artigo.texto: ANTÁLIA, TURQUIA — A terça-feira (17) da COP31 foi dedicada às discussões sobre oceanos, mares, natureza e uso do solo. Seguindo a temática da Conferência, os diálogos realizados no Implementation Hub Pavilion, espaço do setor produtivo brasileiro na COP31, conectaram políticas públicas de transição ecológica a investimentos industriais de alto impacto. O dia trouxe debates sobre estratégias nacionais de descarbonização, modelos de economia circular para a preservação marinha, soluções em minerais críticos e mecanismos de valorização macroeconômica das florestas tropicais. Um dos marcos centrais da programação nesta terça-feira foi a edição especial do Minas Day, voltada à Coalizão de Minerais Essenciais para a Transição Energética. Promovida pelo Instituto Brasileiro de Mineração (IBRAM) e pela Federação das Indústrias do Estado de Minas Gerais (FIEMG), com a presença do governador Mateus Simões, a sessão apresentou dados inéditos do setor produtivo mineiro. A preservação dos ecossistemas aquáticos e a gestão sustentável de matérias-primas integraram o eixo de economia circular ao longo da tarde. O painel promovido pela CNI analisou as tendências regulatórias e os incentivos financeiros para acelerar a transição circular na indústria, contando com a participação da Volkswagen Caminhões e Ônibus, da Associação Brasileira da Indústria de Alimentos (ABIA) e da Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (FINEP). Em seguida, a Agência Brasileira de Desenvolvimento Industrial (ABDI) liderou a sessão "Recircular para não chegar ao mar", que reuniu especialistas e lideranças políticas, incluindo o conselheiro da COP31 Carlos Silva Filho, a senadora Soraya Thronicke (PSB-MS) e representantes da Associação Brasileira de Energia de Resíduos (ABREN). O debate enfatizou a rastreabilidade da cadeia de materiais e a reciclagem como ferramentas essenciais para barrar o descarte inadequado e o vazamento de resíduos plásticos em rios e oceanos. O encerramento dos trabalhos concentrou-se nos instrumentos de valoração ambiental e integridade de mercado. A CNI e o Instituto Clima e Sociedade (iCS) promoveram um painel dedicado às oportunidades do mercado de carbono para a indústria brasileira, discutindo a precificação de emissões, a regulamentação do Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões e os avanços do Artigo 6 do Acordo de Paris. Simultaneamente, a World Climate Foundation, em parceria com a Global Optimism, encerrou as atividades com uma reflexão sobre a resiliência das florestas tropicais enquanto ativos macroeconômicos críticos, sublinhando que a conservação dos serviços ecossistêmicos é pilar indispensável para a estabilidade financeira e a segurança alimentar global. O espaço da indústria na COP31 A CNI marca presença na Zona Azul da Cúpula do Clima com o Implementation Hub Pavilion. O espaço é dedicado a painéis e encontros e reúne lideranças empresariais, representantes de governos, instituições financeiras e organizações internacionais para compartilhar experiências, discutir oportunidades e fortalecer parcerias para a transição a uma economia de baixo carbono. O espaço é promovido pela CNI, em correalização com o Conselho Nacional do SESI, o Serviço Nacional de Aprendizagem Industrial (SENAI) e a World Climate Foundation (WCF). Conta com o apoio do Instituto Amazônia+21, da Facility de Investimentos Sustentáveis (FAIS), do Instituto Clima e Sociedade (iCS) e da U.S. Chamber of Commerce, além do patrocínio da ABDI, da Samarco, da Aegea, da MBRF, da Vale, da Confederação Nacional das Seguradoras (CNseg), do Instituto Brasileiro de Mineração (IBRAM), da Volkswagen Truck and Bus e da Ambev.

artigo.texto: Dubai, United Arab Emirates – Trina Storage, a global leader in energy storage solutions, has once again been recognized on the BloombergNEF (BNEF) Energy Storage Tier 1 List for Q4 2026, marking its 12th consecutive inclusion on the prestigious ranking and completing three consecutive years of Tier 1 recognition. This achievement further reinforces the company's position as a trusted and bankable partner for utility-scale energy storage projects worldwide. The latest BNEF Tier 1 Energy Storage ranking reflects the growing maturity of the global energy storage market and introduces updated assessment criteria with a stronger focus on project financing and bankability. Under the revised methodology, manufacturers are required to demonstrate successful deployment and financing track records through independently financed utility-scale projects. Trina Storage's continued presence on the list highlights the company's proven capability to deliver high-quality, financeable energy storage solutions at scale. "We are honored to be recognized by BloombergNEF for the 12th consecutive quarter," said Mr. Yang Bao, President of Energy Storage Division at Trinasolar. “The evolution of BNEF’s methodology reflects the increasing maturity of the energy storage industry. As customers place greater emphasis on project execution, financing readiness and long-term performance, we remain focused on delivering solutions that create lasting value throughout the project lifecycle.” As solar generation expands across the Middle East and Africa, battery storage can help utilities maintain grid stability and make solar power available after sunset. In Aswan, Egypt, Trina Storage supplied its Elementa 2 system as the exclusive energy storage partner for AMEA Power’s 300 MWh Abydos battery energy storage project, part of Egypt’s first utility-scale solar-plus-storage facility. Trina Storage completed installation and grid connection in 60 days, ahead of schedule. “The next phase of energy storage in the Middle East and Africa will be defined by the ability to deploy at scale while meeting increasingly demanding technical and operational requirements,” said Jack Chen, Head of Energy Storage, MEA Region at Trinasolar. “At Trina Storage, we continue to expand our portfolio with advanced, integrated solutions designed for a range of applications. Our focus is on giving utilities and developers the performance, reliability and flexibility they need for their projects.” The company’s Elementa battery energy storage system incorporates liquid-cooling architecture and advanced battery management technologies designed to support reliable operation across a range of utility-scale applications. Meanwhile, the recently introduced Elementa + Electra integrated DC+AC solution combines high-density battery storage with advanced power conversion technology, simplifying deployment while enhancing system performance and project value. The solution supports demanding utility-scale applications with features including grid-forming capability, black-start functionality, and flexible power control. artigo.texto: TOWN OF MOHAWK — The town of Mohawk has extended its moratorium on battery energy storage systems for another six months to update laws regulating the devices. Town Supervisor Janet DePalma said the town board is expected to review proposed zoning updates next month with a public hearing likely to be scheduled for February to avoid overloading the January organizational meeting. “We just didn't have the time to get everything done before the end of this current moratorium,” DePalma said. The town enacted a six-month moratorium on battery systems earlier this year to give officials time to develop regulations for them. The town board last week extended the pause that would have otherwise expired on Saturday. Officials tasked the planning board with studying the issues and developing recommended zoning regulations for the town board’s consideration. Tighter regulations are expected, but not an outright ban. “We don't want to be unwelcome to what is obviously the state's direction that they want everybody to take. We just want to really set the parameters around how it's done in our town to protect our citizens and to protect our community,” DePalma said. By contrast, other communities are increasingly prohibiting battery systems citing growing safety concerns following fires at lithium-ion battery facilities in Jefferson, Orange and Suffolk counties in summer 2023. Fire broke out at a facility in Warwick in Orange County for a second time in December 2025. The state has since updated its fire code; stricter safety standards took effect this year. Battery bans have been enacted by the city and town of Amsterdam, Florida and Glen in Montgomery County. In Fulton County, the towns of Johnstown, Northampton and Perth have either enacted or extended battery moratoriums this year, as did the city of Johnstown while Gloversville banned them outright. Meanwhile, DePalma said Mohawk is seeking to strike a balance that protects the community while allowing development that aligns with the town’s rural character. It’s the same direction Mohawk has previously taken to more tightly regulate solar development to protect against overdevelopment without barring it completely. “People do want new energy options, but they also want the rural character. So that's what we're really trying to do — is give them that balance of the new options,” DePalma said. As the battery updates are finalized, officials will turn their attention to developing zoning regulations governing data centers. The town adopted a six-month moratorium on data centers in August running through Feb. 13. DePalma said that will likely need to be extended to give the town time to prepare and adopt updated laws. Mohawk enacted its own moratorium after officials found the state’s one-year moratorium on new hyperscale data centers that would consume 50 megawatts of energy or more didn’t go far enough. State Gov. Kathy Hochul signed an executive order in July enacting the partial pause so state agencies and officials can assess the effect of data center development and come up with standards for future projects to protect ratepayers, the environment, the energy grid and communities. However, DePalma has argued the state’s moratorium didn’t give municipalities time to enact local zoning rules applying to data centers of all sizes to fit the needs and wants of their communities. Mohawk officials have acknowledged data centers pose a concern due to their size and their significant demand on resources, including electricity and water. Those worries are shared by other rural communities, which led the town of Perth in Fulton County to enact a one-year moratorium on data centers in June. Yet DePalma expects officials will again look to strike a balance that protects the town and its residents while allowing new development. “I'm hearing both sides of it,” DePalma said. “So, we really are not saying ‘no, we don't want it.’ We're just saying we want to control the narrative. We want to know where they're going, how many there's going to be, how big they're going to be. We want to protect what our community wants protected … They want the new options, but they also want the rural character.”

artigo.texto: A chinesa CATL, apontada como a maior fabricante mundial de baterias, abriu um escritório comercial na Argentina para apoiar sua expansão no mercado local de armazenamento de energia, segundo relatos da imprensa argentina citados pelo South China Morning Post. A empresa pretende partir de projetos de baterias para a rede elétrica em Buenos Aires e alcançar aplicações em minas, centros de dados e parques eólicos da Patagônia. A CATL já fornece equipamentos ao maior projeto de armazenamento do país. Também apresentou seus sistemas a 35 companhias interessadas em uma licitação governamental para armazenamento. Na semana anterior à publicação, a fabricante conversou com geradoras de energia e bancos em Buenos Aires, embora não tenham sido informados valores de investimentos, contratos ou metas comerciais. Principais fatos e números - A CATL abriu um escritório comercial na Argentina. - A unidade servirá de base para a expansão no mercado argentino de armazenamento de energia. - A empresa já fornece o maior projeto de armazenamento do país. - Os mercados visados incluem minas, centros de dados e parques eólicos da Patagônia. - A CATL apresentou seus sistemas a 35 empresas interessadas em uma licitação governamental. - A fabricante conversou com geradoras de energia e bancos em Buenos Aires. Por que isso importa para empresários e investidores A presença comercial da CATL pode ampliar o acesso de empresas argentinas a sistemas de armazenamento para redes elétricas, mineração, centros de dados e geração eólica. Fornecedores, financiadores e operadores de infraestrutura podem encontrar oportunidades em instalação, integração, manutenção e crédito para novos projetos. Ao mesmo tempo, a expansão dependerá do resultado da licitação governamental e da conversão das conversas comerciais em contratos. Como a fonte não informa valores, cronogramas, capacidade dos sistemas ou compromissos firmes, ainda não é possível dimensionar o investimento nem seu efeito efetivo sobre o mercado argentino.

artigo.texto: ZutaCore and Munters Unveil Waterless Chip-to-Rooftop Cooling Architecture for AI Data Centers Key Highlights - Z₂O uses dielectric fluid and two-phase cold plates to transfer processor heat to rooftop equipment, where Munters SyCool rejects it to outdoor air. - The reference design is built around 625-kW IT blocks, with 500 kW of liquid cooling and 125 kW of air cooling. - The modeled pPUE comparison assumes Dulles, Virginia weather, constant full IT load and an 80/20 liquid-to-air cooling split. - ZutaCore says the first installation uses an ASRock Rack server with NVIDIA HGX B300, while independent operating results have not yet been reported. ZutaCore has introduced a new waterless cooling architecture designed to simplify AI data center thermal management by extending two-phase liquid cooling from the processor to the facility's rooftop heat rejection equipment. Unveiled at Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) in Chicago, the ZutaCore Z₂O architecture, developed in partnership with Munters, eliminates several components traditionally associated with liquid-cooled data centers, including cooling distribution units (CDUs), liquid-to-liquid heat exchangers, facility water loops and water-based cooling towers. The architecture uses a sealed dielectric fluid that absorbs heat directly from processors through two-phase cold plates. As the fluid boils, vapor carries heat to rooftop equipment, where it condenses and returns through the same loop. Munters SyCool technology provides heat rejection to the outdoor air, eliminating the need for cooling water. The approach represents an effort to address two increasingly significant constraints on AI infrastructure development: the availability of electrical power and the growing concern over water consumption. Reducing the Energy Cost of AI Cooling According to ZutaCore, the reference architecture developed with Munters achieves a modeled annualized partial power usage effectiveness (pPUE) of 1.03, compared with 1.115 for a conventional high-efficiency chilled-water system. Those figures translate into approximately 74% less energy consumed by cooling infrastructure, based on the modeled difference in facility overhead. The calculations use hourly weather data from Dulles, Virginia, assuming a constant 100% IT load and an 80/20 split between liquid and air cooling. The figures represent modeled performance rather than independently verified operating results. Z₂O is designed around repeatable 625-kW IT blocks, consisting of 500 kW of direct-to-chip liquid cooling and 125 kW of air cooling. The modular approach is intended to support new construction, existing facilities and prefabricated data center deployments. The architecture also incorporates N+1 heat-rejection redundancy and redundant UPS-supported pumps. ZutaCore's HyperCool Cloud software provides system monitoring. "AI operators have fought hard for every megawatt, and they should not be spending it on moving heat," said Dan Wood, ZutaCore's chief product officer. Implications for Data Center Development For developers facing increasingly restrictive power allocations, reducing the electrical requirements of cooling infrastructure could free additional capacity for revenue-producing computing equipment. Eliminating cooling towers, chillers and CDUs could also reduce mechanical infrastructure costs, simplify construction and shorten commissioning schedules. The extent of those benefits will depend on site conditions, system integration and actual operating performance. The elimination of cooling water consumption is particularly relevant in markets where water availability has become a significant consideration in data center permitting and community acceptance. ZutaCore said the first Z₂O installation uses an ASRock Rack server incorporating NVIDIA's HGX B300 platform with integrated two-phase cooling. The architecture also supports ZutaCore's HyperCool and recently introduced OmniTherm cold plates, allowing future processor upgrades without requiring changes to the underlying facility cooling loop. The announcement follows ZutaCore's $100 million-plus Series C funding round earlier this year, which included investments from Mitsubishi Electric, Carrier Ventures and Samsung Electronics. The larger significance of Z₂O is its attempt to extend liquid cooling optimization beyond the server rack. While most direct-to-chip technologies focus on efficiently extracting heat from processors, ZutaCore and Munters are targeting the supporting mechanical infrastructure that contributes to overall facility energy consumption. Whether the modeled performance advantages can be consistently achieved across different climates and operating loads remains to be demonstrated. Nevertheless, the architecture highlights the growing importance of treating cooling as an integrated facility design decision rather than an individual component of the IT infrastructure.

artigo.texto: Governo Lula avalia contestar restrições dos EUA à venda de chips para data centers no Brasil Medida anunciada pela gestão Trump coloca o país entre cinco países que precisarão de autorização para comprar equipamentos avançados utilizados em inteligência artificial O governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva avalia a possibilidade de contestar as novas restrições anunciadas pelos Estados Unidos à venda de chips avançados de inteligência artificial para data centers instalados no Brasil. A medida, divulgada nesta segunda-feira, inclui o país em uma lista de cinco nações que passarão a depender de autorização do governo americano para importar esses componentes, utilizados em grandes centros de processamento de dados. - 'Certamente não é uma má ideia': Trump defende volta de Huang ao comando da Nvidia - Bessent: Secretário do Tesouro dos EUA tenta evitar retorno de Huang e pede reformulação 'drástica' na Nvidia Segundo interlocutores, uma eventual negociação com os Estados Unidos ou contestação das regras não está descartada. Até o momento, porém, o assunto não provocou preocupação significativa dentro do Executivo, e ainda não há uma definição sobre a adoção de medidas em resposta à decisão americana. A avaliação é de que os Estados Unidos têm amplo controle sobre a produção e o fornecimento desses chips, fundamentais para o funcionamento de sistemas avançados de inteligência artificial, o que dá ao país grande influência sobre sua comercialização no mercado internacional. Procurado, o Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços disse que o governo brasileiro tomou conhecimento do comunicado do Departamento de Comércio dos EUA e acompanha com atenção eventuais desdobramentos da medida. "Importante destacar que não se trata de proibição de exportações de semicondutores avançados para o Brasil nem para os demais países citados no comunicado, mas sim de necessidade de autorização para que as operações se concretizem, motivo pelo qual não é possível avaliar, no momento, o efeito concreto da medida sobre as importações brasileiras desses insumos", diz o texto. Os data centers são instalações que reúnem servidores e equipamentos responsáveis por armazenar e processar grandes volumes de informações. Com o avanço da inteligência artificial, esses centros passaram a demandar chips cada vez mais potentes, capazes de realizar os cálculos necessários para desenvolver e operar a tecnologia. A nova norma foi anunciada pelo Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos e também atinge Indonésia, Malásia, Cingapura e Tailândia. O objetivo é impedir que empresas chinesas tenham acesso à tecnologia americana por meio de centros de dados localizados em outros países, contornando as restrições já impostas por Washington. - Terras-raras, espionagem e controle sobre chips: Os temas que vão marcar a cúpula de Trump com Xi nesta semana Desde 2022, os Estados Unidos limitam a venda de chips avançados para a China, exigindo autorizações para a exportação de determinados componentes e equipamentos utilizados em sua fabricação. As regras foram reforçadas em 2023 e agora passam a incluir novas exigências para países considerados pelo governo americano mais suscetíveis ao desvio dessas tecnologias. - Wall Street Journal: Trump deve classificar Nvidia e outras empresas como 'campeãs nacionais' de IA Integrantes do governo brasileiro lembram que houve, anteriormente, preocupação com uma possível falta de chips no mercado internacional, diante do aumento da demanda por equipamentos destinados à inteligência artificial. Essa preocupação, no entanto, é considerada superada. Pelas novas regras, as empresas atingidas precisarão obter licenças do governo americano para importar determinados chips avançados. A regulamentação prevê exceções para companhias sediadas nos Estados Unidos, desde que cumpram exigências de informação, e estabelece que os pedidos de autorização serão analisados individualmente pelas autoridades americanas.

artigo.texto: LOWELL, Mich. — The debate over a potential data center in Lowell Charter Township is continuing, with township leaders now considering new rules for future developments. WATCH: Lowell Township leaders review proposed ordinance for potential data center developments During Monday night's township board meeting, an advisory committee presented a nearly 30-page proposed ordinance outlining requirements developers would have to meet before a data center project could move forward. The proposal received mixed reactions from neighbors. “I think this ordinance has some work to do still,” one neighbor said during public comment. Another neighbor described the proposal as “a great first start.” Tristam Harrington, who has been following the townships data center discussions, said he came into Monday night's meeting skeptical of the proposed ordinance. “We have one chance to get this right because once it goes in, it's over,” Harrington said to the Township Board Monday night. “If we don't put all of the proper and detailed and effective safeguards in place, we have run the real risk of ruining this community forever.” The proposed ordinance would establish requirements for where data centers could be built, how they operate, and what developers must do to protect surrounding communities. That includes addressing concerns such as noise, water consumption, environmental impacts, and emergency response- issues neighbors have raised throughout more than 20 meetings since the project was first announced last November. PREVIOUS COVERAGE: No decision reached after lengthy Lowell Township meeting on Microsoft data center proposal The advisory ordinance committee recommended bringing in third-party consultants to help further develop the proposal and address any remaining gaps. Township Supervisor Jerry Hale agreed with that recommendation. “I think that we do need to hire all the experts to fill in the gaps,” Hale said. After hearing the committee's presentation, Harrington said he came away with a better understanding of the work being done to address neighbors' concerns. “I feel really encouraged by the process and everything that they've done,” Harrington said. “I think we're going to be in a much better position moving forward.” What's next? The proposed ordinance will now go to the Lowell Charter Township Planning Commission for review and recommendations. Township leaders are encouraging members of the advisory committee to participate in that review. “There's still a lot of steps in the process to get to a final ordinance legally,” Township Attorney Bradley Fowler said. After the Planning Commission reviews the proposal, a public hearing will need to be scheduled and held before the ordinance returns to the township board for further consideration. FOX 17 will continue following the township's discussions and provide updates as the process moves forward.

artigo.texto: QUINCY TOWNSHIP, MI (WTVB) – Developers of a proposed battery storage facility in Quincy Township will hold an open house Tuesday to answer community questions, ahead of their application for approval of the project. EDF proposed the Santina Energy facility earlier this year on a 45-acre site in Quincy Township, with about 20 to 25 acres designated for battery equipment. The company says the site on Boone Road was selected partly because it is near ITC transmission lines along the Indiana Northeast Railroad right-of-way. The Bloomington, Minnesota-based company will hold the open house Tuesday from 5:00-7:00 p.m. at Quincy Middle School, with project information and a site plan available for the public to view and comment on. Quincy Township recently adopted new zoning rules and a compatible renewable energy ordinance to maintain local control over projects of this type, limiting battery systems to industrial zones, while EDF proposed an agricultural site. Under state law, EDF could ask the State Public Service Commission to provide approval, regardless of local zoning.

artigo.texto: Floating data centers could help build resilient digital infrastructure in new environments and beyond traditional locations. ABB and Hanwha Ocean have signed an MOU to advance power and control technologies for floating data centers, combining Hanwha Ocean’s offshore design and construction expertise with ABB’s electrification, automation and data center power capabilities. Through May 2027, the companies will explore power system design and operational control technologies suited to the marine environment. This includes assessing power system reliability and quality, and developing control logic to support efficient operations as computing demand changes. The collaboration will also explore how LNG engines and electrical systems can respond to changing data center power demands, helping advance reliable and resilient power solutions for floating data centers.Together, ABB and Hanwha Ocean are combining engineering expertise and power systems know-how to help build the foundations for future marine digital infrastructure. Floating data centers are data centers built on offshore floating platforms, equipped with servers, power systems, and cooling facilities. As the demand for data processing surges, land-based data centers face numerous constraints regarding site selection and power supply; consequently, floating data centers are gaining increasing attention as an alternative solution.

artigo.texto: MOUs signed with GGGI, ICVCM; ministry says GVCM issuance body to be established next year Eight countries, including Singapore, have expressed their intent to join the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM), a high-integrity carbon market initiative led by South Korea. With the latest additions, the total number of signatories to the GVCM cooperation letter of intent stands at nine: South Korea, the Dominican Republic, Morocco, Burkina Faso, Sri Lanka, Singapore, Uganda, Côte d'Ivoire and Paraguay. According to the Ministry of Economy and Finance on Sunday, the nine countries signed the joint cooperation letter of intent on Saturday (local time) at the 31st Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, held in Antalya, Turkey. The GVCM is a multilateral carbon market framework the government is developing to provide common carbon credit issuance standards and infrastructure that multiple countries can use jointly to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Companies will be able to use the framework to pursue greenhouse gas reduction projects in developing countries, generate carbon credits and trade them on international carbon markets. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Lee Hyung-il said in a video opening address that the GVCM is "a platform built together by reflecting the diverse experiences and development needs of participating countries," adding that it "carries great significance as a new multilateral model in which three or more countries participate simultaneously — not a bilateral arrangement." The ministry also signed a trilateral memorandum of understanding with the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) and the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM) to enhance the credibility and quality of the GVCM. The three organizations will pursue knowledge sharing on Core Carbon Principles (CCPs) and provide education and training for GVCM participating countries to improve the market's quality. Moon Ji-seong, director general for international economic affairs at the ministry, said the MOU signing was an opportunity to raise the quality of the GVCM by sharing ICVCM's expertise and experience. The ministry said it plans to complete the establishment of the GVCM issuance body next year and will work to bring in more countries, international organizations and private institutions going forward. oskymoon@heraldcorp.com

artigo.texto: SK Telecom said Monday it has signed a memorandum of understanding with Hyosung Heavy Industries to cooperate on developing gigawatt-scale AI data centers. The two companies will work on securing key equipment for 345-kilovolt substations, testing 800-volt direct-current power distribution technology and identifying new data center projects. Under the agreement, SK Telecom will contribute its AI data center development and operational expertise, while Hyosung Heavy Industries will provide its power infrastructure manufacturing and engineering capabilities. The companies will coordinate supply plans for major equipment, including transformers, to prevent procurement delays from affecting construction schedules. They will also jointly review and test 800V DC distribution, which can reduce power conversion stages and improve data center energy efficiency. They also plan to share expertise in operating and maintaining ultra-high-voltage substations to improve power supply stability and reliability once data centers are operational. The partnership will eventually extend to AI data center development and construction, with both companies seeking new business opportunities and joint business models. "This partnership will help secure the core power infrastructure needed for AI data centers and expand into cooperation on developing and building large-scale facilities," SK Telecom CEO Jung Jai-hun said. "We will strengthen our capabilities in gigawatt-scale AI data center development and take a leading role in the global AI infrastructure market." Hyosung Heavy Industries CEO Woo Tae-hee said the agreement would combine the company's power technology with SK Telecom's data center expertise to establish a stable foundation for electricity supply. jyoungseon8@heraldcorp.com

artigo.texto: LS Electric, a South Korean electrical equipment manufacturer, said Monday it secured a $93.83 million contract to supply power distribution systems for a hyper-scale artificial intelligence data center in the US. Under the agreement, the company will deliver 38-kilovolt high-voltage switchgear and low-voltage switchgear in phases to an unnamed global technology company. Switchgear controls and protects electrical circuits, helping distribute electricity safely throughout large facilities. The latest order extends LS Electric’s involvement in the client's data center project from the initial construction phase to a subsequent expansion. As AI adoption accelerates, demand for computing capacity has grown, placing greater emphasis on “time to power,” the period required for a data center to secure an operational electricity supply. To meet delivery schedules, LS Electric operates manufacturing facilities in Cheongju, South Korea, and the US states of Utah and Texas. The company said its production network enables it to meet the tight delivery timelines of data center projects. Beyond conventional alternating current (AC) distribution, the manufacturer is expanding into direct current (DC) systems, which can reduce energy losses by limiting the power conversions required to operate servers. At its Cheonan plant, LS Electric operates a DC-powered factory equipped with solid-state transformers for voltage conversion, solid-state circuit breakers for electrical protection and energy storage systems. The facility serves as a testing ground for next-generation power grids and data center applications. “The latest contract reflects the quality of our power equipment and our ability to execute projects in North America,” an LS Electric official said. “We will continue expanding our business by providing solutions tailored to the needs of major technology customers.” yejinlim@heraldcorp.com

artigo.texto: Demand for data centers continues to put the pedal to the metal, driven in part by artificial intelligence and the need for more computing capacity. But as developers look for places to build, their attention is on rural America rather than traditional tech hubs. Pinion principal Quint Shambaugh says it’s not just about acreage, but access to the infrastructure needed to support these large-scale facilities. “In North America the primary market data center supply reached 10,903 megawatts in the first half of 2026. That is up over 30 percent from the previous year and vacancy, so open spaces in data centers, still remained under 2 percent. So lots of them are getting built. The ones that are getting built are full and then even to add to that, 80 percent of new construction, so construction that isn’t even up and running yet, that capacity is already sold so it is pre-leased. So a data center currently right now that’s not on the market and that’s getting built, 80 percent of it is already pre-leased.” What does it take to power these data centers? The scale and density of newer builds need a lot of energy. “So AI workloads are driving dramatically higher, and power densities are driving dramatically higher, too. With some AI high-density racks consuming as much as 80 to 100 homes amount of electricity. So with one rack in one data center, it can consume that much energy. And the U.S. data center industry is expected to require roughly 30 gigawatts of new power demand annually to support continued AI growth. So when we look at this, really the core issue is power availability and it is really the dominant constraint of this entire industry.” That’s why access to power infrastructure, water, and land is making rural areas attractive. “Rural assets are becoming exceptionally strategic and are something that these companies are very interested in. Site selection increasingly depends on a combination of power access, transmission infrastructure, fiber connectivity, water resources, and land that you can develop on. All these assets are commonly found in rural America as you all know, and developers are pursuing locations beyond traditional areas and traditional hubs because of grid constraint.” But even when all the assets are in place, there are other challenges that impact whether a project moves forward. “Industry studies are consistently showing that delays in power delivery, permitting, or stakeholder alignment can be more impactful than the actual cost of the site itself. So it’s not the land that’s holding people up, it’s the actual communities that are slowing down these projects. As we recently saw in the midterm elections, I think it was 40 out of 41 ballot initiatives went against data centers. So the two biggest constraints right now, number one is power, but number two is community constraints.” As data center development continues to expand, rural areas with the right mix of infrastructure and resources are expected to remain at the center of site selection discussions.

artigo.texto: The development of next-generation electric vehicles, portable electronics, and advanced energy-storage systems calls for lithium metal batteries that combine high energy density with long-term cycling stability. However, conventional lithium metal anodes face two major challenges: producing uniform ultrathin lithium foils at scale and preventing uneven lithium deposition and continuous lithium consumption during battery operation. Addressing both limitations, a research team has developed a screen-printing strategy that integrates patterned lithium arrays with a chemically reinforced interphase. The resulting ultrathin anodes demonstrate promising performance in both liquid- and solid-state lithium metal batteries, offering a practical approach to high-energy-density battery design. Why This Innovation Matters Ultrathin lithium anodes can substantially reduce inactive lithium mass and increase battery energy density. Yet molten lithium spreads poorly on copper substrates, making it difficult to manufacture uniform, defect-free ultrathin foils. During cycling, unstable interphases and non-uniform lithium deposition further accelerate lithium consumption and dendrite formation. These problems become particularly serious when the lithium inventory is limited. Therefore, achieving scalable fabrication while maintaining stable electrode-electrolyte interfaces is essential for practical high-energy-density batteries. Innovative Design and Mechanism The research introduces a mask-assisted screen-printing method that forms regularly distributed lithium microdiscs on copper rather than relying on continuous molten-lithium coating. By controlling the dimensions and spacing of the patterned arrays, the researchers produced anodes with equivalent lithium thicknesses of 10-28 µm, overcoming the limitations imposed by poor lithium wettability. Meanwhile, Mg(TFSI)2 is introduced into molten lithium to generate a multicomponent nanocomposite containing inorganic species such as LiF, Li3N, Li2S, and Li-Mg compounds. These components provide lithiophilic nucleation sites and contribute to an inorganic-rich solid electrolyte interphase. Together, the discrete architecture and modified interphase promote uniform lithium deposition, reduce mechanical stress, and suppress dendrite growth and parasitic reactions. Outstanding Performance The Li@Mg(TFSI)2 array anodes demonstrate excellent electrochemical stability. In liquid-electrolyte full cells paired with LiFePO4 cathodes, the system maintains a specific capacity above 130 mAh g-1 and Coulombic efficiency exceeding 99.8% over 260 cycles. With high-loading cathodes, the anodes also support stable cycling for up to 120 cycles. The calculated stack-level energy densities reach 504 Wh kg-1 and 1071 Wh L-1 for the 20 µm-equivalent anode configuration. Applications and Future Outlook Importantly, this strategy is compatible with both liquid- and solid-state battery systems. In solid-state cells, the spaces between lithium microdiscs accommodate volume changes, while the reinforced interphase helps maintain stable electrode-electrolyte contact. The successful integration of ultrathin lithium arrays with high-loading cathodes highlights the potential of this approach for future high-energy battery technologies. By combining scalable electrode fabrication with interfacial and structural engineering, this work offers a promising route toward more energy-dense and durable lithium metal batteries.

artigo.texto: South Korea will join the Open Coalition of Committed Carbon Markets (OCCCM), a new international cooperation group aimed at enhancing collaboration on mandatory carbon markets, including emissions trading systems. Minister of Climate, Energy and Environment Kim Sung-hwan announced South Korea's official membership in the OCCCM during a high-level meeting at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) held in Antalya, Turkey, on November 16. The carbon market alliance was proposed by Brazil at COP30 last year and officially launched in May this year with participation from major carbon market operators, including the European Union and China. As of November, 13 countries have joined the coalition. Member countries will share experiences in operating mandatory carbon markets, including emissions trading systems and carbon taxes, and discuss measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV), carbon accounting, and the use of high-quality offset mechanisms. Mandatory carbon markets are systems where governments impose a price on greenhouse gas emissions or regulate emission levels, requiring companies to secure emissions allowances or pay carbon taxes based on their emissions. The carbon market alliance adopted operational regulations in May and established a work plan in September. Countries that operate or are preparing to implement national mandatory carbon markets or carbon pricing systems can participate. During the high-level meeting, Minister Kim will highlight that South Korea was the first in East Asia to introduce a national emissions trading system in 2015, currently managing over 70% of the country's greenhouse gas emissions. He will also share experiences in designing and operating the emissions trading market and the MRV system established in a manufacturing-centered industrial structure, as well as the operation of offset mechanisms. Additionally, he will outline the policy direction for transitioning from a fossil fuel-based economy to a 'carbon-free electricity nation' and introduce the 'Korea Green Transformation (K-GX)' strategy announced by the government last month. The high-level meeting will adopt a COP31 declaration welcoming new member countries and committing to develop the carbon market alliance as a central cooperation body for international collaboration on mandatory carbon markets. Member countries will discuss priorities for 2027 and launch a working group to implement the work plan. Minister Kim stated, "Based on the experience gained from operating the emissions trading system for 12 years, we will actively contribute to the activities of the carbon market alliance and continue to play a leading role in advancing global decarbonization and achieving carbon neutrality through international cooperation." * This article has been translated by AI. artigo.texto: mPlus Corp. Breaks Into the Solid-State Battery Mass-Production Market With an Order in the ₩20 Billion Range From a Global Company - Input - 2026-11-16 08:46:51 - Updated - 2026-11-16 08:49:41 [Financial News] mPlus Corp., a company specializing in rechargeable-battery assembly equipment, is stepping up its push into the next-generation battery market after securing an order worth around ₩20 billion for solid-state battery equipment from a global company. The deal is drawing attention because it marks an expansion of the company’s equipment business, previously centered on electric vehicles (EVs) and energy storage systems (ESS), into solid-state battery mass-production processes. According to industry sources on the 16th, mPlus Corp. recently secured an order worth around ₩20 billion from a global company for solid-state battery assembly and electrode-line equipment. The equipment is expected to be used to build the global company’s solid-state battery production line. The equipment to be supplied incorporates technologies developed in-house by mPlus Corp., including notching, stacking and precision dispensing. The company is also developing Roll Press technology needed for solid-state battery manufacturing. It plans to use these technologies to expand the range of equipment it can supply for solid-state battery production. Solid-state batteries are next-generation batteries that replace liquid electrolytes with solid ones to improve safety and energy density. However, their complex manufacturing processes make securing reliable mass-production technology a key challenge for commercialization. As a result, technological competition is intensifying not only among battery manufacturers but also among makers of equipment for key manufacturing processes. With this order as a springboard, mPlus Corp. plans to focus on securing global customers and diversifying its business. It has also recently been pursuing entry into the market for defense and special-purpose battery equipment, targeting European battery companies. The strategy is to broaden its order base to include solid-state and special-purpose batteries, in addition to equipment for EVs and ESS. Industry observers expect order opportunities for related equipment makers to grow as the solid-state battery market moves beyond research and development and begins preparing for commercialization. In particular, they say that a track record of supplying initial production lines could be a factor in gauging competitiveness in future orders for mass-production facilities. A company representative said, "This order is significant because it gives us a track record of supplying a global customer in the solid-state battery assembly-equipment sector," and added, "We also expect opportunities for additional orders as our customers expand mass production." Meanwhile, mPlus Corp. is expanding its business portfolio to include pouch-type, prismatic and solid-state battery assembly equipment, as well as autonomous mobile robots (AIMR) and control systems. artigo.texto: The Turkish business sector is embracing global carbon markets by leveraging the UN climate change summit, the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31), being held in Antalya. The summit serves as a platform for firms and stakeholders to discuss emerging financial regulations and sustainability standards. Alongside the summit, a carbon market conference was hosted by SEKA Investment and financial services firm StoneX. The conference highlighted that mandatory global carbon trading volumes topped $100 billion per year. Serhat Kisakurek, managing partner at SEKA Investment, said the strong attendance by Turkish firms at COP31 showed the sector’s commitment to the new economic ecosystem, despite some uncertainties over initial carbon pricing. Kisakurek noted that carbon compliance has become a key factor in securing long-term deals and accessing affordable financing for corporations. While industrial giants have adapted to green frameworks, small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are lagging behind, he said, urging these firms to follow suit to maintain their global competitive edge. He added that Türkiye has a significant regional advantage in the green transition due to its established climate laws and regulatory infrastructure supporting compliance. Alfredo Nicastro, global director of carbon markets at StoneX, said the summit is connecting private sector innovators with policymakers, while the global turnout at the event continues to demonstrate growing momentum in Türkiye’s green financial sector. He added that COP31 represents a turning point for Türkiye in becoming a central carbon trading hub for the EU and the wider region.

artigo.texto: Samsung SDI to supply LFP batteries to Jupiter Power SEOUL, Nov. 16 (Yonhap) -- Samsung SDI Co., South Korea's second-largest battery maker, said Monday its U.S. subsidiary has secured a deal estimated to be worth trillions of won to supply lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries to a U.S. energy storage company. Samsung SDI America signed a three-year, 16-gigawatt-hour (GWh) battery supply agreement with Jupiter Power, a U.S. energy storage system (ESS) developer owned by BlackRock, the South Korean company said in a press release. Under the agreement, Samsung SDI will supply LFP batteries for Jupiter Power's ESS, with deliveries scheduled to begin in 2029. Combined with an earlier agreement, the latest deal brings Samsung SDI's cumulative orders from Jupiter Power to about 27 GWh. The batteries will be manufactured at StarPlus Energy, a U.S. joint venture between Samsung SDI and Stellantis NV, in the U.S. state of Indiana. Jupiter Power, owned by U.S. asset management giant BlackRock, is one of the largest developers and operators of energy storage projects in the United States. The contract comes shortly after Samsung SDI began mass production of LFP batteries at the Indiana facility. Industry observers said the deal could help Samsung SDI gain a foothold in the ESS battery market, which has long been dominated by Chinese manufacturers, by leveraging its U.S. production capabilities and non-Chinese supply chain. artigo.texto: Data centers tiveram ampla derrota nas eleições de meio de mandato dos EUA. Foto: Dado Galdieri/Bloomberg Indústrias e ativistas imaginam que parte da capacidade planejada para estados americanos possa vir parar em território brasileiro Bruno Romani Repórter de tecnologia O “tsunami azul” que varreu Donald Trump nas eleições de meio de mandato dos EUA foi também um grande plebiscito sobre inteligência artificial (IA), com candidatos favoráveis à regulação — e opositores dos grandes bilionários do setor — conseguindo ampla votação. Mais especificamente, as urnas deram um grande recado sobre o que a população de lá pensa da presença de data centers em suas comunidades. Agora, indústria e ativistas imaginam que parte dessa demanda possa vir parar no Brasil — para o bem e para o mal. Vale lembrar que o processo eleitoral americano não escolheu apenas novos membros do Legislativo federal e dos Executivos estaduais. Houve também referendos sobre diversos temas, entre eles a paralisação ou a restrição de data centers em vários condados do país. A rejeição foi ampla: segundo a consultoria Redbud, dos 47 referendos, 44 tiveram resultado negativo para o setor e apenas um foi favorável (outros dois ainda não têm resultado). O Goldman Sachs alertou os investidores de que o resultado poderia afetar 45% da expansão de capacidade planejada para o território americano — se isso acontecer, a própria expansão da indústria da IA fica em xeque e começa a se formar um clima terrível de bolha. Na semana passada, essa simples perspectiva fez as empresas de tecnologia perderem US$ 2,5 trilhões em valor de mercado. Elon Musk correu para o X: “Os data centers no espaço parecem bastante atraentes no momento”. Ele, claro, já está fazendo propaganda de um potencial serviço que a SpaceX pode oferecer. Mas nem é preciso ir tão longe: o Brasil já aparece como opção. Sérgio Sgobbi, diretor de relações institucionais e governamentais da Associação das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação (Brasscom), me explicou o que coloca o país em jogo: O cenário nos EUA cria uma oportunidade para o Brasil. Lá, criou-se uma resistência muito forte a data centers, mais por questões econômicas do que ambientais, reflexo da demanda por energia. A gente tem uma matriz diversa. A outra característica é a interligação. A gente tem problemas de distribuição, mas tem uma capacidade interligada que outros países não têm. A Brasscom previa que o Brasil receberia US$ 92 bilhões em investimentos acumulados em equipamentos de TI até 2031 — e o tamanho do bolo é maior, porque a conta não considera custos de construção e de infraestrutura física de suporte, como geradores, sistemas de ar-condicionado/refrigeração, sistemas de combate a incêndio, baterias e no-breaks. Sgobbi admite que a entidade pode voltar à prancheta para refazer as contas após as eleições americanas. Ainda não é possível saber qual será o novo número. Na semana passada, Marcos Peigo, CEO da Scala, disse ao jornal Valor Econômico que o Brasil está diante de uma oportunidade de US$ 500 bilhões. Já o representante da Brasscom tenta dar uma ideia de outra forma. Ele afirma que os aportes em hardware, redes e data centers para IA equivaleram a 1,5% do PIB dos EUA no 1º trimestre de 2026 (contra uma média histórica de 0,7% entre 2015 e 2022). É claro que não haverá transferência automática de toda essa capacidade para o Brasil, mas uma fração disso já significaria valores históricos para o país. Victor Arnaud, presidente da Equinix no Brasil, lembra que o país não é o destino natural da demanda expulsa dos EUA. O norte da Europa, por exemplo, tem mais capacidade instalada do que toda a América Latina — o Google decidiu investir € 13 bilhões na Finlândia. A gigante também anunciou outros US$ 15 bilhões para a Malásia em 2027 e 2028, uma clara indicação de que o Sudeste Asiático também está na fila do pão. E há ainda os rivais locais na América do Sul, cada um com seus atrativos e problemas. A Argentina tem a amizade entre Milei e Trump e o frio da Patagônia (vale lembrar, porém, que um suposto projeto da OpenAI por lá está parado); o Paraguai tem Itaipu e um regramento mais relaxado (mas também uma crise política profunda); e o Chile tem o seu histórico no setor (e um movimento de rejeição que o acompanha). Arnaud reforça que a regulamentação do Redata, a harmonização do ICMS entre os estados e a futura aprovação do Marco da IA são reformas que viabilizam o Brasil, independentemente de onde venha a demanda por data centers. Na sexta (6), a ministra-chefe da Casa Civil, Miriam Belchior, afirmou que a regulamentação do Redata deverá ser debatida com o presidente Lula após a viagem dele à Ásia. Ainda que toda essa tramitação demore a ocorrer, o executivo da Equinix lembrou que um dos principais atrativos do Brasil permanece: O Brasil continua sendo o maior mercado da América Latina e vai continuar crescendo. O usuário daqui não vai falar que não usa mais o celular ou que gosta quando o vídeo demora para carregar. O Pix, o streaming e a vida digital já garantem o crescimento. A Equinix vinha investindo numa média de R$ 1 bilhão por ano e, nos últimos 12 meses, aumentou isso em 50%. Até aqui, com o Redata, a ideia do Brasil era trazer para o território nacional infraestrutura para reduzir o nosso déficit computacional — segundo o Ministério da Fazenda, 60% da nossa demanda roda no exterior. Então, como o país poderia surgir como opção para fornecer capacidade a outros mercados? Sgobbi diz que um data center de grande porte é construído para 100 megawatts (MW), mas costuma iniciar a operação com “apenas 5 MW e expandir conforme a venda de capacidade”. Uma eventual absorção da carga americana poderia fazer os novos data centers no país iniciarem com capacidade maior. Segundo a Bloomberg, o resultado das eleições nos EUA está fazendo a ByteDance, dona do TikTok, estudar a ampliação da capacidade de seus novos data centers no Nordeste. artigo.texto: Hithium has signed a memorandum of understanding with the University of Cambridge to collaborate on long-duration energy storage research, battery technology and the commercialisation of academic work. The agreement was signed during the Global Energy Storage Colloquium in Xiamen, China, on 12 November. Hithium said the partnership will combine Cambridge’s work in materials science, engineering and fundamental research with its own experience in battery development, long-duration energy storage and large-scale deployment. The two organisations plan to establish joint management and research mechanisms, develop research projects, facilitate scientific exchanges and support the translation of research into industrial applications. Hithium said Cambridge researchers will contribute to work on fundamental scientific questions and emerging energy storage technologies, while the manufacturer will provide engineering validation and industrial application scenarios. No individual research programmes, funding commitments or development timescales were disclosed. The partnership comes as Hithium expands its focus on lithium iron phosphate batteries designed for longer-duration stationary storage. BESTmag reported in August that Hithium began production at its $1.8 billion LFP long-duration energy storage manufacturing park in Shandong. The 80-hectare development includes battery cells, modules and complete storage systems alongside materials and upstream processing. The company’s current LDES strategy includes large-format LFP cells intended for discharge durations of four to eight hours. Hithium was also ranked as the world’s second-largest supplier of BESS cells in the first half of 2026, behind CATL. Hithium and Cambridge strengthening bridge from research to deployment Hithium and Cambridge said the collaboration is intended to strengthen links between fundamental battery research, product development and industrial deployment. The agreement also forms part of Hithium’s plans to expand its international research network through partnerships with universities and research institutions. The Xiamen colloquium at which the agreement was signed brought together researchers and industry representatives to discuss battery materials, degradation and lifetime prediction, grid integration, power electronics, thermal-runaway detection and virtual power plants. Hithium said it intends to use the collaboration to bring technical challenges encountered in commercial energy storage projects into academic research, while accelerating the engineering validation of research findings. Photo: Hithium and the University of Cambridge have signed an MoU covering research into long-duration energy storage, battery technology and the translation of academic research into industrial applications. artigo.texto: Data Centers DID YOU KNOW? the Potomac River basin has the largest concentration of data centers in the world. Most of which are nestled in Northern Virginia, now known as “Data Center Alley” – a mega hub of data center infrastructure estimated to handle 70% of all global internet traffic. Northern Virginia is home to one of the world’s largest clusters of data centers. And as more facilities are proposed across the Potomac watershed, there’s a question worth asking: What does all this growth mean for the rivers, streams, and drinking water we depend on? Every time we stream a show, store a photo, or use an AI tool, data centers help make it possible. These large facilities house the computers that keep our digital lives running. But they also need electricity, cooling, and land. Their effects on water vary widely depending on how and where they are built—and with so many projects on the horizon, we need to look at the bigger picture. A data center is an industrial facility that houses expansive, high-powered computing equipment to continuously store and process data for users globally. An average AI data center contains 200,000 computer servers, miles of wiring, batteries, water systems, hundreds of air conditioning units, and is supported by dozens of high-powered, industrial backup diesel generators. Data centers operate constantly, using massive amounts of water in order to cool and power their systems. In our region, they draw this water from Potomac-fed water supplies. This is especially important during the hottest days of the year, when data center water demand spikes at the most water-stressed time of year. Why This Matters for the Potomac and Shenandoah Rivers Data center proposals are multiplying across our region. AI is helping drive that growth, though not every proposed project will necessarily be built. What happens next matters: choices about water use, wastewater, construction, and power infrastructure can shape the health of the Potomac and Shenandoah for years to come. The Potomac River watershed remains a legacy hub and now has more than 350 operating data centers and is projected to surpass 1,000 – placing 200 million square feet of buildings on roughly 20,000 acres of land. Because of the unprecedented construction of these facilities in our watershed, the exact impacts on the environment and water quality remain unclear. However, the primary concerns associated with data centers include: - Water drawdowns - Periodic cooling system discharge - Increased polluted runoff - Construction site pollution - Threats from fuel spills - Threats to drinking water intakes - Risk of substation fires - Toxic e-waste in landfills - Developments on toxic sites - Impacts from power line construction - Power plant operation threats Rapid data center expansion helped the Potomac River earn the title of America’s Most Endangered River in 2026. How PRKN is taking action The extent of data center impacts on river systems and waterways is still not fully understood, and comprehensive analyses and assessments are needed to begin to grasp their effects on our rivers. What we do know is that when unchecked, these installations can pose serious risks to the watershed and the primary clean drinking water source for six million people in the Potomac River basin. PRKN is keeping a watchful eye on the Potomac and Shenandoah rivers for data center impacts and fighting for adequacy of state permitting, such as for cooling system releases, and will call for more public stream monitoring on tributaries where high concentrations of these facilities are upstream from drinking water intakes. Importantly, PRKN will be a voice to ensure that clean water protections are seriously managed in data center development.

In an online earnings call on November 18, the company reported financial results for the first three quarters of 2026: cumulative revenue of just NT$98.73 million (approximately $3.0 million), less than half of the NT$235 million (approximately $7.1 million) posted for all of 2025 and a steep decline from NT$540 million (approximately $16.4 million) for all of 2024. Cumulative gross loss reached NT$105 million (approximately $3.2 million), with after-tax net loss of NT$242 million (approximately $7.3 million) and a loss per share of NT$4.54. This marks the second consecutive year of losses for Ibase Gaming, with no sign of the losses narrowing. "This has indeed been a challenging year for Ibase Gaming," Liao Yi-chung, special assistant to the chairman, said in his opening remarks, acknowledging that the company faces short-term operating pressure while also building the foundation for its next phase of growth. Financial Highlights at a Glance Three Headwinds Combine to Turn Gross Margin Negative Liao attributed this year's weak performance to three factors. First, demand in the U.S. unregulated gaming market has been weak, contracting at least 40% to 50% this year, with customers adjusting both procurement volumes and schedules. Second, existing products are gradually reaching the end of their life cycles, while the next-generation Gaming PC platform still requires customer testing, system integration and validation; during the transition between old and new products, mass-production ramp-up has fallen short of expectations. Third, revenue has fallen rapidly, but fixed operating costs cannot be reduced proportionally in a short period, dealing a severe blow to gross margin and operating profit. "When revenue falls rapidly, existing fixed operating costs cannot be adjusted in tandem, which relatively increases the cost burden," Liao explained. The financial statements show that Ibase Gaming's gross margin for the first three quarters of 2026 was -107%, a marked deterioration from -10% for all of 2025 and far worse than the positive 21% gross margin in 2024. It is worth noting that although cumulative revenue for the first three quarters fell sharply year over year, monthly revenue disclosures show that third-quarter 2026 revenue was about NT$60 million (approximately $1.8 million), up 25.3% from the same period in 2025, indicating that the revenue decline was concentrated mainly in the first half. October revenue of NT$30 million (approximately $910,000) was up 456.3% year over year, also hinting at a recovery from a low base. Still, cumulative revenue for the first three quarters was only NT$98.73 million, and returning to 2025 levels for the full year will remain difficult. Short-Term Debt-Servicing Capacity Flashes Warning Signs Amid the operating losses, Ibase Gaming's financial structure has also deteriorated. As of the third quarter of 2026, total assets had fallen to NT$1.563 billion (approximately $47.5 million), while total liabilities climbed to NT$760 million (approximately $23.1 million), raising the liabilities-to-total-assets ratio from 31% at the end of 2024 to 48%; shareholders' equity fell to NT$803 million (approximately $24.4 million). The current ratio plunged from 150.52% at the end of 2024 to 80.56%, while the quick ratio dropped from 80.71% to 31.90%. "This reflects that the company is indeed facing some management pressure on working capital and short-term liquidity," Liao acknowledged. Going forward, in addition to improving revenue and profitability, the company will place greater emphasis on the efficiency of capital deployment, including inventory management, project payment terms and control of accounts-receivable cash flow. New Businesses Emerge as Bright Spots: ASEAN 20MW Energy Storage and AI Optical Communications Orders Secured Despite the weak core business, Ibase Gaming delivered tangible results in its new business initiatives, providing one of the few bright spots at the earnings call. In the energy business, the company secured an ASEAN 20MW industrial energy storage project this year, extending from pure equipment supply to site demand analysis, project planning and third-party vendor integration — an important milestone in entering large-scale energy storage system integration. In AI optical communications, Ibase Gaming established Guangchi Technology in 2026 to enter bonding and assembly contract manufacturing for silicon photonics thermal components, and has already won orders from a major U.S. client. Liao said this business "is no longer just an early-stage technology deployment, but has begun to enter the stage of actual manufacturing and commercialization," adding that the company is actively expanding capacity and plans to extend into the assembly and testing of finished high-speed optical communications modules. In addition, Ibase Gaming is advancing a modular AI computing center (AIDC) solution that integrates AI servers, energy storage, power management and cooling systems, and is currently in talks with several potential clients. artigo.texto: An aerial view of the world's first 300-megawatt artificial-cavern compressed air energy storage power station, Yuanchu No 1, in Northwest China's Gansu Province. Photo: CCTV News The world's first 300-megawatt artificial-cavern compressed air energy storage (CAES) power station has been connected to the grid in Northwest China's Gansu Province, marking a major step in bringing the technology from experimental testing to large-scale engineering applications, CCTV News reported on Monday, citing China Energy Engineering Corporation (China Energy). The project, known as Yuanchu No 1, provides a new engineering example for diversifying China's compressed air energy storage technologies. The station has four air-storage caverns excavated in rock formations about 110 meters underground. It is equipped with a 300-MW generating unit and has an energy storage capacity of 1,800 megawatt-hours. With a round-trip efficiency of 72 percent, the facility can generate electricity continuously for six hours on a single discharge and has a projected annual power output of 600 million kilowatt-hours. Compressed air energy storage works by converting electricity into energy stored in compressed air, which can later be converted back into electricity when needed. Artificially excavated hard-rock caverns offer an alternative to natural underground storage spaces such as salt caverns. Suitable rock formations are more widely distributed, allowing greater flexibility in site selection, although construction costs are relatively high, according to a report by China Electric Power News published on the website of the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Engineering Thermophysics. The report noted that suitable salt formations are concentrated in parts of central, eastern and southern China, while the country's northern regions, which have extensive wind and solar power installations and strong demand for large-scale energy storage, lack suitable geological conditions for salt cavern storage. The Gansu project reached a key testing milestone in September, when an initial air-injection test at its No. 4 underground storage cavern succeeded, with pressure reaching 12.63 mega-pascals, setting a record for compressed air storage in large artificial caverns, according to China Energy. The grid connection comes amid rapid growth in China's new energy storage sector. The country's installed new energy storage capacity reached 136 million kilowatts by the end of 2025, up 84 percent from a year earlier, according to the National Energy Administration (NEA). Lithium-ion batteries accounted for 96.1 percent of the total, while compressed air storage, flow batteries, flywheels and other technologies made up the remaining 3.9 percent. Energy storage projects with a duration of four hours or longer accounted for 27.6 percent of total installed capacity, up about 12 percentage points from the end of 2024, the NEA said. China is also seeking to diversify its energy storage technologies under its development plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). The plan, jointly issued by the National Development and Reform Commission and the NEA, sets a target of 300 million kilowatts of installed new energy storage capacity by 2030, with an average storage duration of about three hours. artigo.texto: Israel risks becoming a pollution haven in the global race to build AI data centers As the Electricity Authority opens the door to another 1,000MW of data center capacity, the Environmental Protection Ministry warns of rising emissions, health costs and pressure on the country's natural gas reserves. The Electricity Authority has announced plans to position Israel as a global leader in connecting data centers to the power grid. But a senior official at the Ministry of Environmental Protection is warning of significant consequences. "Air pollutant emissions will rise by more than 10% once data centers with a capacity of 3,000 megawatts are established, causing economic damage through increased morbidity and mortality, lost workdays and other costs," she said. The ministry estimates that Israel’s rapid push to establish data centers will cause approximately NIS 2 billion in annual economic damage from the additional electricity generation they require, plus more than NIS 1 billion from the operation of backup generators. The anticipated costs also include higher greenhouse gas emissions and faster depletion of Israel’s natural gas reserves. Beyond the financial damage, the ministry warns of an increase in annual deaths caused by air pollution, which is already responsible for an estimated 5,500 premature deaths in Israel each year. AI is reshaping the global energy landscape, as major technology companies race to build massive data centers around the world. According to the latest forecast from the International Energy Agency (IEA), electricity consumption by data centers is expected to nearly double, from 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 to 950 TWh in 2030, accounting for approximately 3% of global electricity consumption. Over the same period, electricity consumption by data centers dedicated to artificial intelligence is expected to triple. For comparison, 950 TWh is slightly more than Japan’s current annual electricity consumption. In the United States, data centers are expected to account for nearly half of the projected growth in electricity demand through 2030. Local communities are increasingly bearing the costs of this technological expansion, including higher air pollution from facilities that operate polluting backup generators, consume vast amounts of electricity and require large quantities of water for cooling. Data centers are also affecting electricity prices. According to the Federal Reserve, wholesale electricity prices rose by 6.9% last year, driven in part by demand from these facilities. Opposition to data center developments is growing in communities around the world, where residents are also concerned about the large tracts of land these facilities occupy. In the United States, the issue even influenced this month's midterm elections. A September poll by Quinnipiac found that nearly three out of four Americans opposed having a data center in their community. During the elections, 41 ballot measures concerning data centers were put to a vote, with voters rejecting the proposed developments in all but one case. In an NBC exit poll, 23% of voters said data centers were a "decisive" factor in their congressional vote, while another 33% described them as a "significant" factor. The day after the election, Nvidia lost $450 billion in market value. OpenAI has since pledged to use closed-loop cooling systems and to pay for the electricity consumed by its data centers. It has also moved to rebrand its facilities as "computing campuses." In July, the Electricity Authority froze the processing of grid connection requests for data centers with electricity demands exceeding eight megawatts, after approving 2,000MW of capacity. Developers had submitted requests totaling 27,000MW, roughly three times Israel's current electricity consumption and well above the country's record peak demand. The authority recently announced plans to release an additional 1,000MW of capacity, potentially enabling the construction of facilities as large as 200MW, a scale not yet seen elsewhere in the world. "Realizing this allocation is expected to result in data centers accounting for approximately 20% of national electricity consumption, positioning Israel among the world's leaders in the integration of data centers relative to total consumption," the Electricity Authority said. Opening the door to these large facilities is expected to require the construction of at least three new polluting power plants in Israel to meet their electricity needs. But alongside the potential economic benefits, the expansion carries significant environmental and public-health costs that will ultimately be borne by Israeli residents. The concern is that, at a time when communities in other countries are increasingly resisting data center developments, Israel could become a "backyard" for the sector's pollution. In a sharply worded letter, Shuli Nazar, Deputy Director General for Environmental Regulation and Risk Prevention at the Ministry of Environmental Protection, warned of a broad range of risks. In addition to increased air pollution and the resulting rise in morbidity and mortality, she said, higher greenhouse gas emissions would make it harder for Israel to meet its climate targets. According to Nazar, offsetting the additional emissions from data centers would require Israel to set a target of approximately 45% renewable energy by 2035, about 10 percentage points higher than the target recommended by the Electricity Authority. There is considerable skepticism within the energy sector about whether Israel can meet even its existing renewable energy targets. Nazar also warned that implementing the Electricity Authority's plan would accelerate the depletion of Israel's domestic natural gas reserves and shorten their expected lifespan. artigo.texto: Mintech will jointly develop diagnostic equipment with Terra Leader for use in solid-state battery manufacturing processes. Mintech said on Nov. 17 that it signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Terra Leader, a company specializing in digital pressure control, to develop and commercialize diagnostic solutions for solid-state battery manufacturing. The two companies will combine Mintech's electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) technology with Terra Leader's precision pressure-control technology. EIS analyzes internal battery resistance to assess battery condition and performance. Solid-state batteries use solid electrolytes instead of liquid electrolytes, making the contact condition between electrodes and electrolytes an important factor affecting performance. Technologies that maintain uniform pressure during manufacturing and precisely analyze the condition of electrode-electrolyte interfaces are therefore critical. The companies plan to develop an integrated solution that performs temperature and pressure control alongside electrochemical analysis in a single piece of equipment. The goal is to improve manufacturing efficiency and measurement reproducibility by analyzing battery cells without transferring them to separate equipment, while maintaining their manufacturing conditions. Mintech plans to expand its battery diagnostics business, which has primarily focused on lithium-ion batteries, into the solid-state battery sector. It will pursue commercialization targeting global battery manufacturers and materials companies.
