artigo.texto: Enlight and Shemen join race for Israeli data centers with 150MW Haifa project The companies plan to invest in a facility at Hof Shemen, with a NIS 334 million electricity guarantee and a 25-year land lease. The project enters a crowded market as developers compete for the remaining 1,000MW of capacity earmarked for data centers. New names are joining the growing list of entrepreneurs seeking to establish data centers in Israel. Enlight and Shemen Real Estate announced this morning that they have signed an agreement to develop a 150-megawatt data center at Hof Shemen in Haifa. The two companies will jointly establish a special-purpose vehicle (SPV) for the project and have already submitted an application to connect the facility to the electricity grid. Under the Electricity Authority’s regulatory framework, applicants must provide financial guarantees to secure grid connections. The guarantee required for the project is estimated at NIS 334 million, which the two companies will fund in equal shares. The data center is planned to cover between 41 and 82 dunams. The project’s SPV will lease the land from Shemen for 25 years. Annual lease payments will start at NIS 27,000 per dunam during the development phase, gradually rising to NIS 433,000 per dunam once the data center becomes operational. Enlight has also secured an option to purchase 50% of the land designated for the data center at a minimum price of NIS 6.32 million per dunam. The price may increase under a pre-agreed mechanism, and the option can be exercised 30 months after the agreement was signed. Enlight and Shemen are joining a growing field of developers competing for approximately 1,000 megawatts of additional electricity capacity earmarked for data centers. Under the regulatory framework published by the Electricity Authority, up to 20% of Israel’s national electricity supply, equivalent to approximately 3,000 MW, is expected to be allocated to data centers by 2030. Of that amount, approximately 2,000 MW is accounted for by connection requests that have already been approved. The remaining 1,000 MW has become the focus of intense competition among developers seeking to build data centers. For Enlight, a renewable energy company, this is not its first investment in an Israeli data center. In March 2025, it won a tender issued by the Israel Land Authority to build a data center alongside a solar energy facility in Ashalim, in the Negev. Shemen Yielding Real Estate is the successor to Shemen Industries, a company previously engaged in oil production. It is held by Memorandum, a company owned by Haim Fink (44.2%); Zvika Ben-Zvi (22.1%), who also owns logistics company Orsher; and real estate investment fund JTLV3 (22.1%).

artigo.texto: South Korea Joins 'Open Coalition on Compliance Carbon Markets' as New Member International carbon market partnership South Korea to take part in talks on setting rules Minister of Climate, Energy and Environment Kim Seonghwan is being interviewed by The Asia Business Daily at the Han River Flood Control Office in Dongjak-gu, Seoul. 2026.9.21 Photo by Kim Hyunmin View original image South Korea has officially joined the Open Coalition on Compliance Carbon Markets (OCCCM), an international partnership on carbon markets involving the European Union (EU), China and other participants. As a new member, South Korea has secured voting rights at the coalition's high-level meetings and will take part in discussions on international carbon market rules, including Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes and offset credits. Minister of Climate, Energy and Environment Kim Seonghwan officially announced South Korea's membership at a high-level meeting of the coalition held on the sidelines of the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, on the 16th. The coalition is an international partnership that shares experience with compliance carbon markets, such as greenhouse gas emissions trading systems and carbon taxes, and promotes mutual understanding and cooperation among its members on topics including measurement, reporting and verification (MRV), carbon accounting and high-quality offset systems. Brazil proposed the coalition at COP30 last year, and it was launched in May this year with major carbon market operators, including the EU and China, as its core participants. Thirteen countries are currently members. South Korea joined after receiving an invitation from the EU in June, as a follow-up to Korea-EU summit diplomacy. To become a member, a country or regional economic integration organization must have or be developing a domestic compliance carbon market or carbon pricing system. Members can exercise voting rights at high-level meetings. With its membership, South Korea will be able to participate in future discussions on international carbon market rules, including the generation of Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs) under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement and the establishment of common principles for high-integrity offset credits. artigo.texto: [SMM PV Flash] Ecuador Applies Zero VAT and Currency Outflow Tax to Solar and Storage Equipment Ecuador's President Daniel Noboa signed Executive Decree 530, published on November 11 in the Fifth Supplement to Official Gazette No. 407, setting a 0% rate for value-added tax and the tax on foreign currency outflows (ISD) on electricity-sector equipment including solar PV and energy storage systems. A subsequent ministerial agreement, MAE-MAE-2026-0118-AM, lists 55 categories of goods eligible for the 0% VAT rate in the domestic market — solar cells, modules, inverters, power optimisers, controllers, mounting structures, trackers and DC cables — and 104 tariff subheadings eligible for the 0% ISD rate on imports, with storage goods covering stationary cells and modules, battery banks, integrated systems, bidirectional converters and battery management equipment. The new rates took effect on November 12, and the decree lets taxpayers deduct VAT paid on qualifying purchases and imports made between January 1, 2026 and entry into force as an expense for the 2026 income tax year. The measure removes import and transaction taxes on solar and storage equipment, part of Ecuador's push to accelerate private renewable investment after the 2024 supply shortfalls and blackouts.

artigo.texto: A new legislative review estimates that Virginia’s data center tax break generated 22 cents in state tax revenue for every dollar companies saved. Staff for the Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission presented the findings Monday. The report estimates that data centers saved an average of $811.5 million a year from fiscal 2021 through 2025. Researchers estimated that the business activity the tax break attracted generated $179.4 million a year in state taxes, leaving a difference of $632.1 million a year. The revenue estimate excludes local taxes, including property taxes that cities and counties collect from data centers. The exemption lets qualifying data center operators and tenants buy computer equipment and software without paying sales and use tax. Five years of savings from that one tax break accounted for 60% of the $6.8 billion in tax breaks, grants and other business incentives the commission counted over a decade. To figure out what Virginia got back, researchers had to estimate how much data center business would have come to the state anyway. Earlier reviews assumed the tax break drove at least 90% of data center location and expansion activity in Virginia. The new review puts that share at about half. It draws on research into how sales and use tax exemptions affected the number, square footage and energy use of data centers across states. The Virginia Economic Development Partnership said in an Oct. 28 letter that the change had a substantial effect on the estimates. The partnership urged the commission to explain how much its findings depend on that assumption and to keep evaluating its method as more Virginia-specific evidence becomes available. The commission estimated that the exemption supported about 18,100 private-sector jobs a year, including jobs at businesses that supply data centers. It also estimated that the exemption added about $3.9 billion a year to Virginia’s gross domestic product over those five years. A Senate proposal to end the sales tax exemption early helped stall state budget talks this spring. Lawmakers kept the exemption in place in June and added a separate tax on electricity used by data center operators. The electricity tax took effect July 1 and runs through June 30, 2028. The state budget caps deposits from the tax into Virginia’s general fund at $600 million per fiscal year. Lawmakers are still split over the exemption. At an Oct. 26 meeting, Senate Finance Chairwoman Louise Lucas, D-Portsmouth, backed repealing it. House Appropriations Chairman Luke Torian, D-Prince William, urged the state to honor its commitments to the industry while addressing the effects of data center growth on communities. artigo.texto: Restrição para chips de data centers: EUA ainda têm a melhor tecnologia; entenda Governo de Donald Trump está preocupado em manter vantagem na disputa tecnológica com o país asiático O governo dos Estados Unidos decidiu restringir exportações de chips e servidores usados na infraestrutura de processamento de dados para sistemas de inteligência artificial (IA) para empreendimentos em países que possam fornecer capacidade de computação para empresas chinesas, mesmo fora da China, como os componentes fabricados pela Nvidia. A nova norma coloca o Brasil, ao lado de Indonésia, Malásia, Tailândia e Cingapura, na mira das restrições, informou em comunicado o Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos. - Terras-raras, espionagem e controle sobre chips: os temas que vão marcar a cúpula de Trump com Xi nesta semana - Após decisão dos EUA: Governo Lula avalia contestar restrições dos EUA à venda de chips para data centers no Brasil O aperto na restrição busca impedir que a China tenha acesso à capacidade computacional que utilize processadores projetados por empresas americanas mas esteja instalada em terceiros países. Mas qual é o objetivo do governo de Donald Trump? Embora temam o avanço da China na produção de chips de inteligência artificial (IA), os Estados Unidos mantêm ampla vantagem sobre os rivais. Segundo a consultoria Epoch AI, o Ascend 950, principal chip da Huawei, entrega performance equivalente à metade do que entregam os chips H100, da Nvidia, que foram lançados em 2022 — atualmente, a companhia fundada por Jensen Huang já comercializa o H200. A consultoria afirma que a gigante chinesa deve permanecer entre três e quatro anos atrás da Nvidia até, pelo menos, 2030. - 'Certamente não é uma má ideia': Trump defende volta de Huang ao comando da Nvidia Em agosto do ano passado, a DeepSeek tentou treinar a segunda geração de seu grande modelo, o DeepSeek 2, com chips Ascend 950, o que gerou atrasos no projeto. Um ano depois, a Z.ai surpreendeu ao afirmar que, durante o período de testes do GLM 5.3, usou apenas chips chineses para gerar as respostas do modelo, o que foi um sinal de avanço moderado, já que a chamada “inferência” é uma tarefa menos custosa para os chips do que o treinamento de modelos. Os chineses enfrentam alguns gargalos. Um deles é a limitação da high bandwidth memory (HBM, ou memória de alta largura de banda), usada nos chips de IA. A Epoch estima que, se a Huawei usasse somente HBMs feitos na China, atingiria apenas 1% da capacidade de produção de poder computacional da Nvidia. Além disso, a China não tem equipamento especializado para produzir chips de alto rendimento — a holandesa ASML tem o domínio global de máquinas de fotolitografia para a indústria de semicondutores e nunca exportou para a China. Em outubro, uma startup chinesa apresentou um maquinário do tipo, mas analistas estimam que o país está pelo menos uma década atrasado no segmento. Ainda não é possível avaliar o impacto no Brasil da decisão dos EUA de exigir que operadoras de data centers de cinco países obtenham licença prévia para comprar chips avançados de IA — governo, empresas e entidades admitem que preferem esperar para compreender esse movimento. No entanto, há um entendimento de que a determinação do governo Donald Trump cria diferenças competitivas entre as empresas isentas de licença, como as americanas, e as demais. Isso poderia abalar os planos do governo Lula de conquistar a soberania digital, pois as companhias brasileiras terão de se sujeitar às regras. Foi uma reação parecida à de janeiro de 2025, quando Joe Biden, em final de mandato, restringiu o acesso a chips de computador e tecnologias para desenvolvimento de IA. Na época, o Brasil foi enquadrado no grupo dois, sujeito a controles intermediários de acesso à tecnologia. As cotas impediam que as empresas desses países importassem mais de 1,7 mil GPUs de ponta por ano. Assim que tomou posse, Trump revogou a regra.

artigo.texto: Key Takeaways - BYD started in a rented factory in Shenzhen and entered the auto industry through an acquisition in 2003. - BYD has produced more than 19 million NEVs, and its exports rose 93.75% year-on-year in the first 10 months of 2026. BYD (HKEX: 1211) marked its 32nd anniversary on Wednesday with a look back at how it grew from a battery maker in Shenzhen into an automaker with factories in Thailand and Brazil. In its anniversary article, BYD traced its origins to November 18, 1994, when more than 20 people started the business in a rented factory in Shenzhen. The company entered the lithium-ion battery industry in 1996. In 2003, BYD entered the auto industry by acquiring Xi'an Qinchuan Automobile. It launched its first mass-produced car, the F3, in 2005, followed by the F3DM plug-in hybrid sedan in 2008. BYD then expanded into commercial vehicles. It entered the new energy bus market in 2009 and built an electric bus factory in Lancaster, California, in 2013. In 2015, BYD unveiled a strategy covering the entire new energy vehicle (NEV) supply chain and a range of markets. It broadened its electrification efforts beyond passenger cars, buses and taxis to include logistics, ports and mining. As NEV output rose, BYD began building passenger cars overseas. Its 5-millionth NEV rolled off the production line in August 2023. In 2024, BYD completed its first overseas passenger car factory in Rayong, Thailand, where it produced its 8-millionth NEV. On November 18 that year, cumulative NEV production reached 10 million vehicles. BYD began production at its Brazilian factory in 2025, and its 14-millionth NEV rolled off the line there. All 8 of the company's roll-on/roll-off car carriers entered service that year. Earlier this month, BYD announced that its 19-millionth NEV had rolled off the production line, 124 days after it produced its 17-millionth. Chairman and president Wang Chuanfu said on Tuesday at the APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen that BYD had produced more than 19 million NEVs in total. Wang said BYD's Thai factory can produce 150,000 vehicles a year and employs about 6,000 people, more than 95% of them local hires. The company also plans to expand local sourcing and research and development in its overseas markets. BYD exported 1,513,154 NEVs in the first 10 months of 2026, up 93.75% year-on-year. Over the same period, its sales in China fell 27.81% to 2,108,590 vehicles, while global sales declined 2.16% to 3,621,744 vehicles. In March, BYD unveiled its second-generation Blade Battery and new flash charging technology. According to the company, the technology can charge a battery from 10% to 70% in 5 minutes and from 10% to 97% in 9 minutes.

artigo.texto: By Alex Adi At COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, global leaders and climate negotiators are focusing on one of the mechanisms for financing climate action: carbon credits. Under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, countries can trade emission reductions and removals through international carbon markets. But what exactly is a carbon credit, and how can Ghana position itself to turn its environmental initiatives into revenue, create jobs and build cleaner cities? A carbon credit represents one metric tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) reduced, avoided or removed from the atmosphere. For instance, when Ghana protects its forests, converts organic waste into compost instead of allowing it to decompose in landfills, or replaces diesel generators with solar power, it can reduce greenhouse gas emissions. When these reductions or removals are properly measured, independently verified and certified under an approved standard, they can generate carbon credits that are traded in the market. Companies and countries can purchase these credits to meet certain climate commitments or offset emissions, depending on the rules governing the market. In simple terms, Ghana can earn revenue by undertaking activities that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions and selling the resulting verified credits. Ghana’s growing carbon market Ghana has established a Carbon Market Office and a framework to regulate carbon market activities and international transactions. One example of the country’s involvement in the market is the Jospong Group’s Integrated Recycling and Compost Plants. The company secured a bilateral agreement with the Swiss Government at COP28, with carbon credit transactions estimated to be worth US$20 million by 2030. Beyond waste management, Ghana is also generating carbon credits through forest conservation initiatives, including the Ghana Cocoa Forest REDD+ Programme. For a developing economy such as Ghana, the carbon market presents several potential opportunities. Revenue without additional borrowing Carbon credit transactions could provide Ghana with a source of foreign revenue and attract investment without increasing the country’s public debt. Employment opportunities Investment in reforestation, waste sorting, recycling and renewable energy could create jobs for young people, particularly in communities involved in environmental protection and sustainable resource management. Cleaner cities Carbon finance could provide additional incentives for improved municipal waste management, including recycling and composting. These activities could help reduce the volume of waste sent to landfills and ease sanitation challenges in urban communities. Supporting the energy transition Revenue from carbon credits could also support solar energy and clean cooking initiatives, helping households and businesses adopt cleaner energy sources. The need for transparency and accountability Despite the opportunities, carbon market experts have cautioned that Ghana must establish strong safeguards to ensure that the benefits are properly managed and shared. Transparency, independent verification and clear benefit-sharing arrangements are essential to preventing greenwashing and ensuring that carbon credits represent genuine emission reductions or removals. There are also concerns that communities, farmers and other groups directly involved in protecting forests and natural resources could be excluded from the financial benefits if appropriate arrangements are not put in place. For Ghana, therefore, participation in the carbon market must go beyond generating and selling credits. It must also ensure that the people and communities contributing to environmental protection receive a fair share of the proceeds. Carbon trading is not simply a form of aid or charity. It is a market that depends on credible data, proper measurement, independent verification and compliance with established standards. If Ghana strengthens its regulatory framework and ensures that the benefits are fairly distributed, its forests, waste management systems and clean energy initiatives could become valuable sources of climate finance and international investment.

artigo.texto: UK battery company AceOn has launched a range of 12 V sodium-ion battery packs for applications including solar street lighting, roadside equipment, medical devices and remote telemetry, which is UN38.3-certified . The StamiNa+ Core range comprises four packs from 10 Ah to 30 Ah, equivalent to 120 Wh to 360 Wh, and is now available to order following completion of UN38.3 transport testing. UN38.3 is the section of the UN Manual of Tests and Criteria covering the transport safety testing required before rechargeable lithium and sodium batteries can be shipped. Tests include altitude simulation, thermal cycling, vibration, shock, external short circuit, impact or crush, overcharge and forced discharge. AceOn said certification allows it to ship the StamiNa+ Core packs to OEMs and system integrators in the UK, Europe, Africa and other markets. The packs are rated to discharge between –40°C and +70°C and charge between –20°C and +60°C, with a claimed cycle life of 5,000 cycles to 70% remaining capacity. That low-temperature performance is one of the areas where sodium-ion developers are increasingly targeting applications traditionally served by lead-acid batteries. BESTmag reported in September that Aeson was promoting sodium-ion as an alternative to lead-acid for automotive starter and auxiliary batteries, while Clarios, Altris and InoBat have validated sodium-ion cold-cranking performance down to –40°C. AceOn said the new range is aimed at applications where conventional lead-acid batteries can struggle in extreme cold and where lithium-ion chemistry may create safety or supply-chain concerns. The company said it is also seeing interest from the defence sector. All four packs use 32140-format cylindrical sodium-ion cells in a 4S configuration and incorporate an AceOn-designed battery management system providing overcharge, over-discharge, over-current and short-circuit protection, as well as cell balancing. The range comprises two 10 Ah/120 Wh packs, a 20 Ah/240 Wh pack and a 30 Ah/360 Wh model. Maximum current is 5 A for the 10 Ah packs and 10 A for the larger variants. AceOn has also developed a dedicated 15.6 V, 5 A charger for the range. The charger and integrated BMS were designed in-house. The company’s work with sodium-ion dates back to 2017, when it integrated Faradion pouch cells into a modified SolarSDS off-grid solar system. AceOn said that early project provided field experience with the chemistry and led to subsequent development of its own sodium-ion battery management technology, including work on a zero-volt BMS. Sodium-ion cells can tolerate deeper discharge than many lithium-ion chemistries and can use aluminium current collectors on both electrodes rather than requiring copper on the anode side. AceOn said its cells contain no lithium or cobalt and use sodium compounds derived from abundant materials including salt and soda ash. The launch follows growing commercial activity in the 12 V sodium-ion market. BESTmag reported last year that Unigrid had launched a sodium-ion platform as a drop-in replacement for conventional 12 V starter batteries. AceOn is also expanding sodium-ion assembly in Africa. Its new facility near Kampala, Uganda, includes a 3,000 sq ft battery assembly and training centre as well as BMS research and development. The site is intended to supply locally assembled StamiNa+ packs to East African markets. AceOn co-founder and CEO Mark Thompson said: “We first put sodium-ion cells into one of our solar systems back in 2017, when most people had never heard of the chemistry. It proved to us that sodium-ion could do a real job in the field. Nine years on, StamiNa+ Core is a certified range we can ship anywhere in the world. “Solar street lights, roadside signs, medical devices and remote telemetry all need batteries that work in the cold, last for years and don’t depend on cobalt or lithium. That is exactly what these packs are built for, and we’re ready to talk to OEMs and integrators now. “We want to be a leader in sodium-ion pack technology. Our team designs the BMS and charger in-house, we’re now assembling packs in Uganda, and we want to work with cell manufacturers around the world to take this chemistry into every market that needs it.” Photo: AceOn’s StamiNa+ Core range comprises four UN38.3-certified 12 V sodium-ion battery packs from 10 Ah to 30 Ah, alongside a dedicated charger. The packs are rated to discharge at temperatures as low as –40°C. Credit: AceOn.

artigo.texto: Today, a team led by Harvard researchers published a highly anticipated study in Nature Sustainability. For the first time since generative AI took off, we have a peer-reviewed estimate of how much climate pollution comes from keeping America’s biggest data centers running. Headlines about it are already popping up all over. The study estimates that hyperscale data centers across America are emitting up to 31 million metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, roughly as much CO₂ as Denmark emitted in 2024. It also estimates the facilities are taking up roughly 2 percent of U.S. electricity consumption. These are big, important numbers! And yet, they’re also massive underestimations. There are a few reasons why today’s study gets nowhere near the actual amount of climate pollution coming from these ever-buzzing internet slop factories. One is the way the researchers counted the facilities’ emissions. To do this, they estimated how much electricity each data center used, then looked at how the grid in that part of the country makes its electricity—how much comes from gas, coal, renewables, and so on—to estimate how much CO₂ would be released to generate that much power. But not all data center electricity comes from the grid. Indeed, an ever-increasing number of these massive data centers are also building their own, on-site fossil fuel plants. For example, during the study period (May 2024 through April 2025), Elon Musk’s xAI got some of the electricity for its Colossus data center in Memphis from the grid—but it also got some of it by burning gas in turbines right outside the building. Lead author Gianluca Guidi confirmed that Colossus wasn’t among the 403 facilities studied. For the facilities they did study, the researchers couldn’t tell how much power came from the grid and how much was generated on-site. So they applied the regional grid mix to all estimated electricity use, which can undercount emissions at facilities that burn their own gas. Another reason the climate impact of hyperscale data centers is likely understated is that electricity consumption is not the only way these facilities heat the planet. For example, the equipment that keeps the servers from overheating is leaking heat-trapping refrigerants into the atmosphere. And when a data center runs on gas—as so many of them do—methane can escape from wells and pipelines before the gas even reaches the power plant. In addition, there are potentially hundreds of hyperscale data centers that were left out of today’s study on the climate impacts of these facilities. Yes—hundreds. That’s because we don’t actually know how many hyperscale data centers are currently up and running in the United States. (Hyperscale means “the largest and most powerful class of data centers,” according to the study. These are the kinds of facilities that can train and run large language models. See footnote to see how the study defines them).1 The researchers only landed on their number—403—after painstakingly going through a list of 675 possible hyperscale data center locations given to them by a company called Baxtel, which tracks data centers. And by that I mean they had to pull up satellite images for every single facility to answer questions like Is this the data center, or just another building on the same campus? Has it even been built yet, or is this satellite photo just old? And even after they found the right building, they still had to figure out whether it was running before they could figure out how much electricity it might be using. All told, the researchers had to leave 272 possible hyperscale data centers out of the study because they couldn’t find out enough about them. Finally, the study period ends in April 2025—meaning the climate impact of data centers has likely grown substantially. Gianluca Guidi, the study’s lead author, acknowledged this in Monday’s release. “The data center boom hasn’t slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025,” he said. “New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow. That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.” And yet, even with all of these limitations (most acknowledged by the study itself, which is how I know about them), the researchers were able to pull out some important findings. They include: - The generative AI boom is mostly powered by fossil fuels. 53.9 percent of the electricity consumption of hyperscale data centers is fossil-fuel generated, with 38.2 percent coming from methane gas and 15.2 percent coming from coal. - Hyperscale data centers use as much electricity as some U.S. states. They used 82 terawatt-hours of electricity in a year (68–99 terawatt-hours of electricity across scenarios). That’s as much electricity as some individual U.S. states over the course of a year, with the upper estimate approaching the annual electricity consumption of Indiana, Michigan, and Tennessee. It represents about 1.8% of all U.S. electricity consumption. - Hyperscale data centers are consuming more than 3 times as much electricity as they were in 2018. An earlier study done before the generative AI boom put U.S. data centers’ electricity use at about 23 terawatt-hours in 2018. The new study’s central estimate is about 3.6 times as high. - Virginia alone accounted for about a quarter of the electricity use. The researchers counted 142 facilities in Virginia, more than twice as many as in any other state. Powering those facilities was associated with about 7 million metric tons of CO₂. Together, Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa accounted for more than half the electricity used by the data centers in the study. Now, to be totally clear, I’m not saying any of this to bash the study! artigo.texto: LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam powers on battery energy storage system - Official operation of battery marks a key milestone towards operating the factory on 100% renewable energy. - The system is the first of its scale in Vietnam. - The renewable energy solution supported by battery storage and LEGO Manufacturing Vietnams 12,400 rooftop solar panels are expected to avoid the equivalent of 20,000 tonnes of CO2e annually in the first five years of operation¹. LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam has powered on its battery energy storage system, developed in partnership with VietnamSingapore Industrial Park (VSIP), marking a key milestone in the companys ambition to operate its Vietnam factory using renewable energy. Jesper Hassellund Mikkelsen, Senior Vice President of Asia Operations and General Manager of LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam, said: This is an exciting step for the LEGO Groups sustainability ambitions in Vietnam and around the world. By bringing together innovative technology and strong collaboration with our partners, we are turning our renewable energy ambitions into reality and demonstrating what is possible when industry works together. Nguyen Phu Thinh, General Director of VSIP, said: We congratulate LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam for taking a pioneering step in adopting large-scale renewable energy solutions and demonstrating that ambitious sustainability goals can be translated into tangible action. The DPPA between the LEGO Group and VSIP is not only a significant milestone for both organizations, but also a powerful testament to how industrial developers and manufacturers can jointly create a new paradigm for sustainable manufacturing. As part of Vietnams first large-scale renewable energy solution for industrial use, LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam operates its own on-site rooftop solar panels alongside a direct Power Purchase Agreement (DPPA) with VSIP. Under this framework, electricity generated from VSIPs rooftop solar and integrated Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) is delivered directly to the factory via a dedicated transmission line. When generation exceeds demand, VSIPs battery stores the excess power and releases it as needed, ensuring a continuous and highly reliable renewable energy supply. Combined with the existing 12,400 rooftop solar panels on the factorys rooftops, the battery energy storage system is expected to cover approximately 75% of the factorys total electricity demand during the first five years of operation and help avoid approximately 20,000 tonnes of CO₂e emissions each year². LMV is exploring additional power purchase agreements to address the remaining 25% electricity demand and support its continued transition towards renewable energy. Opened in April 2025, the LEGO Groups Vietnam factory has been designed to support the companys long-term growth in the region, while advancing the companys sustainability ambitions. Facts about the battery energy storage system - Agreement type: Direct Power Purchase Agreement (DPPA) with VSIP, signed September 2025 - System: Integrated rooftop solar and battery energy storage solution operated by VSIP, supplying renewable electricity directly to LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam - Forecast renewable coverage: Combined, solar generation and battery storage are expected to support 75% of the factorys electricity demand with renewable energy. - CO2e reduction: Approximately 20,000 tonnes of CO2e per year (based on Vietnam grid emission factor of 0.561 tCO2e/MWh), including the contribution from LEGO Manufacturing Vietnams existing rooftop solar system. Facts about LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam - Jobs: For a full list of job openings, visit our career page or follow LEGO Careers and see how you can build your career. - Employees: 1,350 - Land: 44-hectares, size of 62 soccer pitches - Buildings: Five buildings that cover approximately 150,000 m2 and include office spaces, energy centre, moulding, packing buildings, a high bay warehouse and other buildings critical to factory operations. - Precision manufacturing: All LEGO factories follow the same blueprint, using high-tech equipment to produce bricks with 1/10th of a hairs width precision. - Location: Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Environmental Sustainability Initiatives - Renewable energy: LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam is supported by Vietnams first large-scale renewable energy solution specifically designed for industrial use. The factorys renewable electricity supply is delivered through on-site rooftop solar panels and an adjacent energy centre combining large-scale solar generation with battery energy storage. Until all remaining energy needs can be accounted for through power purchase agreements, renewable energy certificates will be used. - Paper-based bags: The packaging line at LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam packages LEGO bricks in new paper-based bags, which replace single-use plastic bags. - Zero waste to landfill: The factory shares the same ambition as all LEGO operations to generate zero waste from factories which is sent to landfill. - Certification: LEED (Leadership in Energy & Environmental Design) Platinum and Gold certifications have been issued for the factorys main buildings, covering energy, water and waste. - Materials: In 2025, renewable and recycled sources accounted for 52% of the materials purchased to make LEGO® bricks, up from 33% in 2024, primarily through the use of the mass balance approach. - Investment: Sustainability investments increased by 20% in 2025 compared with 2024, and by more than three times compared with 2022. ¹ Avoided emissions are estimated using Vietnams 2026 electricity emission factor. artigo.texto: The Minneapolis City Council passed an ordinance Thursday in a 7-6 vote to strengthen regulations on data centers ahead of the expiration of a six-month suspension on new development passed in June. If approved by Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey, the law will institute overlay zoning, which gives the City Council and City Planning Commission the ability to evaluate new data center proposals on a case-by-case basis. The ordinance also limits the size and geographic location of data centers, which provide storage and transmission of data for internet services. The development of new data centers is limited to two downtown districts that primarily consist of office buildings in an effort to avoid densely populated residential areas. Under the ordinance, data centers using only nonrenewable energy are capped at 50,000 square feet, while those that purchase local green energy can use up to 150,000 square feet. There are eight existing data centers in Minneapolis, with Cologix Data Center being the largest at 45,000 square feet. In an effort to limit noise pollution, servers must be located 20 feet inside a building and at least 100 feet from residential properties. The ordinance also requires potential developers to share expected water and energy use, and how they plan to manage noise. Supporters say case-by-case evaluations by elected officials will strengthen the democratic process. “This amendment is fundamentally about whether we believe residents deserve a meaningful voice in decisions that will shape the future of their neighborhoods,” Ward 2 Council Member Robin Wonsley, who represents parts of southeast Minneapolis and the University of Minnesota area, said. The ordinance follows a failed attempt Monday by progressive council members to pass a full ban, intended to reflect the wishes of the majority of the 1,600 Minneapolis residents who submitted comments to the City Council, Wonsley said. “It doesn’t bring a people-centered downtown, it’s not gonna be our ticket out of our financial woes, and our neighbors don’t want it,” Council Member Soren Stevenson, who represents parts of south central Minneapolis, said. “We should ban it.” The ban did not receive enough support from council members or Mayor Frey to pass. Data centers have been at the center of political deliberations in communities across the country, as the quickly developing Artificial Intelligence industry has increased demand for computational power. Residents in communities with large-scale data centers have faced air, noise and water pollution, as well as lower property values and strain on local energy resources, resulting in frequent power outages and higher utility costs. Council members who oppose stricter regulations say Minneapolis should prioritize the economic investment brought by data center developers. “We need a plan for economic growth, for a thriving downtown core. Being anti-jobs, anti-labor, anti-investment is not a strategy,” Council Member Elizabeth Shaffer, who represents parts of downtown and southwest Minneapolis, said. Council members supporting overlay zoning hope that evaluating individual applications could effectively respond to the rapidly changing conditions of the AI and data center industries. “The industry is rapidly evolving. It changes week by week, both in its financial conditions, in the way that the tech is evolving and also the way that the industry is finding gaps in local policies,” Council Member Aurin Chowdhury, who represents parts of southeast Minneapolis, said. Other council members preferred the existing primary zoning laws, which would establish standardized rules for all data center applications, in order to avoid tedious deliberation. “It’s better for us to have rules, apply them evenly, and not make every data center application a political fight,” Shaffer said. At a rally outside Minneapolis City Hall on Tuesday evening, residents protested in favor of a total ban and, in its absence, the adoption of overlay zoning over primary zoning. Many expressed worry about the pollution and quality-of-life risks from living near large data centers. Kalani Matus of the Climate Justice Committee spoke at the rally opposing any data center development, citing inflated demand driven by intense industry competition and speculation. City Council President Elliott Payne echoed these sentiments in support of overlay zoning at Thursday’s meeting. “The large frontier models are taking on significant debt to build these out under the speculation of future demand that might not actually ever show up,” Payne said. “It’s all speculation. It is a gold rush right now.” J.P. Morgan estimated that the industry’s five largest development companies will spend $697 billion on data center investments by the end of 2026, while major AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic are not expected to make a profit for several years. The City Council’s ordinance will now go to the desk of Frey, who will either approve or veto it. Frey has spoken in support of overlay zoning before, though he has also supported allowing data center development in a larger range of Minneapolis neighborhoods than the ordinance proposes.

artigo.texto: "Expands When Charged, Contracts When Discharged"... A Clue to Solving the All-Solid-State Battery Lifespan Challenge [Reading Science] Hanyang University, Korea Electrotechnology Research Institute, and KIST Develop Bilayer Combining Silver-Carbon and Carbon Nanofiber Layers Capacity Retained at 92% After 250 Charge-Discharge Cycles...11.2 Percentage Points Higher Than Existing Structure Expansion during charging and contraction during discharging are among the main causes of shortened service life in all-solid-state batteries, a next-generation battery technology. Korean researchers have developed a bilayer structure that evenly distributes lithium inside the battery and absorbs volume changes, helping to mitigate the problem of capacity degradation. The National Research Foundation of Korea announced on November 17 that a joint research team led by Professor Lee Jongwon of Hanyang University, Principal Researcher Choi Jeonghee of the Korea Electrotechnology Research Institute, and Principal Researcher Jung Hoonki of the Korea Institute of Science and Technology (KIST) had developed a new bilayer structure that mitigates volume changes during the charging and discharging of anode-free all-solid-state batteries. Fabrication process of a double-layer all-solid-state battery and its lithium storage mechanism. (a) Fabrication of the double-layer structure combining a silver-carbon layer and a carbon nanofiber layer. (b) Lithium stored inside the carbon nanofiber layer and between the two layers after charging. (c) Reduction in internal pressure fluctuations achieved by applying the double-layer structure. (d) How sequential lithium storage mitigates volume expansion and mechanical stress. Provided by the research team led by Professor Lee Jongwon of Hanyang University. View original image All-solid-state batteries are a next-generation battery technology that can reduce fire risks by replacing the liquid electrolyte in conventional lithium-ion batteries with a solid electrolyte. Anode-free all-solid-state batteries, in particular, can reduce weight and volume and increase energy density because they do not use a separate anode active material, such as graphite, during manufacturing. The technology has attracted attention for its potential to extend the driving range of electric vehicles, but volume changes during charging and discharging have been considered a barrier to commercialization. During charging, lithium ions that have moved from the cathode gain electrons and accumulate as metallic lithium, increasing the battery's internal volume. During discharging, the accumulated lithium turns back into ions and moves, reducing the volume. Repetition of this process can destabilize contact between the electrode and solid electrolyte and cause mechanical damage inside the battery, potentially shortening its service life. To address this issue, the team designed a bilayer structure combining a thin silver-carbon layer with a carbon nanofiber layer containing abundant internal voids. The silver-carbon layer guides lithium to accumulate evenly rather than concentrating in specific areas during the initial stage of charging. As more lithium flows in, the carbon nanofiber layer stores it in its internal voids, mitigating volume expansion. By tracking lithium migration and accumulation through structural analysis and computer simulations, the team found that lithium first accumulates in the silver-carbon layer during the initial stage of charging, then fills the voids in the carbon nanofiber layer, and subsequently accumulates between the two layers. Capacity Maintained at 92% After 250 Charge-Discharge Cycles When the bilayer structure was applied to an actual pouch cell, the cell retained 92.0% of its initial capacity after 250 charge-discharge cycles, even at the relatively low pressure of 2 megapascals (MPa). This was 11.2 percentage points higher than the capacity retention rate of a cell using only the existing silver-carbon layer (80.8%). The results demonstrated the potential to improve battery service life by mitigating mechanical damage caused by charging and discharging. The joint research team that developed a bilayer structure for all-solid-state batteries. From left: Professor Lee Jongwon of Hanyang University; Principal Researcher Choi Jeonghee of the Korea Electrotechnology Research Institute; Principal Researcher Jung Hoonki of the Korea Institute of Science and Technology; and co-first authors Kang Junhee and Lee Taeyoung. Photo courtesy of the National Research Foundation of Korea. View original image However, these results were verified under experimental conditions. Before the technology can be applied to actual electric vehicle batteries, stable performance must be achieved in large-area, stacked cells, and long-term charge-discharge durability must be further validated. “This study is significant because it presents a new approach that goes beyond existing technologies for promoting uniform lithium deposition and can also mitigate mechanical damage during charging and discharging,” Professor Lee said. “We plan to develop the technology to deliver stable performance in large-area, stacked all-solid-state batteries and enable long-term operation at room temperature and under low-pressure conditions.” Hot Picks Today "Two Spend 500,000 Won in a Flash, Yet Wait Two Hours?" ... artigo.texto: Charge Power has been appointed to manage two Texas battery energy storage projects totalling 290MW/580MWh through commissioning and into commercial operation in 2027. The two projects comprise a 150MW/300MWh BESS and a 140MW/280MWh system, both connecting to the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) grid. Charge Power will act as an owner’s-side project partner rather than as battery supplier or EPC contractor. Its role will be to coordinate the engineering, procurement and construction contractors, project engineers, equipment suppliers, documentation and grid-connection requirements needed to take both projects from late-stage construction through commissioning to commercial operation date, or COD. COD is the point at which a project has completed the required testing and contractual milestones and can begin normal commercial operation and earn revenue. For projects in ERCOT, the process also involves completing the grid operator’s interconnection and commissioning requirements before the asset can participate fully in the Texas electricity market. Both projects will also use the WARAM platform for project governance, due diligence and compliance. Charge Power said the software is intended to link physical asset requirements with the documentation and evidence needed to demonstrate that those requirements have been met throughout ownership, certification and eventual asset transfer. Founder and president Ravi Pinnelli said: “Texas is one of the most demanding storage markets in the country, and the stretch between construction and commercial operation is where a project either protects its returns or loses them. “We approach every project with an owner-operator mindset, so on these projects our decisions prioritize schedule, revenue, and long-term performance the way the owner would. “Through shifting markets and an evolving energy landscape, our goal is to deliver execution certainty from day one to COD and beyond.” Charge Power said it has commissioned 3GW/7GWh of energy storage since the company was founded in 2022. The company works across US electricity markets including ERCOT, CAISO, MISO and PJM, as well as projects in Canada, India, Japan and the UK. Battery storage deployment has grown rapidly in Texas as developers seek to capture low-cost electricity during periods of abundant generation and discharge it during higher-priced periods of demand. Charge Power cited Modo Energy figures showing ERCOT battery capacity reached 16.5GW/28.8GWh by the end of June 2026, following rapid annual growth since 2020. BESTmag has previously reported on a number of large Texas projects, including Eolian’s 400MW/1.8GWh Padua BESS complex and Energy Vault’s 57MW/114MWh Cross Trails system. The chemistry and equipment suppliers for Charge Power’s two newly awarded projects were not disclosed. Photo: Charge Power’s 240MW/480MWh Anole BESS in Texas. The image illustrates the company’s growing ERCOT project portfolio but is not one of the two newly announced 290MW/580MWh projects. Credit: Charge Power.

artigo.texto: SamsungSDI has secured an additional supply volume of LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries for energy storage systems (ESS) worth 3 to 4 trillion won from U.S.-based Jupiter Power, signaling a major step in expanding its medium- and long-term order book. After already securing production volumes through 2028, the company has also landed large-scale, long-term contracts starting in 2029, broadening its growth foundation in the U.S. ESS market. As of the 16th, SamsungSDI's cumulative U.S. power ESS order book has grown to over 76 GWh (gigawatt-hours), including an additional 16 GWh contract with Jupiter Power. The existing order volume of more than 60 GWh secured by the end of October this year alone is sufficient to keep the U.S. SPE (Star Plus Energy) and Ulsan production lines running at full capacity through 2028. This new contract covers supply over three years starting in 2029, marking another achievement for SamsungSDI in securing long-term supply volumes. To meet growing ESS demand, SamsungSDI is accelerating the expansion of its local production capacity in the United States. In early October, the company began mass production of prismatic LFP batteries for ESS at its SPE plant in Indiana, and started shipping battery cells from mid-October. The produced cells will undergo module and battery box processes before being delivered to customers as finished SBB (Samsung Battery Box) products starting in December. SamsungSDI is working to expand supply capacity by converting existing electric vehicle (EV) battery production lines into ESS LFP battery facilities. It is additionally converting two of the four production lines at its U.S. SPE Plant 1. The company also plans to utilize the U.S. Synergy Cells plant, acquired through the full buyout of its joint venture stake with GM (General Motors) in August, as an ESS production hub. Synergy Cells is currently optimizing designs to convert existing EV facilities into high-capacity LFP battery production lines for ESS. Mass production is scheduled to begin from late 2028 to early 2029, followed by phased expansion of production lines. This expansion of the ESS business is also closely tied to efforts to capture the battery market for AI (artificial intelligence) data centers. SamsungSDI is accelerating its market push by leveraging its status as the world's only company capable of supplying all three essential battery solutions for data centers: BESS (battery energy storage systems), UPS (uninterruptible power supplies), and BBU (battery backup units). As a result, performance has shown signs of recovery. SamsungSDI's cumulative operating profit for the first three quarters of this year reached 456 billion won, turning profitable compared to an operating loss of 1.4232 trillion won in the same period last year. Building on its improved performance, SamsungSDI is strategizing to accelerate its next-generation all-solid-state battery business. All-solid-state batteries use solid electrolytes instead of liquid ones, offering enhanced safety. The company is developing the technology with a target of commercialization in the second half of next year. Since September, it has been supplying all-solid-state battery cell and pack samples for humanoid robots to multiple customers for performance evaluation. It is currently at the stage of refining product specifications for next year's mass production through iterative performance improvements and verification based on customer requirements. The company is also working in parallel to establish a stable supply chain for key materials such as cathode materials and solid electrolytes. A SamsungSDI official stated, "This order reflects recognition of our global technological competitiveness by securing large volumes early on," adding, "We will continue to lead the market with products that combine the performance and safety required by customers."

artigo.texto: As far as we know, San Francisco has three data centers. Two are in Bayview, and one is in Soma. They’re relatively small in terms of energy and water use. The two associated places on Paul Avenue have been around for decades, since the days when we called them “server farms.” The City Planning Department admits other centers may exist, on a smaller scale, since the department has no formal inventory of this type of land use. The Board of Supes recently approved a 45-day moratorium on new centers, and the Land Use and Transportation Committee will consider Monday/16 a year-long extension. The Planning Department has done a study on the issue, and its findings suggests that the city needs at least a moratorium, if not an outright ban. From an environmental justice perspective, data centers are a public nuisance—and to no surprise, all are in low-income neighborhoods with high concentrations of people of color. I don’t think we’re going to see a data center in Pacific Heights. The city also has a major capacity problem. According to the report, big data centers use as much as 50 megawatts of power, which is enough for 25,000 homes. The city’s under immense pressure to approve more housing—and the grid doesn’t have much space available. The current capacity of the power lines coming into San Francisco is 1 gigawatt. Peak usage is about 900 megawatts, and that’s rising, as more residents, businesses, and vehicles are shifting to electric power. A 50 MW data center would overwhelm the grid. PG&E can’t handle this load. Expanding the power lines coming into San Francisco could take at least eight years, and would cost hundreds of millions of dollars. If the city had a municipal utility, it could control new data centers: The City of Santa Clara, which already has 55 existing data centers, has its own municipal utility (Silicon Valley Power, SVP) that stopped taking new applications for service from data centers (but not other development) in 2023 while it assessed the ability to provide power for these uses and while they await the completion of a major transmission expansion project expected to be completed in the next couple years. Then there’s water. From the report: SFPUC has concerns for existing and potential future data centers about the types of chemicals (and their concentrations and amounts) that are being used for cooling systems; whether wastewater discharges from data centers are within the local temperature limit of 125 °F; and whether the combined sewer system has the capacity to handle the data center’s wastewater flow, especially during wet weather. Depending on the water quality, there’s a risk of causing additional corrosion to sewers. SFPUC uses site-specific wastewater discharge permits to regulate non-domestic and temporary discharges into the City’s combined sewer system. Mayor Daniel Lurie loves AI, and if the companies he sees as the city’s economic future want local data centers, I suspect he will by sympathetic. Of course, it we don’t build them here, we’re just outsourcing the problem to other communities. The committee will consider the planning report Monday/16, and the full board will discuss a year-long moratorium Tuesday/17. I don’t use self-checkout. I hate having to take pictures of checks on my phone and sending them to the bank. People used to get paid to do that work; now they’ve lost their jobs, and I’m supposed to do it, for no pay. It’s hard to find an open bank branch with real tellers these days, and sometimes it costs money to get a human on the phone for customer service. When I have an internet outage, my provider’s phone system tells me to seek help on the web; dude, I can’t get to the web. That’s the problem. Not everyone is young and tech-savvy. Some people need people, real people, to help them with their groceries or prescriptions or banking. And the more technology replaces people, the more we are going to have to deal with massive unemployment. The Government Audit and Oversight Committee will consider Thursday/19 a measure that would place limits on self-checkout facilities at grocery stores and pharmacies. The measure would require one employee-staffed checkout center for every three self-check centers, would limit self-check to 15 items, and would mandate one employee to supervise every self-check operations center. The measure has six co-sponsors, enough to ensure it will pass, but not enough to override a mayoral veto. That hearing starts at 10am. Thanks to the AI boom and radical economic inequality, evictions are soaring in San Francisco; landlords are looking for any possible loophole to get rid of rent-controlled tenants who are paying below market rate. One tactic: Cite a “nuisance.” Some landlords in Chinatown tried to use that tool to evict renters who hung their laundry out to dry on a clothesline. It’s been used to evict tenants who have bicycles in public spaces. The Land Use and Transportation Committee will consider Monday/16 an ordinance that would restrict “nuisance” evictions. Among other things, it would ban evictions for damage to the property if the tenants paid to have the place repaired. That hearing starts at 10 am. The union and its representatives would be able to use the threat of a legal filing to gain leverage with hotels during contract negotiations. artigo.texto: In the electric vehicle (EV) battery market, where Korean batteries are under pressure, they have yet to find a breakthrough for a turnaround. As the rise of "Made in China" batteries continues, voices are growing that a counteroffensive must be launched centered on new product lineups such as mid-nickel, lithium manganese-rich (LMR), and all-solid-state batteries. According to battery industry sources and Samsung Securities on Tuesday, CATL's share of Hyundai Motor Group's EV sales was 29% as of September last year. This figure represents a 16 percentage point (p) increase compared to the same period last year. In contrast, during the same period, SK On's share decreased from 52% to 38%, and LG Energy Solution's share fell from 32% to 30%. A similar trend is observed among other automakers. Currently, within the Volkswagen Group, Korean battery makers hold a 53% market share, while Chinese firms account for approximately 45%, according to analysis. The Volkswagen Group, which had used almost 100% Korean batteries, newly adopted CATL batteries in the first half of 2024. In less than three years since then, the market share of Chinese batteries has closed in on that of K-batteries. Jo Hyeon-ryeol, a researcher at Samsung Securities, explained, "With China's Gotion also entering the Volkswagen Group's supply chain this year, it is expected that K-batteries will cede the lead to Chinese firms by 2027." He added, "Similarly, as Hyundai Motor Group has fully launched new vehicles equipped with lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries—an area where China holds an advantage—the market share of Chinese companies is likely to expand further." K-batteries are aiming to increase sales of EV batteries in the United States, where a "No China Zone" has been established, but this too is proving difficult. This is due to the shrinking front-end market resulting from the second Trump administration's abolition of EV purchase subsidies. Through the third quarter last year, GM's EV sales were approximately 214,000 units, and Ford's were about 221,000 units, representing year-on-year declines of 15.6% and 4.4%, respectively. Both companies are experiencing their first negative growth trend since 2020. Domestic battery majors such as LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI, and SK On have adopted a strategy of weathering the EV market downturn by expanding sales of batteries for energy storage systems (ESS). However, as the strength of Chinese firms led by LFP becomes more pronounced year by year, there are concerns that K-batteries may lose their lead in the EV battery market, which is considered the industry's "main battlefield." CATL and others are leveraging cost competitiveness to target not only the LFP segment, where they have shown superiority, but also the ternary cathode market, which has been a stronghold for K-batteries. For K-batteries, it is urgent to regroup and secure market share in the EV battery sector. LG Energy Solution is increasing sales of high-voltage mid-nickel batteries, a mid-to-low-priced product that can serve as a check against Chinese-made LFP, centered on its Poland plant. LMR, which offers higher energy density at a price similar to LFP, is also considered a promising candidate. LG Energy Solution is pushing for the production of next-generation LMR prismatic batteries through Ultium Cells, its joint venture with GM. Whether all-solid-state batteries can emerge as a "game changer" is also a key issue. In the development of all-solid-state batteries, known as the "dream battery" for maximizing performance and safety through solid electrolytes, Samsung SDI is assessed to be in the lead. The company's goal is to mass-produce all-solid-state batteries within next year and apply them to EVs following their use in humanoid robots. A battery industry official said, "Even if we perform well in the ESS market, ceding the EV market to China would inevitably result in a significant blow." He added, "We must be able to create a turning point in the EV battery market next year."

artigo.texto: Essa informação foi compartilhada pelo Sr. Bui Duc Hieu, Diretor Adjunto do Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas, com a imprensa em um evento de lançamento online realizado à margem da 31ª Conferência das Partes da Convenção-Quadro das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima (COP31), em Antalya, Turquia, no dia 13 de novembro. Segundo ele, o desenvolvimento de um mercado de carbono é uma das soluções para apoiar a implementação dos compromissos nacionais de resposta às mudanças climáticas, especialmente a meta de alcançar emissões líquidas zero até 2050. “Constatamos que um mercado de carbono não é apenas uma ferramenta para gerenciar emissões, mas também precisa criar incentivos para que as empresas inovem em tecnologia, melhorem a eficiência energética e invistam em soluções de redução de emissões”, afirmou o Sr. Hieu. No contexto da implementação acelerada do Acordo de Paris sobre mudanças climáticas em todo o mundo , os mercados de carbono estão se tornando uma ferramenta política crucial para promover a redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa, mobilizar recursos para transições verdes e apoiar o cumprimento dos compromissos internacionais. De acordo com representantes do Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas, o Vietnã encontra-se atualmente nos estágios iniciais de implementação de um sistema de comércio de emissões de gases de efeito estufa. Portanto, é necessário buscar recomendações e experiências de outros países e parceiros internacionais em relação à gestão, monitoramento e operação dos mercados de carbono para atingir a meta de operação oficial do mercado até 2029. O Vietnã fez progressos significativos no aperfeiçoamento de sua estrutura institucional e na construção da infraestrutura para seu mercado de carbono. 2026 também marca uma transição crucial do desenvolvimento de políticas para a implementação prática. Até o momento, o Vietnã alocou cotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa para 110 instalações nos setores de energia térmica, siderurgia e cimento para o período de 2025-2026 e colocou em operação o Sistema Nacional de Registro de Cotas de Emissão de Gases de Efeito Estufa e Créditos de Carbono. Notavelmente, a bolsa de carbono doméstica foi oficialmente lançada em 29 de junho na Bolsa de Valores de Hanói . No entanto, estabelecer um novo quadro legal e infraestrutura técnica é apenas o começo. De acordo com o vice-diretor Bui Duc Hieu, durante a fase piloto, o Vietnã precisa continuar aprimorando o sistema de medição, reporte e avaliação das emissões de gases de efeito estufa, além de garantir a coordenação sincronizada entre os órgãos de gestão e os operadores de mercado, e fortalecer a capacidade e a prontidão das empresas para participar. Esses são os requisitos que precisam ser atendidos para que o mercado de carbono se torne, de fato, uma ferramenta eficaz para promover a redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa. Ao elogiar o progresso do Vietnã na tradução do compromisso em ação, John Robert Cotton, Diretor da Parceria para a Transição Energética do Sudeste Asiático (ETP), afirmou que poucos países conseguem fazer a transição de um arcabouço legal para a operação de um mercado de carbono obrigatório em tão pouco tempo quanto o Vietnã. Enfatizando a importância da precificação do carbono para incorporar os custos de emissão aos balanços patrimoniais das empresas, Cotton disse que, a partir de 2029, quando o mecanismo de leilão de cotas começar a ser implementado, o mercado gerará receita para o orçamento do Estado, que poderá então ser reinvestida em atividades de redução de emissões na indústria. Segundo ele, "gargalos" semelhantes que dificultam o funcionamento do mercado também estão sendo encontrados em muitos outros países da região. "Nas Filipinas , a ETP está auxiliando o Ministério das Finanças na realização de uma revisão jurídica dos instrumentos de precificação de carbono. Na Indonésia, estamos trabalhando com o Ministério do Comércio e o Ministério da Indústria para avaliar o impacto das exportações de ferro e aço, cimento, alumínio e fertilizantes nos mecanismos tributários internacionais", afirmou. Reconhecendo o progresso significativo do Vietnã no desenvolvimento de seu mercado de carbono, a Sra. Leticia Guimarães, Chefe da Unidade de Mercado Global de Carbono do PNUD Vietnã, enfatizou: “O Vietnã estabeleceu uma estrutura legal clara e robusta para seu mercado de carbono. O lançamento da Bolsa em junho reafirmou sua posição como um dos países pioneiros na região da ASEAN. Também estamos muito satisfeitos com o lançamento do Portal de Informações de Mercado, que ajuda a divulgar informações importantes, lançando as bases para que as partes interessadas e os investidores tenham confiança nas próximas etapas.”

artigo.texto: HD Hyundai Energy Solution and HD Hyundai Electric said Monday that they will jointly participate in 'RE+ 26,' North America's largest clean energy exhibition, held at the Las Vegas Convention Center in the United States, showcasing their integrated energy business capabilities spanning from solar power generation to energy storage, conversion, and transmission and distribution. HD Hyundai Energy Solution will unveil its 'TOPCon Multi-Cut (G12R TOPCon Multi-Cut)' module for the North American market for the first time. Multi-cut is a technology that divides large-area solar cells into multiple pieces to reduce power loss generated during current flow. Through this, the company achieved a module efficiency of 24.4% by increasing power density. It plans to gradually apply ultra-precision multi-cut technology to its production lines to strengthen the competitiveness of its high-efficiency products. HD Hyundai Electric will introduce battery energy storage systems (BESS) and power grid stabilization technologies. The company will showcase major domestic and international project cases, including the 96th-megawatt-class Anmyeondo BESS project in Sinan, South Korea, and the 100th-megawatt-class Rutile BESS project in Texas, United States. It will also present Grid-Forming technology, which actively controls voltage and frequency to enhance power supply stability, as well as a product lineup of power equipment targeting the North American power grid and data center markets. In the United States, the utilization of energy storage systems is rapidly increasing alongside the expansion of solar power generation. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), U.S. solar power generation increased by 18.3% year-on-year from January to August this year. More than 16% of new large-scale solar facilities built through September this year were installed together with battery storage systems. The importance of grid stabilization technology and the expansion of transmission and distribution infrastructure is also growing due to increasing power demand and the expanded integration of renewable energy into the power grid. The two companies are strengthening their business foundations for targeting the North American market. HD Hyundai Electric is expanding its local business base through the expansion of its North American production subsidiary and the expansion of its BESS business via its Texas subsidiary. HD Hyundai Energy Solution is responding to changes in U.S. supply chain regulations, including requirements related to Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC), based on its domestic integrated cell and module production system. An official from HD Hyundai said, "In the North American market, not only product technological capability but also stable supply capacity and project execution capabilities have emerged as key competitive factors." He added, "Taking this exhibition as an opportunity, we will expand cooperation with local customers and partners and discover practical business opportunities."

artigo.texto: Two days of training end with a diploma reception. Companies eager to hire the new graduates have come ready to hand out jobs that can pay more than $100,000 a year. Welcome to the data center economy. In the race to build out America’s AI infrastructure, tech companies are struggling to find technicians with sufficient skills to install the cooling, server racks, electrical equipment and fiberoptic cables necessary to meet the off-the-charts demand for the revolutionary technology. Even as AI politics have shifted – particularly after recent midterm election – the lack of available labor to build continuing data center projects would almost certainly trump any potential construction slowdown. So the industry is going to extraordinary lengths to teach and hire people to fill those crucial jobs. Several nonprofits, online learning companies and all four of the big AI hyperscalers — Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft — offer various forms of free, accelerated training courses for the technical skills needed to build out data centers. Some of those positions can pay six-figure salaries. And many Americans don’t even know these jobs exist. Graduation on Friday. Orientation on Monday Javonntae Hill studied video game design. He’s in his early 30s and he was looking for a career — but didn’t quite know where to start. His girlfriend saw an advertisement for America’s Workforce Academy, a new training program Meta kicked off in August to help fill the labor skills gap. The company was willing to pay him during his four-week training and guaranteed him placement in a data center job after he received his diploma. Hill figured he’d give it a shot. Over the course of a month, in a classroom of 30 people, he got thrown into a mix of lectures and hands-on training, learning about how to place and run fiberoptic and copper cables and what each cable insulator color specifies. He was nervous: He hoped he could retain all that information for his new job. “Graduation was on Friday,” Hill said. “I started orientation on Monday.” Meta partnered with Associated Builders and Contractors, a construction industry trade group that has been training workers for decades. Unlike traditional training methods, including trade school or an apprenticeship, ABC’s accelerated courses aren’t designed to be comprehensive; they’re designed to get as many people working in data centers as possible. “It’s like the military,” said Joel Thames, head of ABC’s safety and workforce group. “Does boot camp get them trained for any scenario? No. But it gives them a foundational education before they spend time on the job site.” Hill said his nerves were unfounded: He showed up to the Ohio job site overprepared. And grateful. “I could do this for the rest of my life,” Hill said. “I’ve seen postings of jobs available, but I have a lot of loyalty toward Meta.” The problem Despite growing public opposition and a wave of new lawmakers pledging to regulate their expansion, data center construction is virtually unstoppable. AI infrastructure spending is expected to approach $1 trillion a year, annually for the foreseeable future, according to Columbia Business School economist Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh. But construction faces many logistical hurdles, including building permits, power guarantees, materials and financing. Even the deepest-pocketed AI companies that can overcome those obstacles are encountering a consistent roadblock: America has far too few qualified people to build data centers — particularly in some of the remote or rural locations where they’re being built. The United States has a shortage of 1 million engineers needed to meet data center construction estimates, PwC estimates. Many otherwise ready-to-go sites have been delayed for months while they assemble a qualified crew to build them. Only about half of the AI computing capacity scheduled to come online between now and 2028 is actually expected to meet its target date, according to Goldman Sachs. That’s a costly wait: For large AI data centers, a month of delay can cost anywhere from the low tens of millions to well over $100 million, depending on location, scale and contract terms, said Mona Dajani, co-chair of Cooley’s infrastructure, energy and real estate practice. So AI companies are addressing the challenge by ditching requirements for multi-year trade school courses or apprenticeships in favor of accelerated, high-intensity courses designed specifically for data center construction jobs. Many are offering the courses for free. A growing number will even pay learners to take the courses. Classes can run from 15 weeks to just two days, depending on the job. Desperation for labor is so high that AI companies are placing some top graduates on the job the day after they gain their certifications. ‘I had nothing to lose’ Robert Burgess had been bouncing around construction jobs in and around Canton, Mississippi. He knew how to do some low-voltage electrical work and had heard that he could make a lot more money cutting fiber for a telecom or a data center site. Burgess Googled “internet fiber training Mississippi” and a four-week Amazon training program called I2PA (Information Infrastructure Pre-Apprenticeship) surfaced at a local community college. “I had nothing to lose,” Burgess said. “I put in my email, and I got accepted.” Over the course of the training, Burgess learned how electricity is generated and delivered, how servers are installed and how they fit into a data center. Amazon trainers set up a mock data center so that Burgess and his classmates could get hands-on training. At the end: a job fair. Burgess got a job from Yates Construction and Turner Construction, which were partnering on the tail end of a data center construction site in the area. That was in 2024. artigo.texto: O governo dos Estados Unidos emitiu uma norma nesta segunda-feira, 16, que deve dificultar a aquisição de chips de Inteligência Artificial (IA) por empresas de data centers sediadas em cinco países, entre eles o Brasil. A norma publicada pelo Departamento de Comércio não proíbe a compra de chips. Contudo, estabelece que Brasil, Indonésia, Malásia, Singapura e Tailândia deverão obter, além das exigências de licenciamento atualmente em vigor para semicondutores avançados, uma licença adicional para exportação, reexportação ou transferência de chips de alta capacidade. Embora tenha listado cinco países, o governo de Donald Trump busca, na prática, atingir a China com a medida. A ideia é dificultar que empresas chinesas utilizem data centers em outros países para processar demandas de alta capacidade computacional usando tecnologia norte-americana. Conforme a norma, o Brasil e as demais nações são classificados pelo governo dos Estados Unidos como "países que apresentam um risco de desvio superior ao normal". Nesse sentido, a medida afirma que data centers que forneçam um volume significativo de poder computacional a empresas sediadas na China ou em países do chamado grupo D:5 (mercados sujeitos a embargos de armas dos Estados Unidos) deverão obter uma licença no prazo de 90 dias, sob pena de enfrentar futuras restrições à exportação. De acordo com a medida, a exigência de licença não alcança semicondutores destinados a empresas sediadas nos Estados Unidos ou cuja controladora final esteja sediada no território norte-americano. "A norma visa a garantir que as restrições já existentes ao acesso a tecnologias norte-americanas sensíveis não possam ser contornadas por meio de arranjos de computação remota que envolvam data centers em países terceiros", afirma o Departamento de Comércio, em comunicado. A nota oficial ainda afirma que os Estados Unidos "estão empenhados em promover a adoção global de tecnologia norte-americana para fins comerciais legítimos". Sendo assim, o governo busca atuar para que "tecnologias sensíveis não sejam exploradas por meios que ameacem a segurança nacional dos Estados Unidos". Pontos de atenção Em comunicado, a Associação Brasileira das Empresas de Software (Abes) afirma que "acompanha com atenção" a medida anunciada pelo governo norte-americano. A entidade destacou que a norma, enquanto representa uma nova camada de compliance para subsidiárias de empresas sediadas nos Estados Unidos, gera uma "assimetria competitiva" para provedores de nuvem e data centers de capital nacional, por exigir autorizações analisadas caso a caso. Além disso, para a Abes, a inclusão do Brasil em uma lista restritiva pode dificultar a atração de novos investimentos internacionais ao setor de infraestrutura digital brasileiro. Desse modo, a associação defende uma atuação coordenada entre o governo brasileiro e o setor produtivo junto aos Estados Unidos. "Essa atuação deve ter uma agenda objetiva de cooperação em controle de exportações, que demonstre a solidez institucional do Brasil e preserve a fluidez das cadeias globais de suprimentos tecnológicos", ressalta a entidade.
