artigo.texto: Data centers: acordo entre Amazon e Blackstone abrange 13 prédios em Indiana e no Mississippi (Adobe Stock/Divulgação) Repórter de Inteligência Artificial e Tecnologia Publicado em 16 de novembro de 2026 às 10h10. Última atualização em 16 de novembro de 2026 às 10h11. A Amazon anunciou em 16 de novembro de 2026 a venda do controle de 13 prédios de data centers nos Estados Unidos, avaliados em US$ 5 bilhões, para a Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust (BXDC), veículo imobiliário administrado por uma afiliada da Blackstone. A Amazon Web Services (AWS) continuará ocupando todos os imóveis como inquilina, com contratos de prazo médio inicial de 12 anos, que podem chegar a 32 anos com as renovações, e reajuste de 2,75% ao ano. A Amazon receberá dinheiro e ficará com 24,9% das duas sociedades conjuntas que serão donas dos complexos, localizados em Indiana e no Mississippi, que somam 647 megawatts de capacidade. É o primeiro investimento da BXDC desde o IPO, em maio, e a conclusão está prevista para até o fim de 2026. O modelo lembra a sociedade fechada pela Meta com fundos da Blue Owl, em 2025, para o complexo Hyperion, na Louisiana. A Amazon vai passar de proprietária a sócia minoritária e inquilina de 13 prédios de data centers recém-construídos nos Estados Unidos. Em acordo anunciado nesta segunda-feira, 16, um veículo imobiliário administrado por uma afiliada da Blackstone comprará o controle das sociedades que ficarão com os imóveis, avaliados em US$ 5 bilhões. A Amazon Web Services (AWS), braço de computação em nuvem do grupo, vai alugar todos os prédios e continuar usando a infraestrutura. A operação dá à Amazon uma forma de levantar dinheiro com instalações que já construiu e manter a capacidade disponível para seus clientes. Em troca, a companhia assume aluguéis com prazo inicial médio de 12 anos. Se todas as opções de renovação forem exercidas, a média sobe para 32 anos. O reajuste previsto é de 2,75% ao ano, e a própria Amazon garante os pagamentos da subsidiária. Os US$ 5 bilhões correspondem à avaliação bruta dos dois complexos. Na conclusão da operação, a Amazon vai transferir os imóveis para duas sociedades conjuntas, uma para cada complexo, e receber dinheiro e uma fatia de 24,9% em cada uma. A Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust, negociada na Bolsa de Nova York sob o código BXDC, ficará com os outros 75,1%. O pagamento em dinheiro será financiado por duas fontes. A BXDC espera aportar US$ 1,9 bilhão em recursos levantados no IPO. Subsidiárias das sociedades conjuntas devem contratar cerca de US$ 2,5 bilhões em empréstimos hipotecários, garantidos pelos próprios imóveis. Como parte do financiamento também cobrirá custos da transação, a soma dessas duas fontes indica o volume de recursos mobilizados, e o valor líquido a ser recebido pela Amazon ainda depende dos termos do fechamento. É o primeiro investimento da BXDC desde a abertura de capital, em maio. A oferta inicial foi de US$ 1,75 bilhão e, depois que os bancos exerceram integralmente a opção de vender ações adicionais, a captação líquida chegou a cerca de US$ 1,9 bilhão. A conclusão da compra está prevista para até o fim de 2026, sujeita às condições do acordo. O acordo reúne nove prédios no norte de Indiana, no mercado de data centers da região de Chicago, e quatro no Mississippi. Juntos, eles somam 647 megawatts de capacidade elétrica para equipamentos de TI. O número indica a potência que a infraestrutura pode disponibilizar a equipamentos como servidores e sistemas de rede. Para a BXDC, a compra dá acesso a prédios novos com um contrato para ocupar 100% do portfólio. Para a AWS, a locação mantém disponíveis os imóveis de que a operação depende. O contrato segue o modelo conhecido como triple net, em que o inquilino arca, além do aluguel, com despesas como impostos imobiliários, seguro e manutenção. A aquisição foi precificada a uma taxa inicial de capitalização de 7%. O indicador relaciona a renda operacional anual dos imóveis ao valor atribuído a eles. Ele serve para avaliar o preço pago pelo portfólio. O retorno para o acionista da BXDC também depende do custo da dívida e das demais despesas da operação. A parceria permite à Amazon recuperar parte do capital investido nas instalações e continuar usando os prédios. O dinheiro entra no fechamento. Os aluguéis serão pagos ao longo dos anos, com reajuste anual. Para o investidor imobiliário, o atrativo é justamente o fluxo de pagamentos de uma única locatária, respaldado pela garantia da Amazon. Prasad Kalyanaraman, vice-presidente de infraestrutura da AWS, afirmou no comunicado que a parceria permite à empresa continuar ampliando sua operação à medida que cresce a demanda dos clientes. No terceiro trimestre, a receita da AWS cresceu 39%, para US$ 46 bilhões. A expansão exige investimentos em terrenos, energia e prédios, além dos chips e servidores instalados neles. O acordo com a Blackstone traz um investidor para a parte imobiliária dessa conta. A Meta recorreu a uma sociedade com fundos da Blue Owl em outubro de 2025 para desenvolver o complexo Hyperion, na Louisiana. Os fundos ficaram com 80%, e a Meta, com 20%. Os US$ 27 bilhões divulgados naquele acordo correspondem ao custo estimado de desenvolvimento, incluindo construção e infraestrutura de energia, refrigeração e conectividade. No caso da Amazon, os US$ 5 bilhões são a avaliação de imóveis já construídos, que a AWS continuará usando como inquilina. A AWS vai alugar todos os 13 prédios. A Amazon também manterá 24,9% das sociedades que serão donas dos imóveis. Os US$ 5 bilhões são o valor bruto atribuído aos dois complexos. Na conclusão do negócio, a Amazon receberá uma parcela em dinheiro e manterá uma participação minoritária nas sociedades. A BXDC espera concluir a transação até o fim de 2026. O fechamento depende das condições do acordo e do financiamento previsto. artigo.texto: Ascenty constrói data center de IA em Sumaré Projeto tem cliente âncora contratado; companhia mantém três unidades em construção e quatro em expansão no Brasil. A Ascenty está construindo em Sumaré, no interior de São Paulo, um data center dedicado à inteligência artificial, com capacidade inicial de 60 megawatts (MW) para equipamentos de TI e 90 MW de potência total. O empreendimento, chamado Sumaré 3, já tem um cliente âncora contratado, segundo Rodrigo Radaieski, CTO da companhia, em entrevista ao TV.Síntese. O vídeo vai ao ar hoje, às 19h. “É um hyperscale”, afirmou. Segundo o executivo, as bases e os pilares da construção já foram executados. A previsão é disponibilizar a primeira fase em setembro de 2027. O projeto faz parte da expansão da empresa no Brasil, dona de 21 data centers em operação, três em construção e quatro em expansão. Na América Latina, a companhia contabiliza 26 unidades operacionais e um total de 40 ao incluir os empreendimentos em construção e desenvolvimento. Expansão concentrada em São Paulo As obras de expansão no Brasil estão concentradas em São Paulo. Segundo o CTO, a localização atende à demanda dos clientes e à necessidade de reduzir a latência, ou seja, o tempo de comunicação entre os dispositivos dos usuários e os data centers. O executivo afirma que essa proximidade também importa para aplicações de inteligência artificial. A empresa mantém unidades no Rio de Janeiro e em Fortaleza. Radaieski também conta das negociações para novos projetos, que atribuiu ao avanço do Redata, regime de incentivos ao setor. “O Redata acelerou bastante o mercado, então tem muitas discussões, a gente deve fazer anúncios em breve”, disse. No caso de Sumaré 3, a intenção é solicitar o enquadramento no regime após a regulamentação. Além daquela projeto, a Ascenty está adaptando instalações existentes para receber cargas de maior densidade. “Só no ano de 2025 nós fizemos 400 ações dentro dos data centers para buscar essa eficiência energética”, afirmou. Entre os exemplos citados estão ajustes de temperatura, posicionamento de grelhas e circulação do ar. Rede de fibra integra a estratégia A expansão dos data centers é acompanhada pela infraestrutura própria de conectividade. Segundo o CTO, a Ascenty possui 4 mil quilômetros de fibra óptica, somando as redes no Brasil e no México. Essa infraestrutura conecta unidades da empresa, data centers de outros operadores e estações de chegada de cabos submarinos. No Brasil, a rede própria tem conexões em São Paulo, incluindo Praia Grande, no Rio de Janeiro e em Fortaleza. A rede atende tanto clientes corporativos que contratam links quanto empresas que demandam fibras apagadas, dedicadas à conexão entre instalações. Segundo o executivo, os hyperscalers contratam grandes quantidades dessas fibras para interligar data centers, replicar dados e manter redundância. Ele diz que o ativo é estratégico e não há nenhum plano de spin off dele.

artigo.texto: HADLEY — Lightning Hill is the name generations of Hadley residents have given to the peak of Breckenridge Road, where a gravel pit could soon become the location of a stand-alone battery energy storage system. “It is incredibly prone to lightning strikes,” said Linda Hannum, of Sylvia Heights. For residents who have organized to halt the placement of a 5-megawatt facility in the 5-acre site above Zatyrka Park, where there is a playground, gazebo and walking trails, the fact that lightning regularly splits trees and tears off bark makes the location above the town’s aquifer unsuitable for this project. On Thursday, nearly 30 people went to the Hadley Senior Center dining room, joined by another dozen or more attending virtually, to appeal to the Board of Health to take a stand against the development. They contend that the Board of Health could intervene after the Planning Board last month approved site plans, a solar project special permit and a business use in aquifer special permit for ZP Battery Devco’s 5-megawatt system. The meeting came two nights after the Conservation Commission voted 3-0 against the project. Commission members cautioned that they typically only weigh in on matters when wetlands are involved but still determined the project likely wasn’t appropriate for the neighborhood. “We are asking for you to join the Conservation Commission in opposing this project outright,” Hannum said. Planners had initially rejected the development in January 2025, concerned with potential impacts on the aquifer and public safety should there be a fire or leaks, before facing a lawsuit in Hampshire Superior Court in which the company argued the board’s decision was legally untenable and “unreasonable, arbitrary and capricious.” The Lightning Hill nickname for the top of Breckenridge Road, along with the gravel pit remaining an active site with unstable material at its base, are among neighbors’ many objections to the development. Since the agenda only called for public comment on the project, the Board of Health made no decision and took no action on the request. Neither the developer nor the landowner, Karl’s Excavating, was present to rebut any of the information presented. Hannum said she understands that the health board will likely have to prove there is a risk to the aquifer. Her hope is that the information residents provided, supplemented with photographic evidence from the site and pictures of a similar development that caught on fire and burned in Warwick, New York, will be sufficient. Members of the group organizing opposition, though, said they understand this is only a starting point. The aquifer is the big concern for Carol Soules of Sylvia Heights. Soules said the porous soil and fragile and unstable embankments should have necessitated a hydrogeologic study, which was not required for the proposal to proceed. “I feel like there are risks to [the] health and safety of residents,” Soules said. “The developer should find a safer place.” There are potential noise concerns, too. Donna Kurkul of Frallo Drive said residents below the gravel pit can already hear everything that happens there, and the battery noise will be excessive. Gail Mengel of Sylvia Heights said that a catastrophe could happen, and it’s unclear if the town has the resources to handle an emergency, whether a fire or a leak. Greg Owen of Breckenridge Road said the town should mitigate the threat and plan for the worst-case scenarios, adding that the best hazard prevention would be to prohibit such a development altogether. Others suggested that the project would be more appropriate along Route 9, where there are already areas paved over and fewer residential homes. Kristi Nelson of Sylvia Heights said that those concerned with the development are green energy advocates who understand the need to support solar and battery energy storage, but harming drinking water is not a good trade-off. “We feel very strongly it should not be in this location,” Nelson said.

artigo.texto: Pela regra, os operadores de data centers nos cinco países vão precisar de autorização do governo americano para comprar chips de IA avançados da Nvidia e de outros fabricantes americanos. O objetivo é impedir que a China e outros adversários dos EUA usem capacidade computacional instalada fora do país e baseada em processadores projetados nos Estados Unidos. “A regra foi elaborada para garantir que as restrições existentes ao acesso à tecnologia americana sensível não possam ser contornadas por meio de acordos de computação remota que envolvam data centers em terceiros países”, afirmou o departamento em comunicado. Segundo o órgão, os avanços na computação em nuvem tornaram cada vez mais viável acessar remotamente os sistemas americanos de IA. A nova regra busca alinhar esse tipo de acesso às normas que já valem para o acesso físico à tecnologia. As ações da Nvidia chegaram a cair 2,9% nesta segunda-feira, e o índice de semicondutores da Filadélfia recuou até 5,5% Como a regra afeta o Brasil e os outros países da lista Os pedidos de licença serão analisados caso a caso. Empresas com sede nos EUA que operam nos cinco países ficam de fora da exigência e podem continuar enviando chips de IA para lá sem licença. A isenção também vale para data centers usados em sistemas de recomendação de varejistas online e redes sociais. O texto divulgado na segunda-feira prevê que as novas exigências entram em vigor quando a regra for publicada no Federal Register, o diário oficial do governo americano. Escândalo na Nvidia pressiona o Departamento de Comércio A regra saiu dias depois de Jensen Huang deixar o cargo de CEO da Nvidia. Ele admitiu ter tido um caso com Alice Huang, ex-executiva da Megaspeed International, empresa com sede em Singapura. Os EUA suspeitam que Alice seja espiã chinesa, e hoje ela está na China. A Megaspeed é investigada nos EUA por possíveis violações dos controles de exportação e nega irregularidades. Depois da saída repentina de Huang, o Departamento de Comércio e autoridades como o secretário Howard Lutnick passaram a ser mais cobrados pela forma como conduzem os programas de controle de exportação. Nos últimos dias, o secretário do Tesouro, Scott Bessent, culpou Lutnick por não fazer o suficiente para aplicar as restrições que já existem. “Como eu disse, muitos outros departamentos estavam pressionando por isso, e quem redigia era o Comércio”, afirmou Bessent no programa Sunday Morning Futures, da Fox News. O comunicado do Departamento de Comércio diz que a regra foi escrita pelo Departamento do Tesouro e pelo Conselho de Segurança Nacional, e por orientação deles. Isso sugere que a pressão de autoridades de fora do Comércio pesou na publicação. Na semana passada, o site Axios informou que Trump havia autorizado uma nova ofensiva contra empresas suspeitas de desviar chips avançados de IA para a China, mas que Lutnick atrasou a execução da ordem. Nesta segunda-feira, Trump disse que Jensen Huang não colocou a segurança nacional em risco.

artigo.texto: Chris Meiter & Ed Evans from AMAG Technology and Eric Zei from Salient Systems examine why data center security gaps often stem from unfinished integration and unclear ownership, rather than outdated technology. Article Chapters Toggle Data centers are going up faster than almost any other facility type, and the security problem inside them resembles nothing else. A large colocation site moves tens of thousands of people through its doors in a year, working for hundreds of separate tenant companies, most of whom the operator does not employ. Community opposition and organized protests are trying to reshape where these buildings go and how their perimeters get designed. Drones are a concern, though not for what they can see: everything in a data center comes back to cooling, and material dropped into an intake causes an operational event without anyone crossing the fence. Even video retention, a policy question in most buildings, is a contractual obligation with real money attached. Salient Systems and AMAG Technology have worked on these buildings together since 2012. AMAG is among Salient’s closest technology partners, and the work we do together concentrates in exactly this segment: the large operators running multi-tenant sites at scale. So, when an operator tells one of us that the security system isn’t doing what they expected, we compare notes. Comparing notes works because the two halves are not as separate as they look. Access control is often treated as finished technology: badge, reader, door. Visibility is treated as something happening on the video and analytics side. But that mistakes maturity for being solved. A protocol can be decades old and entirely stable, yet still be poorly managed. It is also backwards. Analytics are only ever as good as the access data they compare themselves against. Access events arrive in the video system with the cardholder attached to the alarm, which is what allows an operator to see who badged and to pull the recorded video by clicking the event rather than hunting for a camera and a time. The traffic runs both ways: video can trigger a lockdown, and a credential flagged as stolen can raise an alert with the right camera already attached to it. Video used to be evidence you went back for after somebody reported an incident. Now it is meant to raise the alarm while the incident is still underway. That only works if the access side is alerting personnel to something worth raising. Tailgating is the clearest case. Access control records one valid swipe. Video, counting people, sees two bodies come through. Neither system flags anything alone, because the log says a valid credential was granted and video has no view on how many people should have passed. The alert exists only in the comparison. And in a data center, the second person is rarely an intruder. It is a colleague who did not badge, or a contractor’s second technician on one credential, walking past cages that belong to somebody else. That is what the two systems do when they work. Far more often, what we hear is that they don’t. The complaint is always the same sentence. What is causing it almost never is. In one building the recording servers are eleven years old and the software is four versions behind. That is a budget conversation, and there is no clever way around it. In the other, everything is current and everything works. Nothing was ever finished: the detection zones are drawn so wide that somebody switched the alarms off, the cameras and the doors carry different names in each system, and the clocks drifted apart two years ago without anyone noticing. That one is an afternoon of work. From the operator’s chair the two are indistinguishable. Ed Evans of AMAG Technology puts it at four out of five being the second kind, and suspects that estimate is generous. Neither got that way by accident, and the routes are different. The first route is money. Hardware debt accumulates because security sits behind other IT in the funding order, and a department whose failures stay invisible is easy to defer. Nobody runs a laptop for eleven years. A recording server that has been writing continuously for eleven years draws no comment at all. Version drift is quieter still. One operator can run a dozen sites on the same platform with eight different builds among them and never log it as a fault. That is why someone will watch a capability demonstrated at a trade show and insist their own system cannot do it. It can. Theirs is four versions back. The second route is easier to travel because nothing along it announces itself. A detection zone, a door name, a drifted clock: none of it registers as an incident on its own. Collectively they are the distance between the system as designed and the system as installed, and almost nobody measures that distance. “The system does what it’s told,” Ed says. “It’s just being told the wrong thing.” Colocation multiplies everything that has to be told correctly. “The big thing colocation has to deal with that single-tenant and hyperscale rarely do, is keeping tenants separated from each other, not just keeping outsiders out,” Ed adds. That one difference reaches into every part of the design. Segmentation has to go down to the cage and sometimes the cabinet. Every tenant runs its own authorized-personnel list, with its own churn. Audit evidence has to come out per tenant, PCI for one and HIPAA for the next. And a tailgate into the wrong cage is not an internal write-up. It is a contract problem with a paying customer. An unfinished system is not a technology failure. It is a failure of ownership, and a data center project is structured in a way that almost produces it. On paper, commissioning splits three ways: “Nobody is structurally incentivized to find the gaps,” Ed says. Verification falls to whoever volunteers, and frequently nobody does. artigo.texto: Smartphone batteries have become an important part of the buying decision, especially for people who spend hours gaming, watching videos or scrolling through social media. With the iQOO 15, the company is focusing on battery life through its fourth-generation silicon anode technology. The smartphone comes with a 7,000mAh battery, and iQOO claims that it can deliver up to 10.5 hours of continuous gaming, 32.6 hours of video streaming and 22.6 hours of social media usage on a single charge. But what exactly is silicon anode technology, and how does it help a smartphone battery last longer? To understand this, it is important to know how a smartphone battery works. A battery has two main parts called the anode and cathode. During charging and discharging, lithium ions move between these two parts to store and release energy. Most traditional smartphone batteries use graphite in the anode. Silicon, however, can store more lithium ions than graphite. This means it has the potential to hold more energy in the same amount of space. This is where silicon anode technology comes in. By using silicon-based materials in the battery's anode, manufacturers can increase energy density. In simple terms, a battery can store more power without necessarily becoming much bigger. However, silicon also has a limitation. It expands and contracts during charging and discharging, which can affect battery life and stability over time. Battery makers therefore have to work on ways to manage this expansion. The fourth-generation technology used in the iQOO 15 is designed to improve energy density and battery performance. However, iQOO has not publicly explained every material change that separates this generation from earlier versions. The phone also uses second-generation semi-solid battery technology, which the company says helps maintain stable performance across temperatures ranging from -20°C to 40°C. According to iQOO's laboratory figures, the 7,000mAh battery can offer up to 10.5 hours of continuous gaming. For people who mainly use their phones to watch videos, the company claims up to 32.6 hours of continuous video streaming. Social media users can also get up to 22.6 hours of usage, according to the company's figures. These numbers are based on iQOO's internal testing and should not be treated as guaranteed everyday battery life. Actual results will depend on factors such as screen brightness, network strength, gaming settings, background applications and the type of content being played. The phone also supports 100W wired FlashCharge and 40W wireless charging. It includes bypass charging, which allows power to go directly to the phone's system instead of charging the battery while gaming. This is d esigned to reduce battery heat during long gaming sessions. Another feature is Battery Life Extender mode. The company says this helps users return to their previous activity when the phone is connected to a charger after its battery runs critically low. The iQOO 15 also features Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 processor and an 8K vapour chamber cooling system. These features are meant to support demanding tasks such as gaming while helping manage heat. artigo.texto: COP31 climate negotiations in Antalya, Turkiye, have exposed a major imbalance in international carbon markets: governments and project developers are preparing billions of tonnes of carbon credits for sale, but actual transactions, verified emission reductions and financing reaching climate projects remain far smaller. A new COP31 report identifies $70.9 billion in potential Article 6 carbon-credit supply through 2030, compared with only $1.6 billion in contracted government demand. The State of the Article 6 Carbon Market 2026 report, released on November 13, estimates that 2.36 billion tonnes of carbon credits could become available by 2030. However, sovereign buyers have contracted approximately 53 million tonnes, representing just 2.2 percent of identified potential supply. Only 151,566 tonnes of internationally transferred mitigation outcomes (ITMOs) have actually moved between countries. These figures highlight the difference between potential carbon-credit supply, signed purchasing agreements, completed transfers and measurable climate investment. The report estimates demand associated with national climate commitments at approximately 200 million tonnes by 2030, worth $6 billion at the same assumed price. Since October 2025, governments have announced new tenders and agreements covering 27.3 million tonnes, valued at approximately $819 million. The volume includes Singapore’s procurement programme and Norway’s agreement to purchase up to 12 million tonnes from Indonesia, announced during COP31. These transactions could generate financing for emissions-reduction projects, but contract announcements alone do not establish that developers have received payment or delivered verified credits. Carbon Credit Prices: From $9 Forest Credits to $36 Government Purchases Carbon-credit prices vary significantly according to project type, verification, buyer requirements and eligibility under international climate agreements. According to OPIS’s November 9 COP31 carbon market assessment, Switzerland paid an average of approximately $36.58 per tonne for internationally transferred credits in 2025. Singapore’s initial procurement averaged approximately $27.30 per tonne, while Japanese Joint Crediting Mechanism credits were offered by a trader at $18–22 per tonne during 2026. Some forest-related credits were assessed at substantially lower prices, with OPIS reporting a broad REDD+ price assessment range extending from $0.15 to $9.20 per tonne. OPIS, A Dow Jones Company Sources: OPIS and Fastmarkets. Prices reflect different credit types, contract structures and dates; they are not directly interchangeable. Lower prices are not automatic evidence of fraudulent credits, just as higher prices do not guarantee genuine emissions reductions. The decisive factors are additionality, conservative emissions accounting, permanence, independent verification and safeguards against double counting. Voluntary Carbon Market: 169 Million Credits Retired in 2025 The Fastmarkets 2026 carbon-credit assessment shows that retirements across seven major registries reached approximately 169 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent in 2025, compared with 174.5 million tonnes in 2024. This represents a decline of approximately 3.2 percent, indicating that demand for voluntary credits remained relatively weak despite growing corporate climate commitments. Shell was the largest identified corporate user, retiring 9.75 million credits in 2025, down from more than 14 million in 2024. Eni retired 6.44 million credits, an increase exceeding 80 percent. Gold Standard’s 2025 annual report provides another important comparison. Gold Standard’s 37 million retirements represented approximately 46 percent of its 81 million issuances during 2025. However, credits retired in a particular year may have been issued in earlier years, so this ratio is not a project-level retirement rate. Its $12.4 billion shared-value estimate includes environmental and socioeconomic benefits. It is not carbon-credit sales revenue or verified cash investment. India Leads Historical Voluntary Credit Issuance With 405 Million Tonnes The Berkeley Carbon Trading Project’s voluntary offset database tracks carbon-credit issuance and retirement across major international registries. An analysis published by the US Congressional Research Service found that Indian projects accounted for approximately 405 million tonnes of cumulative voluntary carbon-credit issuance from 2004 through 2025, across 1,855 projects. India ranked first in the dataset for both issued credits and project count. Worldwide voluntary credit issuance reached approximately 253 million tonnes during 2025. India’s domestic carbon market is also developing. According to the International Institute for Sustainable Development’s November 2026 analysis, approximately 490 industrial facilities across seven sectors completed their first compliance reporting cycle under India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme in July 2026. For Indian developers, Article 6 creates potential export opportunities for verified reductions from eligible projects, including methane abatement and qualifying clean-energy activities. However, international transfers require appropriate authorization and accounting adjustments, while domestic compliance credits follow a separate regulatory framework. Can Renewable Energy and Methane Projects Generate Credible Carbon Revenue? Renewable-energy carbon credits face increasing scrutiny because solar and wind projects are commercially competitive in many markets. A developer must demonstrate that carbon-credit revenue supports emissions reductions that would not otherwise occur. Methane-abatement projects can offer more directly measurable benefits when emissions are monitored through reliable equipment and independently verified against credible baselines. The Verra Verified Carbon Standard requires projects to undergo validation, monitoring and third-party verification before credits are issued

artigo.texto: Much attention has been given to artificial intelligence, cloud computing and the technology driving the modern economy. Those topics certainly deserve discussion. Yet for local residents, the more important question is far simpler: What do these projects mean for our communities? The answer begins with jobs and investment, but it does not end there. The arrival of large-scale data centers represents one of the most significant private investments ever contemplated in this region. Drawn by reliable electric power, strategic location, available land and access to major markets, technology companies are increasingly viewing West Virginia as an attractive destination for future development. The benefits begin long before a facility becomes operational. During construction, hundreds and potentially thousands of local and regional workers may be employed in site preparation, building construction, utility installation, electrical work and equipment deployment. These projects create opportunities for heavy equipment operators, electricians, steel workers, concrete specialists, truck drivers, engineers, surveyors and countless others. Once operational, the facilities create a new layer of highly skilled employment opportunities, including data center technicians, network engineers, facility operators, security professionals, maintenance personnel and management staff. These positions typically provide competitive wages, specialized training and long-term career opportunities. Data centers represent extraordinary concentrations of private investment. The land, buildings, electrical infrastructure and equipment associated with these facilities collectively create a property tax base unlike anything most communities have previously experienced. Once placed on the tax rolls, those assets generate recurring revenue year after year. Where does the data center revenue go? Economic development projects are often measured by the number of jobs created. While employment matters, residents should also ask another important question: Where does the revenue go? The answer is straightforward. Tax revenues generated by these facilities are distributed through existing state and local systems and ultimately support essential public services. Those revenues benefit public schools, county government, emergency services, public safety operations, infrastructure improvements, and important statewide initiatives. The combined Monarch and Tamarack developments in Mason County are expected to generate approximately $231.2 million annually in property tax revenue. Of that amount, more than $90 million would support county schools, nearly $47.5 million would flow to county government and more than $7 million would support Fire and EMS services. Additional funding would support statewide initiatives, including the Personal Income Tax Reduction Fund, the Economic Enhancement Grant Fund and improvements to West Virginia's electric grid. Putnam County's proposed Google development, while smaller in scale, would still generate approximately $40.9 million annually in property tax revenue. Local schools would receive approximately $17.4 million each year, the County Commission more than $8.2 million, and Fire and EMS services approximately $1.6 million, with additional revenues supporting statewide priorities. Combined, these projects are projected to generate more than $272 million in annual property tax revenues. For Mason County schools alone, the projected annual distribution exceeds $90 million. Putnam County schools stand to receive more than $17 million annually. These are investments in classrooms, teachers, educational technology, facilities, and opportunities for future generations. County governments would gain resources that could strengthen emergency services, improve infrastructure, address deferred maintenance, expand recreational opportunities and better prepare for future growth. Perhaps most importantly, this revenue stream is not a one-time payment or a temporary grant. It is generated year after year for as long as the facilities remain in operation. This is no longer simply a discussion about technology projects or industrial development. It is a discussion about whether West Virginia can position itself to capture the benefits of one of the fastest-growing sectors of the modern economy. Reasonable questions should be asked. Citizens deserve transparency. Public officials should be held accountable for the decisions they make. Those principles are fundamental to good government and responsible economic development. At the same time, it is important to recognize opportunity when it appears. Years from now, the success of these projects will not be judged by the size of the facilities or the sophistication of the technology they contain. They will be judged by whether they helped build stronger schools, safer communities, better public services, greater economic opportunity, and a higher quality of life for the people who call Mason and Putnam Counties home. That is the true promise of this moment. It is a once-in-a-generation opportunity, and one worthy of thoughtful consideration. Clark S. Barnes, of Scott Depot, is a former state senator and president of the Heritage Hills Development Corporation.

artigo.texto: Data center estaria em trâmite na ONS Mapa traz data center anunciado há quase 2 anos para Maringá, mas ministério não registra criação de ZPE Embora não seja apareça publicamente com o pedido de criação de uma Zona de Processamento de Exportação, no Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços, Maringá consta do Mapa da ONS – Mapa de Datacenters do Brasil do Maravalley, comunidade que mostra a distribuição dos datacenters em operação, construção e planejamento no país. Para se implantar um datacenter é necessário ter uma ZPE, criada mediante edição de decreto presidencial após terem tido seus projetos aprovados pelo Conselho Nacional das Zonas de Processamento de Exportação (CZPE). Até julho não havia nenhum pedido protocolizado no MDIC. A informação no mapa é que, ao lado de outros 17 projetos, foi encaminhado ao Pnast (Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão) e está sob análise do ONS – Operacionador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico. No site não possível constatar a existência do protocolo. Hoje no país são quatro ZPEs ativas: Pecém (PE), Paranaíba (PI), Cáceres (MT) e Uberaba (MG), e outras em instalação: Açu (RJ), Aracruz (ES), Araguaína (TO), Bacabeira (MA), Barcarena (PA), Bataguassu (MS), Imbituba (SC), Senador Guiomard (AC) e Suape (PE). Em 23 de janeiro do ano passado o prefeito Silvio Barros (PP) anunciou que Maringá tinha iniciado à tramitação junto ao governo federal para a criação de uma ZPE, que abrigaria o maior data center de inteligência artificial da América Latina, em parceria com a RT-One, que anunciou recentemente a implantação modular e poderá alcançar capacidade de até 400 megawatts (MW) para equipamentos de tecnologia. A empresa informou que o investimento será de R$ 6 bilhões e que adotará sistema direct-to-chip em circuito fechado (resfriamento líquido). A expansão acelerada dos grandes data centers (especialmente voltados para IA) gerou uma forte polêmica em torno do consumo de energia e recursos naturais. Os servidores funcionam 24 horas por dia e exigem uma quantidade colossal de eletricidade, comparável ao consumo de grandes cidades ou a centenas de milhares de residências por unidade. Além disso, pode impactar na conta de luz, dada a expectativa de que o consumo gere escassez. Além da eletricidade, os sistemas de resfriamento consomem grandes volumes de água e geram ilhas de calor e poluição sonora nas comunidades vizinhas. Oficiamente, o governo federal presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defendeu que a energia “do povo” não deve subsidiar ou ser consumida por essas grandes infraestruturas estrangeiras, sugerindo condicionar a instalação de data centers à autoprodução de energia (como geração própria ou contratos específicos). A recente vitória dos democratas nos Esta Unidos fez investidores das bolsas da Europa ponderarem sobre as incertezas relacionadas ao futuro da inteligência artificial e dos data centers. artigo.texto: Just 400 hyperscale data centers connected in the US used as much electricity as the state of Michigan in a single year, new Harvard research has found. The study, published Monday in Nature Sustainability, also finds that the majority of that electricity was generated using fossil fuels, and data center emissions are three times higher than they were before the AI boom. Federal and state governments do not track data center use separate from the rest of the power sector, despite mounting projections that data centers are putting serious strain on the American power grid. Individual data centers’ power use is often considered proprietary business information, and data center operators and utilities do not have to disclose specific numbers to the public. The Harvard study specifically focuses on hyperscale data centers—the largest types of facilities, which have become flashpoints in community opposition across the country. While often used for AI inference or training, not all of the hyperscalers surveyed in this study are being used for AI. “Hyperscalers have been growing fast, even before the AI boom,” says Jon Koomey, an energy researcher who was not a part of the study. To assemble their dataset, the Harvard researchers put together a list of 403 hyperscale data centers around the country that were operational between May 2024 and April 2025 using a mix of industry research and satellite data. The team then modeled these facilities’ energy use in a variety of scenarios and calculated the energy mix of the regional grids to estimate individual facilities’ carbon emissions. Not all regions were created equal: Data centers in Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa—the first of which is home to Data Center Alley—were responsible for more than 50 percent of the energy use in the study. “Knowing for certain data centers how much they use over a year is a really useful thing,” says Koomey, who notes that a peer-reviewed study is more rigorous than some back-of-the envelope calculations. Koomey has been involved in a regular report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory since 2007 that approximates the energy and water use of the industry. “Sometimes we know it, but sometimes it’s behind an NDA, and no one ever sees it.” While based on recent data, the study may already be outdated—a reflection of how fast the data center industry is moving. The average size of a facility in the new study is 40 megawatts, which is relatively small compared to some of the data centers under development today. Developers are building campuses that are hundreds or even thousands of megawatts, and there are proposals for still larger data centers. “Some of the massive campuses being proposed today are substantially larger than the typical facility in our dataset,” says Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral research fellow at Harvard’s T. H. Chan School of Public Health and the lead author of the study. The study also does not look at developers who choose to build power plants onsite, known as behind-the-meter power—a factor Koomey calls a “wild card” in accurately assessing total data center power use. Plans for behind-the-meter power generation have skyrocketed at proposed data center sites across the US over the past year, with as many as 189 gigawatts in the pipeline earmarked for data centers alone. Many of these plants rely increasingly on inefficient natural gas turbines. BloombergNEF estimated last week that if all of the behind-the-meter power plants in the development queue in the US get built, it could increase overall US emissions by 10 percent. While the federal government hasn’t tracked data center energy use to date, that could change soon, and it could be a boon to researchers and the public. The Energy Information Agency, the arm of the federal government that tracks energy use across various sectors, conducted three pilot surveys of data center power use across 10 states this year. Those pilot surveys are now complete, EIA spokesperson Lee Tucker tells WIRED, and the agency is currently using them to design a potential voluntary survey for the sector.

artigo.texto: By Hervé Jeannin, co-rapporteur for the EESC opinion on the potential of the sodium battery manufacturing sector Europe’s energy transition requires an industrial base capable of delivering it. Batteries power electric mobility, facilitate the integration of renewable electricity and help households and businesses manage their energy consumption. Our ability to manufacture them will shape Europe’s competitiveness and energy security. Yet intense international competition and dependencies on materials, components and equipment are weakening this essential industry. As co-rapporteur for the European Economic and Social Committee’s opinion on sodium battery manufacturing, I am convinced that sodium technologies offer a tangible opportunity to strengthen Europe’s capabilities while making better use of its own resources. Beyond lithium: what makes sodium batteries different? Today, lithium-ion batteries dominate the global market, powering everything from smartphones to electric vehicles and energy storage systems. Their production is heavily concentrated in Asia, particularly China, which leads in battery manufacturing and the processing of key materials. Sodium-ion batteries offer an emerging alternative: they use sodium instead of lithium, reducing reliance on certain critical raw materials. Although they generally store less energy for the same weight, they could be cheaper to produce and are particularly promising for stationary energy storage and more affordable electric vehicles. China is already investing heavily in this technology, making it essential for Europe to develop its own manufacturing capacity before another strategic dependency takes hold. Sodium batteries: an opportunity for Europe Sodium is abundant in Europe. Suitable battery chemistries can reduce dependence on lithium, cobalt and nickel, while the hard carbon used for anodes can be derived from wood or agricultural waste. The EESC highlights the possibility of producing sodium batteries entirely from European raw materials. Turning this potential into strategic autonomy requires European capabilities across the entire value chain, from processing to recycling, and, above all, strong political commitment to driving the development of European solutions encompassing both raw materials and manufacturers. Sodium should complement lithium-ion technologies. Each application calls for a different balance between energy density, cost, safety and durability. Sodium-ion batteries generally have slightly lower energy density, but weight and size matter less for stationary storage than for electric vehicles. Storing renewable electricity for households, businesses and grids therefore represents a particularly relevant market opportunity. Public support must reflect technological maturity. Sodium-ion batteries offer prospects for deployment in the nearer term; sodium–saltwater systems require further research, particularly into solid electrolytes, to explore their potential for marine applications and longer-term storage. Our opinion also identifies the possibility of using sodium recovered from desalination by-products, linking water resilience to energy storage, subject to technical and environmental assessment. From innovation to industrial production The immediate challenge is industrial scale-up. A laboratory breakthrough alone does not create a competitive factory. Companies must demonstrate the reliability of their solutions, secure customers and finance production equipment. Small businesses often struggle to shoulder these risks. The EESC therefore calls for an updated industrial roadmap for lithium and sodium batteries, coordinated by the European Battery Alliance, with targeted investment support and cooperation with research and technology organisations. Investing in Europe’s battery industry The EESC’s opinion on the Battery Booster strategy makes a specific request: broaden funding to cover chemistries beyond lithium and explicitly include sodium. Support should reach SMEs, suppliers and recyclers alongside cell manufacturers, and should not be limited to electric vehicles. Critical chemicals, electrolytes and European-made machinery also deserve investment. Dependence on imported inputs and equipment leaves vulnerabilities that building more cell factories alone cannot resolve. Affordable energy, predictable permitting procedures and timely funding are essential. The EESC calls for stronger and better-targeted funding for the Battery Booster strategy in the next EU Budget. Our opinion on sodium advocates an overall budget of at least EUR 220 billion for FP10. International cooperation must help build lasting European expertise. Both opinions call for technology transfer; the Battery Booster opinion recommends making state aid, public procurement and subsidies conditional on technology transfer and local content. Investment must strengthen European research (80% of current projects are not launched for lack of funding in Europe), skills and suppliers, while ensuring that requirements for products entering the EU market are applied fairly. Sustainability, jobs and regional development Circularity must be built in from the outset. Ecodesign should facilitate disassembly and materials recovery, while production should minimise energy consumption and the use of hazardous substances. Recycling requires economically viable facilities, harmonised collection and the efficient transport of used batteries to authorised facilities within the single market. Materials recovery capacity must grow in step with production. Industrial ambition must also benefit workers and regions. The Battery Booster opinion makes job quality and compliance with EU standards conditions for public support. Adequate staffing, training, investment in prevention and effective inspections are essential. Workers must be involved in identifying risks arising from new processes. artigo.texto: On November 12, 2026, the Federal Reserve Board published a comprehensive Finance and Economics Discussion Series working paper documenting that while U.S. capital commitments for artificial intelligence data centers have surged past $1 trillion, aggregate macroeconomic productivity gains and labor market disruptions remain muted. For university research leaders, economics scholars, and facility directors, the empirical findings highlight severe upstream hardware inflation, substantial import leakage, and mounting compute procurement pressures across higher education. FEDS 2026-074: Quantifying the Capital Boom in Artificial Intelligence Authored by Federal Reserve Board economists Nick Carollo, Leland D. Crane, Daniel Garcia Molina, and Joseph Nichols, working paper FEDS 2026-074—titled Artificial Intelligence and the U.S. Economy: Current Evidence (DOI: 10.17016/FEDS.2026.074)—evaluates how generative AI infrastructure is rippling through national accounts. Crucially, this working paper investigates real macroeconomic variables, capital accumulation, and industry output, keeping its analysis distinct from the central bank’s semi-annual Federal Reserve Financial Stability Report, which focused on debt liquidity and bank credit exposures. The paper documents a massive escalation in planned domestic data-center construction, which climbed from roughly $300 billion in 2024 to more than $1 trillion in announced pipelines by 2025. Applying the project forecasting methodology from Brandsaas et al. (2025), the authors estimate that baseline annual data-center investment will step up from $100 billion in 2024 to over $880 billion by the end of 2027, exceeding 2.0% of U.S. GDP. Approximately one-third of this outlay funds physical structures, while two-thirds is absorbed by high-tech equipment including GPUs, TPUs, high-density memory, and server cooling systems. Data-Center Capex Projections, Import Leakage, and Component Inflation The pace of data-center capital deployment has generated distinct supply-chain pressures and macroeconomic offsets. Key benchmarks established in FEDS 2026-074 include: Crucially, Carollo and colleagues calculate an import share of roughly 50% for high-tech compute hardware, with components primarily sourced from East Asian fabrication and packaging corridors. Because imported equipment enters national accounts as a deduction, this substantial leakage moderates the direct domestic output multiplier. Concurrently, direct inputs like high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and specialized printed circuit boards experienced annualized price increases of nearly 8% through early 2026, reversing a multi-decade trend of technological price deflation. Surging electricity requirements also prompted a sharp rise in power-generation interconnection requests in late 2025. These local infrastructure dynamics align with NBER research by Alvarez et al. (2026), which shows that data centers generate brief construction bursts but minimal long-term local employment. The Solow Productivity Paradox in the Generative Era Despite heavy capital commitments, FEDS 2026-074 finds that generative AI has yielded negligible measurable impact on aggregate U.S. labor productivity and Total Factor Productivity (TFP). Addressing this gap on November 13, 2026, at the UC San Diego Economics Roundtable, Federal Reserve Board Vice Chair Philip N. Jefferson delivered a keynote address titled New Technology, Old Questions: Productivity Puzzles and the Macroeconomy. Jefferson invoked Robert Solow’s famous 1987 paradox that ‘you can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics.’ Jefferson noted that early personal computer investment in the late 1980s required more than a decade of organizational adaptation before aggregate productivity accelerated. Econometric decomposition in FEDS 2026-074 indicates that recent post-2023 productivity pickups primarily reflect cyclical supply-chain normalization rather than AI diffusion. Furthermore, the authors review growth literature: Daron Acemoglu (2025) estimates cumulative TFP gains of only 0.7% over the next decade, while optimistic projections by Filippucci et al. (2025) reach 0.3 to 0.9 percentage points annually. Task-level studies by Jones and Tonetti (2026) and Demirer, Musolff, and Yang (2026) confirm that coding agents accelerate syntax generation, but software deployment remains tightly bounded by human review and integration testing. Federal Reserve Leadership Perspectives: Barr and Waller on Labor and Inequality Central bank governors expanded on these macroeconomic themes during November 2026 addresses. On November 12 at Yale University, Governor Michael S. Barr presented remarks on American Inequality and the Future of AI, analyzing findings from the Federal Reserve’s 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances. Barr warned that because AI infrastructure requires massive capital reserves, financial gains are heavily concentrated among top software firms and high-wealth equity holders, raising distributional risks if routine entry-level cognitive tasks face wage erosion. Conversely, Governor Christopher J. Waller emphasized labor resilience in his November 10 speech at the Bank of England Watchers Conference on The Economic Outlook and Some Thoughts on Labor Market Dynamism. Waller noted that aggregate claims, vacancies, and payrolls show no sign of widespread displacement. This stability is corroborated by New York Fed research (Abel et al., 2025) and independent market analysis from TradingView, which report that only ~10% of workers use AI daily, with firms primarily augmenting existing roles rather than reducing headcounts. artigo.texto: Data centers precisam se conectar às comunidades Sustentabilidade significa ir além da eficiência energética, passando pela otimização de múltiplos recursos e pela criação de impacto positivo para as comunidades que abrigam esses edifícios, avalia Ana Cunha, da Deerns Por Ana Cunha* – A expansão da IA mudou a forma como projetamos e operamos data centers. Com o aumento da densidade e potência dos racks e da demanda por capacidade computacional, questões como energia, água, resfriamento, disponibilidade de rede, emissões e adaptação tecnológica deixam de ser questões isoladas e passam a fazer parte de uma mesma equação que define estrategicamente o valor do ativo “data center” e até a viabilidade do seu licenciamento (permiting) técnico e social. Nesse cenário, falar em sustentabilidade significa ir além da eficiência energética, passando pela otimização de múltiplos recursos e pela criação de impacto positivo, especialmente para as comunidades que abrigam esses edifícios. Torna-se prioritário compreender como diferentes dimensões ambientais, técnicas, regulatórias e sociais se relacionam e como afetam a resiliência e o valor do ativo no longo prazo. Uma mudança que já é perceptível na Europa. Obrigações de reporte e instrumentos como a Taxonomia Europeia, a EED (Diretiva da Eficiência Energética) e a CSRD (Diretiva europeia sobre Relatórios de Sustentabilidade Corporativa) aproximam cada vez mais o desempenho de sustentabilidade das decisões de financiamento, investimento e de relacionamento ou captação de clientes. Sustentabilidade deixa, assim, de ser apenas uma agenda de conformidade e passa a integrar a equação econômica do empreendimento e de aceitação social na fase de licenciamento. Indicadores de desempenho sustentável e operacional também podem influenciar a avaliação de risco econômico e reputacional, a atratividade do ativo e o acesso a instrumentos de financiamento, tão importantes na fase atual de capital “caro”. Isso não significa que o Brasil deva reproduzir o modelo europeu. Os mercados partem de condições diferentes, mas os clientes de data centers de grande escala são cada vez mais internacionais e buscam otimizar práticas, indicadores e valor. A Europa possui um ambiente regulatório mais maduro e enfrenta restrições importantes relacionadas à água, à energia renovável e à capacidade (ou saturação) da rede. O Brasil, por sua vez, conta com uma matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável e vive uma fase de expansão da infraestrutura digital. O ponto de convergência entre eles está na relação entre sustentabilidade e capital. Enquanto o mercado europeu utiliza critérios de desempenho e mecanismos financeiros cada vez mais associados à sustentabilidade, o Brasil pode combinar suas características energéticas com mecanismos fiscais para estimular novos investimentos. O Redata se insere nesse contexto como parte de uma nova equação para a expansão da infraestrutura digital brasileira, embora seus efeitos concretos devam ser avaliados à medida que o mecanismo avance. Mas existe um risco em transformar essa discussão em uma competição por indicadores. O PUE (Eficácia no Uso de Energia) continua sendo uma métrica fundamental para avaliar a eficiência energética de um data center, mas nenhum indicador isolado conta toda a história. Muitas vezes uma solução pode melhorar o PUE e piorar o WUE (Eficácia no Uso de Água); outra pode otimizar o consumo energético e, ao mesmo tempo, dificultar o reaproveitamento do calor residual. Além de que um local energeticamente eficiente ainda pode operar com energia não renovável tendo assim um fraco REF (Fator de Energia Renovável). É por isso que precisamos de uma abordagem sistêmica e multicritérios refletida desde as fases preliminares. Uma decisão de engenharia e de consultoria estratégica de sustentabilidade produz efeitos em diferentes dimensões do projeto, que precisam ser consideradas não só desde a concepção do ativo, mas até mesmo desde a seleção do terreno. Essa visão ganha ainda mais importância diante da inteligência artificial. Um data center preparado para cargas convencionais de cloud não necessariamente terá as mesmas características de uma instalação voltada para cargas de IA. A maior densidade de potência exige novas estratégias e tecnologias de resfriamento e modifica requisitos de infraestrutura. Por isso, a sustentabilidade começa antes do primeiro megawatt. A escolha do terreno, a disponibilidade de energia e água, os riscos climáticos, a arquitetura, o sistema de resfriamento, a possibilidade de reutilização de calor e a capacidade de adaptação futura precisam fazer parte das primeiras decisões. Inovação, porém, não significa simplesmente adotar a tecnologia mais nova. Em infraestrutura crítica, novas soluções precisam ser acompanhadas de segurança operacional e gestão de riscos. A experiência técnica é fundamental para avaliar sua aplicabilidade e integrá-las ao projeto sem dissociar sustentabilidade de funcionalidade, resiliência e custo total de propriedade (“Total Cost of Ownership”). Há ainda uma dimensão que muitas vezes fica fora das discussões predominantemente técnicas que é o território. Um data center não existe isoladamente, pois depende de energia, conectividade, fornecedores, trabalhadores e serviços. Sua implantação também pode gerar impactos sobre a região, e questões como ruído, impacto visual, demanda por água e energia ou ausência de benefícios locais podem comprometer a aceitação do projeto. Por outro lado, a infraestrutura digital também pode contribuir para o desenvolvimento desse local. Reaproveitamento de calor, capacitação profissional, contratação local, conectividade e integração com outros edifícios e sistemas urbanos podem criar benefícios que ultrapassam os limites físicos do data center. É na fase inicial, desde a seleção do terreno, que podem ser identificar as oportunidades de sinergias entre o data center e o território onde será instalado. artigo.texto: A new international platform, named the Global Energy Storage Alliance (GESA), aimed at enhancing cooperation on energy storage was launched at the China Pavilion during COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye. The GESA initiative was established through the joint efforts of the China Energy Storage Alliance (CNESA), China Southern Power Grid Energy Storage Co. and the China Renewable Energy Engineering Institute (CREEI), together with additional industry stakeholders. Discover B2B Marketing That Performs Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms. The alliance seeks to address the role of energy storage in power-system flexibility and renewable energy integration as countries accelerate their adoption of clean energy sources. Senior officials attending the launch included Li Gao, China’s Vice Minister of the Ministry of Ecology and Environment, and Xiong Minfeng, Deputy Director-General of the Department of International Cooperation of the National Energy Administration of China. Also present were Francesco La Camera, Director-General of the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), and Selwin Hart, Special Adviser to the UN Secretary-General on Climate Action and Just Transition. The event took place during a side meeting focused on digital-intelligent innovation and green electricity. GESA was introduced amid mounting challenges faced by the sector, such as energy security concerns, varying technical standards across countries, and gaps in financing and business models, particularly in emerging markets. CREEI International Cooperation Department director, lead scientist and director-general assistant Dr Jiang Hao, stated that the initiative aims to promote large-scale, diversified, and innovation-driven energy storage around the world. The goal is to position storage as a central part of new power systems through international collaboration and support the global energy transition and climate efforts. CNESA secretary-general Liu Wei outlined six priority areas for GESA: facilitating global dialogue, developing databases and standards, advancing technology deployment, fostering business model innovation, enhancing supply-chain coordination, and supporting investment and project cooperation. According to Liu, GESA is intended to serve as an open and inclusive platform for cooperation. China Southern Power Grid Energy Storage Co. deputy general manager Sun Liqun highlighted the evolution of energy storage, identifying challenges such as fragmented standards and difficulties in project development and remuneration. He pointed to gaps in short- and long-duration remuneration, as well as obstacles in financing and business models. Representatives from organisations including Acwa, EVE Energy, the International Hydropower Association, Trina Solar, the Long Duration Energy Storage Council, and the World Resources Institute also attended the launch. The alliance is inviting further participation from industry associations, research institutions, companies, and international bodies worldwide. Recently, at COP31, leaders from Africa and Europe called for greater investment in clean energy and manufacturing to help turn Africa’s renewable resources and critical minerals into jobs and industrial development.

artigo.texto: Support WBUR Kraft-backed data center proposal met with opposition from Sutton residents Residents in Sutton, Massachusetts expressed outrage at a planning board meeting Monday over a proposal to build $16 billion data center campus in their town. The proposed project is backed by The Kraft Group, which owns the New England Patriots. The data center campus would span 10 buildings and draw 900 megawatts of electricity, according to a town memorandum on the project. If built, it would be the among largest data centers in the country. Because the town currently has no zoning laws related to data centers, Sutton’s planning board is exploring options to add a bylaw for data centers to be built in the town. Town officials said at the meeting that the campus would bring in nearly $28 million in tax revenue each year, which could lower the tax bill of an average single-family home and help close the town’s growing budget deficit. But residents in attendance said they are worried about the data center’s impact on the environment, public health and home values. Shawn Buzzell, who has lived in Sutton for three years, stood outside the town hall collecting signatures on a petition before the meeting. He said the petition, which had more than 300 signatures as of Monday night, calls for a special town meeting for residents to vote on the petition’s definition of data centers and prohibit their construction in Sutton. He said he’s against the proposed data center because he’s concerned that it will put residents at risk of higher electricity costs and noise pollution. “They’re sticking them in the middle of people’s neighborhoods,” Buzzell said. “They wedge these in there and it’s not because it’s the right place to put it, it’s because it’s the cheapest place to put it. They end up ruining a lot of people’s lives, destroying quality of life, destroying household resale value, just so they can make themselves a little bit more extra money, and that’s not fair.” Crystal Smith, a Sutton resident for 15 years, said she has been following the news about data centers, but never expected one to be built in the “tiny town” of Sutton. “We don’t have the space for that, we don’t have the resources for that and it would impact way too many things here,” Smith said. About 75 residents attended Monday night’s planning board meeting. Some held signs that read, “NO DATA CENTERS” and “NO DATA CENTERS IN SUTTON.” Others chimed in during the meeting, voicing their disapproval of the project. WBUR reached out to The Kraft Group for comment, but did not receive a response in time for publication. In a memorandum outlining the project, the town said the proposal is tentative. Applications with the town have yet to be filed and "important details on power, water, equipment and site impacts are still to come," the memo reads. Gov. Maura Healey signed an executive order in September requiring data center projects to get local approval before they can obtain state permits. Under the order, data center projects are also required develop energy resources to support their operation or to create a "Ratepayer Protection Fund" if they can't supply their own power infrastructure. The proposed data center would draw 900 megawatts of power, roughly the amount of electricity required to power 450,000 homes.

artigo.texto: Rare look inside Port Washington's $15M AI data center project drawing mixed reactions A $15 million AI data center project in Port Washington, developed by Vantage in partnership with Oracle and OpenAI, is under construction and drawing both community curiosity and criticism. 12 News got a rare look inside one of the largest AI data centers in the country. Get an exclusive look behind-the-scenes in the video player above. The 672-acre site, with an additional 1,000 acres reserved for expansion, is larger than the entire Village of Whitefish Bay. The construction site sees 3,500 workers daily, and Port Washington Mayor Ted Neitzke has been leading van tours of the site to engage locals and address concerns. “Our restaurants are thriving, and our bars are thriving, and our hotels are thriving, and our downtown businesses are thriving,” Neitzke said during one of the tours. The project The first phase of the project includes four data center buildings, each with a footprint large enough to hold two Lambeau Fields. “This is one of the four data center buildings being built here. 800 thousand square feet each,” Neitzke said. “It’s comparable to other data centers that are being built across the country. But definitely as someone who has been in construction for a large part of my life, this is definitely fantastic to watch and build,” he added. Vantage says the center will be operational by early 2028, providing internet and cloud services while storing, processing, and distributing data. “Almost everything you’re seeing here is manufactured, made, or fabricated here in Wisconsin. So it’s not just a Port Washington thing. It’s statewide,” Neitzke said. The project is expected to bring significant tax benefits to the community, transforming agriculturally zoned land assessed at a few million dollars into a site valued at $120 million. This increase is anticipated to support the majority of city services for Port Washington. Responses after tour Tour participants shared their impressions of the project. “It’s really something else,” one attendee said. “I didn’t know what the Vantage Center was really for. And now I know a lot more, so that’s good,” another participant said. When asked if they thought the project was positive for the area, they replied, “Sure. Sure.” Al Poull, whose family has lived on a nearby farm for 126 years, acknowledged the changes brought by the project. “Things change, you know? It’s just the way it is,” Poull said. Criticism Despite the enthusiasm from some locals, the project has faced criticism and opposition. One contentious meeting resulted in the arrest of three women. Clean Wisconsin and other groups have raised concerns about the environmental impact of AI data centers and the power plants required to support them. Video below: Data center dust and noise fight continues near Port Washington “Wisconsin is incredibly vulnerable right now to AI data centers,” a Clean Wisconsin representative said. “When you have something as large as what’s going on in Port Washington, that will be vastly bigger in terms of energy needs than anything Wisconsin has ever seen before, where so much has to be given to that, these are resources we all rely on. That needs to be a conversation that needs to happen well before right now when the construction is going on and it’s almost done,” the representative added. Neitzke acknowledged the unexpected backlash. “Surprised? Yes. Caught off guard is probably the better way to describe it. Did not see that coming,” he said. Transparency The mayor has emphasized transparency during the tours, addressing concerns about water usage, power supply, and electricity rates. “It does not use a lot of water. Power is protected, your electricity rates do not go up,” Neitzke said. He believes the data center is a transformative project for the community. “I really believe that data centers are the newest of all the utilities. And a utility is something everyone needs, right? Clean water, clean sidewalks, electricity, and now information,” Neitzke said. Neitzke has also been advising elected officials across the country on how to navigate similar projects. “Right now, local communities are in an amazing position to negotiate. And I don’t know why anyone wouldn’t. As you saw out there, I mean, it’s an amazing project,” he said. Construction on the data center began in December 2022 and is scheduled to be completed by 2028.

artigo.texto: Brian Fellon is senior vice president at Xpansiv, a market platform for energy and environmental commodities. Winter Storm Fern hit Texas in January 2026 with extreme cold and hazardous precipitation. But unlike Winter Storm Uri in 2021, the lights stayed on. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas’ post-event report captured how the grid remained intact without Energy Emergency Alerts, public conservation calls or systemwide outages. During Fern, ERCOT’s battery energy storage resources were indispensable for covering peak-demand reserves, while all resource types contributed to meeting broader system demand. The critical lesson is that grid performance is highly dependent on coordinating nascent technologies and real-time operations with legacy generation assets. That lesson is now being tested at scale across the country. The U.S. electricity sector is undergoing its most abrupt transformation since deregulation. After nearly two decades of flat demand, load growth is accelerating from data centers, transportation and industrial electrification. The forward demand curve has never been this steep, and ERCOT's long-range planning assumptions contemplate peak load reaching more than four times today’s record levels. Across the PJM Interconnection footprint, forecasted load growth is raising expectations that tens of gigawatts of new supply may be needed over the coming decade to maintain system reliability. This demand jump is colliding with aging grid infrastructure, constrained transmission, record-long interconnection queues and a shifting policy landscape. These factors are reconfiguring wholesale power markets and revaluing baseload and dispatchable generation, while establishing battery storage as essential grid infrastructure. Batteries are often described as a foundational solution because they respond instantly, start and stop without thermal plants’ mechanical constraints, and uniquely shift energy from off-peak to on-peak periods. In practice, the grid does not simply benefit from batteries as fixed capacity in the conventional sense. It benefits from dynamic, flexible battery storage systems that are specifically configured to accelerate responsiveness, along with the telemetry, data feeds, market interfaces and 24/7 readiness required to perform under normal and stressed conditions alike. That distinction matters as storage scales, owners compete for arbitrage opportunities and electricity markets evolve. In organized wholesale markets, dispatch is not a single daily event. It’s a sequence of day-ahead scheduling, intraday adjustments and real-time dispatch, translated into 5-minute price intervals. For chemically-constrained assets like batteries, timelines are crucial because spot market decisions are inseparable from current and future state-of-charge, known as SoC. Every megawatt discharged at a given time affects what can be delivered later. Fortunately, policy and market design are adapting to support this reality. FERC’s Order No. 841 requires ISOs/RTOs to remove barriers to storage participation and adopt participation models that recognize storage’s physical and operational characteristics. That mandate expanded the range of products storage can provide, with more options for revenue production. Although not governed by FERC, ERCOT went even further than Order 841. In December 2025, ERCOT implemented Real-Time Co-optimization Plus Batteries (RTC+B), which co-optimizes energy and reserves in real time while accounting for what battery resources can actually deliver. One month later, during Winter Storm Fern, ERCOT credited RTC+B with helping redistribute ancillary services across the system during a localized transmission emergency. The same change that helped ERCOT lean on batteries during Fern also changed how those batteries earn revenue. As these rules open new ways for storage to participate, the mix of market products that pay off keeps shifting. The new paradigm, and what’s needed Market participants and grid operators need timely, accurate information about what a battery can deliver under variable constraints. Unreliable data or inconsistent operations aren’t theoretical problems, because they show up directly in project economics after commercial operations begin. Similarly, optimization only creates value if it’s converted into timely, accurate and compliant market submissions. There has never been a greater need for validated bid and offer workflows, automated checks against asset constraints and market rules, reliable ISO/RTO connectivity, clear audit trails, and the ability to rapidly adjust trades as forecasts, prices, outages and SoC conditions change. The same need for accuracy and coordination extends into real-time operations. Wholesale markets and grid conditions don’t simply pause at 5 p.m. when the workday ends for most electricity consumers. Scarcity pricing, forced outages and weather disruptions often happen during off-hours. Sophisticated storage operators utilize defined escalation pathways, telemetry monitoring and situational awareness tools to coordinate instantly when grid conditions require immediate support. A practical checklist for battery owners and operators includes: - Treat data and telemetry as mission-critical infrastructure. Validate data quality and latency end-to-end, not just at the device level. - Run multi-market playbooks, not single-product strategies. Markets change; build the adaptive capability to shift with them. - Treat market submission as a core operating capability. Whether built in-house or outsourced, deploy resilient controls, versioned workflows and exception handling. - Operationalize SoC discipline. Establish SoC guardrails tied to existing obligations, revenue targets and forecast uncertainty. Review after-action performance during unforeseen events. ERCOT has shown what adaptive market design can deliver. Other markets should follow. Operators can only do so much on their own. Market rules decide how
