artigo.texto: India's renewable energy ambitions have reached a stage where generating clean electricity is no longer the only challenge. The more difficult task is ensuring that electricity generated during sunny and windy hours remains available when households, industries and businesses need it. With solar and wind capacity expanding rapidly, India faces a fundamental question: how can intermittent renewable energy become a dependable source of round-the-clock electricity?The Union Cabinet's approval of a ₹14,500 crore Viability Gap Funding (VGF) scheme on November 4, 2026, represents a major intervention in addressing this challenge. The programme envisages developing 92 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of grid-scale energy storage capacity between 2026–27 and 2030–31, involving an estimated investment of ₹97,600 crore.Of the proposed capacity, 60 GWh will come from pumped hydro storage projects, 30 GWh from Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), and 2 GWh from emerging storage technologies. The programme also introduces a minimum domestic content requirement of 40% for battery storage projects, reflecting the government's intention to strengthen indigenous manufacturing.The significance of this initiative extends beyond the installation of batteries and storage infrastructure. It represents an attempt to transform the operating architecture of India's electricity system, which has traditionally depended on coal-fired generation to provide reliable power when renewable energy production fluctuates.Solar power generation peaks during daylight hours, while electricity consumption frequently rises in the evening. Wind generation also varies according to weather conditions. Without sufficient storage, renewable electricity may be curtailed during periods of surplus generation, while conventional power plants must compensate when output declines.Battery storage can absorb surplus electricity and release it during peak demand. Pumped hydro storage performs a similar function by using electricity to move water to an elevated reservoir and subsequently releasing it through turbines.Together, these technologies can reduce renewable energy curtailment, improve grid flexibility and limit the need for additional coal-based balancing capacity. However, storage cannot eliminate coal dependence immediately, particularly during prolonged periods of low renewable generation.According to the Ministry of Power, India's grid-scale energy storage requirement is projected to reach 411 GWh by 2031–32. The newly approved programme is therefore an important addition, but it will meet only part of the country's anticipated requirement.A more complex challenge lies in India's dependence on China for battery cells, components and processing technologies. China dominates several critical stages of the global lithium-ion battery supply chain, particularly lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, which are widely used for stationary energy storage because of their cost advantages and durability.According to a May 2026 analysis by the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA), China accounts for approximately 74% of global lithium refining, 80% of cobalt refining and 98% of LFP cathode active material production. India's domestic lithium refining capacity remains negligible, while its battery cell manufacturing industry is still developing.The same analysis estimated that India's advanced chemistry cell battery demand could increase from 28 GWh in 2025 to approximately 272 GWh by FY2030. Despite the government's ₹18,100 crore production-linked incentive programme, only 1.4 GWh of cell manufacturing capacity had been commissioned under the scheme by early 2026.This creates a strategic contradiction. India is investing heavily in renewable energy to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels, but its transition could create another form of external dependence through imported batteries and processed minerals.Assembling battery packs domestically does not necessarily constitute technological self-reliance if the cells, cathodes, anodes, electrolytes and manufacturing equipment continue to come from China. Changing this situation requires coordinated intervention across the entire battery value chain.India must accelerate domestic cell manufacturing while developing facilities for processing lithium, nickel and other critical minerals. The Cabinet's simultaneous approval of a ₹2,814 crore capital-support scheme for critical mineral processing provides an opportunity to connect mineral refining with battery manufacturing.India should also expand long-term mineral supply partnerships with countries such as Australia, Argentina and Chile, encourage Indian companies to acquire overseas mineral assets, and develop recycling facilities capable of recovering valuable materials from used batteries.Equally important is investment in alternative battery technologies, including sodium-ion systems, which could reduce dependence on lithium for some stationary storage applications. Domestic research institutions and manufacturers need sustained support to commercialise these technologies at competitive costs.The Ministry of Heavy Industries has acknowledged that Chinese dominance in technology and mineral processing creates difficulties for Indian manufacturers, including restricted access to some refining technologies. Addressing these constraints will require technology development, international partnerships and a predictable domestic market.Financing presents another major challenge. Battery storage projects require substantial upfront investment, while revenues depend on electricity price differences, storage utilisation, contractual arrangements and the financial health of electricity distribution companies.The VGF scheme can improve project viability by reducing initial capital costs. artigo.texto: Open house event sheds light on proposed battery energy storage system in Sandcut TERRE HAUTE, Ind. (WTWO/WAWV) — Concerned residents from Sandcut got the chance to learn more about a proposed battery energy storage system that could be coming to the area. The event was an open house-style event where people could go from station to station to speak with officials from the NextEra Energy Resources group that is in charge of the proposed project. Taylor Christian is the lead project manager for NextEra Resources, and he mentioned what the battery energy storage system actually is. "Energy storage is essentially a grid reliability mechanism," Christian said. "It stores energy whenever the demand is low and the supply is high. Then it puts that energy back onto the grid whenever you see periods of higher demand and lower supply." Officials said this project is just for energy purposes. "This is not tied to any Vigo County data center or any Vigo County, any other development in Vigo County really. This is an energy source project that we're proposing in Vigo County." Dustin Houser is a resident of Sandcut who came to the open house, and he mentioned that there are several concerns with this proposed project. "The largest concerns that I have are noise pollution, light pollution and environmental concerns," Houser said. "The animals are going to get driven off in our area, which we've had even bald eagles coming back in our area. So, we don't want them to go away." Another concern residents have is the possibility of the batteries catching fire. "When they catch fire," Houser said. "They release a lot of chemicals in the air and they can't put the fire out. They have to let the fire burn out itself. Smoke will linger; there's been reported fires that have lasted up to 17 days, and they have to evacuate the area because of the hazardous materials that are in the air." This is just a proposed project at this time, but Sandcut residents hope changes can be made. "The commissioner's office needs to understand and undo the rezoning that they just did," Houser said. "Residents live out in the country for a reason. We like the quiet. We like the dark. We enjoy looking at the agriculture." Officials with NextEra Energy Resources said this proposed project can bring 175 jobs to the area during construction and millions of dollars in tax revenue to the area. artigo.texto: Saída de Jensen Huang da Nvidia e o risco oculto dos data centers no Brasil A troca de comando na Nvidia não é só questão de liderança. Para o Brasil, que atrai bilhões em data centers, o risco real é a dependência de um único fornecedor de chips. Jensen Huang deixou a presidência da Nvidia em 12 de novembro sem um sucessor definitivo. O mercado reagiu ao fato como uma questão de liderança corporativa. Mas o problema mais relevante está a milhares de quilômetros de Santa Clara: no Brasil, que começa a receber investimentos bilionários em infraestrutura de inteligência artificial, a troca de comando expõe uma fragilidade estrutural que pouca gente está discutindo. A dependência quase total de um único fornecedor de tecnologia transforma qualquer instabilidade na Nvidia em risco financeiro direto para projetos brasileiros. Por que a Nvidia domina os data centers e o que isso significa A Nvidia não vende apenas chips. Ela entrega o pacote completo: processadores de aceleração, servidores, redes de interconexão e o ecossistema de software CUDA, usado por milhões de desenvolvedores no mundo. É como comprar um carro inteiro de um único fabricante, do motor ao sistema de navegação. Para o cliente, isso reduz a complexidade da instalação. Para a Nvidia, cria uma relação de dependência difícil de romper. Essa estratégia deu à empresa uma participação estimada acima de 80% no mercado de chips para treinamento de IA. Os concorrentes existem, como mostram os resultados recentes da AMD no segmento de data centers, mas nenhum se aproxima da escala e da integração que a Nvidia oferece. O lançamento sequencial de gerações como Blackwell e Rubin reforça a vantagem competitiva, e a reserva antecipada de capacidade fabril nas fundições especializadas torna quase impossível para rivais escalarem na mesma velocidade. O custo invisível da dependência tecnológica Para entender o risco brasileiro, é preciso pensar em termos concretos. Um data center de grande porte no Brasil exige centenas de milhões de reais em investimento inicial. Parte desse capital vai para equipamentos Nvidia: servidores com GPUs de última geração, sistemas de rede proprietários e licenças de software. Depois da instalação, trocar de fornecedor significa retreinar equipes, substituir hardware e reescrever código otimizado para CUDA. Economistas chamam isso de custo de mudança de fornecedor, um problema clássico de investimentos em ativos específicos. Projetos como o supercomputador planejado para o Nordeste do Brasil já ilustram essa dinâmica. O investimento é feito em função de uma tecnologia específica, com cronogramas de entrega amarrados ao roadmap de produto da Nvidia. Se a troca de comando alterar prioridades comerciais, atrasar lançamentos ou redirecionar produção para mercados mais lucrativos, o impacto no Brasil é imediato: equipamentos atrasados, custos financeiros correndo sem geração de receita e financiadores exigindo juros mais altos. Essa situação não é hipotética. A tensão geopolítica envolvendo a Nvidia e a China já demonstrou que decisões estratégicas da empresa afetam cadeias de fornecimento globais. Uma mudança de liderança adiciona incerteza a um cenário que já era complexo. O que a manchete não conta: risco financeiro de segunda ordem O problema não se limita ao dono do data center. Ele atinge toda a cadeia de financiamento. Quando um banco ou fundo de investimento financia um projeto de infraestrutura de IA, ele projeta fluxos de caixa para os próximos anos com base em premissas de entrega de equipamentos, vida útil da tecnologia e continuidade do suporte. Qualquer dúvida sobre esses fatores altera o perfil de risco do projeto. Na prática, isso significa que uma transição de liderança na Nvidia pode encarecer o custo de capital de um data center brasileiro mesmo sem nenhuma mudança na economia local. É um canal de transmissão de risco que foge do radar da maioria dos analistas, porque não aparece em indicadores macroeconômicos tradicionais. A Malásia entendeu essa dinâmica ao diversificar suas fontes de investimento em infraestrutura de IA, atraindo tanto empresas americanas quanto chinesas. O Brasil, até aqui, não demonstrou a mesma sofisticação na negociação desses contratos. O melhor argumento contra essa preocupação É justo reconhecer que a Nvidia é maior do que uma pessoa. A empresa tem 30 mil funcionários, uma estrutura de engenharia consolidada e contratos de longo prazo com as maiores empresas do mundo. A saída de um CEO, mesmo um tão identificado com a marca, não significa colapso operacional. A Apple sobreviveu a Steve Jobs. A Microsoft floresceu depois de Bill Gates. Empresas maduras costumam ter resiliência institucional. Além disso, o mercado de chips para IA é tão aquecido que a demanda por GPUs Nvidia continuará superando a oferta independente de quem estiver no comando. Os investimentos globais em data centers já ultrapassaram centenas de bilhões de dólares anuais e seguem acelerando. Esses argumentos são válidos, mas não eliminam o risco de curto e médio prazo. A Nvidia sob Huang tinha uma visão de produto e uma capacidade de execução que eram indissociáveis da figura do fundador. Uma transição mal conduzida pode não destruir a empresa, mas pode criar exatamente o tipo de incerteza que encarece projetos em mercados emergentes como o Brasil. O que o Brasil precisa fazer diferente Atrair investimentos em data centers é necessário, mas não suficiente. O desafio brasileiro é transformar compra de tecnologia em capacidade produtiva autônoma. Isso exige pelo menos três frentes simultâneas. Primeira: negociar contratos de fornecimento de longo prazo com cláusulas de proteção contra atrasos e mudanças estratégicas do fornecedor. Segunda: investir na formação de profissionais brasileiros capazes de operar e adaptar essas tecnologias, reduzindo a dependência do ecossistema proprietário. Terceira: evitar concentração excessiva em um único fornecedor, abrindo espaço para alternativas como AMD, Intel e até chips

artigo.texto: Um estudo publicado na Nature Sustainability estimou que 403 centros de dados hiperescaláveis identificados nos Estados Unidos usaram de 68 a 99 TWh de eletricidade entre maio de 2024 e abril de 2025 — o equivalente a 1,5% a 2,2% do consumo elétrico total do país. A estimativa foi relatada pela Ars Technica e não corresponde apenas a centros de IA: os pesquisadores não conseguiram separar a computação de IA dos serviços tradicionais oferecidos por esses locais. O resultado é uma estimativa modelada, não a soma de leituras diretas de cada instalação. Terawatt-hora (TWh) mede energia consumida ao longo do tempo; megawatt (MW), usado para indicar a capacidade elétrica dos centros, mede potência. Antes de comparar números de consumo de data centers, confira se eles abrangem o mesmo tipo de instalação e o mesmo período. O que a estimativa de consumo dos data centers dos EUA abrange A conta considera 403 centros hiperescaláveis identificados no país durante um período de um ano, de maio de 2024 a abril de 2025. Além de não isolar a carga de IA, a amostra pode incluir instalações que nem sequer são centros de dados de IA. A seleção começou com 675 instalações candidatas. O estudo reteve 403 após excluir locais sem capacidade elétrica informada ou cujas características de construção, refrigeração e conexão elétrica não puderam ser verificadas. Cada centro incluído tinha, em média, cerca de 40 MW de capacidade elétrica; esse valor não é o consumo anual de energia. Emissões estimadas e fontes de eletricidade A Ars Technica relatou que a geração da eletricidade estimada corresponde a 21 milhões a 31 milhões de toneladas de CO₂, cerca de 0,5% das emissões de CO₂ dos EUA provenientes de combustíveis fósseis. Segundo a reportagem, o cálculo considera a intensidade de emissões da geração elétrica na região da rede que atende cada instalação. A estimativa de emissões não inclui a geração de energia no próprio local, fora da rede. A mistura de geração elétrica atribuída aos centros incluídos foi de 54% de fontes fósseis, principalmente gás natural, 25% de fontes renováveis e 21% de energia nuclear. Quais dados do estudo estão disponíveis ao público A página do estudo informa que os dados de cada instalação são restritos por um acordo de uso. Já as exportações agregadas por estado e por autoridade de equilíbrio da rede, além do código de análise, são públicos. Os registros públicos não incluem identificadores, endereços e coordenadas das instalações nem atributos comercialmente sensíveis. A página do estudo na Nature Sustainability descreve esses limites de acesso.

artigo.texto: US Energy Storage Installations Cross 200 GWh: Report Energy storage installations reached 48.3 GWh in 9M of 2026 November 18, 2026 Follow Mercom India on WhatsApp for exclusive updates on clean energy news and insights The U.S. has surpassed 200 GWh of cumulative energy storage installations with 14.3 GWh of energy storage capacity added in the third quarter (Q3) of 2026, according to the U.S. Energy Storage Market Outlook Q4 2026 released by the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. The country’s cumulative storage capacity is expanding as grid operators, and energy buyers increasingly deploy storage to reduce energy costs and strengthen grid reliability. Installations during the first nine months (9M) of 2026 totaled 48.3 GWh. Utility-scale storage accounted for most additions in Q3, with 12.2 GWh deployed. Commercial and industrial storage installations totaled 1.3 GWh, while residential storage additions stood at 746 MWh. The report raised its forecast for cumulative U.S. energy storage deployments by 2030 by 3.7% to 708 GWh across grid-scale and behind-the-meter segments. Texas led utility-scale energy storage deployments through 9M, adding 12.3 GWh. Arizona and California followed, adding 7.7 GWh and 6.8 GWh, respectively. Eleven states surpassed their previous year’s annual energy storage installation records. These were Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama, and Illinois. According to a recent SEIA analysis, the rapid deployment of solar and energy storage contributed to a 42% decline in average wholesale electricity prices in Texas and a 51% decline in California between summer 2021 and summer 2026. Pete Tillotson, Senior Analyst at Benchmark Minerals, noted that states are moving from targets to centralized procurements. Across utility mandates and bulk capacity contracts, energy storage pipelines are growing because of both investment appetite and flexibility requirements. Manufacturing Capacity Battery manufacturing capacity in the U.S. also expanded during the period. A new battery cell manufacturing facility commenced operations in Tennessee in July, followed by another facility in Indiana in October. These additions brought the country’s total battery cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, representing a 50% increase. SEIA also called on the U.S. Congress to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which it said would accelerate energy storage deployment, reduce project costs, and expand access to lower cost and reliable electricity. The U.S. added 4.7 GW/17.2 GWh of utility-scale battery energy storage systems in Q2 2026, taking cumulative operational capacity past the 50 GW milestone, according to the American Clean Power Association. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, more than 16% of the utility-scale solar capacity added in the U.S. through September 2026 was co-located with operational battery storage, compared to just 2% in 2017.

artigo.texto: RWE starts construction of its first battery in Italy Essen/Rome, 10 November 2026 RWE has started construction of its first Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in Italy. The 62,5-megawatts (MW) Ragusa battery will be located in Sicily. It will consist of 42 containers with lithium-ion batteries, being able to deliver its maximum output for 4 hours. This corresponds to a nominal storage capacity of 262,5 megawatt hours (MWh). Commissioning is scheduled for the end of 2027. Sopna Sury, CEO RWE Renewables Europe & Australia, said: The start of construction of our Ragusa battery storage marks an important milestone. ”We have been operating in Italy for many years, using the energy from the wind and the sun. In a world of growing renewable energy, battery storage systems are crucial for stabilising the grid and ensuring that electricity is used when it is needed most. Ragusa battery will be capable of covering the evening peak demand of around 21.000 households for 4 hours. We look forward to establishing further battery storage capacity in Italy soon – in addition to wind and solar power – in order to support Italy in building a resilient energy system.” Ragusa battery will provide balancing energy to stabilise the electricity grid. It also features the technology necessary to provide new grid forming services such as instantaneous reserve (inertia). In addition to the batteries, RWE will build the associated grid infrastructure. This includes a high-voltage transformer to connect to the 150-kV grid. Battery storage at RWE As a driver of the energy transition, RWE develops, builds and operates battery storage systems in the US, Europe and Australia. Globally, RWE currently operates battery storage systems with a total capacity of around 1.7 gigawatts (GW) and 3 GW are under construction. As an integral part of its growth strategy, RWE plans to significantly expand its battery storage capacities worldwide. RWE Renewables Italia – strong presence in Italy’s renewables market RWE is a key player in the Italian renewables market. The company takes an integrated project approach that incorporates the development, construction and operation as well as the marketing of wind farms and solar plants. With 18 onshore wind farms, one photovoltaic plant and three agrivoltaic plants in operation, RWE currently manages a total installed capacity of approximately 670 MW in Italy, enough to supply green electricity to more than 550,000 Italian households. In addition, RWE currently has around 200 MW of further wind and solar capacity under construction in Italy. artigo.texto: Restrições de chips dos EUA ao Brasil afetam data centers O governo dos Estados Unidos, sob a administração de Donald Trump, incluiu o Brasil em uma lista de países que passam a ter restrições para importar chips avançados destinados a data centers. A medida, anunciada pelo Departamento de Comércio, vale mesmo quando os semicondutores são fabricados fora da jurisdição americana. A partir desta segunda-feira (16), fornecedores precisarão de autorização do governo americano para enviar os processadores a empresas brasileiras, com pedidos analisados caso a caso. Além do Brasil, a relação inclui Singapura, Tailândia, Malásia e Indonésia. Segundo a norma, esses países apresentam risco acima do normal de desvio ilegal dos chips para China ou Macau — alvos de embargos junto com Rússia, Irã, Coreia do Norte, Síria e Cuba. O objetivo é evitar que empresas chinesas usem sedes no exterior para treinar modelos de inteligência artificial com uso de chips restritos a Pequim. Risco de desvio para China Os territórios classificados como elevado risco de desvio, assim como o Brasil, abrigam grandes complexos de processamento de dados ligados a big techs orientais, como ByteDance (dona do TikTok), Tencent (dona do WeChat), Alibaba e Huawei. A norma norte-americana exige que empresas dos cinco países solicitem licenças de exportação dos EUA para os chips mais avançados, em um esforço para reduzir o contrabando desses produtos. “A regra foi elaborada para garantir que as restrições existentes ao acesso a tecnologia norte-americana sensível não possam ser contornadas por meio de acordos de computação remota envolvendo data centers em países terceiros”, afirmou o Departamento de Comércio em comunicado. A medida busca fechar brechas que permitiam o uso indireto de tecnologia americana por entidades sob embargo. Prazos e isenções previstos Os produtos já enviados estão isentos das novas normas por 30 dias. Os fornecedores que prestam volume relevante de serviços de computação avançada para o grupo sob embargo têm 90 dias para obter uma licença junto ao Escritório de Indústria e Segurança do Departamento de Comércio. As novas restrições não se aplicarão a sistemas usados por varejistas online e empresas de mídia social, que, segundo o departamento, não representam a mesma ameaça à segurança nacional. Em janeiro de 2025, nos últimos dias do governo Joe Biden, os Estados Unidos já haviam incluído o Brasil em um grupo intermediário de países com acesso limitado a chips avançados de inteligência artificial. A classificação previa cotas para a importação desses componentes. A nova regra amplia o controle, passando de cotas para licenciamento individual. Impacto para o setor de tecnologia A exigência de licenças caso a caso pode afetar a expansão de data centers no Brasil, especialmente aqueles que dependem de chips de última geração para processamento de inteligência artificial. Empresas brasileiras que operam grandes infraestruturas de nuvem e serviços de IA podem enfrentar atrasos e custos adicionais para obter os componentes necessários. O Departamento de Comércio não detalhou os critérios exatos para aprovação das licenças. Para o comércio e a indústria do interior paulista, a medida pode ter efeitos indiretos, uma vez que a digitalização de processos e o uso de serviços em nuvem dependem de data centers eficientes. A disponibilidade limitada de chips avançados pode impactar a oferta de serviços de computação em nuvem no país, com possíveis reflexos em custos para empresas de todos os portes. A fonte não detalhou estimativas de impacto econômico. A decisão americana reforça a tendência de controle tecnológico em um cenário de disputa geopolítica. O Brasil, como destino de investimentos em data centers, terá de se adaptar às novas exigências para manter o fluxo de importação de semicondutores avançados. A medida pode estimular o desenvolvimento de alternativas locais ou a busca por fornecedores de outros países, mas a fonte não detalhou planos nesse sentido. Perguntas Frequentes Por que os EUA incluíram o Brasil na lista de países com restrições para comprar chips para data centers? O Brasil foi incluído porque, segundo a norma, apresenta risco acima do normal de desvio ilegal desses chips para China ou Macau, que são alvos de embargos. Quais outros países estão na lista de restrições dos EUA para compra de chips para data centers? Além do Brasil, a lista inclui Singapura, Tailândia, Malásia e Indonésia. O que os fornecedores precisam fazer para enviar chips avançados para o Brasil a partir de 16 de junho? A partir de 16 de junho, os fornecedores precisarão de autorização do governo americano para enviar processadores avançados a empresas brasileiras, com pedidos analisados caso a caso.

artigo.texto: Berea unanimously passes data center moratorium Year-long measure stops city from accepting, processing or approving data center applications and permits BEREA, Ky. (WKYT) - The city of Berea adopted a year-long data center moratorium by unanimous vote Tuesday night, becoming the latest municipality in Kentucky to adopt some form of data center moratorium. The decision gives the city another year to decide the permanent future of data centers. What the moratorium does During the moratorium, the city will not accept, process or approve data center applications or permits. Public comments before the vote The unanimous vote came after a handful of public comments in which residents raised concerns about draws on resources such as water and power. Council member comments Council member Katie Startzman was one of the driving forces behind the legislation. “I haven’t heard from one person who is in favor of data centers unless they were someone who was a lobbyist for the industry. So I think it’s pretty clear where people stand,” Startzman said. She has seen what surrounding cities and towns have done with their moratoriums and believes they are a tool to more closely study the issue before making a decision that affects residents. She said the entire council was in agreement on that. “This was not something that was challenging for us to come to consensus on. I think we all pretty immediately agreed that data centers have no place in Berea,” Startzman said. Advocate reaction Katie Dapkus has been advocating against data centers across central Kentucky. She is optimistic seeing other cities adopt similar moratoriums. “I think it’s sort of a domino effect. All of our elected officials are being lobbied hard, but the people were sort of left in the lurch, and I think people are collectively waking up to what’s happening and demanding more from our leadership,” Dapkus said. What’s next One sitting council member said he hopes the next council is bold enough to enact a complete ban if that is what Berea residents want to see. The future of data centers in the city has yet to be determined. Other communities with regulations Berea joined nearby towns and cities, including London, Nicholasville, Versailles and Winchester, that have some form of data center regulations in place. Woodford County is the only county in the area to enact a total ban. Copyright 2026 WKYT. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: A recent report compiled by the Environmental Integrity Project found, to quote from coverage of the report in The Guardian by Tom Perkins, “Data centers are spurring a boom in fossil fuel pipeline projects at a time when the Trump administration is gutting rules that protect from disasters along the lines.” A federal records review completed as part of the report identified 200 pipeline projects that are proposed or in the works, which would collectively span some 17,000 miles. The pipelines would help serve at least 98 gas-fired power plants meant to serve data centers. If all lines are completed, they would carry about 40% more natural gas daily than what the existing system carries. The U.S. already records about 1.7 pipeline accidents, spills, fires or explosions per day, according to data from the U.S. Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration, which is housed within the U.S. Department of Transportation. “The pipelines could also destroy thousands of acres of federally protected wetlands,” Perkins continues. “At least 81 of the projects are expected to damage more than 19,000 acres of federal protected wetlands, the report found. This also comes as the Trump administration attempts to strip 94% of federal wetland protections.” Gov. Patrick Morrisey has just announced that Appalachian Power will commit $17 billion to building three new natural gas-fired plants in the state, expected to be operational by 2031, and $7.5 billion to upgrade its coal-fired plants in the state through 2050. Meanwhile, according to a piece in The Guardian by Oliver Millman, the nonprofit institute Climate Action Tracker has found that “The world is heading for an ‘irrevocable overshoot’ of global temperature thresholds that will plunge billions of people into disastrous climate impacts because governments have stalled for so long to cut planet-heating emissions.” An analysis by the Environmental Defense Fund recently found that the Trump administration handed out $950 million in taxpayer dollars to 24 coal plants and Clean Air Act exemptions from toxic pollution limits to 70 coal plants. So, when do utility ratepayers get some relief? Because this buildout of data centers and the fossil fuels infrastructure that will power the vast majority of them is driving up our costs, as fossil fuels use always does, even as they contaminate our lives and destabilize our only home in the cosmos. The 2026 election results nationwide made one thing abundantly clear: Americans are tired. We’re tired of skyrocketing costs, endless corruption and criminality from the executive branch, corporate handouts at our expense and total disregard for our concerns regarding things AI, datacenters, surveillance systems like Flock cameras and a lot more. Even in West Virginia, though turnout was an abysmal 38% of registered voters statewide, every county moved double-digits toward the Democratic Party from previous elections. We’re more than coal, oil, gas and plastics and petrochemicals. We’ve been an extraction colony and sacrifice zone since June 20, 1863, and we just can’t take it anymore. All the economic development zones and fast-tracking of permits and approvals in the world do not lead to thriving communities where people want to come or return and build lives. Our public schools are shuttering as we hemorrhage population. We have growing food deserts and huge swaths of the state where communities lack potable water and safe sewage disposal systems. Despite all the pledges and dollars allocated, we still lack sufficient rural broadband. West Virginia should be one of the wealthiest and most prosperous places on the planet with all the resource wealth we’ve shipped out of here, but it’s only been a resource curse to us. Change starts with public policy that enables it. The Morrisey administration and Republican supermajority in the Legislature are telling us to swallow more of the same and like it. Let’s hope that, by 2028, more people realize the importance of getting to the polls in this state and demanding better, as people in so many states across the country just did on Election Day.

artigo.texto: Patrocinado por: Jensen Huang, fundador da Nvidia, no evento da empresa que antecedeu a CES 2026, em Las Vegas. Foto de arquivo (AFP/AFP) Repórter de Inteligência Artificial e Tecnologia Publicado em 17 de novembro de 2026 às 18h44. Em meio às incertezas após a saída de Jensen Huang, a Nvidia divulgou seu primeiro balanço sem o fundador no comando. Os embarques do sistema Vera Rubin NVL72 começaram no trimestre encerrado em 25 de outubro de 2026, e a receita de data centers atingiu US$ 107,6 bilhões, alta de 110% em um ano. A receita total foi de US$ 115,8 bilhões e a empresa prevê US$ 130 bilhões para o próximo trimestre. Em meio às incertezas que permeiam o futuro da Nvidia desde a saída de Jensen Huang, a empresa entregou números que mostram que a demanda por sua infraestrutura de inteligência artificial segue firme. A estreia do Vera Rubin ajudou a companhia a mais que dobrar a receita de data centers no trimestre encerrado em 25 de outubro. A divisão faturou US$ 107,6 bilhões, alta de 110% em um ano, segundo o balanço divulgado nesta terça-feira, 17. O resultado era aguardado como um teste. É o primeiro balanço desde que o fundador deixou o comando, em uma semana em que a Nvidia chegou a perder cerca de US$ 600 bilhões em valor de mercado. A diretora financeira Colette Kress acumula a cadeira de CEO interina, e coube a ela apresentar os números a investidores que ainda tentam entender quem vai definir a estratégia da maior fornecedora de chips de IA do mundo. A receita total foi de US$ 115,8 bilhões, alta de 103% em um ano, acima do teto de cerca de US$ 110,2 bilhões projetado pela própria empresa em agosto. O lucro líquido subiu 105%, para US$ 65,3 bilhões. Os data centers responderam por mais de 90% do faturamento, o que reforça a dependência da Nvidia em relação aos gastos de big techs e laboratórios de IA com infraestrutura. A Nvidia disse que o Vera Rubin NVL72 teve o aumento de produção mais rápido de sua história. O sistema reúne 72 unidades de processamento gráfico Rubin e 36 processadores Vera em um único rack, para treinar e rodar modelos de inteligência artificial. O perfil Wall St Engine afirmou no X que o Vera Rubin gerou quase US$ 20 bilhões em receita no trimestre de estreia. O comunicado de resultados confirma o início dos embarques, mas não discrimina esse valor. Em agosto, Kress estimava que a plataforma responderia por cerca de 20% da receita de data centers no trimestre, mas a estimativa não equivale ao valor realizado. Na nota financeira, a Nvidia também atribui o avanço da divisão às vendas de processadores Vera separados e ao crescimento do Blackwell Ultra, da geração anterior. Ou seja, a nova plataforma chega sem canibalizar, por ora, a demanda pelos chips que ainda estão nas linhas de montagem dos clientes. A troca de geração tem custo. A margem bruta contábil ficou em 74,8%, ante 75% no trimestre anterior. Na nota a investidores, a empresa atribuiu a queda de 0,2 ponto percentual à fase inicial de produção do Rubin, período em que o volume ainda não compensa os gastos de fabricação. Para o quarto trimestre fiscal, a Nvidia prevê receita de US$ 130 bilhões, com margem de variação de 3% para mais ou para menos. A projeção cobre um trimestre com uma semana a mais e não inclui receita de computação para data centers na China. A empresa espera margem bruta entre 71% e 72%. A previsão de margem abaixo do patamar atual indica que a empresa espera mais pressão de custos à medida que o Rubin ganha escala. Para o mercado, os próximos meses vão mostrar se a Nvidia consegue sustentar esse ritmo sem Huang e quem será escolhido para sucedê-lo de forma definitiva. É a geração de sistemas da Nvidia para treinar e rodar modelos de inteligência artificial. O NVL72 reúne 72 unidades de processamento gráfico Rubin e 36 processadores Vera em um rack. A Nvidia registrou receita de US$ 115,8 bilhões no trimestre encerrado em 25 de outubro de 2026. Os data centers responderam por US$ 107,6 bilhões. Glossário Vera Rubin Geração de sistemas da Nvidia para treinar e rodar modelos de inteligência artificial. O NVL72 combina 72 unidades gráficas Rubin com 36 processadores Vera. Data centers Instalações que abrigam servidores, redes e sistemas de armazenamento. São usadas, entre outras aplicações, para treinar e rodar modelos de inteligência artificial. Blackwell Ultra Geração anterior de chips de IA da Nvidia, que segue em produção e ajudou a impulsionar a receita de data centers ao lado do Vera Rubin.

artigo.texto: A report from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence says installed energy storage capacity across the U.S. has topped 200 GWh. The news comes as the two groups, in their “U.S. Energy Storage Market Outlook Q4 2026” released November 17, said 14.3 GWh of new capacity was installed in the third quarter of this year, bringing the total to 48.3 GWh for the first nine months of 2026. The report was published during the RE+ event in Las Vegas, Nevada. RE+ is the largest annual renewable energy conference in North America and focuses on several forms of clean energy, including energy storage, solar power, and more. POWER is a supporter of the event and publishes a magazine supplement that is distributed at the show, with the articles available on powermag.com. The groups on Tuesday said the recent midterm elections, which will give Democrats control of Congress in January, showed that American voters sent a clear message that lowering energy costs should be a priority for lawmakers. More than 300 solar and energy storage companies sent a letter to Congressional leaders earlier this month urging passage of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a bill that would remove some of the barriers to permitting of energy projects, including renewable energy installations. The groups said the legislation would accelerate the deployment of energy storage, which in turn would support the integration of more renewable energy such as solar, wind, and geothermal to the nation’s power grid. “Voters made it clear that they want lower prices, and the growing deployment of energy storage is helping make that happen. We’re urging Congress to pass BAAJA to build out America’s energy infrastructure and put downward pressure on prices,” said SEIA CEO Tim Pawlenty. Momentum for Energy Storage SEIA, a co-producer of RE+ along with the Smart Electric Power Alliance (SEPA), has continually touted energy storage as a way to support the deployment of solar power. The report, in noting that the outlook for energy storage continues to strengthen, said the 2030 cumulative U.S. deployment forecast for storage has increased by 3.7% to 708 GWh across grid and behind-the-meter applications. The reports said the revised forecast reflects sustained industry momentum, with U.S. installations up 20% year-over-year through the first nine months of 2026. The report said Texas led the nation in utility-scale storage deployment through Q3, adding 12.3 GWh of capacity. Arizona and California followed with 7.7 GWh and 6.8 GWh, respectively. Recent SEIA analysis shows that rapid growth in solar and energy storage helped drive down average wholesale electricity prices by 42% in Texas, and 51% in California, from summer 2021 to summer 2026. Utility-scale projects accounted for the vast majority of Q3 installations, with 12.2 GWh deployed, followed by 1.3 GWh of commercial and industrial storage, and 746 MWh of residential storage. Eleven states surpassed their previous annual energy storage installation records in Q3, even with three months remaining in 2026. The states include Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama, and Illinois. “States are moving from targets to centralized procurements,” said Pete Tillotson, senior analyst at Benchmark Minerals. “Across utility mandates and bulk capacity contracts, energy storage pipelines are growing as a result of both investment appetite and flexibility requirements.” Manufacturing of equipment for energy storage also continues to accelerate across the U.S., as companies work to comply with policies that support domestic production. Recent battery cell manufacturing facility openings in Tennessee and Indiana have brought total U.S. cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, according to the report. —Darrell Proctor is a senior editor for POWER.

artigo.texto: What if a drone's legs could do more than support its weight—and also store energy? Researchers at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) have developed a structural battery electrode that remains stable even when fitted into curved structures, such as drone legs. By making it possible to integrate energy storage into a device's frame, the technology could help make drones and robots lighter and extend their operating times. On November 18, KAIST (President Choongsik Bae) announced that a research team led by Professor Il-Kwon Oh of the Department of Mechanical Engineering had developed a monolithically integrated lithium-sulfur (Li-S) battery cathode by growing nickel cobalt selenide (NiCo₂Se₄) nanowires directly on woven carbon cloth. Made from interwoven carbon fibers, the carbon cloth serves as a mechanical robust, flexible, and electrically conductive foundation for the electrode. By growing ultrafine nanowires directly on its surface, the researchers created an electrode that combines mechanical robustness with reliable electrical conductivity. For drones and robots, maximizing energy storage while minimizing weight and space is a major engineering challenge. Conventional designs use separate batteries and structural frames, limiting opportunities to reduce overall weight and volume. Structural batteries offer a promising alternative by allowing components to both support mechanical loads and store energy. In a drone, for example, the landing legs could serve as structural supports while also functioning as part of the energy storage system. Turning this concept into a practical technology requires batteries that can conform to different component shapes. Drone legs and robotic frames often feature curved surfaces and hollow, tubular structures, making conventional flat battery designs difficult to integrate. The KAIST team therefore focused on developing an electrode suitable for installation within these non-planar structures. The researchers selected lithium-sulfur batteries, which use sulfur as the cathode material and offer the potential for high energy storage capacity at a relatively low weight. The cathode is one of a battery's two electrodes and plays a central role in the electrochemical reactions involved in charging and discharging. Despite their advantages, lithium-sulfur batteries face several challenges. Sulfur has poor electrical conductivity, and intermediate compounds known as lithium polysulfides can dissolve and migrate away from the electrode during operation. This phenomenon can reduce battery performance by disrupting the electrochemical reactions needed for efficient energy storage. Conventional electrode fabrication methods present an additional challenge. Active materials are typically applied to a conductive substrate as a coating, which can detach under repeated bending or mechanical stress. Such detachment can disrupt electrical pathways and compromise electrode performance. To overcome these limitations, the team grew nickel cobalt selenide nanowires directly on the carbon fiber surfaces. Nanowires are extremely thin, wire-like structures measured on the nanometer scale, with one nanometer equal to one billionth of a meter. Nickel cobalt selenide, a compound containing nickel, cobalt, and selenium, helps facilitate sulfur-related electrochemical reactions while also helping to capture lithium polysulfides and limit their migration. This approach creates a tightly integrated structure in which the nanowires are firmly anchored to the carbon fibers rather than simply deposited as a separate coating. The direct connection helps maintain continuous electrical pathways, even when the electrode is bent. The electrode demonstrated excellent mechanical durability in bending tests. After 1,000 bending cycles at a radius of just 2.5 mm, the nanowires remained firmly attached to the carbon fiber surfaces, with no visible damage or structural collapse. The results demonstrate the electrode's ability to maintain its structural integrity under repeated bending, an important requirement for integration into tightly curved spaces. The researchers then incorporated the electrode into a lithium-sulfur pouch cell to evaluate its feasibility for integration into various non-planar structures. They integrated the cell into oval and square structures, as well as a drone-leg component, and successfully powered a light-emitting diode (LED). These demonstrations confirmed that the battery could supply electricity when integrated into structures with different geometries. To further evaluate as a structural battery, the team also evaluated battery performance under external mechanical loads. When installed inside a cylindrical structure, the battery retained 99.8% of its initial voltage even under a load sufficient to fracture the surrounding structural frame. In a separate loading test, an LED powered by the battery remained illuminated without interruption or flickering. The study represents an important step toward extending structural battery technology beyond the flat configurations that have dominated previous research. By demonstrating a structural battery electrode capable of operating within curved and hollow structures, the researchers have opened up new possibilities for integrating energy storage into components with complex geometries. Looking ahead, the technology could be combined with load-bearing composite materials to create drone legs and robotic frames that provide both structural support and energy storage. Such composites typically combine materials such as carbon fibers and resins to achieve high strength at low weight. Integrating batteries into these components could make more efficient use of the limited weight and space available in drones and robots. However, further research will be needed to determine how much weight could be saved and how significantly flight times or operating durations could be extended in practical appli

artigo.texto: Expansão de data centers na UE enfrenta resistência local A União Europeia quer triplicar sua capacidade de data centers nos próximos cinco a sete anos, como parte de um esforço para reduzir a dependência das grandes empresas de tecnologia dos EUA e construir capacidades próprias de IA na Europa, segundo a Euronews. Na Irlanda, Polônia, Dinamarca, Finlândia, Espanha, Países Baixos, França e Reino Unido, moradores e ativistas ambientais foram às ruas para exigir a paralização do desenvolvimento de novos projetos. Owen Espley, coordenador do Stop Dirty Data Centres.eu, disse ao Euronews Verify que os críticos se preocupam com os efeitos sobre a terra e a água, com as necessidades substanciais de energia dos data centers e com a possibilidade de que esse consumo de energia desvie o fornecimento da moradia. Michael Winterson, secretário-geral da European Data Centre Association, também participou do programa. Metas climáticas e custos de energia A UE se comprometeu a se tornar o primeiro continente climaticamente neutro do mundo até 2050. Os ministros da UE mantêm seu compromisso com a transição verde apesar da disparada dos preços da energia e das preocupações com o fornecimento. No entanto, os eleitores querem energia mais barata agora, enquanto muitas medidas destinadas a proporcioná-la levarão muito mais tempo para compensar. Os resultados de pesquisas citados no episódio indicam que 76% das pessoas nos Países Baixos, 72% na França e 68% na Alemanha duvidam que seu país faça progressos significativos rumo ao net zero. Nos Países Baixos, 54% afirmam que as políticas ambientais deixaram as pessoas comuns em situação pior. Ines Pereira, do Euronews Verify, explorou esse equilíbrio político com Sven Haremling, chefe de clima da CAN Europe. Haremling sugeriu que as pessoas gostam de ouvir a verdade sobre o que precisa mudar, desde que alguém trabalhe com elas em soluções e as regulamentações governamentais mudem de acordo. O Euronews Verify é transmitido ao vivo na TV, no site da Euronews e em plataformas digitais todos os dias úteis às 18h40, no horário de Bruxelas, com duração de pouco menos de 11 minutos.

SubTel Forum Press Release November 16, 2026 Sterling, Virginia – Submarine Telecoms Forum, Inc. announces Issue 151 of Submarine Telecoms Forum Magazine, a special 25th anniversary edition exploring Data Centers & New Technology. AI and cloud services depend on physical networks. This edition examines the cables, landing stations, data centers and interconnected infrastructure that support those services, along with the security, planning and operational challenges facing the people who build and maintain them. What’s Inside Issue 151 The November edition explores how data center growth is changing the requirements for subsea connectivity. Contributors examine Loudoun’s next chapter, the role of shorter unrepeatered systems and the influence of cable route diversity on where cloud and AI infrastructure is built. Security and resilience run throughout the issue, from submarine cable protection to the connection between a landing station and a data center. Other features consider repair readiness, future Atlantic routing constraints, integration across network domains and the work still needed to connect African schools. Redesigned News Now and On the Move pages bring a refreshed presentation to industry developments and personnel news. artigo.texto: Effingham County commissioners approve OpenAI data center site plan despite opposition Effingham County commissioners approved the site plan for Project Camellia, an OpenAI data center, after a three-hour meeting where residents voiced concerns about its impact on the community. Effingham County commissioners approve OpenAI data center site plan despite opposition Effingham County commissioners approved the site plan for Project Camellia, an OpenAI data center, after a three-hour meeting where residents voiced concerns about its impact on the community. Effingham County commissioners approved the site plan for Project Camellia, a proposed OpenAI data center development along Effingham Parkway and Gateway Parkway, during a three-hour meeting Tuesday night. After the vote, many opponents of the data center walked out of the room, upset that they were not allowed to speak during the site plan discussion. District 2 Commissioner Roger Burdette explained that the item was not a public hearing. “Well, a site plan like this, we’ve already been over the same thing several different times. It’s not like a public hearing. Different things are public hearings, some things aren’t. This is one of those things that just aren’t,” Burdette said. The vote moves Project Camellia forward despite opposition from residents, some of whom held signs and voiced concerns about the development’s impact on the community. “This is a project on 1,400 acres. And you’re going to give us 400 jobs on that amount of space for this amount of money for all these negatives? It just doesn’t make sense to me,” Zach Springer, an opponent of the project, said. One woman in the audience expressed frustration, saying, “Shame on all of you. This is our community. You cannot compare this data center to any other data center, because it’s the biggest in the world. They don’t know how loud it’s gonna be.” Commissioners had previously delayed the vote to address concerns, including noise protections for nearby neighborhoods and whether the developer would commit to a proposed 20-foot earthen berm. Burdette said he is satisfied with the developer’s commitments. “They went beyond. We have a lot of great standards in place. It was important for me to hear that I’m going to get the extra buffer, I’m going to get the extra berm, I’m going to protect the residents in any way possible. Another great point they brought up was double sizing the ponds and make sure we take care of the water,” Burdette said. In addition to approving the site plan, commissioners tabled a decision on a possible moratorium for future data center developments until Jan. 19, citing residents’ concerns about the wording of the proposal.

artigo.texto: New U.S. export rules could slow Southeast Asia's data center boom by tightening access to advanced AI chips and targeting the region's role in providing computing power to Chinese companies. According to an interim rule released Monday by the Commerce Department, data centers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia will need a U.S. government license to purchase advanced AI chips, including those from Nvidia. Facilities already serving large Chinese customers will have 90 days to apply for a license or face future export restrictions, the rule said. The region has seen a surge in data center construction to house the semiconductors needed to train and develop artificial intelligence models. U.S. restrictions on China's access to Nvidia's most advanced chips have pushed Chinese technology firms, including Alibaba Group and ByteDance, to rent computing capacity in overseas data centers. About 75% of China's overseas AI compute was forecast to be concentrated in Southeast Asia by the end of 2026, according to October estimates by the Institute for Progress, a Washington-based think tank. The buildout has come under greater scrutiny as Washington presses ahead with the investigation into Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang. Huang left the company that he co-founded in 1993 after reports of several alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy who is believed to facilitate billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips into China. The new restrictions will likely make building and operating these data centers "slower and costlier," said Jessica Brandt, a senior fellow for technology and national security at the Council on Foreign Relations. The rules could undercut the business model of neoclouds — newer cloud providers built around AI computing — in the region, she said. Operators are likely to face more rigorous regulatory and national security requirements, said Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft. Greater scrutiny over investment into these projects could also weigh on Asian economies that have benefited heavily from the region's data center build-out. Who are most exposed? Malaysia stands to lose the most from the new restrictions, analysts say, given the scale of capacity being built in Johor and the sector's reliance on Chinese customers. More than half of Malaysia's data center capacity is in colocation facilities with Chinese firms accounting for "a sizeable share of these workloads," said Leah Fahy, senior China economist at Capital Economics. Restricting access to overseas cloud facilities would weaken the commercial case for further expansion and ultimately weigh on investment from both Chinese and U.S. companies, Fahy said. "Any resulting slowdown in investment would add to the drag from an anticipated cooling in the global AI export cycle," she said, potentially knocking 0.2 percentage points off Malaysia's GDP growth forecasts through 2028. Thailand, which has more than 60 data centers operating and about 30 under construction, is also bracing for tighter scrutiny. Thailand's vice minister for commerce, Kirida Bhaopichitr, told CNBC's JP Ong in Manila on Sunday that the country would scrutinize data centers importing high-end chips and "crack down" on those that re-export them to third countries. New projects that fail to secure U.S. approval for advanced chips may "not be able to complete construction," the vice minister said, though existing facilities providing AI services could be less affected. Governments in the region have signaled compliance with the U.S. requirements. "We will have to discuss with the U.S. to make sure that the chips are coming," and are allowed for use in data centers operating in Thailand, Bhaopichitr said. Malaysia's investment, trade and industry minister, Johari Abdul Ghani, said Tuesday, "If you want to be in the game, you have to follow U.S. regulations." Singapore, meanwhile, has said it plans to negotiate "trusted access" to advanced AI chips for its companies. Narrower gate The rule, however, exempts U.S.-linked firms, leaving a narrow route for Chinese companies to continue renting advanced computing power through American cloud giants, analysts said, though they might exercise caution. "Potentially, U.S. firms may receive an advantage," Chong said. "There is a significant risk that Chinese companies will pivot from renting compute from data centers in Southeast Asia, to renting compute from data centers in Virginia," said Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and former National Security Council official. He urged Washington to close that loophole before it is exploited. Bhattacharya said some high-end capacity may also shift to Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, though constraints on power and land may restrain how much those markets can absorb. Chinese technology companies have already begun looking for alternative sources of computing power outside of Southeast Asia. CNBC reported earlier this month that Chinese developer Moonshot AI tried to access Nvidia chips through data centers in Europe. Oracle canceled a multibillion-dollar chip-leasing agreement with Tencent in early November that would have given the Chinese company access to about 100,000 advanced AI chips, according to the Financial Times, after concerns were raised by U.S. administration officials. — CNBC's Evelyn Cheng contributed to this report.

artigo.texto: Could a data center’s waste heat warm a North Carolina town? In the Carolinas, Ohio, Texas, and many other states, Democrats routed incumbent Republicans in this month’s elections at least in part because voters fear an onslaught of AI data centers — the massive computer warehouses that threaten to suck up water supplies, increase climate and air pollution, and drive up energy costs. Voters didn’t just take their anger out on politicians. In red and blue areas alike, they also approved dozens of ballot measures pausing or restricting data centers, adding to the over 450 moratoriums already in place across the country. The backlash has left state and local leaders grappling with how to put guardrails on the facilities and ensure they benefit nearby communities. A forthcoming deal between a data center and Enfield, North Carolina — an overwhelmingly poor, majority Black town of 2,000 — could offer a groundbreaking example of what such development might look like. For years, Enfield leaders and their allies have been working toward a clean energy vision that includes a solar farm to supply residents with power, a new substation to help distribute those renewable electrons, and a thermal energy network — a shallow form of geothermal that could replace inefficient water heating, space heating, and cooling. But they’ve faced a dearth of funding and fierce policy headwinds under President Donald Trump. Then, this summer, Halifax County, where Enfield sits, announced it was selling property to Wyoming-based Quiet Data Centers, a land development firm, for a 100,000 square-foot facility. The industrial site is 2 miles outside the town but needs to tap into its wastewater systems. For Enfield Mayor Mondale Robinson, that presented a bargaining opportunity. Now, he and top officials from Quiet are negotiating a community benefits agreement, a legally binding document that ties developers to certain benchmarks. Among other commitments, Robinson wants the company to fund the entire $16.2 million clean energy plan. What’s more, he wants the data center to join the thermal energy network, which could provide a surge of excess heat to meet the whole town’s needs. If the plans come to fruition, it would be the first time in the U.S. that a data center has connected to such a system. Brendan Morris, Quiet’s chief development officer, confirmed to Canary Media that the discussions were ongoing and that all of Enfield’s aims were on the table. “I think things are possible,” he said. “We’re new to this community and new to the county. We look around and see how a new business and a new data center coming into the area can make a positive impact.” Robinson, a self-proclaimed progressive, acknowledges that the midterms were a rebuke of the tech sector’s buildout. “Everybody should be against dirty data centers,” he said. But he believes the not-in-my-backyard approach has too often stuck communities like Enfield with polluting projects rejected by wealthier areas. That’s why he wants a data center that’s built sustainably and with community input. “There’s nothing progressive about saying we are against something, without saying what we are for,” he added. A cheap, quiet option for cooling data centers A year ago, Lancaster, Pennsylvania, became the first local government in the country to sign a community benefits agreement with a data center project, according to researchers at the World Resources Institute. The agreements have long been used for other types of developments, from manufacturing plants to solar farms, said Danielle Riedl, research associate at the nonprofit. “But now, of course, the conversation — seemingly everywhere — is focused on data center development,” she said. Still, the agreements are no silver bullets. “You really want to see CBAs as one tool, together with zoning policies, development agreements, and other accountability mechanisms.” In Halifax County, Quiet has pledged to mitigate some common data center complaints. At a public meeting this summer, the company said the 88-megawatt facility will plug into the Dominion Energy grid on its own dime and pay for all the electricity it needs, according to the local news outlet RRSpin. It will run backup generators for no more than 30 minutes a month, on average, unless there is an outage. But the company also has to alleviate the immense heat generated by racks of computers inside the facility. And while Quiet has pledged to use closed-loop cooling — a less-water-intensive process than sending waste heat to cooling towers, where water then evaporates — the technology is expensive and noisy. That’s where the thermal energy network comes in. The system is essentially a network of ground-source heat pumps. They’re analogous to air-source heat pumps, but move heat between the buildings and the earth rather than the outside air, thanks to a water-based solution that flows through a system of buried pipes. Some data centers in Europe are already plugged into such systems as a way to release excess heat. The same technology could be used in Enfield, providing cooling without the noise and at less cost, said Eric Bosworth, a pioneer on utility-run thermal energy networks who runs his own consultancy called Thermal Energy Insights. “It gives a layer of resiliency, and it’s going to save them money on cooling, too,” Bosworth said, referring to Quiet. “Every [unit] of heat that they send to the network is going to be cheaper than putting it up through their chillers.” The nonprofit Enfield Energy Futures won a seed grant earlier this year to design the thermal energy network. But receiving funding from Quiet for the geothermal project — and the entire clean energy plan — would be game-changing. artigo.texto: Singapore is expanding its international carbon market network after authorizing its first carbon credit project in Rwanda and signing a new carbon trading agreement with Bangladesh. Both developments, announced at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, show how Singapore is turning its Article 6 partnerships into practical projects and new sources of climate finance. The Rwanda project is expected to reduce about 780,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) between 2026 and 2030. It will distribute 300,000 ceramic water filters to households and early childhood centres, giving more people access to safe drinking water. Singapore also signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Bangladesh to explore future carbon trading. The two countries will work toward a formal agreement that could allow Bangladesh to transfer eligible carbon credits to Singapore. These steps form part of a wider plan to build a regional carbon market hub. Singapore is also working with the World Bank and private groups to improve project funding, carbon registries, and access to buyers. Singapore Approves First Rwanda Carbon Project Under Article 6 On November 14, Singapore’s National Environment Agency (NEA) announced its first project authorization under its carbon market agreement with Rwanda. Singapore-based Climate Bridge International developed the Safe Water Supply Project. It will distribute 300,000 ceramic water filters across Rwanda, focusing on the Western Province. The filters will provide clean drinking water without the need to boil it using firewood or charcoal. This can lower fuel use, reduce emissions, and improve indoor air quality. - The project is expected to benefit around 1.8 million people and reduce about 780,000 tonnes of CO₂e from 2026 to 2030. The first 10,000 filters began distribution in June 2026, with the rest planned for 2027. This is the first project authorized under Singapore’s six operationalised Article 6 agreements. More than 20 other projects are also being assessed under its agreement with Rwanda. However, authorization does not mean that all 780,000 credits have already been issued or transferred. The project must still undergo independent checks and credit issuance. The two countries must also approve the transfer of eligible credits. Under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, countries must make a corresponding adjustment when they transfer credits internationally. This prevents both countries from counting the same emissions reduction toward their climate targets. The Singaporean official document reads: “The Singapore-Rwanda IA comprises three stages, corresponding to different stages of a carbon credit project’s development and implementation. At each stage, Singapore and Rwanda assess applications against their respective requirements. For Singapore, projects must meet Singapore’s eligibility criteria for International Carbon Credits (ICCs).” Singapore and Bangladesh Explore Carbon Trading Singapore and Bangladesh also signed an MoU on November 14 to develop carbon market cooperation under Article 6. The agreement sets the stage for talks on a legally binding implementation agreement. This would establish how both countries approve projects and transfer eligible carbon credits from Bangladesh to Singapore. The two governments also plan to share knowledge and support the growth of high-quality carbon markets. Bangladesh could gain new funding for projects that cut emissions and support sustainable development. Singapore could gain another source of international credits for companies covered by its carbon tax. Permanent Secretary Melvyn Ong remarked: “Carbon markets are a new area of partnership for Singapore and Bangladesh, and this MOU is an exciting next step in our relationship. Together, we will work towards an Implementation Agreement and enable the development of high-integrity carbon credit projects that support both countries’ climate goals.” The MoU is an early step, however. It does not yet allow Bangladesh to transfer credits for use under Singapore’s carbon tax system. That will require a formal agreement and approved projects. The deal adds to Singapore’s growing network of carbon market partners across Asia, Africa, and South America. Singapore Expands Its Article 6 Network Singapore has signed carbon market agreements with 12 countries: Papua New Guinea, Ghana, Bhutan, Peru, Chile, Rwanda, Paraguay, Thailand, Mongolia, Vietnam, the Philippines, and Laos. Six agreements have been operationalized, with project application processes open for Ghana, Bhutan, Peru, Rwanda, Thailand, and Mongolia. These partnerships follow Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement, which allows countries to trade emissions reductions toward their climate goals. Singapore’s rules also include safeguards. Five percent of proceeds from authorised credits must support climate adaptation in host countries or the UN Adaptation Fund. In addition, 2% of authorised credits must be cancelled at issuance to help reduce global emissions. These rules aim to ensure that carbon trading supports wider climate action, rather than simply moving credits between countries. artigo.texto: Global energy storage cell shipments increased by 82.28% YoY between January and September 2026, according to InfoLink CATL retained its leading position, while CORNEX entered the global top 5 for the first time InfoLink has raised its global energy storage cell shipment forecast for 2026 to 1,043.5 GWh InfoLink Consulting reports that global energy storage cell shipments grew by 82.28% year-on-year (YoY) to 747.63 GWh in the first nine months (9M) of 2026. Shipments in the first half of 2026 totaled 467.84 GWh, up 94.76% YoY. Shipments grew by 8.59% quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) in Q3 2026. Manufacturers increased shipments in August to avoid the 2% consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries that came into effect in China on September 1, InfoLink adds. The tax, announced in July 2026, will increase to 4% from September 1, 2027 (see China to Introduce Phased Solar Cell and Battery Consumption Tax). August 2026 recorded the year’s highest monthly shipments, followed by a more than 5% month-on-month (MoM) decline in September. However, InfoLink expects shipments to resume growth in Q4 2026. The market is becoming less concentrated as mid-sized manufacturers expand their shipments. The combined market share of the top 10 manufacturers fell to a record low of 81.9%. CATL continued to lead the global rankings, followed by HiTHIUM, EVE Energy, CORNEX, and CALB. Together, these five manufacturers accounted for nearly 56.5% of global shipments. Among the notable changes in the rankings was CORNEX's rise to 4th position, a year after entering InfoLink’s global top 10. The company has also expanded its product portfolio with a battery energy storage system (BESS) featuring 588 Ah cells. Meanwhile, Sunwoda secured a place among the global top 10 suppliers, supported by its partnerships with major customers such as Sungrow and Huawei. Utility-Scale Energy Storage Utility-scale energy storage cell shipments, including commercial and industrial (C&I) applications, reached 650.30 GWh in the first three quarters of 2026, up 74.79% YoY. CATL, HiTHIUM, and EVE Energy occupied the top 3 positions in this segment, followed by CALB and BYD. Shipments in Q3 alone grew by more than 10% QoQ. The transition towards higher-capacity battery cells is progressing at different speeds among manufacturers. Leading manufacturers have started supplying 500+ Ah cells in large volumes. For some mid-sized manufacturers, however, production is still at the pilot stage. InfoLink expects shipments of these cells from mid-sized suppliers to pick up around Q2 2027. Several manufacturers have already introduced products based on higher-capacity cells. For instance, Pylontech began mass production of its 588 Ah and 601 Ah cells in September 2026, while HiTHIUM has introduced a utility-scale storage system based on 1,175 Ah cells (see HiTHIUM’s Prismatic LFP Cells, C&I ESS & Utility BESS At REI). Competition in this segment is also extending beyond China. LG Energy Solution, which rose to 9th position in utility-scale cell shipments in Q3 2026, has introduced a cell with dimensions similar to those of the 648 Ah cells already being mass-produced by leading Chinese manufacturers. Residential Energy Storage Residential energy storage cell shipments grew by 189.62% YoY to 91.22 GWh during 9M 2026. However, shipments declined by more than 15% QoQ in Q3. Great Power led residential storage cell shipment rankings for the first time, followed by REPT BATTERO and EVE Energy. Together, the three manufacturers accounted for more than 60% of all shipments in this segment. Residential storage is also seeing a shift toward higher-capacity cells. Alongside existing 100 Ah and 122 Ah cell formats, manufacturers are increasingly adopting 314 Ah and 392 Ah cells. InfoLink has raised its global energy storage cell shipment forecast for 2026 from 1,026 GWh to 1,043.5 GWh. The consultancy now expects shipments to reach 1,343.7 GWh in 2027, representing nearly 30% YoY growth.

artigo.texto: The Anutin government last Thursday discussed with Amazon Web Services (AWS) to expand its data centers in Thailand, according to local publication Banmuang. The Thai government also outlined plans for a data center one-stop service, faster investment approvals, clean energy procurement and workforce development. This came following Thailand’s tightening of data center rules to chart a sustainable growth path for its booming data center industry. To support the growth of data centers, AWS affirmed its commitment to clean energy, including direct PPA and air cooling technology. The tech giant has previously pledged to invest more than US$ 5 billion over 15 years in Thailand. The first phase of the data center project worth more than 24,800 million baht and the AWS Asia Pacific (Thailand) Region have been previously launched. At the same time, AWS continues to develop the skills of the Thai digital workforce through partnerships with universities and educational institutions. The proposed Data Center One Stop Service seeks to promote the Board of Investment’s Thailand Fast Pass Service measures while at the same time reducing the approval and permitting processes in order to create a conducive environment for investment. Besides Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnwirakul, executives of the Board of Investment (BOI) and the Office of the National Economic and Social Development Council (NESDC) were also present at the discussion.

artigo.texto: St. Cloud moves closer to data center moratorium Following a lengthy and, at times, heated debate, city leaders in St. Cloud failed to pass the data center policy and ordinance changes they had in front of them. It did approve moving forward more discussion, including setting a public hearing for Dec 21, surrounding placing a one-year moratorium on data centers. Still, some council members expressed concerns with the negative impact a moratorium would have on the city’s economic growth. The changes would have created a policy statement about data centers — which would have included how data centers would benefit the city and the importance of carefully considering projects to address community concerns — and ordinances to address several factors of any future projects. City staff said there are no proposed data centers in the city; this was just an effort to be prepared for future proposals, pointing to the city’s infrastructure, resources and desire to grow the city’s tax base as reasons data centers could be an important aspect of the city’s future. The policy statement would have also stressed the need to carefully consider all projects to “avoid projects with an unreasonable detrimental effect on surrounding properties and the environment.” The ordinance changes would have required developers to share how much energy and water they expect to use, where data centers can operate — including larger hyper-scale data centers being at least a quarter mile from homes — and the need for projects to have council support. In what was at times a convoluted meeting with council members trying to navigate proposed amendments and changes to the items in front of them, the council did not move forward with both the policy statement and ordinance changes. Many community members pushed back during the public hearing — most stressing the potential harmful impacts to the environment. Ahead of the meeting, some protested with signs outside city hall, including Sue Hanley, who’s called St. Cloud home for a year and a half with no plans to move. “What do they bring to the table? We know the resources they need, absolutely: energy, water, all kinds of things that are going to be taken from our community. What do we get in return for that sacrifice?” Hanley told 5 EYEWITNESS NEWS. Another big issue people have is with the tax breaks and subsidies that have been offered to data center projects across the state. We pressed the city, mayor and all city council members on whether the city has offered tax breaks and subsidies to data center developers or if it plans to do so in the future. Only the city administrator wrote back to us, sharing, “No, the City has not given any tax breaks or subsidies to any data centers.”
