artigo.texto: 16 November 2026 Thailand Carbon Markets Club Joins Carbon Market Partners in ASEAN to Renew Memorandum of Collaboration at COP31 in Turkey On November 12, 2026, the signatories to the ASEAN Common Carbon Framework (ACCF), comprising Thailand Carbon Markets Club (TCMC), the Malaysia Carbon Market Association (MCMA), the Singapore Sustainable Finance Association (SSFA), the Indonesia Carbon Trade Association (IDCTA), and the ASEAN Alliance on Carbon Markets (AACM), signed a renewal of their Memorandum of Collaboration (MoC) for a further two years at COP31 in Türkiye. The renewal reaffirmed their shared commitment to regional cooperation and to developing high-integrity, interoperable carbon markets across ASEAN. As part of the renewal, Aboitiz Foundation, Inc. from the Philippines formally joined the ACCF and signed the MoC as an observer. Its participation broadens regional representation in the ACCF and reflects growing interest among ASEAN member states in linking national carbon market development with regional coordination. The renewal also marks progress in aligning approaches on the demand side. AACM and CMC joined IDCTA, SSFA, and MCMA in supporting the Shared Principles under the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets, a government-led initiative co-chaired by Kenya, Singapore, and the United Kingdom. Launched in November 2025 at the COP30 Business and Finance Forum, the Shared Principles set out six pillars for the credible corporate use of carbon credits alongside deep decarbonization. With all five signatories now supporting the Shared Principles, the ACCF will explore ways to contribute to and advise global initiatives, including those led by the Coalition, so that carbon market development reflects ASEAN’s circumstances. Under SSFA’s chairmanship, which began in the second half of 2026, the ACCF established five priorities for its 2026–2028 strategy. - Bring the ACCF’s work into formal ASEAN processes. - Broaden the signatory base to ensure wider and more balanced regional representation. - Bring ASEAN carbon markets into closer alignment with global standards. - Coordinate with the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets and contribute ASEAN perspectives to its work. - Establish an ASEAN Community of Practice (CoP) as a structured platform for sharing knowledge and consulting on longer-term ACCF projects. The ACCF’s work covers three main areas. - Supply and demand - Develop interim guidance for companies on using high-integrity carbon credits to support demand. Build capacity among financiers through a preliminary due diligence framework for assessing key criteria for carbon project financing. - Market infrastructure - Examine the legal nature and status of verified carbon credits and explore ways to reduce cross-border barriers, better align market rules, and enable the use of credits interchangeably across ASEAN carbon markets. - Capacity building - Work with international partners to provide technical and advisory support for carbon project financing and bring the ACCF’s work to ASEAN forums. Since its establishment at COP29 in November 2024, with MCMA serving as chair for the first 18 months, the ACCF has gained wider regional recognition. It was acknowledged in the Joint Media Statement of the 57th ASEAN Economic Ministers’ Meeting and the ASEAN Joint Statement on Climate Change to COP30. It was also cited in the ASEAN Capital Markets Forum’s Guidance for an ASEAN Voluntary Carbon Market. Over the past year, the ACCF has supported national and independent carbon standards aligned with benchmarks set by the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM) and the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA), helping strengthen the integrity and market acceptance of ASEAN carbon credits. Under its renewed strategy, the ACCF will prioritize putting its work plans into practice alongside policy alignment and capacity building. These efforts aim to strengthen confidence in ASEAN-origin carbon credits, facilitate cross-border cooperation, and support the region’s climate objectives. Mrs. Gloyta Nathalang, Senior Executive Vice President, Sustainability Management and Corporate Communications, Bangchak Corporation Public Company Limited, and Chair of Thailand Carbon Markets Club (TCMC), said, “ASEAN’s strength lies in its diversity. Cooperation between governments and businesses can build on the region’s progress in developing carbon markets, strengthening credit quality and interoperability while respecting national priorities. Through these efforts, we hope to help channel financing toward high-quality projects that deliver measurable emissions reductions and benefits for local communities.” Ms. Oi-Yee Choo, ACCF Co-Chair, Co-Lead of SSFA’s Carbon Markets Workstream, and CEO of Climate Impact X, said, “This renewal marks the next phase for the ACCF. As chair, SSFA will work closely with the Singapore government, which will assume the ASEAN chairmanship in 2027, to complement its market-building efforts from the private sector. artigo.texto: Arrests and scuffles with police. Shouts of “shame.” Litigation, petitions and public comment sessions stretching past midnight. This is how Coloradans are reacting to the arrival of large-scale data centers in the Centennial State. Smaller data centers have operated in Colorado for years, tucked into unassuming office parks and downtown skyscrapers. But a new era of hyperscale data centers made for the age of artificial intelligence has begun in Colorado and — despite near-universal pushback in the communities where they are planned — more developments are underway as governments and regulators struggle to keep up. “This has moved so fast, the data center demand is so incredibly strong and powerful that it’s really caught local governments like us off-guard,” Aurora mayor Mike Coffman said. “There’s a feeling of vulnerability right now. It came so fast, so hard, it’s forced me to push back – and I’m pretty pro-business.” Four large data centers are in the planning phases or under construction in Colorado, several of which are competing to become the state’s largest. Combined, their max power needs could equal those of more than 819,000 homes — or 16 times the amount of power used by Denver International Airport. The development comes despite a patchwork of regulations, moratoriums and local opposition that has slowed — though not stopped — industry growth. In Aurora, plans for a 500-megawatt facility next to a neighborhood are moving forward, despite the mayor’s pledge to stop it at all costs. If built, the facility’s power needs could outstrip the city’s entire residential use. In Weld County, a successful petition drive sought to stop an artificial intelligence data center planned there, but it’s unclear whether a ballot measure could halt the project. In Colorado Springs, the City Council voted to put off a vote on a data center until the spring, but the developer said he plans to continue working on the project in the interim. If built, the data center would be the largest power user in the city, by far. There is no standard definition of “hyperscale” data centers, but the term is generally used to describe large facilities that use lots of power and often the computing power needed for artificial intelligence. The Colorado utility regulators writing new rules for large electrical loads (like data centers) are looking at facilities that draw at least 50 megawatts, though they are considering lowering that threshold to 20 megawatts for new customers. A megawatt of power can power approximately 1,100 homes, according to Xcel Energy. Local governments remain the primary regulators of data centers big and small in Colorado. The state lacks broad regulation of the industry, prompting city councils and county commissions of a variety of political persuasions to pass their own rules or enact moratoriums. Larimer County is seeking public comment on a proposed ban on hyperscale data centers, defined as any facility that would draw more than 30 megawatts of power. Brighton in late October enacted a moratorium weeks after residents learned of a 2.5 million-square-foot data center proposed for the Adams County town. The company later withdrew its application. Denver, Arvada, Commerce City, Pagosa Springs, Boulder County and Jefferson County are some of the more than one dozen local governments that enacted a temporary moratorium on data center development. The topic has drawn the attention of governor-elect Phil Weiser, who said at an event in October that his first legislative priority would be a bill to “put guardrails on data centers,” though he did not support an all-out ban. “Communities need to be listened to,” he said. “These data centers shouldn’t be shoved down the throat of communities.” Opposition to data centers is not always about the specifics of a project, said Jason Green, whose company Raeden is building a 50-megawatt facility in Colorado Springs. Instead, developers feel like they are defending against the broad swell of growing hostility against the industry — and the artificial intelligence technology it fuels — as a whole. “There isn’t a data center project in the U.S. that in some form isn’t caught up in the referendum of data centers,” said Green, who has worked in the data center industry for more than 25 years. That broader conversation is also playing out in discussions about potential statewide legislation regulating the industry, said state Sen. Cathy Kipp, who sponsored a failed bill in the last legislative session to regulate data centers. The issue is not about left or right politics, she said, but about regular people bearing the costs to their quality of life from projects that make huge amounts of profit for wealthy companies. “People see these very wealthy companies coming in, building whatever they want, taking our precious resources and people are saying, ‘Why should we support this?'” she said. “It’s no longer left or right, it’s up and down.” Data center capital of the state? When Amy Wiles bought her home in Aurora in 2020, the realtor told her that the open fields abutting her neighborhood would eventually become a small, walkable cluster of shops and restaurants on the eastern edge of Colorado’s third-largest city. Wiles never got her neighborhood coffee shop. Instead, the land became home to the state’s largest data center. And Wiles, now a city councilmember, has found herself deeply embroiled in the debate about how local communities should regulate the booming, unpopular industry. The ward she represents sprawls across the city’s northeast corner and has a lot of attributes data center developers value: large parcels of undeveloped land, relatively easy access to power and water resources, proximity to an urban core and — an increasing rarity on the Front Range — a lack of a moratorium against data center development. artigo.texto: Salt Lake adopts 180-day pause on data center development SALT LAKE CITY (KUTV) — The Salt Lake City Council adopted a temporary ordinance pausing data center development in the city for up to 180 days, giving officials time to study regulations for the industry. The council plans to use the pause to consult with residents, industry representatives, experts and other levels of government. From there, the council "intends to initiate formal petitions to amend the Salt Lake City Code to adopt zoning regulations pertaining to data centers." The 180-day period is the maximum allowed under state law, Councilwoman Victoria Petro said. The vote comes after permit applications for a proposed data center in Salt Lake City’s Northpoint area drew opposition from nearby residents. The ordinance will temporarily pause any progress on that and any other data center projects on Salt Lake City land. Dennis Bangerter, who lives across the street from the proposed site, said he believes development approvals are moving too quickly. “We’re just kind of caught in the middle of a puzzle that they’re trying to do too many things,” he said. Chris Souther, who lives nearby, said he has noticed more noise and air pollution as the neighborhood has changed. He says that has impacted more than just the quality of life, but also property value. "My life savings is gone because the city decided to commercialize to make a bigger tax base for themselves," Souther said. Petro said residents have not had enough input into the development of the data center industry. “You can’t leave our neighbors out of it,” she said. “You have to engage them.” Petro represents the area and said residents’ concerns about noise, light, energy use and water use will be part of the council’s review. “I am constantly working against clocks trying to preserve the sanity for my neighbors who want to stay," Petro said. Petro said the council will seek input from residents, experts and other stakeholders during the pause. She hopes the city will develop “an evidence-based, truth-based way to regulate an industry that could either be beneficial or harmful.” But Petro cautioned that the city may have limited ability to stop the Northpoint project. She said it is already vested and the landowners have the zoning they need. “We will struggle to even play defense,” Petro said. “The only way we can be sure things will be different is if our constituents and every other stakeholder comes to the table and finds a path forward.” Petro said the council is not inherently opposed to data centers, but is concerned about the speed of development, lack of information, and potential harm to residents, the environment and wildlife. “We are hostile to abuses of our environment and our neighbors that could make a project like this detrimental for time to come,” she said. _____

artigo.texto: 13/11/2026 A Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica) pretende apresentar uma ADI (Ação Direta de Inconstitucionalidade) no STF (Supremo Tribunal Federal) para questionar o custeio do leilão de baterias, disseram fontes à Agência iNFRA. Pelas regras atuais, os encargos da contratação dos sistemas de armazenamento serão pagos apenas pelos geradores. Mesmo com o risco de um “desgaste político”, os agentes temem que o leilão marcado para dezembro ocorra com “fragilidades regulatórias”, de acordo com interlocutores. Também está previsto que empresas associadas entrem com uma ACP (Ação Civil Pública) na Justiça pedindo a suspensão do certame até a aprovação do PL (Projeto de Lei) 3.716/2026, que compartilha os encargos com os consumidores. O objetivo, de acordo com fontes, é pressionar pela rápida tramitação do projeto no Congresso. A estratégia foi aprovada no conselho da Abeeólica há cerca de três semanas, mas foi decidido que só dariam andamento a ela após se certificarem de que o PL não seria aprovado a tempo do certame. Segundo fontes, a expectativa era que o projeto fosse debatido na reunião de líderes partidários da Câmara dos Deputados na última terça-feira (10) e votado no plenário nesta quinta-feira (12). Isso viabilizaria a apreciação no Senado na próxima semana. A matéria, no entanto, não entrou na pauta da Câmara. O leilão está previsto para 2 e 4 de dezembro. Relatório Contribui para a percepção de risco do setor a probabilidade de que outros temas do setor sejam incluídos na matéria. Isso poderia atrasar ainda mais a aprovação do texto. A avaliação de fontes é que há margem para uma tentativa de rever pontos debatidos na MP (Medida Provisória) 1.304, transformada na Lei da Reforma do Setor Elétrico (Lei 15.269/2025). O PL está sob relatoria do deputado Danilo Forte (PP-CE), próximo a pautas de agentes renováveis, mas que não são consensuais no setor e entre os parlamentares. Um dos principais temas já defendidos pelo deputado é a ampliação do ressarcimento financeiro aos geradores pelo curtailment (cortes de geração obrigatórios). Ele conseguiu aprovar uma emenda na Câmara durante a tramitação da MP 1.304, mas que foi vetada pelo presidente Lula. Outros temas que podem estar no relatório, como circula nos bastidores, são a obrigatoriedade de que projetos de hidrogênio verde contratem energia de usinas novas ou recém-construídas, além do retorno dos incentivos nos custos dos fios de transmissão para fontes renováveis. Apesar de serem pautas benéficas às eólicas, segundo fontes, a Abeeólica defende que o relatório do PL 3.716 fique livre de temas polêmicos. Isso facilitaria a aprovação de forma célere, sem colocar em risco a realização do certame na data prevista. Mudanças no edital O diretor-geral da ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica), Sandoval Feitosa, disse à imprensa que qualquer modificação legal sobre o leilão iria requerer o adiamento do certame. Segundo ele, a reguladora precisaria de prazo para ajustes no edital. No MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia), no entanto, a percepção é que o edital aprovado não exige alterações caso o custeio seja estendido aos consumidores, disseram fontes. Existe ainda a possibilidade de incluir no projeto que tramita no Congresso emenda para dispensar a ANEEL do prazo necessário para modificações no edital. Contudo, há relatos de resistências a isso. Posição do governo O governo federal evitou apoio ao PL antes das eleições, pelo risco de ter atrelado a si o discurso de aumento de custos aos consumidores de energia elétrica. No entanto, técnicos do MME estariam alinhados à proposta, de acordo com fontes. O tema também foi levado à Casa Civil, que teria solicitado aos geradores um estudo comprovando que a medida não seria prejudicial aos consumidores e de que forma contribuiria para o sistema elétrico. Segundo relatos, a avaliação é que o órgão da Presidência da República estaria mais sensibilizado à pauta. Fonte: Agência Infra

artigo.texto: Portugal has opened two tenders offering a combined 1,050 MVA of grid capacity for energy storage Of the total, standalone batteries account for 750 MVA, while renewable projects with co-located storage receive 300 MVA Applications will be accepted till December 22, 2026, according to DGEG Portugal has opened two competitive tenders offering a combined 1,050 MVA of grid connection capacity for energy storage projects as the country expands battery storage deployment. The tenders, launched by Portugal’s Directorate-General for Energy and Geology (DGEG), allocate 750 MVA for standalone battery energy storage systems (BESS) and 300 MVA for renewable power generation projects with co-located storage. Developers can apply for a minimum capacity of 50 MVA per application. There is no maximum capacity limit per applicant. Applications for both tenders must be submitted by December 22, 2026. The 750 MVA tender is designed exclusively for standalone battery storage installations across different grid connection points. Developers will bid for capacity and indicate their preferred grid connection locations. Projects must have installed storage power equivalent to at least 100% of their awarded grid injection capacity. They must also provide a minimum of four hours of storage at maximum injection power. The second 300 MVA tender is for renewable energy generation projects paired with battery storage. The storage component must have a minimum power rating equivalent to 20% of the awarded grid injection capacity. It must also provide at least four hours of storage at maximum injection power. The tender includes additional consideration for agrivoltaic projects that combine solar power generation with agricultural activities on the same land. The framework also provides financial benefits to municipalities hosting the projects. Local authorities will receive a share of auction revenues and annual compensation from project developers. The two tenders are part of Portugal’s broader efforts to strengthen electricity storage, improve grid flexibility and support renewable energy integration. Portugal’s National Energy Storage Strategy sets a target of 6.9 GW of installed storage capacity by 2030.

artigo.texto: Elon Musk Tesla’s Powercore could change how data centers get power Tesla unveiled Powercore, a solid-state transformer that could ease one of the grid’s worst bottlenecks. Tesla has unveiled Powercore, a solid-state medium voltage transformer that also handles the jobs of an inverter and a circuit breaker in a single unit. “Solid state medium voltage transformer, inverter and breaker – reliable, safe and secure,” the company’s Tesla Megapack account posted on X Tuesday, adding that the product is “Made in America” and will be “Operating 2027.” Elon Musk followed with his own post: “Advanced solid state transformers at scale from Tesla.” Tesla rates Powercore at 7.4 MW, or 9 MVA, of continuous output at 34.5 kV AC, with grid-forming support for 10 MVA of peak power. Specs shared by Sawyer Merritt list a peak efficiency of 98.86 percent, a DC range of 800 to 2,000 volts and a built-in solid-state breaker that clears faults in about 100 microseconds. Tesla has not announced pricing, a factory location or a first customer. The product fills a gap Tesla left open last year. When it introduced Megapack 3 and Megablock in September 2025, Tesla said it would build its own transformers, but shared almost nothing about them. Megablock groups four Megapack 3 units with a transformer and switchgear into a single medium voltage block, as Teslarati reported. Powercore appears to be that missing piece. A typical battery or solar project today uses low voltage inverters to turn DC into AC, then a large oil-filled transformer to step that power up to grid voltage. A solid-state unit handles both steps with power electronics, which means less equipment, a smaller footprint and no flammable oil. Grid-forming capability lets it actively help hold voltage and frequency steady rather than simply following the grid. Introducing Powercore Solid state medium voltage transformer, inverter and breaker – reliable, safe and secure 7.4 MW/9 MVA continuously at 34.5 kVac w/ grid-forming support for 10MVA of peak power Made in America. Operating 2027 https://t.co/sHxqnpWJrf — Tesla Megapack (@Tesla_Megapack) November 17, 2026 Timing is a big part of the pitch. Lead times for conventional transformers have stretched into years as AI data centers and renewable projects crowd utility interconnection queues. Tesla energy executive Max de Zegher pointed to the problem in a post Musk shared, noting that “transformers have barely changed since the 1890s: copper coils in a tank of oil,” while batteries, solar and compute all run on DC. Powercore, he wrote, delivers “one conversion and about half the losses.” Tesla has also said its Megapack supply for 2027 is nearly sold out. Tesla deployed 13.7 GWh of energy storage in the third quarter, its second best quarter on record. On Tuesday, the company also said customer solar systems deployed by Tesla Energy now generate more than twice the electricity its global operations consume each year.

artigo.texto: AI Models & Platforms LS ELECTRIC to Supply Switchgear for US AI Data Center Expansion Add Unite.AI to your preferred sources on Google Key PointsLS ELECTRIC's new $93.83 million contract is a follow-on order from an existing data… View more - LS ELECTRIC's new $93.83 million contract is a follow-on order from an existing data center customer. - Repeat awards hinge on meeting hyperscale delivery schedules across its Korea and US production sites. - LS ELECTRIC is also developing DC distribution systems at its Cheonan facility for future AI data centers. LS ELECTRIC announced on November 16, 2026, that it had signed a power-system supply contract worth approximately $93.83 million (KRW 130 billion) for a global big-tech company’s U.S. hyperscale AI data center project. The contract covers 38 kV high-voltage switchgear and low-voltage switchgear, which will be supplied sequentially for the data center’s power network. The high-voltage equipment distributes incoming electricity to individual facilities and protects equipment when power abnormalities occur. LS ELECTRIC participated in the customer’s large local data-center project from its initial construction phase. The new contract continues its high-voltage switchgear awards into the expansion phase, making it a follow-on order from an existing customer and directly connecting the supplier’s role to the project’s continued buildout. Delivery Capacity Underpins the Expansion Order LS ELECTRIC identifies time to power—the interval before a data center receives electricity and can begin operating—as a central competitive concern in AI infrastructure. It attributes its repeat awards to meeting the customer’s quality requirements and hyperscale delivery schedules from the project’s early stages. Its named production bases are the Cheongju smart factory in South Korea, LS ELECTRIC Utah and the Bastrop Campus in Texas. The company presents that footprint as the foundation of its delivery competitiveness. For this expansion order, the delivery requirement has a concrete operational dimension: the equipment contract depends on industrial capacity and scheduling as well as product specifications. Recent Contracts Span the Power System A separate October 2026 announcement disclosed a KRW 168.9 billion ($125.23 million) long-term agreement with another U.S. big-tech company covering 2027–2028. The announced amount represents products scheduled for delivery in 2027, while the scale of the 2028 business remains subject to further discussions. That agreement covers 38 kV high-voltage switchgear. Possible additional supplies of low-voltage switchgear, distribution transformers and ring main units remain under discussion, creating a potential broader equipment package around the committed deliveries. LS ELECTRIC announced on October 1, 2026 a KRW 181.2 billion ($133.41 million) contract for 345 kV extra-high-voltage transformers. Deliveries are scheduled in phases to nine substations through 2030 for a North American hyperscale AI data center project. Read together, the company’s records describe work across both data-center distribution equipment and the higher-voltage infrastructure required to power large AI projects. AC Business and DC Development Beyond conventional alternating-current (AC) distribution, LS ELECTRIC is pursuing next-generation direct-current (DC) systems for AI data centers. It describes its Cheonan DC Factory as the first manufacturing site to commercialize DC distribution. Solid-state transformers, solid-state circuit breakers and energy-storage systems are used there to test next-generation grids and data-center environments. The contract highlights the commercial connection between power delivery and AI compute: new capacity cannot be energized until electrical equipment is in place. LS ELECTRIC’s repeat role ties its switchgear business to that schedule, while the Cheonan test site provides a route into future DC designs as hyperscale projects expand and their power architecture evolves.

artigo.texto: Superando desafios e abraçando o superciclo de investimentos em data centers. Segundo Do Thanh Thang, Diretor de Otimização de Operações para o Leste Asiático da Schneider Electric, os data centers em todo o mundo estão apresentando um forte crescimento. Este também é o momento em que o mercado está entrando em um super ciclo de investimentos. O rápido desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial ( IA ), da computação em nuvem e da economia digital está transformando os centros de dados, de meras infraestruturas de armazenamento em plataformas essenciais para a economia digital. À medida que a IA se desenvolve, a demanda por poder computacional, armazenamento, conectividade e processamento de dados aumenta, exigindo que a infraestrutura dos centros de dados seja moderna, flexível e escalável. Em seu discurso no recente seminário "Data Centers no Vietnã: Infraestrutura Estratégica para a Era da IA", organizado pelo jornal Industry and Trade Newspaper, o Sr. Ha Dang Son, Presidente do Centro de Pesquisa em Energia e Crescimento Verde, afirmou que a tendência de transformação digital e a revolução digital são necessidades urgentes para o Vietnã e a região no período vindouro. Segundo pesquisadores do mundo todo, o mercado de data centers e serviços relacionados à digitalização e inteligência artificial na região Ásia-Pacífico representa atualmente cerca de 34% da demanda global, sendo que a ASEAN sozinha responde por aproximadamente metade desse valor. A tendência de digitalização e desenvolvimento de data centers já está presente em países vizinhos como Singapura , Tailândia e Malásia. No entanto, o Vietnã é considerado um dos países de crescimento mais rápido da região. “Isso também representa um desafio significativo para o investimento em infraestrutura e a preparação de serviços relacionados para garantir o desenvolvimento. Os investimentos em data centers devem assegurar sustentabilidade e competitividade com outros países da região”, afirmou Ha Dang Son. O Sr. Ha Dang Son analisou que, com o aumento da densidade e da eficiência dos centros de dados, a densidade energética por rack disparou em comparação com o passado, chegando a ser de 3 a 4 vezes maior. Para modelos específicos, o nível é ainda mais alto (podendo atingir 1 MW para uma única unidade de gerenciamento de dados). "Isso levanta a questão de como ainda podemos criar centros de dados altamente eficientes, garantindo simultaneamente um fornecimento de energia sustentável que esteja alinhado com a tendência verde emergente", afirmou o Sr. Son. Além disso, o sistema de refrigeração (que representa aproximadamente 20-30% do consumo de energia) também precisa ser otimizado. Este é um problema relacionado ao planejamento e à seleção dos padrões mais adequados às características específicas do Vietnã, visto que cada país terá características diferentes dependendo da localização do data center. Do ponto de vista de uma unidade de investimento e operação de data centers, o Sr. Nguyen Tien Long, Diretor Adjunto de Negócios da FPT International Telecommunications Co., Ltd. (FTI), uma subsidiária da FPT Telecom, identificou três tendências em mudança nos sistemas de data center que atendem à IA. Você também pode gostar Em primeiro lugar, a eficiência energética por unidade de área, bem como por utilização de racks, aumentou significativamente nos últimos tempos. Em segundo lugar, o investimento em sistemas de refrigeração é necessário para atender às demandas de sistemas de computação de alto desempenho. O Sr. Long explicou que estávamos acostumados com data centers tradicionais que utilizavam sistemas de refrigeração a ar. No entanto, para data centers de alta densidade, precisamos migrar para um novo sistema chamado Refrigeração Líquida. Em terceiro lugar, esses sistemas exigem velocidades de conexão muito altas. Antes, nos conectávamos a 1G, 10G ou até mesmo 100G, mas agora precisamos de conexões de 800G ou 1 Terabit. Segundo o Sr. Long, os atuais centros de dados do Vietnã utilizam principalmente refrigeração a ar. Portanto, o desafio é a modernização para um novo sistema de refrigeração líquida, bem como a atualização de outros componentes dentro do centro de dados. Isso apresenta desafios técnicos significativos e exige um cronograma de implementação rigoroso para atender às demandas dos clientes e do mercado. 60% dos novos centros de dados serão destinados a aplicações de IA. A respeito desse assunto, o Sr. Do Thanh Thang, Diretor de Otimização de Operações para o Leste Asiático da Schneider Electric, afirmou o forte desenvolvimento de data centers em todo o mundo. Segundo o Sr. Thang, estamos em um superciclo de investimentos em data centers. O relatório mais recente da JLL, do início de 2026, indica que o mundo deverá adicionar aproximadamente 100 GW de data centers globalmente entre agora e 2030, o que representa uma duplicação da capacidade. Desse total, 60% dos novos data centers atenderão aplicações de IA. “Em países vizinhos, já surgiram grandes data centers (também conhecidos como fábricas de IA). Essas fábricas de IA são projetadas especificamente para atender a todas as necessidades ao longo do ciclo de vida da aplicação de IA, desde o treinamento e o refinamento até a consulta e a inferência”, explicou o Sr. Thang. Como parceira global em tecnologia de energia, a Schneider Electric observa um forte impacto dessa onda de investimentos nas necessidades de fornecimento de energia, sistemas de refrigeração e gerenciamento de energia para data centers. Você também pode gostar O Sr. Do Thanh Thang salientou que a densidade de potência normal atual ronda os 5 a 10 kW por rack, mas que será muito superior no futuro. Os fabricantes já estão mesmo a considerar um cenário de 1 MW por rack. Além disso, os centros de dados de IA operam de maneira muito diferente dos centros de dados convencionais. Por exemplo, o treinamento de IA exige a mobilização de um número muito grande de chips de GPU, às vezes milhares funcionando simultanea

artigo.texto: AI is burning through compute and power, and the Anthropic IPO, Nvidia leadership questions, and fresh regulatory scrutiny have pushed that reality into sharp focus for investors. Money chasing AI is not just flowing into model developers; it is pulling attention toward the digital plumbing behind them. This article explains how three US stocks exposed to that story could either benefit from, or be hurt by, this surge in demand. The stocks covered below are just a sample, and the full screen surfaced another 65 US-listed companies tied into data centers, power gear, cooling and related infrastructure with equally compelling stories that are not included here. To analyze, compare and identify your own highest conviction angles on this theme, head straight into the US Data Center and Power Infrastructure Benefiting from AI Compute Growth screener. Overview: Carrier Global provides large scale HVAC, cooling, energy management and refrigeration systems for buildings and transport, including data center thermal solutions worldwide. Operations: Carrier Global generates most revenue from Climate Solutions Americas at about US$11.2b, with Europe, Asia Pacific and transport adding roughly US$11.6b. Market Cap: US$44.3b Carrier Global matters for this AI power and cooling screen because its industrial HVAC and energy platforms touch exactly the thermal bottlenecks investors are watching. The analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St describes how that data center push is starting to reshape the story. "Carrier Global is building a larger presence in AI and data center cooling, with about $2 billion of 2026 data center revenue already in backlog, an over $8 billion company backlog that is heavily tied to commercial and data center projects, and a dedicated U.S. manufacturing site planned to roughly double Americas data center capacity, which can support future revenue and earnings." What happens to Carrier Global's earnings profile if that growth engine collides with one unresolved pressure on profitability and capital intensity? If that tension is on your mind, read the full narrative for Carrier Global to see how AI data center demand, capital needs, and profitability pressures could be decoupling. Overview: Vertiv Holdings Co builds the power, thermal management and life cycle services that keep AI-focused data centers and digital infrastructure running worldwide. Operations: Vertiv generates about US$8.8b of revenue in the Americas, with Asia Pacific contributing roughly US$3.1b and Europe, Middle East and Africa about US$2.7b. Market Cap: US$77.8b Vertiv sits right in the AI plumbing story, supplying the high density power and liquid cooling hardware that lets hyperscale and colocation operators turn Anthropic style compute commitments into live capacity. According to pdixit1, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community, the order book already reflects that shift in a significant way. "The liquid cooling market is already growing at roughly 20-30% annually as hyperscalers like Microsoft, Google, and Amazon race to build AI infrastructure. Vertiv's Q4 2025 organic orders surged 252% year-over-year, and its $15 billion backlog is equivalent to roughly 1.5 years of trailing revenue." An open question is what happens to Vertiv's margin profile if a single unseen pressure in how AI customers deploy that backlog begins to change. If that deployment risk is what concerns you, the full narrative for Vertiv Holdings Co explains how Vertiv could convert its backlog into accelerating value or encounter real roadblocks. Overview: SPX Technologies supplies engineered HVAC cooling systems and related technologies that help manage heat in data centers and other critical infrastructure. Operations: SPX Technologies generates about US$1.8b from HVAC solutions and roughly US$767 million from Detection and Measurement products, with most turnover in the United States. Market Cap: US$7.8b SPX Technologies matters for this screener because its cooling hardware touches the thermal limits of AI data centers, and John_Eric, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community, captures how quickly that part of the story has scaled. "Its HVAC backlog, meaning the confirmed, contracted, not-yet-delivered future revenue sitting on the books, grew 59% organically in a single year, to $919 million. Management just raised its own estimate of the data-center capacity it can eventually ship to $1.1 billion annually, up from $750 million." artigo.texto: State environmental regulators have resumed reviewing data center permits, bringing an end to an earlier directive from Gov. Greg Abbott ordering a pause on permit approvals related to data center projects. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality received notice on Friday from Abbott’s office that officials at the state’s electric grid had completed gathering information on potential community impacts from data centers — one of multiple issues Abbott asked grid officials and electricity regulators to evaluate. “The agency has resumed its normal permit review process and will evaluate applications under all applicable state and federal laws and regulations,” TCEQ spokesperson Laura Lopez said in a written statement. In August, Abbott had called on the Electric Reliability Council of Texas and electricity regulators to audit all data centers trying to connect to the grid, as well as gather information about tax incentives, power use, water use and potential neighborhood impacts. Abbott at that time paused approval of any grid interconnections for data centers while the audit was completed. In his Sept. 21 letter to TCEQ calling for the environmental permitting pause, Abbott said the agency needed to wait until ERCOT “completes its review.” Environmental advocates at Public Citizen, responding to the news of the resumed permits, called on TCEQ commissioners to resign. “The TCEQ is asserting that ERCOT has concluded its assessment of the community impacts of data centers, and without sharing those results with communities or detailing how the TCEQ will incorporate the findings into permitting decisions, agency leadership has begun unilaterally issuing data center permits,” said Kathryn Guerra, the TCEQ watchdog campaign director for Public Citizen, in a statement. Intense opposition to data centers had been growing all year in communities across the state, where Democrats and Republicans alike fought projects they worried would destabilize the electric grid, lead to more pollution from new gas-fueled power generators and guzzle up water in a state with serious drought concerns. TCEQ handles permits related to air pollution at facilities and stormwater runoff on construction sites. The agency faced criticism in October from Public Citizen and FracTracker Alliance. The groups noticed that some data center-related construction permits were being cleared anyway — counter to Abbott’s order. TCEQ said it suspended the permits and then it shut down its entire automated electronic filing system and required physical applications be submitted for staff to review. Then in a staggering upset on Nov. 3, Abbott lost his reelection to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who on the campaign trail vowed to keep data center approvals paused until legislators pass new state laws. Neither Abbott’s office nor Hinojosa’s media team on Tuesday immediately responded to a request for comment. “Texans are tired of this political theatre,” said Sam Law, researcher at FracTracker Alliance, in a written statement shared by Public Citizen. “We need real leadership, transparency, and a true moratorium on data center development.” ERCOT provided an update on its review of community impacts to electric regulators at the Public Utility Commission of Texas on Nov. 5. ERCOT reported receiving responses from 93% of 465 projects, which provided enough information for “a statistically meaningful analysis for the final report.” ERCOT officials plan to report their full findings to the PUC on Dec. 10 and discuss them at the next PUC open meeting Dec. 17.

artigo.texto: St. Cloud is latest Minnesota city to consider new rules for data centers Go Deeper. Create an account or log in to save stories. Like this? Thanks for liking this story! We have added it to a list of your favorite stories. Quick Read St. Cloud officials will hear from residents Monday night about possible new restrictions for data centers. St. Cloud hasn't yet received any proposals from developers who want to build a large data center, as other Minnesota communities have, but the City Council is considering adopting an ordinance so it's prepared for any future requests. The proposed rules would separate smaller data centers from hyperscale facilities — those with at least 2,000 computer servers housed in buildings larger than 10,000 square feet, or that use at least 50 megawatts of electricity. Under the ordinance, hyperscale data centers could only be located in the city's industrial district, at least a quarter mile from residential areas, and would require a conditional use permit. They must be connected to the city’s water system. Turn Up Your Support MPR News helps you turn down the noise and build shared understanding. Turn up your support for this public resource and keep trusted journalism accessible to all. Data center developers also would have to study noise, vibration, environmental and community impacts. They would also be required to incorporate sustainability measures, including water conservation and renewable energy. After Monday’s public hearing, the council could vote on the ordinance or postpone action. Why Minnesota is attracting data centers Tech companies are eyeing Minnesota for data centers because of its relatively cool climate and available land, water and electricity. More than a dozen large projects have been proposed around the state. Meta is already building a hyperscale data center in Rosemount. Google plans to build massive data center campuses in Hermantown and Pine Island, although environmental groups are fighting those projects in court. Many Minnesotans have raised concerns about the impacts of a mega-sized facilities, including noise and light pollution, water and energy use. Proponents say they will bring construction jobs, property tax revenue and other economic benefits. Some of St. Cloud’s neighboring cities, including Waite Park and St. Joseph, have passed one-year moratoriums on new data centers. Others, including Sartell, have adopted similar regulations. Monticello, a city about 25 miles southeast of St. Cloud, adopted a data center ordinance in April. Its City Council will consider at a Nov. 30 meeting whether to allow a hyperscale project to move forward. In Minneapolis, a temporary moratorium that blocks most new data centers, with some exceptions downtown, expires Nov. 21. On Thursday, the Minneapolis City Council narrowly approved new data center regulations on a 7-6 vote, including a controversial proposal to require council approval of any new data center. The Minneapolis City Council plans to reconvene Nov. 20 to address a possible veto — one day before the moratorium ends.

artigo.texto: Maharashtra’s emissions trading scheme is being presented as a way to make industrial pollution control financially meaningful rather than relying only on penalties and restrictions. Announced at an Impact Assembly in Mumbai organised by The Earthshot Prize, the proposed expansion will initially cover Maharashtra before being extended to Rajasthan, according to a report by Loksatta – Mumbai. The initiative is expected by its proponents to help improve air quality for about 21 crore people across the two states. The central idea is to place an overall limit on the pollution that participating factories can emit and allow permits linked to unused pollution capacity to be traded. A factory that emits less than its permitted level could sell its surplus allowance to another industrial unit. In theory, this creates two simultaneous pressures: cleaner factories can gain financially, while factories that continue to emit more face a higher economic cost. That design changes the logic of industrial regulation. Conventional enforcement generally focuses on setting standards, inspecting facilities and penalising violations. An emissions market adds a price signal to those requirements. The purpose is not to make pollution acceptable, but to make pollution reduction financially valuable and continued high emissions financially burdensome. Whether that shift produces cleaner air will depend on how the cap is set, how emissions are measured and how consistently the system is enforced. The supplied announcement does not provide those operational details. The model is based on Gujarat’s experience, which the report describes as a successful experiment and as the world’s first system to establish an economic trading mechanism around industrial pollution. Under the model, factories receive an overall pollution limit. Units that remain below their limits can trade their unused permissions, while units that exceed their own reduction capacity can bear the cost of acquiring additional permissions. The arrangement is intended to reward investment in pollution-control equipment and production systems. A factory that reduces particulate emissions could potentially create a tradable surplus, giving it a financial return in addition to the environmental benefit. The incentive is therefore different from a rule that simply requires every unit to install the same equipment or meet the same reduction pathway. It attempts to direct reductions towards facilities that can achieve them more efficiently, although the source material does not specify how the Maharashtra programme will identify those facilities. Particulate matter is the immediate pollution concern identified in the announcement. Fine particles released by industrial activity contribute to deteriorating air quality, and industrial development can intensify that problem when emissions controls do not keep pace with production. The Maharashtra proposal thus links industrial policy with urban and regional public health. The impact will not be confined to factory premises: emissions move through the air sheds in which workers, nearby communities and urban residents live. This is particularly important for a state with large industrial and urban regions, but the announcement does not identify the districts, industrial clusters or categories of factories that will enter the first phase. It also does not state the number of facilities to be covered, the initial emissions cap, the particulate pollutants to be traded or the date on which trading will begin. Those details are not peripheral. They will determine whether the scheme operates as a meaningful reduction programme or merely as a compliance mechanism with limited effect on actual air quality. The institutional arrangement announced so far places the Emissions Market Accelerator in a supporting role. The organisation will assist with expanding the Gujarat model to Maharashtra and later Rajasthan. The report does not identify the precise responsibilities of the Maharashtra government, the Maharashtra Pollution Control Board or other regulatory bodies in administering the market. It also does not specify who will issue allowances, verify factory emissions, maintain the trading platform or impose consequences for inaccurate reporting. Those administrative functions are central to the credibility of any pollution market. A tradable allowance has value only when the underlying emissions data are reliable and when the total quantity of allowances is controlled. If a factory’s emissions are under-measured, its apparent compliance may not reflect its actual pollution. If the overall cap is too generous, trading can continue without delivering a significant reduction. If enforcement is inconsistent, firms that invest in cleaner technology may not receive the expected economic advantage. The announcement’s reference to approximately 21 crore people is a measure of the proposed geographic reach rather than evidence of an achieved health outcome. That figure combines the populations of Maharashtra and Rajasthan as the scheme is expanded. The supplied material does not include baseline air-quality data, projected particulate reductions, health indicators or an implementation timetable. It therefore establishes the scale of the policy ambition, but not yet its measurable environmental performance. The sequencing is also significant. Maharashtra is to receive the first phase of the expansion, followed by Rajasthan. This suggests that the programme will be adapted across states rather than introduced simultaneously. However, the report does not explain whether both states will use the same emissions limits, monitoring standards or trading rules. Differences in industrial composition, regulatory capacity and pollution sources could affect how the model works in each jurisdiction. artigo.texto: ANOTHER TOWN may be taking the first steps toward its own comprehensive data center bylaw amid a wider trend of towns adopting effective prohibitions on large-scale data center facilities. The Tewksbury Select Board has an item on its agenda Tuesday for a discussion on a data center bylaw with little information beyond that. The agenda item comes after residents spoke during recent Select Board meetings about the desire to implement Tewksbury’s own moratorium on data centers. When resident Sandra Poole spoke during the Nov. 4 Select Board meeting, she noted that she had drafted a data center moratorium policy herself. She expressed concern that the town could find itself in a similar situation to the Hillman Street battery storage site proposal, which drew backlash from surrounding residents and ultimately fell through earlier this year after the company withdrew its application. Board members Eric Ryder and Mark Kratman both noted that they had wanted to make it through the special Town Meeting last month before taking this issue up, and suggested that the conversation starting now would allow a bylaw proposal to make it to the annual Town Meeting next spring. “I have looked at what some of our surrounding communities have done, and it is something I intend on discussing with the town manager and other board members as well to get their inputs,” Ryder said during the Nov. 4 meeting. It will take some time before we can say what form a data center ban or moratorium would take in Tewksbury, if there is a big enough desire for such a thing at all, but if the town follows the same route as other nearby communities it could be one less option for a location for large scale data centers. In its fall Town Meeting last month, Chelmsford Town Meeting representatives voted to impose a total ban on medium- and large-scale data centers, leaving room for smaller data centers already commonly in use. This Saturday, Wilmington’s special Town Meeting will consider a similar prohibition. Data centers have been around in some form since the widespread adoption of the internet, but as the demand increases for larger facilities increases in our still young artificial intelligence era, so too do the concerns about the resource draw required by these facilities, and the effects they may have on the surrounding area via pollution or persistent noise. Notably, Tewksbury already has a definition for data center in its bylaws, but it is very much behind on the times. In Tewksbury’s zoning bylaws, a data center is defined as “A physical location that stores computing machines and their related hardware equipment. It contains the computing infrastructure that IT systems require, such as servers, data storage drives, and network equipment. It is the physical facility that stores a company’s digital data.” There is no mention there of the physical footprint of the facility, its water use, energy requirements, or any of the things people have been expressing concern over when it comes to data centers in the age of AI. If there is a desire to prohibit large data centers in Tewksbury, or any community without explicit policies toward them in 2026, those factors will be the likely place to start. — Peter Currier Will another one bite the dust? AFTER DRACUT finally caved and approved MBTA Communities zoning, Wilmington remains the last community in Greater Lowell to still be out of compliance with the state law. Dracut’s decision last week followed a similar change of heart from Tewksbury last month as the number of noncompliant towns ticks down. On Saturday Wilmington will consider effectively the same zoning overlay Town Meeting has considered twice before, the only difference being that the town has had the opportunity to be hit with the consequences of noncompliance, namely through lost grant funding and the potential for the state to come in and set its own zoning. Instead of losing any say in the matter, Wilmington is going through the “paper compliance” strategy, where a zoning overlay is created in areas where there is not likely to be any new multifamily housing built in the near future. The slow capitulation of the noncompliant communities also comes after voters in Massachusetts very narrowly rejected a ballot measure to allow single-family homes to be built on lots as small as 5,000 square feet. That kind of measure wouldn’t have solved the housing crisis on its own by any means, but paired with other solutions, and cities and towns not pretending like the housing crisis is every other community’s problem but their own, it could have helped. Instead we get state mandates that anger large parts of the population and don’t actually accomplish what they set out to do because they made too big of a loophole. — Peter Currier It is TIF season in Lowell A WEEK after the Lowell City Council approved a tax increment financing agreement with Draper, TIFs are on the agenda again on Tuesday in the form of a motion by Councilor Corey Robinson and Mayor Erik Gitschier. artigo.texto: According to a new SEIA & Benchmark Mineral Intelligence report US energy storage installations have exceeded 200 GWh Utility-scale projects accounted for 12.2 GWh of Q3 additions, led by Texas, Arizona, and California Analysts forecast cumulative installations to reach 708 GWh by 2030 The US energy storage market has crossed 200 GWh of cumulative installed capacity, as battery deployments continue to expand across all segments, as per a new report. The total 215.9 GWh includes 14.3 GWh of new capacity in Q3 2026, taking installations during the first nine months of the year to 48.3 GWh. The figures are from the U.S. Energy Storage Market Outlook Q4 2026 (ESMO), released by the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. According to the report, utility-scale projects accounted for the bulk of Q3 installations, adding 12.2 GWh. Three GW-scale projects came online during the quarter, supporting growth in the utility-scale segment. Commercial and industrial (C&I) storage contributed 1.3 GWh, while residential systems added 746 MWh. The report said battery energy storage system (BESS) installations in Q3 at 14.3 GWh remained flat quarter-on-quarter (QoQ), but increased 23% year-on-year (YoY) for the first three quarters of 2026. Overall US installations were up 20% YoY during the January-September period. Texas led utility-scale storage deployment through Q3, adding 12.3 GWh. Arizona followed with 7.7 GWh, while California recorded 6.8 GWh. The report also highlighted the impact of solar and energy storage deployment on electricity prices. According to SEIA analysis, the growth of these technologies helped reduce average wholesale electricity prices by 42% in Texas and 51% in California between summer 2021 and summer 2026 (see Solar & Storage Cut Wholesale Electricity Prices In CAISO & ERCOT). Eleven states had already exceeded their previous annual energy storage installation records by the end of Q3, despite three months remaining in 2026. These included Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama, and Illinois. As states move from targets to centralized procurements, Benchmark Minerals Senior Analyst Pete Tillotson says energy storage pipelines are growing across utility mandates and bulk capacity contracts, thanks to “investment appetite and flexibility requirements”. In 2026, analysts project the annual installed BESS capacity of the US to reach 73.8 GWh, up 26% from 59 GWh installed in 2025 which was an increase of 30% over the previous year, comprising both utility and behind-the-meter (BTM) installations. This implies around 26 GWh of new additions in Q4 2026. SEIA and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence have raised their forecast for cumulative installations by 2030 by 3.7% to 708 GWh across grid-connected and behind-the-meter (BTM) applications. Annual installations are projected to exceed 129 GWh by 2030. Along with installations, domestic manufacturing is also seeing an uptick as per the report. Ultim Cells of LGES and General Motors began Lithium-ion Phosphate (LFP) commenced cell production for stationary storage in Tennessee in July 2026, while Samsung SDI opened LFP production at its StarPlus Energy facility in Indiana in October. This brought the total US battery cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, a 50% increase, according to the report. Battery module manufacturing capacity exceeded 109 GWh following the opening of an additional facility in Q3. Analysts forecast that LFP will account for 92% of lithium-ion BESS deployments in 2026, up from 77% in 2023. Lithium-ion batteries are expected to account for over 97% of all BESS installations in 2026. Other technologies, including flow batteries, sodium-ion and lead acid batteries, continue to lag behind lithium-ion. Recently US flow battery and sodium-ion cell manufacturer ESS Tech filed for relief under Chapter 7 (see US Battery Maker ESS Tech Files For Chapter 7 Bankruptcy). The complete report is available for purchase on Benchmark Mineral Intelligence website. Meanwhile on the policy front, following the results of the mid-term elections in the US, SEIA said more than 300 solar and storage companies recently urged Congressional leaders to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). The industry says the legislation could accelerate storage deployment, reduce project costs, lower prices, and improve access to affordable electricity.

artigo.texto: Empresa suíça apresentou em Londres a estratégia para que a computação de IA deixe de pressionar a rede elétrica e passe a ajudar a sustentá-la. E se o prédio que mais consome energia de uma cidade pudesse, em certos momentos, devolver eletricidade para a rede? É essa a aposta que a Hitachi Energy, empresa suíça de tecnologia para redes elétricas, levou ao seu Investor Day, evento para investidores realizado em Londres em novembro de 2026. A ideia é transformar os data centers de inteligência artificial, hoje vistos como grandes consumidores, em contribuidores do sistema elétrico. O pano de fundo é uma corrida. A computação de IA pode ser instalada em pouco tempo, mas as usinas, linhas e subestações que a alimentam levam muito mais para ficar prontas. Esse descompasso é o problema que a empresa quer atacar. Um consumo que não para de crescer Segundo a Hitachi Energy, a demanda global por eletricidade deve quase dobrar até 2050, empurrada pela eletrificação de transportes, edifícios e indústrias. Os data centers entram como um acelerador extra: a estimativa é que consumam cerca de 950 terawatt-hora por ano até 2030, quase o dobro do nível atual e mais do que o consumo anual de eletricidade do Japão. Para dar conta disso, a Agência Internacional de Energia calcula que o mundo precisará construir ou modernizar aproximadamente 80 milhões de quilômetros de linhas de energia nos próximos 25 anos. É o equivalente a toda a rede global em operação hoje. Como um data center vira fornecedor de energia No modelo defendido pela empresa, o data center não depende só de uma grande conexão com a rede. Ele combina geração no próprio local, armazenamento de energia, eletrônica de potência (equipamentos que controlam e convertem a corrente elétrica) e gestão inteligente de consumo. Quando a geração local supera a demanda dos computadores, o excedente pode ser exportado. Esses sistemas também podem prestar serviços técnicos à rede, como resposta de frequência, regulação de tensão e suporte de potência reativa, o que ajuda a integrar mais energia renovável, que oscila conforme sol e vento. Para quem opera data centers, a empresa vê acesso mais rápido à energia, uso mais enxuto de capital, maior resiliência e novas receitas com venda de eletricidade e serviços de rede, sujeitas às condições de mercado de cada local. A parceria com a Ansaldo e o truque das frequências A solução nasce de uma parceria estratégica recém-anunciada com a Ansaldo Energia. A Ansaldo entra com turbinas a gás e geração; a Hitachi Energy, com transformadores, equipamentos de alta tensão, eletrônica de potência, armazenamento e automação de rede. Uma peça central é o conversor estático de frequência. Ele permite que quem gera e quem recebe a eletricidade operem em frequências diferentes. Na prática, turbogeradores de 50 Hz da Ansaldo poderiam atender mercados de 60 Hz, como os Estados Unidos, sem redesenhar a turbina. Segundo a Hitachi Energy, o princípio já foi testado em larga escala: desde 2014, uma instalação de 413 MW na Alemanha converte energia de 50 Hz em 16 2/3 Hz para a rede ferroviária da Deutsche Bahn. Combinada a armazenamento e controles avançados, a eletrônica de potência também ajuda a lidar com as variações bruscas de carga típicas da computação de IA. As metas financeiras para 2030 Segundo a Hitachi Energy, a empresa busca crescimento anual composto de receita na casa dos 15% entre os anos fiscais de 2024 e 2030, com margem EBITA ajustada de 19% a 21%. A carteira de pedidos deve se aproximar de US$ 100 bilhões, sustentando receitas anuais de cerca de US$ 38 bilhões. Para o ano fiscal de 2026, a projeção é de receita de US$ 23,6 bilhões e margem EBITA ajustada de 15,7%. A companhia estima que clientes industriais e data centers representem uma oportunidade de mercado anual de US$ 130 bilhões até 2030. Para sustentar o crescimento, executa um programa global de investimentos de US$ 9 bilhões em fábricas, engenharia e tecnologia, e persegue retorno sobre o capital investido de 30% a 40%. Elevou ainda a meta de contribuição da IA em suas próprias operações para mais de US$ 350 milhões anuais no EBITA ajustado até 2030, e quer ampliar serviços digitais, como manutenção preditiva, com a plataforma HMAX. O que isso pode significar para a Amazônia A pauta é global, mas o debate chega à região. Data centers exigem energia firme e abundante, e a Amazônia tem rede em que muitas comunidades ainda dependem de geração isolada. A discussão de como integrar geração local, armazenamento e serviços de estabilidade à rede é a mesma que atravessa os sistemas da região, onde fontes renováveis precisam conviver com a necessidade de estabilidade. O material da empresa não cita projetos na Amazônia, mas o modelo mostra uma tendência: quem planeja infraestrutura digital precisará planejar junto a energia que a sustenta, e a forma como isso for feito definirá quem se beneficia, as comunidades do entorno ou apenas o próprio data center. Os próximos passos serão acompanhados nos resultados trimestrais da companhia e na implantação das primeiras soluções integradas com a Ansaldo Energia, que dirão se a promessa de data centers como ativos da rede sai do papel até 2030. artigo.texto: San Francisco lawmakers will have a busy, varied agenda this week as they consider legislation on issues ranging from hotel workers’ ability to sue their employers over health issues to restrictions on data centers, along with hearings on traffic safety and revitalizing Market Street. Meanwhile, commissions review surveillance policy and the state of cleanup at the former Hunters Point shipyard. El Niño, data centers, and traffic safety One of the first events on this week’s calendar is a Monday meeting of the city’s Disaster Council, chaired by Mayor Daniel Lurie and Department of Emergency Management Executive Director Mary Ellen Carroll, to review preparations for anticipated extreme weather events associated with El Niño. The meeting comes as officials consider the potential for heavier rainfall, flooding, and other weather-related disruptions from the climate pattern, and Lurie’s declaration of a city emergency last month, to expedite department response. The council includes the heads of the Police and Fire departments, Public Health, Public Works, the Port, the Municipal Transportation Agency and other city departments. A presentation for the meeting obtained by The Voice outlines the roles of different departments to coordinate preparedness, protect the city’s waterfront, drainage systems, transport, and public spaces from flooding, and generally “mitigate what we can and prepare to respond to impacts we cannot prevent.” Later that day, the Supervisors’ Land Use Committee considers items related to the interim moratorium on data centers, including a move to extend the freeze for another 10 months. The debate comes amid growing scrutiny of the potential environmental and land-use consequences of data centers, including their substantial electricity and water requirements. The committee will likely refer the extension and other items to the full board for approval on Tuesday; as an extension of emergency legislation, it will require nine votes for passage. The committee will also reopen a hearing convened by Board President Rafael Mandelman, along with colleagues Stephen Sherrill and Danny Sauter, on traffic enforcement and street safety. The hearing was originally convened in 2022, when it revealed significant deficits in enforcement, including a 97 percent decline in citations between 2014 and 2022, with less than half issued for the five violations most commonly associated with serious collisions. Subsequent meetings have found little improvement, and a 2025 Civil Grand Jury report found that police failed to prioritize traffic safety and had inadequate staffing. Health Commission reviews Hunters Point cleanup Also on Monday, the Health Commission will hear a presentation from the Department of Public Health on the Hunters Point Naval Shipyard. The presentation, by Health Officer Susan Philip and other department officials, will cover remediation and restoration updates, health promotion in Bayview-Hunters Point, community outreach and regulatory oversight. The presentation includes updates on the July 2026 vegetation fire at the shipyard’s Parcel E-2 landfill, which burned an estimated two to three acres and damaged monitoring equipment and stormwater controls. The Navy subsequently repaired the damaged systems, while state regulators and the Health Department monitored the response. Full board: Strengthening the Healthy Buildings Ordinance Set for approval on first reading at Tuesday’s Board of Supervisors meeting is a Covid-era ordinance requiring hotels to follow specified cleaning and disease-prevention practices, including frequent cleaning of high-contact common areas. A proposed amendment would allow hotel employees and their unions to sue hotels for civil penalties and other remedies. The bill is sponsored by District 11 Supervisor Chyanne Chen, with Mandelman and colleagues Connie Chan, Shamann Walton and Jackie Fielder as cosponsors. After being held on ice at the Rules Committee since April, it was revived with amendments earlier this month. In a Nov. 14 oped in the Chronicle, Lynn S. Mohrfeld, president and CEO of the California Hotel and Lodging Association, criticized the proposal as expanding outdated pandemic-era requirements. The group has also placed ads on social media to coincide with the vote. Budget Committee: Can relocating courts jumpstart Mid-Market? On Wednesday, the supervisors’ Budget and Finance Committee will consider a bill sponsored by District 6 member Matt Dorsey and almost all his colleagues to enable “Sober Spaces” by increasing availability of public facilities such as community rooms to recovery groups at no cost, along with a fund to support such meetings when hosted by private nonprofit-owned facilities. Dorsey will also preside over a hearing on how to use city-owned assets to help revitalize Market Street. One presentation associated with the hearing explores the leveraging of courthouses for economic impact, and Dorsey has floated the idea of moving the Hall of Justice and related offices to the struggling Mid- Market area. Police Commission: Surveillance cameras Meanwhile the Police Commission will hear a briefing on on its live monitoring of surveillance cameras owned by private entities and other non-city organizations. Current city laws allow officers to access private camera feeds in emergencies involving imminent danger, certain significant public-safety events and active criminal investigations, with restrictions. They were enacted after a controversy in 2020 over the practice during the George Floyd protests. The department’s presentation reports that all requests for live monitoring from the third quarter of 2023 through the first half of 2026 were approved. During the first six months of this year, SFPD made 11 requests, involving 40 hours and 58 minutes of monitoring, and reported 10 arrests. artigo.texto: O que são mega data centers, onde estão os projetos no Brasil e por que precisamos de leis rigorosas para proteger o povo e a natureza das Big Techs. A era da Inteligência Artificial (IA) virou uma corrida tecnológica que exige cada vez mais territórios, recursos e dados. Mas dá tempo de agir antes que os danos se tornem irreversíveis. No Brasil, mega projetos das gigantes da tecnologia avançam em meio a isenção de impostos, enquanto comunidades e consumidores enfrentam os prejuízos. “Antes de seguir expandindo os data centers que só aumentam os lucros bilionários das Big Techs, o Brasil deve saber o custo e definir as regras para que o povo brasileiro não pague a conta dos impactos” explica Julia Catão, especialista em Tecnologia do Greenpeace Brasil. O que são Mega Data Centers? São centros de dados de hiperescala que concentram milhões de servidores para processar, armazenar e transmitir enormes volumes de dados, podendo consumir energia equivalente a países inteiros, sobrecarregando as redes elétricas locais e milhões de litros de água potável. A principal diferença está no tamanho e na capacidade: os data centers operam os serviços digitais que usamos no dia a dia (enviar mensagens, assistir a vídeos e acessar plataformas); já os mega data centers são instalações computacionais de escala industrial e atendem sobretudo às Big Techs para desenvolvimento de IA. Quais os impactos dos Mega Data Centers? Diferente de estruturas menores, os mega data centers causam danos de proporção industrial e prejudicam principalmente a população local: - Aumento na conta de luz: usam a rede local e elevam os custos da energia nas residências – nos EUA, as tarifas chegaram a triplicar para mercados, custo que é repassado aos consumidores. - Consumo de água: apesar de existir “circuito fechado”, há perdas e reposição; nos EUA, o consumo anual chegou a 1 trilhão de litros d’água. - Poluição sonora: geradores fazem ruído insuportável, alto e constante, afetando a qualidade de vida das famílias vizinhas. - Emissões de gases de efeito estufa: a possibilidade de usar fontes fósseis, ampliando as emissões que agravam a crise climática. - Pressão sobre os territórios: ocupam áreas enormes que podem chegar a mais de 100 campos de futebol, disputando terras, água e energia com comunidades locais. - Concentração de poder: domínio de empresas estrangeiras sobre o mercado e as infraestruturas impede o avanço tecnológico no país. Nos EUA, onde mais tem data centers no mundo, a população fez vários protestos contra e o tema foi decisivo nas eleições. Nova York suspendeu novas instalações de hiperescala até ter leis mais rígidas e países europeus também pausaram projetos como Irlanda, Holanda e Dinamarca. Quais são os projetos de Mega Data Center no Brasil? O Brasil já possui data centers (cerca de 225 e quase metade fica no estado de São Paulo), mas projetos de hiperescala estão chegando em todo país: instalações maiores e com muito mais impactos. O mais avançado está em construção no território indígena do povo Anacé, em Caucaia (CE), região metropolitana de Fortaleza. Segundo o Governo do Ceará, abrigará as tecnologias de IA do TikTok e a previsão é começar a operar no segundo semestre de 2027. Confira abaixo projetos de mega data centers em andamento no Brasil. Lei Redata e a importância de regular data centers no Brasil No Brasil, o Redata (Lei 15.504/2026), sancionada em setembro, criou o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter. Na prática, concede isenções de impostos para atrair centros de dados ao país — uma renúncia fiscal estimada em R$ 7 bilhões, segundo Secretaria Especial da Receita Federal, ou seja, recursos públicos que deixam de ser arrecadados. Aprovado sem participação social ou diálogo com as comunidades atingidas, o Redata abre brechas preocupantes, como o incentivo à combustível fóssil. O desenho da lei favorece as Big Techs em detrimento do povo brasileiro e do clima global. Enquanto estados norte-americanos e países europeus discutem limites rígidos, o Brasil se torna alvo da expansão acelerada. O que são Big Techs e quem controla a corrida da Inteligência Artificial? As Big Techs são gigantes da tecnologia que estão entre as empresas mais ricas e influentes do mundo, como Google, Amazon, Meta, Nvdia, Microsoft e TikTok – seus fundadores e administradores ocupam o topo da lista de bilionários da Forbes. São exemplos de como a “inovação” acontece quando é controlada por poucos: lucros recordes, cortes de empregos e a falsa promessa de que automação trará benefícios, porém na prática acumulam violações trabalhistas, sociais e ambientais. Por que regular Big Techs e Data Centers? Regular não é censurar ou frear o desenvolvimento tecnológico, é assegurar que a população faça parte com salvaguardas que respeitem os ciclos da natureza, o bem-comum e que tragam retorno para a sociedade. Para isso, precisamos de criar regras: - Regulação das Big Techs (ambiente digital e democracia): estabelece limites e responsabilidades para as grandes empresas de tecnologia, incluindo transparência sobre algoritmos, proteção de dados e direitos digitais. - Regulação de data centers (infraestrutura física e recursos naturais): impõe análise de riscos e leis firmes para a construção e operação desses empreendimentos, considerando os impactos socioambientais. Parem os mega data centers! Nove organizações — Instituto Terramar, Amazônia Sem Data Center, CTRL+Z, Data_Labe, Instituto Decodifica, Mulheres pelo Clima do Vale do Paraíba, Coding Rights, Filha do Sol e Greenpeace Brasil – se uniram para frear o avanço de data centers de IAs no Brasil até que sejam assegurados: - Consentimento e Transparência: Participação social ativa e consulta livre, prévia e informada para as comunidades tradicionais. - Licenciamento Ambiental completo: Estudo e relatório de impacto assegurando transição energética justa e proibindo instalação em áreas de importância ecológica. - Fim da isenção de impostos: Quem lucra com i

artigo.texto: Lawmakers call for national data center construction pause Lawmakers say pause would give Congress time to pass artificial intelligence regulations WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Members of Congress are calling for a national moratorium on data center construction until the artificial intelligence field can be regulated. They said data centers are not helping local communities and, in many cases, are actively harming them. Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Mass.) said the White House is not doing enough on artificial intelligence. “The alarm bells are flashing. And the president and the White House are asleep at the switch when it comes to AI,” he said. McGovern said big tech leaders are becoming oligarchs and are enriching themselves at the expense of local communities with data centers. “These billionaires want to come into our communities, tell us what to do, and make a profit by driving up our utility prices, and wrecking our environment,” he said. Rep.-elect William Lawrence (D-Mich.) said data centers do not provide the same community value as an automotive plant. “The value, the billions of dollars that is being raised to build these data centers, is built on the promise that it’s going to put people out of work,” he said. Lawmakers said pausing new construction would give Congress time to pass regulations and protect communities from future construction. Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine) said she wants transparency in dealings between big tech and the government. “We don’t want back door deals and secret handshakes between big tech and the government. We want transparency, community engagement, and strong regulations that protect our air, water, climate and communities,” she said. It is not yet clear whether the plan has enough support to pass in the next Congress. The Trump administration has attempted to rename AI - artificial intelligence - as SI - super intelligence.
