artigo.texto: SpaceX plans $50B data center campus in Cochise County COCHISE COUNTY, AZ (AZFamily) — SpaceX has announced plans to build a $50 billion data center campus in Cochise County, and several community groups are organizing to stop it. SpaceX, Elon Musk’s rocket and AI company, has created an online link for the facility that includes a rendering of the proposed campus. The data center would sit on nearly 750 acres near Willcox Playa and would be the largest in the state. Developers have changed their tactics amid opposition to data center facilities. Many now are trying to work with communities to get projects approved. SpaceX is highlighting the economic impact of the project. Residents raise concerns Tara Clayton lives in Cochise County and is the organizing director for Rural Arizona Engagement. The group fought and killed a large data center project in Pinal County over the summer. “I’ve been hearing from the community that they’re extremely concerned about the integrity of this SpaceX data center,” Clayton said. “Whether they’re telling us the absolute truth about some of these benefits that we might be receiving or the chemicals that might be involved in this facility, how it could potentially impact our water supply here locally or local wildlife, quality of life,” Clayton said. Clayton said it’s important that the county leaders listen to the community and take their opinions into account. Environmental questions Ken Gillingham, a professor of environmental and energy economics at Yale University, has been researching data centers. He said SpaceX has used diesel generators to power some of its facilities. “SpaceX has acquired a reputation for not being the most environmentally oriented of the large hyperscalers,” Gillingham said. “There are other claims that they have not been following environmental protections in a very, very serious way.” Jobs, grid upgrades and state review SpaceX said the project would create more than 5,000 construction jobs and 1,000 permanent jobs. According to the company’s application, SpaceX would invest more than $3 billion in power grid upgrades. Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes said in an interview with On Your Side’s Christine Stanwood that she has concerns and that her office is taking a closer look. Mayes raised the question of “whether that would destabilize our grid in the southwest and maybe even potentially in the West.” SpaceX claims the project would reduce neighbors’ electricity bills and lower property taxes. What’s next The project still must go before the county’s Planning and Zoning Board, which will hold a hearing Dec. 9. Arizona’s Family Investigates called and emailed the Planning and Zoning department and all three members of the Board of Supervisors but has not heard back. artigo.texto: America’s hyperscale data centers together use as much electricity as some entire U.S. states and produce millions of metric tons of carbon dioxide over the course of a year, according to a new study published Monday in Nature Sustainability. The number of hyperscale data centers, which are larger and more powerful than traditional data centers, and are often used to train and run large-scale AI models, has exploded in recent years. Between 2019 and 2024, the number of data centers around the world doubled from a little over 500 to over 1,100, with more than half located in the United States. That number is only expected to grow: the research firm Synergy estimates that the total capacity of U.S. data centers will double in the next three years, largely driven by the growth of hyperscale data centers. American voters rallied against data center development in the midterm elections this November, with many citing economic and environmental concerns. In 40 out of 41 local ballot initiatives across the country, citizens voted to limit or prevent data center development. Yet few studies have quantified just how much electricity each hyperscale data center uses, and what fuels generate the electricity, the researchers say. “Even though there were a lot of [public and scientific] statements about the environmental impact of data centers, when we started this research, we realized that there was basically very little, if none, peer-reviewed data,” says Francesca Dominici, director of the Harvard Data Science Initiative and senior author of the paper. The study provides one of the first facility-level estimates of the electricity use and carbon dioxide emissions of hyperscale data centers since the rise of AI. The researchers used satellite imagery to build a list of 403 hyperscale data centers across the U.S., and then estimated the annual electricity consumption for each facility between May 2024 and April 2025 under a range of operating scenarios. They then used data from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to calculate their emissions. They found that, together, the data centers used between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity—with the upper estimate equivalent to what some states, like Indiana, Michigan, and Tennessee, use in a year. In the lower scenario, the facilities still consumed approximately the annual electricity sold to customers in Wisconsin, roughly 70 TWh, or Minnesota, around 65 TWh. More than half of the electricity powering the data centers comes from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The facilities studied produced a combined estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide—roughly the annual emissions of Denmark. Half of the electricity use of all the data centers studied was concentrated in just four states: Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa, the report found. Virginia has long been known as “data center alley” due to its high number of data centers, but size and power capacity can also impact electricity consumption. The researchers identified 26 hyperscale facilities in Iowa, combined electricity consumption for which was approximately 7.2 TWh, with the average facility having substantially higher estimated electricity demand than the average facility in Virginia, where 142 hyperscale facilities account for approximately 21.4 TWh of annual electricity consumption. However, the emissions impacts were not always the same. Virginia, Iowa, and Ohio have the most emissions attributable to hyperscale data centers, while Oregon, which is home to more hyperscale data centers than Iowa and Ohio, has significantly fewer emissions due to a cleaner energy grid. “For the same amount of electricity consumed, the regional electricity mix associated with data centers in Wyoming produces approximately seven times more carbon dioxide than in Oregon,” says Gianluca Guidi, Harvard data scientist and the study’s lead author. “So these environmental impacts are not necessarily inevitable. Geography matters.” Without clean energy alternatives, U.S. data centers are projected to consume more natural gas than most countries by 2035, according to a report from BloombergNEF. The electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely even higher than the research shows. The team did not have enough data to assess every single hyperscale data center in the U.S. at the time, and more data centers have emerged since their study concluded in April 2025. The researchers hope to continue to quantify the environmental impacts of hyperscale data centers to better understand their impact on air pollution, water, and health, adding that, as AI continues to scale, its infrastructure growth must be done sustainably. “We tend to imagine AI as something that is almost immaterial, but in the end, the infrastructure power is profoundly physical,” says Guidi. “Behind every algorithm, there are enormous buildings, power plants, water resources, and ultimately also communities that live with the consequences.”

artigo.texto: One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built. A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference to track moving forward. Finding the centers The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts. In a way, that makes this a very conservative estimate, since 272 facilities believed to be large data centers were left out. But if you’re interested in AI data centers, specifically, it’s also true that some of the facilities included may not fall in that category. That fact also introduces some uncertainty in the actual power usage of these data centers. Relying on other research, they use a range—some conventional data centers run at an average of about 48 percent of capacity, while AI training loads have been running higher, at around 70 percent. Putting that together, the total power usage for the year by these 403 data centers was estimated at 68 to 99 terawatt-hours. That amounts to 1.5 to 2.2 percent of total US electricity use, on par with the total used by Wisconsin or Indiana.

artigo.texto: Proposta já está pronta no Ministério da Fazenda e, se aprovada pelo presidente, deve virar medida provisória no início de 2027. Um órgão com cerca de 150 funcionários e um colegiado de cinco diretores, com mandatos, pode passar a comandar o mercado regulado de carbono do Brasil. A proposta de criação de uma autarquia especial está pronta no governo federal e aguarda a decisão do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, segundo a secretária extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono do Ministério da Fazenda, Cristina Reis, em entrevista ao UOL publicada em 10 de novembro de 2026. A expectativa é que o tema seja levado ao presidente ainda neste ano. Havendo aval, será editada uma medida provisória para criar a estrutura. Uma solução “engatilhada” para depois da COP31 Cristina Reis afirmou que o desenho do novo órgão já está concluído e que o debate deve ganhar força após a conferência do clima. A proposta está pronta. A gente está com uma solução engatilhada. Nessa volta da COP31, essa discussão vai ser mais aprofundada. Apesar disso, a secretária admite que o calendário é incerto. A proposta ainda depende de discussões dentro do governo e da palavra final da Presidência. “Tem muitas discussões a serem feitas, então é mais provável que fique para o começo do ano que vem”, disse. Como seria o novo órgão A autarquia teria um colegiado de cinco diretores, incluindo um diretor-presidente, todos com mandatos definidos. O quadro de pessoal seria de aproximadamente 150 funcionários. O órgão ficaria vinculado ao Ministério da Fazenda e teria estrutura própria para conduzir a regulamentação e a operação do mercado. Ele substituiria a Secretaria Extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono, criada para conduzir a primeira fase de implementação do Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE), nome formal do mercado regulado de carbono no país. Até que a autarquia esteja efetivamente constituída, com pessoal contratado e estrutura montada, a Secretaria Extraordinária continuaria em funcionamento. A transição, portanto, evita um vazio de gestão. Quem vai pagar a conta O financiamento é o ponto ainda pendente. Inicialmente, a autarquia dependerá de recursos do Orçamento da União, o que exige definição antes da criação formal da estrutura. No futuro, o próprio mercado deve ajudar a custear a governança do sistema. Pela legislação, 15% das receitas arrecadadas por meio de leilões e outros mecanismos de cobrança poderão ser destinados à governança, o que inclui a manutenção da autarquia. Para onde vai o restante do dinheiro A mesma regra define o destino das demais receitas. Outros 75% serão direcionados ao Fundo Clima, e 10% poderão financiar projetos de interesse público, especialmente iniciativas sociais envolvendo comunidades tradicionais e povos indígenas. Para a Amazônia, esse último ponto é o que mais tende a ter efeito direto. A região concentra grande parte dos territórios indígenas e das comunidades tradicionais do país, potenciais beneficiárias dessa fatia, embora os critérios de acesso dependam da regulamentação que o novo órgão terá de conduzir. Os próximos passos O primeiro passo é a discussão da proposta com o presidente Lula, prevista para este ano. Se houver aprovação, a medida provisória que criaria a autarquia deve ser editada, na estimativa da secretária, no começo de 2027, enquanto a definição do financiamento segue em aberto. artigo.texto: Ohio Becomes the Epicenter of Data Center Backlash After Tax Credits Cost State’s Schools $374 Million Angela Huffman, a sixth-generation farmer, spent 15 years in agriculture policy in Columbus, OH, and Washington, DC. But her focus lately has been 10 miles from her Wharton, OH, sheep farm. On June 4, Huffman picked up her local newspaper, the Daily Chief-Union. The above-the-fold headline revealed a developer was eyeing a $900 million data center in nearby Upper Sandusky. The headline "stopped me cold," Huffman says. The proposal would have planted a 146-acre Smartland Energy data center campus, with a natural gas power plant, on the north edge of town. "We were already worried about a big development coming in and extracting the town's resources," Huffman tells Realtor.com®. Townsfolk were already concerned after another recent proposal for a soybean processing plant. "What does that do to the community?" she says. Huffman, CEO of Farm Action, says her family has owned its nearby farm for six generations. Organizing concerned neighbors, they began filling planning commission meetings and peppering officials with questions about the impact of the development. They also questioned if it should be approved on industrial zoning, as neighbors had hoped. A petition opposing the project drew 1,100 signatures. Many residents worried about how such a major project could change their rural way of life. And Upper Sandusky wasn't alone. Ohio was the heart of data center resistance in the midterms. Voters in 18 of its 88 counties backed 21 bans or restrictions on development of those projects. One of those was in Upper Sandusky, where voters approved a charter amendment blocking large data centers within the limits of the 6,600-person town. "They wanted to use about a third of the water the whole town uses today," Huffman says. "I'm not against AI or development, but can a town of this size absorb a development like that?" Data center tax breaks come into view But the state already hosts dozens of large centers. And they already exact a cost. A new study shows that the state's data center tax break derived its schools of almost $374 million in revenue in 2025 alone. Republican Gov. Mike DeWine paused the tax breaks in May after the state realized developers were exempted from $2.1 billion in taxes in 2024 and 2025, far more than initally projected. Gov.-elect Amy Acton has promised further scrutiny. Good Jobs First and Policy Matters Ohio studied where those missing tax dollars would have gone. The state's Fair School Funding Plan allocates some sales tax to schools. So by exempting data center developers from the 5.75% sales tax, those schools missed out on revenue. "Ohio lawmakers made a choice to give data center companies a blank check, and now Ohio's schools are paying the price," said Hannah Halbert, Policy Matters Ohio's executive director. "In 2025 alone, the state gave up enough revenue from this single tax break to fully update the Fair School Funding plan and close the gap." This comes at a time when homeowners were being asked to make up the difference. Many Ohio schools aimed to raise money through levies this year, but many were unsuccessful. The Ohio Policy Education Institute found just 24 of 66 levies on the May 2026 ballot had passed. Upper Sandusky's school district was one of the losers—missing out on $383,000 in revenue, according to the report. While voters have approved levies for its schools in 2015, 2018, and 2023, it's still been forced to cancel classes this year because it can't install air conditioning in century-old buildings that are too expensive to rebuild. "Our schools were struggling," Huffman says. "It tells you a lot about when these big tech companies come along, and if they are paying their fair share." Wider backlash Voter anger has put data center incentives in the spotlight. NBC exit polls show 76% of voters opposed data center building in their communities, and a majority considered them "crucial" to their votes. Polls show broad concerns that the pace of data center construction could drive up power costs, raise land prices, and create environmental problems. Recent Realtor.com research on data centers found they're increasingly moving into rural areas. That's despite a major spending spree by the industry. Ohio was barraged with $1.8 million in data center ads in the fall, Pew Research Center found—more than Texas, Wisconsin, and other large states. AI and crypto political action committees spent an estimated $65 million backing Republican Sen. John Husted, who lost reelection to Democrat Sherrod Brown on Nov. 3. Developers, after all, have big plans in the state, having pitched $168.7 billion in new projects. Regulation of data center developments and AI could be a major factor for new Democratic leaders in Columbus and Washington, DC. Sober to that reality, tech stocks tanked after the election. Acton says she supports a conditional moratorium on data centers. She wants to see them cover their utility costs, build with union labor, and abide by environmental standards. She also says she wants to see incentives "reined in" for the large developments. AI companies address future scrutiny Artificial intelligence companies have spent the days since the election promising they'll work with cities and residents on data centers. OpenAI published a "blueprint for responsible development" promising to slow the technology. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone cited a commitment "to pay our own energy and water costs so they're not passed onto consumers, fund new and upgraded grid infrastructure, and support local communities." Ohio isn't alone, either. Virginia, another data center hot spot, spent over $4 billion in data center incentives over 10 years, according to a state report. In her keynote speech, Rwanda's Minister of Environment emphasised that Africa needs bankable projects capable of attracting investment and supporting economic development. And that is exactly the point. Carbon finance could play a central role in mobilising capital, creating jobs and supporting a more sustainable development pathway. But something caught my attention: across discussions, meetings and keynote speeches, plenty about carbon finance and investment opportunities was discussed. Yet, Article 6.4 and its Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism (PACM) were almost absent from the conversation. For many of the people actually developing and financing projects, Article 6.4 remains more of a theoretical framework than a practical opportunity. Developers do not really oppose the mechanism, they simply do not see a compelling reason to adopt another complex system in a market that is already extremely difficult to navigate. Developers are already dealing with changing methodologies, host-country authorisations, corresponding adjustments and increasingly demanding buyer requirements. Article 6.4 introduces yet another set of rules and approval processes without demonstrating a clear commercial advantage. After years of negotiations, the mechanism is finally becoming operational. As of October 2026, five methodologies have been approved, including two new clean-cooking methodologies. Meanwhile, 1,512 projects and programmes have requested transition from the old Clean Development Mechanism (CDM), with 418 having received host-country approval by June. Transitioning existing projects, however, is not the same as attracting new investment under the new methodologies. In conversations with experts and developers, one concern kept emerging: methodological conservatism increasingly seems to be treated as synonymous with environmental integrity. Stricter baselines and more demanding monitoring requirements could significantly reduce credit issuance. Developers must also account for mandatory deductions of 5% for the Adaptation Fund and at least 2% for overall mitigation, alongside administrative fees, host-country levies and, where applicable, reversal-risk buffer contributions. To understand the potential economic impact, I ran a quick-and-dirty simulation. This is not a financial model or an Article 6.4 price forecast, just a simple exercise to illustrate how project economics could change. Let's assume a project originally generates 100,000 credits annually, sold at $10 each, generating $1 million in carbon revenue. If more conservative accounting reduces issuance by 40%, and we apply the mandatory 7% UNFCCC deductions, only 55,800 credits remain available for sale. What price would the developer need to charge to maintain the same carbon revenue? In the most demanding scenario, a credit previously sold at $10 would need to sell for almost $30 just to preserve the same carbon revenue. Is the market prepared to pay that difference? The concern is not conservatism itself, but the accumulation of conservative assumptions without sufficiently recognising improvements already made to address historical over-crediting. Conservatism should ensure accurate crediting, not become an objective in itself. Meanwhile, international carbon markets are progressing. According to Sylvera, projected demand for internationally adjusted credits under CORSIA and government purchasing programmes could approach one billion tonnes through 2030. Unlike Article 6.4, these pathways can leverage established standards, methodologies and registries that developers already know, and which are beginning to support deliveries to governments and airlines. Why move to an entirely new mechanism when existing systems are already opening access to compliance markets? The answer may come from future demand. The European Commission has proposed auctioning up to 260 million EU ETS allowances to finance the purchase of international credits between 2036 and 2040. At an illustrative EUA price of €120 in the late 2030s, this could generate approximately €31 billion in purchasing resources. This is not a guaranteed budget or credit price, but it illustrates the scale of the potential opportunity. Such purchasing power could make Article 6.4 more attractive, establish a new market benchmark and potentially encourage other countries to follow a similar approach. But this raises two fundamental questions. Will buyers pay the higher prices needed to make these projects viable, while keeping international credits cost-effective? And perhaps more importantly, will enough eligible and authorised credits be available? Lower issuance per project means more investment is needed to generate the same volume. Host-country authorisation remains a sovereign decision, while credit-vintage eligibility and restrictions across NDC periods create additional uncertainty. For Europe, securing up to 260 million credits between 2036 and 2040 would require a substantial project pipeline developed and financed years in advance. The market cannot wait until 2036 to start developing the projects Europe may need in 2036. This brings me back to the message from Rwanda's Minister of Environment: “Africa needs bankable projects.” Article 6.4's success will ultimately depend on strong demand signals and its ability to reduce risks for project developers and investors. This means simplifying procedures, providing greater regulatory certainty, establishing a clear and transparent pathway for host-country authorisation, and turning regulatory ambition into bankable projects that attract capital and deliver measurab

artigo.texto: A Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) informou seus clientes que pretende interromper o fornecimento de chips para operadores de data centers que alugam mais de 50% de suas unidades de processamento gráfico (GPUs) para empresas chinesas, de acordo com uma reportagem da CNBC publicada na terça-feira, 17 de novembro de 2026. A política anunciada surge num momento em que as autoridades americanas introduzem medidas adicionais destinadas a limitar o acesso das empresas chinesas à tecnologia avançada de inteligência artificial americana, incluindo recursos computacionais fornecidos por meio de serviços de nuvem no exterior. A CNBC, citando duas pessoas familiarizadas com o assunto, informou que a Nvidia havia alertado seus clientes nos últimos meses sobre as possíveis implicações da proposta da Lei de Segurança de Acesso Remoto (RASA). A legislação ampliaria a autoridade do governo dos EUA para regulamentar o acesso a serviços de computação em nuvem, aproximando as restrições de acesso remoto dos controles já existentes sobre as exportações físicas de semicondutores. Segundo o relatório, a Nvidia também alertou que as regras propostas poderiam gerar riscos legais tanto para os fabricantes de semicondutores quanto para seus clientes. A Nvidia teria definido uma meta de 51% de clientes fora da China O Financial Times noticiou no início de novembro que a Nvidia havia instruído verbalmente seus clientes de data centers a alocar pelo menos 51% de seus serviços a clientes não chineses em contratos futuros. A exigência relatada afetaria operadoras cujos modelos de negócios dependem fortemente do fornecimento de capacidade computacional para empresas chinesas. De acordo com os atuais controles de exportação dos EUA, a Nvidia está impedida de vender certos processadores de IA avançados diretamente para a China. No entanto, os órgãos reguladores têm tido autoridade mais limitada sobre o acesso à mesma tecnologia por meio de infraestrutura em nuvem localizada fora do país. A legislação RASA proposta visa abordar essa distinção, estendendo a supervisão regulatória aos serviços de computação remota. Segundo a CNBC, o projeto de lei foi aprovado pela Câmara dos Representantes dos EUA em janeiro, mas ainda não havia recebido a aprovação do Senado. O Departamento de Comércio dos EUA introduz restrições adicionais ao acesso remoto O Departamento de Comércio dos EUA, por meio do Bureau de Indústria e Segurança (BIS), anunciou na segunda-feira uma regra final provisória destinada a impedir que empresas chinesas acessem remotamente processadores de IA restritos, informou a CNBC. A medida faz parte dos esforços de Washington para fortalecer a aplicação dos controles de exportação de semicondutores e abordar o uso de centros de dados em terceiros países para obter capacidade computacional. A questão atraiu atenção após relatos de que empresas chinesas de inteligência artificial buscavam acesso a hardware da Nvidia por meio de instalações no exterior. Em 5 de novembro, a CNBC noticiou que a desenvolvedora chinesa de IA Moonshot AI havia tentado acessar processadores da Nvidia por meio de data centers na Europa. Anteriormente, em julho, o governo Trump havia acusado a Moonshot de obter acesso aos chips por meio de centros de dados no Leste Asiático. Essas alegações dizem respeito a possíveis métodos de acesso a recursos computacionais restritos e não comprovam, por si só, que ocorreram violações dos controles de exportação. O secretário do Tesouro pede maior fiscalização da Nvidia Os acontecimentos seguem a saída do CEO da Nvidia, Jensen Huang, o que gerou maior atenção às práticas de gestão e controle de exportação da empresa. O secretário do Tesouro dos EUA, Scott Bessent, pediu no domingo uma “reestruturação drástica” na Nvidia, de acordo com a CNBC. Suas declarações vieram na sequência de relatos que alegavam que Huang havia se envolvido em um relacionamento extraconjugal com uma mulher que, segundo as autoridades americanas, era suspeita de realizar atividades de espionagem em nome da China. As alegações relatadas não foram comprovadas como evidências de irregularidades. Bessent também sugeriu que outros executivos da Nvidia deveriam ser investigados quanto ao cumprimento das restrições de exportação dos EUA. Em entrevista à Fox News, ele questionou se a Nvidia teria incentivado vendas que ele classificou como potencialmente ilegais, numa tentativa de aumentar a receita e os lucros. Os comentários representam preocupações levantadas pelo Secretário do Tesouro, e não conclusões definitivas sobre a conduta da Nvidia. Nvidia destaca as limitações da supervisão de produtos pós-venda A Nvidia já abordou anteriormente os desafios associados ao monitoramento de como seus processadores são usados após a venda. Em um documento enviado à Comissão de Valores Mobiliários (SEC) em agosto, a empresa afirmou que buscava cumprir os requisitos de controle de exportação aplicáveis, mas reconheceu as limitações em sua capacidade de supervisionar os produtos depois que eles saem de sua posse. A Nvidia afirmou não ter “controle físico de seus produtos após a venda”, explicando que depende de programas de conformidade operados por clientes e parceiros comerciais. A divulgação ilustra as dificuldades que os fornecedores de semicondutores enfrentam no monitoramento do uso final de processadores avançados, principalmente quando o hardware é implantado em infraestrutura de nuvem que atende clientes em várias jurisdições. As alterações relatadas nas políticas de vendas da Nvidia, juntamente com a legislação proposta e as novas medidas do Departamento de Comércio, podem afetar os operadores de centros de dados que fornecem serviços de computação de IA para empresas chinesas. A Nvidia também é negociada na B3 por meio da BDR (BOV:NVDC34). Este conteúdo é apenas para fins informativos e não constitui aconselhamento financeiro, de investimento ou de qualquer outra natureza profissional. artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA A LS ELECTRIC fornecerá equipamentos de manobra para a expansão de um data center de IA nos EUA Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Pontos-chaveO novo contrato de US$ 93,83 milhões da LS ELECTRIC é um pedido de acompanhamento de um… Ver mais - O novo contrato de US$ 93,83 milhões da LS ELECTRIC é um pedido de acompanhamento de um cliente existente de data center. - As premiações repetidas dependem do cumprimento dos cronogramas de entrega de hyperscale em suas unidades de produção na Coreia e nos EUA. - A LS ELECTRIC também está desenvolvendo sistemas de distribuição DC em sua instalação de Cheonan para futuros data centers de IA. A LS ELECTRIC anunciou, em 16 de novembro de 2026, que havia assinado um contrato de fornecimento de sistemas de energia no valor de aproximadamente US$ 93,83 milhões (130 bilhões de KRW) para um projeto de data center de IA hiperescalável nos EUA de uma empresa global de tecnologia de grande porte. O contrato abrange painéis de manobra de alta tensão de 38 kV e painéis de manobra de baixa tensão, que serão fornecidos em etapas para a rede elétrica do data center. Os equipamentos de alta tensão distribuem a eletricidade recebida às instalações individuais e protegem os equipamentos quando ocorrem anomalias no fornecimento de energia. A LS ELECTRIC participou do grande projeto de data center local do cliente desde a fase inicial de construção. O novo contrato dá continuidade às encomendas de painéis de manobra de alta tensão na fase de expansão, tornando-se um pedido subsequente de um cliente existente e vinculando diretamente a atuação da fornecedora à continuidade da construção do projeto. Capacidade de entrega sustenta o pedido de expansão A LS ELECTRIC identifica o prazo até a energização — o intervalo antes que um data center receba eletricidade e possa começar a operar — como uma preocupação competitiva central na infraestrutura de IA. A empresa atribui os pedidos recorrentes ao atendimento dos requisitos de qualidade do cliente e dos cronogramas de entrega para instalações hiperescaláveis desde as etapas iniciais do projeto. Suas bases de produção nomeadas são a fábrica inteligente de Cheongju, na Coreia do Sul, a LS ELECTRIC Utah e o Bastrop Campus, no Texas. A empresa apresenta essa presença como o alicerce de sua competitividade em entregas. Neste pedido de expansão, o requisito de entrega tem uma dimensão operacional concreta: o contrato de equipamentos depende tanto da capacidade industrial e do cronograma quanto das especificações dos produtos. Contratos recentes abrangem todo o sistema elétrico Um comunicado separado de outubro de 2026 divulgou um acordo de longo prazo no valor de 168,9 bilhões de KRW (US$ 125,23 milhões) com outra empresa de tecnologia de grande porte dos EUA, abrangendo 2027–2028. O valor anunciado corresponde aos produtos programados para entrega em 2027, enquanto a dimensão dos negócios de 2028 continua sujeita a novas discussões. Esse acordo abrange painéis de manobra de alta tensão de 38 kV. O possível fornecimento adicional de painéis de manobra de baixa tensão, transformadores de distribuição e unidades de manobra em anel continua em discussão, criando a possibilidade de um pacote de equipamentos mais amplo em torno das entregas já comprometidas. A LS ELECTRIC anunciou, em 1º de outubro de 2026, um contrato de 181,2 bilhões de KRW (US$ 133,41 milhões) para transformadores de tensão extra-alta de 345 kV. As entregas estão programadas em etapas para nove subestações até 2030, para um projeto de data center de IA hiperescalável na América do Norte. Em conjunto, os registros da empresa descrevem atividades tanto em equipamentos de distribuição para data centers quanto na infraestrutura de tensão mais alta necessária para fornecer energia a grandes projetos de IA. Negócios em corrente alternada e desenvolvimento em corrente contínua Além da distribuição convencional em corrente alternada (CA), a LS ELECTRIC está desenvolvendo sistemas de próxima geração em corrente contínua (CC) para data centers de IA. A empresa descreve sua Cheonan DC Factory como a primeira unidade fabril a comercializar a distribuição em corrente contínua. Transformadores de estado sólido, disjuntores de estado sólido e sistemas de armazenamento de energia são usados ali para testar redes elétricas de próxima geração e ambientes de data center. O contrato destaca a relação comercial entre o fornecimento de energia e a capacidade computacional de IA: não é possível energizar uma nova capacidade até que os equipamentos elétricos estejam instalados. A atuação recorrente da LS ELECTRIC vincula seu negócio de equipamentos de manobra a esse cronograma, enquanto a unidade de testes de Cheonan oferece um caminho para projetos futuros em corrente contínua, à medida que os projetos hiperescaláveis se expandem e sua arquitetura de energia evolui.

artigo.texto: SALEM — The massive, whitewashed buildings of Shetland Park loom over Salem Harbor, looking much like the cotton mills they used to be. Decades ago, with its mechanical looms and thousands of low-paid textile workers, this was probably the noisiest spot in town. Today, it’s remarkably quiet. The modern tenants — law offices, a food pantry, a medical clinic, a charter school — make good neighbors for the apartment dwellers just across Congress Street, in the low-income neighborhood known as The Point. But now Shetland Park’s owner has designs on bringing back the thrum of industry. It has proposed a small-scale data center for the complex, one that would bring the constant hum of cooling fans and the occasional roar of three big diesel generators. Many in Salem want no part of it. “There’s probably a place for data centers,” City Councilor Ty Hapworth said. “It’s probably not in a dense city like Salem.” The outcry against the Salem proposal echoes the surging nationwide resistance to giant “hyperscale” data centers. In October, public opposition halted a $4 billion project in Westfield. And in a town near Worcester, Sutton residents turned out in force last week to oppose a plan by the Kraft Group to build one of the nation’s biggest hyperscale facilities. Such massive data centers are essential for training powerful artificial intelligence systems from companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta. Their developers are up against ferocious opposition from citizens in Massachusetts and across the country, who fear the data centers will drain local water supplies, jack up electricity rates, and generate intense noise and air pollution. The Pew Research Center estimates there are about 3,000 data centers in the United States. Most of them are relatively small — like the one that’s been sitting atop the Macy’s department store in Boston’s Downtown Crossing for nearly 30 years — and use little cooling water or electricity. We rely on them for nearly every part of our digital lives, from shopping and banking to streaming video, yet until recently, few people noticed they existed. Lately, though, anything called a “data center” draws fire, however small. In Salem, upstate New York-based Prime Group Holding, which owns the 30-acre Shetland Park, had no trouble getting a building permit in May. But in September, amid intense backlash from city residents, Salem’s zoning board of appeals canceled the permit. The about-face was driven in part by concerns that Prime Group hadn’t been entirely honest about its intentions. The company had originally proposed a much smaller facility, claiming it would be used by an unnamed “IT services company.” Only after getting the permit was the project scaled up to drugstore size, requiring three diesel generators to provide backup power instead of the single generator in the original plan. Prime Group has a less-than-transparent name for the new version, calling it a “low-latency inference point,” and insists it’s not a data center, even though it would be a roomful of computers providing artificial intelligence services to local businesses. “It did feel a bit disconcerting that they would change plans midstream and try to characterize their project as something that it clearly was not,” Salem Mayor Dominick Pangallo said. Now, the city has banned the construction of data centers, except by organizations that need them for their own use, such as hospitals or government agencies. Prime Group did not respond to requests for comment. The company has until late November to challenge the zoning board’s decision in court. Across the state line, in Concord, N.H., a similar battle is playing out. City planners are having second thoughts about an already approved plan for a small data center on vacant commercial land near Interstate 93 in East Concord. The planning board may vote later this month to halt the development. Kelly Morgan, an S&P Global analyst who tracks the data center industry, said 110 US data center projects had been canceled or delayed this year through October, with the overwhelming majority scrubbed because of citizen opposition. Most were to be large data centers, using at least 50 megawatts of electric power from the local grid. But Morgan listed the cancellation or delay of eight projects requiring 36 megawatts or less. And her list did not include the Salem and Concord data centers. “I suspect it is people hearing the word ‘data center’ and not distinguishing by size or impact, just reflexively saying, ‘No thanks,’” Morgan said. Levitate, a Bothell, Wash.-based AI infrastructure and data center company, obtained a building permit in East Concord to erect a 15-megawatt, 7,500-square-foot data facility on a parcel of undeveloped land about a quarter mile from Interstate 93. The area couldn’t be more different from Salem. There’s little nearby except trees and a few businesses, including a shipping company, a data networking contractor, and a company that repairs roads and bridges. No homes, no apartment buildings. Just trees and traffic whirring past on the interstate. During a recent visit, managers of local businesses declined to speak on the record, but expressed no concern about a possible data center in the neighborhood. One seemed mystified that anybody would object. But object they did, after Concord’s city planner ruled in June that the Levitate project was a permissible use of land zoned for industrial use. Faced with broad opposition, the board deferred final action until Nov. 18. Speaking at the hearing, Levitate chief executive Ryan Howard described the data center as “a small compact design with an intentionally low impact on public resources.” He said that local power company Unitil could deliver the needed electricity without driving up electric rates. artigo.texto: The largest data centers in the US collectively emit an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon emissions annually â almost as much as Denmark, according to a study published in the journal Nature Sustainability. Harvard researchers found 403 data centers used almost 2% of US electricity, with most of the power being generated from fossil fuels. Sites in Iowa, Ohio, and Virginia accounted for about half the estimated emissions. The study provides the first peer-reviewed estimates of emissions generated by US data centers since the start of the AI boom, although it is not a comprehensive inventory. Without a publicly available list of facilities, researchers pieced together information using a commercial dataset, satellite imagery, and data on the power mix supplying each regional electricity grid. The findings are likely an underestimate as they exclude data centers that researchers could not sufficiently verify, as well as facilities that rely on on-site power generation.

artigo.texto: The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) has launched its second Bulk Energy Storage solicitation to procure approximately 1 GW of energy storage capacity. The solicitation is open to various eligible energy storage technologies and is part of a plan to procure 3 GW of bulk energy storage through at least three annual solicitations. The initiative is part of the state’s 2022 Energy Storage Roadmap, which aims to deploy 6 GW of energy storage by 2030. Projects supported under the programme will be required to comply with updated energy storage safety codes, including requirements for safe site selection, first responder training, and emergency response plans. NYSERDA will provide incentives through its Index Storage Credit mechanism, but payments will only begin after projects have received the necessary permits, been installed and become operational, and passed peer reviews and quality assurance inspections. NY Green Bank will also offer financing options to developers and investors to support project development. In September 2026, NYSERDA awarded contracts to eight battery storage projects and 13 large-scale renewable energy projects. Together, these projects represent 1.7 GW of new capacity and over $3.7 billion in private investment. BESS projects will add 950 MW of capacity, with durations ranging from four to eight hours while the 13 renewable energy projects will add over 719 MW of capacity and comprise solar, onshore wind, and hydropower. The projects are expected to be operational by the end of 2030.

artigo.texto: CATL presented its battery-storage systems in Buenos Aires to 35 companies interested in a government storage tender, according to a report published November 17, 2026. The presentation took place the week before that report. The account describes a pitch to prospective bidders, not a tender award to CATL. (South China Morning Post) The 35-company audience gives CATL’s reported presentation a clear measure of its commercial reach. Which storage markets is CATL pursuing in Argentina? The reported pitch covered potential battery-storage uses for mines, data centers and Patagonian wind farms. These are prospective markets identified by CATL representatives, not additional signed projects. (South China Morning Post) The presentation builds on CATL’s reported activity with Argentine generator Central Puerto. For more on that work, see NeoTeo’s earlier coverage of CATL’s storage projects in Argentina. Financing imported storage equipment Financing also came up at the Buenos Aires event: battery containers are imported from China, and Christian Deymonnaz, a representative of Bank of China’s Argentine branch, proposed project loans denominated in yuan. Readers following the broader financial side of technology and business can find finance coverage at NTV88. (South China Morning Post)

artigo.texto: Pakistan is seeking investment and technological partnerships with Finland in electric vehicles (EVs), battery energy storage and advanced industrial technologies as the country works to expand its electric mobility sector. The opportunities were discussed during a meeting between Prime Minister’s Adviser on Industries and Production Haroon Akhtar Khan and a Finnish delegation led by Jarno Syrjälä, Finland’s Under-Secretary of State for International Trade. During the meeting, both sides explored potential cooperation in electric vehicles, battery storage solutions, mineral processing and advanced industrial technologies. Haroon Akhtar Khan highlighted Pakistan’s recent policy initiatives, including the National Industrial Policy, National Tariff Policy and New Energy Vehicle Policy. He said electric vehicles had become an important part of modern transportation and encouraged Finnish companies to explore investment opportunities in Pakistan’s EV and industrial sectors. The adviser also invited Finnish businesses to consider investment in Pakistan’s mineral processing industry. Finnish companies, including Metso and Wärtsilä, are already involved in projects such as Reko Diq. Other Finnish firms, including Nokia and Vaisala, also have an established presence in the country. He added that the government was working to simplify regulatory procedures and remove obstacles to facilitate foreign investment. The discussions also focused on the 14th Finland-Pakistan Business Summit, scheduled to take place in Islamabad on November 16 and Karachi on November 17. The event aims to strengthen business-to-business ties and create new opportunities for companies from both countries. Although no specific Finnish investment, EV manufacturing plant or battery production project was announced, the discussions signal Pakistan’s efforts to attract foreign expertise and technology to support its electric mobility ambitions. Greater cooperation with Finnish companies could help Pakistan develop its EV ecosystem, strengthen battery storage capabilities and expand its industrial technology base.

artigo.texto: This week: Two high-stakes data center public hearings in Spotsylvania and Stafford SPOTSYLVANIA, Va. (7News) — Two important hearings will take place this week in Spotsylvania and Stafford counties on proposed massive data center projects. On Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, the Stafford County Planning Commission will hold a public hearing on the massive Kings Corridor data center complex on and near the Rappahannock River. On Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, the Spotsylvania County Board of Supervisors will hold a public hearing on the Crossroad Technology Campus in the Lee Hill area. The data center applicant is requesting a special use permit in Spotsylvania County to develop a 555-acre data center campus. One property is at 3215 Eagle Drive. The other two properties have not been assigned addresses. According to the county, the properties are located on the north side of Eagle Drive (Route 736), Lee Hill School Drive (Route 635), and Mills Drive (Route 17) and lie adjacent to the CSX Railroad corridor on the west side. RELATED | Spotsylvania Planners recommend approval for 555-acre Amazon data center In September, 7News reported that the Spotsylvania County Planning Commission recommended approving a new data center campus in the Lee Hill area. The planning commission voted 4-2 to approve the Crossroads Technology Campus. The data center mega-site would sit across the street from a park, and homeowners have told 7News they’re concerned about how close it will be to their homes. Right now, the 550-acre site is filled with trees and wildlife. Much of it would be leveled for a data center campus with multiple buildings, including three substations to power the data center complex. RELATED | Spotsylvania residents push back on data centers and the county’s low data center tax Over the summer, 7News reporter Nick Minock spoke with homeowners living next to the proposed data center development. “We are worried about all sorts of things. Will it affect our home prices?” asked Trillane Burlar. “Will we be able to sleep at night with the noise? Will our children get asthma from the additional particulates in the air from the generators?” “I would really like to see a limit on how many data centers we bring here,” said Cynthia Staats. “At the bare minimum, we need to slow it down. We need to understand what the long-term impacts are to our neighborhoods, communities, water, [and] utilities.” “Not only do we love our home because it's our sanctuary and it's our place where we come to restore and revive, but we also have invested a lot of money in our home, and we would like to know that it continues to appraise,” said Sarah Burlar. “I've been looking much more into the environmental impacts, the noise problem that's going to be affecting everyone, because constant hum and noise is actually bad for our health,” said Kevin Johnson. “We wouldn't be able to sit on our decks and enjoy the peacefulness of our neighborhood with having the 24/7 light and noise pollution; that is a big, big concern of ours,” said Catherine Williams. “3,100 feet is too close.” RELATED | Stafford residents oppose massive data centers proposed near Rappahannock River Meanwhile, several Stafford County residents who live in a neighborhood on the Rappahannock River are concerned about a proposal that would place data centers and a substation near – and in some cases right next to – their homes. “I hate it,” said Arlene, who would live directly next to the data centers. “It makes me want to cry.” The data center complex, known as Kings Corridor, would cast a shadow over Arlene’s house during the day, and bright lights from the data centers would shine through her windows at night. “It makes me very sad, and I'm praying that it doesn't come about,” said Arlene. “And we should keep it farm.” The location the data center developer is eyeing is currently farmland and an agricultural area with homes and subdivisions next door. The developer is proposing four sites along Route 3, also known as Kings Highway, for massive data center complexes. Homes are right next to all four locations. The newly proposed data center alley is a short drive from Fredericksburg, King George County, and George Washington’s boyhood home in Stafford County. One of the data center locations is right across the river in Spotsylvania County. The homeowners there would have a view of an industrial site instead of a serene river with trees at Bald Eagle's nest. RELATED | Stafford County postpones data center project hearing after county staff urged denial “They need to know that there is one very large data center being put literally right across a river from a very large subdivision, and they're very likely going to see the light effect of that at night,” said Stafford County resident Kevin French. David lives in the house right next to Arlene’s home, and he’s concerned about data center noise. “I've had a choice [to live anywhere in] the entire country,” said David, who is a veteran and physician. “I chose here, and this is an idyllic area with a lot of nature. We've got a river here. We've got eagles. We've got wildlife. That'll all disappear.” The Parsons are concerned about their property value and the data centers impacting the water next to their homes, which run on well water, but that’s not all. “I'm just worried about the Rappahannock because it is an endangered river,” said Sharon Parsons. The developer’s attorney, Charles Payne, told 7News that at full build-out, Kings Corridor is projected to generate $245 million annually for the county, which is just over 20% of the county's total budget. The developer's attorney told 7News the data center money would support school funding and essential county services “while easing growing tax pressure on homeowners.” The developer points out that Stafford County homeowners’ real estate tax bills have increased 57% in five years. “Our plan also invests more than $80 million in County water infrastructure projects, keeps 55

artigo.texto: India’s most industrialized state, Maharashtra, will launch the country’s first sulfur dioxide (SO2) trading market on December 1, with an aim to bring cleaner air to its population of more than 130 million people. The market builds off successful particulate pollution markets in the state of Gujarat, becoming the third emissions market in India and demonstrating the emerging popularity of the tool to reduce pollution and potentially greenhouse gas emissions while maintaining economic growth. “Maharashtra is tackling pollution while its economy is growing fast, not after. That is the most important time to act, and usually the hardest—but not with markets. Markets can help make cleaner air part of economic progress,” says Michael Greenstone, the Milton Friedman Distinguished Service Professor at the University of Chicago and the founding co-chair of the Emissions Market Accelerator (EMA), a joint initiative of the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago (EPIC) and the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL) that is helping Maharashtra run the market. Emissions markets set a limit on how much pollution industrial plants can release in total. Plants that cut their pollution can sell unused allowances to others, rewarding industries for cleaning up. The Maharashtra market will cover 104 industrial facilities across 17 highly polluting sectors, covering about 80 percent of the state’s industrial emissions. At full implementation, the market will produce health benefits of around $6.5 billion over five years. Speaking at the launch of the market, Shri. Siddhesh Ramdas Kadam, Chairman of the Maharashtra Pollution Control Board, said, “Our approach is not to control, but to grow together with industry. Without the active participation of the industries, and the support of our knowledge partners, the University of Chicago, the Emissions Market Accelerator and J-PAL, this would not have been possible.” Alongside Maharashtra and Gujarat, nine other Indian states are developing or exploring markets, with the help of the EMA. At the same time, discussions are underway to expand internationally, with a partnership already in place in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. History of Results The concept of emissions markets is not new. When power plants were polluting the air and leading to acid rain in the United States during the 1990s, the country started the world’s first large-scale, national cap-and-trade market for pollution. In its first 10 years, the market slashed sulfur dioxide (SO2) emissions by 40 percent, with the benefits exceeding the costs by a 40 to 1 ratio. From there, markets began to take off in Europe, Canada and other countries. But it wasn’t until 2019 that the world learned pollution markets could also work—and indeed thrive—in the Global South, where growth is paramount and pollution is an urgent and deadly threat. “It’s a remarkable moment,” says Greenstone. “The country that pioneered pollution markets has largely stopped building them, while India is demonstrating their potential. Countries looking for ways to grow and clean their air at the same time should be watching closely.” Evaluating the Proof-of-Concept Greenstone and his colleagues Rohini Pande and Nicholas Ryan from Yale University and Anant Sudarshan from the University of Warwick—all Scientific Advisors to EMA—worked with the Indian state of Gujarat in collaboration with J-PAL South Asia and EPIC India to pilot the world’s first particulate pollution market in the industrial city of Surat. Their pilot was conducted as an experiment, so the results from facilities participating in the market could be compared to a control group of facilities following existing, conventional air pollution rules. This rigorous approach enabled researchers to identify the causal impacts of the program. Their 2019 pilot was published in 2025 in a leading economics journal and found that facilities participating in the market cut pollution by up to 30 percent and spent about 11 percent less to do it, with near perfect compliance. The benefits outweighed the costs at least 25 times over. Following the success of the pilot, the Gujarat government expanded the market to cover the control group of facilities. It also launched a second market in the city of Ahmedabad—Gujarat’s largest city and a major industrial hub. Today, 20 million people are breathing cleaner air in Gujarat due to these markets. The Gujarat government became an Earthshot Prize finalist for this work. Scaling in the Global South With the proof-of-concept in hand, the Emissions Market Accelerator was formed in 2025 to help governments throughout the Global South scale the approach. The EMA is working with the government of Rajasthan to develop a market and is exploring the concept with eight other Indian states and the city of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. “J-PAL is proud to have worked alongside the Gujarat government and EPIC for more than a decade to pilot, evaluate, and scale this innovative approach and now through the Emissions Market Accelerator expand it further across India and other countries,” said Esther Duflo, Abdul Latif Jameel Professor of Poverty Alleviation and Development Economics at MIT, co-founder and director of J-PAL, and a 2019 Nobel laureate at the launch of the EMA. What it Means for Carbon What Maharashtra learns about measuring and trading pollution could have implications far beyond the state and even the country. About a quarter of global greenhouse gas emissions are covered by compliance markets—led by the European Union and China. But India is developing its own carbon market, set to be the world’s largest once it’s fully operational. With 86 percent of future emissions growth expected to come from economies like India’s, the country’s broader experience using markets could help shape how other fast-growing economies address both pollution and carbon emissions moving forward.

artigo.texto: Investing.com -- Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) has told customers it will stop selling chips to data-centre operators that rent more than half of their graphics processing units (GPUs) to Chinese companies, CNBC reported on Tuesday, as Washington moves to tighten restrictions on China's access to U.S. artificial intelligence technology. The chipmaker has in recent months warned buyers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act (RASA) would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, similar to its powers over physical hardware, CNBC reported, citing two people familiar with the matter. Nvidia also warned that the legislation could expose both chipmakers and buyers to legal risks, the report said. The Financial Times reported earlier this month that Nvidia had verbally told data-centre clients to direct at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese customers under future contracts. RASA passed the U.S. House of Representatives in January but has yet to clear the Senate, CNBC reported. U.S. export controls restrict Nvidia's advanced chips from being sold to China, but regulators have had limited powers to restrict access through cloud services hosted overseas. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced an interim final rule on Monday aimed at preventing Chinese companies from remotely accessing AI chips, CNBC reported. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that Chinese artificial intelligence startup Moonshot AI had sought access to Nvidia chips through data centres in Europe. The Trump administration accused Moonshot in July of accessing the chips through data centres in East Asia. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia following the departure of Chief Executive Jensen Huang, amid reports of an alleged extramarital affair with a woman U.S. authorities reportedly suspect of spying for China, CNBC reported. Bessent suggested that other Nvidia executives should also face scrutiny over compliance with export controls. He told Fox News he wanted to know whether the company had pushed what he described as seemingly illicit sales to boost revenue and earnings.

artigo.texto: Minneapolis Downtown Council CEO calls for veto of data center ordinance MINNEAPOLIS (FOX 9) - A new Minneapolis data center ordinance is setting up a fight between downtown business leaders and the City Council. Downtown business group pushes back Adam Duininck said he has spent the past six months trying to convince council members that some of downtown's 9 million vacant square feet could be used for data centers. He said that could help shift more of the property tax burden away from homeowners and renters. Local perspective: Duininck pointed to the Sleep Number building in downtown Minneapolis as an example he wants to repeat. The building recently sold for $235 million, which was about eight times its previous assessed value of about $30 million, and Duininck credited the AI data center inside for that increase. "We took I think 10 of the council members through the Sleep Number building behind us on a tour," said Duininck. "We want to try to make things easier for people to invest money in the city, it should be a clear process, a clear timeline," said Duininck. The backstory: Duininck said he worked with the council on some regulations, including square footage and location, but said the final approval amendment added at the end could push developers away. "I think it’s just a total non-starter," said Duininck. He said the extra council vote would add more time and risk to projects that already go through the planning commission process. "Every developer would have to plan in time and risk and do a fair amount of community engagement. That sort of thing is going to happen anyways through the planning commission. This is just another step for the city council to insert themselves in the process," said Duininck. What the new ordinance does Late last week, the City Council passed the ordinance after a full ban failed. As part of that compromise, any new data center would need council approval, could go only in existing buildings and could not be the primary use of a building. "We want to make sure that our community is protected from data centers, the impacts that it has on our planet. We want to better understand the impacts that it has on our water, and we want to have a better say on how we shape our city," said Councilmember Aurin Chowdhury, who authored the ordinance. By the numbers: The city says downtown now has eight data centers serving tech companies. City staff said many more around Minneapolis support the computing needs of existing businesses, and council members said they heard from Xcel Energy that there is interest in up to eight more downtown projects. The ordinance also bars data centers from the first or second floor, requires disclosure of energy, water and generator use, calls for a sound attenuation plan and requires a decommissioning plan if a site stops operating. Data centers larger than 50,000 square feet would also have to enter an Xcel Energy program and pay a premium for renewable energy credits, according to Chowdhury. What we don't know: FOX 9 reached out to ask whether Frey will veto the ordinance, but had not heard back. Frey must decide by Nov. 19, and the city's six-month moratorium on data centers expires Nov. 21. Duininck said there are two to three data center projects in talks downtown right now, but he said those projects could be in jeopardy if the ordinance moves forward. "It’s unfortunate and now we’ll have to figure out a way forward," said Duininck. The Source: A Minneapolis City Council press conference, Downtown Council CEO Adam Duininck, property records and past FOX 9 reporting.

artigo.texto: Council rejects ordinance lifting Jackson’s data center ban JACKSON, Miss. (WLBT) - Jackson’s temporary ban on data centers will remain in place following a contentious Jackson City Council meeting on Tuesday. After hearing from multiple residents, the council voted down a decision to lift the ban, which Ward 3 Councilman Kenneth Stokes says is needed to “untie the mayor’s hands” so he can bring in economic development. “The only thing we’re doing is asking the mayor to have the opportunity to listen to some of the proposals that are out there,” he said. “We don’t have a clue what they are, but we know these other cities are getting money. They’re building up.” “Why do we as Jackson, the capital city ... Why can’t we have an opportunity to bring money to this city?” he added. Stokes was joined by Ward 1 Councilman Ashby Foote in supporting rescinding the measure. Council members Vernon Hartley, Kevin Parkinson, Tina Clay, Brian Grizzell, and Lashia Brown-Thomas voted in opposition. The moratorium will remain in place until April 4. While it’s in effect, the city will not accept, process, or approve any applications for permits related to new data center projects or expansion projects for existing data centers. Foote believes the atmosphere at Tuesday’s meeting was part of the reason the repeal ordinance failed. “Council meetings have become very negative. We can’t let that negativity keep the city from pursuing economic development that could get the city back on its feet,” he said. Several people attended the meeting to speak out against the proposal, including Ward 3 resident Jackie Warren Tatum, who thanked the council for putting the moratorium in place. “For months, despite Stokes’ absences, we voiced our concerns regarding the negative impact of data centers. And we’re learning about the spills up in Southaven, the unbearable noise, and many other things,” she said. “Please do not repeal and rescind this moratorium.” Tatum was referring to a chemical spill at the SpaceXSI data center in Southaven. Mississippi Today reports that a contractor caused “5,000 to 6,000 gallons of a propylene glycol mixture to spill into a neighboring drainage ditch.” The Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality (MDEQ) was still determining when it happened, the publication stated. Yolanda Daniel also urged the council to leave the ban in place until the city fully studies data centers and their potential impact on the community. “A moratorium exists precisely to provide the time necessary for fact-finding, public input and evaluation of alternatives. Seeking to terminate that process early raises a simple, but important question: Has the council fully evaluated other economic development opportunities capable of generating jobs, investment, tax revenue, and long-term prosperity for Jackson and Jackson residents?” she asked. “The responsible course remains unchanged. Allow the moratorium to remain.” Want more WLBT news in your inbox? Click here to subscribe to our newsletter. See a spelling or grammar error in our story? artigo.texto: Osaka, Japan-headquartered Kansai Electric Power is acquiring a minority interest in Prospect Power Storage, a 150-MW/600-MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) owned by Elevate Infrastructure and ArcLight Capital Partners. Elevate (a portfolio company of ArcLight) and ArcLight announced the deal on November 16. Prospect Power currently is the largest standalone BESS in commercial operation in the PJM Interconnection, the power grid operator that serves all or part of 13 states across the U.S. Mid-Atlantic and Midwest regions. Prospect Power is located in Rockingham County, Virginia. The companies on Monday said the investment by Kansai is part of Elevate’s strategy “to develop and operate critical energy infrastructure at scale while attracting sophisticated long-term strategic capital.” The groups said the BESS is an important installation in an area with growing electricity demand driven by data centers, artificial intelligence, and electrification. Utility-Scale Battery Energy Storage “Prospect Power demonstrates Elevate’s ability to execute utility-scale battery storage projects from acquisition through commercial operation and deliver flexible capacity where the grid needs it most,” said Joshua Rogol, CEO of Elevate. “As electricity demand accelerates, projects like Prospect Power are increasingly important to strengthening grid reliability and supporting economic growth. We look forward to continuing to bring projects of this scale online across our portfolio.” The groups said that Kansai’s investment “further expands the group of global strategic and institutional investors partnering with Elevate and ArcLight and reinforces the ability of the platform to combine deep energy infrastructure expertise, operational execution, and long-term capital.” “Battery storage is becoming increasingly critical as energy demand grows and power markets require greater flexibility and reliability,” said Angelo Acconcia, managing partner of ArcLight. “Prospect Power demonstrates the value of bringing large-scale storage infrastructure into service in high-growth markets, and Kansai’s investment is a strong validation of both the quality of the asset and the growing need for storage as part of the nation’s power infrastructure.” “Prospect Power is a high-quality operating asset in an important U.S. power market, and we are pleased to partner with Elevate and ArcLight through this investment – our first battery storage project outside Japan,” said Takayuki Doi, executive officer of Kansai’s Global Business. “We look forward to leveraging the experience gained through Prospect Power and exploring opportunities for further collaboration in battery storage and other energy infrastructure in the United States.” Elevate brought Prospect Power into commercial operation in May of this year. The project is fully contracted under a 15-year power purchase agreement with Dominion Energy Virginia. —Darrell Proctor is a senior editor for POWER.

artigo.texto: EUA restringem venda de chips de IA para data centers no Brasil Regra exige licença para exportar semicondutores avançados ao País; medida também restringe oferta de serviços de computação em nuvem. O governo dos Estados Unidos incluiu o Brasil em uma lista de cinco países que passarão a depender de licenciamento específico para adquirir determinados semicondutores avançados utilizados em inteligência artificial. A medida, anunciada hoje (16) pelo Departamento de Comércio norte-americano, também abrange Indonésia, Malásia, Singapura e Tailândia e estabelece tratamento diferenciado para empresas controladas por grupos sediados nos Estados Unidos. A exigência consta da regulamentação provisória Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors, identificada pelo código RIN-0694-AK50 e divulgada pelo Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), órgão responsável pelo controle de exportações norte-americanas. O documento estabelece que a exportação, reexportação ou transferência de semicondutores avançados para os cinco países dependerá de autorização do governo dos Estados Unidos, ressalvadas as exceções previstas. Segundo o Departamento de Comércio, esses destinos apresentam risco de desvio de equipamentos superior ao considerado normal pelas autoridades norte-americanas. Trata-se de uma classificação adotada pelo governo dos EUA para justificar os novos controles, sem identificação, no documento, de operações irregulares específicas realizadas no Brasil. A medida não representa uma proibição geral de comercialização desses processadores. Os pedidos de licença serão analisados individualmente, considerando critérios de segurança nacional e política externa dos Estados Unidos. Empresas norte-americanas terão exceção à exigência A regulamentação estabelece que a nova exigência de licença baseada no país de destino não será aplicada a semicondutores destinados a empresas sediadas nos Estados Unidos ou cuja controladora final tenha sede naquele país, desde que sejam cumpridas as obrigações de informação previstas pelo BIS. Isso significa que a localização dos equipamentos no Brasil não será o único critério considerado. A estrutura societária da empresa destinatária também determinará a aplicação da exigência específica de licenciamento. A exceção, porém, não representa dispensa de todas as demais regras norte-americanas de controle de exportações. Para os pedidos sujeitos à autorização, o BIS informa que considerará a eficácia dos mecanismos nacionais de controle de exportações e o grau de cooperação das autoridades do país destinatário com o governo dos Estados Unidos. O Departamento de Comércio também poderá adotar medidas adicionais contra países que, segundo sua avaliação, tolerem tentativas de contornar as restrições. Entre as possibilidades estão novas exigências de licenciamento, restrições comerciais e inclusão de empresas em listas de controle. Regra também alcança acesso remoto a data centers Além das restrições de exportação para o Brasil e os outros quatro países, a norma cria um mecanismo separado de controle sobre a utilização remota de capacidade computacional instalada em data centers. Nesse caso, o objetivo declarado pelo governo norte-americano é impedir que empresas sujeitas a restrições tenham acesso indireto a processadores avançados por meio de serviços de computação em nuvem oferecidos em outros países. O mecanismo estabelece a necessidade de licença para determinadas operações com semicondutores destinados a data centers que forneçam, direta ou indiretamente, capacidade computacional superior a 12 milhões de unidades agregadas de Total Processing Performance (TPP) a empresas sediadas, ou controladas por companhias sediadas, em Macau ou em países classificados no grupo D:5. O limite considera a capacidade disponibilizada por uma instalação individual ou por diferentes data centers conectados digitalmente. Essa exigência é distinta da nova regra de licenciamento baseada no destino dos semicondutores. Portanto, o limite de 12 milhões de TPP não constitui um teto geral de processamento para data centers brasileiros. A regulamentação também prevê obrigações de identificação dos clientes e verificação de suas estruturas de controle societário. Há uma exceção específica para sistemas comerciais de recomendação, como os empregados por plataformas de comércio eletrônico e redes sociais, vinculada ao controle de acesso remoto, e não à exigência geral de licenciamento aplicável aos cinco países. Restrição surge após sanção do ReData no Brasil A mudança na política norte-americana ocorre dois meses depois da sanção do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (ReData), instituído pela Lei nº 15.504, de 15 de setembro de 2026. O programa brasileiro estabelece incentivos tributários para investimentos na instalação, modernização e ampliação de data centers, incluindo infraestruturas destinadas à computação em nuvem, ao processamento de alto desempenho e ao treinamento e à inferência de modelos de IA. O regime prevê benefícios para a aquisição de equipamentos destinados ao ativo imobilizado de empresas habilitadas, condicionados ao atendimento de contrapartidas estabelecidas na legislação. Entre as obrigações está a disponibilização de pelo menos 10% da capacidade de processamento, armazenamento e tratamento de dados beneficiada pelo regime para o mercado interno, além do cumprimento de requisitos de sustentabilidade e investimentos em pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação. A nova exigência norte-americana acrescenta uma condição de licenciamento às operações de aquisição de determinados semicondutores avançados destinados ao Brasil, independentemente dos incentivos tributários previstos na legislação brasileira. Vigência depende de publicação oficial A regulamentação também formaliza a revogação dos dispositivos da chamada AI Diffusion Rule, anunciada em janeiro de 2025, durante o governo Joe Biden.
