artigo.texto: Linxon and Fluence form Strategic Collaboration to advance integrated energy storage delivery - Collaboration combines Fluence's energy storage technology with Linxon's Mission Ready EPC approach, building on an initial 200 MWh project award in ERCOT. RALEIGH, N.C. and ARLINGTON, Va., November 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Linxon and Fluence Energy, Inc. today announced a strategic collaboration to pursue and deliver battery energy storage system projects through a more integrated OEM-EPC model. The collaboration combines Fluence's energy storage technology and expertise with Linxon's high-voltage engineering, grid integration and project execution capabilities. The collaboration has already contributed to securing a 200 MWh battery energy storage project in Texas' ERCOT market. Linxon and Fluence are also jointly pursuing additional opportunities across the energy storage and grid infrastructure markets. Linxon's high-voltage engineering, grid connection and complex EPC execution capabilities complement Fluence's energy storage technology and expertise. Together, the companies can address customer requirements spanning the battery energy storage system and the infrastructure required to connect it safely and reliably to the grid. Energy storage projects can separate technology supply, grid connection and EPC execution into distinct scopes, creating technical, commercial and schedule interfaces that must be resolved later in the project lifecycle. Linxon and Fluence intend to address these interfaces earlier by coordinating system requirements, engineering, constructability, procurement, commissioning and project execution from the development stage. By aligning technology, engineering, constructability, procurement, project execution and commissioning from the early stages of a project, Linxon and Fluence aim to reduce interfaces, anticipate risks and create a more competitive and predictable delivery model for customers. From managing interfaces to Engineering the Mission together At the center of the collaboration is a simple principle: align the battery system and grid infrastructure through a coordinated approach to planning, integration, and delivery. The objective is not simply to place two separate scopes alongside each other. It is to align technology, grid integration and project execution earlier, allowing the companies to identify interfaces, improve constructability and establish execution readiness before mobilization. Fluence brings its energy storage technology and expertise, while Linxon brings its EPC system integration and execution capabilities through its Mission Ready EPC approach. The collaboration incorporates Linxon's Mission Ready EPC approach, which focuses on preparing projects for successful execution before mobilization. Through early readiness planning, interface management, constructability reviews, risk identification, standardization and local capability development, Mission Ready EPC is designed to improve execution readiness and delivery predictability. The companies intend to apply these principles across future opportunities while maintaining the flexibility required to address customer specifications, market conditions and local project requirements. Together, the companies intend to create an integrated framework that can be applied across projects and markets, improving execution consistency while maintaining the flexibility required for specific customer needs. Building competitiveness before execution Earlier collaboration between the Fluence OEM and EPC is expected to create opportunities for standardized interfaces, repeatable engineering, improved constructability and more coordinated procurement and execution planning. The approach is also intended to support the progressive development of the engineering knowledge, training, field competencies and local delivery ecosystems required for future energy storage deployment. For customers, this can support earlier risk identification, clearer accountability and a more coordinated path from technology selection through grid connection and project delivery. "We want to redefine the traditional relationship between an OEM and an EPC," said Nicolas Sanloup, Managing Director Americas at Linxon. "This is not about one company providing technology and another executing around it. It is about engineering the mission together from the beginning. By combining Fluence's technology expertise with Linxon's Mission Ready EPC approach, our ambition is to anticipate interfaces, build competitiveness into the solution and develop local capabilities ahead of demand." "By bringing technology and EPC execution closer together from the outset, we have an opportunity to simplify project delivery and create a scalable and repeatable approach for our customers," said Jeff Monday, SVP and Chief Growth Officer, Fluence. "This collaboration reflects the purpose of Fluence PACE, our newly launched strategic partner program, which formalizes how we work with select partners whose capabilities complement our strengths. Our work with Linxon demonstrates how that model can support customers while creating opportunities for continued growth." A new way to deliver energy infrastructure The Linxon–Fluence collaboration is designed to move the OEM–EPC relationship from a transactional interface toward an integrated delivery ecosystem, combining technology, project integration and execution around a common mission. For customers, the ambition is clear: fewer interfaces, earlier alignment, greater competitiveness and more predictable execution. One technology strategy. One execution strategy. One mission. About Linxon Linxon is a global leader in Engineering, Procurement, and Construction (EPC) solutions for electrical substations and infrastructure projects. We develop and deliver turnkey infrastructure solutions that power progress, drive growth and benefit communities, clients, and the environment through sustainable engineering excel

artigo.texto: Rochester City Council approves one-year pause on data centers Interim ordinance passes 5-1 after public hearing ROCHESTER, Minn. (KTTC) – The Rochester City Council approved a one-year moratorium on data centers within city limits through passage of an interim ordinance. The Monday evening vote followed a public hearing on the topic. The majority of those who spoke were in support of the measure. The council heard from 10 people. Eight supported the interim ordinance, which was prepared by Rochester’s Community Development Department. Several social and environmental issues were raised. Those opposing the move said a one-year moratorium isn’t necessary for the council to responsibly address potential data center projects. According to city leaders, there are no pending applications. “There’s a lot of questions at this table. There’s a lot of questions in the audience. And we need to know more about how it’s going to impact our community,” said Randy Schubring, Rochester City Council president. The vote was 5-1. Councilmember Shaun Palmer opposed the proposal and raised concerns over the wording of the interim ordinance. In addition to the one-year moratorium, the action authorizes a comprehensive study on best practices related to data center developments. Find stories like this and more, in our apps. artigo.texto: Gerando resumo A Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica (Abeeólica) ingressou com uma ação civil pública, com pedido de tutela de urgência, para suspender a realização dos leilões de reserva de capacidade (LRCap) para contratação de sistemas de armazenamento por baterias, marcados para 2 e 4 de dezembro próximos, bem como os atos destinados à adjudicação, homologação e celebração dos contratos decorrentes do certame. A ação, apresentada na 17ª Vara Federal Cível do Distrito Federal contra a União e a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel), questiona a legalidade da realização dos leilões sem a adequada definição do regime de custeio e, adicionalmente, a legitimidade da imposição desse encargo aos geradores de energia. Para a Abeeólica, o trecho da Lei nº 15.269/2025, conhecida como lei de modernização do setor elétrico, que determinou que o custo da contratação das baterias seja pago apenas pelos geradores de energia, ofende a ordem econômica, a isonomia, a legalidade e a segurança jurídica, por isso defende o reconhecimento de sua inconstitucionalidade. “Os leilões não podem ser realizados nas condições atuais. O vício está, antes de tudo, na própria regra que atribui aos geradores o custeio das baterias. O encargo que remunera as baterias tem natureza de preço público, e não de tributo. A consequência relevante dessa natureza é a exigência de nexo entre o custeio e a fruição ou o benefício da utilidade remunerada, o que inexiste no caso. Ao impor o custo a quem não é o beneficiário final, a lei produz transferência injustificada de ônus dos usuários finais aos geradores, por meio de medida desproporcional”, argumenta a ação, que cita que os custos de contratação de reserva de capacidade de maneira geral são arcados pelos usuários finais do sistema. Leia também - Bandeira tarifária em novembro segue verde, sem adicional na conta de luz - Moura estende parceria com chineses e investe R$ 200 milhões em fábrica de PE - Subsídios criam o modelo Robin Hood às avessas e deixam País com sobra de energia e risco de apagão A ação também aponta a existência de vício relacionado à estruturação dos leilões por falta de conclusão da regulamentação que definirá a metodologia de cálculo do montante que cada gerador pagará. “E a minuta da regulamentação em discussão pretende fazer alguns geradores pagarem até quatro vezes mais que outros, por critério que a lei não previu. Ao fazê-lo, a Aneel extrapola a delegação do § 6º e sua competência regulatória (art. 2º da Lei 9.427/1996). Esse vício diz respeito aos próprios leilões e subsistiria ainda que a lei fosse válida", diz. A presidente da Abeeólica, Elbia Gannoum, afirmou ao Estadão/Broadcast que a decisão de judicializar o leilão foi tomada a despeito do avanço de um projeto de lei que visa alterar a lei sobre o custeamento das baterias, em discussão no Congresso Nacional, devido ao prazo limite para entrar com a ação civil pública antes do certame. “Esse prazo limite se esgotou ontem, dia 16, e precisamos entrar com essa ação, e ela, de certa forma, reforça o sinal para o Legislativo resolver logo essa questão legal, porque existe essa ação civil pública e existe uma flagrante inconstitucionalidade nessa cobrança”, afirmou. Ela comentou que a Abeeólica também está preparando uma Ação Direta de Inconstitucionalidade (Adin) contra o trecho da lei que define os geradores como responsáveis por custear os sistemas de baterias. “A alocação do custo, por essa lei, foi totalmente equivocada, porque a bateria é um recurso que todo o sistema elétrico brasileiro recebe o benefício, o bônus, porém o ônus da bateria foi alocado só para os geradores de energia eólica e solar, então há um problema claríssimo de alocação ineficiente do custo, que o gerador não pode bancar, principalmente num sistema em que está gerando tanto curtailment (cortes de geração)”, disse, salientando que o sinal de investimento ficou deturpado, gerando insegurança entre empreendedores.

artigo.texto: Marisa Wanzeller, da Agência iNFRA* A Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica) pretende apresentar uma ADI (Ação Direta de Inconstitucionalidade) no STF (Supremo Tribunal Federal) para questionar o custeio do leilão de baterias, disseram fontes à Agência iNFRA. Pelas regras atuais, os encargos da contratação dos sistemas de armazenamento serão pagos apenas pelos geradores. Mesmo com o risco de um “desgaste político”, os agentes temem que o leilão marcado para dezembro ocorra com “fragilidades regulatórias”, de acordo com interlocutores. Também está previsto que empresas associadas entrem com uma ACP (Ação Civil Pública) na Justiça pedindo a suspensão do certame até a aprovação do PL (Projeto de Lei) 3.716/2026, que compartilha os encargos com os consumidores. O objetivo, de acordo com fontes, é pressionar pela rápida tramitação do projeto no Congresso. A estratégia foi aprovada no conselho da Abeeólica há cerca de três semanas, mas foi decidido que só dariam andamento a ela após se certificarem de que o PL não seria aprovado a tempo do certame. Segundo fontes, a expectativa era que o projeto fosse debatido na reunião de líderes partidários da Câmara dos Deputados na última terça-feira (10) e votado no plenário nesta quinta-feira (12). Isso viabilizaria a apreciação no Senado na próxima semana. A matéria, no entanto, não entrou na pauta da Câmara. O leilão está previsto para 2 e 4 de dezembro. Relatório Contribui para a percepção de risco do setor a probabilidade de que outros temas do setor sejam incluídos na matéria. Isso poderia atrasar ainda mais a aprovação do texto. A avaliação de fontes é que há margem para uma tentativa de rever pontos debatidos na MP (Medida Provisória) 1.304, transformada na Lei da Reforma do Setor Elétrico (Lei 15.269/2025). O PL está sob relatoria do deputado Danilo Forte (PP-CE), próximo a pautas de agentes renováveis, mas que não são consensuais no setor e entre os parlamentares. Um dos principais temas já defendidos pelo deputado é a ampliação do ressarcimento financeiro aos geradores pelo curtailment (cortes de geração obrigatórios). Ele conseguiu aprovar uma emenda na Câmara durante a tramitação da MP 1.304, mas que foi vetada pelo presidente Lula. Outros temas que podem estar no relatório, como circula nos bastidores, são a obrigatoriedade de que projetos de hidrogênio verde contratem energia de usinas novas ou recém-construídas, além do retorno dos incentivos nos custos dos fios de transmissão para fontes renováveis. Apesar de serem pautas benéficas às eólicas, segundo fontes, a Abeeólica defende que o relatório do PL 3.716 fique livre de temas polêmicos. Isso facilitaria a aprovação de forma célere, sem colocar em risco a realização do certame na data prevista. Mudanças no edital O diretor-geral da ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica), Sandoval Feitosa, disse à imprensa que qualquer modificação legal sobre o leilão iria requerer o adiamento do certame. Segundo ele, a reguladora precisaria de prazo para ajustes no edital. No MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia), no entanto, a percepção é que o edital aprovado não exige alterações caso o custeio seja estendido aos consumidores, disseram fontes. Existe ainda a possibilidade de incluir no projeto que tramita no Congresso emenda para dispensar a ANEEL do prazo necessário para modificações no edital. Contudo, há relatos de resistências a isso. Posição do governo O governo federal evitou apoio ao PL antes das eleições, pelo risco de ter atrelado a si o discurso de aumento de custos aos consumidores de energia elétrica. No entanto, técnicos do MME estariam alinhados à proposta, de acordo com fontes. O tema também foi levado à Casa Civil, que teria solicitado aos geradores um estudo comprovando que a medida não seria prejudicial aos consumidores e de que forma contribuiria para o sistema elétrico. Segundo relatos, a avaliação é que o órgão da Presidência da República estaria mais sensibilizado à pauta. *Colaboraram: Lais Carregosa e Geraldo Campos Jr.

artigo.texto: Samsung’s Solid-State Battery and the Shaky 64% Silver Demand Claim Key Takeaways - The 64% silver claim traces to one X post from August 2024, and its author later described the figure as "completely unverified" after Kitco, MarketWatch and Morningstar carried it. - Samsung SDI has not disclosed silver loading per cell or pack; the Ag-C layer is a five-micrometre-class coating, so a plausible range is a few hundred grams to about 1 kg per EV pack. - The claim needs 16 million vehicles, equal to four of every five EVs sold in 2025, yet Samsung targets mass production only in the second half of 2027, starting with luxury vehicles and robots. - Against the Silver Institute's 2025 data, the 16,000-tonne figure falls to about 61% of mine production and about 46% of total demand. - Silver's demand case stands without Samsung; the signals to watch are a Samsung loading disclosure, real 2027 production volumes and the pace of Toyota's 2027-2028 rollout. The most quoted number in the silver bull case right now is not a Samsung number. The claim that Samsung‘s solid-state battery could consume 64% of the world’s annual silver mine supply traces back to a single post on X in August 2024. Its author later called his own figure “completely unverified”. That admission has not slowed the figure down. Kitco, MarketWatch, Morningstar and a long tail of silver-investment sites have carried it, and each retelling made it sound more solid than the last. If you hold silver or are thinking about it, you may be pricing in a story rather than a specification. This piece separates what Samsung has disclosed from what was guessed, and gives you a method for testing the next commodity demand claim that lands in your feed. Where did the 64% silver claim come from? In August 2024, Kevin Bambrough, a retired investment professional, posted an estimate of how much silver Samsung’s planned battery might need. About ten days later, Kitco published it on 19 August 2024, and the figure began its run through financial media. His arithmetic took four steps: - Each cell might use as much as 5 g of silver. - A typical 100 kWh EV pack might hold about 200 cells, giving roughly 1 kg of silver per vehicle. - Roughly 20% of about 80 million vehicles built each year (about 16 million) might adopt the battery. - That adds up to 16,000 tonnes of silver a year. Set against a rough 25,000-tonne annual mine output, you get 64%. Use the Silver Institute’s 2025 mine production of 846.6 Moz (about 26,300 tonnes) and the figure drops to about 61%. Against total 2025 demand of 1,130.6 Moz (about 35,166 tonnes), it falls to about 46%. The viral 64% figure relies on cascading estimates, concluding that 16 million vehicles would require 16,000 tonnes of silver a year. How the caveats disappeared The original post was hedged. Bambrough said official figures were unavailable, that 5 g might be high and that the true number could be as low as 0.5 g per cell. In replies, he said he had used AI to estimate grams per cell and cells per pack, and he cited a 3-10 g range without naming its source. None of that survived the trip into headlines. By late 2025, he was pushing back on people treating it as fact: His later verdict on his own estimate: “completely unverified.” Then, in 2026, a widely circulated analysis attributed the figure to technical disclosures from Samsung SDI. No such documents have been published. The same retellings blended a 600-mile range, a 20-year life and a 9-minute charge into one battery, even though those benchmarks came from separate Samsung announcements. A headline figure that cannot be traced to a primary source is a hypothesis. You should treat it as one before it shapes any allocation decision. Readers who want the bullish framing in full can read it in our deep-dive into the solid-state battery silver thesis, which sets out the mispricing pattern commodity investors repeat. When big ASX news breaks, our subscribers know first What has Samsung actually disclosed about silver in its battery? Strip out the guesswork and a real technology remains. Samsung SDI describes its all-solid-state battery as anode-free, meaning the cell is built without a conventional graphite or lithium-metal anode. Instead, lithium plates onto the current collector during charging and forms the anode in place. That is where silver comes in. A thin silver-carbon (Ag-C) layer helps lithium spread evenly rather than clumping, according to Korea JoongAng Daily (1 July 2026). Reports describe it as thinner than a hair, a five-micrometre-class coating. The pouch cell matters because robot packs hold a couple of kWh, against roughly 70-75 kWh in an average EV. Silver scales with stored energy, so early robot cells would use little of it. The production timing is a company target, not a guarantee. The gaps are wider than the facts: - The silver-to-carbon ratio in the layer - Silver per cell, per kWh and per pack - Final cell size for the prismatic EV product - Whether recipes differ between pouch and prismatic formats A plausible range runs from a few hundred grams to about 1 kg per EV pack; even Bambrough’s low-end 3 g per cell gives 600 g. Because the silver sits in an interfacial layer rather than a bulk electrode, you should read 1 kg as the ceiling of that range, not the baseline. How does silver demand work, and why do adoption assumptions matter? A new use for silver only matters relative to the size of the market it enters. Mine supply is the metal dug out each year. Total demand adds industrial use, jewellery, silverware and investment buying, and the gap is filled by recycling and existing stocks. Now test the adoption assumption against those totals. The International Energy Agency (IEA) counted just over 20 million electric cars sold in 2025 (about 21 million in its Global Energy Review), roughly a quarter of new-car sales. The speculative claim of 16,000 tonnes of battery demand represents a massive share of the 846.6 Moz (~26,300 tonnes)

artigo.texto: Eight area emergency departments extinguished a Poynette garage fire just after noon on Sunday, Nov. 15. No one was injured by the blaze. According to an update from Carie Myers, public information officer for the Poynette-Dekora Fire Department, a call at 12:19 p.m. reported flames coming from a garage near Seward Street in the Village of Poynette. Fire units were enroute by 12:26 p.m. Both Poynette-Dekora EMS units were on calls at the time, so medical support was requested from Arlington EMS. “Our partners with the Poynette Police Department were first to arrive on the scene, locating the garage fire in the alley behind the residence,” wrote Myers on Facebook. “Our PPD officer immediately took action, initiating an aggressive attack on the fire with a fire extinguisher until fire resources arrived.” Crews kept the fire contained to the garage and the fire was reported under control by 12:53 p.m. Battery safety An official cause has not been determined, Myers wrote, but “preliminary information indicates the fire may have originated from an e-bike battery that was charging inside the garage.” She noted that the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) has highlighted lithium-ion battery safety as part of its fire prevention education efforts, “Incidents like this serve as an important reminder of the potential dangers associated with these batteries when they are not property stored, charged or maintained,” she wrote. The NFPA advises consumers to stop using these batteries if they observe odor, a change in color, too much heat, a change in shape, leaking or odd noises. Lithium-ion batteries should not be disposed of in traditional recycling bins or they could ignite, the NFPA states. Instead, they should be taken to a safe battery recycling location, such as those listed at call2recycle.org.

artigo.texto: A expansão das fontes fotovoltaica e eólica na última década diversificou os modais do setor elétrico brasileiro (SEB), historicamente organizado em torno das hidrelétricas. Deste crescimento, porém, deriva o desafio de compatibilizar a geração de eletricidade a partir de fontes não despacháveis à flexibilidade do sistema, sem a qual a assincronia entre oferta de energia e oscilações de consumo exige cortes na geração. Chamados de curtailment, os cortes no sistema interligado nacional passaram de 18 TWh em 2024 para 58 TWh em 2025, segundo o ONS. O mesmo país que investe pesadamente na ampliação da oferta de energia, restringiu cerca de 20% da geração potencial solar e eólica no ano passado. Neste cenário, os sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias (“BESS”), assumem protagonismo no SEB. Eles guardam energia nos períodos de excedente, fornecendo-a nos horários de maior demanda. Desempenham parte das funções de flexibilidade associadas aos reservatórios hidrelétricos e às termelétricas. Enquanto a Lei Federal nº 15269/2025 garantiu reconhecimento institucional aos sistemas de armazenamento, a Portaria MME nº 136/2026 balizou as regras para os leilões de reserva de capacidade previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro deste ano, criando condições para uma grande expansão do BESS no futuro próximo. Estes avanços institucionais, porém, contrastam com as regras ambientais, ainda em embrionária fase de construção. Diante disto, muitos agentes setoriais se apegam à crença de que o licenciamento do BESS será “simples” porquanto sua potencial associação a empreendimentos preexistentes reduziria a extensão das intervenções necessárias à implantação da nova tecnologia. Mesmo admitida a possibilidade de instalação do BESS em áreas antropizadas, os critérios adotados pelas oito unidades da federação que já regularam o enquadramento ambiental da tecnologia impõem limites às expectativas de simplicidade. Piauí e Rio Grande do Sul adotam a área útil, mas classificam o potencial poluidor como médio e baixo, respectivamente, e estabelecem limites distintos de não incidência de licenciamento. Bahia e Pará utilizam a potência; Ceará e Rio Grande do Norte, a capacidade de armazenamento. Goiás e Rio de Janeiro incluem baterias em categorias que também abrangem subestações. Em São Paulo e Minas Gerais, como na maioria dos estados, não foram identificados critérios de enquadramento para o BESS. Não surpreende, portanto, que as primeiras licenças ambientais emitidas para os sistemas de armazenamento de energia abranjam diferentes modalidades. Na Bahia, em julho de 2025, uma licença de alteração incluiu o sistema de armazenamento no Complexo Fotovoltaico Cedro. Em novembro do mesmo ano, o Rio Grande do Sul concedeu licenças prévias e de instalação unificadas aos BESS Pontal e Lagoa, vinculados a complexos eólicos. No dia 27 daquele mês, o Piauí emitiu licença prévia ao BESS Lagoa do Barro Associado, enquadrado em tipologia específica. Esses casos, além de contrariarem a doce ilusão de que a instalação das baterias em áreas intervindas afastaria automaticamente a incidência do rito ordinário, indicam que o BESS não será absorvido de modo homogêneo pelos órgãos licenciadores brasileiros. Os arranjos distintos (autônomo ou integrado) ajudam a explicar essa heterogeneidade, mas a ausência de diretrizes nacionais específicas pode submeter até mesmo projetos comparáveis a exigências severamente desiguais. Neste sentido, a normatização do licenciamento do BESS no Brasil aponta para um modelo híbrido. Sistemas diretamente associados a usinas solares, parques eólicos ou instalações de transmissão tendem a ser licenciados de forma integrada ao empreendimento principal, enquanto projetos standalone, especialmente aqueles voltados à oferta de potência e à prestação de outros serviços ao sistema, tendem ao enquadramento autônomo. A questão se torna particularmente sensível porque a expansão do BESS e a construção das regras ambientais específicas para a tecnologia coincidem com a reformulação do próprio licenciamento pela Lei Federal nº 15.190/2025. Com dispositivos do novo marco questionados no STF, os vultosos investimentos previstos para o BESS estão à mercê de algum grau de insegurança jurídica. Há, por fim, uma dimensão material que não pode ser subestimada. Baterias de íons de lítio apresentam riscos ambientais concretos (thermal runaway, incêndio e vazamento químico) e, após sua vida útil, tornam-se resíduos que exigem logística reversa, reciclagem e reprocessamento industrial. Essa estrutura permanece frágil no Brasil. O debate setorial avançou mais na dimensão operacional que na construção de uma cadeia robusta de pós-uso para baterias de grande porte. Assim, o desafio do licenciamento alcança tanto o BESS quanto a infraestrutura necessária ao tratamento e à destinação de suas baterias.

artigo.texto: Trinity Capital Inc. Provides $100 Million in Debt Financing to Accelerate Phononic's Growth and Manufacturing Expansion for AI Data Centers PHOENIX , Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Trinity Capital Inc. (NYSE: TRIN), a leading alternative asset manager, today announced the commitment of $100 million in debt financing to Phononic, a North Carolina-based company developing solid-state cooling solutions for AI data centers. The financing will support accelerated growth and manufacturing capacity expansion to meet increasing customer demand. Phononic's proprietary Thermal Control Systems™ provide software-defined cooling for AI infrastructure by combining high-performance thermoelectric devices with intelligent controls. Compact, solid-state devices and an integrated software control layer deliver precision cooling at the point of need for critical components, including GPUs, high-bandwidth memory, networking silicon, and the optical transceivers that connect them. Phononic's Thermal Fabric™ software layer monitors conditions throughout the data center and dynamically adjusts thermal control in real time as AI workloads change. Together, these solutions are designed to unlock greater AI infrastructure performance, optimize compute and facility capacity, and reduce energy and water consumption. "As AI hardware continues to evolve, we believe precise, real-time cooling at the chip level is becoming increasingly important," said Phil Gager, Senior Managing Director of Tech Lending at Trinity Capital. "Phononic has built the thermoelectric technology and software to address that need, and we're pleased to back their team as demand for their solutions continues to build." Phononic enters its next phase of growth as a profitable company backed by leading venture and growth-equity investors. With demand accelerating across AI infrastructure, the company is expanding manufacturing capacity to meet growing customer requirements and scale delivery of its intelligent thermal control solutions. "AI infrastructure is advancing at an unprecedented pace, and cooling has become a critical bottleneck to growth, limiting both facility capacity and compute and optical performance. Our customers are demanding disruptive thermal control solutions that can overcome these limitations at scale," said Dr. Tony Atti, CEO and Founder of Phononic. "Our partnership with Trinity Capital enables us to accelerate manufacturing capacity expansion to meet that demand and support the next wave of growth across AI infrastructure." About Trinity Capital Inc. Trinity Capital Inc. (NYSE: TRIN) is an alternative asset manager that seeks to deliver consistent returns for investors through access to private credit markets. Trinity Capital sources and structures investments in well-capitalized growth-oriented companies across five distinct lending verticals: Tech Lending, Equipment Finance, Healthcare & Life Sciences, Sponsor Finance, and Asset Based Lending. As a long-term, trusted partner for innovative companies seeking tailored debt solutions, Trinity Capital has deployed more than $6.8 billion across over 511 investments since inception in 2008 (as of September 30, 2026). Headquartered in Phoenix, Arizona, Trinity Capital's dedicated team is strategically located across the United States and Europe. For more information on Trinity Capital, please visit trinitycapital.com and stay connected to the latest activity via LinkedIn. About Phononic Phononic is a leader in software-defined thermal control for AI infrastructure, combining breakthrough solid-state cooling technology with intelligent hardware and software to unlock greater performance, efficiency, and reliability. Deployed across major U.S. hyperscalers, Phononic's solutions deliver precision thermal control at the source for optical connectivity, GPUs, high-bandwidth memory, and other critical AI components. Through its Thermal Control Systems™ and Thermal Fabric™ intelligence layer, Phononic enables real-time, workload-responsive thermal optimization that helps mitigate throttling, improve energy efficiency, and maximize AI infrastructure performance. For more information, visit www.phononic.com. artigo.texto: Residents urged to speak up as Salix weighs data center ordinances SALIX, Iowa (KTIV) - Community members gathered in Salix Monday evening for an informational meeting to discuss how local ordinances could shape the future of their community. This comes amid debate over a proposed Google data center. Attendees learned about data centers and asked questions about their potential local impact. Salix City Council members Gene Monk and Tim Skidmore attended the meeting. Organizers encouraged residents who want to see changes to continue speaking at City Council meetings and contacting elected leaders. “I think people need to show up. If there’s no one at the city council meeting, no one calling their numbers, they’re not going to change their minds,” said Jessica Mazour, conservation program coordinator for the Iowa Sierra Club. Woodbury County homeowner Janet Yanak said one of her biggest takeaways was the importance of getting local ordinances right. She also expressed concern about a data center’s potential impact on water and air quality. “The one thing that really did stick with me is how important it is to get these ordinances in and get them right,” Yanak said. “We really need some strict, some protective ordinances to protect not only the cities, but the citizens.” Residents were also encouraged to talk with their neighbors, write letters to the editor and contact state lawmakers about data center legislation. artigo.texto: Ekinops unveils PTM300 compact modular platform for ultra-high-capacity datacenter connectivity New 3RU* optical platform delivers up to 32 Tb/s capacity with ultra-low power consumption per bit, open management and multi-vendor interoperability PARIS , Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Ekinops (Euronext Paris - FR0011466069 – EKI), a leading provider of optical networks, connectivity and SASE cybersecurity solutions for telecom service providers and enterprises, today announces the release of PTM300, a new compact modular optical platform designed for high-capacity datacenter interconnect (DCI) and scale-across optical networking applications. Designed to bring carrier-class optical transport into a datacenter form factor, PTM300 delivers up to 32 Tb/s of client and line capacity in just 3RU, supporting up to 40 x 800 Gb/s coherent pluggable interfaces. The platform combines ultra-high density and ultra-low 0.08W per Gbps (watts per gigabit per second) power consumption with redundant power and cooling, front-to-back airflow, and Open management interface based on Openconfig and Netconf/Yang for easy integration into open, standards-based environments. It is also compatible with Ekinops' Celestis NMS for unified network management within an Ekinops optical network further simplifying integration. With PTM300, Ekinops is extending its optical networking portfolio to address increasing interconnection bandwidth requirements between datacenters with compact modular platforms that seamlessly enable the transition from the telco environment. High density without compromising openness and performance PTM300 can be deployed over direct fiber, existing Ekinops optical line systems or third-party infrastructure using alien wavelengths. Beyond DCI, it is designed to address metro, regional and long-haul transport applications as well as service regeneration for router-hosted IPoWDM applications. *RU = Rack Unit "The rapid growth of cloud and AI is creating unprecedented bandwidth requirements between data centers, as well a greater demand for service providers to deliver wavelength services to these locations. With PTM300, we are bringing together ultra-high capacity, ultra-low power consumption, operational simplicity and openness in a compact platform designed to help operators scale their optical networks while protecting existing infrastructure investments," said Philippe Moulin, Chief Operating Officer of Ekinops. PTM300 will be generally available in December 2026 with first customer deployments expected in Q1 2027. All press releases are published after Euronext Paris market close. artigo.texto: TECO Showcases AI Data Center and EV Powertrain Solutions in Poland WARSAW, Poland , Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- TECO Electric & Machinery Co., Ltd. (TWSE: 1504) will join the Taiwan Electrical and Electronic Manufacturers' Association (TEEMA) at the TEEMA Technology Park Industry Day – Poland, held November 17–18 in Warsaw. TECO will showcase its HULK 3.0 and HULK 6.0 Modular Data Center (MDC) solutions alongside next-generation EV powertrain systems, highlighting its integrated capabilities in AI infrastructure and electrification. HULK Series Accelerate AI Infrastructure Deployment HULK 3.0, designed for initial AI computing infrastructure deployment, features a 10-module configuration with an IT load capacity of 2.7 MW. It can accommodate 16 advanced computing systems and 12 IT racks. The cooling system combines Coolant Distribution Units (CDUs) and Computer Room Air Conditioning (CRAC) systems to support initial AI computing deployments. HULK 6.0, targeting high-density AI data center campuses, features a 22-module configuration with an IT load capacity of 4.2 MW per data hall. It can accommodate up to 16 advanced computing systems and 24 IT racks. The solution integrates power distribution, cooling, fire protection, and monitoring systems to meet the high reliability and electromechanical integration requirements of large-scale AI computing facilities. Through factory prefabrication and modular system integration, TECO reduces the complexity of on-site construction, enabling planned delivery timelines of as little as nine months for both solutions, with a design Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) target of 1.2. These solutions allow hyperscale cloud providers, AI cloud and GPU computing service providers, and data center colocation operators to deploy infrastructure in phases, according to their evolving needs. High-Efficiency Hairpin Motors Drive Electrification TECO will also showcase its OD180 hairpin motor and EV powertrain portfolio, covering 50–410 kW and 250–800 V. Featuring high slot-fill windings, these motors deliver improved power density, reduced copper losses, enhanced cooling performance, and higher torque output within compact installation spaces. Applications include light commercial vehicles, 15–32-ton trucks, 9- and 12-meter electric buses, and off-highway equipment such as construction, agricultural, and mining machinery. By integrating motors, controllers, and reduction gearboxes, TECO provides complete EV powertrain solutions that improve efficiency, shorten development timelines, and support diverse commercial and industrial electrification needs. Through participation in the TEEMA exhibition, TECO aims to strengthen partnerships with Polish and European industries to expand opportunities in AI infrastructure and electrification markets. TECO has delivered nearly 1 GW of data center infrastructure worldwide and holds over 85% of Taiwan's electric bus powertrain market. artigo.texto: Hyperscale Data, Inc. Announces Intent to Launch Previously Announced Exchange Offer on or about November 20, 2026 LAS VEGAS , Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Hyperscale Data, Inc. (NYSE American: GPUS), an artificial intelligence ("AI") data center company ("Hyperscale Data" or the "Company"), today announced that it intends to commence its previously announced exchange offer to purchase up to 192,308,000 shares of its Class A Common Stock, $0.001 par value per share ("Common Stock") in exchange for units (the "Units") consisting of (a) $2.00 in cash and (b) one share of preferred stock with a stated value of $24.00 per share (the "Preferred Stock"), per 100 shares of Common Stock on or about November 20, 2026. The Company previously announced that it anticipated formally launching the exchange offer on or around November 17, 2026. Due to the recent global outages of various enterprise services, the Company is now anticipating formally launching the exchange offer on or about November 20, 2026, subject to board approval, regulatory approval and customary closing conditions. Details regarding the proposed exchange offer and instructions for stockholders interested in participating will be provided in the Offer to Exchange and related documents, which will be filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the "SEC") and distributed to the Company stockholders. The exchange offer will not be made to any person in any jurisdiction in which either the exchange offer, or solicitation or sale thereof, is unlawful. This press release is for informational purposes only and shall not constitute an offer to buy or sell Common Stock or any other securities. Any solicitation of offers to buy the Common Stock will only be made pursuant to an Offer to Exchange and related materials to be sent to the Company stockholders on the commencement of the exchange offer. Company stockholders should read such materials carefully when they become available because they will contain important information, including the terms and conditions of the proposed exchange offer. The tender offer documents will be available without charge at the SEC's website at http://www.sec.gov and will be delivered without charge to all stockholders of the Company who so request it. It is anticipated that the exchange offer will be made pursuant to the exemption from registration requirements of the Securities Act of 1933, as amended, contained in Section 3(a)(9) thereof. Under that exemption, if Common Stock exchanged is freely tradeable, the Preferred Stock received in exchange therefor will be freely tradeable. If the Common Stock is restricted, the Preferred Stock will be restricted to the same degree. For more information on Hyperscale Data and its subsidiaries, Hyperscale Data recommends that stockholders, investors and any other interested parties read Hyperscale Data's public filings and press releases available under the Investor Relations section at hyperscaledata.com or available at www.sec.gov. About Hyperscale Data, Inc. Through its wholly owned subsidiary Sentinum, Inc., Hyperscale Data owns and operates a data center at which it offers colocation and hosting services for the emerging AI ecosystems and other industries. Another of Hyperscale Data's wholly owned subsidiaries, Ault Capital Group, Inc. ("ACG"), is a hybrid private equity firm and operating company that acquires, finances, builds and actively manages businesses across financial services, digital assets, industrial services, hospitality, defense technologies and other sectors. Hyperscale Data currently expects the divestiture of ACG (the "Divestiture") to occur in 2027. Upon the occurrence of the Divestiture, the Company would be an owner and operator of data centers to support high-performance computing services, as well as a holder of the digital assets and the third wholly owned subsidiary of the Company, Omnipresent Robotics, LLC. Until the Divestiture occurs, the Company will continue to provide, through ACG and its wholly and majority-owned subsidiaries and strategic investments, mission-critical products that support a diverse range of industries, including an AI software platform, equipment rental services, defense/aerospace, industrial, automotive and hotel operations. In addition, ACG is actively engaged in private credit and structured finance through Ault Lending, LLC, a licensed lending subsidiary. Hyperscale Data's headquarters are located at 11411 Southern Highlands Parkway, Suite 190, Las Vegas, NV 89141. On December 23, 2024, the Company issued one million (1,000,000) shares of a newly designated Series F Exchangeable Preferred Stock (the "Series F Preferred Stock") to all common stockholders and holders of the Series C Preferred Stock on an as-converted basis. The Divestiture will occur through the voluntary exchange of the Series F Preferred Stock for shares of Class A Common Stock and Class B Common Stock of ACG (collectively, the "ACG Shares"). The Company reminds its stockholders that only those holders of the Series F Preferred Stock who agree to surrender such shares, and do not properly withdraw such surrender, in the exchange offer through which the Divestiture will occur, will be entitled to receive the ACG Shares and consequently be shareholders of ACG upon the occurrence of the Divestiture. artigo.texto: Argentum AI Signs $630M Data Center Collaboration With Kyndryl to Deploy NVIDIA GPUs 20-year, 10-megawatt agreement underpins deployment of B300 systems for AI inference SAN FRANCISCO and NEW YORK, Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Argentum AI, a premium GPU cloud provider, and Kyndryl (NYSE: KD), a leading provider of mission-critical enterprise technology services, today announced a 20-year, $630M data center collaboration for an initial 10 megawatts (MW) of capacity at Kyndryl'sBoulder, Colorado facility to power deployment of NVIDIA GPU systems. Argentum is deploying NVIDIA B300 systems at the site in a fully Tier III environment, creating advanced, enterprise-grade infrastructure to run demanding AI applications at scale. Deployment is underway. The agreement provides Argentum access to a facility built for the power density of current-generation GPU systems and gives Argentum's customers a faster path to high-performance inference capacity. artigo.texto: Linxon and Fluence form Strategic Collaboration to advance integrated energy storage delivery Linxon and Fluence form Strategic Collaboration to advance integrated energy storage delivery - Collaboration combines Fluence's energy storage technology with Linxon's Mission Ready EPC approach, building on an initial 200 MWh project award in ERCOT. RALEIGH, N.C. and ARLINGTON, Va., November 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Linxon and Fluence Energy, Inc. today announced a strategic collaboration to pursue and deliver battery energy storage system projects through a more integrated OEM-EPC model. The collaboration combines Fluence's energy storage technology and expertise with Linxon's high-voltage engineering, grid integration and project execution capabilities. The collaboration has already contributed to securing a 200 MWh battery energy storage project in Texas'ERCOT market. Linxon and Fluence are also jointly pursuing additional opportunities across the energy storage and grid infrastructure markets. Linxon's high-voltage engineering, grid connection and complex EPC execution capabilities complement Fluence's energy storage technology and expertise. Together, the companies can address customer requirements spanning the battery energy storage system and the infrastructure required to connect it safely and reliably to the grid. Energy storage projects can separate technology supply, grid connection and EPC execution into distinct scopes, creating technical, commercial and schedule interfaces that must be resolved later in the project lifecycle. Linxon and Fluence intend to address these interfaces earlier by coordinating system requirements, engineering, constructability, procurement, commissioning and project execution from the development stage. By aligning technology, engineering, constructability, procurement, project execution and commissioning from the early stages of a project, Linxon and Fluence aim to reduce interfaces, anticipate risks and create a more competitive and predictable delivery model for customers. From managing interfaces to Engineering the Mission together At the center of the collaboration is a simple principle: align the battery system and grid infrastructure through a coordinated approach to planning, integration, and delivery. The objective is not simply to place two separate scopes alongside each other. It is to align technology, grid integration and project execution earlier, allowing the companies to identify interfaces, improve constructability and establish execution readiness before mobilization. Fluence brings its energy storage technology and expertise, while Linxon brings its EPC system integration and execution capabilities through its Mission Ready EPC approach. The collaboration incorporates Linxon's Mission Ready EPC approach, which focuses on preparing projects for successful execution before mobilization. Through early readiness planning, interface management, constructability reviews, risk identification, standardization and local capability development, Mission Ready EPC is designed to improve execution readiness and delivery predictability. The companies intend to apply these principles across future opportunities while maintaining the flexibility required to address customer specifications, market conditions and local project requirements. Together, the companies intend to create an integrated framework that can be applied across projects and markets, improving execution consistency while maintaining the flexibility required for specific customer needs. Building competitiveness before execution Earlier collaboration between the Fluence OEM and EPC is expected to create opportunities for standardized interfaces, repeatable engineering, improved constructability and more coordinated procurement and execution planning. The approach is also intended to support the progressive development of the engineering knowledge, training, field competencies and local delivery ecosystems required for future energy storage deployment. For customers, this can support earlier risk identification, clearer accountability and a more coordinated path from technology selection through grid connection and project delivery. "We want to redefine the traditional relationship between an OEM and an EPC," said Nicolas Sanloup, Managing Director Americas at Linxon . "This is not about one company providing technology and another executing around it. It is about engineering the mission together from the beginning. By combining Fluence's technology expertise with Linxon's Mission Ready EPC approach, our ambition is to anticipate interfaces, build competitiveness into the solution and develop local capabilities ahead of demand." "By bringing technology and EPC execution closer together from the outset, we have an opportunity to simplify project delivery and create a scalable and repeatable approach for our customers," said Jeff Monday, SVP and Chief Growth Officer, Fluence . "This collaboration reflects the purpose of Fluence PACE, our newly launched strategic partner program, which formalizes how we work with select partners whose capabilities complement our strengths. Our work with Linxon demonstrates how that model can support customers while creating opportunities for continued growth." A new way to deliver energy infrastructure The Linxon–Fluence collaboration is designed to move the OEM–EPC relationship from a transactional interface toward an integrated delivery ecosystem, combining technology, project integration and execution around a common mission. For customers, the ambition is clear: fewer interfaces, earlier alignment, greater competitiveness and more predictable execution. One technology strategy. One execution strategy. One mission. artigo.texto: The last several days have not been good for big tech. On Thursday, Microsoft Outlook, which handles most of the business email in America, suddenly shut down. Then, on Friday, the FAA grounded every flight in the country, apparently because of technical upgrades that went wrong. These fiber-optic faceplants happen to come at a moment when much of the country, mostly at the local level, is seeing fierce opposition to data centers, not only because of environmental concerns and energy prices but also because of real concerns that tech is becoming too big a part of our lives. In Maryland, the story of Taylor Frazier-McCollum, a community activist who helped block a $5 billion data center project planned for the site of an abandoned mall, went viral, with the left praising the power and bravery of the individual and the right mocking her alternative idea for the site: a trampoline park. In fairness, this Maryland activist does not come across as particularly adroit or searing in her insights. On the other hand, like many Americans, she understands implicitly the advantages a trampoline park or a Topgolf location can bring to her community. The benefits of a data center seem murky by comparison. This kind of attitude toward data centers has many very smart people pulling their hair out in frustration. For them, the economic and technological benefits, including beating China in the AI race, obviously far outweigh the concerns of nonexperts like Frazier-McCollum. In fact, many proponents of data centers argue that China is funding propaganda to slow our growth in the sector, even as data centers start popping up all over China like umbrella salesmen in a Manhattan rainstorm. This is true. China, the Eddie Haskell of the planet, is absolutely "giving us the business" by stoking anti-data center fervor. But it is important to remember that data centers aren’t controversial because of Chinese information operations; rather, Chinese information operations exist because data centers are controversial. FOREIGN ADVERSARIES RUNNING 'PSYOP' TO FUEL ANTI-AI AND ANTI-DATA CENTER MOVEMENT, WAR OFFICIAL SAYS Up until about six months ago, data centers were not a major national news story. In fact, the place one was most likely to hear about them was local talk radio in small towns across rural America, where many people care more about who the county commissioner is than who lives at 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. The concerns you hear from callers on these shows sound downright mundane compared to the fervent calls from experts to win the new space race against China and unleash the power of AI. But for many who live there, water rights and easements mean more than geopolitical fisticuffs. This is why, in a strange way, this week’s tech mishaps, which inconvenienced millions of Americans at work and at airports, present an opportunity for the tech industry to explain in more practical terms why we need so many data centers. Implicit in the pro-data center argument has been the idea, often offered with a bit of disdain, that it is absurd to oppose data centers by posting about them on devices that cannot operate without data centers. And OK, point taken, but the snark doesn’t help. 8 EVERYDAY THINGS THAT WOULD QUIT WORKING WITHOUT DATA CENTERS In fact, Democrats, one could say cynically, capitalized on the anger many Americans felt at being talked down to by the big tech set, using it to great electoral advantage, especially in traditionally right-leaning rural areas. But Democrats, no matter who leads them, cannot maintain their blanket disapproval of data centers for long, as this weekend showed. It was safe enough to call for data center moratoriums in the races of 2026, but as they seek to govern, Democrats will need data centers. Let’s face it, nobody is going back to typewriters and fax machines, and nobody wants to sit in seat 24B for five hours on the tarmac at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport. RED COUNTIES WITH DATA CENTER PROJECTS SWUNG AWAY FROM GOP IN MIDTERMS, ANALYSIS FINDS At the local level, much of the data center fuss is already working itself out through the sausage-making of politics and the courts. Some communities, like the Amish, will eschew the infrastructure projects completely and lose out on the pot of gold. But most will find a happy compromise once enough concessions are pried from developers. For now, proponents of data centers would be wise to point to events like the Outlook outage and the flight groundings, without sneering, as the very reason we need so many data centers to power the conveniences we have all grown accustomed to. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP With the midterms behind us and our tech infrastructure on thin ice, now is the time for the case to be made that, one way or another, our future lies in data centers.

artigo.texto: RS offers ebm-papst solutions for rack-level thermal challenges in high-density data centers ebm-papst DiaForce, AxiForce, and RadiCal series fans help mitigate rack-level hot spots, minimize harmonic vibration, reduce parasitic power draw, and improve energy efficiency in critical data center infrastructure. FORT WORTH, Texas , Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- RS, a high-service global product and service solutions provider for industrial customers, offers high-performance ebm-papst air-moving products engineered to solve rack-level thermal management challenges in high-density data centers, including several series of robust, compact, and versatile fans. As processing demands soar, these proven fan technologies allow data center operators, system builders, and thermal engineers to optimize airflow, overcome high static pressure resistance, minimize harmonic vibration, reduce parasitic power draw, and reliably protect critical assets from thermal damage and mechanical stress. Rapid growth in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and high-performance computing has pushed server rack power densities from 3–5kW a decade ago to 40–100kW or more per rack today. Because server chips convert nearly all electrical energy into heat, unmitigated thermal energy creates localized hot spots that facility-level air conditioning cannot effectively dissipate, risking component degradation, silicon melting, and unplanned downtime that averages around $9,000 per minute. While liquid cooling adoption is growing, fan-based forced-air cooling remains the global standard for roughly 90% of data centers due to lower capital costs, easier maintenance, legacy facility compatibility, and zero risk of fluid leaks near high-voltage electronics. Effectively cooling these densely populated server chassis requires specialized fans engineered to overcome extreme aerodynamic resistance from PCBs, power supplies, and cabling without introducing excessive noise, harmonic vibration, or energy penalties. ebm-papst offers a variety of precision engineered fans through RS that directly resolve these common rack-level thermal and mechanical constraints. Key product lines include: - DiaForce series diagonal compact fans: Designed to combine the high volumetric airflow of axial fans with the high static pressure capabilities of centrifugal blowers, these single-stage units deliver up to 50% higher air performance than single-stage axial fans with static pressure matching traditional counter-rotating units. Their unique single-motor diagonal design cuts motor count in half compared to dual-motor counter-rotating setups, significantly reducing the harmonic vibration energy that causes hard drive read/write errors while lowering acoustic noise by 6–12 dB(A) with superior tonality. Available in standard 40mm, 80mm, and 120mm footprints, DiaForce fans provide high-efficiency cooling for high-density server chassis and uninterruptible power supply systems. - AxiForce series compact axial fans: Engineered specifically for high-static-pressure server rack environments, these compact axial fans feature optimized blade aerodynamics, lower noise profiles, reduced electrical power draw, and robust environmental construction compared to legacy axial designs. They are available in compact frame sizes ranging from 40mm to 200mm, directly corresponding to vertical rack unit (U) heights from 1U chassis (40mm) up to 4U and larger enclosures (120mm and 172mm). This structural alignment enables reliable, space-efficient thermal protection across server chassis, power supplies, and rack enclosures. - RadiCal series AC and EC centrifugal fans: Featuring backward-curved impellers from 190mm to 250mm with aerodynamically shaped blades, these centrifugal fans minimize energy losses, flow separation, and turbulence to achieve maximum aerodynamic efficiency. Available with GreenTech EC motor technology and variable speed controls, they reduce energy consumption by up to 50% compared to traditional AC alternatives to curb facility-wide parasitic power draw. Their high-volume airflow capabilities make them ideal for computer room air conditioners, air handling units, supply fan grids, rear-door heat exchangers, and in-row cooling architectures. "As data centers scale to handle generative AI and high-performance computing, thermal management has shifted from a facility-wide consideration to a precise, component-level engineering discipline," said Steve Berestecky, Director of Information Technology & Clean Room Air Technologies at ebm-papst. "Evaluating fans strictly on total volumetric airflow is no longer sufficient when dense internal components create intense aerodynamic impedance. By matching static pressure requirements, optimizing air velocity at critical component sites, and utilizing intelligent PWM control loops, ebm-papst solutions like our DiaForce, AxiForce, and RadiCal series fans allow engineers to master thermal density, curb parasitic power consumption, and protect operational uptime." To learn more about high-performance ebm-papst air-moving products available through RS, visit the links embedded here and check out the new RS Expert Advice article, "High-density rack-level data center cooling," featuring Steve Berestecky. artigo.texto: GCC and EXIST Sign Carbon Market Cooperation Agreement at COP31 The Global Carbon Council and Turkiye's Energy Exchange, Enerji Piyasalari Isletme A.S., known internationally as Energy Exchange Istanbul (EXIST), have signed a Memorandum of Understanding to deepen cooperation on carbon market development and to examine trading of GCC-issued carbon credits in Turkiye, according to QNA. The agreement was signed at the Arab Climate Pavilion, jointly hosted by the GCC and the League of Arab States, during the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Turkiye. The memorandum was signed by Dr. Yousef Alhorr, Founding Chairman of the GCC, and Taha Meli Arvas, CEO and Vice Chairman of the Board of EPIAS. The cooperation is intended to facilitate use of the GCC's internationally recognized carbon crediting program in Turkiye, open new paths for market participants to access high-integrity carbon credits, and reinforce technical capacity as the country builds its carbon market framework. Combining Standards Expertise with Market Operations The arrangement pairs the GCC's experience in carbon crediting standards, project registration and credit issuance with EPIAS's expertise in running organized energy and environmental markets. It aims to support transparent market mechanisms that connect credible emissions reduction projects with buyers and investors, while contributing to corporate climate strategies and national climate objectives. Under the memorandum, the two organizations will explore listing and trading of the GCC's Approved Carbon Credits on EPIAS trading platforms, subject to applicable regulations and market requirements. They will also examine whether the credits could be recognized under Turkiye's future compliance carbon market framework. The proposed cooperation could widen market access for project developers and buyers and encourage the registration, issuance and use of high-quality carbon credits through transparent trading processes. Capacity Building and Technical Support Beyond trading, the agreement emphasizes capacity building and knowledge exchange. The GCC and EPIAS intend to hold workshops, webinars, seminars and other activities to improve understanding of carbon market requirements among potential participants and local stakeholders. The GCC will also support access to publicly available information on its crediting program, registry and methodologies. The cooperation may draw on the expertise of the Gulf Organisation for Research and Development, the GCC's parent organization, to support market readiness and technical capacity development in Turkiye. Possible areas of support include training on greenhouse gas accounting, monitoring, reporting and verification, carbon border adjustment requirements, and sustainability disclosure under the Turkish Sustainability Reporting Standards, which are aligned with IFRS S1 and S2. The parties may also explore applying GORD digital solutions, including SustainoAI, for greenhouse gas accounting, ESG reporting and financed-emissions calculations, along with broader technical assistance on decarbonization and energy efficiency. Positions of the Signatories Dr. Alhorr commented that credible carbon markets depend on connecting high-integrity credits with transparent, well-functioning market infrastructure, and that the cooperation with EPIAS creates an opportunity to strengthen those connections in Turkiye while supporting the knowledge and institutional capacity markets need to grow responsibly. He indicated that a broader objective is to help climate projects attract investment, deliver measurable emissions reductions and contribute to sustainable economic development. Taha Meli Arvas commented that effective carbon markets require more than trading platforms, depending instead on reliable standards, transparent processes and participants with the knowledge and capacity to engage confidently. He said the cooperation with the GCC aims to explore new opportunities for carbon credit trading, strengthen technical expertise and support market development in line with Turkiye's regulatory priorities and evolving market needs. The agreement reflects a shared interest in strengthening Turkiye's carbon market ecosystem through internationally recognized standards, technical cooperation and the exchange of expertise. By combining carbon crediting with organized market operations, the GCC and EPIAS aim to support credible and accessible market mechanisms that can translate climate commitments into measurable outcomes. - 1. artigo.texto: Rwanda carbon market goes to Antalya with 29 projects on its register Rwanda has registered 29 carbon market projects and opened its Article 6 agreement with Singapore to renewable energy and clean cooking proposals, and at COP31 in Antalya, where Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva leads the delegation, its pavilion programme includes the launch of a carbon registry and a distributed renewable energy fund. Credits from Rwandan carbon projects have sold at between $14 and $45 a tonne and brought in about $1.5 million, the Rwanda Environment Management Authority (REMA) said in September, from a register of 29 projects running across renewable energy, electric mobility, forestry, waste management, agriculture and land conservation. Some of those projects are already selling credits and others are with external auditors for verification, according to REMA, whose Deputy Director General, Faustin Munyazikwiye, said the projects “are at different stages of development”. Rwanda became Singapore’s first East African partner under Article 6 when the two governments signed an implementation agreement on 6 May 2025, Singapore’s sixth such agreement overall, under which Singapore-based companies can use eligible Rwandan credits to offset up to 5% of their taxable emissions. Singapore will put the value of 5% of the authorised credits towards adaptation in Rwanda and cancel 2% at first issuance, and the call for proposals that opened on 30 January covers renewable energy and efficiency alongside clean cooking, electric mobility, waste management and improved forest management. The joint committee overseeing the agreement, which Munyazikwiye co-chairs, met in Kigali on 16 October to speed up approvals, and the lessons from it are the subject of a session at Rwanda’s COP31 pavilion that will also launch the country’s carbon registry. At the same pavilion the Rwanda Green Fund is launching its Distributed Renewable Energy Fund, the first fund of its investment arm, the Ministry of Environment said on 10 November, alongside a biodiversity window and the Cabinet-endorsed Country Platform for Climate and Development, which coordinates national climate priorities with the investment raised for them. Household electricity access reached 85.4% by the end of 2025, with 60.1% of households on the national grid and 25.3% relying on solar, according to Rwanda Energy Group, and the government’s target is universal access by 2029. The World Bank’s Renewable Energy Fund project, which runs subsidies and loans for solar home systems through local savings and credit cooperatives, aims to connect at least 445,000 households from a $15 million subsidy window, and Franz Drees-Gross, the World Bank Group’s Regional Director for Infrastructure in Western and Central Africa, called Rwanda “a shining example for Africa of what it takes to electrify a country”, The New Times reported in October. Under its third nationally determined contribution, submitted last year, Rwanda commits to a 53% cut in greenhouse gas emissions by 2035, about 14.86 million tonnes, with 7% of the reduction to come from its own resources and 46% depending on external finance or technical support, against a total finance need of $12 billion to 2035. Its delegation is asking COP31 for a clear roadmap to the $300 billion a year climate finance goal agreed at COP29, and for high-integrity carbon markets under Article 6. Rwanda will also use COP31 to call for universal ratification of the Kigali Amendment, which commits countries to cut their use of climate-warming hydrofluorocarbons by 80% by 2047, after Kigali hosted the 38th Meeting of the Parties to the Montreal Protocol from 2 November on the amendment’s tenth anniversary. Full implementation could avoid up to 0.5°C of warming by 2100, and close to 1°C with more efficient cooling, and the Minister of Environment, Dr Bernadette Arakwiye, told the Kigali meeting that “signals only matter when they are backed by clear rules”. Speaking in Kigali in October, Arakwiye said the government is studying whether “a share of the proceeds from carbon transactions can be recycled through the Rwanda Green Fund”, so that the credits Rwanda sells now pay for the feasibility studies and baseline data its next projects need before investors will look at them. artigo.texto: St Bess collects $413m in property taxes up to October Loading article... WESTERN BUREAU: Despite the widespread devastation caused by Hurricane Melissa, St Elizabeth is reporting a steady collection in property tax payments, netting $413.6 million in the first seven months of the 2026-2027 financial year. The improved revenue performance has triggered calls from councillors for a greater portion of the revenue to be channelled into community development projects, particularly in areas still recovering from the hurricane. Black River Mayor Richard Solomon, who is also the chairman of the St Elizabeth Municipal Corporation, said the $413,626,794 collected up to October 31 represents 64.2 per cent of its $644.26-million annual target. The sum collected is approximately $144.14 million short of matching the $557.76 million collected for the entire 2025-2026 financial year, with five months remaining. Deputy Mayor Donald Simpson, councillor for the Malvern Division, commended the residents for honouring their tax obligations despite the financial challenges. “I think it’s a great achievement. We really have to congratulate the citizens of the parish because, you know, people in general don’t like to be taxed,” he said. “But when you go through these sorts of circumstances and you still remember that you have to pay your property tax and you make it your duty to pay property tax, I think we really have to congratulate the citizens of St Elizabeth.” Solomon endorsed the sentiments, noting that property tax revenue is important for the efficient operation of municipal corporations and funding for local government services. He hailed the collection team for its outreach efforts, particularly the mobile collection unit, which has been visiting communities to facilitate payments. According to the corporation’s report, property tax collections for October 2026 exceeded those collected in the corresponding month last year by approximately $10.27 million. The parish’s annual property tax target was reduced by approximately $11.85 million, from $656.12 million in 2025-2026 to $644.26 million for the current financial year. Audie Myers, councillor for the Siloah Division, stressed that residents should reap tangible benefits from the funds collected. “We want to see it reflected now in the parish. It’s time for us to get something now within the parish to do something on the roads,” said Myers, declaring that residents were making sacrifices to meet their tax obligations. Everton Fisher, councillor for the Balaclava Division, suggested that the funds could be used to assist communities still struggling with the hurricane’s impact. Solomon also acknowledged the need for taxpayers to see direct benefits from improved collections. “We have to revisit the timetable and see how best we can connect this programme, so that people can realise the benefits that can be derived from the improved collection,” he said. albert.ferguson@gleanerjm.com

artigo.texto: Google bets on superhot geothermal to power Oregon data centers The geothermal startup Quaise Energy has landed a major first customer for its novel, superhot project in central Oregon. On Tuesday, the Houston-based firm announced that Google has agreed to buy 50 megawatts of carbon-free power from Quaise’s first commercial project, called Project Obsidian, near the Newberry Volcano. Quaise will deploy advanced drilling techniques and unique rock-melting technology to access significantly hotter geothermal resources than traditional plants can. Google said it plans to use the energy to help run its existing data center operations in northwest Oregon as early as 2030. The deal is valued at more than $500 million, Quaise confirmed. The startup is working to find offtakers for an additional 200 MW in future capacity at the Oregon site. “We started Quaise to make the Earth’s most abundant energy source universally accessible — and this agreement marks a critical next step, not just for Quaise but for the entire clean energy sector,” Carlos Araque, Quaise’s CEO and president, said in a Tuesday statement. Quaise is one of at least four U.S. geothermal companies to land agreements with tech giants to pursue next-generation plants. Fervo Energy, the startup that’s furthest along in project development, recently inked a landmark deal to supply Google with nearly 400 MW of clean electricity from the Cape Station facility in southwest Utah. Sage Geosystems and XGS Energy are both partnering with Meta to develop facilities in Nevada and New Mexico, respectively. Tech firms are seeking to secure sources of clean, around-the-clock power for their vast buildout of data centers. For geothermal startups, winning customer contracts like these is an essential step toward raising the financing they need to build first-of-a-kind facilities. Their technologies, while promising, have yet to be deployed widely at commercial scales — and questions remain about how effectively they’ll be able to operate over long periods of time. Google is investing in other nascent technologies, too, including long-duration energy storage and advanced nuclear power. “The scale of power that we’re looking for and also the scale of impact we’re trying to have on the grid requires us to foster that ecosystem,” Lucia Tian, who leads Google’s advanced energy technologies team, told the Wall Street Journal. Quaise said its Oregon project will cost about $350 million to build. The company raised $180 million in equity financing in August, which included investment from the oil-and-gas drilling firm Nabors Industries. (Another startup, Mazama Energy, recently nabbed $135 million to accelerate its own superhot geothermal project near the Newberry Volcano.) At the Project Obsidian site, Quaise will initially use oil-and-gas drilling technologies to develop an enhanced geothermal system. The emerging approach involves fracturing rocks and pumping them full of water to create artificial reservoirs. Surrounding rocks heat the water, which is used to drive turbines on the surface to produce power. Fervo is deploying this method at Cape Station, which began selling power from an initial 33-MW unit in September — becoming the first utility-scale, next-gen geothermal facility to hit such a milestone worldwide. Quaise’s goal is to go deeper and hotter. After using conventional tools to drill down some 2.5 miles, the company plans to switch to its millimeter-wave drilling techniques, which involve deploying high-frequency beams that melt and vaporize rocks. Quaise aims to tap into superhot rock, with temperatures above 572 degrees Fahrenheit, to derive more energy from a relatively smaller number of wells. The startup is still testing the unique technology it plans to deploy for the Google-backed power plant. Quaise said it drilled through more than 330 feet of granite at its field site in central Texas last year, and is now working to reach down over 3,200 feet, or about 0.6 mile, at the same site. Maria Gallucci is a senior reporter at Canary Media. She covers emerging clean energy technologies and efforts to electrify transportation and decarbonize heavy industry.

artigo.texto: O governo dos Estados Unidos incluiu o Brasil na lista de países sujeitos a restrições para a compra de chips avançados destinados a data centers. A medida também atinge Singapura, Tailândia, Malásia e Indonésia. Com a decisão, a exportação desses processadores para empresas brasileiras dependerá de autorização do Departamento de Comércio dos EUA, com análise individual de cada pedido. Segundo o Escritório de Indústria e Segurança (BIS), o objetivo é impedir que tecnologias americanas consideradas sensíveis sejam acessadas indiretamente por meio de centros de processamento de dados instalados em outros países. A restrição pode dificultar a expansão de data centers e projetos de inteligência artificial no Brasil, setores que dependem de processadores de alto desempenho. A medida não representa uma proibição total das vendas, mas estabelece novas exigências para sua autorização.
