artigo.texto: A SOLV Energy (NASDAQ:MWH) anunciou uma carteira de projetos de US$ 9,2 bilhões em 30 de setembro de 2026, ao apresentar suas atividades comerciais e planos de desenvolvimento de infraestrutura durante a conferência de energia limpa RE+ 2026 em Las Vegas. A empresa afirmou que o tamanho médio de seus projetos agora ultrapassa 400 megawatts de capacidade de corrente contínua (MWdc), com o crescimento dos negócios concentrado nas regiões Sudoeste, Centro-Sul e Centro-Oeste dos Estados Unidos. A conferência marca a primeira participação da SOLV Energy na RE+ desde que se tornou uma empresa de capital aberto no início de 2026. A empresa fornece serviços de engenharia, aquisição e construção, além de operações e manutenção, suporte técnico e soluções de infraestrutura de alta tensão para projetos de energia. A aquisição amplia os serviços de transmissão e alta tensão A SOLV Energy destacou sua recente aquisição da ASB Energy Services, que amplia suas capacidades em transmissão, distribuição, infraestrutura de alta tensão e serviços de campo. A aquisição amplia a gama de serviços que a empresa pode fornecer nas fases de desenvolvimento, construção e operação de projetos de infraestrutura energética. A SOLV Energy afirmou que a maioria de seus clientes atualmente utiliza mais de um de seus serviços, incluindo engenharia, aquisição e construção, operação e manutenção, serviços técnicos e soluções de alta tensão. A empresa indicou que esse modelo de serviço permite dar suporte aos clientes em diferentes estágios da vida útil de um ativo energético. George Hershman, CEO da SOLV Energy, comentou sobre a demanda por infraestrutura energética. “A necessidade de energia confiável e escalável continua a crescer, criando oportunidades em todas as etapas do ciclo de vida dos ativos de energia”, disse Hershman. “Os clientes procuram parceiros que possam entregar projetos com sucesso e dar suporte ao desempenho dos ativos a longo prazo.” Os clientes estão cada vez mais focados em requisitos de infraestrutura de longo prazo A SOLV Energy afirmou que seus clientes estão cada vez mais considerando suas necessidades de infraestrutura em períodos mais longos, em vez de abordar projetos individuais de forma independente. A empresa atribuiu essa tendência à mudança na demanda por eletricidade e à necessidade de desenvolvimento e gestão coordenados dos ativos energéticos. Helena Kimball, Diretora de Receitas da SOLV Energy, afirmou que os clientes estão buscando parcerias com fornecedores de serviços capazes de dar suporte a múltiplos projetos à medida que suas necessidades aumentam. “Em vez de avaliar projetos individualmente, muitos estão buscando estabelecer relacionamentos com parceiros em quem confiam e com quem podem crescer ao longo do tempo”, disse Kimball. A empresa afirmou que sua combinação de serviços de construção, manutenção, técnicos e de alta tensão visa atender a essas necessidades de longo prazo. O crescimento do armazenamento de energia e dos centros de dados está entre as prioridades do setor A SOLV Energy também confirmou que Hershman tem participação agendada em um debate informal organizado pela Associação das Indústrias de Energia Solar (SEIA) no dia 17 de novembro. A discussão abordará os desenvolvimentos na infraestrutura de energia, incluindo o papel do armazenamento de energia e a expansão dos centros de dados. Essas áreas estão se tornando parte de discussões mais amplas do setor sobre demanda de eletricidade, capacidade de infraestrutura e integração de recursos adicionais de geração de energia. A participação da SOLV Energy no evento ocorre após a divulgação de sua carteira de pedidos de US$ 9,2 bilhões e do aumento no tamanho médio dos projetos para mais de 400 MWdc. artigo.texto: Supported by Congress Looks to Charge Data Centers Billions in Sweeping Energy Plan The permitting bill could make it easier to build data centers for A.I. but a novel provision would also force data centers to pay much more for power. Weeks after voters lashed out at data centers in the midterms, Congress is debating a sweeping overhaul of federal permitting rules that could help tech companies more quickly build the facilities. The bill would speed up federal environmental reviews of a variety of energy projects, including transmission lines and gas pipelines, making it easier for developers to get the power they need to run data centers. But that help comes with a huge catch: Data centers would also have to pay much more for their electricity under a provision in the bill that would charge the facilities extra for access to the electric grid. That measure would upend decades of federal power rules and potentially save billions of dollars over the next decade for households and other ratepayers. The push to impose higher costs on data centers underscores how thorny the politics around A.I. have become in Washington. Massive, energy-hungry data centers are spreading rapidly across the country, straining electrical networks and triggering anger in many communities. Voters this month approved at least 40 local ballot initiatives to restrict the facilities. Some environmentalists who oppose the permitting bill have cast it as a boon to tech companies, arguing that the legislation could accelerate the development of data centers powered by natural gas. The bill would pare back federal environmental laws to speed construction of a many types of projects, including gas pipelines, wind and solar projects, high-voltage transmission lines, roads, public transit and housing. By contrast, supporters have framed the bill as an opportunity to get tough on A.I. firms. “The day of data center freeloading ends when this bill passes,” said Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, Democrat of Rhode Island and a co-author of the bill. “Data centers now have to pay for the extra costs that they bring to the grid when they come online. They do not get to have all that extra cost dumped out onto the utility’s rate base and picked up by all of the other ratepayers.” Related Content Advertisement

artigo.texto: The U.S. Commerce Department on November 16 issued an interim rule that restricts indirect access to advanced American AI chips through overseas data centers, Bloomberg reported, as President Donald Trump prepared to travel to the Philippines and China. The rule adds export-license requirements for covered chips shipped to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil. It also gives overseas data centers that serve certain foreign customers 90 days to obtain licenses. We already walked through the mechanics in our earlier report on the five-country license requirement and 90-day deadline. This piece takes a different angle. It asks what these AI chip curbs mean for the people who rent GPU time, train models and serve inference from Southeast Asia and Brazil, and for the AI model market that leans on that compute. Trump was scheduled to meet Xi Jinping in China, and the timing colors how Washington, Beijing and regional capitals read the move. Reporting so far leaves several details open, including chip model numbers, performance thresholds and the names of affected data centers. We mark those gaps as we go, and we keep every figure tied to what outlets have actually confirmed. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The AI Chip Curbs at a Glance Start with what is on the record. The measure is an interim rule from the Commerce Department, and it works through export licensing rather than a ban on any single product. It covers advanced chips from NVIDIA Corporation and other U.S. manufacturers. It also reaches the data centers that sell access to that hardware, which is the part that makes it different from a classic shipment rule. One caution on framing. Some headlines say the curbs hit Asian data centers. That wording summarizes the story, but the confirmed measure is a licensing and remote-compute restriction that applies to specified countries and uses. Brazil sits on the list too, so the geography is wider than Asia alone. Why Remote Access to AI Chips Became the Target Traditional export controls govern boxes crossing borders. A buyer who cannot import accelerators directly can still rent time on servers somewhere else, send training jobs over the internet and collect the results. That path never touches a customs desk. The new rule goes after it by putting obligations on the data centers that provide the computing power, not only on the sellers of the silicon. The Associated Press framed the action as an effort to restrict China from indirect access to AI technology. That matches the language in the rule as reported, which targets overseas data centers providing “significant volumes of computing power” to companies headquartered in countries including China, Russia and Iran. Those data centers must obtain U.S. licenses and conduct end-user checks. This shift matters because earlier limits focused almost entirely on hardware. Our analysis of why US chip export controls fell short showed how much room remained once a buyer found a third-country intermediary. Washington now treats rented compute as the same kind of exposure as purchased compute. Whether that works in practice depends on enforcement, and the reporting does not describe any company-specific enforcement action yet. The Five Countries and the Higher-Than-Normal Risk Label Reuters reported that the rule names Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil as places where advanced chips face a “higher-than-normal risk” of diversion or rerouting to unauthorized buyers. Shipments of covered chips to those countries now need a U.S. export license. The label describes risk, not a finding of wrongdoing, and the reporting we reviewed does not accuse any of the five governments of facilitating diversion. The list reads like a map of where data center capital has been landing. Singapore and Malaysia have drawn heavy investment in server capacity, and Bloomberg’s headline called the region an Asian data center hotbed. Indonesia and Thailand are building out as well. Brazil is the odd one out geographically, which tells you the logic here is about transshipment risk and compute hosting, not a regional campaign against Asia. For operators in those countries, a license requirement changes timelines more than it changes demand. A shipment that used to clear in routine fashion now waits on a federal decision. Procurement teams will need to model that delay into capacity plans. How long licenses take is not stated in the reporting, so any estimate today is a guess. The 90-Day Clock for Overseas Data Centers Covered overseas data centers have 90 days to obtain licenses if they want to keep providing the specified services. If the clock runs from the November 16 announcement, that window closes around mid-February 2027. Reports do not say when the 90 days formally begin, so treat that date as arithmetic and not as a published deadline. What happens at the end of the window is also unclear. The practical reading is that a site without a license must stop providing the covered service to the restricted customers, or lose access to further covered chips. The reporting available does not spell out penalties, and we will not guess at them here. Compare that with the usual rhythm of export policy. Rules often land with immediate effect and leave industry scrambling. A 90-day runway gives operators time to audit customer lists, find out who sits behind each account and file paperwork. It also gives Washington leverage, because a data center that wants a license has a reason to cooperate on end-user checks. Who Is Exempt: U.S.-Headquartered Operators The new country-specific licensing requirements do not apply to U.S.-headquartered companies operating data centers in the five countries. artigo.texto: A Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias) pediu à Justiça Federal uma liminar para suspender os primeiros leilões de armazenamento de energia em baterias do país, previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro. A entidade, que representa a indústria nacional de geração eólica, protocolou na 2ª feira (16.nov.2026) uma Ação Civil Pública para impedir a realização do certame até que sejam definidas as regras sobre quem pagará pela contratação dos sistemas e como as despesas serão divididas. A duas semanas da disputa, a associação argumenta que é inconstitucional o trecho da lei que determina que somente os geradores arquem com os custos das baterias. Também contesta a proposta da Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) para distribuir as despesas entre as diferentes fontes de geração. O processo questiona os critérios de rateio sugeridos pela agência, com participação entre 25% e 100%, conforme a flexibilidade de cada fonte. Pelo modelo, geradores eólicos, solares e nucleares pagariam mais; as usinas térmicas teriam custos intermediários, e as hidrelétricas arcariam com as menores parcelas. Para a Abeeólica, algumas empresas poderiam pagar até 4 vezes mais que outras, sem critérios jurídicos claros. As regras de divisão das despesas foram submetidas pela Aneel a consulta pública, mas ainda não receberam aprovação definitiva. A entidade afirma que, sem regulamentação concluída, os agentes de geração não conseguem calcular os riscos e os impactos econômicos antes de apresentar ofertas. A ação, protocolada na 17ª Vara Federal Cível do Distrito Federal, pede a interrupção de todas as fases do certame, da disputa à adjudicação, homologação e assinatura dos contratos. A associação sustenta que as baterias devem reforçar a segurança e a estabilidade de todo o sistema elétrico nacional, beneficiando diretamente os consumidores conectados à rede. Por isso, argumenta que deixar a conta exclusivamente com os geradores viola princípios de isonomia, livre concorrência e segurança jurídica. A controvérsia envolve a Lei 15.269 de 2025, que atribuiu aos geradores os custos da contratação. Nos leilões tradicionais de reserva de capacidade, a cobrança é feita de todos os consumidores finais. Para a Abeeólica, as baterias deveriam seguir essa regra, pois também se destinam a garantir potência ao sistema. A ação cita estimativas do TCU (Tribunal de Contas da União) de que os contratos do leilão podem totalizar de R$ 108 a R$ 153 bilhões. No Congresso, há discussões para mudar a lei e retirar dos geradores a obrigação exclusiva de custear os sistemas. Em 13 de outubro, a Câmara aprovou urgência para o PL (Projeto de Lei) 3.716 de 2026, apresentado pelo deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP) e relatado pelo deputado Danilo Forte (PP-CE). A proposta revoga o trecho da lei de 2025 e prevê a aplicação da regra geral de divisão dos custos. Segundo a Aneel, se o texto for aprovado antes do leilão, será necessário alterar o edital: as despesas passariam a ser compartilhadas pelos usuários finais do SIN (Sistema Interligado Nacional), incluindo os consumidores. As baterias armazenam energia produzida quando há maior oferta e a devolvem à rede nos períodos de aumento do consumo. Na geração solar, podem ser carregadas durante o dia e acionadas no início da noite, quando a produção solar diminui e a demanda é maior. O armazenamento ajuda a reduzir o desperdício e dá flexibilidade ao sistema, permitindo equilibrar rapidamente geração e consumo. Ainda assim, não substitui os investimentos necessários para ampliar as redes de transmissão e distribuição.

artigo.texto: BOSTON — Opponents of data center development have launched a campaign to put new restrictions before Massachusetts voters in 2028, as a $16 billion project proposed in Sutton sharpens the debate. The Committee to Restrict Data Centers, which filed initial paperwork with state regulators in September, announced the campaign Thursday and launched sign4restrictingdatacenters.org, where residents can pledge support for a ballot petition and request a signature form by mail. The Kraft Group is pursuing a data center campus in Sutton that, if completed, would rank as the fourth-largest data center in the country. The proposal has drawn opposition from residents of the central Massachusetts town, adding to the unfolding national debate over AI development, electricity consumption, water use and potential effects on utility bills. The website urges visitors to help restrict data centers, citing concerns about increasing electric bills, water consumption and noise from equipment that can “sound like jet engines.” It also calls for local voter approval of proposed facilities. At the bottom of the site, organizers included a declaration: “No Ai was used on this site.” The committee’s proposal, designated Petition 26-08 by the attorney general’s office, would establish requirements for new data centers and expansions of existing facilities, including a two-thirds vote of approval by residents in the host community. Under the petition, a data center could not receive a municipal permit unless its electricity supplier agreed not to shift costs onto other customers and committed to providing enough electricity from 100% renewable resources to meet the facility’s needs without reducing renewable energy available to others. Operators would also have to guarantee recovery of infrastructure costs if a facility closes, reduces capacity or violates its contract. The proposal also requires water suppliers to certify that existing systems can accommodate a facility without materially affecting service to existing customers in the host or neighboring communities. Operators would need drought-related water reduction plans. Municipalities would have to publicly disclose permitting documents online, and voters would decide whether to approve a proposed facility at an election at least 180 days after the community announces its permitting decision and releases the relevant documents. The state auditor could audit data centers and their electricity and water suppliers, with municipalities authorized to require facilities to cease operating until certain violations are corrected. The committee is chaired by Jim Fleming, a political consultant who operates a signature-gathering company and said he has connections to communities that have raised concerns about data center projects, including Westfield and Holyoke. Sen. John Velis, a Westfield Democrat, is also promoting the campaign. “The completion and proposed construction of data centers around the state has caused local community groups to organize to either stop or delay new centers,” Velis said in the committee’s press release, citing concerns about electricity costs, environmental uncertainty, water usage and noise. Fleming submitted the proposal shortly before this year’s August filing deadline, and Attorney General Andrea Campbell’s office certified it in September. The committee is not planning to collect signatures for the first available deadline this month, Fleming said. Organizers have until Nov. 18 to submit 74,574 signatures, representing 3% of the votes cast in the 2022 gubernatorial election, to qualify for the next stage of the process. Because the proposal is intended for the 2028 ballot, they can pursue the initial signature threshold next fall, when the requirement will be based on votes cast in this month’s gubernatorial election. That approach gives organizers more time to build public support and leaves them an opportunity to submit alternative versions of the proposal by next August’s filing deadline. Fleming indicated the language already approved by the attorney general may not be the version ultimately advanced. Filing early also puts lawmakers on notice as they begin a legislative session in January. If enough signatures are collected next fall, the Legislature would have until early May 2028 to act on the proposal. If lawmakers do not pass it, supporters would need to gather a smaller round of signatures by early July to secure a spot on the November ballot. Fleming said the prospect of a ballot question is intended, in part, to prompt legislative action before voters are asked to decide the issue. “If the legislature passes a law like this that is good, and not just an executive order, then we will wrap this entire process. And this will hopefully encourage them to do this,” he said. The petition would go further than Gov. Maura Healey’s executive order, signed Sept. 8, which established requirements for state agencies reviewing large data center projects. The order generally applies to facilities exceeding 25 megawatts, while the petition sets a lower threshold of 5 megawatts of peak annual demand. Healey’s order directs state agencies, including the Department of Environmental Protection and the Energy Facilities Siting Board, to develop policies addressing electricity, water, environmental impacts and community benefits. It requires developers to procure incremental clean electricity, with an alternative compliance payment available, and directs agencies to develop ratepayer protections. Unlike the proposed ballot measure, the order does not require a communitywide vote. Instead, it calls for community benefit agreements and municipal guidance. It also applies only to facilities built or expanded after it took effect. Like any executive order, it can be amended or revoked by a future governor. artigo.texto: Relatórios Estudo de Harvard conclui que os combustíveis fósseis fornecem energia à maioria dos data centers hiperescaláveis dos EUA Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Pontos-chaveOs combustíveis fósseis forneceram aproximadamente 54% da eletricidade atribuída aos… Ver mais - Os combustíveis fósseis forneceram aproximadamente 54% da eletricidade atribuída aos data centers de hiperescala dos EUA. - As emissões atribuídas a um data center dependem da matriz de geração da sua rede regional. - O estudo não conseguiu separar o uso de eletricidade específico da IA da computação de uso geral em instalações individuais. Um estudo liderado por Harvard, publicado em 16 de novembro de 2026 na Nature Sustainability, estima que 403 data centers hiperescaláveis dos EUA consumiram aproximadamente 82 terawatts-hora (TWh) de eletricidade no cenário central, o equivalente a cerca de 1,8% do consumo total de eletricidade dos EUA. Os combustíveis fósseis forneceram cerca de 54% da geração atribuída, principalmente gás natural, com 38%, e carvão, com 15%. A estimativa central das emissões atribuíveis de dióxido de carbono (CO2) foi de aproximadamente 25,7 milhões de toneladas métricas, dentro de uma faixa de 21 a 31 milhões de toneladas métricas entre os cenários. Nos diferentes cenários de carga das instalações, o consumo estimado de eletricidade variou de aproximadamente 68 a 99 TWh. Harvard afirmou que a estimativa mais alta se aproxima do consumo anual de eletricidade de estados como Indiana, Michigan e Tennessee. Como foram elaboradas as estimativas das instalações As estimativas abrangem o período de maio de 2024 a abril de 2025. Os pesquisadores usaram imagens de satélite para compilar a lista de instalações e modelaram o consumo anual de eletricidade de cada local em diferentes cenários operacionais. Em seguida, usaram dados da Agência de Proteção Ambiental para atribuir as emissões de acordo com a combinação de usinas de energia na rede regional de cada instalação. O artigo descreve seu método central de contabilização como um método de atribuição baseado na localização e na produção total da autoridade de balanceamento. Na prática, a abordagem distribui entre as instalações a geração e as emissões das usinas da rede regional pertinente. O resultado é uma estimativa das fontes de eletricidade e das emissões discriminada por instalação, em vez de leituras diretas dos medidores de cada local. As redes regionais moldam a pegada Segundo a medida de produção total ponderada pelo consumo de eletricidade usada no artigo, a intensidade de carbono foi de aproximadamente 314 gramas de CO2 por quilowatt-hora, em comparação com a média de produção total dos EUA, de aproximadamente 348 gramas. Essa média agregada mais baixa coexiste com grandes variações regionais: cerca de um quarto da eletricidade foi consumida em regiões da rede com intensidade de carbono acima da média nacional, e muitas instalações estavam concentradas em áreas onde a geração a carvão contribui significativamente para o abastecimento. Virginia, Oregon, Ohio e Iowa responderam, em conjunto, por mais da metade do consumo de eletricidade analisado. Portanto, uma média nacional não representa todos os complexos de data centers; as emissões atribuídas a uma instalação dependem da combinação de fontes de geração de sua rede regional. O que as estimativas não esclarecem Os dados disponíveis não abrangiam todos os data centers hiperescaláveis dos EUA, e os pesquisadores não conseguiram separar, em cada instalação, a eletricidade usada em operações especializadas em IA daquela destinada à computação de uso geral. As instalações dão suporte a serviços como computação em nuvem, treinamento de grandes modelos de linguagem e implantação global de ferramentas de IA; por isso, os totais não podem ser interpretados como consumo exclusivo de IA. O autor principal, Gianluca Guidi, afirmou no anúncio de Harvard que o consumo de eletricidade e a pegada de carbono relatados “já podem ser substancialmente maiores agora, em 2026”. Trata-se de uma projeção baseada nas instalações construídas e nos complexos ampliados após o período do estudo, além do crescimento contínuo da demanda por computação de IA, e não de uma nova medição. O estudo não mediu diretamente os efeitos sobre a saúde, que os pesquisadores planejam investigar em trabalhos futuros. A autora correspondente, Francesca Dominici, descreveu duas vias: o dióxido de carbono impulsiona as mudanças climáticas, que afetam a saúde por meio de ondas de calor, fumaça de incêndios florestais, inundações e outras vias; além disso, as usinas de combustíveis fósseis liberam material particulado fino, óxidos de nitrogênio e dióxido de enxofre, associados a doenças cardíacas e pulmonares e à morte prematura. As pessoas que vivem perto dessas usinas e a favor do vento em relação a elas podem arcar com custos para a saúde mesmo estando longe do próprio data center. Dominici afirmou que o objetivo é oferecer ao público, aos formuladores de políticas, aos investidores e aos incorporadores uma base mais concreta para decidir onde instalar data centers e como abastecê-los de energia. Essa estrutura amplia a contabilização, que deixa de se limitar a um único total nacional e passa a abranger as redes regionais e suas usinas — o nível em que se encontram a escolha de locais para data centers hiperescaláveis, o fornecimento de eletricidade e as emissões atribuíveis.

artigo.texto: SNOQUALMIE, Wash. — In the race to meet the nation’s growing power demands, states and utilities are rapidly building new “battery farms” that can store energy for when customers need it most. But as the facilities grow, so too does community opposition. The systems store banks of batteries in buildings or shipping containers. While they can take many forms, developers are increasingly building large, multi-acre projects designed to meet the needs of local utilities. The electricity stored by such systems nationwide has grown tenfold since 2022, and it’s projected to double again by the end of 2028. State lawmakers and renewable energy advocates say battery storage is urgently needed to stabilize the grid and support the transition to clean power. But in some communities, residents are wary of proposals to build industrial battery systems in their neighborhoods, noting that battery fires can produce toxic smoke and are difficult to extinguish. As the backlash has grown, nearly 200 communities have passed or proposed moratoriums to block battery farms from being built near them. Backers say modern systems are designed to be much safer than previous versions, with data showing that fire risk has dropped significantly. But some industry leaders fear the perception of danger — along with a rising tide of community activism stirred by the buildout of data centers — could threaten an industry that’s becoming integral to the nation’s energy future. ‘Meteoric growth’ Most energy storage on the U.S. grid takes the form of battery energy storage systems, commonly known as BESS. Such facilities host banks of batteries, typically lithium-ion — a technology that has become more capable and cost-effective with the development of electric vehicles. At present, battery storage capacity nationwide exceeds 50 gigawatts, up from just 5 gigawatts at the beginning of 2022. Another 54 gigawatts is slated to come online in the next two and a half years. That projected total of more than 100 gigawatts would be enough to power roughly 75 million homes, although battery farms are designed to provide electricity for one to four hours, as opposed to the more continuous supply of conventional power plants. “The meteoric growth is continuing,” said Noah Roberts, executive director of the U.S. Energy Storage Coalition, an industry group. “For state policymakers who are focused on the energy transition and decarbonizing the grid, (battery) storage is essential.” Policymakers and energy planners have increasingly pushed for battery farms as more renewable energy sources have come online. Solar farms, for instance, can produce massive amounts of cheap electricity during the afternoon hours — but peak demand is in the evening, when people get home from work and turn on household appliances. With batteries on the grid, that surplus solar energy can be stored and saved for when it’s needed, instead of firing up more costly “peaker” gas plants to meet evening demand. Industry leaders say battery systems can also improve reliability and affordability, even in states without clean energy goals. They note that Texas and California are home to a majority of the battery projects on the grid so far. While typically on opposite ends of the political spectrum, both states produce large amounts of wind and solar energy, while facing heavy power demands that have at times required energy conservation measures and put the grid at risk of blackouts. Battery systems, backers say, have already stabilized their grids considerably. Adding to the appeal of battery farms is the fact that they can be put in place quickly, in a matter of months, compared with much longer timelines for other energy projects. “As we’re dealing with a power supply crisis, energy storage is the obvious solution for adding capacity and getting more out of the grid that we’ve already paid for,” Roberts said. State policies have been a driver of the industry’s growth. Thirteen states have enacted targets requiring their utilities to deploy certain amounts of energy storage by specific dates. In Maryland, Democratic Del. Lorig Charkoudian authored a law in 2025 directing state regulators to issue bids for projects totaling 1,600 megawatts of energy storage. “It’s basically a no-regret path,” Charkoudian said in an interview earlier this year. “Over time once we bring more renewables on, they will be that much more valuable because there’s battery storage.” Charkoudian noted that the Trump administration has stalled permitting for offshore wind and other renewable projects, while phasing out clean energy tax credits. The federal push against those forms of energy has made battery farms a more attractive option, as they’ve met with less resistance and still qualify for a 30% tax credit. Community concerns For all of the potential that battery farms offer the grid, some communities are not eager to host them. Much of the opposition centers around the risk for out-of-control fires and toxic smoke. Most prominently, the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County, California, caught fire in early 2025, burned for several days and released 55,000 pounds of toxic metals into nearby wetlands. Lithium-ion batteries, when ignited, can trigger a reaction known as thermal runaway that is nearly impossible to extinguish. Across the country, community activists have been alarmed to see battery farms proposed near schools, playgrounds and senior care facilities. “They’re making us collateral damage,” said Phoenix Artemisia, an activist in Watsonville, California, who has helped lead efforts to oppose a proposed battery storage facility there. “We have 12 schools within two miles of us here, but these out-of-state developers are telling us what we’re going to do in our backyard.” The Watsonville project has stirred up significant community opposition, Artemisia said, prompting the developer to seek approval from state regulators in order to bypass local officials. artigo.texto: Oklahoma currently has 64 data centers operating or in progress. Editor’s note: This story was updated on 11/16/2026 with new information from the U.S. Data Center map, and updates to local project. Our Data Center Info Hub features an interactive map, data center profiles, frequently asked questions, and a form to ask us your questions about data centers in your area. Driven by affordable land, access to power, and growing demand for cloud and AI services, companies ranging from global tech giants to regional providers are expanding their presence in Oklahoma. According to the US Data Center Map, data as of Oct 2026. https://dcmap.us, Oklahoma has: - 64 data center projects overall - 34 operational data centers - 6 data centers under construction - 20 data centers planned - 2 paused data center projects - 2 inactive data centers Below is a running list of data center projects across the state. This article will be updated as new facilities are announced, approved, or completed. Claremore Project Mustang (Approved) Project Mustang is an approved data center development at the Claremore Industrial Park by Beale Infrastructure. Plans call for multiple data center buildings and office space, with power supplied by Grand River Dam Authority and water and wastewater services provided by the City of Claremore. City leaders say the property is already zoned for industrial use and that the developer would pay for required infrastructure upgrades. The Claremore City Council approved plans Monday, May 18, for “Project Mustang.” Claremore City Hall reached standing-room capacity during the meeting, with dozens of people waiting outside and rotating in to comply with fire code limits. Public comment lasted nearly two hours before the council voted on the proposal. Related Story: Claremore approves Project Mustang data center plan The agreement allows Beale Infrastructure to seek a 25-year ad valorem tax exemption for each phase of the project. Company representatives said the development would still contribute more than $250 million toward Rogers County schools, municipal services and community programs over time. Some residents have raised concerns about water usage, environmental impacts and transparency. City officials and the developer say the project would not raise taxes or utility rates and could bring long-term investment and jobs. Muskogee County Google Data Centers (Summit and Council Hill) (Early Development) Google plans to build two new data center campuses near Summit and Council Hill as part of a $9 billion investment in Oklahoma. The facilities are expected to support Google’s cloud and AI services, including Search, Maps and Google Cloud. The company says the projects will be paired with clean energy agreements expected to add hundreds of megawatts of renewable power to Oklahoma’s grid. Construction timelines have not been released. Related Story: Google to build two data centers in Muskogee County as part of $9B Oklahoma investment In April, OG&E announced that it will power the Muskogee data centers as well as a data center coming to Stillwater (see below) “OG&E is pleased to support Google and together advance growth in our home state, ensuring our current customers benefit from data center expansion that meets the technology needs of the 21st century economy at some of the lowest rates in the country,” said Sean Trauschke, Chairman, President and CEO of OGE Energy Corp. “This unique agreement is a model for future data center partnerships and forms the basis for a new large-load tariff that OG&E will submit in the coming weeks that protects our current customers from bearing the costs of this growing demand and Oklahoma’s goals for economic growth.” Core Scientific (Under Construction) A Core Scientific data center in Muskogee at 4800 S 24th St W. is operational, as of Aug. 14, 2026, according to the U.S. Data Center map. Two more Core Scientific high-performance computing (HPC) data centers in Muskogee are under construction. Oklahoma City American Tower EDC Oklahoma (Planned) American Tower EDC Oklahoma is a construction-ready edge data center* development located at 1309 Northeast 122nd Street in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. According to American Tower, the facility would be on 83.5 acres and provide 4MW of capacity. The American Tower EDC Oklahoma company says that zoning has been approved and that the facility can be ready in 18 months once a customer signs an anchor lease. *An edge data center is a smaller, decentralized facility positioned near the source of data generation. Cerebras Systems operates a 10-megawatt data center in Oklahoma City in partnership with Scale Datacenters. The facility supports large-scale AI computing and uses a closed-loop, direct-to-chip liquid cooling system. CloudBurst Oklahoma City Campus - 3 Data Centers (Under Construction) The CloudBurst Oklahoma City Campus is planned to be an expansive location with a total capacity of 200MW covering at least three data centers. It is planned for the area near 2000 S Council Rd. Cogent Data Center (Operational) The Cogent Data Center in Oklahoma City is 5,294 square feet of colocation space designed for 42U cabinets. The Cogent data center is what’s known as a “carrier hotel,” meaning that it has equipment, space, and/or bandwidth available for rental to retail customers. Lumen Technologies operates the Oklahoma City 1 data center, supporting enterprise, government and network infrastructure. MIDCON Recovery Solutions operates a 60,000-square-foot data center in northwest Oklahoma City’s Quail Springs Business Park, designed to meet Tier IV standards. RACK59 operates a 30,000-square-foot colocation data center at 7725 West Reno Avenue, offering redundant power and on-site substation access. TierPoint operates multiple Oklahoma City facilities providing colocation and enterprise services ValorC3 operates a 65,000-square-foot Tier III+ data center designed to withstand severe weather, including EF5 tornadoes.

artigo.texto: BOTETOURT COUNTY, Va. – A Botetourt County judge is taking more time to decide whether construction on a controversial 300-acre Google data center campus should be halted. Following a hearing Monday, the judge gave attorneys for the three parties involved, Botetourt County, Google shell company Helio, and Botetourt County resident Robert Dallas, until Friday to submit additional briefs explaining their arguments. The judge said he wants more time to review the evidence and relevant case law before deciding whether the county violated Virginia’s Freedom of Information Act. John Fishwick, who represents Dallas, argued the county failed to adequately disclose that supervisors would be voting on the project’s performance agreement during a June 2025 meeting. Fishwick said the county did not provide the public with enough information about the agreement before the vote, arguing that the lack of disclosure violated state law. “We think we have a strong case. We think we’ve made it,” Fishwick said. “We’re pleased with how the evidence came in today. We put a lot of evidence in front of the judge. Ultimately, that’ll be his call.” The county maintains it made information about the project available to the public, including posting the performance agreement online after the deal was finalized. “Once the deal was consummated, it was all out in the open. Anyone could issue a FOIA request for the deal. The deal was placed on the website,” said Julian Harf, an attorney representing Botetourt County. However, the judge questioned the timing of that disclosure, pointing out that the details of the agreement were not made public until several hours after supervisors voted on it. “I have a fundamental disagreement as far as the temporal issue and whether you can disclose three and a half hours after the vote, and that somehow satisfies the statutes,” the judge said. The judge also acknowledged a fundamental disagreement between the parties over what qualifies as disclosure under the state’s open meeting requirements. A ruling could come as early as Monday, after the judge has had additional time to review the arguments and determine whether the remedies Dallas is seeking are permitted under the Freedom of Information Act.

artigo.texto: Lawmakers call for national data center construction pause WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Members of Congress are calling for a national moratorium on data center construction until the artificial intelligence field can be regulated. They said data centers are not helping local communities and, in many cases, are actively harming them. Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Mass.) said the White House is not doing enough on artificial intelligence. “The alarm bells are flashing. And the president and the White House are asleep at the switch when it comes to AI,” he said. McGovern said big tech leaders are becoming oligarchs and are enriching themselves at the expense of local communities with data centers. “These billionaires want to come into our communities, tell us what to do, and make a profit by driving up our utility prices, and wrecking our environment,” he said. Rep.-elect William Lawrence (D-Mich.) said data centers do not provide the same community value as an automotive plant. “The value, the billions of dollars that is being raised to build these data centers, is built on the promise that it’s going to put people out of work,” he said. Lawmakers said pausing new construction would give Congress time to pass regulations and protect communities from future construction. Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine) said she wants transparency in dealings between big tech and the government. “We don’t want back door deals and secret handshakes between big tech and the government. We want transparency, community engagement, and strong regulations that protect our air, water, climate and communities,” she said. It is not yet clear whether the plan has enough support to pass in the next Congress. The Trump administration has attempted to rename AI - artificial intelligence - as SI - super intelligence. artigo.texto: In March, Super Micro faced a crisis. Two employees at the U.S. server giant, including one of its co-founders, had just been charged in federal court with attempting to transfer Nvidia AI chips to China, in violation of U.S. export laws. Weeks later, Super Micro retained the services of Ballard Partners, a lobbying firm known for its close ties to the Trump administration. Ballard would help the company with “advocacy regarding AI data center infrastructure policy” and “export control regulations affecting advanced computing hardware,” according to records maintained under the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Super Micro is one of three firms involved in Southeast Asia’s data center boom that have called on Ballard since the beginning of Trump’s second term. The region has emerged as a hotbed for server companies providing remote access to Nvidia chips for Chinese AI companies. Ballard’s other clients include EdgeConneX, a U.S. firm that operates data centers in Kuala Lumpur and Jakarta, with three more under construction elsewhere in Malaysia and the Philippines, and Equinix, another data center operator for which Ballard has been “tracking executive orders and action regarding power, energy, and data center development.” Equinix, too, has expanded operations in Southeast Asia since Trump retook office. Ballard’s work on behalf of data center operators raises questions about vectors of influence in the Trump administration, whose approach to chip export policy has come under fresh scrutiny following revelations about Jensen Huang’s affair with former Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang (黃樂). Super Micro has also returned to the spotlight this week, following a statement from Singapore’s government saying that the company had provided “limited cooperation” with its investigation into Alice Huang last year. Since the second quarter of this year, Super Micro has paid Ballard $100,000 each month as the company has come under increasing scrutiny for its role in a network of AI infrastructure providers that Nvidia assembled in East Asia to get around U.S. export controls. Both men left the administration around the time that Waltz — who accidentally added a journalist to a group chat containing classified battle plans for Yemen — transitioned out of his role as national security advisor. The firm’s clients have included Lenovo, a Chinese computer maker that a House committee accused of building a back door for the Chinese government to spy on users in late 2023. Lenovo denied these allegations. Ballard has also worked for ByteDance, the Chinese tech giant that struck a joint venture deal to keep operating its social media platform TikTok in the U.S. earlier this year. It is currently building two data center campuses, in Cyberjaya and Johor, designed specifically to handle AI workloads. “These facilities also serve as gateways for global cloud and cloud-based services expanding throughout Southeast Asia and beyond,” reads a description of the project on the company’s website. artigo.texto: Industrial Manufacturing Norway Halts Data Center Projects as AI Booms Norway says stoppage is necessary to ensure 'proper operation' of the power system Released Monday, November 16, 2026 Written by Martin Lynch, European News Editor for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary As global AI data center growth accelerates, Norway has opted to press pause on related grid connection applications in an effort to regulate the kinds of data centers it wants built in the future. Stemming the AI Boom Norway's government has introduced a halt to grid connection applications for data center projects in an attempt to regulate the growing demands on its power grid. Statnett, the national grid operator, has introduced a "temporary suspension of further reservation of network capacity for data centers" and claimed the stoppage is necessary to ensure "proper operation" of the power system. It said it wants to ensure a "controlled growth of data centers in Norway and that they are as beneficial to society as possible". The government is now working on a number of measures and aims to introduce a licensing scheme for data centers in the coming year. The ban could stay in place until August 2027. According to Industrial Info Resources data, there are 74 active data center projects planned worth more than US$39 billion in investment. The Global Market Intelligence (GMI) Industrial Manufacturing Project Database offers a list of detailed project reports. The Government Take "We are facilitating more and faster development of power and networks, but it is neither desirable nor possible to develop enough to cover the power demand that comes from data centers that want to establish themselves in Norway," said Minister of Energy Terje Aasland. "We must have enough power in the right place for socially beneficial purposes. That is why we are taking action now." Torgeir Micaelsen, minister of digitalization and public administration, added: "Data centers are part of our critical infrastructure. They contribute to value creation, secure digital services and greater digital independence for Norway. But we have been clear that we do not want all types of data centers in Norway. We need those that contribute the most social benefit. Therefore, the government is starting work on a licensing scheme that will set requirements and conditions for the establishment and operation of data centers." The Problem According to Statnett, it has so far this year received applications for around 26,000 megawatts (MW) of new consumption in Norway, with data centers accounting for three quarters of those requests. Aasland said: "That's more than all of Norway's consumption today." Statnett said that today, data centers with a total power consumption of 800 MW have been connected to the grid, 4,200 MW have been reserved grid capacity and 9,100 MW are in the capacity queue. In addition, there are requests for connection of a further 18,000 MW. In comparison, the maximum power consumption in Norway is just over 25,000 MW. Norwegian data centers used 3.2 terawatt hours (TWh) of electricity last year according to a report from Menon Economics last month. That's four times more than three years ago. Proposed Measures - Licensing: The first step the government will take is to introduce a licensing scheme for establishing and operating data centers in Norway. Micaelsen said that priority in licensing will be given to data centers serving defense, police, emergency response services, healthcare services and other critical infrastructure, including mobile networks and the financial system. Norway will restrict access to land and electricity for global cloud companies and cryptocurrency businesses. Data centers that conduct crypto business will not be considered socially beneficial, according to the government. - Digital security and preparedness: Requirements and conditions that support digital security and preparedness, as well as contribute to the necessary AI computing power in Norway, the Nordic region and Europe, will be considered. - Modernize the connection obligation: The government will modernize the regulations that oblige network companies to connect consumption to the electricity grid, so that it is better adapted to the actual situation where the grid queue far exceeds what is possible to handle. - Get more of the costs covered: The government wants large new power consumers to contribute more to covering the costs of developing a new grid and costs incurred in system operation. It is assessing whether a distinction can be made between new large consumption and large expansion of existing consumption. - New contributions to power production: The government will talk to the data center industry about how it can help build new power sources to deal with increased demand using gas-fired power plants with carbon capture and storage, and offshore wind. - Consider state ownership: The government will investigate different models for state ownership in data center projects of particular societal benefit. Unhappy Industry Reaction The Norwegian Data Center Industry (NDI) has reacted by claiming the move by the government and Statnett will create uncertainty for billions of dollars in investment. "Billions of kroner are invested every month in Norwegian data centers, with most of it going to the supplier industry," said NDI Chief Executive Officer Reynir Johannesson. "This is about construction workers, electricians and engineers all over the country. They deserve to know what rules apply in both the short and long term." He added: "The government uses the electricity queue as a justification, but does not launch a single measure that clears the queue. Poland cut its queue by 90% in a few months earlier this year by requiring applicants to put money on the table. artigo.texto: Lansing residents push town board to ban data centers, crypto mining LANSING, N.Y. (WBNG) --More than 20,000 people have signed a petition opposing a proposed AI data center in Lansing. Residents are now taking that opposition to the Town Board and pushing for a ban on data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities. The company TeraWulf has proposed a 300-megawatt facility along the shores of Cayuga Lake. Residents say the potential costs to their community are too high. Resident Renee Vogelsang said, “AI data centers suck up all of our energy, raise our electricity bills, waste our water, and harm our climate and environment.” What the proposal includes The proposed project would include three buildings to house computing equipment. Plans also call for clearing more than 40 acres of forested land and constructing new power infrastructure. Residents worry about the impact on the lake, local wildlife and the region’s tourism industry. Resident John Dennis said, “And in terms of jobs, the Finger Lakes ecotourism and wineries produce 4.6 billion in annual visiting spending a year, and it’s time for the 10 miles of the town of Lansing’s border on the lake to become integrated back into that economy.” Dennis said he believes the region should be focused on protecting the natural resources that already support its economy. Assemblymember raises cost concerns State Assemblymember Anna Kellis, who represents the 125th District, said the concerns go beyond the immediate impact of construction. She said taxpayers could be left paying for the infrastructure needed to power the facility. “But what will still be here is the debt that is then passed on to all taxpayers for paying for the capital infrastructure for the grid, the energy grid that was built up in order to provide those electrons and that energy to those data centers,” Kellis said. “We are the ones who would be stuck with that cost.” Kellis also pointed to potential increases in electricity costs, greenhouse gas emissions and water usage. She said the economic promises made by data center developers do not necessarily guarantee long-term benefits for the communities hosting them. Resident Ken Wolkin, who lives near Cayuga Lake, also shared concerns. “They are bullies who encroach and impinge upon our legislative and democratic processes and they continue to push their development plans even despite our sustained and ongoing refusal to consent to a data center in Lansing,” Wolkin said. Town Board considers zoning change The Town Board is considering a zoning change that would make data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities disallowed uses in Lansing. A vote on the proposal is currently scheduled for Wednesday. The date could change. Residents who have spent months organizing against the project said the decision could help determine the future of their community. Copyright 2026 WBNG. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: UK-EU carbon market plan sparks clash over British energy bills Ahead of Friday's UK-EU summit in Brussels, ministers say linking carbon markets shields £6.5 billion in exports, while critics warn it raises energy bills. Chief editor: Ken Kariuki 0701401086 Britain and the European Union are preparing to link their carbon markets at a Brussels summit on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, prompting a sharp dispute between Downing Street and free-market critics over whether the deal will protect exporters or raise domestic energy bills. In an official factsheet published Tuesday, Nov. 17, the UK Cabinet Office said linking the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS) with the EU ETS could add up to £3.8 billion a year to the British economy and shield about £6.5 billion in steel and aluminium exports from the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). Critics at the Prosperity Institute, writing in City AM on Wednesday, Nov. 18, countered that aligning with higher European carbon prices would raise British carbon prices by around 32% and leave the wider economy worse off. The clash highlights a central policy trade-off behind Prime Minister Andy Burnham's European reset: shielding export-heavy manufacturers from EU border tariffs requires accepting higher domestic carbon-price floors across power generation and industry. How Carbon Market Linkage Works Both the UK ETS and EU ETS operate as cap-and-trade systems that require power plants, heavy factories, and airlines to buy permits for their greenhouse gas emissions. Because the UK system has traded at lower carbon prices than the EU's scheme, British exports entering the bloc face CBAM charges designed to equalize carbon costs at the EU border. Linking the two trading schemes would create a shared permit price and secure mutual exemptions from border carbon levies. Beyond emissions trading, the Cabinet Office factsheet outlines a food and drink trade deal projected to add up to £5.1 billion annually by cutting border paperwork, alongside a Youth Experience Scheme for study, work, and travel. Downing Street's economic case rests on protecting export competitiveness. By avoiding CBAM charges on approximately £6.5 billion of steel, aluminium, and related industrial exports, ministers argue the linkage prevents new trade friction while keeping Britain inside its manifesto red lines against rejoining the EU single market, customs union, or freedom of movement. Competing Cost Estimates and Evidence Limits Critics argue the government's calculation omits the domestic cost of converging toward EU permit prices. Writing in City AM, Prosperity Institute researcher Joseph Dinnage pointed to a 2024 Frontier Economics report cited by ministers, noting that while separate markets could cost British exporters £0.2 billion to £0.8 billion in EU CBAM payments between 2026 and 2030, keeping UK carbon prices lower would simultaneously save the domestic economy £3.5 billion to £8 billion in carbon taxes. Neither side's headline number tells the full story on its own. The Cabinet Office's £3.8 billion figure represents an upper-bound economy-wide projection ("up to") rather than a guaranteed windfall, while the Prosperity Institute's recommendation to abolish the Climate Change Levy, Carbon Price Support, the UK ETS, and the proposed UK CBAM would eliminate domestic carbon pricing altogether, leaving British steelmakers exposed to EU border tariffs and raising Exchequer revenue questions. Brexit Politics and Delayed Long-Term Options The carbon dispute unfolds alongside broader political caution inside Labour ahead of Friday's summit with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and EU leaders. Speaking at the Lord Mayor's Banquet in London on Monday evening, Nov. 16, Burnham declared that "the Brexit we were given has not worked" and said Britain had "lost more than we gained" over the past decade. Yet by Tuesday, Burnham indicated there was "no rush" to set out broader options for Britain's long-term EU relationship, postponing a planned options framework until December amid cabinet unease over reopening Brexit divisions. Meanwhile, former prime ministers Boris Johnson and David Cameron cautioned against moving toward rejoining the bloc, and the Cabinet Office's factsheet stressed that Friday's agreements require no payments into the EU budget beyond proportionate administrative costs for shared databases and IT systems. Whether the summit delivers immediate industrial relief will depend on the final permit-linkage terms published in Brussels on Nov. 20. How did this story land? No sign-in required. Choose up to two. Oklahoma leaders discuss nuclear power, data centers during State of Business Forum At a State of Business Forum, leaders said Oklahoma is in position to attract new nuclear development and AI data centers. Oklahoma is exploring nuclear power and data centers as key industries to drive its economic future, with leaders discussing the state’s potential at the State of Business Forum Tuesday. But to attract the next wave of jobs and investment, Oklahoma will have to compete. The conversations were part of the forum hosted by the State Chamber of Oklahoma, where industry leaders explained why Oklahoma is catching their attention. "Having a state that’s willing to hold its hand up and say, ‘Hey we want to host this stuff here. We have the right infrastructure. We’re an energy state, and we’re hungry for opportunities,’ Oklahoma fits all those in a unique way," Jacob DeWitte, co-founder of the nuclear power company Oklo, said. DeWitte moved to Tulsa last year as Oklahoma submitted its bid for a federal nuclear lifecycle innovation campus. He said the state’s oil and gas history could position it as a leader in nuclear energy. "I think, ultimately, Oklahoma has the potential and positioning to be really the hub for new nuclear development," DeWitte said. >> Video Below: Oklahoma reveals new details of nuclear facility bid, but many questions remain The demand for artificial intelligence is also driving interest in data centers, and Amazon’s Brian Huseman stressed the importance of Oklahoma seizing this opportunity. "Although I work for Amazon, I am definitely on team Oklahoma. I do not want to see our state like in 10 years regret that we were not able to take part in the building of this new kind of interstate highway system," Huseman said. Chad Warmington, president and CEO of the Oklahoma State Chamber, said the state needs to act quickly to attract companies. "The companies that are going to come here are going to come here because we move quickly, and I think we have the regulatory framework in place to do that," Warmington said.

artigo.texto: Data centers – O Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos prepara uma regulamentação que exigirá autorização do governo americano para a compra de chips avançados de inteligência artificial por operadoras de data centers de cinco países, incluindo o Brasil. A medida também abrange Indonésia, Malásia, Cingapura e Tailândia. A iniciativa pretende impedir que a China e outros países considerados adversários tenham acesso indireto à tecnologia americana por meio do aluguel de capacidade computacional em estruturas instaladas no exterior. LEIA: Novo curso do Sindplay ensina a transformar ideias em soluções inovadoras Segundo o Departamento de Comércio, a norma busca evitar que as restrições existentes sejam contornadas por acordos de computação remota. As empresas afetadas também terão de realizar verificações mais rigorosas sobre seus clientes. A expectativa é que as novas exigências dificultem o uso de chips americanos no treinamento de modelos avançados de IA por organizações de países considerados de alto risco, como China, Rússia e Irã. A regulamentação surge após o escândalo envolvendo a Nvidia e seu ex-CEO, Jensen Huang, que renunciou ao cargo depois de vir à tona seu relacionamento com Alice Huang, ex-executiva de uma companhia de Cingapura investigada por suspeita de envolvimento em espionagem para a China. A empresa nega irregularidades. O episódio aumentou a pressão sobre autoridades americanas responsáveis pela fiscalização das exportações de tecnologia. O secretário do Tesouro, Scott Bessent, criticou a atuação do Departamento de Comércio, comandado por Howard Lutnick, por considerar insuficientes os mecanismos de controle existentes. A discussão também expôs divergências dentro do governo Trump. Enquanto o Departamento de Comércio supervisiona as regras, o Tesouro e o Conselho de Segurança Nacional defendem medidas mais rigorosas para impedir que empresas chinesas obtenham acesso indireto aos processadores. A nova norma, que prevê análise individual dos pedidos de licença, deverá entrar em vigor em até 90 dias. Empresas americanas que operam nos países afetados terão exceções, assim como data centers utilizados em sistemas comerciais de recomendação de varejistas on-line e redes sociais. O anúncio ocorre poucos dias antes da viagem de Donald Trump à China, onde o presidente americano deverá se reunir com Xi Jinping para uma cúpula econômica. As restrições também provocaram reação no mercado financeiro. Na manhã do anúncio, ações da Nvidia recuaram mais de 2%, enquanto Intel e Micron registraram perdas superiores a 6% e 7%, respectivamente. O índice Philadelphia Semiconductor, que reúne empresas do setor, caiu mais de 5%. artigo.texto: As LIPA eyes more battery storage, LI developer envisions alternative method As New York State doubles down on large energy-storage plants which could lead to a second wave of lithium-ion based projects and alternative battery technologies before the end of the decade, a Long Island entrepreneur is proposing one of the first plants using an alternative called flow-batteries. Last week, the state announced a second bulk-energy storage solicitation, seeking projects that could add 1,000 megawatts of battery storage plants across the state by 2030. It expands on awards from the first round announced this summer that saw two of eight new projects awarded for Long Island -- in Holtsville and Manorville. All are part of Gov. Kathy Hochul’s plan for 6,000 megawatts of battery storage by 2030, and come as Long Island continues to collectively resist the strategy with moratoriums in nearly all towns. Concerns here are based largely on reports of thermal runaway events at four New York plants in 2023, including one in East Hampton, where high levels of forever chemicals were reported earlier this month at a site dealing with a spreading toxic plume following fire suppression efforts. The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority’s competitive solicitation announced on Nov. 12 is “open to a range of eligible storage technologies,” the agency said. Non-lithium batteries are eligible for 25-year contracts in the new solicitation, versus 15-year contracts for lithium-ion battery proposals, NYSERDA said in responses to Newsday. - As New York State doubles down on soliciting for large energy-storage plants proposals, a Long Island entrepreneur is proposing one of the first plants using an alternative called flow-batteries. - Last week, the state announced seeking projects that could add 1,000 megawatts of battery storage plants across the state by 2030. - Meanwhile, Larry Siegel, a businessman from Wantagh with a background in energy finance, said he is in the early stages of developing a non-lithium ion battery storage project for eastern Long Island which would use flow-battery technology to provide 5 megawatts of storage for the grid. NYSERDA’s NY Green Bank will help fund the new battery projects with a “range of financing options” to advance energy storage, the agency said, and its siting team will work “closely with local governments to provide tailored education, technical assistance and model local laws.” LIPA expressed support for the state’s latest battery solicitation, saying in a statement that it “welcomes NYSERDA’s efforts to advance innovation in energy storage and help promising technologies become commercially viable options for meeting New York’s energy needs.” Meanwhile, Larry Siegel, a businessman from Wantagh with a background in energy finance, said he is in the early stages of developing a non-lithium ion battery storage project for eastern Long Island which would use flow-battery technology to provide 5 megawatts of storage for the grid. Siegel, in an interview, said his newly formed Tobay Energy has identified a location for the plant on a site less than an acre. He said he recently met with PSEG Long Island, which runs the grid under contract to LIPA, about connecting his project to the electric grid. It could be ready by 2028, he said. Flow batteries use liquid electrolytes rather than solid lithium-ion cells to store energy, using zinc bromine or vanadium to the store power for up to four hours of discharge onto the grid. Batteries can help stabilize the grid in the face of intermittent energy from solar and wind arrays, one of the reasons they are crucial as LIPA prepares to make way for up to 924-megawatts of wind energy early next year. Siegel said he’s still finalizing a design and specific manufacturer for the project, and that much will depend on the cost of connecting to local power lines. “All over Long Island, there’s a demand for a large number of these batteries, but it’s just very hard to build them because of the moratoriums,” Siegel said, noting that Islip Town recently approved a ban on batteries over a certain size that could nix a LIPA contract for a 79-megawatt battery. “Even Brookhaven is not in a rush to approve them,” Siegel said of the town where multiple projects have been proposed because it has a special zone for batteries and no moratorium. More recently, town supervisor Dan Panico has assured concerned residents nothing will be approved until the town is sure they are safe. Siegel said flow batteries are not subject to thermal runaway fires that lithium batteries are, and said they are already in use in the state and across the country. He pointed to a July contract awarded to manufacturer Eos Energy to build zinc-based battery storage systems for a “Golden Dome for America” defense system for the U.S. Department of War. “It’s going to cost me more” to work with flow-energy batteries, Siegel said. “There’s less profit in it because the costs are higher, but I think it’s the way to go.” The Wantagh resident, who said he previously worked for the U.S. Department of Energy, grew up in Patchogue. “I know the market, I see other site locations that will never get built,” said Siegel, who has attended community meetings where residents have objected to lithium-ion batteries. “I know what’s going on out here. There are a lot of projects that have been abandoned on Long Island.” His proposed flow battery of 5 megawatts has challenges, he acknowledged. “I do have a hurdle to convince investors about these flow batteries,” he said. “They have questions. artigo.texto: Loudoun County leaders approve 10-month pause on data center applications LOUDOUN COUNTY, Va. - Loudoun County's Board of Supervisors voted Tuesday night to put the breaks on future data center development with a 10-month pause on data center applications. What we know: The vote comes after an hours-long meeting where supervisors heard from frustrated residents and industry leaders. Before the decision, some residents were losing hope. The pause is intended to give supervisors time to take a closer look at how much more growth the area can actually handle, including the impact on electricity, infrastructure and neighborhoods. During Tuesday's meeting, supervisors raised concerns about the backlog that could result from putting a halt to all new digital infrastructure projects. The Data Center Coalition argued that these facilities should drive Loudoun County's economy, and generated about $1.3 billion in tax revenue in 2026. They also argued that the county should not abruptly change course in a way that creates uncertainty, invites legal challenges and disrupts investments. On Tuesday night, the coalition warned that developers could take legal action. Certain developers with existing zoning applications, like ZRTD applications, may still move forward, depending on the status of their projects and a case-by-case review. The Source: Information in this article is from a Loudoun County Board of Supervisors hearing and original FOX 5 DC reporting.

artigo.texto: Durham has just 75 days of easily accessible water remaining if no rain falls, and Falls Lake has dropped to its lowest level since the drought crisis of 2007. As water supplies dwindle across the Triangle, some residents are pointing the finger at a rapidly growing industry: data centers. Other WRAL Top Stories Comments on recent WRAL social media posts about the drought have raised concerns about the facilities consuming large amounts of drinking water. But water consumption figures provided by Raleigh and Durham show that other customers account for much more of the cities' water demand. Drought is caused by a lack of precipitation, but water consumption can determine how long communities' supplies last. How much water do Durham's data centers use? Durham officials have identified six customers with facilities that could be classified as data centers. Four of those facilities collectively consume approximately 1.88 million gallons of water per month, accounting for just 0.2% of the city's overall water use. At the other two facilities, officials cannot distinguish water used to cool data centers from water used for other purposes. Data center water consumption also tends to increase during the hotter summer months, according to the city. Residential customers account for the largest share of Durham's water demand: - Residential: 52% - Commercial and industrial: 36.6% - Institutional, including schools and places of worship: 11.4% Durham estimates it has 145 days of total water supply remaining, including 75 days of easily accessible water. Those projections are based on a 30-day running average of demand on the city's reservoirs and assume no rainfall. Who uses the most water in Raleigh? In Raleigh, nearly two-thirds of water demand comes from residential customers. Just 4% goes to the entire industrial category. Raleigh Water official Ed Buchan said the utility serves a handful of traditional data centers, including facilities that handle banking information, but no large-scale generative AI data centers. “But we don't really have any significant demand from industrial customers, and certainly none from generative AI,” Buchan said. “So that is not an issue in our service area.” Despite the Triangle's rapid population growth, Raleigh's water demand has increased relatively modestly over the past two decades. In 2007, Raleigh Water's average demand was 52 million gallons per day. Today, it's about 60 million gallons per day, including water supplied to additional wholesale customers. Buchan attributes that trend in part to more efficient household appliances and conservation habits that developed during the previous drought crisis. One of the biggest drivers of additional water demand during the summer is lawn irrigation, which can account for 17 million to 18 million gallons of water per day. Not all data centers use the same amount of water Water consumption can vary significantly depending on how a data center is designed and cooled. Cooling towers and evaporative cooling systems can consume large amounts of water, while closed-loop systems and air cooling can substantially reduce water consumption. Durham officials said a proposed data center in Research Triangle Park would use city water for standard office needs but not for cooling. Instead, the facility has proposed using reclaimed water from Durham County. Officials also said data centers would be subject to the same drought-related water restrictions as other customers. Can North Carolina handle future data center demand? In Richmond County, where Amazon Web Services is developing a massive data center campus, economic development officials say they evaluated the project's water needs alongside engineers and public works staff. “We're not having to expand our water treatment plant,” a Richmond County economic development official told WRAL earlier this year. “We have plenty of capacity to supply AWS at peak buildout in the hottest days of the summer.” Amazon is also funding water distribution infrastructure upgrades needed to serve the campus, according to county officials. Those assessments are based on projected demand, rather than actual water consumption from a fully operational campus. In the Triangle, both Raleigh and Durham have temporarily paused approvals for certain new data center developments as they consider regulations for future projects. Raleigh's moratorium lasts six months, while Durham's lasts nine months. Buchan said Raleigh Water has contacted utilities across the country that already serve large data centers to learn how they manage the industry's water demand. While the available figures do not indicate that data centers are a major driver of current water demand in Raleigh or Durham, the industry's rapid expansion raises a longer-term question: how much additional demand can North Carolina's water systems handle, particularly during prolonged drought? Water officials urge conservation Raleigh Water is encouraging customers to conserve water even though mandatory restrictions have not been implemented. Buchan recommends reducing lawn irrigation, taking shorter showers and checking homes for leaks. “That said, the whole region is clearly in a very serious drought situation,” Buchan said. “So we would ask our customers and anybody listening to this to try to conserve water, no matter where you're at.”
