artigo.texto: Na Cúpula do Clima das Nações Unidas COP31, em Antalya, Turquia, o Vietnã lançou oficialmente o portal público CarbonVN. Este evento marca um ponto de virada na infraestrutura digital, ajudando o mercado de carbono doméstico a acelerar a integração e a antecipar os fluxos globais de financiamento climático. Segundo informações do PNUD Vietnam, o portal de informações públicas CarbonVN foi desenvolvido sob os auspícios do Ministério da Agricultura e Meio Ambiente , implementado diretamente pelo Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas (DCC) com o apoio do PNUD. Esta plataforma permite que empresas, investidores, instituições financeiras e cidadãos acessem facilmente dados sobre cotas de emissão, créditos de carbono, listas de projetos registrados e políticas relacionadas. O Vietnã lançou o portal de informações públicas CarbonVN na COP31, fornecendo cotas de carbono transparentes e dados de mercado para investidores (Foto: PNUD Vietnã). Os sistemas de informação pública e os sistemas nacionais de registo constituem a infraestrutura digital essencial. Para os investidores financeiros, a transparência e a rastreabilidade dos dados são pré-requisitos para a avaliação de ativos e o investimento. Essa iniciativa coincide com o lançamento, pelo Vietnã, de uma plataforma piloto de negociação de carbono na Bolsa de Valores de Hanói (HNX), um passo rumo à meta de emissões líquidas zero até 2050. A digitalização de todos os dados de transações e cotas ajuda a suprir a lacuna de informações, aumentando a confiança das instituições financeiras internacionais que buscam projetos de redução de emissões no Vietnã. A onda de conectividade global e a oportunidade para fluxos de investimento de bilhões de dólares. Paralelamente ao progresso do Vietnã, na COP31, a Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Comércio e Desenvolvimento (UNCTAD) lançou oficialmente a Rede Global do Mercado de Carbono. Essa iniciativa reúne importantes bolsas de valores, bancos e instituições financeiras internacionais, como a Climate Impact X ( Singapura ), a Bolsa de Valores da Indonésia, a Verra e o Conselho de Desenvolvimento de Serviços Financeiros de Hong Kong (China). Segundo a UNCTAD, os mecanismos de precificação de carbono estão se expandindo rapidamente em todo o mundo. Os sistemas de comércio de emissões (SCE) e os impostos sobre o carbono agora abrangem quase 30% das emissões globais, gerando mais de US$ 107 bilhões em receita pública até 2025. A maioria dos créditos de carbono voluntários gerados atualmente é fornecida por países em desenvolvimento a compradores em países desenvolvidos. Ao comentar sobre o papel do mercado, Nan Li Collins, Diretora de Investimento e Empreendedorismo da UNCTAD e Presidente da Iniciativa das Nações Unidas para Bolsas de Valores Sustentáveis, enfatizou que os mercados de carbono podem contribuir para a precificação das emissões e para a mobilização de financiamento para atividades de resposta às mudanças climáticas. No entanto, a eficácia do mercado depende de confiança, integridade e uma infraestrutura de mercado que funcione de forma eficiente. A rede da UNCTAD concentra-se na padronização de tecnologias digitais , medição e verificação para minimizar os custos de transações transfronteiriças. A sincronização da infraestrutura digital CarbonVN do Vietname com os padrões internacionais oferece aos projetos verdes nacionais uma oportunidade significativa de acesso a uma rede global de compradores. As instalações de produção industrial estão intensificando a redução de emissões para aproveitar as oportunidades do mercado internacional de créditos de carbono (Foto: MASI). Antecipando mecanismos internacionais e fluxos de financiamento verde. De acordo com o Relatório de Políticas sobre Precificação de Carbono, o quadro legal do Vietnã abriu importantes vias para atrair investimentos internacionais. O Decreto 112/2026/ND-CP estabeleceu três métodos para a transferência de resultados de redução de emissões para o exterior, em conformidade com o Artigo 6º do Acordo de Paris e com padrões independentes. Em nível bilateral, o Vietnã assinou um acordo de implementação nos termos do Artigo 6.2 com Singapura e um Memorando de Cooperação sobre o Mecanismo Conjunto de Crédito (JCM) com o Japão, além de conduzir negociações com a Coreia do Sul e a Suíça . Esses acordos permitem a transferência dos resultados de redução de emissões licenciados e a implementação dos mecanismos de ajuste correspondentes. Juntamente com o mercado de crédito, os fluxos de crédito verde doméstico estão ganhando uma base mais sólida graças à Decisão 21/2025 sobre a lista de classificação verde, que inclui 45 tipos de projetos em 7 setores. Com a verificação transparente dos dados de emissões por meio do Portal CarbonVN, as empresas que reduzem efetivamente as emissões terão uma vantagem significativa no acesso a crédito verde e na emissão de títulos verdes. A infraestrutura transparente da CarbonVN, combinada com os mecanismos de cooperação internacional previstos no Artigo 6, está gradualmente transformando a redução de emissões em recursos financeiros concretos. Este é um pré-requisito fundamental para que o Vietnã avance para a fase operacional de um mercado formal de carbono com leilões até 2029, trazendo gradualmente capital verde global diretamente para projetos nacionais de transição energética e tecnologias de baixo carbono.

artigo.texto: 247 – A COP31 apresentou nesta terça-feira (17) um acordo internacional para diminuir o impacto ambiental dos data centers, estruturas responsáveis pelo processamento de dados e pelo funcionamento de tecnologias digitais. De acordo com a Sputnik, o Brasil e outros oito países aderiram ao Compromisso de Antália sobre Inteligência Artificial nos eventos que ocorrem na Turquia. A iniciativa estimula a redução das emissões, o uso eficiente de água e energia e a adoção de práticas sustentáveis. O pacto não estabelece metas obrigatórias, mas prevê avaliações anuais durante as conferências climáticas até 2030. A presidência turca da COP31 desenvolveu a iniciativa em parceria com a União Internacional de Telecomunicações (UIT) e a Organização das Nações Unidas para a Educação, a Ciência e a Cultura (Unesco). A proposta busca enfrentar os efeitos ambientais associados à expansão da infraestrutura digital, especialmente diante do crescimento das atividades que dependem de centros de processamento de dados. Acordo busca reduzir consumo de energia e água O Compromisso de Antália estabelece diretrizes para incentivar práticas ambientais nos data centers. Entre as prioridades estão a ampliação da eficiência energética, a redução do consumo de água e o aumento da participação de fontes limpas no abastecimento dessas instalações. A iniciativa também contempla a economia circular, modelo que incentiva o reaproveitamento de materiais e a redução do desperdício ao longo dos processos produtivos. Outro ponto envolve o gerenciamento de equipamentos eletrônicos que chegam ao fim de sua vida útil. O documento defende procedimentos adequados para o descarte desses resíduos, buscando diminuir os impactos ambientais associados à infraestrutura tecnológica. O conjunto de orientações procura estimular mudanças na operação dos centros de processamento de dados, considerando tanto as necessidades energéticas quanto a utilização de recursos hídricos. Brasil participa de compromisso internacional A adesão brasileira coloca o país entre os participantes do entendimento anunciado durante a conferência climática na Turquia. Além do Brasil, outras oito nações assumiram o compromisso de incentivar medidas voltadas à sustentabilidade da infraestrutura digital. O caráter voluntário da iniciativa permite que os governos participantes desenvolvam ações sem a imposição de metas vinculantes de redução de emissões. O acordo estabelece, ainda assim, um mecanismo de acompanhamento anual nas conferências do clima, com avaliações previstas até 2030. A proposta busca manter a discussão sobre os impactos ambientais dos data centers na agenda internacional, permitindo que os países acompanhem as iniciativas implementadas ao longo desse período. Ausência de big techs dos Estados Unidos gera dúvidas Embora o entendimento tenha recebido o apoio de nove países, a iniciativa ainda enfrenta questionamentos sobre sua capacidade de produzir resultados concretos. O principal ponto de incerteza envolve a ausência das maiores empresas de tecnologia dos Estados Unidos, que figuram entre as principais operadoras mundiais da infraestrutura de processamento de dados. Sem a participação dessas companhias, o alcance das medidas dependerá da adesão voluntária dos governos e dos operadores interessados em incorporar as recomendações. O documento também não determina percentuais obrigatórios de redução das emissões, fator que limita sua capacidade de impor mudanças diretamente às empresas do setor. Mesmo com essas restrições, os participantes pretendem acompanhar anualmente o desenvolvimento das ações, mantendo o tema nas próximas conferências internacionais sobre o clima. Inteligência artificial poderá contribuir para soluções climáticas O compromisso não aborda apenas os impactos ambientais associados à operação dos sistemas digitais. A iniciativa também incentiva o desenvolvimento de aplicações de inteligência artificial voltadas ao enfrentamento das mudanças climáticas. Entre os exemplos apresentados está a utilização da tecnologia para melhorar a previsão de eventos climáticos extremos. O acordo também contempla mecanismos de cooperação tecnológica com países em desenvolvimento, buscando ampliar o acesso a instrumentos digitais que possam contribuir para a agenda ambiental. Essa orientação relaciona o desenvolvimento de sistemas de inteligência artificial à necessidade de reduzir seus efeitos ambientais e, simultaneamente, aproveitar suas aplicações no monitoramento e na resposta aos desafios climáticos. Pacto inclui proteção aos trabalhadores diante da automação Outra dimensão do Compromisso de Antália envolve as consequências da automação sobre o trabalho. O documento contempla medidas destinadas à proteção dos trabalhadores diante das transformações associadas à utilização crescente de inteligência artificial. A proposta integra essas preocupações sociais às diretrizes ambientais e tecnológicas, ampliando o alcance das discussões sobre a infraestrutura digital. No Brasil, o conteúdo do acordo apresenta pontos de convergência com iniciativas como o programa Computadores para Inclusão, mencionado entre as ações relacionadas à agenda tecnológica nacional. A proposta brasileira de sediar o Instituto de Inteligência Artificial para Mudanças Climáticas (AICI) também se relaciona aos objetivos do compromisso, especialmente no desenvolvimento de aplicações tecnológicas voltadas à questão ambiental. Com a adesão de nove países, o Compromisso de Antália estabelece uma agenda de cooperação sobre emissões, consumo de energia, utilização de água, resíduos eletrônicos e aplicações climáticas da inteligência artificial. O acompanhamento anual até 2030 permitirá observar os avanços das iniciativas voluntárias, em um cenário no qual as maiores empresas norte-americanas de tecnologia ainda não participam do pacto. artigo.texto: Utilities could be left holding the bill for billions in infrastructure spending committed in anticipation of artificial intelligence data centers that are delayed, downsized or canceled, industry observers and experts told Utility Dive. Opposition to data center construction has crossed traditional party lines, while Democratic gains in the midterms are adding pressure on earlier-stage investments across key markets. Together, these dynamics raise the stakes for project approvals and utility cost recovery, they say. “From a financing perspective, prolonged uncertainty will increase the cost of capital, reduce available leverage and make investors more hesitant to commit significant development dollars before power is secured,” said Andrejka Bernatova, managing partner of investment firm Dynamix Capital Partners, which invests in energy infrastructure. Even in regions that theoretically have enough capacity to accommodate new large loads, projects may struggle to secure a credible path to power on the timelines they need. “Interconnection, permitting, and financing all matter, but they are part of the same execution question of whether the team can get reliable power to the site and actually deliver,” Bernatova said. “A customer commitment or a large announced capacity number does not answer that by itself.” Ultimately, Bernatova expects investors to favor markets that offer certainty around power availability and timelines, potentially eroding the competitive advantage of markets like Texas, which until recently attracted substantial data center investment. Over the summer, Gov. Greg Abbott, R, announced a pause on new data center interconnections pending an audit of the queue. In the midterms, he lost his bid for reelection to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who has pledged to maintain pressure on the industry after taking office next year. Ballot-box rebuke puts utility investment safeguards in focus Nearly all of the 46 municipal ballot measures tracked by Bloomberg that addressed data center development resulted in restrictions, moratoriums or bans. That unfavorability extends to a substantial share of the development pipeline. An estimated 191 GW of planned data center capacity faces new risk, with exposure concentrated in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, where incoming Democratic governors campaigned on pausing or restricting construction, according to a report from energy analytics firm Orennia that was shared with Utility Dive. Texas accounts for nearly half of the pre-construction in development in the U.S., so a statewide approval freeze would have an outsized impact on the national buildout, but the “impact of delayed or unrealized data center build-out on power prices varies widely across technologies and markets,” Orennia said. If 20% of projected data center demand in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas region fails to materialize, solar and wind generators could see their average wholesale revenue fall 38% and 37%, respectively, according to the report. Implied heat rates, a measure of the economics of gas-fired generation relative to fuel costs, could decline 39%. In the same scenario, two-hour battery storage arbitrage spreads could fall below new-build break-even requirements. In PJM, delaying half of the planned data center buildout by two years could reduce four-hour battery storage arbitrage spreads by 16% and lower solar and wind capture prices and implied heat rates by about 12% through 2030, the modeling suggests. The election results are unlikely to produce sweeping federal AI legislation but could lead to congressional hearings and greater transparency requirements, according to D.C.-based research and advisory firm Capstone. Its analysts expect much of the policy debate to take place at state utility commissions and local siting boards. Despite a proliferation of large-load tariffs over the past year, safeguards may still leave customers exposed in the event of a slowdown, some say. “Existing tariffs and regulatory frameworks likely won’t fully protect customers because they were designed for a different century,” Louisa Eberle, principal at the Regulatory Assistance Project, warned in a written statement. Eberle also called for reforms to utility business practices “to turn this data center surge into updated infrastructure, cleaner energy and a better deal for average customers.” The push for lower electricity bills is prompting policymakers to look more closely at how utilities use existing grid infrastructure. Richard Caperton, vice president of policy at SPAN, a maker of smart electrical panels, anticipates greater emphasis on data center projects that can be served without major new grid investments. “I’m really thrilled to see governors like Abigail Spanberger [in Virginia] campaign on affordability and then embrace utilization as the solution,” he said. In April, Gov. Spanberger signed legislation requiring Dominion Energy and Appalachian Power to report how effectively they use existing grid infrastructure. The State Corporation Commission can use those metrics to establish improvement targets and evaluate utility spending. “Winning candidates who emphasized lowering electricity prices are already looking for ways to deliver on their promises quickly,” Caperton said. “I expect that will lead to more policies and programs that boost grid utilization being ratified and implemented in early 2027. How those policies affect data center development and utility investments will vary by state.” A ‘necessary’ shakeout puts project commitments to the test Stephen Rose, CEO of infrastructure software provider Render Networks, said he expects to see a “pause and necessary shakeout” in data center development. “Fully permitted projects with real capital will keep moving,” Rose said. “The speculative end takes the hit: developers land-banking without firm power, and the contractors who staffed up for projects that won't break ground.” Rose cited AEP Ohio's large-load tariff,

artigo.texto: Will the Paris Agreement's carbon market generate high-quality carbon credits? (Dan Tri Newspaper) - The new mechanism under Article 6.4 of the Paris Agreement has begun operating with stringent standards, causing the number of project credits granted to decrease by up to 40%, opening up a rigorous screening process for Vietnamese businesses. Once seen as a financial "lifeline" to help businesses go green, the carbon credit market has recently faced a wave of skepticism regarding its actual quality. The tendency for projects to exaggerate emission reduction figures and lack sustainability has deterred even global tech giants. For example, in April, Microsoft temporarily suspended its purchases of new carbon elimination credits, reflecting the heightened caution of international buyers. Under that pressure, Article 6.4 of the Paris Agreement – the centralized credit granting mechanism directly overseen by the United Nations – officially entered the implementation phase with the goal of restoring order to the carbon game. Tightening the credit disbursement valve: A 40% drop in output. A major turning point occurred in February, when the Monitoring Body of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) approved the first credits under Article 6.4 for a clean cooking stove project in Myanmar. Notably, this project had originally been registered under the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) during the Kyoto Protocol era. According to an analysis by the Clean Air Task Force (CATF) – an international non- governmental organization specializing in independent climate research – when compared using the new methodology and more cautious calculation factors for non-renewable biomass, the project received approximately 40% fewer credits compared to the previous CDM system. You may also like The "evaporation" of nearly half of the credit output is clear evidence that the United Nations is tightening its calculation formula. The new mechanism forces parties to prove that emissions reductions are real, rather than relying on exaggerated scenarios. To date, the regulatory body has only approved five methodologies, including landfill gas capture, industrial N2O treatment, renewable energy, and clean cooking. The transition from legacy CDM projects to Article 6.4 is also progressing quite slowly. Although the deadline for host countries to approve transfers is June 30th, early 2026 figures show that only about 13% of submitted CDM credits have been approved. This indicates that many governments are considering retaining credits for domestic emission reduction purposes, rather than selling them off internationally on a massive scale. The "gold standard" for quality and the challenging problem of forests. In principle, one carbon credit represents one ton of CO2 equivalent that is reduced or removed from the atmosphere. However, for a credit to have sustainable commercial value, Article 6.4 sets out five stringent conditions: complementarity (the project only survives thanks to the carbon funding), longevity (how long the carbon is stored), accurate emission baseline, emission leakage risk (not shifting pollution elsewhere), and an independent measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV) system. While industrial engineering projects have relatively clear measurement processes, the credit-based aspects of forestry and land use present the greatest challenge. Crops can be destroyed by natural disasters, pests and diseases, or accumulated carbon in the soil can be released when ownership changes. An assessment by the non-profit organization CATF, reviewing 20 forest credit rules in North America, has revealed a number of gaps in baseline determination and carbon return risk mitigation. Although forest credits once accounted for nearly 40% of the voluntary market, the methodology for reforestation and reforestation was only introduced into the UNFCCC review process in October, and there is no date set for final approval of the framework. The dilemma between upholding environmental standards and facilitating the flow of private capital is a major headache. If regulations are too lenient, accreditation credits will become useless. Conversely, if procedures are too complicated and accreditation costs too high, developing countries will struggle to access the market. This directly impacts Vietnam's roadmap. You may also like The wave of international standardization is directly impacting Vietnam's progress. On April 1st, the Government issued Decree 112/2026/ND-CP (effective from May 19th). This is an important legal document that clearly stipulates the mechanism for exchanging emission reduction results under both Article 6.2 (bilateral agreements between governments), Article 6.4, and other voluntary forms. Previously, on August 14th, the Government also approved Resolution 235/NQ-CP, officially formalizing the Article 6 cooperation agreement signed with Singapore , effective from September 2025. This handshake paves the way for Vietnamese businesses to sell internationally accredited credits to the island nation. According to UNEP-CCC data as of November 5th, Vietnam has 3 bilateral agreements and 20 registered activities under Article 6.2, although no credits have yet been officially issued through the Article 6.4 channel. On the domestic stage, the carbon exchange has also been operational since June 29th. According to data from the UNDP, the total pilot quota for the 2025-2026 period is approximately 511 million tons of CO2 equivalent, directly allocated to 110 large facilities in three heavy-emission sectors: thermal power, iron and steel, and cement. On November 13th, Vietnam further announced the launch of the Carbon Market Information Portal at COP31 to ensure transparency of all project data for investors. artigo.texto: EUA impõem restrição ao Brasil em compras de chips para data centers O governo dos Estado Unidos incluiu o Brasil na lista dos países que enfrentarão restrições para importar chips fabricados no país norte-americano para data centers. Com a decisãodo Escritório de Indústria e Segurança do Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos (BIS, na sigla em Inglês), fornecedores brasileiros precisarão de autorização do governo de Donald Trump para enviar os processadores avançados a empresas brasileiras, com pedidos analisados caso a caso. Segundo o Departamento de Comércio, a norma visa garantir que as restrições existentes ao acesso a tecnologias americanas sensíveis não possam ser contornadas por meio de acordos de computação remota que envolvam centros de dados em países terceiros. Além do Brasil, a restrição inclui Singapura, Tailândia, Malásia e Indonésia, que, segundo a norma, apresentam risco acima do normal de desvio ilegal desses chips para China ou Macau —alvos de embargos junto com Rússia, Irã, Coreia do Norte, Síria e Cuba. Norma norte-americana exige que empresas dos países restringidos solicitem licenças de exportação dos EUA para os chips mais avançados, em um esforço para reduzir o contrabando desses produtos. A proposta dos EUA aborda o cenário tecnológico em evolução. “Alinhando ainda mais as proteções que regem o acesso remoto a recursos computacionais avançados com os controles existentes sobre o transporte físico de tecnologia americana sensível”, disse o Departamento de Comércio. continue lendo - O que se sabe sobre a reunião para a 'paz mundial' que reunirá Trump, Xi e Putin AFP · há 1 hora - Justiça ordena transferência de Peña a prisão militar após denúncias de privilégios Estadão Conteúdo · há 2 horas - Alliana diz que pagamento a aposentados do Ueno Bank acontecerá nesta semana AFP · há 3 horas - Rascunho da COP31 defende acelerar o fim do uso dos combustíveis fósseis AFP · há 6 horas

artigo.texto: Regional carbon market leaders gather for the ASEAN Common Carbon Framework (ACCF) collaboration at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, with the Philippines joining as an Observer through Aboitiz Foundation, representing the CarbonPH Coalition and the Philippines Nature-based Solutions (NbS) Group. From left: Steven Marcelino, Deputy Chair for International Affairs, ASEAN Alliance on Carbon Markets; Oi-Yee Choo, ACCF Co-Chair and CEO of Climate Impact X; Dr. Renard Siew, President of the Malaysia Carbon Market Association; Khun Gloyta Nathalang, Chair of the Thailand Carbon Markets Club; and Faiha Azka Azzahira, Vice Head of Community Development, Indonesia Carbon Trade Association. The Philippines is strengthening its participation in Southeast Asia’s emerging carbon markets through private-sector engagement with the ASEAN Common Carbon Framework (ACCF), contributing to regional efforts to promote carbon market integrity, cooperation, and climate finance. Aboitiz Foundation, representing the CarbonPH Coalition and the Philippines Nature-based Solutions (NbS) Group, is joining the ACCF as an Observer and participating in the signing of its Memorandum of Collaboration (MoC) at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye. The engagement provides an opportunity to bring Philippine perspectives and experience to regional discussions on carbon market standards, financing, and cross-border cooperation. It also highlights the growing role of Philippine private-sector initiatives in advancing forest restoration, nature-based climate solutions, and sustainable investment opportunities. The signing coincides with the renewal of the ACCF’s Memorandum of Collaboration for another two years, reaffirming regional commitments to developing connected, transparent, and high-integrity carbon markets across ASEAN. “ASEAN has the natural capital and economic dynamism to become a significant player in global carbon markets. Through the CarbonPH Coalition and our work in nature-based solutions, we hope to contribute Philippine perspectives and practical experience to this regional effort,” said Ginggay Hontiveros-Malvar, Aboitiz Chief Reputation and Sustainability Officer and President of Aboitiz Foundation. “Our aim is to help build a carbon market where integrity attracts investment, climate action creates economic opportunity, and communities share in the value being created,” she added. The Philippines’ participation builds on ongoing private-sector efforts to strengthen the country’s emerging carbon market ecosystem through industry collaboration, knowledge-sharing, and capacity building. Among these initiatives is the CarbonPH Coalition, which brings together stakeholders to explore opportunities for credible carbon market development and nature-based climate solutions. Complementing these efforts, both CarbonPH Coalition and NbS Group have a long-term nature-based solutions initiative focused on forest restoration, biodiversity conservation, watershed protection, community development and recommended governance frameworks. These efforts highlight the Philippines’ potential to develop nature-based carbon projects that support environmental protection, attract climate financing, and create economic opportunities for local communities. They also provide practical experience that Philippine stakeholders can bring to regional discussions as ASEAN works toward a more connected and credible carbon market. Established in 2024, the ACCF brings together carbon market organizations from Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Thailand, alongside the ASEAN Alliance on Carbon Markets, to strengthen regional coordination and advance the development of high-integrity carbon markets. Under its 2026–2028 strategy, the framework is prioritizing broader ASEAN representation, alignment with international standards, stronger market infrastructure, and technical cooperation to support credible carbon financing and cross-border market development. This representation creates an avenue for Philippine private-sector stakeholders to contribute local perspectives, share practical experience, and learn from regional carbon market initiatives. For the Philippines, the engagement marks another opportunity to strengthen regional partnerships, support the development of credible carbon market mechanisms, and attract investment in climate solutions that benefit both the environment and local communities.As ASEAN advances cooperation on carbon markets, Philippine private-sector participation can help connect regional climate financing opportunities with local conservation efforts, sustainable livelihoods, and long-term environmental resilience.

artigo.texto: Malta Maritime Forum calls for a fairer emissions trading system Prime minister's arguments at EU summit lauded Malta Maritime Forum calls for a fairer system and backs the Prime Minister’s stand in the national interest. The Malta Maritime Forum (MMF) has welcomed the 'firm position' taken by the prime minister at the recent European Political Community meeting in Ireland, where, it said, he echoed the MMF’s criticism of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS). The MMF views the ETS as harming Europe and Malta, and must be changed. "The ETS was poorly designed. It was passed in record time, without a proper, broad consultation process with the maritime industry. The result is an impractical system that created unfair competition for European ports," it said. "The ETS is not delivering the climate results it promised. The EU cannot apply its laws outside its own territory. As a result, Europe is losing business, investment and maritime connectivity to North Africa, where the ETS applies differently or may not apply at all," it explained. " Whilst shipping routes are increasingly diverting southwards, emissions are not falling; they are simply moving elsewhere, together with the jobs and investment that go with them." Robert Abela made the same point at the summit meeting, saying the EU is shooting itself in the foot with ETS. The impact of ETS is disproportionate on Malta relative to other Member States because it has no alternatives such as rail or inland waterways to keep goods moving, and it is the most open economy in the EU27. The MMF said it is ready to continue working with the government on fair and practical solutions and to present them to the EU with a unified national voice. One key proposal is to apply the ETS to the cargo, whether containerised or not, rather than to the vessel carrying it. " Any solution must ensure a level playing field and avoid putting EU ports and shipping services at an unfair disadvantage," it stressed. artigo.texto: GCC e EXIST assinam acordo de cooperação para o mercado de carbono na COP31 O Global Carbon Council e a bolsa de energia da Turquia, Enerji Piyasalari Isletme A.S., conhecida internacionalmente como Energy Exchange Istanbul (EXIST), assinaram um Memorando de Entendimento para aprofundar a cooperação no desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono e examinar a negociação de créditos de carbono emitidos pelo GCC na Turquia, segundo a QNA. O acordo foi assinado no Pavilhão Climático Árabe, organizado conjuntamente pelo GCC e pela Liga dos Estados Árabes, durante a 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas, em Antália, na Turquia. O memorando foi assinado pelo Dr. Yousef Alhorr, presidente fundador do GCC, e por Taha Meli Arvas, CEO e vice-presidente do Conselho de Administração da EPIAS. A cooperação tem como objetivo facilitar o uso do programa de certificação de carbono do GCC, reconhecido internacionalmente, na Turquia, abrir novos caminhos para que os participantes do mercado acessem créditos de carbono de alta integridade e reforçar a capacidade técnica à medida que o país constrói seu marco regulatório de mercado de carbono. Unir expertise em padrões à operação de mercados O arranjo combina a experiência do GCC em padrões de certificação de carbono, registro de projetos e emissão de créditos com a expertise da EPIAS na operação de mercados organizados de energia e ambientais. O objetivo é apoiar mecanismos de mercado transparentes que conectem projetos confiáveis de redução de emissões a compradores e investidores, contribuindo ao mesmo tempo para as estratégias climáticas corporativas e para os objetivos climáticos nacionais. Nos termos do memorando, as duas organizações vão explorar a listagem e a negociação dos Créditos de Carbono Aprovados do GCC nas plataformas de negociação da EPIAS, sujeitas às regulamentações e aos requisitos de mercado aplicáveis. Também vão examinar se os créditos poderiam ser reconhecidos no futuro marco regulatório de mercado de carbono regulado da Turquia. A cooperação proposta poderia ampliar o acesso ao mercado para desenvolvedores de projetos e compradores e incentivar o registro, a emissão e o uso de créditos de carbono de alta qualidade por meio de processos de negociação transparentes. Capacitação e apoio técnico Além da negociação, o acordo enfatiza a capacitação e o intercâmbio de conhecimento. O GCC e a EPIAS pretendem realizar workshops, webinars, seminários e outras atividades para melhorar a compreensão dos requisitos do mercado de carbono entre potenciais participantes e partes interessadas locais. O GCC também apoiará o acesso a informações disponíveis publicamente sobre seu programa de certificação, seu registro e suas metodologias. A cooperação poderá contar com a expertise da Gulf Organisation for Research and Development, organização-mãe do GCC, para apoiar a preparação do mercado e o desenvolvimento de capacidade técnica na Turquia. Entre as possíveis áreas de apoio estão o treinamento em contabilidade de gases de efeito estufa, monitoramento, relato e verificação, requisitos de ajuste de carbono na fronteira e divulgação de sustentabilidade segundo os Padrões Turcos de Relato de Sustentabilidade, alinhados às normas IFRS S1 e S2. As partes também poderão explorar a aplicação de soluções digitais da GORD, incluindo a SustainoAI, para contabilidade de gases de efeito estufa, relatos ESG e cálculos de emissões financiadas, além de assistência técnica mais ampla em descarbonização e eficiência energética. Posições dos signatários O Dr. Alhorr comentou que mercados de carbono confiáveis dependem da conexão entre créditos de alta integridade e uma infraestrutura de mercado transparente e bem estruturada, e que a cooperação com a EPIAS cria uma oportunidade de fortalecer essas conexões na Turquia, ao mesmo tempo que apoia o conhecimento e a capacidade institucional de que os mercados precisam para crescer de forma responsável. Ele indicou que um objetivo mais amplo é ajudar projetos climáticos a atrair investimentos, entregar reduções de emissões mensuráveis e contribuir para o desenvolvimento econômico sustentável. Taha Meli Arvas comentou que mercados de carbono eficazes exigem mais do que plataformas de negociação, dependendo, em vez disso, de padrões confiáveis, processos transparentes e participantes com conhecimento e capacidade para atuar com segurança. Ele afirmou que a cooperação com o GCC visa explorar novas oportunidades de negociação de créditos de carbono, fortalecer a expertise técnica e apoiar o desenvolvimento do mercado em linha com as prioridades regulatórias da Turquia e as necessidades cambiantes do mercado. O acordo reflete um interesse comum em fortalecer o ecossistema de mercado de carbono da Turquia por meio de padrões reconhecidos internacionalmente, cooperação técnica e intercâmbio de expertise. Ao combinar a certificação de carbono com a operação de mercados organizados, o GCC e a EPIAS buscam apoiar mecanismos de mercado confiáveis e acessíveis capazes de traduzir compromissos climáticos em resultados mensuráveis.

artigo.texto: Samsung SDI – AI data center backup battery wins CES 2027 Innovation Award Samsung SDI’s space-saving UPS battery for AI data centers earned a 2027 CES Innovation Award for power, energy density and fire safety. Samsung SDI’s prismatic battery solution for uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems won the 2027 CES Innovation Award for the world’s largest electronics trade show set to take place in Las Vegas in January. The Korean battery maker said Tuesday its SDI U8A3-UPS, an uninterruptible power supply that provides emergency power to critical facilities like AI data centers during blackouts, won in the enterprise tech category. The system was recognized for its very high power output, high energy density and fire safety, Samsung SDI said. It uses prismatic cells made with lithium manganese oxide, which makes it 33 percent more space-efficient than conventional products, so fewer units are needed to deliver stable power. It can also supply backup power during sudden surges in demand from AI computing, which helps prevent server failures and data loss. artigo.texto: O leilão de reserva de capacidade marcado para 2 e 4 de dezembro coloca a sobra de eletricidade renovável no centro de uma disputa comercial entre Tesla, Petrobras e fabricantes chineses. Em 2025, o Brasil cortou ao menos 20% da geração eólica e solar, segundo a S&P Global, em um corte forçado conhecido como curtailment, provocado por falta de demanda ou de linhas para escoar a produção. O mundo instalou 108 GW em baterias em 2025, alta de 40% sobre o ano anterior, segundo a Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA). Esse avanço alimenta a corrida de grupos chineses contra Tesla e Petrobras num mercado estratégico para a transição elétrica da América do Sul. No Brasil, a matriz predominantemente hidráulica também conta com usinas reversíveis, que possuem dois reservatórios e cumprem papel semelhante ao de grandes baterias. O Ministério de Minas e Energia separou os certames: em 2 de dezembro, o leilão com exigência de conteúdo local; em 4 de dezembro, o aberto a todos os fornecedores. O relatório global do Schneider Electric Research Institute (SERI), “System Costs of Electricity: A new Baseline for the 21st Century Economy”, analisou 40.500 combinações de custos envolvendo geração solar, baterias e rede elétrica. A conclusão é que a integração entre painéis e armazenamento pode diminuir o gasto total do sistema em até 40% nos anos 2030, com os custos projetados, desde que a eletrificação da demanda avance junto, com data centers, veículos elétricos e bombas de calor. Quando a nova demanda ocupa a capacidade liberada pelas baterias, os custos fixos se dividem por um volume maior de energia vendida, derrubando o preço por megawatt-hora. Se oferta e consumo não crescerem em sintonia, os custos podem subir temporariamente antes de cair. O relatório ainda mostra que a duração dos equipamentos importa. Se os tempos de armazenamento empregados em diferentes ativos forem incompatíveis, o gasto total do sistema pode ficar até 35% acima do patamar atual. Tesla e BYD confirmaram interesse no leilão, que também terá Petrobras, Auren, Eneva e Weg, segundo o portal Zigg. Mais de 6 mil projetos foram cadastrados. No mercado brasileiro, a Voltxs aposta na locação de sistemas de armazenamento (BESS), em vez da venda, para reduzir o custo inicial das empresas. O modelo, segundo a empresa, permite adotar baterias sem grande desembolso inicial. Nos períodos de tarifa reduzida, o sistema guarda eletricidade e a entrega quando o preço aumenta, diminuindo a fatura de demanda contratada. Entre os clientes potenciais estão indústrias, data centers, shoppings, hospitais, aeroportos, agronegócio, mineração e centros logísticos. A disputa agendada para 2 e 4 de dezembro será o primeiro teste em escala nacional desse arranjo. O sucesso dependerá de alinhar oferta, consumo e financiamento, enquanto o setor acompanha se as baterias convertem o excedente em ativo econômico.

artigo.texto: O Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos publicará norma que obriga operadoras de data centers no Brasil, Indonésia, Malásia, Cingapura e Tailândia a obterem licença prévia para comprar chips avançados de inteligência artificial destinados a esses centros de dados, produzidos pela Nvidia e por outros fabricantes americanos. A medida visa impedir que a China e outros adversários dos EUA acessem capacidade computacional localizada no exterior que utiliza processadores projetados nos Estados Unidos. A decisão ocorre na esteira do escândalo que levou à renúncia do ex-CEO da Nvidia, Jensen Huang, na semana passada, após revelação de relacionamento com uma executiva chinesa suspeita de espionagem. Os países listados apresentam risco de contrabando acima do normal, segundo o governo americano. A norma foi elaborada para garantir que restrições existentes a tecnologias americanas sensíveis não sejam contornadas por acordos de computação remota envolvendo data centers em terceiros países. A regulamentação fecha brecha que, na visão de muitos em Washington, permitia à China contornar a proibição de compra dos chips de IA mais avançados. Ela estabelece restrições para data centers no exterior que forneçam volumes significativos de capacidade computacional a empresas sediadas em países de alto risco, lista que inclui China, Rússia e Irã. Os centros também deverão realizar verificações rigorosas sobre clientes. A regra, que entra em vigor em 90 dias, deve prejudicar a capacidade dessas empresas de usar chips americanos para treinar modelos avançados de IA. Ações de fabricantes de chips caíram na manhã desta segunda-feira. Papéis da Nvidia recuaram mais de 2%, da Intel mais de 6% e da Micron mais de 7%. O Philadelphia Semiconductor Index caiu mais de 5%, e o Nasdaq também abriu em baixa. O plano surge dias antes da viagem do presidente Donald Trump à China para cúpula econômica, na qual se reunirá com Xi Jinping. A proposta foi divulgada dias após Huang renunciar, após admitir relacionamento extraconjugal com Alice Huang, ex-executiva da Megaspeed International, empresa de Cingapura investigada por possíveis violações de controles de exportação e suspeita de envolvimento em espionagem para a China. A empresa nega irregularidades, e Alice Huang está atualmente na China. Após a queda de Huang, o Departamento de Comércio e autoridades de alto escalão, incluindo o secretário Howard Lutnick, enfrentaram maior escrutínio. O secretário do Tesouro Scott Bessent responsabilizou Lutnick por não ter feito o suficiente para garantir cumprimento das restrições. A norma alinha regras de acesso remoto às restrições já existentes para acesso físico. Há exceção para empresas com sede nos EUA que operam nos países listados, que podem continuar enviando chips sem licença, e para envios a data centers usados como sistemas comerciais de recomendação por varejistas online ou redes sociais. Analistas afirmam que a aplicação ficará a cargo do Departamento de Comércio, e ainda não está claro como será implementada. A minuta estabelece que as exigências entram em vigor com a publicação no Federal Register, que ainda não havia ocorrido até as 9h desta segunda. A possibilidade de a China acessar chips via aluguel de capacidade em data centers do Sudeste Asiático e outras regiões tem sido fonte de divergências no governo Trump. O escândalo da Nvidia elevou o tema aos mais altos escalões, gerando atritos entre o Departamento de Comércio e outros setores. O anúncio afirmou que a norma foi redigida pelo Departamento do Tesouro e por determinação deste e do Conselho de Segurança Nacional, instituições que defendiam regras mais rigorosas. Licenças serão analisadas caso a caso. Nos últimos meses, Scott Bessent, Marco Rubio e Jamieson Greer defenderam restrições abrangentes, enquanto Lutnick resistia a uma versão mais enxuta.

artigo.texto: The voluntary carbon market debate we’re having is wrong For several years now, one question has dominated the technical debate over voluntary carbon markets: should host countries be required to apply “corresponding adjustments” — accounting entries that prevent the same emission reduction from being counted twice — when their carbon credits are purchased by foreign companies? The question sounds like a dry accounting matter. It is not. Depending on how it is answered, the result could be either a more credible voluntary carbon market or a smaller and less effective one — with the costs falling disproportionately on the countries and projects that need climate finance most. A new EDF paper, Corresponding Adjustments and the Voluntary Carbon Market makes the case that the debate, as currently framed, is asking the wrong question. What corresponding adjustments are — and where they apply A corresponding adjustment is an accounting entry applied to a host country’s national emission balance when it transfers a mitigation outcome internationally. The logic is simple: If a country sells reductions to a foreign buyer, it should not also count those reductions toward its own Paris Agreement commitment. The same tonne of CO₂ cannot discharge two obligations simultaneously. This accounting obligation is legally clear in two contexts. Under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement, CAs are required for government-to-government transfers of mitigation outcomes. Under CORSIA, the international aviation offsetting scheme, CAs are required when airlines use credits to discharge their compliance obligations. Both cases involve legal obligations being discharged through the same transaction — which is precisely why double-counting matters. The contested question is different: Should CAs also be required for purely voluntary transactions, where a company purchases credits to support its own net zero commitment, not to satisfy any legal obligation? Two questions that keep getting conflated The CA debate suffers from a persistent failure to distinguish between two fundamentally different questions. - The accounting question: Are CAs legally required for voluntary corporate transactions under the Paris Agreement? The answer is no. The Paris Agreement and its implementing decisions are entirely silent on what corporate climate claims may or may not be made on the basis of carbon credits. The leap from “sovereign accounting requires CAs for government-to-government transfers” to “corporate offsetting claims require CA-backed credits” is a normative position, not a treaty requirement. - The policy effectiveness question: Would mandating CAs for voluntary transactions, in practice, produce better climate outcomes? This is an empirical question — and the honest answer is that we do not yet have the evidence to resolve it. Conflating these two questions has consequences. When CAs are treated as a matter of accounting integrity, those who oppose them are forced to defend double-counting. When they are treated as a policy instrument with costs and benefits, the burden shifts to proponents to demonstrate that the benefits outweigh the costs. The second framing is the correct one. Do CAs improve climate outcomes? Whether mandating CAs would strengthen or weaken global climate outcomes depends on three empirical parameters that remain poorly understood. - Host country responsiveness: If countries systematically reduce their own domestic climate ambition when private carbon finance flows in — substituting international private money for domestic public commitment — then even additional project-level credits generate no net global benefit. This is the displacement concern at the heart of the pro-CA argument. It is a legitimate concern. But the evidence for it, across the heterogeneous landscape of VCM host countries, does not yet exist at the scale needed to justify a blanket policy response. - Supply sensitivity: World Bank modelling suggests that CA-related fees could exceed $25 per tonne of CO₂ in many host countries — enough to render the most finance-dependent, highest-additionality projects unviable. For projects where carbon revenues are the margin between proceeding and not, this is not a marginal cost. The authorization infrastructure needed to implement CAs efficiently is also, as of today, absent in most potential host countries. Mandating CAs before that infrastructure exists would not reform the market — it would freeze it. - Buyer differentiation: The pro-CA position assumes that CA backing is what makes corporate claims credible. But neither the ICVCM’s Core Carbon Principles, the VCMI’s Claims Code of Practice, nor the SBTi’s framework for beyond-value-chain mitigation currently requires CA backing for valid corporate claims. If buyers and the public do not, in practice, distinguish meaningfully between CA-backed and non-CA credits when the underlying quality is high, the market case for mandating CAs weakens considerably. Who pays when we get CA requirements wrong? The cost structure of CA requirements is not neutral. The most additional projects — those entirely dependent on carbon revenue to proceed — face the steepest barriers from authorization fees. Low-additionality projects, which would happen regardless of carbon finance, are comparatively unaffected. A policy designed to protect environmental integrity should not systematically penalize the most genuinely additional activities. The geographic pattern is similarly concerning. The countries with the greatest mitigation potential and the greatest need for climate finance are typically those with the least authorization infrastructure. The CDM precedent is instructive: Administrative requirements contributed to a heavy concentration of activity in a small number of large, institutionally sophisticated economies, with relatively little reaching least-developed countries. There is no reason to assume CA requirements would produce a different distribution.

artigo.texto: Solar and battery storage can do a lot of the heavy lifting in a renewable electricity system. Add wind, and supplying reliable power gets nearly 20% cheaper, according to new analysis from energy think tank Ember. Wind fills gaps when solar output drops, so the system needs fewer batteries to keep electricity flowing. Ember’s analysis, produced with the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC), found that adding wind to solar and battery storage cuts the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour. The median cost of solar and wind power covering all demand is $89/MWh, with batteries and a little backup. More wind means fewer batteries Solar and wind don’t follow the same schedule. Their output varies by time of day and across seasons, allowing one to offset the other’s shortfalls. That matters because storing enough electricity to get through a long stretch of weak solar output gets expensive. Wind reduces the amount of energy the batteries need to store in the first place. In the US, adding wind reduces the modeled battery requirement to meet 90% of demand from 20 hours of electricity use to 12 hours. Europe sees the same reduction, while China’s requirement falls from 18 hours to 12. The savings also put cheaper renewable power within reach of more regions. With wind included, regions that account for 75% of global electricity demand can meet 90% of their electricity demand at less than $100/MWh. With solar and batteries alone, that share is only 50%. “We already know that solar and wind are cheap,” said Daan Walter, principal at Ember. By combining solar, wind, and batteries, we can deliver reliable power at remarkably low costs almost everywhere in the world. That’s a pretty fundamental shift in the economics of energy. What happens when it’s cloudy and still? The researchers also looked at prolonged periods of low output. Globally, weighted by electricity demand, a week of low solar output occurs roughly four times a year. A week in which both solar and wind output are low occurs only about once every four years. That’s a global average, so individual locations will have different experiences. Ember defines a lull as seven consecutive days of output below half the source’s average. Combining wind and solar reduces the gaps in low output. New coal and gas doesn’t make financial sense The findings also raise questions for developers planning new fossil fuel plants. Ember identifies 845 GW of coal and gas capacity in planning worldwide. Adding wind raises the share located in regions where solar, wind, and battery storage can meet 90% of demand for under $100/MWh from 71% to 90%. In China alone, wind brings another 91 GW of planned coal and gas capacity into the range where renewables are cheaper. Include backup to cover all demand, and 706 GW of the planned fossil fuel capacity sits in regions where the renewable-based alternative costs less than $100/MWh. Without wind, that figure falls to 520 GW. For investors financing fossil fuel plants in the pipeline that are expected to run for decades, there is likely already a cheaper renewable alternative available to meet the same electricity demand, so it’s worth scrutinizing the project’s economics. Ember’s interactive Wind + Solar + Battery Atlas lets users explore reliable electricity costs in their own region. artigo.texto: The UL-certified, ITC-eligible system is built at the company’s award-winning Megafactory 1, with deployments planned at commercial sites across North America AUSTIN, Texas and VANCOUVER, British Columbia, Nov. 17, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Moment Energy today unveiled Nova, its next-generation battery energy storage system (BESS). Nova is the world's first BESS made with repurposed electric vehicle batteries to achieve both UL 1973 and UL 9540 certification. The certifications help support its use in commercial, industrial and large-scale energy storage applications. Nova is now in production at the company’s award-winning Megafactory 1 for deployment across North America. The BESS enables commercial customers to reduce energy costs, improve site reliability and uptime, and integrate clean energy into their operations. Moment Energy has already deployed systems powering critical infrastructure including airports, hospitals, agricultural and manufacturing sites. Nova is made in North America and independently verified as fully compliant with Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements. Moment Energy has also been independently verified as a non-Prohibited Foreign Entity. Together, this makes Nova the only third-party verified BESS eligible for the U.S. federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) in 2027 and beyond. "Access to affordable power is a defining factor determining where businesses can grow and what they can build. Today, businesses across North America are being throttled by power capacity constraints,” said Edward Chiang, Co-Founder and CEO of Moment Energy. “We see a future where reengineered EV batteries become essential infrastructure for powering businesses and onshoring manufacturing and supply chain. Nova brings that vision to life, combining safety, engineering and North American manufacturing to deploy the safest and highest-performance batteries ever made: EV batteries to supercharge our aging grid.” Designed for Performance, Flexibility and Long-Term Value The Nova platform is designed to integrate batteries from multiple types of EVs into its flexible stationary storage platform. Moment Energy’s proprietary AI-powered battery management system (BMS) continuously evaluates and optimizes batteries across different states of health to maximize performance, efficiency and reliability throughout the system's life. Each Nova block delivers 200 kW of power / 500 kWh of energy within a 2.94 m by 1.80 m (9.65 ft x 5.9 ft) footprint. This compact, scalable design brings substantial energy storage capacity to commercial sites where space is an important consideration, while also enabling Nova to deploy in large-scale installations in the tens of MWhs. Nova helps commercial energy users save by supporting grid services and utility bill savings, as well as providing resilient backup power during grid outages. Nova’s swappable architecture allows individual battery packs to be replaced as they age over time, instead of replacing the entire system. Durable infrastructure such as the enclosure and concrete pad can remain undisturbed, while the battery packs are serviced and replaced. This design extends the system's lifespan to more than 20 years with Moment Energy’s capacity augmentation service. "With Nova, we’ve solved the engineering challenges that have prevented BESS made with EV batteries from scaling commercially,” said Gurmesh Sidhu, Co-Founder and Chief Product Officer of Moment Energy. “Every element of the platform has been engineered to maximize flexibility, simplify servicing and give customers confidence that the system will reliably power their critical infrastructure for decades." Batteries Made in North America As battery storage becomes increasingly critical for commercial energy users, battery supply has become a global issue of international trade and national security, with the large majority of batteries currently imported from China. By establishing a new domestic supply chain from the abundant supply of retiring EV batteries, Moment Energy's Nova allows the U.S. and Canada to keep critical minerals and battery software in North America. Repurposing is an important step in the circular economy, unlocking years or even decades of residual value in a battery after its useful life for electric vehicle applications is over, preventing batteries from entering landfills. Nova brings that value into commercial energy infrastructure through a platform engineered, manufactured and supported in North America. Engineered and Certified for Safety Nova is the first BESS built from EV batteries that is certified to UL 9540 by UL Solutions. Nova has achieved UL 1973 and UL 9540 certifications, key safety certifications also commonly held by first-life battery systems, and has been tested to UL 9540A for evaluating thermal runaway fire propagation in BESS. With these certifications, Nova meets the listing requirements of electrical codes of the United States and Canada for stationary storage. Additionally, Megafactory 1 is certified to UL 1974, the standard for sorting, grading and repurposing electric vehicle batteries. “Repurposing electric vehicle batteries for stationary energy storage creates new technical considerations that must be carefully evaluated,” said Jeff Smidt, senior vice president of Testing, Inspection and Certification, Industrial, at UL Solutions. “UL Certification demonstrates that the evaluated battery and energy storage system met applicable safety requirements. This achievement provides important third-party evidence supporting the responsible use of repurposed batteries in commercial and industrial energy storage applications.” Nova combines these UL certifications with integrated safety features and engineering for demanding commercial environments: Nova’s rigorous safety engineering allows the system to be installed in the outdoor built environment, alongside the buildings and facilities it serves. artigo.texto: Duke Energy has unveiled plans to invest up to $756 million in its largest battery storage complex yet, adding 410 megawatts (MW) of grid capacity in Wayne County, North Carolina. Announced on November 17, 2026, the two-phase H.F. Lee Battery Storage project is scheduled to begin construction in early 2027 and enter service by late 2028. Situated adjacent to Duke Energy‘s existing H.F. Lee natural gas power plant in Goldsboro, the complex will more than double the 308 MW of battery storage the utility currently operates across 14 North Carolina sites. By building on a former coal plant property using North American-manufactured batteries, the development qualifies for a 50% federal tax credit designed to reduce costs for ratepayers. Two-Phase Buildout Doubles North Carolina Storage Fleet The installation is divided into two four-hour lithium-ion battery systems. H.F. Lee Battery Storage 1 will deliver 260 MW when it comes online in fall 2028, followed by the 150 MW H.F. Lee Battery Storage 2 facility by the end of 2028. At full output, the combined 410 MW complex will supply enough instantaneous electricity to power roughly 300,000 homes during peak demand periods. That capacity is more than four times the size of Duke Energy’s current largest operational battery facility in North Carolina, a 100 MW site in Knightdale. Work on the Goldsboro site will reuse grid interconnections at the H.F. Lee Energy Complex, where a 920 MW combined-cycle natural gas plant replaced a retired 1951 coal-fired station in 2012. How Do Federal Tax Credits and Grid Rules Shape the Deal? Federal clean-energy tax incentives form a central pillar of the project’s economics. Locating the batteries inside a designated energy community alongside domestic content requirements for North American battery manufacturing unlocks a 50% federal tax credit, lowering the net capital cost passed on to utility customers. The announcement arrived one day after the North Carolina Utilities Commission issued a November 16, 2026 order advancing 2,700 MW of new battery storage toward a 5,400 MW fleet target by 2034. Within its broader 2025 Carolinas Resource Plan, the utility has outlined plans for 6,540 MW of battery storage by 2035 as it shifts capital toward dispatchable capacity following Duke Energy’s decision to halt offshore wind plans off North Carolina and advances four planned solar projects in Florida. Local Tax Base and Workforce Impact in Wayne County County officials estimate the two battery facilities could generate up to $2 million in additional annual property tax revenue once operational. Duke Energy is already Wayne County’s largest taxpayer, contributing $5.8 million each year for its existing H.F. Lee generating complex and related local power infrastructure. Nine permanent full-time positions will support operations at the Goldsboro battery complex alongside regional solar and storage assets. Kendal Bowman, Duke Energy’s North Carolina President, said the utility is “reinvesting in our existing power plant communities that have powered North Carolina and South Carolina for decades,” while Wayne County Board of Commissioners Chairman Joe Daugherty noted that the tax revenue and grid reliability will support long-term industrial recruitment across Eastern North Carolina. Across the broader U.S. grid-storage pipeline targeting 2028 delivery, construction is also underway on the 553 MWdc Cold Creek Solar and Storage Project in Texas after developer Doral Renewables closed nearly $900 million in project financing earlier in 2026. Project Overview - Project Name: H.F. Lee Battery Storage (H.F. Lee Battery Storage 1 and 2) - Developer / Owner: Duke Energy (Duke Energy Progress) - Location: Goldsboro, Wayne County, North Carolina, USA - Project Type: Utility-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) - Project Value: Up to $756 million - Capacity: 410 MW total (260 MW Phase 1 and 150 MW Phase 2; four-hour duration) - Status: Announced; pre-construction - Milestone Date: November 17, 2026 (project announcement) - Construction Start: Early 2027 (anticipated) - Target Completion: Fall 2028 (Phase 1); late 2028 (Phase 2) - EPC Contractor: Not publicly disclosed - Permanent Jobs: 9 full-time regional operations roles (construction jobs not publicly disclosed) - Economic Impact: Up to $2 million in estimated additional annual county tax revenue Project Team - Developer and Operator: Duke Energy - State Utility Regulator: North Carolina Utilities Commission - Local Government Host: Wayne County Government - Regional Economic Development Partner: North Carolina Global TransPark Economic Development Region - EPC Contractor: Not yet disclosed

artigo.texto: Luiz Araújo, da Agência iNFRA O governo federal formalizou nesta semana as regras do ProBioQAV (Programa Nacional de Combustível Sustentável de Aviação), que estabelece metas de redução das emissões de carbono para as companhias aéreas. A regulamentação da ANAC (Agência Nacional de Aviação Civil), publicada na terça-feira (17), prevê um período de transição, com redução ou dispensa das metas caso as empresas comprovem a indisponibilidade de SAF (Combustível Sustentável de Aviação). Criado pela Lei do Combustível do Futuro, o programa prevê metas anuais de redução das emissões em voos domésticos, começando em 1% em 2027 e chegando a 10% a partir de 2037. A obrigação alcançará companhias que emitirem mais de dez mil toneladas de carbono por ano em operações de passageiros ou cargas. O cálculo considerará o consumo de combustível de cada empresa e o percentual de redução previsto para o período. O principal instrumento para o alcance das metas é o uso do SAF. Contudo, as regras permitem o cumprimento das obrigações sem abastecimento físico, já que os créditos serão contabilizados a partir dos CS-SAF (Certificados de Sustentabilidade do SAF), documentos que comprovam a redução de emissões e podem ser comercializados. Também admitem o uso parcial de combustíveis de menor emissão, certificados estrangeiros e créditos do SBCE (Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões), limitados a 15% da meta em 2027 e 2028, 10% em 2029 e 5% a partir de 2030. A possibilidade de redução ou dispensa das metas por falta de SAF valerá enquanto não estiver em funcionamento a plataforma de emissão e registro dos CS-SAF. Para obter a flexibilização, as companhias deverão comprovar tentativas de aquisição do combustível, apresentando informações sobre a disponibilidade do produto, respostas dos fornecedores e motivos que impediram o abastecimento. Até a entrada em operação do sistema, o uso de SAF poderá ser comprovado por documentos equivalentes aos exigidos para a emissão dos certificados. A regulamentação também permite que as companhias aproveitem, no ano seguinte, reduções de emissões superiores às metas exigidas. O mecanismo deverá observar as condições estabelecidas pela ANAC e poderá ser utilizado para compensar parte das obrigações futuras. A medida se soma aos instrumentos alternativos previstos para o cumprimento das metas anuais. Fiscalização e penalidades O acompanhamento será feito por três instrumentos, cujos procedimentos foram detalhados em portaria complementar: o PME (Plano de Monitoramento de Emissões), o RE (Relatório de Emissões) e o RC (Relatório de Cumprimento). O primeiro detalhará os métodos de medição do consumo de combustível e das emissões, enquanto os demais apresentarão os dados anuais e a comprovação do cumprimento das metas. O prazo excepcional para entrega do PME será 15 de dezembro deste ano. O RE deverá ser apresentado até 31 de março do ano seguinte ao período de referência, e o RC, até 31 de maio. A ANAC será responsável pela verificação das informações, sem exigir, como regra geral, auditorias independentes. O descumprimento das obrigações poderá resultar em multas de R$ 84 mil pela ausência do PME ou do RE e de R$ 750 por tonelada de carbono que deixou de ser reduzida. O pagamento da penalidade não eliminará a obrigação, e o saldo pendente deverá ser incorporado à meta do ano seguinte. A regulamentação também prevê sanções por inconsistências nos relatórios, ausência de documentos e irregularidades na utilização de certificados ambientais. Embora as regras da ANAC já estejam formalizadas, a implementação integral do ProBioQAV ainda depende da regulamentação e da entrada em operação do sistema de certificados sob responsabilidade da ANP (Agência Nacional do Petróleo, Gás Natural e Biocombustíveis).

artigo.texto: The 400 largest data centers in the United States emit more greenhouse gas emissions in one year than the entire nation of Denmark, according to a new report from Harvard University. From May 2024 to April 2025, data centers accounted for nearly 2% of total U.S. energy consumption and produced more than 25 million metric tons of CO2. Amna Nawaz spoke with the study's lead author, Gianluca Guidi. Amna Nawaz: The 400 largest data centers in the United States emit more greenhouse gas emissions into the air in one year than the entire nation of Denmark. That's according to a new report from Harvard University. The study found that, from May 2024 to April 2025, data centers accounted for nearly 2 percent of total U.S. energy consumption and produced more than 25 million metric tons of carbon dioxide, a level two or three times higher than an earlier estimate in 2018. I'm joined now by the lead author of that study, Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral research fellow at Harvard focusing on AI and public health. Gianluca, welcome to the "News Hour." Thanks for joining us. Gianluca Guidi: Yes, thank you for having me. Hello, everyone. Amna Nawaz: So, what was most surprising to you from this report? What really stood out to you in the way of the findings? Gianluca Guidi: Yes. So think about it, right? So Denmark is an entire country, and with millions of people, homes, hospitals, and industries. And we're talking about, like, comparable annual carbon emissions from just 403 data centers. So those are just like 400 buildings. And that's an extraordinary scale. And those facilities are just only a fraction of the industry and how the industry looks like right now. Amna Nawaz: You point out in the report too you weren't even able to capture all of the information from many data centers. So what do we not yet know about the impact that they could be having? Gianluca Guidi: Yes, that's a great question. The study dates back like -- it's almost a year-old by now. And since then, there's been, like, an incredible build-out. We have preliminary results of newer studies that tells us there are around 1,000 hyperscale data centers. So that's just more than the double of what we reported in our study. Amna Nawaz: So many more data centers, meaning the numbers in here, in actuality, now the scope of emissions could be much higher than your report suggests. Is that correct? Gianluca Guidi: That is correct. Yes, that is correct. And together with the emissions, you have the water consumption and potentially also public health consequences. So, in a way, we have that a technology that is actually moving faster than our ability to understand its consequences. Amna Nawaz: Tell us more about that, the intersection of the build-out of these data centers and the impact on public health. What are you finding there? Gianluca Guidi: Yes. In this specific study, we haven't addressed yet the public health, but what's happening basically is that, once you have a powered demand and a power that is produced at the power plant level, not only you're producing, we're producing carbon emissions, but we're also producing hazardous pollutants that travel and eventually somebody breathes them, and the effects for the health are pretty dangerous. And there's plenty and ton of scientific research about this. Amna Nawaz: The power pull as well when we talk about the power use in -- of these data centers, there are states you point out, like Virginia, Iowa, Oregon, and Ohio that account for half of the electricity use. Why is that and what kind of downstream impacts does that have for residents in the area? Gianluca Guidi: Yes, that's correct. So, basically, the states offer the infrastructure, the land and the electricity that large data centers need. But there's a catch. So the benefits of these expansion aren't necessarily felt by the same communities that bear its environmental costs. So, more electricity demands can mean more power plans and, therefore, as we're saying, more pollution and more pressure on local infrastructure. So those consequences don't stop at the data center's fence. Amna Nawaz: There are those who will argue, Gianluca, I'm sure you have heard, that we need to build out these AI data centers, that the country has to do it to remain competitive, that it's necessary for our economy, for national security, and that the impact of that on the environment or for residents in the area is a necessary evil, in other words. Would you agree with that? Is that -- can that argument be made? Gianluca Guidi: Yes, I see that, and there's a big backlash happening right now. I wouldn't call them like a necessary evil. I mean, I am an AI researcher myself, and I have to say I'm really excited about this technology and what it can do. but there are better ways to build it, so -- that might cost more, they might take longer. The question is whether we're willing to prioritize doing it right over doing it first. Amna Nawaz: The report, as you mentioned, is now several months old, almost a year-old. There are a lot of things you don't address in it. For the average citizen to understand how this might impact their lives, what are the questions you think need to be answered next? Gianluca Guidi: Yes, here's what concerns me the most. We're building this AI infrastructure faster than we can independently understand its consequences. So, our study, as you were saying, was just published, like -- but the data are already over a-year-old. So scientific evidence shouldn't arrive after the infrastructure, and neither should, I believe, the public participation. And the main concerns would be the water consumption, the electricity, so such that putting the power grid into like -- in strain and potentially therefore, as I was saying before, the public health consequences. Amna Nawaz: That is Gianluca Guidi of Harvard. He's a postdoctoral research fellow there focusing on AI and public health. Gianluca, thank you so much for your time. It's good

artigo.texto: More Online: City Budget, Data Center Moratorium, Carbondale Odors Already this week, Dalton’s elected officials have adopted a $50.868 million budget for the 2027 fiscal year, which begins Jan. 1, and voted, in a split decision, to indefinitely table a proposed moratorium on data centers. And there’s plenty more on the calendar. The Whitfield County Commission will hold the first of two work sessions devoted to planning the county’s 2027 budget Wednesday, Nov. 18, at 5:30 p.m., with the second scheduled for Thursday, Nov. 19, also at 5:30 p.m. Both meetings will take place in the Board of Commissioners Meeting Room at the Whitfield County Courthouse, 205 N. Selvidge St., Dalton. According to county officials, the sessions are the initial planning meetings for commissioners to review past spending, anticipated revenues and departmental requests before developing a proposed budget for public review and eventual consideration by the board. The Joint Development Authority also met earlier this week, while residents continue seeking answers and assistance regarding odors associated with Essentia Protein Solutions, a food-grade protein and broth manufacturing plant operating in Carbondale Business Park. Meanwhile, student-athletes are wrapping up the fall sports season as winter sports get underway, and the holiday season is getting into full swing throughout Dalton, Whitfield County and Northwest Georgia. With so much news, so many events and activities taking place across our community, The Dalton Daily Citizen is placing a greater emphasis on timely online reporting, bringing readers local news as stories are completed rather than waiting for the next print edition. Readers can watch daltoncitizen.com in the coming days for reports on these topics and other developments throughout the community. We are also developing an online holiday events calendar, to be hosted on our website through Google Calendar. Residents and organizations will be able to submit events for consideration, helping create a convenient place for readers to find holiday activities throughout the area. Events may also be featured in our print editions as space permits.
