artigo.texto: Botswana battery storage plan puts 100MWh beside the Mmadinare solar cluster Botswana Power Corporation has published plans for a 25MW battery with 100MWh of storage beside the Mmadinare solar cluster, with the World Bank funding its construction, as Botswana presents a climate plan at COP31 in Antalya that ranks energy generation as its largest opportunity for carbon market activity. Botswana Power Corporation has published a revised environmental and social management plan, dated 6 November, for a battery storage system of 25MW and 100MWh in 20 battery containers and five power conversion units, to be built on 2 hectares of a 40-hectare plot 8km south-east of Mmadinare in the Bobirwa District, beside the 100MW Mmadinare Solar PV Cluster. The plan, submitted to the Department of Environmental Protection in Selebi Phikwe, says the World Bank will fund the initial construction, pencilled in for 2027 over 9 to 12 months, and that the battery is designed to firm the output of the adjoining solar cluster and to provide peak-shaving and frequency services for the region. More than 243,288MWh had flowed into the grid from the solar cluster by its official launch on 31 August, with availability and reliability above 99% since operations began, according to BPC’s Chief Executive, David Kgoboko. Scatec, the Norwegian IPP that built and owns the plant, sells its power to BPC under a 25-year power purchase agreement. Solar plants at Bobonong, Phakalane, Shakawe and Mmadinare produced about 82,520MWh in the first quarter of 2026, or 9.1% of domestic generation against 3.2% a year earlier, by Statistics Botswana’s figures reported in Mmegi, while imports fell 29.8% on the previous quarter and the Morupule A and B coal plants supplied 90.8% of local generation. Under its revised Integrated Resource Plan the government wants renewables to supply 50% of the generation mix by 2030, up from about 8%, and in April President Duma Boko broke ground at Maun on a 500MW solar plant with a 500MWh battery, which BPC is executing with Okavango Solar under a government-to-government partnership with Oman and a 30-year power purchase agreement. The World Bank’s Renewable Energy Support and Access Accelerator project, approved in July 2024 with an $88 million loan and $34 million in Green Climate Fund finance, includes 50MW of utility-scale battery storage. Botswana’s third nationally determined contribution, which its delegation is presenting at COP31 in Antalya, rates energy generation as having the “largest” potential for carbon market activities and nature-based removals a “significant” one, with bushfire management and refrigerant transitions at “moderate” and a “lower volume” expected from energy efficiency, according to Argus. Its draft carbon market framework, which Carbon Pulse reported the plan targets for the first quarter of 2027, would keep the cheaper mitigation for Botswana’s own target and offer the higher-cost activities abroad as internationally transferred mitigation outcomes under Article 6, and it names both Article 6.2 and the Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism as suitable routes for energy generation. Mitigation under the unconditional target will need $224 million between 2026 and 2035, the NDC says, and the conditional mitigation need for the same period is $1.5 billion. The second NDC, submitted in December 2024, had put the conditional need to 2030 at $2.7 billion, of which about $50 million has been secured, Argus reported. On removals, the NDC cautions against overselling the low-cost mitigation Botswana needs for its own unconditional target, and the government will seek $4.32 billion in climate finance at COP31, the state news agency BOPA reported. Before commissioning, the battery will need grid-connection and regulatory approvals from the Botswana Energy Regulatory Authority, the ESMP says, and amendments to BERA’s own Act that would recognise independent transmission providers and introduce electricity trading are due in Parliament’s November sitting, according to Mmegi’s report of remarks by BERA’s Chief Executive, Never Tshabang, at the National Business Conference in Francistown in October. Fieldwork for the ESMP found no one living on the 40-hectare plot that the Ngwato Land Board allocated to BPC, so no resettlement plan is needed, and the battery compound will fence about 2 hectares, leaving the other 38 open for the livestock of neighbouring farmers and for the communities who collect non-timber forest products there.

artigo.texto: As the world looks for ways to restore degraded land and remove carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere, oasification offers another approach to nature-based restoration. It focuses on improving how drylands capture and retain water, allowing vegetation to recover and ecosystems to become healthier. Beyond its environmental benefits, oasification could also create opportunities for carbon removal projects and nature-based finance. But how does it work, and can it become part of the growing carbon market? What Is Oasification? Understanding the Concept Oasification is a land-restoration approach that aims to reverse desertification by improving how degraded land captures and retains water. It focuses on restoring the natural conditions needed for vegetation to grow, particularly in arid and semi-arid regions where water is limited. The concept was developed by Spanish researchers Andrés Martínez de Azagra, Jorge Mongil, and J. Rojo. Their 2004 paper, Oasification: A Forest Solution to Many Problems of Desertification, describes how small earth structures can collect and infiltrate rainwater and surface runoff, improving soil moisture and supporting vegetation growth. Oasification is closely linked to the fight against desertification, which occurs when land in dry regions loses its productivity due to climate conditions and human activities such as deforestation, overgrazing, and unsustainable farming. The scale of this challenge is significant. According to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD), drylands cover approximately 40.6% of Earth’s land area, excluding Antarctica. The UN also reported that 77.6% of the world’s land experienced drier conditions between 1990 and 2020 than during the previous 30 years. Unlike approaches that focus mainly on planting trees, oasification first addresses the land’s ability to capture and retain available water. It can complement reforestation by creating better conditions for vegetation to establish and survive. How Does Oasification Work? Restoring Land by Making Better Use of Water Oasification works by improving how degraded land collects, absorbs, and retains rainwater. Rather than relying on large irrigation systems, it uses relatively small structures and land-management techniques to direct available water toward areas where vegetation can grow. One common technique is rainwater harvesting. Small basins, trenches, terraces, and contour barriers are built along slopes to slow down surface runoff. These structures collect rainwater that would otherwise flow downhill and carry away valuable topsoil. The captured water can then seep into the ground, increasing soil moisture and supporting plant growth. Another important part is soil restoration. By slowing water runoff, oasification helps reduce erosion and allows soil particles and nutrients to settle. This can improve soil conditions and create a better environment for seeds, roots, and microorganisms. Vegetation is then introduced or allowed to recover naturally. Native trees, shrubs, grasses, and other suitable plants help stabilize the soil, provide ground cover, and support local biodiversity. Their roots also help improve soil structure and water infiltration. The process works as a cycle. Better water retention supports plant growth, while growing vegetation protects the soil and adds organic matter. Over time, these improvements can help degraded land recover its productive capacity. However, oasification must be adapted to local conditions. Rainfall, soil type, slope, and available water all influence which techniques will work. It is not a one-size-fits-all solution, but an approach that combines water management, soil protection, and vegetation recovery. Not all carbon added to the soil remains stored permanently. Some organic matter decomposes and releases CO2 back into the atmosphere. Projects must, therefore, measure net changes in carbon stocks over time. Oasification and Carbon Sequestration: How Restored Land Can Capture CO2 Beyond restoring degraded land, oasification could also contribute to climate change mitigation by increasing the amount of carbon stored in vegetation and soil. This is where the approach becomes particularly relevant to nature-based carbon removal and carbon markets. Plants absorb carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere through photosynthesis and store carbon in their trunks, branches, leaves, and roots. When oasification improves soil moisture and supports vegetation growth, it can create better conditions for increasing this natural carbon storage. As trees and other plants grow, they can accumulate more carbon in their biomass. Soil also plays an important role. Fallen leaves, dead roots, and other organic materials break down and add carbon to the soil. Greater vegetation cover can help protect this organic matter from erosion and support the long-term buildup of soil organic carbon. The scale of the opportunity is significant. The IPCC estimates that approximately 20–30 billion tonnes of carbon have been released into the atmosphere through desertification-related processes, including deforestation, overgrazing, and conventional tillage. This highlights the climate value of protecting and restoring degraded land. However, carbon storage does not happen immediately. Vegetation needs time to establish, while soil carbon gains can take years or even decades to become measurable. Results also depend on rainfall, soil conditions, plant species, and long-term land management. The IPCC identifies natural vegetation restoration and tree planting on degraded land as activities that can enrich carbon in topsoil and subsoil over time. It also recognizes that measures to combat desertification can support soil carbon sequestration. For oasification projects, this means carbon benefits could come from two main sources: - increased carbon in growing vegetation, and - additional organic carbon stored in the soil. artigo.texto: Setting ground rules: City of Irondale votes on data center regulations Irondale, Ala (WBMA) - Irondale City Council says it is setting the ground rules for possible future data center developments. Tuesday night, the City voted to adopt regulations for future data center project proposals. City Councilman Aaron Sims says he had been researching data centers for months, and used that information to draft the new ordinance. Under Irondale's new code, if a future data center required upgrades to the power grid, the developer would be fully responsible for funding the upgrades. The code also requires any future data center to use a 'closed loop' water system, that is designed to cut down on excessive water use. Irondale Mayor James D. Stewart, Jr., says as of now, there are no data center projects on the table for the city.

artigo.texto: Meta climática de 2040 da UE sob pressão por acordo no mercado de carbono Um documento vazado analisado pela Euronews indica que as reformas do Sistema de Comércio de Emissões da União Europeia, o EU ETS, poderiam enfraquecer a meta climática de 2040 do bloco. A Presidência irlandesa do Conselho da UE suavizou uma proposta que será discutida por embaixadores da UE na quarta-feira, em meio ao aumento da pressão política para conciliar as metas de emissões com a competitividade industrial e os altos custos de energia. O texto de compromisso busca garantir apoio político para o mercado de carbono após 2030, mas defensores do clima alertam que as concessões destinadas a proteger a indústria europeia podem reduzir a contribuição do sistema para a meta de 2040, deixando outros setores econômicos para cobrir a lacuna. Licenças gratuitas e planos de investimento O texto do Conselho mantém a proposta de julho da Comissão Europeia de desacelerar a redução das licenças de carbono, estender as permissões gratuitas para a indústria e trazer créditos de carbono internacionais para o mercado da UE, de modo que as emissões domésticas possam ser compensadas por meio de projetos no exterior. Segundo a proposta da Presidência irlandesa, as empresas industriais manteriam 80 por cento de suas licenças gratuitas se apresentarem um plano de investimento, mesmo que depois não realizem os investimentos de descarbonização propostos. Os 20 por cento restantes dependeriam do início da construção de projetos elegíveis. As licenças gratuitas são permissões que as empresas recebem sem comprá-las em leilão, concebidas para proteger os produtores da UE da concorrência em países com regras climáticas menos rigorosas, como a China e os Estados Unidos. A proposta representa uma concessão política significativa às indústrias preocupadas em perder essas licenças e levanta questões sobre se o ETS oferecerá incentivo suficiente para cortar emissões. Créditos internacionais e a meta de 2040 Sobre os créditos de carbono internacionais, o Conselho manteve a proposta da Comissão de reservar licenças equivalentes a 260 milhões de toneladas de CO2 para financiar sua compra. Também deixa em aberto uma possível fase-piloto entre 2031 e 2035 para testar o sistema antes da implementação plena. O Conselho manteve requisitos rigorosos de qualidade e integridade para os créditos internacionais, tornando a trajetória de redução do ETS cada vez mais dependente de sua disponibilidade. Se as indústrias não puderem comprá-los, a meta climática de 2040 poderá ser comprometida, já que ela exige pelo menos 85 por cento de redução líquida doméstica das emissões, com os créditos internacionais respondendo pelos 5 por cento restantes. Cronograma das negociações e divisões entre os Estados-membros A Presidência irlandesa busca consenso entre os 27 países da UE antes que as negociações avancem para questões politicamente mais sensíveis, como ambição climática e repartição de encargos. Ela espera fechar um acordo no Conselho de Meio Ambiente em 11 de dezembro, enquanto o Parlamento Europeu deve votar durante sua sessão plenária de 14 a 17 de dezembro em Estrasburgo. A presidência enfrenta uma batalha difícil diante das profundas divisões entre os Estados-membros e da complexidade das negociações. Segundo um segundo documento analisado pela Euronews, os países da UE já estão divididos sobre a velocidade com que a oferta de licenças de carbono deve encolher, se as empresas devem usar créditos internacionais para cumprir obrigações e até que ponto os setores industriais devem ser protegidos do aumento dos custos de carbono. Em conjunto, essas demandas correm o risco de diluir o ETS justamente quando se espera que ele impulse grande parte da próxima fase de cortes de emissões do bloco. Os governos em geral querem preservar o ETS como fonte de receita para a descarbonização, mas crescem as preocupações com os custos impostos a indústrias de uso intensivo de energia que competem com fabricantes na China ou nos Estados Unidos. Algumas capitais argumentam que o número de licenças deve cair para elevar o preço do carbono e incentivar o desinvestimento em combustíveis fósseis, enquanto outras temem o impacto da retirada das licenças gratuitas sobre indústrias em dificuldade. Uma redução mais lenta aliviaria a pressão sobre usinas e fábricas, potencialmente moderando os preços do carbono e dando às empresas mais tempo para se adaptar, mas também significaria menos cortes de emissões nos setores cobertos pelo ETS, tornando a meta de 2040 mais difícil de alcançar. Análise questiona compatibilidade da reforma Uma análise recente do Oko-Institut, encomendada pelo grupo ambientalista WWF Alemanha, alertou que a reforma do ETS proposta pela Comissão é incompatível com a meta da UE de cortar as emissões líquidas em 90 por cento até 2040. Lisa Okken, especialista em política industrial do WWF Alemanha, disse que a Comissão está optando por correr riscos na proteção climática em vez de resguardar o futuro da indústria europeia, e argumentou que a reforma proposta carece do sinal de preço do carbono necessário para impulsionar uma modernização urgente. Segundo ela, a lacuna está sendo preenchida com medidas contábeis complicadas e flexibilidade excessiva. Ambientalistas também manifestaram preocupação com uma proposta que permitiria emissões adicionais além do teto existente em troca de futuras remoções permanentes de carbono por meio de tecnologias caras destinadas a capturar CO2 do ar. O estudo observou que ainda não está claro se tais remoções podem ser entregues na escala necessária, já que a capacidade necessária não existe hoje.

artigo.texto: Moratorium? Tax break? Colorado cities face data center policy choices As data centers continue to pop up across Colorado, municipalities are facing a difficult choice: weighing the economic benefits against growing concerns from the communities they serve. While some municipalities are passing moratoriums on data centers, Douglas County leaders recently granted a $19 million tax break in business personal property taxes to a new Flexential data center that's under construction in Parker. That data center is set to open next year. Across Colorado, community members have been saying no to data centers. "A lot of people feel very blindsided about the data centers popping up, and so they don't feel heard, which I understand, and I understand their disappointment," one Douglas County resident said in a recent meeting. "We needed this moratorium, and you all failed us, and you failed yourselves," an Aurora resident said in another meeting. Residents have shared worries about water, electricity, noise and pollution. "I'm scared for the water, scared for the pollution, scared for my air, my quality of life. The noise that this data center might create- that's why I'm so disappointed in this," one Colorado resident recently said. But one CEO in the rapidly growing industry says data centers are a necessity in modern life. Flexential's CEO and a public policy expert weighed in on the heated debate surrounding them. "Your connected life can't happen without a data center," said Ryan Mallory, CEO of Flexential. "All of the social media apps that you're using run through our sites, as well as a lot of the streaming services that everybody's using at home." Headquartered in Denver, Flexential has data centers across the country. Its fifth Colorado center is in development in Parker. "This is an industrial shell that has power and cooling that customers can then put their own IT infrastructure into," Mallory said. While Mallory says AI-focused customers only make up 11% of Flexential's centers, he says AI data centers are fueling the U.S.'s economic growth right now. "The GDP in the United States is growing about 3%, 3.5%. That's fueled primarily by AI infrastructure data centers," Mallory said. But with communities mobilizing against them, how should local leaders respond? "It's a lot of hard and fast feelings," said Billy Wynn, the lead author of a recent report on data centers, prepared by the Romer Institute of Evidence-Based Policy for the city of Colorado Springs. "It's a very nascent and kind of burgeoning issue," Wynne said. The report recommends municipalities handle data center applications with transparency, invite the public to participate and develop standard rules and processes. "Do it in a transparent way, develop policies that are broadly applicable, not case by case, ad hoc negotiations. Give the public a bona fide opportunity to express their interests, concerns, questions," Wynne said. "[We] really want to be treating different facilities as similarly as much as possible." It also recommends clarifying evidence-based standards around water and energy use. Mallory says Flexential uses an efficient closed-loop system rather than evaporative cooling. "Our site in Parker will use the same amount of water as about six homes," Mallory said. He says data centers bring tax revenue that can be beneficial for communities. Wynne says there are a lot of unknowns in the rapidly changing space, and evidence should guide communities weighing data centers. "Let's do our best to look at the facts, and then have a more informed debate about it," Wynne said. Flexential's CEO also spoke on the impact of the recent election on data center buildout after the stock market plummeted following the midterms. While Mallory attributes that to standard volatility, he does think that Democratic lawmakers could slow data center permitting and buildout. "At the end of the day, the people that lose out isn't going to be Flexential. It's going to be the communities that we serve," Mallory said.

artigo.texto: Our Next Energy Inc. (ONE), a Novi-based U.S. energy storage technology company and battery manufacturer, has signed an agreement with New York’s Wen Acquisition Corp. to take ONE public and trade on the Nasdaq Stock Market under the ticker symbol ONEE. “Over the last five years, LFP (lithium iron phosphate) has grown from roughly 20 percent to 60 percent of the global battery market, yet China produces approximately 99 percent of the world’s LFP cells,” says Mujeeb Ijaz, founder and CEO of ONE. “We built ONE to close that gap with a secure American and allied supply chain. “We believe our combination with Wen will give us a public platform to scale ONE into this $40 billion addressable market with access to growth capital as we scale our operations to meet rising demand.” Most LFP cells made in America today come from foreign-owned factories or rely on licensed Chinese technology. ONE uses its own domestic technology, from electrode active materials through fully integrated energy storage systems. Two recent federal actions make that distinction matter, according to ONE. The FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) extends battery restrictions to cells and components produced by a foreign entity of concern (FEOC) or under FEOC technology licenses. Executive Order 14421, signed in August 2026, restricts battery energy storage systems and other grid equipment tied to covered foreign entities from the U.S. bulk-power system. ONE says it’s well positioned to meet this moment. It makes its cells in Van Buren Township and integrates them in Novi with its own battery management systems (BMS) into packs and containerized energy storage systems for defense, rail, and grid customers that require safety, durability, and a secure domestic supply chain. “ONE has done the hard part of building an American LFP cell and pack business, with factories operating and customers in markets that increasingly require domestic supply,” says Julian Sevillano, CEO of Wen. “With two operating factories, binding customer contracts, and federal policy appearing to move its way, ONE is positioned to lead the reshoring of critical battery manufacturing in the United States.” The boards of directors of both Wen and ONE have approved the proposed transaction, which is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to approval by Wen’s shareholders and ONE’s stockholders and the satisfaction of other customary closing conditions, including Wen’s registration statement on Form S-4 being declared effective by the Securities and Exchange Commission, the expiration or termination of the waiting period under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act of 1976, as amended (HSR Act) and the satisfaction or waiver of a minimum cash condition. Additional information about the proposed transaction, including a copy of the business combination agreement, will be provided in a Current Report on Form 8-K to be filed by Wen with the SEC and available at sec.gov. For more information about ONE, visit one.ai.

artigo.texto: O Brasil pode perder para o exterior a próxima onda de investimentos em data centers. A conclusão saiu de um painel em Lisboa que juntou a ANP, a agência que regula petróleo, gás natural e biocombustíveis, e a Eneva, do mercado de gás e energia, em torno das regras tributárias e energéticas do setor. O calendário aperta. Interlocutores ouvidos pela Agência iNFRA relatam que as tratativas dentro do Executivo avançaram e que o decreto do Redata, o Regime Especial de Tributação voltado aos Serviços de Data Center, deve sair ainda em novembro. Falta pacificar, porém, o ponto mais espinhoso do setor elétrico. Uma das hipóteses na mesa obriga os empreendimentos a contratar energia nova para se abastecer, exigência batizada de adicionalidade energética. Quem deu o tom do alerta foi Pietro Mendes, diretor da ANP, na Conferência Ibero-Brasileira de Energia (Coniben) 2026, em Lisboa, segundo apuração do site especializado Megawhat. Ele cobrou do governo federal celeridade para fechar as regras definitivas do programa. Na avaliação dele, o país já parte em desvantagem na disputa global por novos hubs de processamento de dados. Segundo ele, o país vai perdendo oportunidades e investimentos, e o capital acaba indo para outro lugar. O gás natural já consta da legislação do programa. Mendes, porém, criticou duas ideias em circulação, a de condicionar a participação das térmicas à captura e ao armazenamento de carbono e a de priorizar o biometano no abastecimento. A captura de carbono serve para mitigar os impactos da queima de combustíveis fósseis, mas vira barreira se transformada em obrigação, avaliou o diretor. Sobre o biometano, ele reconheceu papel relevante na transição energética e lembrou o limite atual, uma produção sem escala para usinas de grande porte. Critérios rígidos demais, na mesma leitura, castigariam o gás num país cuja matriz elétrica já tem peso enorme de fontes renováveis. Diretrizes engessadas, completou, espantam investidores internacionais de grande porte. O contraponto veio de Christiano Vieira, diretor de Regulação da Eneva. Para ele, a regulamentação precisa ir além da origem limpa da eletricidade contratada e contabilizar o custo de manter o abastecimento garantido. Data centers exigem eletricidade sem pausa, enquanto sol e vento variam ao longo do dia. Para Vieira, não faz sentido montar um modelo energético só com renováveis e deixar a conta da segurança do abastecimento para todos os usuários do sistema. O executivo defendeu preservar as metas de descarbonização e abrir caminho para que os empreendedores ofereçam potência e confiabilidade a preços competitivos, de térmicas a gás a sistemas de armazenamento. Citou empreendimentos que demandam entre 300 MW e 500 MW, escala que exige reforço no fornecimento. Baterias ajudam a dar qualidade à energia usada em aplicações de inteligência artificial. Não bastam, ponderou Vieira, para sustentar o funcionamento ininterrupto que os empreendimentos exigem. O decreto esperado para ainda este mês vai arbitrar o equilíbrio entre descarbonização, segurança de suprimento e custo. Errar a mão, na avaliação do diretor da ANP, empurra o capital para a concorrência internacional.

artigo.texto: - Owner’s-side partner will manage both ERCOT projects through commissioning to commercial operation date (COD), slated for 2027, strengthening grid resilience and helping lower power prices for Texas consumers. - Project wins build on boutique energy services firm’s expanding BESS portfolio in the Southwestern U.S. AUSTIN, Nov. 16, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Charge Power Inc.—the hands-on, owner’s-side energy storage partner—today announced it was awarded two battery energy storage system (BESS) projects in Texas to manage through commissioning: a 150-megawatt (MW) / 300-megawatt-hour (MWh) project and a 140 MW / 280 MWh project. Together, the projects will add 290 MW / 580 MWh of storage capacity to the ERCOT grid as Charge Power continues to build out its footprint in the rapidly expanding Southwestern U.S. energy storage market. On both projects, expected to reach commercial operation in 2027, Charge Power will integrate EPC contractors, project engineers, suppliers, documentation, and the ERCOT interconnection checklist—among other parties and processes—on the owner’s behalf. Its role is to close gaps in project delivery so that projects energize on time and earn from day one. During Charge Power’s involvement, both projects are also onboarding the WARAM platform for project governance, due diligence, and compliance. WARAM connects physical energy-asset requirements to the evidence that proves them, keeping that record current through ownership, certification, and transfer. “Texas is one of the most demanding storage markets in the country, and the stretch between construction and commercial operation is where a project either protects its returns or loses them,” said Ravi Pinnelli, founder and president of Charge Power. “We approach every project with an owner-operator mindset, so on these projects our decisions prioritize schedule, revenue, and long-term performance the way the owner would. Through shifting markets and an evolving energy landscape, our goal is to deliver execution certainty from day one to COD and beyond.” The wins extend Charge Power’s track record of protecting project outcomes for BESS owners. Since its founding in 2022, the company has commissioned 3 gigawatts (GW) / 7 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of energy storage, and its hands-on approach has saved owners more than $10 million in estimated avoided liquidated damages. Charge Power’s recent project awards come as energy storage demand in Texas continues to surge. Battery capacity on the ERCOT grid roughly doubled each year from 2020 through 2024 and grew another 76% in 2025, reaching 16.5 GW / 28.8 GWh by the end of June 2026, according to Modo Energy. Utility-scale storage captures lower-cost power when it is plentiful on the grid and delivers it when demand peaks, reducing the cost of power for consumers, cutting reliance on carbon-heavy peaker plants, and strengthening grid reliability. Batteries also respond in milliseconds to stabilize the grid and help it ride through extreme weather and sudden plant outages. According to an American Clean Power Association analysis, in Texas alone, storage deployed since 2023 has saved consumers over $750 million in electricity costs. About Charge Power Charge Power is the independent, hands-on, owner’s-side partner for energy storage. A boutique energy services firm with offices in Austin, Texas and Toronto, the company approaches every project with an owner-operator mindset from design through commissioning and beyond. It closes the gaps between contractors during project delivery, keeping everything aligned on the owner’s behalf, so projects energize on time and earn from day one. As a battery energy storage system (BESS) specialist with deep grid and market expertise, Charge Power optimizes long-term performance and fixes small problems before they become expensive ones, preserving revenue and uptime—and protecting project outcomes. The result: execution certainty in an evolving energy landscape. Founded in 2022 by BESS industry veterans, Charge Power has commissioned 3 GW / 7 GWh of energy storage across U.S. energy markets — including CAISO, ERCOT, MISO and PJM — as well as Canada, India, Japan and the U.K. Learn more at www.chargepowerinc.com. A photo accompanying this announcement is available at https://www.globenewswire.com/NewsRoom/AttachmentNg/bfcf648e-9e62-4fc7-b864-ad0ce895e8dc Media contact Chris Larson Media Communications chris.larson@chargepowerinc.com Media gallery

artigo.texto: EUA restringem venda de chips de IA para data centers no Brasil Nova norma exige licença governamental para exportação por suspeita de “desvios” em 5 países O Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos publicou nesta 2ª feira (16.nov.2026) uma norma que exige licença governamental para a exportação, reexportação ou transferência de chips avançados de inteligência artificial destinados a data centers fora do território norte-americano. O Brasil está entre os 5 países com restrições imediatas. Leia a íntegra da norma provisória (PDF – 694 KB). A norma não impede o Brasil de adquirir chips norte-americanos. O que muda é a necessidade de aprovação prévia do governo dos EUA para cada operação. A regra foi elaborada pelo Departamento do Tesouro e pelo Conselho de Segurança Nacional dos EUA e publicada pelo BIS (Bureau of Industry and Security), órgão do Departamento de Comércio. O objetivo declarado é impedir que restrições já existentes ao acesso a tecnologias sensíveis fabricadas nos EUA sejam contornadas por meio de arranjos de computação remota em data centers instalados em outros países. Além do Brasil, Indonésia, Malásia, Singapura e Tailândia integram o grupo de países classificados como de “risco elevado de desvio de tecnologia”. Para essas nações, passa a ser obrigatória a autorização do governo norte-americano antes de qualquer exportação ou transferência de semicondutores avançados. “Esses países estão sendo incluídos em resposta a preocupações de que itens de computação avançada, sujeitos aos requisitos de licenciamento do EAR [Regulamentos de Administração de Exportações], estejam sendo desviados –sem autorização– para entidades e países que suscitam preocupações”, diz o documento do governo norte-americano. A exigência de licença não se aplica a chips destinados a empresas com sede ou cuja controladora final tenha sede nos Estados Unidos, desde que determinados requisitos de reporte sejam cumpridos. O secretário de Comércio pode incluir outros países na lista, mediante consulta ao secretário de Estado ou ao assessor de Segurança Nacional da presidência. O Departamento de Comércio afirmou que vai monitorar ativamente países que tolerem o descumprimento da norma. As consequências estabelecidas para casos de evasão são: - restrições a importações; - novos requisitos de licença para exportação de semicondutores avançados; - rebaixamento do status do país no regime de controle de exportações dos EUA; - proibições temporárias de exportação para pessoas físicas ou jurídicas estrangeiras envolvidas nessas atividades. Segundo o Departamento de Comércio, a medida responde ao avanço da computação em nuvem e da infraestrutura de “superinteligência”, que tornaram crescentemente possível o acesso remoto a capacidades computacionais avançadas dos EUA por meio de data centers localizados fora dos países sujeitos às restrições de exportação vigentes. CASO NVIDIA A norma foi publicada dias depois do escândalo envolvendo Jensen Huang, ex-CEO da Nvidia. A fabricante de chips abriu uma investigação interna para apurar se o executivo foi alvo de espionagem –a mulher com quem ele se relacionou fora do casamento é suspeita de ser uma espiã chinesa. Huang já criticou as restrições impostas pelos EUA à venda de chips para a China.

artigo.texto: SiTime Addresses $2 Billion Opportunity in Data Center Bandwidth Upgrades with Two New Clock Families FemtoClock 4 and VersaClock 8 Bring 20 Years of Heritage to 2X Faster Ethernet and Connectivity Standards SANTA CLARA, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 17, 2026-- SiTime Corporation (NASDAQ: SITM), the Precision Timing company, today introduced FemtoClock™ 4 and VersaClock® 8, two clock families designed for the latest connectivity protocols that double bandwidth over previous generations. The families are designed for networking and computing applications in the data center rack. Together they address a $2 billion serviceable addressable market (SAM) over the next five years. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261117222922/en/ FemtoClock 4 and VersaClock 8 Bring 20 Years of Heritage to 2X Faster Ethernet and Connectivity Standards “Insatiable demand for AI, along with rising performance requirements, is driving the need for greater density and speed,” said Piyush Sevalia, executive vice president and chief business officer of SiTime. “The FemtoClock and VersaClock families have a 20-year heritage and multiple generations of products. Over this period, they have led the industry in performance, density and shipments, and have become the default choice for many customer designs. Engineers know these architectures well. This familiarity enables them to design with confidence, get the most from these programmable clocks and reuse existing software. The result is higher-performance, denser AI hardware that generates revenue sooner. Built on this successful track record, FemtoClock 4 and VersaClock 8 extend SiTime’s lead in Precision Timing.” These clocks are built to solve the bandwidth challenge and the industry is tackling it right now; 224G serializer-deserializer (SerDes) links are being rapidly adopted in data center switches and AI servers to double Ethernet bandwidth, and PCI Express® (PCIe®) 7 is doing the same for interconnectivity between CPUs, xPUs, memory, storage and smart network interface cards (SmartNICs). In faster, denser systems, the margin for error is smaller. FemtoClock 4 delivers resilient clock signals for Ethernet networking with ultra-low jitter and high clock density in a single device. VersaClock 8 serves PCIe interconnectivity with a flexible, compact, low-power design that is ideal for hot and dense compute trays. According to Dell’Oro Group, 1.6 Tbps ports in AI back-end switches are expected to ramp at least five times faster than 800 Gbps, driven by adoption across scale-up, scale-out and scale-across networks. This bandwidth is critical to maximizing utilization of expensive xPU resources. “The AI infrastructure build-out is exposing bottlenecks that go well beyond GPU compute performance,” said Dave Altavilla, president and principal analyst at HotTech Vision and Analysis. “Moving data efficiently across increasingly complex systems is becoming a critical design challenge, particularly as Ethernet and PCIe bandwidth requirements continue to climb. Precision Timing plays an important role here, especially as higher signaling speeds leave less margin for jitter and signal degradation. SiTime’s latest clock families reflect how these underlying technologies are evolving to meet the precise needs of the next generation of AI data center architectures.” Product Features FemtoClock 4 is a jitter attenuator and clock generator for top-of-rack and spine switches built on 224G SerDes. Key features include: - 19 fs RMS phase jitter at 312.5 MHz in clock generator mode (12 kHz to 20 MHz, 4 MHz high-pass filter) - Up to six frequency domains across 18 outputs - Fewer devices for top-of-rack switches that generally need more than 40 clocks VersaClock 8 is a programmable clock generator providing reference clocks for CPUs, xPUs, memory and storage. Key features include: - About 10 fs reference clock jitter for PCIe 7 - 30 fs RMS phase jitter at 312.5 MHz (12 kHz to 20 MHz, 4 MHz high-pass filter) - Low power limits self-heating; operates at up to 105°C - 5-, 9- and 12-output variants in QFN packages from 4x4 mm to 6x6 mm - 12-output variant is about 40% smaller than a comparable solution Availability FemtoClock 4 and VersaClock 8 are in production and available now. FemtoClock 4 part numbers: RC38616, RC38412, RC32418 and RC32412. VersaClock 8 part numbers: RC31312A, RC31309A and RC31305A. Additional Resources About SiTime SiTime is the Precision Timing company. Our people and products help engineers build the impossible. Customers trust SiTime solutions in more than 400 applications, including AI hardware, autonomous vehicles, low Earth orbit satellites and wearables. Built on decades of innovation, our oscillators, clocks, resonators and software deliver higher system performance, greater resilience and better reliability. For more information, visit www.sitime.com. artigo.texto: O Brasil está abraçando uma oportunidade que ninguém quer deixar escapar. Com investimentos bilionários anunciados, a expansão acelerada da inteligência artificial e a crescente importância da capacidade computacional, atrair grandes data centers virou uma aposta de desenvolvimento econômico e tecnológico. Mas a pressa para entrar nessa corrida pode estar passando por cima de uma avaliação criteriosa sobre os ganhos e principalmente sobre as perdas para o país. Essa conta começa pelo que o conceito de "nuvem" esconde. O uso da IA mobiliza servidores que demandam muitíssima energia e refrigeração, apoiados em instalações que ocupam território e dependem de redes elétricas e de fontes de água. Por isso, a conveniência digital tem uma contrapartida material e ambiental. Esse tema ganhou outra dimensão durante o 2º Seminário de Inteligência Artificial, Meio Ambiente e Justiça Socioambiental, organizado pelo Lapin (Laboratório de Políticas Públicas e Internet) em Fortaleza, entre os dias 8 e 10. A programação incluiu uma visita ao território Anacé, nas proximidades do Complexo Industrial e Portuário do Pecém, onde está sendo construído um grande data center para o TikTok. Assim, a discussão deixou de ser apenas sobre tecnologia e ganhou endereço e rostos. Essa promessa foi encampada pelas propostas dos principais candidatos à presidência da República, incluindo as de Lula. Ampliar a capacidade computacional, desenvolver serviços de IA, estimular pesquisa e gerar empregos qualificados são objetivos legítimos. Mas investimentos bilionários não garantem, por si só, benefícios distribuídos nem ganhos tecnológicos proporcionais aos recursos que o Brasil oferece. Nos Estados Unidos, governos locais já impõem restrições aos data centers. Se quem recebe esses empreendimentos há mais tempo começa a impor limites, o Brasil precisa entender que questionamentos não representam necessariamente oportunidades perdidas, fazendo parte de uma busca pelo equilíbrio necessário. Veja esse artigo em vídeo: Esse equilíbrio exige questionar a ideia de que temos energia limpa sobrando. Nossa matriz elétrica é predominantemente renovável, mas há cortes por limitações da rede, segurança operacional e falta de demanda em certos horários. De janeiro a abril de 2026, eles atingiram 2.843 MW médios de geração eólica e solar, sendo 2.233 MW no Nordeste. Essa energia desperdiçada não pode ser automaticamente direcionada aos data centers, pois isso depende da localização, da capacidade da rede e de novos investimentos em transmissão e conexão. Além disso, data centers precisam dissipar o calor dos equipamentos e algumas tecnologias de refrigeração consomem volumes expressivos de água. Mesmo nos mais modernos, não basta medir a eficiência hídrica, pois uma instalação grande pode ter baixo consumo relativo e ainda retirar muita água do local. No Pecém, além da captação subterrânea, o projeto prevê 120 geradores de emergência a diesel, entre outros impactos sobre o território. - Assine gratuitamente minha newsletter sobre IA, experiência do cliente, mídia e transformação digital - Inscreva-se no meu podcast (escolha a plataforma): Spotify, Deezer, Apple Podcasts ou Soundcloud No dia 15 de setembro, o Brasil instituiu o Redata, regime que reduz tributos sobre equipamentos em troca de pesquisa no país, atendimento ao mercado interno, uso de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão e eficiência hídrica. Mas parte dos critérios depende de regulamentação, e é preciso demonstrar que o retorno público justifica a enorme vantagem privada. "Quando o governo fala de soberania digital e acha que trazer data centers para o território é garantia de soberania, ele está errado", afirma Cynthia Picolo, diretora-executiva do Lapin. Ela distingue as meras presenças físicas do controle sobre suas finalidades, a gestão dos recursos naturais e a governança. "Ter a infraestrutura no território não é o mesmo que controlá-la." Soberania também exige respeitar quem vive no território. Os Anacé afirmam que seu protocolo de consulta não foi respeitado, enquanto o Ministério Público Federal e a Defensoria Pública da União questionam a suficiência do licenciamento daquele data center. Ao defender a repartição justa de benefícios, a defensora pública Thalita Verônica ressaltou durante o evento que "isso não se confunde com escola, estrada, água potável, que já são uma obrigação do Estado". Fazendo do jeito certo Não se trata, portanto, de rejeitar a tecnologia ou de impedir investimentos, mas de estabelecer as condições para que eles beneficiem o país respeitando os direitos da população. "Para mim, é possível atrair data centers de uma forma sustentável, ética e segura", explica Edson Prestes, professor da Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul. "Mas, para isso, a gente não pode 'colocar a carroça na frente dos bois'." Isso começa antes da aprovação e dos incentivos, avaliando a disponibilidade de água, a capacidade elétrica, a vegetação, as áreas protegidas e os direitos das comunidades tradicionais. Não basta examinar o terreno do data center, sendo necessário avaliar toda a infraestrutura que o sustenta e os impactos somados aos de outros empreendimentos. O licenciamento deve exigir estudos proporcionais ao porte e ao potencial de impacto, com participação pública. E a fiscalização não pode terminar na licença. As empresas envolvidas devem divulgar dados verificáveis sobre consumo e eficiência no uso de água e de energia, emissões e resíduos. Picolo defende o acompanhamento dos efeitos da disputa por recursos sobre as comunidades e outras atividades locais. Cabe ao poder público fiscalizar impactos e contrapartidas durante toda a operação, com verificação independente dos dados apresentados. Além disso, o investimento só se transforma em desenvolvimento quando deixa conhecimento e capacidade no país. Isso exige formar profissionais, fortalecer centros de pesquisa, transferir tecnologia e desenvolver fornecedores nacionais. Os recursos destinados à pesqui

artigo.texto: How Google's data center investment has impacted Pryor schools While some communities are weighing promises from data center developers, the City of Pryor has already spent years seeing what that kind of investment can mean for local schools. In Pryor, students can end the school day with a paddle in hand through after-school activities the district offers at no cost. Superintendent Lisa Muller said a stronger tax base, boosted by Google’s investment, has helped make programs like that possible. “We're able to provide that as a free program for our students after school,” Muller said. Google’s data center sits inside the Pryor school district, and Muller said the investment significantly increased school revenue. The funding comes in part from property taxes Google pays. In addition, Google has received tax breaks, and the state makes up for that tax revenue and sends it to Pryor schools. Pryor’s original agreement with Google included that money from the company’s tax exemptions going to the district. The impact extends beyond the school district. For the 2025 tax year, the Oklahoma Tax Commission lists about $34.2 million in Google-related reimbursements for Mayes County. That figure is countywide, but Pryor benefits as well. “It’s difficult to separate out, you know, what portion comes from the companies out at the, the industrial park versus what comes from other taxpayers within the district,” Muller said. The laws governing those incentives have changed since Google made its agreement in Pryor. Since 2021, new data centers can’t qualify under the same program. Certain existing facilities can still qualify for breaks on eligible equipment. “And so that's when we end up with these very different structures, that change over time just to fit the needs of the community,” said Trystine Payfer with Google. Payfer said new deals can include company payments in place of property taxes or other negotiated payments to the community, and what reaches schools depends on how each agreement divides those payments. “And this is all separate, of course, from the additional grants and scholarships and sponsorships that we do once we enter a community,” Payfer said. Muller said the additional revenue has helped Pryor keep classes small and pay staff above state minimums. “So just on the sort of the big picture question, like, does money matter? The answer is, is unambiguously yes,” Muller said. Northwestern economist Kirabo Jackson, who studies what happens when schools spend more, said how districts use additional funding is key. “You want to make sure that money is going towards things that improve instruction. You want to make sure that's going towards curriculum, that improves things. You want to make sure it's going towards reducing class size,” Jackson said. Muller said Pryor has seen academic improvement over time tied to the Google investment, and she pointed to staffing and class sizes as part of that progress. “We also maintain small class sizes here in Pryor and are able to pay our, our staff above the state minimums as well,” Muller said. The district’s state report card has continuously improved since the investment began, and the district has funding to provide opportunities and transportation for students and families even after the school day ends.

artigo.texto: Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust Announces $5 Billion Acquisition of Stabilized Data Center Portfolio NEW YORK--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 16, 2026-- Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust Inc. (NYSE: BXDC) today announced that it has signed a definitive agreement to acquire a 75% majority interest in two joint ventures with Amazon Web Services (“AWS”), in a transaction valued at approximately $5 billion reflecting an initial capitalization rate of 7.0%. The transaction represents BXDC’s inaugural investment and advances its strategy of acquiring and owning high-quality, stabilized data centers leased to leading cloud provider customers on long-term contracts. The joint ventures will own 13 newly constructed powered shells across two AWS data center campuses, with AWS retaining a 25% interest in the joint ventures. AWS will lease back 100% of the portfolio on a triple net basis with an initial lease term of 12 years and a fully extended lease term of 32 years. Nick Pell, Chief Executive Officer and President of BXDC, said, “We are thrilled to announce BXDC’s inaugural investment and our partnership with Amazon, a leading global technology company with a long-term commitment to innovation. The quality, basis and tenant profile of these assets make this an attractive match for the deployment of our IPO proceeds. Given the deep expertise across our platform, we believe BXDC is well positioned to capitalize on a highly compelling opportunity and deliver value for our shareholders.” "As we scale to meet growing demand for our customers, we're committed to building in a way that strengthens the communities where we operate,” said Prasad Kalyanaraman, VP of AWS Infrastructure. “We're focused on delivering long-term local benefits, from creating good jobs and free workforce training programs to supporting local priorities. Partnering with Blackstone allows us to continue expanding responsibly while keeping communities at the center of how we build.” The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026 and is subject to certain closing conditions. Morgan Stanley, CBRE Capital Markets, Citi, Goldman Sachs, J.P. Morgan, and Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. are serving as financial advisors on the transaction. Simpson Thacher & Bartlett LLP is serving as legal advisor to Blackstone. About Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust (NYSE: BXDC) is a recently listed company focused on acquiring and owning mission-critical data center assets that power the modern digital economy. BXDC targets newly-constructed, income-generating, stabilized data center properties leased to investment-grade hyperscale tenants on long-term contracts. Our investment strategy is designed to generate stable, long-term cash flows and deliver current income to shareholders, with growth potential through contractual rent escalations and accretive acquisition opportunities. BXDC is externally managed by an affiliate of Blackstone (NYSE: BX), the world’s largest alternative asset manager and the largest financial investor in data center and digital infrastructure assets globally. Further information is available at www.bxdc.com. About Blackstone Blackstone is the world’s largest alternative asset manager. artigo.texto: Stem and Copec Expand Partnership to Advance Energy Storage and Intelligent Energy Management Across Latin America Building on the Granja Solar project in Chile, the companies will jointly serve utility-scale and commercial and industrial customers across key regional markets HOUSTON--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 16, 2026-- Stem, Inc. (NYSE: STEM), a global leader in AI-enabled clean energy software and services, today announced a partnership agreement with Copec Flux, the renewable energy subsidiary of Copec S.A., to jointly deliver energy storage and energy management solutions, initially focusing on Chile, with plans to explore opportunities in Colombia and other Latin American markets. The agreement expands an existing relationship established through the Granja Solar project in Chile, where Copec Flux is deploying Stem's PowerTrack™ Energy Management System (EMS) as the master control system for a 135 MW solar facility being retrofitted with a 420 MWh battery energy storage system. Announced in May 2026, the project provides a foundation for extending the companies' collaboration to additional customers and markets. “Our partnership with Copec Flux is about making advanced energy technology more accessible to customers while simplifying how projects are deployed and operated,” said Arun Narayanan, Chief Executive Officer of Stem. “By combining our technology with Copec Flux's local capabilities, we can help customers bring projects online faster, improve operational performance, and maximize the long-term value of their energy investments.” Under the partnership, Stem will provide its PowerTrack software and controls technology, including EMS, power plant controls (PPC), and cloud-based monitoring and analytics, while Copec Flux will lead local engineering, project delivery, and operational services. The joint offering will serve utility-scale developers and asset owners as well as commercial and industrial (C&I) customers, providing a coordinated approach to deploying, monitoring, and managing solar, storage, and hybrid energy assets. “Energy storage is becoming critical for reliability across regional grids,” said Juan Cristóbal González, CEO of Copec Flux. “Collaborating with specialized technology providers like Stem allows us to test software capabilities at Granja Solar and identify the most efficient ways to support our clients' energy needs.” The expanded relationship reflects Stem's broader strategy to grow its international footprint through partnerships that combine its software and controls capabilities with established regional providers. As demand for flexible, intelligent energy infrastructure continues to grow, the companies see opportunities to extend the delivery model established at Granja Solar to additional projects and customers throughout Latin America. For more information on Stem and the PowerTrack, visit stem.com. About Stem Stem is a global leader in energy intelligence and the operating system for clean energy: where assets connect, sites are optimized, and value is captured. Powered by decades of operational experience and purpose-built AI, our PowerTrack™ platform is the layer that sits between raw data and confident action, making every decision-maker smarter, every asset more productive, and every transition more certain. From asset monitoring to portfolio optimization and control, PowerTrack delivers everything energy professionals need in one place. With projects managed across 55 countries, we have spent nearly 20 years empowering asset owners, operators, and developers to take command of what comes next, with the certainty to act, the trust to commit, and the intelligence to lead. Learn more at stem.com. About Copec and Copec Flux Copec is one of Chile's leading energy companies, with nearly 90 years of experience serving individuals, businesses, and industries across the country. Historically recognized for its leadership in fuel distribution and convenience services, the company is evolving into a broader energy and mobility platform, with growing investments in renewable energy, electromobility, and energy storage. As part of this strategy, its subsidiary Copec Flux develops, builds, and operates solar and energy storage projects across Chile, delivering integrated clean energy solutions for utility-scale, commercial, and industrial customers. Through its nationwide footprint, operational capabilities, and long-term commitment to innovation and sustainability, Copec seeks to play a key role in accelerating Chile’s energy transition and development. artigo.texto: ICE Launches New Tool to Quantify Data Center Construction Risk ATLANTA & NEW YORK--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 17, 2026-- Intercontinental Exchange, Inc. (NYSE: ICE), one of the world's leading providers of financial market technology and data powering global capital markets, today announced the launch of the ICE Data Center Site Analytics Tool. The tool helps developers, investors, lenders, and municipalities assess the feasibility and delay risk of data center projects before capital is committed. Data centers are among the largest components of U.S. private sector investment today, with cumulative global spending projected to reach $7 trillion by 2030 to meet the demand for compute power, according to McKinsey & Company. Although data centers have been a clear driver of U.S. economic growth, local factors such as utility costs, environmental concerns, and community opposition are increasing the probability of halted or delayed projects. Trained on thousands of data center permitting and project outcomes across the U.S., the ICE Data Center Construction Disruption Model, a key part of the ICE Data Center Site Analytics Tool, is designed to estimate the probability that data center construction may face disruption within 24 months. When tested against historical permit outcomes to analyze the probability of disruption, the model achieved 77% accuracy. “Data center capital is moving faster than local permitting and community consensus, and that gap is now a material financial risk,” said Larry Lawrence, Head of the Geospatial Intelligence team at ICE. “On a median-sized $2.7 billion project, a 12-month delay can cost $162 million to $270 million, so giving developers and communities a common, data-driven view of those costs can lead to better-informed agreements.” The ICE Data Center Site Analytics Tool covers more than 3,100 U.S. counties and tracks thousands of existing U.S. data centers across 47 embedded geospatial data layers, estimating disruption probability through three categories of inputs: - County permit history, including past delay and stoppage rates, filing volume and trends, project value, and fees. - Local site characteristics, including nearby electricity and water costs, plus tract-level education, broadband, poverty, and unemployment. - Market conditions, analyzing the ICE U.S . Mortgage Rate Lock Index at the time of filing. The ICE Data Center Site Analytics Tool is part of ICE Geospatial Intelligence, which links location-specific data to financial assets and securities. The platform spans 1.6 billion global building footprints, 13 million corporate asset locations, more than 100 million U.S. properties and more than 50,000 municipal bond issuers. Learn more about ICE Geospatial Intelligence: ICE Geospatial Intelligence | ICE About Intercontinental Exchange Intercontinental Exchange, Inc. (NYSE: ICE) is a Fortune 500 company that designs, builds, and operates digital networks that connect people to opportunity. We provide financial technology and data services across major asset classes helping our customers access mission-critical workflow tools that increase transparency and efficiency. ICE’s futures, equity, and options exchanges -- including the New York Stock Exchange -- and clearing houses help people invest, raise capital and manage risk. We offer some of the world’s largest markets to trade and clear energy and environmental products. Our fixed income, data services and execution capabilities provide information, analytics and platforms that help our customers streamline processes and capitalize on opportunities. At ICE Mortgage Technology, we are transforming U.S. housing finance, from initial consumer engagement through loan production, closing, registration and the long-term servicing relationship. Together, ICE transforms, streamlines, and automates industries to connect our customers to opportunity. artigo.texto: Proposed Lansing data center ban draws packed hearing, boos and debate A proposal to ban data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities drew a packed auditorium Tuesday night, with supporters urging Lansing officials to protect local resources and opponents warning against closing the door to potential investment. 48 people signed up to speak at the public hearing at Lansing Middle School. Each was given two minutes, with a 9 p.m. cutoff for the proceedings. Many attendees wore red to show support for the ban. Some speakers opposing it, including TeraWulf representatives, were met with boos and shouted interruptions. Board members repeatedly asked the audience to stop shouting and clapping so speakers could continue. The debate comes amid opposition to TeraWulf’s proposed artificial intelligence data center at the former Cayuga Power Plant site near Cayuga Lake. The proposed zoning amendment would define data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities but exclude them from the town’s list of permitted uses, making them prohibited under the zoning code. The change would apply townwide rather than serve as a decision on a single project application. Before the hearing, neighbors and community advocates held a press conference supporting the proposed ban. Speakers stood in front of signs reading “No Data Center on Cayuga Lake.” “We enthusiastically support the board moving forward with a ban on data centers and crypto mining facilities in the town,” said Renee Vogelsang, a member of the FLX Strong coalition. Supporters cited concerns about water resources, electricity demand, noise and the potential effects on nearby neighborhoods. Lisa Lincoln and Mark Zuss said they live approximately 3 1/2 miles from the proposed site. In a joint interview, they raised concerns about how the development could affect the lake and their quality of life, including potential noise from the facility. TeraWulf representatives urged the board to continue considering the project, arguing that development could generate new tax revenue and support schools, public services and infrastructure. One representative also discussed the possibility of a community benefits agreement providing recurring financial contributions toward local priorities. Those contributions were presented as potential benefits, rather than a finalized agreement. Another TeraWulf representative argued that opposing the ban should not be interpreted as endorsing the proposed development. “Voting no to this ban doesn’t mean automatic support of the data center,” the representative said. “It means we should thoughtfully review individual projects as they come along.” A resident speaking against the ban also urged officials to consider potential economic benefits and raised concerns about possible legal challenges. The hearing gave the board sharply differing views on whether Lansing should prohibit the facilities or continue reviewing proposals individually. A vote on the proposed zoning change was tentatively scheduled for Wednesday, Nov. 18, at Lansing Middle School.

artigo.texto: Installed energy storage capacity in the United States has surpassed 200 GWh, according to the U.S. Energy Storage Market Outlook Q4 2026, produced by the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. During the third quarter of 2026, 14.3 GWh of battery energy storage systems (BESS) entered operation. These additions brought total deployments during the first nine months of the year to 48.3 GWh, representing a 20% year-on-year increase. The volume installed between July and September was 1% lower than in the same quarter of 2025. However, the cumulative results for 2026 reflect growth in both grid-connected projects and behind-the-meter storage. Utility-scale projects account for most deployments Utility-scale projects represented most of the storage deployed during the first nine months of 2026, with 40.8 GWh, while the behind-the-meter segment added 7.5 GWh. In the third quarter alone, the utility-scale market added 12.2 GWh across 45 projects. Three projects with gigawatt-hour-scale capacity began operations during the period. Commercial and industrial storage added 1.3 GWh during the quarter, an increase of 29% year on year. Between January and September, this segment reached 5.4 GWh, exceeding the 4.8 GWh installed during the whole of 2025. SEIA and Benchmark attribute part of this growth to data centre expansion and the difficulties these consumers face in securing sufficient grid capacity. BESS can be combined with on-site solar or wind generation to manage demand, shift renewable output and provide short-duration backup power. Residential storage, meanwhile, added 746 MWh during the third quarter, up 16% year on year and the highest volume recorded for a third quarter. Nevertheless, installations through September remained 12% below the level recorded during the first nine months of 2025. Texas leads state-level deployment Texas led utility-scale energy storage deployment through the end of the third quarter, adding 12.3 GWh of capacity. Arizona ranked second with 7.7 GWh, followed by California with 6.8 GWh. Eleven states had already surpassed their previous annual energy storage installation records by the end of September: Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama and Illinois. The report identifies a shift in state policy from setting storage targets to conducting procurement processes. During 2026, New York awarded contracts to eight projects totalling approximately 950 MW in its first bulk energy storage solicitation, while Illinois secured around 600 MW in its first dedicated procurement. A previous SEIA analysis attributed part of the reduction in average wholesale electricity prices between the summers of 2021 and 2026 to the combined growth of solar and energy storage: 42% in Texas and 51% in California. seia.org 2030 forecast increases to 708 GWh SEIA and Benchmark raised their forecast for cumulative US energy storage capacity in 2030 by 3.7%. The updated outlook expects the country to reach 708 GWh across grid-connected and behind-the-meter systems. The revision reflects the number of projects under development, state procurement programmes and the growing need for flexibility across the electricity system. Energy storage can shift electricity from periods of high production to hours of greater demand, respond to fluctuations in renewable generation and provide grid services. Its deployment can also reduce the need to use additional generation facilities during demand peaks. Battery cell manufacturing capacity reaches 92.4 GWh US manufacturing capacity for energy storage cells also increased during the third quarter. Production of lithium iron phosphate cells for stationary energy storage began at a facility in Tennessee in July. Another facility opened in Indiana in October, increasing total US cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, a 50% rise. The report estimates that lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry will represent 92% of lithium-ion BESS deployments in 2026, up from 77% in 2023. Overall, lithium-ion batteries are expected to account for more than 97% of installations. Industry calls for permitting reform The report’s publication coincides with a request from more than 300 solar and energy storage companies for Congress to approve the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). The companies argue that the reform would shorten permitting procedures for energy infrastructure, reduce development costs and accelerate the connection of new projects. SEIA maintains that expanding energy storage infrastructure can increase the capacity available to meet electricity demand growth and support the integration of renewable generation into the US grid.

artigo.texto: - The Integrity Council has signed a cooperation agreement with South Korea’s Ministry of Economy and Finance and the Global Green Growth Institute. - The partnership will support the development of the Global Verified Carbon Market framework. - The work will focus on sharing expertise on carbon credit quality standards and the Integrity Council’s Core Carbon Principles. The Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (Integrity Council, also known as ICVCM) has agreed to work with the Republic of Korea and the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) to help shape an emerging framework for international cooperation on carbon markets. The three parties signed a tripartite memorandum of understanding (MoU) on November 15, bringing together the te Integrity Council, South Korea’s Ministry of Economy and Finance and GGGI, which serves as the interim secretariat for the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM). The agreement is intended to support the framework’s development and help ensure that its design meets a global standard for high-integrity carbon credits. The benchmark will be based on the Integrity Council’s Core Carbon Principles (CCPs) and its Assessment Framework. Partnership Targets Common Standards The GVCM is an emerging initiative through which participating countries aim to cooperate on carbon markets. Under the arrangement, the Integrity Council will share technical expertise with GGGI and help countries participating in, or considering joining, the new framework understand the principles and assessment requirements. The cooperation reflects an effort to build integrity into the GVCM as it takes shape, rather than address shortcomings after the framework is established. Relevant: ICVCM Publishes Article 6 And Domestic Policy Framework Guide For Governments Amy Merrill, chief executive of the Integrity Council, said the partnership would contribute to the development of interconnected carbon markets while supporting a consistent international threshold for credit quality. GGGI Executive Director Sang-Hyup Kim said confidence in the credibility of emissions reductions was essential for carbon credits to channel finance into projects that cut emissions. Early collaboration with the Integrity Council, he added, could help prevent costly changes later and maintain the confidence of participating countries. artigo.texto: CATL is exploring an air-breathing battery. Could it give EVs 2,000 km of range? A report by Chinese technology outlet IT Home has revived claims that lithium-air batteries could deliver electric vehicle ranges of up to 2,000 km and achieve five times the energy density of solid-state batteries. The chemistry’s theoretical specific energy is often cited at around 3,505 Wh/kg. However, this figure describes electrochemical potential, not the performance of a complete automotive battery. The CATL connection comes from Chief Scientist Wu Kai, who identified lithium-air technology as a long-term research direction at the 2026 Equipment Powerhouse Forum. As we previously reported, CATL’s broader battery roadmap places sodium-ion and all-solid-state technologies closer to commercialisation, while lithium-air remains a longer-term research prospect. CATL has not announced a 2,000 km production-car target or a commercial launch schedule for the technology. The gap between theoretical energy density and automotive performance remains substantial. Oxygen management, chemical stability, rechargeability and the supporting equipment all present significant engineering challenges. How lithium-air batteries work Conventional lithium-ion batteries store lithium within two electrodes, with lithium ions moving between the anode and cathode during charging and discharging. Lithium-air batteries instead use metallic lithium as the negative electrode and oxygen from the surrounding environment as the positive reactant. During discharge, lithium reacts with oxygen to form lithium peroxide (Li₂O₂) inside a porous cathode. Charging reverses the reaction, releasing oxygen and returning lithium ions to the anode. Drawing oxygen from outside the cell rather than storing the positive reactant in a conventional cathode material gives the chemistry high theoretical specific energy. The frequently cited 3,505 Wh/kg figure relates to the theoretical lithium-peroxide reaction and includes the oxygen reactant mass. Higher figures approaching 12,000 Wh/kg use a different calculation boundary that excludes oxygen mass. Neither represents the energy density of a complete automotive battery. Electrolytes, electrodes, protective components and air-management equipment all add weight and volume. Laboratory progress has not solved the durability problem Automotive interest in lithium-air batteries predates CATL’s research. IBM launched its Battery 500 project in 2009, targeting a metal-air battery capable of powering an electric car for 500 miles (805 km) on a charge. The multinational research programme involved academic and industry partners but did not produce a commercially available automotive battery. More recent research has addressed lithium-air batteries’ chemical limitations, particularly the accumulation of discharge products inside porous cathodes. A 2025 study by researchers at the University of Science and Technology of China, including Professor Peng Tan, examined how electrolyte oxygen-transport properties influence reaction mechanisms in lithium-oxygen batteries. Using thick electrodes, the researchers showed how mass-transfer resistance can change reaction pathways at different positions within an electrode. The work provides insight into electrode design but does not establish an automotive solution to cathode blockage. A separate result came from researchers associated with Jilin University and the Chinese Academy of Sciences. A 2024 study published in Advanced Energy Materials reported an optimised lithium-air pouch-cell configuration achieving 757.5 Wh/kg with an in-situ gelled polymer electrolyte. The researchers also demonstrated 241 cycles under specified laboratory conditions of 500 mA/g and 1,000 mAh/g. This is a laboratory result, not a commercially validated automotive battery-pack rating. Researchers at the Illinois Institute of Technology and Argonne National Laboratory reported another approach in a 2023 Science paper. Their solid-state lithium-air architecture used a four-electron reaction to form lithium oxide (Li₂O), rather than the more conventional lithium-peroxide pathway. The battery completed at least 1,000 charge-discharge cycles at room temperature. Its theoretical energy-density potential was estimated at 1,200 Wh/kg, not measured as an achieved commercial-cell rating. These results show progress beyond theoretical calculations, but different chemistries, operating environments and measurement boundaries make direct comparisons difficult. None establishes a production-ready passenger-car battery. Three engineering roadblocks for passenger cars 1. Air management adds weight and complexity A lithium-air battery needs oxygen while limiting exposure to moisture and carbon dioxide. These contaminants can trigger unwanted reactions that degrade the lithium anode, electrolyte and cathode. Moisture can react with metallic lithium, while carbon dioxide can form lithium carbonate (Li₂CO₃). Deposits inside the porous cathode can restrict oxygen transport and reduce usable capacity. An automotive system would therefore need controlled air intake, filtration and humidity management, potentially alongside additional gas-handling equipment. These components add weight and volume while consuming energy. A 2023 study in the Journal of Energy Storage proposed mechanical balance-of-plant systems for lithium-air vehicles. It estimated that the supporting equipment would consume 5.4% of battery power in its proposed vehicle configuration. The figure is design-specific, but illustrates the additional energy demand of operating lithium-air cells in a vehicle. 2. Rechargeability and efficiency remain difficult Lithium peroxide must be removed from the cathode during charging. Reversing the discharge reaction requires additional energy and can generate reactive oxygen species that attack the electrolyte and other cell components. These side reactions contribute to capacity loss and limited cycle life. Lithium-
