artigo.texto: Following the signing of the connection construction agreement earlier this year, the grid connection agreement marks a further significant step towards delivering the project. Together, the two agreements establish the key contractual framework for construction and subsequent operation of the grid connection. The BESS will have a storage duration of four hours and will be connected directly to the extra-high-voltage grid. It will be able to store electricity during periods of high generation or low demand and release it back to the grid when needed. Stadorf will make an important contribution to integrating renewable energy, increasing the flexibility of the power system and making efficient use of existing energy infrastructure. Michael Zimmermann, Managing Director of Elements Green Deutschland, said: “Signing the grid connection agreement marks another milestone for Stadorf. Together with the connection construction agreement, we now have the key contractual foundations in place for connecting this 400 MW project to the grid. This is significant progress for Elements Green and underlines our ability to successfully advance complex energy infrastructure projects of this scale.” Stadorf is part of Elements Green’s extensive German battery storage pipeline. The company is developing several large-scale battery storage projects for connection to the extra-high-voltage grid and is pursuing a long-term strategy as an integrated developer, investor and operator of energy infrastructure. “Germany needs not only additional renewable generation capacity but, above all, the high-performance and flexible infrastructure to make the energy transition a technical and economic success. Large-scale battery storage systems such as Stadorf will play a central role in this,” Zimmermann added. With the key grid connection agreements now in place, Elements Green is focusing on the next stages of technical and commercial implementation. This includes detailed planning of the grid connection infrastructure, preparations for construction and continued coordination with the project and technology partners involved.

artigo.texto: Duke Energy customers across North Carolina are facing higher electricity bills starting in January, but new rules will require large data centers to shoulder more of the financial risks associated with their growing energy demand. After opening in downtown Raleigh one year ago, Alejandro Leon Jr., owner of Olé Sports Bar and Lounge, said a new challenge is on the horizon for his establishment: Higher electricity bills. Other WRAL Top Stories “We’ve been eating that up and now unfortunately with that spike its obvious that the consumers are going to have to pay all that up front. Very unfortunate," Leon said. Leon says the rate hike would put business owners like himself in a crunch. “I was pretty disappointed that North Carolina approved the spike," Leon said. For Durham resident Midori Brooks, who recently received a $900 electricity bill, the prospect of another rate increase means she may need to take on a second job. Brooks has lived in the same home since 1995 and has watched her electricity bills climb. She recalls paying about $225 to $250 a month in previous years. Now, even with her husband working full time and Brooks working part time, the family is struggling to keep up. “I have to figure out whether I'm gonna pay at least a portion of the light bill and still be able to feed my three grandkids,” Brooks said. About $200 of her recent $900 bill was a past-due balance, she said, reflecting how difficult it has already become for her family to keep up with electricity costs even before the new rate increases take effect. The North Carolina Utilities Commission on Monday approved two-year rate plans for Duke Energy Carolinas and Duke Energy Progress, largely accepting negotiated settlements that reduced the utility's original requests. Residential electricity rates are projected to rise about 9.5% over the next two years for Duke Energy Carolinas customers and 9.3% for Duke Energy Progress customers. Duke released new figures Tuesday detailing how those increases will translate into monthly electricity bills. The increases will begin Jan. 1, 2027, in the middle of the winter heating season. How much more will customers pay? According to projections released Tuesday by Duke Energy, a typical residential customer using 1,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity per month would see the following increases: Duke Energy Carolinas (Charlotte, Durham, the Triad and much of western North Carolina): - January 2027: $6.53 more per month - January 2028: An additional $4.66 per month - Total monthly increase by 2028: $11.19 Duke Energy Progress (Raleigh, much of eastern North Carolina and the Asheville region): - January 2027: $9.62 more per month - January 2028: An additional $5.89 per month - Total monthly increase by 2028: $15.51 That amounts to approximately $134 to $186 in additional annual electricity costs by 2028 for a typical household, based on Duke's projections. Actual bill impacts will vary depending on electricity usage and other charges. Under the settlements, Duke would collect approximately $834 million in additional annual revenue across all customer classes by the second year of the rate plans. Regulators authorized a 9.8% return on equity for both utilities, down from Duke's initial request of 10.95%. That figure represents the authorized return on shareholder equity invested in the utility, not the percentage increase in customers' electricity bills. The rate plans include approximately $7.2 billion in capital investments over two years, along with a mechanism to refund customers for certain infrastructure projects that are delayed or canceled. Duke also agreed to contribute a combined $20 million in shareholder funds to support electricity bill assistance and home repairs that help low-income households access weatherization programs. Duke said it worked with customers and other stakeholders to reduce its initial rate increase requests while maintaining investments needed to strengthen the power grid and accommodate North Carolina's growth. “We listened to our customers and worked closely with stakeholders to find a more cost-effective way forward,” said Kendal Bowman, Duke Energy's North Carolina president, in a statement Tuesday. “This outcome keeps affordability at the forefront while allowing us to make the investments needed to strengthen reliability and support North Carolina's continued growth.” For some low-income customers, however, the financial impact could be significantly greater. A $42 monthly credit available to qualifying customers through Duke's Customer Assistance Program is scheduled to expire at the end of December, just as the new rates take effect. Brooks said some of the programs that Durham families have relied on for help with utility bills have lost funding. “I know I'm struggling, so I can imagine how the seniors are going to be struggling with a fixed income,” Brooks said. The commission directed Duke to submit revised revenue calculations within 10 days of its orders and updated rate schedules for approval within 30 days. New rules for data centers For the first time, regulators established a separate electricity rate schedule for large data centers with power demands of at least 50 megawatts. The decision comes as artificial intelligence and cloud computing drive unprecedented growth in electricity demand across the Carolinas. Between March 2024 and April 2026, Duke signed contracts to provide 6.7 gigawatts of electricity capacity to new large customers in North Carolina and South Carolina. Data centers account for 92% of that contracted demand, according to the commission. Meeting that demand will require billions of dollars in new power plants, transmission lines and other infrastructure. Regulators found that Duke's existing and proposed billing structures did not adequately address the financial risks associated with that expansion. artigo.texto: Geral COP31 propõe controle de emissões de data centers O crescente impacto ambiental dos data centers entrou na mira de um novo pacto global lançado durante a COP31, em Antália, na Turquia. Batizado de Compromisso de Antália sobre Inteligência Artificial e articulado pela presidência turca junto à União Internacional de Telecomunicações (UIT) e à Unesco, o acordo, anunciado nesta terça-feira (17), busca frear a pegada ecológica da infraestrutura digital, exigindo maior eficiência energética e hídrica dos centros de processamento de dados. Articulado pela presidência turca em parceria com a União Internacional de Telecomunicações (UIT) e a Unesco, o acordo conta com a adesão do Brasil e incentiva o uso de energias limpas, a eficiência no consumo de água e energia, a economia circular e o descarte adequado de lixo eletrônico nos centros de processamento de dados. Embora tenha caráter voluntário e não estabeleça metas obrigatórias de corte de emissões, o pacto prevê acompanhamento anual nas conferências do clima até 2030. Além do Brasil, oito países aderiram ao pacto, incluindo Coreia do Sul e a gigante chinesa Alibaba. Entretanto, o acordo enfrenta dúvidas sobre seu alcance prático por não ter atraído as principais big techs dos Estados Unidos, maiores operadoras globais dessa infraestrutura. A iniciativa incentiva ainda o uso da própria IA para soluções climáticas, como previsão de eventos extremos, prevê apoio tecnológico a países em desenvolvimento e inclui medidas de proteção aos trabalhadores diante da automação — ponto alinhado a ações brasileiras como o programa Computadores para Inclusão e a proposta de sediar o Instituto de Inteligência Artificial para Mudanças Climáticas (AICI). Brasil é o 4º país a apresentar novo relatório de transparência do Acordo de Paris Também nesta terça-feira (17), o Brasil tornou-se a quarta nação do mundo a cumprir a etapa das regras de prestação de contas do Acordo de Paris. O principal destaque do levantamento é a queda de 27% nas emissões nacionais de gases de efeito estufa entre 2022 e 2024, resultado extraído da série histórica analisada desde 1990. Coordenado pelo Ministério da Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação (MCTI) e aprovado pelo Comitê Interministerial sobre Mudança do Clima, o material integra dados científicos e resultados de políticas públicas em uma única publicação para dar mais agilidade aos processos. Além de detalhar o cumprimento das metas climáticas brasileiras, o relatório traz um diagnóstico sobre os riscos do aquecimento global e as estratégias de adaptação do país, reunindo também informações sobre educação ambiental, pesquisas científicas e as necessidades de financiamento e transferência de tecnologia. De acordo com a pasta, o documento, que foi submetido em inglês — idioma oficial da ONU —, terá em breve versão em português no portal do ministério e o conteúdo enviado passará pelo crivo de especialistas internacionais e por um fórum multilateral da convenção para revisão técnica. artigo.texto: Sutton residents continue ardent opposition to Kraft-backed data center At a packed planning board meeting in Sutton, Massachusetts, Monday night, residents were adamant in trying to convince the planning commission to shut down a Robert Kraft-backed data center proposal before it goes any further. The proposal from the Kraft Group and its Unified Global Packaging Group business involves building a massive data center on a former sand lot on the north side of Sutton. It would include 10 buildings and draw roughly 900 megawatts of power, which is enough to power a city. Residents said they are worried about that kind of drain on the power grid and on local water resources. They are also dreading the noise. "I'm frustrated that it's even being thought of as a possibility here," said Crystal Smith. Some residents are trying to fast-track an effort to shut the project down. Shawn Buzzell has launched a petition against the project. He already has signatures in the town of less than 10,000 residents. "I think that a development of a smaller scale might be something that the town would entertain," Buzzell said. "Just not in this fashion and not on this scale." The planning board meeting comes on the heels of a Select Board meeting that generated staunch opposition and public outcry over the project. "We are governing backwards. Right now as a town— we are taking steps out of order; we haven't done the proper action in the past to address this issue before a proposal like this arrived on our doorstep with a big red bow," said Sarah Osterman Stone. The planning board said Monday night that it's in no hurry and said they would not rule out a 1-year moratorium on data centers while they explore adding a bylaw. Like many towns, Sutton is facing a budget deficit, and the town select board says it's their responsibility to at least consider investments that would cover the gap and lower property taxes, posting a statement on the town website that reads in part: "Considering an opportunity is not the same as supporting it," the town said. "Our obligation is to understand it fully: its potential benefits, its potential costs, and its potential impacts. Only with that understanding can the Town, and ultimately Town Meeting, make an informed decision." The Kraft Group also released a statement, saying that it's always looking for meaningful, long-term economic investments: "We are committed to working collaboratively with local officials, residents and other stakeholders as the planning process moves forward to pursue a responsible development that delivers lasting benefits to the community. Most importantly, this project will only move forward if the community and the town of Sutton want it."

artigo.texto: It's not just the U.S., the movement against data centers is global It’s not just the U.S., the movement against data centers is global Activists protesting data centers in their backyards are teaming up to learn tactics from allies around the world. "We are coordinated and we are together," said one Spanish activist. STEVE INSKEEP, HOST: The opposition to data centers that American voters expressed in the midterms is a worldwide phenomenon. Voters around the U.S. have made it harder for communities to build big projects tied to artificial intelligence. And in other countries, local groups are joining forces to slow the AI buildout. NPR's Ruth Sherlock reports. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) UNIDENTIFIED DEMONSTRATORS: (Chanting in Spanish). RUTH SHERLOCK, BYLINE: In Zaragoza in northeastern Spain, demonstrators fill an avenue. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) UNIDENTIFIED DEMONSTRATORS: (Chanting in Spanish). SHERLOCK: They're protesting against a data center Microsoft wants to build beside a much-loved local forest. MONICA GRACIA: AI is causing a lot of problems. SHERLOCK: Monica Gracia says she was inspired to join by the loud opposition to data centers in the United States. GRACIA: I think that's one of the reasons why this place is so full of people. SHERLOCK: While many environmental problems are local, most of the push to build data centers around the world comes from U.S. tech giants. So opponents who are fighting their construction are teaming up, says Spanish activist Aurora Gomez. She founded Tu Nube Seca Mi Rio - Your Cloud Dries My River. AURORA GOMEZ: We have connection with, of course, USA, Africa, Australia and even some parts of Asia. We are coordinated, and we are together. SHERLOCK: She says Spanish groups were inspired by activists in the U.K. to crowdfund money for legal bills. LUIS GARCIA: We are exercising our rights. SHERLOCK: Luis Garcia is from Ecologistas en Accion. He's part of a court case to stop his local government from allowing a giant expansion of Amazon data centers. GARCIA: We know they have way more means than we do. But the crowdfunding proves we have gathered a lot of support from so many people - individuals, organizations. SHERLOCK: There's evidence these tactics are working. The European Data Centre Monitor that tracks this opposition says more than 70 European projects were rejected or restricted in the first four months of this year alone. UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: (Speaking Spanish). SHERLOCK: This movement is both global and hyperlocal. In the main square of the tiny village of Quart on the rural plains of Spain's Aragon region, colorful bunting flaps in the wind from a recent celebration by the town's tight-knit community. (SOUNDBITE OF BUNTING FLAPPING) SHERLOCK: Also strung up on the wall here is a giant banner - we drink water, not data centers. CARLOS OLIVAN: (Speaking Spanish). SHERLOCK: It's a slogan to protest a giant data center being built at the edge of the village. Resident Carlos Olivan describes it as a seven-headed monster. OLIVAN: (Speaking Spanish). SHERLOCK: So Olivan and the villages are getting organized. OLIVAN: (Speaking Spanish). SHERLOCK: "We're trying in a very small group to make visible the scale of what's happening so people understand, empathize and mobilize," says Olivan. They began with a referendum in the village. OLIVAN: (Speaking Spanish). SHERLOCK: "Ninety-five percent of people were against this," he says. They'll use the referendum results to pressure authorities to try to stop the project. (SOUNDBITE OF CONSTRUCTION WORK) SHERLOCK: Laura Cosculluela says she got involved in the opposition after seeing what happened in other countries. LAURA COSCULLUELA: We have a lot of data from the U.S., especially, which is the place where it's been going on for longer and where there are more data centers, so it's the most reliable source. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) UNIDENTIFIED ANNOUNCER: (Speaking Spanish). SHERLOCK: Back at the protest in downtown Zaragoza in Aragon, local activist Maria Pena Calvo says action matters even if it feels small. MARIA PENA CALVO: (Speaking Spanish). SHERLOCK: "Because putting sticks in the wheels, putting stones in their path, can make some companies simply give up or go elsewhere. It's down to citizens," Pena Calvo says, "to defend every inch of their land." Ruth Sherlock, NPR News, Zaragoza, Spain. (SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. UNYX 09 Now that we have covered October 2026 wholesales, let’s focus on the latest launches on the Chinese market. After a record 19 in September, we have 11 new entrants in October, 8 of them Chinese. To fully understand the scope of the Chinese market, make sure you consult our Exclusive Guide to all 161 active Chinese Brands. 1. Lynk & Co 20 (5,082 sales) The Lynk & Co 20 (领克 20)—formerly marketed as the Lynk & Co Z20 prior to its September 2026 refresh and renaming—is the brand’s all-electric (coupe crossover SUV. Built on Geely’s Sustainable Experience Architecture (SEA2), the updated 2026 model introduces an 800V high-voltage platform with 6C ultra-fast charging, standard LiDAR hardware, and a significantly expanded front storage area. The 20 follows “The Next Day” second-generation design language, featuring a closed front fascia, signature claw-style LED daytime running lights, and an aerodynamic drag coefficient of 0.25 Cd. It is equipped with frameless doors and side mirrors, hidden rain gutters, a full-width rear LED light bar integrated into the rear spoiler. The 20 comes at 4,495 mm long, 1,845 mm wide and 1,573 mm high with a 2,755 mm wheelbase. Inside, the 20 is driven by the Flyme Auto cockpit ecosystem (with the Super Eva AI voice assistant) across a 15.4-inch 2.5K floating central touchscreen, a 10.2-inch digital instrument cluster and a 13.8-inch head-up display. It is built on an 800V high-voltage architecture with single-motor Rear-Wheel Drive (RWD) configurations using Geely’s Aegis Golden Brick LFP batteries. It comes either as a 61.52 kWh battery for 545 km of CLTC range or a 70.01 kWh for 630 km of range. Promotional launch price stands between 118,800 and 158,800 yuan (16,200-21,600€ or US$17,800-23,800) and competes with the likes of the Zeekr X, Smart #1, BYD Yuan Plus (Atto 3) and Geely Galaxy E5. The 20 received 14,663 orders within 1 hour of market launch and registered over 5,000 units in October. The Z20 peaked at 6,368 sales in January 2025 for its 2nd month in market, so we’d want the same to consider the 20 as a success. Bar for success: 6,500 monthly sales 2. VW ID.ERA 8X (3,500 sales) The ID. ERA 8X is a mid-to-large 5-seat extended-range electric vehicle (EREV) SUV. Positioned directly below the 6-seat ID. The exterior design is anchored by a full-width “Universal Light Wing” LED strip, L-shaped daytime running lights, and “six-core high-energy” matrix headlights with dynamic welcome animations. Includes flush aerodynamic door handles, a full-width rear light bar and a roof-mounted LiDAR sensor. It comes at 5,020 mm long, 1,997 mm wide and 1,750 high with a 2,970 wheelbase. The cockpit is equipped with the “Yunqi” smart cockpit powered by a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8295P chip and VW OS. It features dual high-definition screens for the driver and front passenger, an industry-first “Smart Surface” magic screen, and a windshield head-up display. It is standard equipped across all trims with a 192-line roof LiDAR (part of a 26-sensor suite) running the Momenta R7 World Model for Highway NOA, Urban NOA, and end-to-end automated parking. The ID.ERA 8X is available in a choice of single-motor RWD with a 51.1 kWh battery for 373 km of CLTC pure electric range and 1,567 km combined range and dual-motor with a 451 km CLTC pure electric range and 1,602 km of combined range. AURA T6 has been truly successful, selling 12,032 units in October. The want the ID.ERA 8X to reach at least half that amount to be successful. Bar for success: 7,500 monthly sales 3. It pushes the brand into the ultra-long-range luxury sedan segment at an aggressive price point. The Great Han features an ultra-low drag coefficient of 0.197 Cd. It comes at 5,256 mm long, 1,999 mm wide and 1,510 high with a 3,130 mm wheelbase. The Great Han features a three-screen dashboard anchored by a high-resolution 3K central touchscreen, paired with real-wood trim, Nappa leather upholstery and a 31-speaker surround-sound audio system. There are also electrochromic dimming rear windows. artigo.texto: Resumo - Data centers nos EUA oferecem vagas com salários acima de US$ 100 mil por ano - Faltam técnicos para refrigeração, racks, parte elétrica e fibra óptica - Treinamentos de dois dias já terminam com cerimônia de diploma - Amazon, Google, Meta e Microsoft oferecem cursos gratuitos e acelerados - Falta de mão de obra supera qualquer freio na construção civil do setor - Muitos americanos nem sabem que esses empregos existem Nos Estados Unidos, a construção da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial criou um gargalo inesperado: faltam técnicos. Na disputa por profissionais, empresas de tecnologia já oferecem vagas com remuneração acima de US$ 100 mil por ano. E parte dessas contratações recai sobre pessoas que acabaram de concluir cursos relâmpago. A trajetória pode ser rápida: bastam dois dias de formação para que os alunos recebam seus diplomas numa solenidade. Mal o certificado fica pronto e as companhias, sedentas por mão de obra, já brigam pelos novos profissionais. Por que faltam técnicos Para dar conta da demanda disparada pela tecnologia, as companhias precisam de gente capaz de montar os sistemas de refrigeração, instalar racks de servidores, lidar com equipamentos elétricos e puxar os cabos de fibra óptica que sustentam os data centers. O problema é que encontrar profissionais com essas habilidades virou um desafio. Ainda que o ambiente político em torno da IA venha se transformando, sobretudo após as últimas eleições de meio de mandato, a falta de trabalhadores pesa mais do que qualquer eventual desaceleração nas obras. Diante disso, o setor vem se organizando para formar e contratar quem possa preencher essas vagas. Cursos gratuitos e salários de seis dígitos Diferentes origens respondem pela qualificação desses trabalhadores. Para capacitar nas habilidades técnicas que a edificação de data centers requer, cursos rápidos e sem custo são oferecidos por entidades sem fins lucrativos, por plataformas de ensino digital e pelas quatro gigantes da nuvem com inteligência artificial: Amazon, Google, Meta e Microsoft. Há posições nesse setor cuja remuneração chega à casa dos seis dígitos. Mesmo assim, a maioria dos americanos nem imagina que empregos assim estejam disponíveis. Javonntae Hill é um exemplo de quem entrou nesse universo. Formado em design de videogames e na casa dos 30 anos, ele procurava uma carreira, mas não tinha clareza de por onde começar.

artigo.texto: Public Pushback Complicates Data Center Buildouts Developers face closer scrutiny of utility costs, water use, and local benefits as community concerns complicate approvals and investment decisions. Public concern over electricity costs, water demand, and neighborhood impacts is pushing data center development toward tighter restrictions, including in states where leaders previously welcomed the investment. The shift is forcing developers to reassess whether expected permits, tax benefits, and utility arrangements will survive rising community resistance. In Pennsylvania, gubernatorial candidate Stacy Garrity initially praised Amazon’s $20 billion data center investment and urged the state to attract more projects before backing a pause on new development and stronger requirements. Gov. Josh Shapiro also moved from promoting investment and faster permitting to supporting stricter environmental standards and transparency requirements, according to Spotlight PA. Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley reversed his opposition to a moratorium during the campaign and ultimately backed a pause while supporting the elimination of the industry’s state sales tax exemption. After the election, he said he was considering requirements around resource-use disclosures, community support, and protections against shifting energy costs onto residents, according to an Associated Press report. If those exemptions disappear, developers could face higher equipment costs, larger bills for power infrastructure, and construction delays while new approval requirements take shape. November’s local ballot measures added to the pressure, with voters in multiple communities backing new restrictions on data center development. For developers, the immediate questions center on zoning decisions, utility agreements, and environmental approvals that could reshape both project timelines and costs. Sreenivas Duvvuri Venkata, research analyst for services at IDC, said developers now need to reassess which projects can realistically move forward. “Community acceptance has become material to timely execution of data center projects, alongside power availability, interconnection timelines, and environmental permits,” he told Data Center Knowledge. Venkata said builders should prioritize projects based on the constraints still to be resolved, not just on cost and capacity. Data center projects that broke ground between the third quarter of 2025 and the third quarter of 2026 waited an average of just over two years from announcement to construction, up from about 18 months for projects launched between early 2020 and mid-2025, according to GlobalData. Permits, Tariffs, and Grid Upgrades Can Reshape Project Timelines Different authorities control different parts of a project’s viability. Venkata pointed to state environmental permits and incentive agreements, utility commission decisions on tariffs and cost allocation, and local rezoning and conditional-use approvals as distinct exposure points. That means a project with land secured may still face unresolved questions about who will pay for grid upgrades or whether its planned generation equipment can operate as proposed. Developers need to map those decisions against procurement and construction commitments before locking in schedules. Alston Mason, president of energy solutions at Oldcastle Infrastructure, told Data Center Knowledge that on-site generation can introduce another permitting process. “They can have the power plan figured out and still be waiting on environmental permits for the equipment,” Mason said. “If that review takes longer, the project team has to evaluate what work can move forward in the meantime and adjust sequencing as more information becomes available.” Schedule changes also have to account for suppliers serving multiple markets. Recent Data Center Knowledge coverage of construction labor shortages highlighted the strain on specialized crews, reinforcing the need to align approvals with labor availability and equipment delivery capacity. “When you’re evaluating a site, the question is whether suppliers have the capacity to [deliver] the right components when construction timelines demand them,” Mason said. Developers Face Pressure to Put Commitments in Writing Residents want to know what a facility will require before construction begins, including where its water will come from and whether households could end up bearing higher electricity costs. Labor shortages and supplier constraints can further complicate scheduling, making it important to involve energy and water partners while designs are still flexible enough to address community concerns, Mason said. “If the developer is funding infrastructure upgrades that serve residents, like neighborhood roads and connectivity, people want to know what’s planned, who will benefit, and when,” he said. Publishing those commitments alongside power and water plans gives residents a way to track delivery and forces developers to reflect those promises in the project’s economics. “Enforceable commitments are key to winning approval,” Venkata said. Venkata said developers may face conditions that include full responsibility for utility costs, renewable energy requirements, closed-loop cooling, and limits tying projects to designated industrial sites. Reduced tax benefits, higher power costs, and long-term payment obligations can affect viability just as much as approval delays. Moving to another market does not eliminate those pressures. Developers still need to determine whether infrastructure, suppliers, and permitting schedules support the target opening date rather than assuming a more welcoming location is immediately buildable. “For an individual site, it still comes down to land, power, and water,” Mason said. “All three have to be available on a timeline the project can work with.”

artigo.texto: Economia Brasil pode contestar restrições dos EUA à venda de chips para data centers O governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva está considerando a possibilidade de questionar as novas limitações impostas pelos Estados Unidos sobre a comercialização de chips avançados de inteligência artificial destinados a data centers no Brasil. Essa medida, anunciada nesta segunda-feira, colocou o Brasil entre cinco países que precisarão de autorização do governo americano para importar esses componentes, utilizados em grandes centros de processamento de dados. Fontes próximas ao governo dizem que uma possível negociação com os EUA ou contestação das regras ainda está em aberto. Por enquanto, o tema não gerou grande preocupação dentro do Executivo, e não há uma decisão tomada sobre eventuais respostas à decisão dos americanos. Os Estados Unidos detêm um controle significativo sobre a fabricação e distribuição desses chips, que são essenciais para o funcionamento de sistemas avançados de inteligência artificial, o que lhes confere forte influência sobre o comércio internacional desse mercado. Os data centers são locais que reúnem servidores e equipamentos responsáveis por armazenar e processar grandes quantidades de informações. Com o avanço da inteligência artificial, esses centros passaram a exigir chips mais potentes, capazes de realizar os cálculos necessários para desenvolver e operar essas tecnologias. A nova regulamentação foi divulgada pelo Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos e também inclui Indonésia, Malásia, Cingapura e Tailândia. O objetivo é evitar que empresas chinesas acessem tecnologia americana por meio de centros de dados instalados em outros países, burlando as restrições já impostas por Washington. Desde 2022, os EUA limitam a venda de chips avançados para a China, exigindo autorização para a exportação de certos componentes e equipamentos usados na fabricação desses chips. Em 2023, as regras foram reforçadas e agora abrangem novas exigências para países que o governo americano considera mais vulneráveis ao uso indevido dessas tecnologias. Membros do governo brasileiro apontam que anteriormente houve preocupação com a possível escassez de chips no mercado global, devido ao aumento da demanda por equipamentos para inteligência artificial, mas essa preocupação foi superada. Segundo as novas regras, as empresas afetadas terão que obter licenças do governo dos EUA para importar determinados chips avançados. A regulamentação prevê exceções para empresas baseadas nos Estados Unidos, desde que cumpram os requisitos de fornecimento de informações, e determina que os pedidos de autorização serão analisados caso a caso pelas autoridades americanas.

artigo.texto: Hitachi Energy fecha primeiro contrato de IA para energia de data center no Brasil Acordo com a BCR-i prevê manutenção preditiva em subestação de 560 MVA que atende data center no estado de São Paulo. A Hitachi Energy assinou seu primeiro contrato HMAX Energy no Brasil com a BCR-i Brasil para implementar um sistema de monitoramento e manutenção preditiva em uma subestação de 560 MVA que atende um data center no estado de São Paulo. O acordo prevê o uso de IA para analisar as condições dos equipamentos elétricos e identificar riscos de falhas operacionais. A solução combina informações coletadas dos ativos elétricos, monitoramento em tempo quase real e modelos analíticos para orientar intervenções técnicas. Segundo a Hitachi Energy, o serviço busca substituir parte das rotinas de manutenção baseadas em intervalos predeterminados por procedimentos orientados pelas condições dos equipamentos. Subestação atende infraestrutura digital A instalação é operada pela BCR-i Brasil, grupo especializado em gestão de infraestrutura e serviços técnicos, e a capacidade de 560 MVA corresponde à potência aparente da subestação. Raphael Campos, Head de Operação e Manutenção da BCR-i Brasil, afirma que o contrato permitirá integrar os serviços de operação elétrica da companhia às ferramentas de análise de dados fornecidas pela Hitachi Energy. “Garantir a máxima confiabilidade no fornecimento de energia é fundamental para atender a setores que exigem alta disponibilidade, como os data centers”, afirma o executivo. A Hitachi Energy ficará responsável pelo fornecimento do HMAX Energy, que reúne serviços de acompanhamento técnico e ferramentas de IA aplicadas à gestão dos ativos durante seu ciclo de vida. “Os data centers estão no centro da era da IA e operam com a expectativa de 100% de disponibilidade. Isso exige uma transformação na forma como a infraestrutura energética é gerenciada, incorporando mais inteligência, capacidade de antecipação e integração”, diz Fernanda Alves, gerente do Service Hub para a América Latina na Hitachi Energy. Expansão pressiona demanda por energia O acordo ocorre em meio ao crescimento da infraestrutura de processamento e armazenamento de dados no Brasil, associado à expansão da computação em nuvem e das aplicações de IA. Segundo projeções da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) citadas pelas empresas, o consumo de eletricidade no Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) deverá crescer 4% ao ano até 2030, quando a carga elétrica total poderá atingir 98,8 GW. A expansão dos data centers é apontada como um dos fatores de aumento da demanda. A continuidade do fornecimento elétrico é um requisito operacional dessas instalações, que dependem de energia para servidores, sistemas de armazenamento, equipamentos de rede e refrigeração. Nesse contexto, o modelo contratado pela BCR-i busca identificar alterações no desempenho dos componentes elétricos antes que provoquem interrupções nos serviços. (Com assessoria de imprensa)

artigo.texto: New Delhi/Mumbai: The Maharashtra Government on Tuesday announced the country's first sulphur dioxide (SO2) emissions trading scheme to improve air quality. The scheme will be implemented by the Maharashtra Pollution Control Board (MPCB) in collaboration with Emissions Market Accelerator, Environment and Climate Change Minister Pankaja Munde said. Speaking at an event in Mumbai, Munde said the government wanted to develop, in collaboration with industries, solutions that balance environmental protection with economic development. Under the emissions trading scheme, participating industrial units will be given permits specifying their permissible sulphur dioxide emissions. Industries that can reduce emissions at a lower cost will be able to make additional reductions and sell their surplus permits, while those facing higher costs of emission reduction can purchase them, an official release said. Michael Greenstone, professor of economics at the University of Chicago, director of the Energy Policy Institute and co-chair of Emissions Market Accelerator, said research had shown that market-based schemes could achieve effective emission reductions while lowering the cost of pollution control for industries. The MPCB and the University of Chicago Trust also signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to use artificial intelligence and machine learning in environmental regulation and industrial inspections. The initiative will be implemented through the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago India. Under the agreement, the two institutions will jointly develop and pilot an AI-based framework for environmental inspections. The system will analyse data available with the MPCB to identify industrial units that are more likely to violate environmental regulations, the release said. Training programmes will also be organised for MPCB officials and field inspectors on AI, environmental data analysis and the use of modern technologies. A decision on expanding the system across Maharashtra will be taken based on the findings of the pilot project. artigo.texto: Demand for electricity to power data centers is hindering the state’s plans to reduce pollution and fight climate change. Under an ambitious law signed by Gov. JB Pritzker in 2021, the state set out to retire all fossil-fuel power plants between now and 2050. Stream NBC 5 for free, 24/7, wherever you are. But big new data centers are requiring so much electricity that it’s become difficult for the state to shut down all coal, gas and oil sources used to meet demand, a pair of state reports released Monday found. The reports confirmed fears that environmental and climate advocates have had for more than a year. Cleaner sources of power, including wind and solar farms, are not being built quickly enough to keep up with the new demands from the data centers being used to power artificial intelligence. That’s bad news for the planet because oil, gas and coal create carbon dioxide, the major contributor to global warming. The same pollution causing climate change is also bad for our health, causing respiratory problems and exacerbating a number of other threats. “Fossil fuel power plants emit thousands of tons of lung-damaging chemicals,” said Brian Urbaszewski, director of environmental health at Respiratory Health Association in Chicago. “These are chemicals that have an immediate and harmful effect on people.” In central and southern Illinois, seven coal plants still operate. The goal has been to shut four of them down by 2030 and that goal remains, according to one of the two reports. Three publicly owned coal-fired plants have longer timelines before they are closed. Local Eleven so-called peaker plants, which burn oil or natural gas as power backups, were expected to close in 2030 or 2031. But power demands from data centers mean those plants should continue to operate until 2033 to help prevent blackouts, the report recommends. Those peaker plants are limited-use, oil-fueled or gas-power sources shut down for most days in any given year, but are designed to guard against blackouts and can be fired up when energy use is peaking, like on the hottest day of the year, when many air conditioners are running. In Chicago, peakers are still active at the long-closed Fisk coal-fired power plant in Pilsen. There are also peakers in Waukegan, where a former coal plant that has operated for more than 90 years will keep operating until 2033 under the state recommendation. “That’s disappointing,” said Mayra Mendez, executive director of Clean Power Lake County. She said the Waukegan peakers produce strong smells that cause a burning sensation in the nose. “Our community is tired of dirty energy.” Some advocates feared the state would recommend building new natural gas plants but that is not being advised, state officials said. The state will continue to rely on nuclear power and upgrades to plants in hopes of producing more energy which is free of carbon dioxide, according to the reports. Enough power for now Illinois is not running out of power yet but the forecast for data centers is so large, and the operations potentially being built so quickly, the situation could create an emergency to provide more electricity. Each new hyperscale data center can require enough electricity to power a mid-sized city. State lawmakers in Springfield are expected to debate the impact of data centers and power demand, possibly next month. Hearings on the state findings are expected later. The reports are the Resource Adequacy Mitigation Plan released by the Illinois Power Agency and the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency and the Integrated Resource Plan, released by the Illinois Commerce Commission.

artigo.texto: Criticism of data centers is less about the physical building infrastructure and more about the public’s broad concerns about artificial intelligence and tech companies, according to several University of Virginia studies. Maura Austin, a research scientist at the University of Virginia’s National Security Institute, said that as data center pushback has intensified over the last few months, it’s largely been bipartisan. But, Austin said, people are thinking about data centers “as combined with their thoughts on AI, and they are harboring a strong distrust for the federal government and for Big Tech as well. And those feelings of distrust translate into an uneasiness about the future and about the economic instability that they believe is being wrought by AI and the developments there, and they’re taking out that unease in their resistance to data centers.” Broadly, Austin said, many people have a negative feeling about data centers but can’t explain why. As a result, they point to the physical buildings. There are hundreds of data centers across Northern Virginia, and many are in Loudoun County. In some cases, local governments are working to change the way data center projects are approved, in an effort to slow their growth. Generally, Austin said, residents who live close to new data center projects don’t envision benefits locally. “They don’t expect data centers to bring jobs,” Austin said. “They don’t expect to experience any more benefits from AI by having a data center close by, which makes sense. I don’t think that you get faster access to AI models just because you have a data center down the street.” There are concerns about noise, water usage and data centers driving up energy bills, Austin said, which means data centers are “occupying this particularly tricky space, where they are not bringing any known benefits to the local community, and they are bringing a lot of expectations for costs and burdens.” Some tech companies, Austin said, are working to make water use more transparent or taking responsibility for energy infrastructure and announcing they’ll absorb the costs. But, based on the studies’ findings, “What people are looking for is to feel more secure in their economic futures,” she said. Spending on proenvironmental efforts, local libraries or schools, or direct payments to households would all increase support for data center projects, Austin said the research found. Direct payments to households were the best-performing initiative to increase the public’s support for data centers. “We’re relying on the acceptance of the people in these communities in order to continue this critical infrastructure build-out, and the way forward is to meet the people at the negotiations table, and that means listening to their concerns and listening to their needs,” Austin said. artigo.texto: EUA fecham a brecha do acesso remoto: data centers no exterior precisarão de licença para servir a China O Departamento de Comércio publicou nesta segunda (16) uma regra provisória que exige licença sempre que um data center, em qualquer país, fornecer mais de 12 milhões de TPP a empresas sediadas na China, Macau e outros destinos restritos. O Brasil entra numa lista separada de cinco países. O Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos publicou nesta segunda-feira, 16 de novembro de 2026, uma regra provisória — uma *interim final rule* — desenhada para impedir que empresas chinesas tenham acesso a chips avançados de inteligência artificial por via remota. O alvo é uma brecha conhecida: em vez de comprar ou receber fisicamente o equipamento, a empresa aluga capacidade computacional em data centers fora dos Estados Unidos, inclusive em países que não estão sujeitos às mesmas restrições. Abaixo, o que exatamente a regra exige, os dois mecanismos que ela cria — o limite de capacidade computacional e a lista de cinco países que inclui o Brasil —, o que fica de fora, o que acontece a partir de agora e por que o anúncio cai justamente na semana em que Xi e Trump se encontram. 1 · O que foi publicado, em resumo Ponto de atenção — a regra não proíbe chips nem data centers. Ela cria uma etapa burocrática: a licença. Quem precisa dela é quem exporta, reexporta ou transfere o equipamento sabendo que ele alimentará um data center que dará volume relevante de computação a empresas de um grupo restrito. Sem licença, a operação não pode acontecer — e a análise é caso a caso, não automática. 2 · Como a brecha funcionava A lógica é simples e foi explicada por praticamente toda a cobertura. Os Estados Unidos já impediam que empresas chinesas comprassem os chips de IA mais avançados — aqueles fabricados por companhias como a Nvidia — e que os recebessem em território chinês. O que não estava igualmente controlado era o caminho indireto: uma empresa chinesa pode contratar, em Singapura ou na Malásia, o uso de um data center equipado com esses mesmos chips americanos. Nada é exportado para a China; só a capacidade de computação é acessada por rede. A formulação do próprio BIS, no comunicado que acompanha a regra, é esta: “A regra foi desenhada para garantir que as restrições existentes ao acesso à tecnologia americana sensível não possam ser contornadas por meio de arranjos de computação remota envolvendo data centers em países terceiros.” O que dá nome ao problema é o volume. Vinte mil chips em um data center estrangeiro não mudam nada; um data center configurado para servir grandes volumes de computação a um único cliente chinês, sim. É essa diferença de escala que a regra tenta capturar com um limite numérico, em vez de tentar controlar toda operação de nuvem. 3 · O primeiro mecanismo: o limite de 12 milhões de TPP O coração da regra é um número. A unidade de medida é o TPP — *total processing performance*, a métrica que o controle de exportação americano usa para medir a potência de um chip de computação avançada. A partir de agora, quando o exportador sabe que o equipamento irá para um data center que fornecerá mais de 12 milhões de TPP agregados a uma empresa restrita, a licença é obrigatória. Alguns pontos importantes sobre como esse limite funciona: · O cálculo é agregado: soma a capacidade dos chips, e não a de um chip isolado. · A soma vale para um data center ou para data centers interligados, que compartilhem recursos como um sistema único — o que impede a fragmentação artificial do volume entre instalações. · Quem é alcançado pela regra: empresas sediadas na China, em Macau ou em países do chamado Grupo D:5, e também empresas cujo controlador final tenha sede nesses lugares. · A regra alcança o acesso indireto: um cliente que esteja fora do grupo restrito entra no escopo quando treina modelos para uma empresa alcançada, participa desse treinamento ou fornece modelos a ela. A comparação que ajuda a dimensionar o limite: 12 milhões de TPP correspondem, aproximadamente, à capacidade máxima de cerca de 750 chips Nvidia H100 ou H200. Não é um limiar baixo — é um volume de cluster, e não o uso individual de nuvem. 4 · O segundo mecanismo: a lista de cinco países A regra tem uma segunda parte, independente da primeira. Ela passa a exigir licença para exportar, reexportar ou transferir semicondutores avançados cobertos pelo controle com destino a cinco países: A justificativa oficial é que esses países “apresentam risco de desvio acima do normal”. Para os três primeiros — Indonésia, Malásia e Singapura —, há um motivo específico: são os três centros da rede da Megaspeed, a empresa que estaria comprando milhares de chips da Nvidia para fornecer capacidade computacional a empresas chinesas e, com isso, contornar as restrições já existentes. Há uma exceção relevante nessa parte da regra: a exigência de licença não se aplica a chips destinados a empresas sediadas nos Estados Unidos ou cujo controlador final tenha sede americana, desde que cumpridos os requisitos de relatório periódico. É importante não confundir essa exceção com o controle de uso final da seção anterior: são dois mecanismos distintos, com escopos distintos. 5 · O que fica de fora A regra exclui explicitamente um caso, e a definição dessa exceção é reveladora. Ficam fora da proibição os usos de acesso computacional dedicados exclusivamente a **sistemas comerciais de recomendação** — aqueles que ordenam, filtram ou sugerem produtos, serviços ou conteúdo —, sujeitos a condições de relatório. A definição, porém, fecha a porta logo em seguida: a exceção não alcança sistemas projetados ou usados para **gerar** novo texto, imagens, áudio, vídeo, software ou outro conteúdo, mesmo que também tenham função de recomendação. Em outras palavras: a regra deixa de fora o motor de recomendação de uma loja ou de uma rede social e mantém dentro o treinamento e a operação de modelos generativos. artigo.texto: St. Cloud rejects new rules for data centers, moves closer to moratorium Go Deeper. Create an account or log in to save stories. Like this? Thanks for liking this story! We have added it to a list of your favorite stories. Quick Read The St. Cloud City Council rejected new rules for data centers after a lengthy public hearing Monday night. Instead, the council voted 4-3 to consider a one-year moratorium on new data centers after getting more public input next month. The policy would have changed St. Cloud’s comprehensive plan to make clear that the city is open to considering new data centers, but only in certain locations and with regulations to protect residents from negative effects. The proposed regulations would have separated smaller data centers from hyperscale facilities — those with at least 2,000 computer servers housed in buildings larger than 10,000 square feet, or that use at least 50 megawatts of electricity. Turn Up Your Support MPR News helps you turn down the noise and build shared understanding. Turn up your support for this public resource and keep trusted journalism accessible to all. Hyperscale data centers could only be located in the city's industrial district, at least a quarter mile from residential areas, and would require a conditional use permit. Data center developers also would have to study noise, vibration, environmental and community impacts. They would also be required to incorporate sustainability measures, including water conservation and renewable energy. Those proposed regulations will be set aside, at least for now. Instead, the City Council plans to set a public hearing and possible vote on a moratorium for Dec. 21. Council member Mark Johnson voted in favor of the moratorium, saying the city should take a go-slow approach. “It's still new overall, and I do think within a year we're going to hear a lot from data centers already in existence,” Johnson said. “And if it's all worked wonderful, OK. We may not be the first ones to have one in our area, but we will know it's been proven, tested.” Weighing the pros and cons of data centers A crowd packed the city council chambers for the public hearing, and nearly two dozen people spoke against allowing data centers. Many raised concerns about their potential noise, water consumption and energy use, as well as the rapid rise of artificial intelligence. Resident Susan Lau told the council that allowing data centers could harm the quality of life in St. Cloud in the future. “What we do will impact our environment and our children and their children,” she said. “It might not still be the data center, because it might be long gone by then. But maybe we could invest in something that would be more beneficial down the road.” St. Cloud has some smaller data centers but has not received any formal development proposals for the hypersized facilities that have generated controversy in other Minnesota communities. But St. Cloud does have features that are attractive to large data center developers, including ample water and electricity, large tracts of land, industrial buildings and an available workforce, said Matt Glaesman, the city’s community development director. Council member Tami Calhoun voted for the moratorium after initially supporting the policy. She said she shares some of the same concerns as residents, but supports a policy that builds in guardrails and would communicate the city’s criteria in advance. “It says, ‘We have these very high expectations before you come in here, because we want to protect our city and we want to protect our residents,’” Calhoun said. Some council members voted against the moratorium, citing potential benefits of data centers, including jobs and tax revenue. Council member Dave Masters said he thinks the city “can’t be afraid of the future.” “Technology moves very quickly,” Masters said. “By putting in these moratoriums, I feel like it is a way that we’re going to put our heads in the sand and stand back and let progress go ahead.”

artigo.texto: Demand for electricity to power data centers is hindering the state’s plans to reduce pollution and fight climate change. Under an ambitious law signed by Gov. JB Pritzker in 2021, the state set out to retire all fossil-fuel power plants between now and 2050. But big new data centers are requiring so much electricity that it’s become difficult for the state to shut down all coal, gas and oil sources used to meet demand, a pair of state reports released Monday found. The reports confirmed fears that environmental and climate advocates have had for more than a year. Cleaner sources of power, including wind and solar farms, are not being built quickly enough to keep up with the new demands from the data centers being used to power artificial intelligence. That’s bad news for the planet because oil, gas and coal create carbon dioxide, the major contributor to global warming. The same pollution causing climate change is also bad for our health, causing respiratory problems and exacerbating a number of other threats. “Fossil fuel power plants emit thousands of tons of lung-damaging chemicals,” said Brian Urbaszewski, director of environmental health at Respiratory Health Association in Chicago. “These are chemicals that have an immediate and harmful effect on people.” In central and southern Illinois, seven coal plants still operate. The goal has been to shut four of them down by 2030 and that goal remains, according to one of the two reports. Three publicly owned coal-fired plants have longer timelines before they are closed. Eleven so-called peaker plants, which burn oil or natural gas as power backups, were expected to close in 2030 or 2031. But power demands from data centers mean those plants should continue to operate until 2033 to help prevent blackouts, the report recommends. Those peaker plants are limited-use, oil-fueled or gas-power sources shut down for most days in any given year, but are designed to guard against blackouts and can be fired up when energy use is peaking, like on the hottest day of the year, when many air conditioners are running. In Chicago, peakers are still active at the long-closed Fisk coal-fired power plant in Pilsen. There are also peakers in Waukegan, where a former coal plant that has operated for more than 90 years will keep operating until 2033 under the state recommendation. “That’s disappointing,” said Mayra Mendez, executive director of Clean Power Lake County. She said the Waukegan peakers produce strong smells that cause a burning sensation in the nose. “Our community is tired of dirty energy.” Some advocates feared the state would recommend building new natural gas plants but that is not being advised, state officials said. The state will continue to rely on nuclear power and upgrades to plants in hopes of producing more energy which is free of carbon dioxide, according to the reports. Enough power for now Illinois is not running out of power yet but the forecast for data centers is so large, and the operations potentially being built so quickly, the situation could create an emergency to provide more electricity. Each new hyperscale data center can require enough electricity to power a mid-sized city. State lawmakers in Springfield are expected to debate the impact of data centers and power demand, possibly next month. Hearings on the state findings are expected later. The reports are the Resource Adequacy Mitigation Plan released by the Illinois Power Agency and the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency and the Integrated Resource Plan, released by the Illinois Commerce Commission. artigo.texto: New York Must Get Its Review of Data Centers Right. Here’s How. NY Public Service Commission must rigorously evaluate data center development during pause A dam is poised to break in New York. Nearly 12 gigawatts of proposed AI data center development (enough to power TWO New York City’s) could soon overwhelm our electricity system, flooding it with new demand for electricity, driving up energy costs, and threatening achievement of New York’s climate and environmental justice laws. The only thing holding the flood back right now is an Executive Order (EO 62) that Governor Hochul issued in July, which paused development of data centers with a capacity of 50 megawatts (MW) or greater. Communities in other states with prolific AI center buildout have decried the broad spectrum of harmful impacts that their construction and operation creates, including their ceaseless noise, reliance on dirty power supplies, water use, and destruction of thousands of acres of land. In re-electing her, New Yorkers are expecting that Governor Hochul maintain her cautious approach toward AI data centers. EO 62 directed the Department of Public Service (DPS) to complete a Generic Environmental Impact Statement (GEIS). Until it’s completed, the moratorium will remain in place. This review process requires the Public Service Commission (Commission) to identify potential environmental impacts, broadly defined, that would flow from different development scenarios of AI data centers and to scrutinize measures that could reduce those impacts. As part of the scenario review, the Commission can compare the impacts of a scenario where no additional AI data centers are developed versus one where expansion is permitted. This is what the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) did with high-volume hydraulic fracturing (i.e., “fracking”), resulting in the state’s ban on the practice, as well as the recent moratorium on a similar industry, proof-of-work cryptocurrency mining. The environmental review process involves several stages. As a first step, the Commission outlined its proposed scope of review, essentially a work plan, in September. This “Draft Scope” is woefully inadequate and will lead to an outcome that will not protect New Yorkers, our natural resources, or our electric grid. Earthjustice, independently as well as with partner organizations, submitted comments explaining that to get back on track the Final Scope must: - Be broadened to consider all data center impacts, not just those that flow from “interconnection reforms”; - Define roles for other involved agencies with relevant expertise, including the DEC and the Department of Health; - Include an alternative scenario with no new data center expansion; - Ensure compliance with the CLCPA and the Environmental Justice Siting Law (EJ Siting Law); - Specify in greater detail robust interconnection reforms and cost allocation standards that fully protect ratepayers; and - Consider a mandatory data center permit as a policy mechanism to protect communities. The Draft Scope either fails to incorporate these issues altogether or otherwise insufficiently considers them. Of particular concern is the State potentially approaching AI data center development as worthy of accommodation, through essentially unlimited power supply, rather than serious scrutiny under the CLCPA and EJ Siting Law. Starting from a place of accommodation would frustrate the basic purpose for enacting legislation. Already, many developers in other states have been moving forward without sufficient oversight, bypassing the usual planning or regulatory processes in the name of “speed to power.” Protecting New Yorkers requires starting with a different question: Can AI data center growth be reconciled with state law, chief among them the requirements of the CLCPA and EJ Siting Law, and if so, under what conditions? The Commission recently held a Technical Conference at which presenters explained that data center development in New York could result in thousands of MW of new natural gas powerplants by 2035, making it nearly infeasible for the state to comply with the CLCPA’s requirement that the state’s electricity system be 100% emissions free by 2040. Locking in harmful, polluting new gas generation to accommodate AI data centers does not have to be a foregone conclusion, however, and the Commission has a legal obligation to scrupulously examine alternative policy mechanisms to avoid that outcome. There is no shortage of better alternatives. With respect to electric grid impacts, Earthjustice and its clients and partners across the state have submitted to the Commission multiple comments detailing how it can reform the existing interconnection rules and cost allocation standards to (1) ensure compliance with New York’s climate and justice laws; (2) protect ratepayers from bearing the additional costs that AI data centers create when they want to connect to state’s grid; and (3) permit AI data center development. In addition to reforms that would place AI data centers into a separate rate class, require firm up-front and enduring financial commitments, and introduce minimum contract terms, the Commission should also develop a Bring Your Own New Clean Energy (BYONCE) policy. BYONCE is self-explanatory: it avoids additional fossil fuel generation buildout by requiring that data center developers meet their facility’s new energy demand with renewable energy. This policy must be carefully designed to avoid greenwashing or otherwise diverting resources away from broader decarbonization efforts. A BYONCE policy that benefits all would require AI data center developers to bring new (additional) and nearby (in the same geographic area) renewable energy and storage resources ready to match a facility’s full energy demand when it begins operation. artigo.texto: A demora na regulamentação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata) e a possibilidade de exigências ambientais excessivamente restritivas para o uso de gás natural podem comprometer a atração de investimentos para o Brasil. O alerta foi feito por Pietro Mendes, diretor da Agência Natural do Petróleo, Gás Natural e Biocombustíveis (ANP), durante a Conferência Ibero-Brasileira de Energia (Coniben) 2026, realizada em Lisboa, em Portugal. Pietro também cobrou maior agilidade do governo na definição das regras do Redata, diante da competição internacional por investimentos em infraestrutura digital. “A gente vai perdendo oportunidade, vai perdendo investimento, aí sim o capital vai para outro lugar”, afirmou. Embora o gás natural já esteja contemplado na legislação do programa, Pietro Mendes criticou discussões sobre a adoção de critérios que condicionariam a participação das termelétricas a gás ao uso de tecnologias de captura e armazenamento de carbono (CCS) ou priorizariam o suprimento com biometano. Segundo ele, o biometano tem papel importante na transição energética, mas ainda não dispõe de escala de produção suficiente para atender à demanda de grandes termelétricas. Mendes ainda ressaltou que a definição de critérios muito restritivos pode penalizar o gás natural em um país cuja matriz elétrica já apresenta elevada participação de fontes renováveis. Segurança do suprimento No mesmo painel, Christiano Vieira, diretor de Regulação da Eneva, defendeu que a regulamentação do Redata considere não apenas a origem renovável da energia contratada pelos data centers, mas também os custos associados à segurança do suprimento. Segundo o executivo, os empreendimentos possuem demanda contínua de eletricidade, enquanto fontes como solar e eólica apresentam variações de produção ao longo do dia. Nesse cenário, mesmo que um data center contrate energia exclusivamente renovável, o sistema elétrico continuará precisando de recursos capazes de garantir o atendimento nos períodos de menor geração. “Não tem sentido você fazer um modelo energético só com renováveis […] e deixar a conta da segurança ser arcada por todos os usuários do sistema”, disse o diretor da Eneva. Para Christiano Vieira, a regulamentação deve preservar os objetivos de descarbonização do programa, mas também permitir que os empreendedores apresentem soluções competitivas de potência e confiabilidade, incluindo térmicas a gás natural e sistemas de armazenamento. O executivo citou como exemplo a instalação de data centers com demandas de 300 MW a 500 MW, que podem exigir recursos adicionais para assegurar o fornecimento de energia. As baterias também devem desempenhar um papel importante, especialmente na qualidade do suprimento para aplicações de inteligência artificial. No entanto, segundo ele, o armazenamento não elimina a necessidade de soluções capazes de sustentar o atendimento contínuo. Segundo Christiano, na integração entre gás e eletricidade, a Eneva consegue oferecer flexibilidade de atendimento por contar com produção própria de gás e infraestrutura de regaseificação, mas mecanismos semelhantes precisam ser viabilizados para outras usinas conectadas à malha de transporte. O executivo também defendeu tarifas de transporte competitivas e criticou tratamentos regulatórios diferenciados que favoreçam determinadas fontes sem necessariamente produzir ganhos de eficiência.

artigo.texto: A busca por maior autonomia e controle sobre informações corporativas sensíveis levou organizações brasileiras a intensificarem a alocação de cargas críticas em infraestruturas locais de computação em novembro de 2026, conforme avaliação divulgada pela fornecedora de data center e serviços gerenciados Global Gate. O movimento, sustentado por exigências crescentes de conformidade regulatória e mitigação de vulnerabilidades transfronteiriças, estabelece a soberania de dados como parâmetro central na tomada de decisões tecnológicas de alta gestão, superando o modelo de contratação pautado exclusivamente em custos nominais de armazenamento e disponibilidade. A discussão institucionalizada no ecossistema corporativo transcende o conceito básico de residência física de hardware. A soberania de dados compreende a capacidade irrestrita de uma organização estabelecer protocolos proprietários de acesso, determinar a governança do tratamento de ativos intangíveis e blindar operações contra legislações externas. Segundo a análise da empresa, oscilações nas relações diplomáticas, alterações em tratados de comércio internacional e revisões regulatórias em potências estrangeiras passaram a figurar na matriz de risco corporativo de companhias que mantêm sistemas dependentes de jurisdições externas. Geopolítica digital e riscos de extraterritorialidade O panorama macroeconômico global impõe desafios complexos aos departamentos de tecnologia da informação. Mecanismos normativos internacionais, a exemplo de legislações extraterritoriais que autorizam requisições governamentais de registros digitais independentemente da localização física de servidores multinacionais, aumentaram a insegurança jurídica entre corporações brasileiras. A interdependência de ecossistemas em nuvem pública operados fora do território nacional expõe operações estratégicas a sanções unilaterais, embargos tecnológicos ou alterações súbitas de termos de uso impostas por cortes estrangeiras. Para as companhias com atuação no mercado nacional, a adequação integral à Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD) e às exigências de órgãos fiscalizadores setoriais demanda previsibilidade na custódia de arquivos. A manutenção de ambientes digitais sob a autoridade jurídica exclusiva dos tribunais brasileiros simplifica auditorias e resguarda segredos industriais. Jean Jader Martins, diretor da Global Gate — divisão do Grupo Bludata, conglomerado com mais de quatro décadas de experiência tecnológica —, avalia que a evolução das prioridades corporativas decorre de uma readequação estrutural de portfólio. Conforme sustenta Martins, o processo decisório tradicional concentrava-se em métricas operacionais diretas de escala volumétrica e valor por gigabyte. Atualmente, os comitês de governança priorizam o conhecimento da cadeia de custódia, as credenciais de manipulação de dados e as garantias institucionais de conformidade. A proximidade física com o provedor e a transparência em relação aos protocolos de defesa cibernética constituem salvaguardas essenciais para a sustentabilidade e a continuidade operacional dos negócios. Pesquisa global reflete apreensão da liderança executiva A percepção de vulnerabilidade no ambiente digital não está restrita aos quadros técnicos de segurança da informação e engenharia de sistemas. Levantamento conduzido internacionalmente pela consultoria Everpure indicou que falhas ligadas à soberania de dados atingiram patamar crítico de responsabilização funcional. De acordo com o relatório, 88% dos executivos de nível C-level consideram que incidentes de inconformidade jurisdicional ou perda de controle regulatório sobre dados podem culminar na rescisão de seus próprios contratos de trabalho. A mesma sondagem apontou que 91% dos líderes entrevistados temem repercussões financeiras severas e prejuízos duradouros à reputação corporativa em decorrência de eventos associados à custódia irregular de informações. O receio de desvalorização de marca e imposição de multas regulatórias catalisa a revisão de arquiteturas corporativas de nuvem, impulsionando a busca por parceiros locais capazes de assegurar atendimento a marcos legais locais. Parâmetros técnicos de infraestrutura e padrões Tier III A migração para centros de processamento nacionais requer garantias técnicas de tolerância a falhas e contingência operacional contínua. Para viabilizar a hospedagem de cargas críticas sem interrupções operacionais, o mercado B2B direciona investimentos para instalações certificadas pelo padrão Tier III do Uptime Institute. Esta classificação atesta a existência de manutenção concorrente, assegurando que qualquer componente de distribuição de energia ou climatização possa ser reparado ou substituído sem a paralisação dos sistemas de processamento. Dentro desse arranjo estrutural, a fornecedora reporta a operação de dois centros de dados desenhados para atender sistemas de alta sensibilidade. O primeiro complexo está localizado em Blumenau (SC), constituindo o primeiro data center do estado catarinense a receber a certificação Tier III. O segundo ponto de presença atua na região metropolitana de Vinhedo (SP), oferecendo redundância geográfica e capacidade de balanceamento de carga para clientes corporativos de diversas regiões industriais do país. - Residência jurídica estrita: Salvaguarda contratual e técnica de que os volumes armazenados respondem exclusivamente ao ordenamento processual e civil brasileiro. - Arquiteturas de Disaster Recovery: Rotinas de contingência automatizadas entre sítios remotos com baixa latência, reduzindo o tempo de recuperação (RTO) e o ponto de recuperação (RPO). - Isolamento de nuvem privada: Estruturas dedicadas que mitigam os riscos de ataques laterais comuns a ambientes compartilhados hiperconvergentes. - SLA de sustentação assistida: Suporte técnico local com responsabilidade única sobre hardware, conectividade e segurança de borda. artigo.texto: O fato: O governo de Donald Trump anunciou nesta segunda-feira (16) novas restrições à exportação de semicondutores avançados utilizados em inteligência artificial. O Brasil foi incluído, ao lado de Singapura, Tailândia, Malásia e Indonésia, entre os países que precisarão de autorização americana para receber determinados chips destinados a data centers. Focus Poder apurou que esse obstáculo poder ser um problema para a plena instação de novos Data Centers no Ceará. Segundo a Reuters, reproduzida pelo UOL, a decisão pretende impedir que empresas chinesas utilizem centros de processamento instalados em terceiros países para acessar tecnologia americana submetida a controles de exportação. Por que importa para o Ceará: A restrição surge em um momento decisivo para a estratégia de transformar o Ceará em um dos principais polos de infraestrutura digital da América Latina. O Estado concentra projetos de data centers com investimentos anunciados de centenas de bilhões de reais, atraídos pela disponibilidade de energia renovável, pela infraestrutura de cabos submarinos de Fortaleza e pelas condições oferecidas pela Zona de Processamento de Exportação (ZPE) do Pecém. O novo obstáculo é particularmente relevante porque os chips avançados, especialmente os utilizados no treinamento de modelos de inteligência artificial, estão entre os equipamentos estratégicos desses empreendimentos. O projeto chinês: O exemplo mais expressivo é o complexo destinado à ByteDance, empresa chinesa controladora do TikTok, em implantação na ZPE do Ceará pela Omnia Data Centers, em parceria com a Casa dos Ventos. O Governo do Ceará informa que o empreendimento poderá mobilizar aproximadamente R$ 200 bilhões ao longo de quatro fases, com desenvolvimento previsto até 2033. A expectativa divulgada é alcançar capacidade total de 1 gigawatt, com os primeiros 40 megawatts de carga de tecnologia da informação previstos para operar até o terceiro trimestre de 2027. É justamente a presença de grandes empresas chinesas em estruturas internacionais de processamento de dados que está no centro das preocupações manifestadas por Washington. Isso não significa, entretanto, que o projeto cearense tenha sido acusado de qualquer irregularidade ou que sua implantação esteja suspensa. Os demais investimentos: O Ceará também recebeu a aprovação de um projeto vinculado à Voltalia Energia do Brasil, com previsão de R$ 181,7 bilhões em investimentos em Caucaia, conforme anúncio da prefeitura em agosto. Outro empreendimento é o Grand Réseau, da francesa Qair, projetado para a região do Pecém, com investimento estimado em R$ 15 bilhões. Nesse caso, além das questões internacionais, o projeto enfrenta dificuldades regulatórias relacionadas ao acesso à rede de transmissão de energia, após decisões desfavoráveis da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel). Os valores representam investimentos projetados, sujeitos às etapas de licenciamento, financiamento, contratação e execução. Não equivalem a recursos já desembolsados. O Redata: A decisão americana ocorre justamente quando o Brasil busca consolidar uma política de incentivos para a instalação de centros de processamento de dados. O Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata) foi instituído pela Lei nº 15.504, sancionada em setembro de 2026. A legislação teve origem em projeto apresentado pelo deputado federal cearense José Guimarães (PT) e relatado no Senado pelo também cearense Cid Gomes (PSB). O programa estabelece benefícios tributários para aquisição de equipamentos, incluindo a suspensão de impostos federais, com contrapartidas relacionadas à utilização de energia de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão. A regulamentação do regime ainda estava em preparação pelo governo federal, com expectativa de anúncio na semana iniciada em 16 de novembro. O paradoxo: Enquanto o Brasil procura reduzir a carga tributária para ampliar sua competitividade na economia digital, os Estados Unidos passam a impor uma nova exigência administrativa e geopolítica sobre uma das tecnologias mais importantes para os investimentos. A combinação cria uma situação delicada: os incentivos fiscais brasileiros podem tornar a instalação de data centers financeiramente mais atraente, mas não garantem o acesso aos semicondutores necessários para determinadas operações de inteligência artificial. O que muda na prática: A nova regulamentação americana não estabelece uma proibição generalizada à venda de chips para o Brasil. Os fornecedores deverão solicitar licenças ao governo dos Estados Unidos, com análise individual dos pedidos. Há exceções previstas, inclusive para determinadas operações de empresas americanas, observadas exigências de conformidade. Os controles também podem alcançar semicondutores fabricados em outros países quando utilizarem tecnologias sujeitas à jurisdição americana. Assim, o efeito sobre cada empreendimento dependerá de sua estrutura societária, dos equipamentos utilizados, dos fornecedores e da finalidade da capacidade computacional instalada. A disputa geopolítica: O endurecimento das regras integra a competição entre Estados Unidos e China pelo domínio da inteligência artificial. Washington procura evitar que empresas chinesas contornem restrições comerciais mediante o uso remoto de centros de processamento instalados fora do território chinês. O Brasil aparece nessa disputa como destino de grandes investimentos internacionais em infraestrutura digital. A decisão evidencia que a localização física dos data centers não elimina a influência das regras americanas sobre a cadeia tecnológica. Entrelinhas: A ambição cearense de se tornar um polo global de processamento de dados passa a depender de fatores que ultrapassam a oferta de energia, os incentivos tributários e a infraestrutura logística.
