artigo.texto: Pulaski County Judge-elect Wendell Griffen has asked to intervene in a federal lawsuit brought by a company working to build a $6 billion data center near Wrightsville. AVAIO Digital, the company behind the data center, sued Pulaski County in federal court over an ordinance the Quorum Court passed recently, saying they would be harmed if the measure, which puts limits on the construction and operation of huge industrial sites, goes into effect. On top of the lawsuit, AVAIO filed a request for a temporary injunction in an attempt to stop the ordinance from being implemented while the case is under consideration. Griffen said he should be allowed to intervene because AVAIO’s lawsuit will be his responsibility in just a few weeks. “I am the county judge-elect and on Jan. 1, I will be legally obligated to defend the implementation of that ordinance,” he said in an interview on Monday. “Between now and Jan. 1, I need to be able to see how the county is defending against the lawsuit, which I believe is baseless and without merit.” The case is before U.S. District Court Judge Lee Rudofsky, who is scheduled to hear the arguments relating to the temporary injunction order on Friday. The ordinance was passed in September and then vetoed by County Judge Barry Hyde, who gave a number of reasons for his action, including that he thought the ordinance opened the county to legal action. The Quorum Court, however, was able to override Hyde’s veto. Griffen used Hyde’s stance as another reason to be allowed to intervene. “The incumbent County Judge’s opposition to the Ordinance creates a potential divergence between the current administration’s litigation position and the interests of the incoming administration,” Griffen wrote in his request to the court. In hopes of being allowed to intervene, Griffen also readied his legal position further, filing another two motions, one addressing a rebuttal to AVAIO’s argument for a temporary injunction and the other a paragraph-by-paragraph response to AVAIO’s lawsuit. At this point, Griffen said in his response to the temporary injunction request, there is no reason to seek injunctive relief. “The county has not implemented the ordinance, meaning there has not been a stop-work order so their construction is continuing as we speak,” Griffen said.

artigo.texto: Last December, a Wythe County Board of Supervisors meeting was standing room only. Residents at the time said they were blindsided by the announcement of the first data center in the county, to be built on public land in an industrial park. The following year involved the announcement of a second, bigger data center on private land, sparking fears from local opponents that more were on the way. After an open house with one of the data center developers in October, many said they were still searching for answers. “Our ecosystems in Southwest Virginia are what make us so special,” said Maranda Edwards, a Wytheville resident, while at the open house. “We need to preserve that. People like looking out their windows and seeing the deer. With data centers, that’s going to go away, and that’s frustrating to know.” For Edwards and her family members, who live out in the county, zoning regulations could have shone light on plans for the data centers before they were a done deal, she said. Wythe County is one of a handful of localities in Virginia that has no zoning codes. Data centers — or any other development — can be built on private land without public notice or government intervention aside from state permitting in limited circumstances. As of early November, the process to put codes in place has been progressing at the urging of dozens of county residents who say they want the regulations to act as a deterrent for data center developers. Several said that as conservatives who otherwise wouldn’t want zoning implemented, they see a need for it in their community because of data centers. Across several counties in Southwest Virginia, a similar movement has taken root in meeting halls where officials have stressed the importance of getting specific data center zoning ordinances on the books. Most residents who speak at their public meetings have said they agree their localities need rules for data centers, though some are skeptical of their efficacy and have asked for multi-year moratoriums. No locality in Southwest Virginia has enacted a moratorium so far. For local governments, data centers can be a source of millions of dollars in property tax revenue, and some local officials have said they don’t want to write them off entirely. Wythe County zoning In early November, the Wythe County Planning Commission voted 5-2 to send its drafted ordinance and map for a board of supervisors public hearing, the next step in a process to get zoning codes on record. The commission recommended a July 1 implementation date. A vote on the ordinance and the map would occur after the public hearing, which hasn’t been scheduled yet. The process started several years ago before data centers became a major concern for people in Wythe County, according to Matt Hankins, deputy county administrator. At the time, it was another major type of development rankling residents: solar farms. In 2023, solar farm companies began building on hundreds of acres in the county, to the chagrin of residents around them, Hankins said in an interview. After looking at the options, he found the only way the county could make it possible to regulate solar farms on a local level was by enacting zoning codes. “We’ve had that conversation,” he said. “As part of it, residents said, ‘We’ve looked at zoning before. Come back to us with a light-touch ordinance that respects personal property rights and gives us some level of input and management over these projects as they come in.’” The data center issue is similar in nature to solar farms, he said, and has motivated groups of residents to advocate for zoning. The ordinance he and his team have worked on isn’t perfect, Hankins said, but it reflects the character of the county and the end goal of putting it in place, which is to ensure public input for major changes to the county’s landscape. The new codes would require a special exceptions permit for data centers, according to the draft document, which involves a public hearing and a vote from the board of supervisors. They would be allowed in commercial and industrial zones. Though some have called for a complete ban, Hankins said that it’s not legal to strike a particular use of private property from all areas of the county. The two data centers already in the works will also have to be grandfathered into the new codes, Hankins said. Wythe County residents have organized protests and spoken in droves at public meetings over the past year, asking for a way to halt the development of the data centers that have already been announced. They’ve voiced concerns over potential environmental impacts to the air and water, and the damage to their rural quality of life, if large-scale processing centers are built near their homes. At a public hearing hosted by the planning commission in late October, the majority of 17 people who spoke said they were in favor of zoning, specifically to protect the county from data centers. Those who were against zoning said they did not believe the codes would be protective enough against data centers to warrant restrictions on what they could do with their property. “Maybe we do need zoning to keep them out,” said Virginia Riggins, a county resident, during the October hearing. “But if they’re already here, it’s too late. Too little too late.” But for others, the possibility of Wythe County becoming a hotspot for dozens of data centers is the primary fear. Andrew Kegley has lived in the county for 46 years, he said in an interview. Like some, he believes the zoning has come too late, he said, but he is relieved it’s close to the finish line. He thinks it’s a dire need before other data center developers begin to see the county as a place to build without friction from the local government. He wants the effective date to be as soon as possible, he said. He advocated for Jan. 1 during the October hearing. “In an ideal world, we wouldn’t need zoning, nor would we be confronted with noxious developments like data centers

artigo.texto: Soneil Spark revela Sistema Móvel de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias rebocável na RE+ 2026 A Soneil Spark apresentou esta semana seu Sistema Móvel de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias, uma unidade de bateria modular portátil instalada em um reboque rebocável, segundo a Solar Power World. A empresa, que oferece soluções modulares de energia sob medida, exibe o produto na RE+ 2026. O Mobile BESS foi projetado para fornecer energia de reserva temporária e energia fora da rede, captando eletricidade da rede elétrica, de um gerador ou de fontes solares. Sonya Jain, diretora-executiva da empresa, afirmou em comunicado que a energia acompanha o negócio aonde ele for e que a unidade pode ser rebocada até locais onde a demanda por energia cresce; os clientes podem começar com uma única unidade e acrescentar outras conforme as necessidades mudarem, acrescentou ela. A Soneil Spark descreveu a instalação como simples, sem necessidade de guindaste, valas ou espera por interligação à rede elétrica. A empresa posiciona o sistema para canteiros de obras que podem estar a meses de receber o serviço permanente, sets de filmagem e eventos em que o ruído e a fumaça dos geradores são problemáticos, equipes de concessionárias que restabelecem a energia após tempestades e minas ou fazendas remotas além do alcance da rede. Em locais que já usam geradores, o Mobile BESS se sincroniza com eles para cobrir picos e lacunas de partida, permitindo que os geradores operem por menos horas. Em locais onde o uso de diesel é restrito, a empresa afirmou que a unidade oferece uma alternativa silenciosa. Diferentemente do armazenamento em contêineres, destinado a ser instalado uma única vez, o Mobile BESS foi construído para ser rebocado e operar em qualquer clima, segundo a empresa. Entre as aplicações-alvo estão locação de geradores e equipamentos, construção civil, energia de emergência e de reserva, concessionárias, empreiteiras elétricas, eventos, cinema e entretenimento, além de locais fora da rede, como mineração e agricultura. Uma opção híbrida acrescenta a recarga de veículos elétricos. artigo.texto: AI companies are missing a key reason people hate data centers: They’re ugly Of all of the millions of dollars being spent on these sites, barely anything is allocated to visual design. The U.S. is experiencing a huge boom in AI investment, and data centers are at the epicenter. But amid power outages, criticisms around water usage, and moral quandaries, the infrastructure is facing intense backlash from communities earmarked for site development. The new AI Infrastructure Coalition (AIIC)—a trade organization whose members include Google, Meta, Microsoft, and other tech giants—hopes that pledges to limit resource use, prioritize local hiring, and invest in community projects will ease the mounting friction. But all this forgets one crucial thing: People don’t want to live next to eyesores. Of all of the millions of dollars that data center developers are spending on these structures, barely anything is allocated to their visual design. And while I would expect the largest expenses to be what they are—AI servers, electrical and power infrastructure, cooling systems, and labor—the buildings’ aesthetics mustn’t be sidelined. Far more time and money must be spent on this part of the equation. Otherwise, AI companies risk simply adding to the growing list of reasons to resist construction. Neighborhoods are already resisting development and the backlash is reaching the leading data center locations. In Texas, for example, Governor Greg Abbott has gone so far as to implement a statewide moratorium requiring an energy audit for AI companies, halting grid approvals in the meantime. And the governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa, has said she’ll go farther, with a moratorium until the legislature passes new data center laws “to protect Texans.” AI companies and developers will need to get creative to deal with the scale of the challenge, and while I accept that improving how centers look may not solve everything, investing more in their visual appeal would certainly help. Because, fundamentally, people tend to view nicer-looking things more favorably. We are superficial creatures, and psychological researchers have even found that people attribute greater moral standing to animals, objects, and buildings that they perceive as more beautiful. Data centers could certainly do with that boost. Current designs tend to have the opposite effect. Huge gray commercial units are simply not nice to look at, and economically speaking, can spark homeowner concerns about whether they’ll be able to sell their property if they choose to. Owners are already on edge, given that home sales are down, and property delistings—sellers pulling homes off the market—are hitting near-record rates. At a time when the residential market is volatile, the arrival of a massive gray industrial unit is even more unlikely to be welcomed. It matters to everyone in the local area because Americans have a deep-rooted sense of pride in their communities, especially the way they look. The look and feel of a town really makes a difference to the people who live there, and I regularly see just how much pride a homeowner takes in having a pristine, clean-cut lawn or an aesthetically pleasing home exterior. It is why Homeowners Associations (HOAs) keep popping up. Nationwide there are more than 370,000 communities managed by HOAs, encompassing more than 77 million residents. These HOAs set guidelines for home appearance and waste management, among other matters. The associations take maintaining standards very seriously. Nearly half of all HOA violations are based on landscaping or architectural concerns, and they are met with penalties and fines. It could not be clearer to me that residents care deeply about these kinds of design elements—and that data center developers are missing an easy win with local communities by overlooking sites’ aesthetics. Putting more thought into the building’s shape, ensuring the entrance has a well-maintained lawn and foliage, or making architectural modifications that match other local buildings can make a meaningful difference in how a site looks. And it could go a long way toward making residents more amenable to them. Don’t get me wrong. I’m not saying that enhancing visual design will lead to a U-turn in public opinion. There are still plenty of resource-driven concerns that I know will worry communities far more than the building’s exterior. But, by and large, the AIIC is trying to addressing these concerns in its recent pledges. What developers, and the AIIC for that matter, are missing is the aesthetic consideration. It carries a surprising amount of weight, and given that the leading states for data center development—Virginia and Texas—are also home to some of the largest numbers of HOA communities, it cannot be left to fly under the radar any longer. Beautifying data centers is the low-hanging fruit that could help shift the dial back in developers’ favor. Without it, the appearance of these ugly buildings will steadily add more fuel to the flames, with communities continuing to resist construction in their backyards.

artigo.texto: Parceiro institucional: Simon Stiell, secretário-executivo da ONU para Mudanças Climáticas: “A inteligência artificial e outras tecnologias de ponta são uma faca de dois gumes” (UNFCC / Flickr) Repórter de ESG Publicado em 17 de novembro de 2026 às 17h00. Última atualização em 18 de novembro de 2026 às 04h54. “A inteligência artificial e outras tecnologias de ponta são uma faca de dois gumes. A nossa tarefa é reduzir seus riscos, ampliar seu potencial transformador e colocá-las para trabalhar de forma responsável”, afirmou Simon Stiell, secretário-executivo da ONU para Mudanças Climáticas, durante discurso na COP31, em Antália, na Turquia. A declaração resume o desafio que levou a grande conferência climática a lançar, na segunda-feira, 16, um pacto global para tornar a IA mais sustentável, uma iniciativa da presidência turca e da União Internacional de Telecomunicações (UIT), com participação da Unesco. Ao mesmo tempo que pode ajudar a reduzir emissões, integrar fontes renováveis de energia e antecipar desastres climáticos, a tecnologia depende de uma infraestrutura de data centers que consome massivamente eletricidade e água. Com adesão do Brasil, o Compromisso de Antália sobre Inteligência Artificial (Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge) mira essas duas frentes: reduzir a pegada de carbono enquanto ampliaa seu uso como ferramenta de combate à crise climática. O acordo é voluntário e prevê compromissos para melhorar a eficiência energética da infraestrutura digital, incentivar o uso de fontes limpas e ampliar a transparência sobre as emissões associadas à IA. Durante a mesa-redonda de alto nível que marcou o lançamento, Stiell alertou que o "boom" da tecnologia não pode impor custos ambientais e econômicos à população. “Não podemos pedir às pessoas que aceitem contas mais altas, mais poluição que aquece o planeta e maior desigualdade hoje em troca de promessas de um amanhã melhor”, destacou. O secretário-executivo também lembrou que o aumento da demanda dos data centers já pressiona os sistemas elétricos e pode comprometer as metas climáticas nacionais (NDCs) quando essa expansão é sustentada por combustíveis fósseis. O Compromisso de Antália estabelece quatro frentes de atuação para conciliar o avanço tecnológico com os objetivos do Acordo de Paris de limitar a temperatura a 1.5ºC em relação aos níveis pré-industriais. A primeira trata da infraestrutura necessária para desenvolver e operar sistemas de inteligência artificial e incentiva a construção de data centers mais eficientes, a redução do consumo de água e eletricidade e a utilização de fontes de energia de baixa ou nenhuma emissão de carbono. A segunda frente aborda o desenvolvimento e o uso responsável da IA ao longo de todo o seu ciclo de vida. Isso inclui desde a fabricação dos equipamentos até o descarte de componentes eletrônicos, com incentivo à reutilização de materiais e à economia circular. O terceiro eixo busca ampliar a transparência sobre a pegada ambiental da tecnologia. O pacto incentiva empresas e governos a avaliar e divulgar informações sobre consumo de recursos e emissões, utilizando metodologias padronizadas que permitam acompanhar os impactos. Por último, o compromisso prevê apoio financeiro e tecnológico para ampliar o uso da IA em soluções climáticas, especialmente nos países em desenvolvimento, nas nações menos desenvolvidas e nos pequenos Estados insulares, que estão entre os mais vulneráveis aos efeitos do aquecimento global. Entre as aplicações estão ferramentas para prever eventos climáticos extremos, melhorar a eficiência das redes elétricas, integrar fontes renováveis e ajudar setores como agricultura e indústria na descabonização. Segundo o anúncio, os participantes poderão assumir compromissos específicos conforme suas capacidades, incluindo exigências ambientais para data centers, investimentos em infraestrutura computacional e capacitação profissional. A implementação contará com apoio de padrões internacionais desenvolvidos pela UIT, e os avanços serão acompanhados anualmente nas COPs do clima até 2030. Em 2027, o país anfitrião será a Etiópia. Por outro lado, o pacto não estabelece metas obrigatórias e uniformes na mitigação das emissões. Seu funcionamento depende do que for assumido voluntariamente por cada país e da capacidade de ação. O Brasil oficializou sua adesão ao compromisso durante a COP31. Representando o governo brasileiro, o secretário de Telecomunicações do Ministério das Comunicações, Hermano Tercius, participou do debate sobre os impactos ambientais, econômicos e sociais da inteligência artificial. Além da sustentabilidade, o país levou à mesa um alerta com os efeitos da automação sobre o mercado de trabalho. “Destacamos uma preocupação do governo brasileiro com a proteção dos trabalhadores diante das transformações e da substituição de vagas causadas pela IA, defendendo a garantia e a manutenção desses postos de trabalho”, afirmou Tercius, em comunicado. Segundo o Ministério das Comunicações, a participação brasileira reforça a posição de que o desenvolvimento tecnológico deve caminhar junto com o crescimento econômico, a inclusão social e a preservação ambiental. A adesão não significa, por enquanto, que o Brasil tenha anunciado metas nacionais específicas para reduzir o consumo energético ou as emissões de data centers. O comunicado do governo também não detalha investimentos associados à implementação. Em seu discurso, Stiell defendeu também que o acesso à infraestrutura computacional, ao financiamento e aos dados confiáveis seja ampliado para as nações em desenvolvimento. O representante da ONU citou aplicações capazes de alertar famílias sobre enchentes, ajudar agricultores a se preparar para períodos de seca e permitir que redes elétricas utilizem mais energia solar e eólica com menos desperdício. Para ele, a IA só poderá se consolidar como uma solução em prol do clima se seus benefícios forem distribuídos de maneira mais ampla. O alerta aparece em um estudo liderado

artigo.texto: - Salt Lake City paused new data centers for six months to review regulations. - The City Council voted unanimously, addressing concerns over a proposed Northpoint project. - Mayor Mendenhall supported the pause to reassess zoning and environmental impacts. SALT LAKE CITY — Utah's capital city quickly pushed through a new ordinance pausing all new data centers within city limits for up to six months so it can better review a proposed project on its west side. The Salt Lake City Council voted unanimously on Tuesday to approve the measure after quickly adding it to its agenda this week. It essentially creates a moratorium on new data centers, allowing the city and potentially the state to adopt new data center regulations. "While policy would be the best protection for everyone in the long term — and I will advocate for that at any level of government — I'm also going to use any amount of soft power I have to influence whoever can make a decision to back off plans that can hurt people or the land out there," Salt Lake City Councilwoman Victoria Petro told KSL before the vote. The measure popped up on the City Council this week in an apparent response to a proposed data center that recently made headlines. A San Francisco-based architect filed a commercial building permit with the city for a one-story data center in June. Little else is known about the project, which would be located at 2258 W. 2950 North in Salt Lake City's Northpoint neighborhood. Qlevr LLC, a Florida-based digital infrastructure company, then applied for an air quality permit at the same site with the Utah Division of Air Quality on Sept. 30. That, too, only provided vague details, only saying it would run on grid power with fuel storage tanks and diesel-fired emergency generators. "That particular development is a thorn in my side," said Petro, whose district covers the Northpoint area. She explained that the development flew under the city leadership's radar until recently, and the developer hasn't provided much readily available information. The location is particularly vexing for her and the city. Salt Lake City recently completed a new plan for the Northpoint area to map out developments within the city's final rural edge. That came as residents pleaded with the city to help stop massive warehouses that wreaked havoc on them. It would potentially create a new challenge with noise and environmental concerns. "This is just heaping trauma upon trauma on one community," she said, adding that many residents aren't anti-data center but against the impacts they can have without any type of regulation. What the city voted on Tuesday follows a similar moratorium that Salt Lake County leaders approved in September, but that measure only applied to unincorporated land within the county, not Northpoint. It's also similar to a six-month pause the city approved in March to cap nonresidential water to 200,000 gallons per day. What started as a temporary measure to potentially thwart an immigration detention center on the west side ended up in a permanent ordinance approved in September. The new pause would give the city time to craft a new policy to address data centers, as the concerns over them mount. It would also carry through mid-May, potentially allowing the state to craft new data center policies that could go into effect by the time Tuesday's order expires. State leaders suggested making improvements to data center policy earlier this month after it seemed to be one of the key local issues during this year's election cycle. It's a "healthy pause" for the city, Salt Lake City Mayor Erin Mendenhall said earlier on Tuesday, asserting that the city's technology plans and zoning never considered data centers at the scale that has been proposed in recent years. Many vary in how they use water, which is something the city is very interested in, so she believes it makes sense to review new centers before approving them. "I think it's appropriate for our city and any other city that does land use to reconsider and take a hard look at zoning that's out there so that we can make sure what happens here is reflective of our capacity," she said.

artigo.texto: ROCHESTER — A timeline for a temporary moratorium on data center development in Rochester remains uncertain. “I don’t expect it to take longer than a year, and our hope is to get there sooner,” Community Development Director Irene Woodward told the Rochester City Council during a roughly 90-minute review of the proposal Monday. ADVERTISEMENT The council voted 5-1 to approve the moratorium, making way for staff study of potential data center impacts, along with developing definitions and guidelines for future development. The development pause begins with official notice of approval. “It gives us the opportunity to define the application process,” Woodward said, noting the goal is to ensure the community and developers know what is possible and what the development process entails. Council member Shaun Palmer, who cast the sole vote against the moratorium, questioned whether existing model ordinances could be adopted in an effort to reduce the potential timeline to three months. Woodward said model ordinances will be reviewed, but it will take time to tweak one, if used, since staff must ensure it meets community expectations and fits within the city’s unified development code without causing new conflicts. Council member Dan Doering said time is needed, but the move doesn’t mean data centers won’t be allowed under revised ordinances. “It’s not about automatically saying no to them,” he said. “It’s about fully knowing the pros and cons before making a long-term decision that could have a profound impact on our community.” ADVERTISEMENT Woodward said the city cannot outright ban data centers, but regulations can ensure development fits community expectations. While the process for developing future regulations is expected to involve public engagement efforts, the City Council heard concerns from both sides of the issue Monday. With 11 people speaking during a public hearing, the majority encouraged the council to support the moratorium as presented by staff, voicing concerns about environmental impacts and development issues seen in other communities, including Pine Island. “I am pleased that you are looking at this proactively and not just waiting until a center is on our doorstep and a deal is already made and proposed,” Rochester resident Mary Vlazny told the council. Evan Vlaeminck, an asset manager for the Rochester Technology Campus, which sits on the former IBM campus, said he’s concerned the moratorium could harm existing businesses needing to expand their data centers during the moratorium period. “A year is a very long time, certainly with respect to business,” he said. “Many deals can come and go in that time.” Council member Andy Friederichs suggested limiting the moratorium to new development, making way for expansion, but the proposal failed to get the needed support. ADVERTISEMENT The moratorium allows existing operations to operate and adapt to changing needs, but it’s also intended to be broad enough to rule out expansions that could transform existing facilities into something beyond their existing scope. Woodward said existing Rochester data centers were developed before the city implemented its new development code in 2023, and no applications for development or expansions are under city review. Whether an expansion would be restricted by the moratorium would depend on several factors, she said, noting a building permit application would spur a review to determine if the proposed work is allowed. She said the uncertainty related to requirements in existing code is what prompted the moratorium and planned study of data center impacts. “There are different ways to define a data center, and that is what we don’t have clearly defined,” she said. The temporary pause on potential development is the latest effort throughout the state. Egan lays claim to being the first Minnesota city to enact a temporary moratorium on development of new data centers. The Feb. 17 Eagan City Council decision came as four data centers were under construction in the Twin Cities suburb with a population of nearly 69,000. ADVERTISEMENT Meanwhile, a split Minneapolis City Council took action on Nov. 12 to approve new development rules, which will require council approval for individual data centers after proposals are made. The decision follows a review that included a five-month moratorium, which was implemented in June. Woodward said Rochester’s moratorium is designed to end earlier, if the council approves updates to the city’s development code. “We are planning to keep this moving,” she said of the timeline and state statute that allows a one-year moratorium with the possibility of requesting an 18-month extension. “If we bring back an ordinance before that time, the moratorium would expire.”

artigo.texto: By Lucia Yu, Senior Manager of Development, Key Capture Energy MANORVILLE – Long Islanders opened their electric bills this year to increases of up to 20%. The state’s grid operator forecasts that Long Island’s power grid will be operating with very slim margins starting in 2027. Battery energy storage is one of the fastest ways to help address both rising costs and the risk of blackouts. Key Capture Energy is developing battery energy storage projects across Long Island, including KCE NY 37 in Manorville. The two questions our team hears the most are “why here?” and “is battery energy storage safe?” Why Long Island? Long Island’s grid connections to the rest of the state are stretched thin, and getting energy here can be a challenge, especially on summer afternoons and evenings when air conditioners and appliances are all running at once. That raises the risk of blackouts on an island that has already seen its share of outages. In February, a winter storm knocked out power for nearly 50,000 Long Island residents and just a few months later, heavy wind and rain resulted in blackouts and brownouts that impacted more than 10,000 customers. Without continued investment in the grid, even standard weather events could become increasingly difficult for Long Island’s electric grid to manage. Storage is uniquely able to address both costs and the potential of electrical shortfalls. Batteries charge when power is cheap and plentiful and store it for when it’s needed, like on hot summer afternoons that are the hours that strain the grid and drive up prices. That’s why New York set a goal of 6 gigawatts of storage by 2030, a buildout that State regulators have said could save nearly $2 billion in system costs. KCE NY 37 is a part of that buildout. In September, NYSERDA selected it as one of eight projects in the state’s first bulk energy storage solicitation. It will provide millions of dollars in local taxes, union construction wages and other community benefits. Is battery energy storage safe? Simply put, yes. There are roughly 1,000 large scale projects like KCE NY 37 operating across the country and since today’s modern safety testing codes have been in place, the occurrence of fires at BESS facilities has plummeted. Here in New York, the state updated its fire code to be one of the strictest in the country. Today, every project must undergo an independent third-party safety review during the local permitting process to ensure these updated codes are met and develop an Emergency Response Plan in coordination with the local fire department. Developers are also required to offer training for local first responders prior to a facility starting operations and annually afterwards. KCE has met with the Manorville Fire Department and Brookhaven fire officials to discuss the project. We look forward to ongoing dialogue with local emergency personnel to finalize a comprehensive emergency response plan and address any outstanding questions. These steps and the pre-operational fire department training will ensure that first responders are equipped and ready in the very unlikely event of a safety incident at the facility. New York’s fire leaders have said again and again that battery storage is safe when it is built to New York’s updated code. Residents are also right to ask what the 2023 East Hampton battery storage fire means for their community, particularly after PFAS contamination was found in nearby groundwater. The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) is continuing to investigate that contamination, but its preliminary findings identify the facility’s fire suppression system, rather than its batteries, as the likely source of any contamination. That system used Novec 1230, a chemical fire-extinguishing agent that can break down into a PFAS compound if combined with water. KCE NY 37 and our projects across Long Island will not use Novec 1230 or a similar suppression agent. Unlike East Hampton’s indoor facility, which also utilized an older battery chemistry called nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC), KCE’s projects will use outdoor systems with lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) batteries built to New York’s updated fire safety codes. Everyone should be confident in the safety of today’s modern BESS systems, including KCE NY 37, because they incorporate the lessons learned from incidents like the East Hampton fire and are specifically designed to prevent and mitigate the impacts of a fire, in the rare case one were to happen. Battery energy storage built to New York’s updated safety codes is safe. It can ease Long Island’s energy challenges, help stabilize electric bills, and ensure businesses and households have the reliable grid needed to power Long Island’s economy. Lucia Yu is Senior Manager of Development at Key Capture Energy (KCE). KCE is a battery energy storage developer and operator headquartered in Albany with projects across New York.

artigo.texto: Chinese battery maker CATL opens office in Argentina — South China Morning Post Chinese battery manufacturer Contemporary Amperex Technology Co Ltd (CATL) has opened a commercial office in Argentina, South China Morning Post reports, citing Argentine media. The company plans to use it to expand supplies of energy storage systems. CATL already supplies batteries for the country’s largest electricity storage project and has presented its solutions to 35 companies interested in a government tender. Last week, CATL representatives met in Buenos Aires with generating companies and banks. The company said it intends to become the leading supplier of energy storage systems in Argentina. The office is also expected to become a base for developing storage projects for mining enterprises, data centers and wind power plants in Patagonia. Projects and tenders Argentina’s largest private electricity producer, Central Puerto, uses CATL cells in two projects with a combined capacity of 205 MW. Construction of the larger one, the 150 MW Nuevo Puerto facility, is about 80% complete. Commercial operation is planned to begin in mid-December under a 15-year contract with distribution company Edenor. Last year, Argentine authorities announced the first tender for 500 MW of energy storage systems near Buenos Aires to reduce the number of power supply disruptions. Due to high demand, contracts were concluded for 713 MW: they were signed directly with distributors, while Cammesa, which manages the wholesale electricity market, acted as guarantor. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram. In July, Argentina’s Energy Secretariat allocated another 700.5 MW among 20 projects in other regions of the country. The auction received 235 technical applications, and the estimated investment volume amounted to $700 million. Average prices were about a quarter lower than in the first round. Renewable energy developer Genneia received 421 MW, or about 60% of the total volume. Financing in yuan Financing remains one of the main issues for market participants, as battery containers are imported from China. Christian Damonaz of the Argentine unit of Bank of China proposed lending in yuan and said that this currency offers acceptable rates and stability against the US dollar. ICBC’s Argentine unit provided Genneia with 358.8 million yuan, or $50 million, last year for renewable energy projects. CATL also reported that its revenue from energy storage systems rose 87.5% year-on-year in the first half of the year. According to Harry Lau, the company’s representative in Latin America, CATL has contracts in the region for more than 15 GWh of energy storage systems, including for the Oasis de Atacama project in Chile.

artigo.texto: COLUMBUS, Ohio — A leaked Ohio bill could allow data centers to qualify as "public utilities," giving them the ability to seize private property. Ohioans rejected data centers on every ballot measure this election, but after that massive loss, Republican lawmakers may be moving to allow tech hubs one way or another. For decades, Gretchan Francis has been fighting to keep her multigenerational family farm. "It's not the farm that it once was," Francis said in an interview. "It's only 60 acres; it's not 160 acres." Using eminent domain law, which allows the government to take property for public use, the state has seized her land numerous times for highway development. "I understand that it is necessary, but I think it has to be done in the right way," she said. While ODOT has always been able to do this, farmers like her are fearing that new legislation would take their livelihoods for a controversial cause. A draft bill leaked to us exclusively would expand the list of who qualifies to take land. The draft changes the definition of "public utility," from just an entity being owned or operated by municipal corporations, an electric cooperative and an agency holding a certificate of public convenience and necessity granted by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. The legislation adds "and an agency holding a certificate of environmental compatibility and public need from the power siting board for constructing an electric transmission line and associated facilities or gas pipeline and its associated facilities." This could mean a transmission developer may be able to seize land to power or place a data center, according to legal experts. "That would be devastating," Francis said. "I think anybody would feel the same way if their personal land was taken for a data center. That sounds like it's a corporate, private, for-profit type of need, not for a public need." In June, we discovered that the Ohio Business Roundtable, a powerful trade group that lobbies at the Statehouse, recommended that lawmakers change eminent domain law, and “should extend possession authority to energy infrastructure projects once public use and necessity have been established.” RELATED: Ohio farmers fear new proposal would allow data centers to take property The Ohio Farm Bureau, which is adamantly against changing eminent domain, had been preparing for this fight since. "We are aware of efforts to further erode the limited protections that landowners have, allowing for quick take of property without first paying for the property and determining a landowner’s rights and compensation through a court of law," the Bureau’s Evan Callicoat said. The Farm Bureau isn't opposed to data centers, but they are opposed to a violation of property rights, Callicoat said. He feared that with this proposed idea, it's broad enough that farmers could lose their land to data centers, not getting paid for it for months or years. The Roundtable calls the program "deposit and build," and it's modeled after a system that 45 other states use. "This recommendation is about making sure that Ohio's grid is reliable and affordable for Ohioans and that economic development can continue in the state," the Roundtable's Alexandra Denney said in an interview Monday. The Ohio Power Siting Board controls the installation of utility facilities, including power lines, some gas pipelines, and wind farms. The Public Utilities Commission of Ohio can also help utility companies acquire land. A utility will approach a homeowner for land and must provide them with a "fair" market price. If the owner refuses to sell, the utility company will take them to court and will need to determine "necessity" for the land. If a court sides with the utility company, deeming it necessary to take, the appraised value of the land is given to a court account. However, the owner can appeal this decision to fight for more money. While this court battle is going on, construction is not allowed to begin. The draft bill changes the appraisal process, making it easier to seize land immediately. "Ratepayers and Ohioans are paying the price because it's driving up costs and it's also delaying the critical infrastructure that we need to have a reliable grid," Denney said about construction delays. While Denney was aware of the appraisal portion of the legislation, she categorically denied any changes to eminent domain. After I read the bill out loud, she said she would need to "look at" the changes in the definition of public utilities. She said that Ohioans choosing to restrict or ban data centers in 21 different cities has nothing to do with the timing of this proposal. "That is not the intent of the Ohio Business Roundtable to expand the ability to use eminent domain to anybody that doesn't already have that ability," Denney said. Soon-to-be Senate President Republican Bill Reineke (R-Tiffin), who is working on the bill, echoed her sentiment. “We keep talking about lowering costs, and one way we can do that is expanding infrastructure for public utilities to keep rates down. That’s what this is about," Reineke said in a statement. "It’s important to me that landowners keep their rights, and this would not extend eminent domain to anyone who doesn’t already have that privilege — rather, it is a framework to simplify our existing process that would put us in line with 45 other states." He added that one of his top focuses was to make sure there was enough energy and lower costs. artigo.texto: Data centers dos EUA emitem tanto CO₂ quanto a Dinamarca, aponta Harvard | Vero NotíciasData centers dos EUA emitem tanto CO₂ quanto a Dinamarca, aponta Harvard Os 403 maiores data centers dos Estados Unidos emitiram 25,7 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono entre maio de 2024 e abril de 2025, volume equivalente às emissões anuais da Dinamarca, segundo estudo da Universidade de Harvard. Publicado nesta segunda-feira (16) na revista Nature Sustainability, o levantamento aponta que as emissões desses centros de dados triplicaram desde 2018, impulsionando preocupações sobre o impacto ambiental da infraestrutura digital. Virgínia, Oregon, Ohio e Iowa concentraram mais da metade do consumo de eletricidade analisado. Segundo os pesquisadores, a maioria dos centros utilizava energia gerada a gás, e o estudo busca ampliar a transparência sobre os impactos ambientais da inteligência artificial. Um estudo do Ministério da Fazenda estima que a aprovação do projeto de lei que regulamenta economicamente as big techs pode gerar benefícios de R$ 15,3 bilhões a R$ 50,6 bilhões anuais para consumidores e empresas brasileiras. Os valores representam entre 0,1% e 0,4% do PIB. O levantamento, elaborado pela Secretaria de Reformas Econômicas, analisou 20 segmentos do mercado digital, incluindo comércio eletrônico, publicidade, aplicativos de transporte e inteligência artificial. Os setores movimentaram cerca de R$ 410 bilhões em 2025. O Ministério da Fazenda estima que ampliar a concorrência entre plataformas digitais pode gerar benefícios de R$ 15,3 bilhões a R$ 50,6 bilhões anuais para consumidores e empresas, com menores preços e comissões. O estudo avalia um projeto que amplia os instrumentos do Cade para fiscalizar grandes plataformas e combater barreiras à concorrência. O texto tramita com urgência na Câmara e aguarda votação no plenário. O ajuste fiscal pode reduzir em R$ 280 milhões os recursos destinados a projetos esportivos, estimam as organizações Atletas pelo Brasil e Instituto Esporte e Educação. As entidades divulgaram comunicado contra a medida. O projeto amplia de 10% para 20% o corte linear de benefícios tributários. As organizações pedem que a Lei de Incentivo ao Esporte seja excluída da redução para preservar o financiamento dos projetos. O Ibovespa caiu 1,83% nesta segunda-feira (16), aos 169.295,41 pontos, em meio a preocupações com as contas públicas brasileiras e ao aumento da aversão ao risco nos mercados internacionais. Investidores avaliam se o pacote fiscal será suficiente para estabilizar as contas. O Morgan Stanley reduziu sua recomendação para o Brasil e projetou o Ibovespa em 160 mil pontos no fim de 2027. O secretário especial da Receita Federal, Robinson Barreirinhas, afirmou nesta segunda-feira (16) que o projeto de ajuste fiscal não restringe os créditos tributários da Contribuição sobre Bens e Serviços (CBS). Segundo Barreirinhas, os créditos da CBS continuarão podendo ser compensados. O texto permite restringir outras compensações tributárias caso o governo esteja distante da meta fiscal, incluindo créditos ligados a benefícios fiscais.

artigo.texto: The Hidden Efficiency Gap in Data Center Containment The Gap Nobody Budgeted For Data center operators measure nearly everything to ensure efficiency at the highest level, from inlet temperatures to rack density, airflow per kilowatt to PUE. Yet an unobtrusive gap above the hot contained aisle or missing roof above the cold contained aisle has been leaking conditioned air, forcing the cooling system to work harder than it needs to be, driving up cooling costs since the day the facility was commissioned. And no one has been measuring its detriment to performance. It’s easy to miss. The open seam sits at ceiling height for HAC or above the racks for CAC and is barely perceptible to some. However, the gap rarely appears on an efficiency dashboard, because it’s not an oversight nor a design defect. The gap is a deliberate allowance, that’s been quietly shaping the cooling bill of almost every contained facility that has relied on it. The real story is not that the gap exists. It’s why the industry has treated it as an unavoidable compromise. Why the Gap Exists The open seam above the hot aisle containment or missing roof above the cold aisle for cold aisle containment is a result of fire code, not a construction fault. In the United States, a combination of national model codes, specialized National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) regulations 13 (installation of sprinkler systems) and 75 (protection of IT equipment) standards, along with the International Fire Code plus state or local municipal amendments enforced by local Authorities Having Jurisdiction (AHJs), regulate data center fire safety. A sprinkler can only protect what its water spray can reach. Fire code mandates require the unobstructed dispersal of sprinkler heads to protect the space, and a he ad that is blocked, shadowed, or poorly positioned may fail to control the fire. The problem is that a fully sealed ceiling impedes sprinkler coverage. It can be done. The sprinkler layout could be designed at the same time as the rack, tray, and containment layout rather than afterward. But this would require renewed verification and approvals after any increase or relocation of racks and cabinets, change of cable trays or busways, additional lighting or cooling lines, or modification of containment and airflow. With the rapid evolution of AI racks, adding higher-density or higher-power equipment (such as liquid cooling or battery systems) also changes the hazard classification and can trigger additional requirements. To adhere to fire code and not impede sprinkler coverage, data center designers made the easier call and left a gap. It is a reasonable, safety-first decision that allows for adaptation and refitting as and when required. It is also one that operators have paid for ever since, in wasted cooling energy. The industry has long treated this as a fixed trade-off between containment and compliance. While that choice has protected facilities, safety and efficiency have been set against each other, and efficiency has lost by default. This trade-off has gone unchallenged for years, because no one could offer containment that fire protection engineers and code officials would accept as fully sealed. What the Gap Costs at Scale Containment has one job: to keep hot exhaust air and cold supply air from mixing. Every pathway that lets them meet forces the cooling plant to compensate. It matters more than its size suggests. The loss is not a one-off event to be fixed after an incident. It is a constant, built into the facility's operating cost from the first day of operation. Sealed When it Should Be The answer is a contained cold or hot aisle that stays fully sealed in normal operation and changes its behavior in an emergency. Two components work together to make that possible: - A melting fuse plug with airflow flaps: A sealed ceiling with airflow flaps that under normal operating conditions stay closed. If aisle temperatures rise, the melting fuse plug is activated, opening the airflow flaps releasing hot air to the sprinkler activation. - Dissolving panels: When the sprinklers activate, the EPA approved non-combustible panels dissolve on contact with water; sprinkler discharge is never blocked and panels never fall, so there is no obstruction to egress. The principle is simple: containment is in full effect when conditions are normal, but when safety requires the space, the flaps and dissolving panels combine, giving operators efficiency when they need it and safety when it counts. Reviewed and Approved Promising efficiency gains in a life-safety context can often lead to mistrust. Efficiency improvements that cannot demonstrate fire code compliance are not improvements at all. They are liabilities waiting to surface during inspection, or worse, during an incident. Most efficiency gains ask a lot: major capital, long downtime or a redesign from the ground up. The distinction here is that this is not a workaround. It is a design that has been reviewed and approved directly by fire protection engineers and AHJs. It also works for both new builds and legacy facilities. - New builds can specify either fully sealed hot or cold aisles with airflow flaps from the outset, so the gap is never created. - Legacy facilities can close a leak or add a roof system over the cold aisle that has existed since commissioning, without rethinking the architecture. In both cases the result is the same: fully sealed hot aisles with airflow flaps that meet fire code without compromising safety. Compliant Containment The hot aisle seam above hot aisle containment and missing roof system above the cold aisle for cold aisle containment has been tolerated for as long as it was thought to be the price of compliance, but that reasoning no longer holds. Each day these openings stay open is another day of avoidable cooling cost. artigo.texto: Researchers at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology have developed a structural lithium-sulfur battery cathode capable of maintaining stable electrical performance inside curved and hollow structures. Led by Professor Il-Kwon Oh from the Department of Mechanical Engineering, the research team fabricated the electrode by growing ultrafine nanowires directly onto woven carbon cloth, creating a monolithically integrated scaffold designed to serve simultaneously as a mechanical support and an energy storage medium for drones and robotic systems. In robotics and unmanned aerial vehicle engineering, maximizing energy storage capacity while minimizing device weight and occupied volume remains a primary design constraint. Conventional vehicle architectures rely on separate structural airframes and discrete, rigid battery packs, restricting the extent to which overall platform weight can be reduced. Structural energy storage addresses this challenge by converting load-bearing airframe parts, such as landing gear or robotic limbs, into functional battery components. Implementing multifunctional structural batteries in practice requires energy storage cells that conform to non-planar structural geometries. Unmanned aerial vehicle landing legs and robotic support frames frequently incorporate curved, hollow, or tubular surfaces that cannot accommodate conventional flat battery configurations. To resolve this geometric restriction, the KAIST team focused on engineering an electrode architecture capable of conforming to tightly curved, three-dimensional enclosures without sacrificing mechanical durability or electrochemical activity. The engineering team selected a lithium-sulfur electrochemical system, which utilizes sulfur as the active cathode material. Lithium-sulfur chemistries provide theoretical potential for high energy storage capacity at a relatively low material weight compared to traditional alternatives. Within this system, the cathode acts as a critical functional electrode that governs the redox reactions occurring during electrical charge and discharge cycles. Despite these theoretical storage advantages, lithium-sulfur systems encounter operational obstacles that hinder long-term performance. Elemental sulfur has poor electrical conductivity, and intermediate compounds termed lithium polysulfides dissolve into the electrolyte during operation. The migration of these dissolved polysulfides away from the cathode disrupts the reversible electrochemical reactions required for efficient energy retention, accelerating capacity loss over repeated cycling. Conventional electrode fabrication techniques introduce additional structural vulnerabilities when subjected to physical movement. Active materials are typically applied as a surface slurry coating onto a conductive substrate, making the layer susceptible to cracking or complete delamination under repeated bending or external mechanical stress. When active material detaches from the underlying current collector, the electrical pathways are severed and the electrode degrades rapidly. To overcome delamination and polysulfide migration simultaneously, the KAIST researchers grew nickel cobalt selenide nanowires directly on the surfaces of interwoven carbon fibers. Nanowires are ultrafine structures with dimensions measured on the scale of nanometers, where one nanometer represents one billionth of a meter. The nickel cobalt selenide compound, consisting of nickel, cobalt, and selenium, catalyzes sulfur-related redox reactions while chemically anchoring lithium polysulfides to limit their dissolution and migration away from the reaction zone. Because the nickel cobalt selenide nanowires are grown directly out of the woven carbon cloth substrate rather than spread as a secondary surface coating, the cathode establishes firmly anchored, continuous electrical conduction pathways. In cyclic mechanical deformation tests, the monolithic electrode underwent 1,000 bending cycles at a tight curvature radius of 2.5 millimeters. Following testing, the nanowires remained intact and securely attached to the carbon fiber surfaces, displaying no structural collapse, cracking, or material detachment. To verify the practical viability of the electrode within non-planar enclosures, the researchers assembled the material into functional lithium-sulfur pouch cells. They incorporated the resulting cells into multiple curved and angular housings, including oval, square, and drone-leg structural components. In each configuration, the integrated lithium-sulfur battery successfully powered a light-emitting diode, demonstrating reliable electrical discharge across varied structural contours. The team also subjected the integrated structural battery to external mechanical load testing to evaluate electrical stability under severe mechanical strain. When installed within a cylindrical housing, the battery retained 99.8 percent of its initial operational voltage even under external mechanical forces sufficient to fracture the surrounding structural frame. In a parallel loading evaluation, a connected light-emitting diode maintained steady illumination without flickering or interruption during structural failure. Looking toward practical deployment, the authors noted that the electrode architecture could eventually be paired with load-bearing composite materials, such as carbon fiber and resin matrices, to construct multifunctional drone legs and robotic airframes. However, the researchers emphasized that further experimental research remains necessary to quantify precisely how much structural weight can be eliminated and the degree to which operational flight times or robot mission durations can be extended in operational conditions. The study, titled “Monolithically integrated NiCo2Se4 nanowire–carbon cloth cathode scaffolds for non-planar lithium-sulfur structural-battery integration,” was published in the journal Advanced Composites and Hybrid Materials

artigo.texto: Publicidade Receba notícias do Congresso em Foco: Relações exteriores Congresso em Foco 16/11/2026 15:52 O Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos passou a exigir licença do governo norte-americano para exportação, reexportação ou transferência de semicondutores avançados de inteligência artificial destinados ao Brasil. A nova regra, divulgada nesta segunda-feira (16) pelo Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), órgão responsável pelos controles de exportação, também alcança Indonésia, Malásia, Singapura e Tailândia. Segundo o governo dos Estados Unidos, os cinco países foram incluídos na nova exigência por apresentarem um risco considerado "acima do normal" de que equipamentos avançados de computação sejam desviados para empresas ou países submetidos a controles norte-americanos. A medida atinge chips de alto desempenho utilizados, entre outras aplicações, na infraestrutura necessária para desenvolver e operar sistemas avançados de inteligência artificial. Os pedidos de licença envolvendo os cinco países serão analisados individualmente pelas autoridades norte-americanas, que avaliarão se a operação pode contrariar interesses de segurança nacional ou de política externa dos Estados Unidos. Há ainda uma exceção para determinadas operações cujo usuário final seja uma empresa sediada nos EUA ou controlada por uma companhia norte-americana, desde que sejam cumpridas exigências de informação ao governo. A regra faz parte de uma ofensiva mais ampla do governo dos Estados Unidos para impedir que empresas de países sujeitos a restrições, especialmente aquelas vinculadas a destinos classificados no grupo D:5, tenham acesso indireto à capacidade computacional de chips norte-americanos. O grupo inclui países como China, Rússia, Irã e Coreia do Norte. O governo norte-americano identificou como uma das preocupações o uso de data centers instalados em terceiros países. Nesse modelo, uma empresa impedida de comprar diretamente determinados semicondutores poderia acessar remotamente a capacidade de processamento de equipamentos instalados em outro território. O Departamento de Comércio afirma que a nova norma busca fechar essa possibilidade e aproximar as regras de acesso remoto das restrições já aplicadas ao envio físico da tecnologia. Tags Temas

artigo.texto: In a recent study, researchers investigated biodegradable polymer electrolytes engineered for use in green electric double-layer capacitor devices. The research examined solid polymer blend electrolytes composed of chitosan and methylcellulose paired with potassium thiocyanate salt and modified using glycerol as a plasticizing agent. The development addresses the implementation of environmentally friendly biopolymer matrices capable of supporting functional electrochemical storage systems, with an emphasis on establishing sustainable materials for capacitor applications. Impedance spectroscopy evaluations demonstrated that the addition of glycerol plasticizer effectively enhanced the overall electrical properties of the chitosan/methylcellulose/potassium thiocyanate electrolyte system. By incorporating glycerol into the ternary biopolymer blend, the investigators identified clear modifications in electrical response compared to unmodified formulations. These impedance findings confirmed that plasticization served a critical functional role in optimizing the bulk electrical characteristics required for practical solid polymer electrolyte performance. Structural and morphological analyses confirmed that glycerol incorporation induced measurable physical alterations within the solid polymer blend. X-ray diffraction measurements showed a reduction in diffraction peak intensity alongside noticeable peak broadening, indicating structural reorganization in the polymer electrolyte network. Furthermore, scanning electron microscopy revealed a homogenous dispersion of glycerol throughout the solid polymer electrolyte matrix, demonstrating uniform integration of the plasticizer across the combined chitosan and methylcellulose structure. The dielectric behaviour of the electrolyte system provided additional insights into the internal charge transport dynamics. The loss tangent peaks exhibited a systematic shift toward higher frequencies, which the authors identified as direct evidence that the time required for ion transport decreased as plasticizer concentration increased. Complementing these observations, an electric modulus study was performed to suppress electrode polarization phenomena and enable clear observation of the relaxation peaks associated with ionic motion. Conductivity testing revealed that the plasticized polymer electrolyte reached a maximum ionic conductivity of 2.305 x 10^-4 S/cm, a performance level deemed adequate for device production. To clarify the transport mechanism, transference number measurements were performed on the electrolyte. The measurement confirmed that the dominant fraction of conducting species consisted of ions, establishing that ionic mobility governs the electrical conductivity of the plasticized polymer blend rather than electronic transport pathways. Electrochemical stability assessments using linear sweep voltammetry confirmed the capacity of the electrolyte to resist electrical breakdown under applied voltage. Furthermore, cyclic voltammetry was conducted to examine ion storage and interface reactions at the boundary between the electrodes and the electrolyte. The resulting cyclic voltammograms displayed a characteristic rectangular pattern, while galvanostatic charge-discharge testing produced an almost ideal profile, confirming that the fabricated capacitor operates through non-faradaic charge storage processes. Overall performance testing of the assembled electric double-layer capacitor demonstrated low equivalent series resistance and high specific capacitance as key experimental outcomes. The resulting energy storage device achieved energy densities ranging from 9.6 to 7.61 Wh/kg and power densities ranging from 1791 to 1475 W/kg across testing conditions. The researchers noted that these combined structural and electrochemical results substantiate the operational viability of biodegradable solid polymer electrolytes in advancing green capacitor storage technology. artigo.texto: St. Joseph County Council advances proposal to ban non-legacy hyper-scale data centers The Area Plan Commission voted unanimously against the proposal earlier on Tuesday SOUTH BEND, Ind. (WNDU) - The St. Joseph County Council took the next step Tuesday on a proposal that would ban non-legacy hyper-scale data centers, hours after the Area Plan Commission voted unanimously against it. Tuesday was the first reading of the proposal, which would prohibit future hyper-scale data centers in unincorporated parts of St. Joseph County that exceed one million square feet. County Council President Bryan Tanner sent the proposal to the Land Use Planning Committee. Tanner said the proposal also creates definitions that are not currently in the county’s development code. “It is institutionalizing a new definition that hasn’t historically existed in our development code for what a hyper-scale data center is,” Tanner said. “There will also be a new definition for what is considered a legacy data center.” Officials said a meeting focusing on public comment and discussion of the proposal will be held in December. artigo.texto: A movement opposing data center development in Rapid City appears to be gaining momentum in City Hall. Put simply, residents pressed the City Council with two options: halt data centers in the community or face potential recall petitions. As City Hall packed Monday night, citizens broke decorum standards, applauding, cheering and offering City Council an ultimatum. No one spoke in favor of data center development at the meeting. Several called back to advocate Jeff Shelton’s comments last week, pushing for a year-long moratorium on the matter, some threatening potential recall petitions, and recommending Council put the matter on the agenda at the Monday meeting. This comes as Council was considering but ultimately pushed back ordinances tied to data center development. Justin Huntley is the former flood plan and air quality manager for the city. He said it’s time to act. “Part of the programs I was involved with – we worked on the data center ordinance," Huntley said. "A lot of people put a lot of time into that. By delaying that ordinance, you’re leaving the window open for things to happen that nobody in this city wants. I would just ask that you, immediately, either approve the ordinance as written and amend it as needed, or apply the moratorium as soon as possible.” Resident Gabbi DeMarce said it simply doesn’t have to be this way. “You are looking at only a fraction of residents in Rapid City that do not support decisions made that subsidize, support, or depend on harmful, unnecessary projects like data centers, simply because it has always been that way," DeMarce said. "I urge you all to extend this moratorium. You have nothing to lose from data center companies and everything to lose in public trust and support.” A recent, Council-backed survey of residents found deep seeded opposition to data center development. Resident Taylor Gunhammer’s impassioned plea perhaps best reflects the growing tension in Council chambers. “It’s not Peter Thiel’s community, it’s not Elon Musk’s community, and we won’t stand for you selling it to them – we don’t want it," Gunhammer said. "We, the people, are not the hammer in your hand, you are the hammer in ours. If you serve the people of this community, as you claim to, there is nothing to discuss. We gave our ruling. You don’t have one. You work for us.” Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun has called upon the Council to act quickly. Council ultimately did not motion put the matter on the Monday night agenda.

artigo.texto: Japan said on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) that Southeast Asian nations will be able to access its crude oil storage facilities as part of efforts to prepare the region for a future energy crisis. The announcement came as leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) met in Manila, where energy security has been high on the agenda. Keep track | ASEAN Summit LIVE updates: PM Modi at ASEAN-India Summit; Quad meeting likely after President Trump arrives Addressing regional leaders, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said her country's "hydro-tanks" would be available for use under the proposed initiative for cooperation on oil stockpiling. ASEAN members have been grappling with fuel shortages and price hikes after the West Asia conflict squeezed the flow of crude to the region. The regional bloc has previously called for "unimpeded" passage through the Strait of Hormuz, which was closed following U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. Under the Japanese POWERR Asia initiative, ASEAN nations will be able to use Japan's excess storage capacity for crude oil. "We have suggested to utilise our crude oil stockpiling facilities in Japan, which is not utilised," Japan's Foreign Ministry press secretary Toshihiro Kitamura told reporters on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit. "By utilising those unused facilities in Japan, we can stockpile the other countries' crude oil and in case of crisis... it's a kind of joint stockpiling system." Japan has 254 days' worth of oil reserves, Mr. Kitamura said, while at the outbreak of the West Asia war in February some ASEAN countries had less than a month's worth. An ASEAN-backed study for joint stockpiling of oil has also recommended using facilities in Thailand and Indonesia, but Kitamura said a final decision had not been made. "It's under specific discussion," Mr. Kitamura said. "But as a government in Japan, we are ready to work with ASEAN countries to utilise our own facilities," he said. Longer term, Tokyo plans to assist ASEAN countries to build their own "stockpiling facilities". "I think this is very important in order to prepare ourselves for future possibilities, crises." Philippine Energy Secretary Sharon Garin said a memorandum of cooperation signed with Japan on Monday (November 16) included assistance to "put up many more facilities to store more oil, whether (that) is diesel, gas or crude oil", in the archipelago nation. "What this means is the Philippines will be more prepared in ensuring there is adequate oil for our homes and businesses, whatever the situation is," Ms. Garin told reporters. "With our reserves in place, we would be better positioned to support our transport, markets, and industries." Published - November 17, 2026 02:50 pm IST

artigo.texto: Empresas, profissionais e instituições ligados ao setor de data centers podem participar da Pesquisa Nacional de Data Centers, que recebe respostas até o dia 30 de novembro. A iniciativa busca reunir informações sobre o mercado brasileiro e identificar desafios e oportunidades para o desenvolvimento da infraestrutura digital no país. A pesquisa é conduzida pela Agência Brasileira de Desenvolvimento Industrial (ABDI), em parceria com o Centro de Pesquisa e Desenvolvimento em Telecomunicações (CPQD), como parte do Projeto ECOS – Data Centers Sustentáveis. O levantamento pretende reunir dados e opiniões de empresas, operadores, fornecedores, instituições públicas, universidades e outras organizações que atuam no segmento. Entre os temas abordados estão investimentos, infraestrutura, disponibilidade de energia, conectividade, formação de profissionais, sustentabilidade, regulação e inovação tecnológica. As informações coletadas serão utilizadas na elaboração de um diagnóstico sobre o setor de data centers no Brasil. O estudo deverá servir de base para identificar oportunidades de expansão, fortalecer a cadeia produtiva nacional e orientar possíveis políticas públicas relacionadas à infraestrutura digital e à soberania tecnológica. Além do questionário, o projeto realizou entrevistas técnicas, visitas presenciais e workshops em diferentes regiões do país. Os encontros foram organizados para discutir questões específicas de cada mercado regional. Em Campinas (SP), os debates abordaram infraestrutura energética e digital, inovação tecnológica, ambiente regulatório e oportunidades para ampliar a participação da indústria nacional na cadeia de data centers. Em Fortaleza (CE), o foco esteve na conectividade internacional por cabos submarinos, no potencial de geração de energia renovável, na infraestrutura de transmissão e nas condições para atrair novos investimentos. Já em Porto Alegre (RS), as discussões trataram da resistência da infraestrutura digital a eventos climáticos extremos, da segurança operacional, da conectividade regional e da continuidade de serviços essenciais. A participação na pesquisa permanece aberta até 30 de novembro e pode ser feita por organizações e profissionais ligados ao setor. Como participar: o questionário está disponível no site da ABDI, na página do Projeto ECOS – Data Centers Sustentáveis: https://www.abdi.com.br/projeto-ecos/#participe-da-pesquisa

artigo.texto: OLYPHANT — More than 200 people cheered on 27 Lackawanna County residents who urged council Tuesday not to settle a data center developer’s lawsuit and forgo the public hearing process for Project Triboro in exchange for $101 million. Council chose not to listen. Olyphant Borough Council voted 5-2 during a special meeting to approve the settlement with ERCOR Triboro LLC allowing it to move forward with plans to develop seven 420,000-square-foot data centers and a substation within the footprints of four previously approved warehouses off Marshwood Road and Route 247. Council President Jimmy Baldan and council members Beth Frushon, Eric Hartshorn, Tony Delfino and Fred Hartman voted in favor of the settlement. Council Vice President Robert Hudak and Councilman Mike Abda dissented. In an identical 5-2 vote, the council members approved a 15-year, $101 million community benefits agreement with ERCOR Triboro that was widely opposed by the community. Project Triboro will still be subject to the land development process under Olyphant’s planning commission as they modify their plans from warehouses to data centers — a detail project representatives stressed Tuesday night. But Project Triboro will not be required to navigate the conditional use hearing process, where residents would have had the opportunity to cross-examine data center representatives at public hearings and present their own evidence. Victor, New York-based ERCOR sued Olyphant in June in a bid to sidestep that process and develop its data centers as principal permitted uses. People crowded the Rescue & Restore Church sanctuary during the nearly three-hour meeting that culminated in council’s decision. As furious residents shouted at council and data center officials, half a dozen Olyphant police swarmed the front of the sanctuary after a hasty adjournment following the votes. “Give us each a million dollars for our house, then you could have our freaking town you dirtbags,” a woman yelled as the meeting adjourned. “I hate you all.” Borough police maintained a heavy presence throughout the night, including shutting down Willow Avenue and surrounding streets for the duration of the meeting. Police received credible threats of violence; officers arrested a Taylor man Tuesday, charging him with terroristic threats and harassment, Police Chief James DeVoe said. The man’s name was unavailable Tuesday night. Following a brief presentation by ERCOR Triboro and Emergent Data Centers, who partnered with ERCOR to design and develop the data centers, residents addressed council. Every speaker opposed the settlement and CBA, either asking council to table its decision or to outright deny it. Lifelong resident Nicole Pasko, 27, one of the first speakers Tuesday, stood before council and described her pride in Olyphant and its small-town charm. “By allowing this corporation to buy you and your cooperation, you are directly sewing shut the mouths of your constituents,” Pasko said. “Grow a backbone and say, ‘No.’ Listen to those that voted you into these positions. Your vote tonight shows exactly what you think about the people of our town, our opinions and our futures.” As residents discussed the night’s proceedings on the sidewalk in front of Rescue & Rescue Church after the decision, Lackawanna County Commissioner Bill Gaughan said council’s complete disdain for public comment was embarrassing. Gaughan, who also spoke during the meeting, criticized council members for failing to explain their decision. “For them again not to explain their vote is a complete dereliction of duty on their part,” Gaughan said, calling it their basic responsibility. “They didn’t even do that, and it just shows a complete lack of respect for the people.” Check back for updates.
