artigo.texto: HILLSBORO, Texas (KXXV) — The proposed Provident data center has now pulled out of its agreement to come to Hillsboro. - “They’re taking a lot of the farmland, and I’m not happy about that," said Sheila Brazil. - In August 2026, the city announced that Provident no longer had the property under contract. “We’re going to have to pay their water and their electric bill, and I don’t think that’s fair," said Shelia Brazil, a Hill County resident. In this case, Sheila Brazil thinks less is best. Brazil, a Hill County resident, said that with Provident Data Centers backing out of coming to Hillsboro, she’s completely okay with it. “They’re taking a lot of the farmland, and I’m not happy about that," said Brazil. According to the City of Hillsboro, the city's economic development corporation entered into a contract with Provident in September 2024 for the potential sale of approximately 300 acres. In August 2026, the city announced that Provident no longer had the property under contract. “That contract on the land, everything before close is a matter of due diligence. So they were going through their processes to see whether the project could come to fruition. There’s a lot of uncertainty, statewide, around data centers, and at the time they were in a month-to-month contract extension period and decided to terminate," said Jessica Trew, the executive director for the Hillsboro Economic Development Corporation. Trew explained that the initial contract for Provident was for nine months to complete its due diligence. Afterwards, she said the company started asking for contract extensions. Trew said she’s unsure why Provident ended the contract. 25 News reached out to Provident Data Centers, but we have not heard back. TA Smith, the founder of the Texas Coalition Against Data Centers, said he’s not sure what to believe. "Everyone keeps saying Provident is backing out… are they? They might have backed out on paper; they may have publicly backed out, but have they actually left?" said TA Smith, founder of the Texas Coalition Against Data Centers. But Provident may not be the only data center backing out on projects. Data Center Watch reports at least 75 data center projects worth billions were blocked or delayed in the first quarter of 2026. Smith said regardless of the reason, this is good news. “At the moment it gives you a sigh of relief, but again next month it’s a different story and that same company…there’s nothing against them coming back...here’s a new proposal with a new zoning board committee," said Smith. Trew said the EDC isn’t for or against data centers, and the property once sought by Provident cannot be used for farmland. Brazil said whatever comes to Hill County can impact many people. “And we care about what comes up, what comes here, and what’s going to affect us," said Brazil.

artigo.texto: As developers pursue new data center projects in SF, the Board of Supervisors voted Tuesday to extend a moratorium on new facilities, citing unanswered questions about their environmental impacts and demands on the city's power grid. San Francisco supervisors voted unanimously Tuesday to extend the temporary ban for 10 months and 15 days, as the Chronicle reports. The extension, recommended by the Land Use and Transportation Committee on Monday, gives the Planning Department more time to examine the facilities' potential effects and develop regulations before the city considers approving additional projects. The vote follows a report released last week by the Planning Department that identified significant gaps in the city's understanding of existing data centers, including their electricity and water consumption, pollution, and effects on surrounding neighborhoods, as SFist reported previously. The department stopped short of recommending whether San Francisco should allow more facilities, but outlined several policy changes officials could consider, including restricting standalone data centers in residential and commercial areas and requiring developers to assess impacts on nearby communities. According to Mission Local, the report also recommended updating the city's definition of a data center, which currently relies on language dating back to 2001, to better align with the state's definition. The department's assessment examined the city's three standalone facilities but acknowledged that San Francisco does not maintain a complete inventory of smaller data centers operating inside other buildings. Data Center Map, meanwhile, identifies 15 potential facilities throughout the city, many of them downtown. Two of the larger standalone facilities are located along Paul Avenue in Bayview Hunters Point, a neighborhood that has experienced disproportionate air pollution for decades due to industrial operations, truck traffic, and a former PG&E power plant that closed in 2006. District 10 Supervisor Shamann Walton, who represents the neighborhood and introduced the original moratorium in October, said the city needs to understand how the facilities affect residents before allowing additional development. “We really don't know the impact of data centers to our communities,” Walton said before Tuesday's vote. The Planning Department's report also warned that larger facilities could place substantial demands on an electricity grid already approaching its transmission capacity. A 50-megawatt data center could use as much electricity as 25,000 new homes, potentially competing with housing, hospitals, and businesses for limited power resources, as previously reported. Other concerns include air pollution and noise from backup generators. Developers have explored potential data center projects at the shuttered SF Centre mall downtown and in Dogpatch. NOVVA, an existing facility at 400 Paul Ave. in Bayview, had also planned to expand from nine to 36 megawatts by 2028, but those plans are now on hold. The moratorium comes as San Francisco attempts to balance its ambitions to remain a center of the AI industry against the infrastructure demands of the facilities needed to support it. As the Chronicle notes, Mayor Daniel Lurie has made attracting tech investment part of his economic strategy, while labor groups have argued that data centers could create union construction jobs and help fund needed infrastructure improvements. In a letter Monday, Building and Construction Trades Council leader Rudy Gonzalez, who ran Supervisor Connie Chan’s campaign for US Congress, opposed a permanent ban, arguing that developers should have a path to approval if they meet enforceable environmental and labor standards and cover the costs of the infrastructure they require. He also urged the city to distinguish large commercial facilities from smaller research and development sites. Walton acknowledged the union's concerns and said he intends to involve labor and community groups in developing future restrictions. Per the Chronicle, public speakers at Monday's committee hearing, meanwhile, questioned whether data centers would deliver meaningful employment benefits, given the relatively small number of workers needed to operate them. Others raised concerns about pollution and the concentration of facilities in communities already facing environmental burdens. San Francisco now joins Oakland and Seattle in extending temporary restrictions while officials work on regulations. As SFist reported last week, Oakland supervisors also voted unanimously to extend that city's moratorium for another 10 months and 15 days, through October 5, 2027. Oakland is reviewing potential effects on its electricity grid, water supply, and air quality after receiving inquiries from developers, including Behring Companies, which proposed putting a data center inside a downtown office building. (MegaWhat) A disputa envolve o rateio dos custos da contratação do armazenamento. - A regra atual prevê que os custos fiquem apenas com os geradores de energia. - A Abeeólica argumenta que, na contratação de reserva de capacidade, os custos são distribuídos entre os usuários finais do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). - Segundo os geradores, os benefícios do armazenamento são de natureza sistêmica para todo o SIN, portanto os custos devem ser divididos por todo o setor. - Entidades que representam os consumidores defendem que a expansão das fontes renováveis intermitentes gerou a necessidade de capacidade firme, por isso, o custo do armazenamento deve ficar com o segmento de geração, sem onerar as tarifas da população. - Veja as principais discussões levantadas pelo setor na consulta pública sobre os leilões. Em paralelo, continua travado no Congresso Nacional o projeto de lei 3.716/2026, que muda o rateio dos custos. O relator, deputado federal Danilo Forte (PP/CE), havia prometido apresentar o parecer na semana passada, o que não ocorreu. - O autor do projeto, o deputado federal Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania/SP), diz que não há justificativa para que a contratação de armazenamento tenha uma regra de custeio diferente daquela aplicada aos demais mecanismos de reserva de capacidade. artigo.texto: ACME Solar Holdings Limited has announced the commissioning of an additional Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) component with a capacity of 52.32 MW / 209.28 MWh for its firm and dispatchable renewable energy project in Bikaner district, Rajasthan. The newly commissioned storage component is scheduled to achieve its commercial operation date (COD) on November 19, 2026. Following this latest development, the cumulative commissioned capacity of the project’s battery energy storage component has reached 247.67 MW / 990.68 MWh. The overall installed storage capacity of the project stands at 247.67 MW / 1,321 MWh, marking further progress in the company’s efforts to strengthen its renewable energy and storage portfolio. The project is being developed through a wholly owned subsidiary of ACME Solar Holdings Limited. The company has also entered into a Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with SJVN Limited for the supply of electricity generated under the firm and dispatchable renewable energy project. The commissioning of the additional BESS capacity represents an important step towards improving the project’s energy storage capabilities and supporting the reliable supply of renewable power. Battery storage systems play a significant role in managing the intermittent nature of renewable energy generation by storing electricity and making it available when required. With the latest addition, ACME Solar continues to advance its integrated renewable energy development strategy, combining solar power generation with battery storage solutions. The project also highlights the growing importance of energy storage infrastructure in supporting India’s transition towards a more reliable and flexible renewable energy system. artigo.texto: Singapore is stepping up carbon market cooperation with several countries at the 31st UN Climate Change Conference, signing an implementation agreement on carbon credit cooperation with Kenya and renewing a memorandum of understanding with Colombia on Monday (16 November). The signing ceremony took place at the Singapore Pavilion at the conference venue. Since signing its first memorandum of understanding on carbon credit trading in 2022, Singapore has established cooperation with more than 30 countries. According to a statement from the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry, the implementation agreement with Kenya establishes a legally binding bilateral mechanism for transferring high-quality carbon credits with corresponding adjustments under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Businesses are expected to be able to submit carbon credit projects for government authorisation from 2027. “Corresponding adjustments” refer to an accounting mechanism that ensures the same emissions reductions are not counted by both the buyer and the seller. This is Singapore’s 13th implementation agreement on carbon credit cooperation, and its third with an African country, after Ghana and Rwanda. In her speech, Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu said: “We meet amid global headwinds, but Singapore remains steadfast in our commitment to climate action. No country can tackle climate change alone.” She said it was heartening for Singapore to work with like-minded countries, and praised Kenya for demonstrating considerable leadership in the green transition. In 2024, over 90% of Kenya's electricity was generated from renewable sources. In 2024, Kenyan projects accounted for about one fifth of voluntary carbon market revenues across Africa. Singapore and Kenya signed a memorandum of understanding on carbon credit cooperation in 2023. Typically, the two sides first sign a memorandum of understanding to set the direction for cooperation, before entering substantive negotiations and eventually signing a legally binding implementation agreement. Singapore and Kenya, both founding members of the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets, have actively advocated the development of high-quality carbon markets. Fu noted that Singapore and Kenya have complementary strengths. Kenya is one of Africa’s most established carbon markets, with a clear legal framework in place, while Singapore is a financial and carbon services hub. Together, this can help credible projects in Kenya attract the investment they need. Expanding cooperation with Colombia This is Singapore’s second memorandum of understanding on carbon credit cooperation with Colombia. The first memorandum, signed with the South American country in 2022, has expired. The new memorandum of understanding not only continues the partnership but also broadens its scope. It establishes a framework for dialogue, technical cooperation, exchanges of experience and the exploration of opportunities for cooperation in carbon markets and areas related to Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Fu stressed that the two countries would work towards a legally binding implementation agreement that could take their cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement to the next stage. “Colombia has tremendous potential for high-quality climate action – in its forests and natural ecosystems, in energy and industry, and in waste.” Besides its cooperation with Kenya and Colombia, Singapore also approved its first carbon credit project from Rwanda last Saturday (14 November) and signed a memorandum of understanding on carbon market cooperation with Bangladesh.

artigo.texto: BYD supera Toyota na preferência por eletrificados, diz pesquisa Pesquisa da Webmotors mostra que metade dos donos de eletrificados tem modelos chineses; pós-venda ainda é desafio para novas fabricantes As marcas chinesas estão ganhando espaço na preferência dos consumidores brasileiros e já superam montadoras tradicionais em diferentes indicadores do mercado automotivo, segundo pesquisa da Webmotors Autoinsights. A BYD ultrapassou a Toyota na intenção de compra de veículos eletrificados, enquanto fabricantes como Omoda Jaecoo, Geely e GAC também aparecem entre as marcas emergentes mais consideradas pelos motoristas. No levantamento sobre eletrificados, realizado em junho com mais de 1.200 usuários da plataforma, a BYD lidera a intenção de compra, com 24% das menções, ante 17% em 2025. A Toyota, que ocupava a primeira posição no ano passado, caiu de 28% para 19%. A presença chinesa também aparece entre quem já possui um eletrificado. Cerca de metade dos proprietários ouvidos tem um carro de marca chinesa. A BYD concentra 25% das menções, seguida por Toyota (14,2%), GWM (9,4%) e Caoa Chery (4,7%). Omoda Jaecoo, GAC e Geely também aparecem na lista. O avanço também aparece nas buscas da plataforma. Entre junho de 2025 e junho de 2026, os contatos de compradores com vendedores de eletrificados da BYD cresceram e chegaram a 2,9 vezes o volume registrado pela Toyota. A GWM teve alta de 119% no período. Para Eduardo Jurcevic, CEO da Webmotors, a competitividade das fabricantes chinesas está relacionada à escala de produção e à oferta de tecnologia. "As marcas chinesas chegaram a esse mercado com uma vantagem de escala: a eletrificação já representa 52% das vendas de carros de passeio na China, e o país exportou 2,6 milhões de eletrificados em 2025, alta de 104% em um ano. Isso permitiu trazer um portfólio amplo de híbridos e elétricos, com preços e condições muito competitivos", afirma. Apesar do avanço, a confiança nas fabricantes ainda é um obstáculo. Em outra pesquisa da Webmotors, realizada em setembro, apenas 17,6% disseram que comprariam uma marca nova ou pouco conhecida. Outros 44,8% descartam essa possibilidade. Quando as marcas são apresentadas pelo nome, porém, a resistência diminui. Omoda Jaecoo lidera a intenção de compra entre as fabricantes emergentes, com 30,8%, seguida por Geely (27,9%) e GAC (22,5%). A principal preocupação dos consumidores é a disponibilidade de peças e serviços de manutenção, citada por 28,9% dos entrevistados. O custo-benefício aparece em seguida, com 28,2%. "O pós-venda é, sim, a principal barreira, mas não é a única, e não se vence de uma vez só", afirma Jurcevic, acrescentando que a reputação das fabricantes e o valor de revenda também pesam na decisão de compra.

artigo.texto: Client news A&O Shearman advises Macquarie Capital on strategic joint venture with Revera Energy for UK battery storage A&O Shearman has advised Macquarie Capital on the formation of a strategic joint venture with Carlyle-backed Revera Energy, a global independent energy platform backed by global investment firm Carlyle, under which Macquarie Capital will make an initial investment alongside Revera in two transmission-connected battery energy storage system (BESS) projects in Scotland. The projects, both now under construction, are Windyhill BESS (200 MW / 400 MWh), located in Bearsden, which reached financial close and notice to proceed in February 2026 and remains on track for commercial operations in Q4 2027, and Hunterston BESS (400 MW / 800 MWh), located in North Ayrshire, which reached financial close and notice to proceed in September 2026, with commercial operations expected in Q3 2028. The partnership provides scope for further investment opportunities across Revera’s UK portfolio, including the 400 MW Kincardine BESS, and supports the UK's Clean Power 2030 Action Plan. The A&O Shearman team was led by partner Dan Graham and senior associate Arabella Robinson, with support from associates Ine Deblaere and Livia Gauntlett. The team also included energy, natural resources and infrastructure partners Edward Moser and Alexander Chenery, senior associates Saskia Volhard Martin and Arvindh Rai, and associates Kamilla Marianayagam and Aidan Swietochowski; tax partner James Burton, counsel Sorsha Taylor and associate Maria Clezy; antitrust partner Thomas Masterman and associate Amol Vani; and environment and sanctions partner Matthew Townsend and senior associate Danae Wheeler. artigo.texto: Springfield City Council to consider defining data centers, extending pauses on applications Three proposals on Monday’s agenda would add a city code definition and extend pauses through Feb. 24 SPRINGFIELD, Mo. (KY3) - The Springfield City Council on Monday night will take up three proposals. One would define what a data center is under city code. The other two would extend pauses on development and utility applications while the city works on potential regulations. The current pause expires Tuesday. The proposed extensions would run through Feb. 24. What the proposals would do Council Bill 2026-235 would amend the city’s Land Development Code by adding definitions related to data centers. The bill is up for second reading tonight. Council members can amend or adopt it, and a vote is required for it to be adopted. Unless an amendment is offered, the bill would be voted on tonight. The other two proposals would extend existing pauses on development and utility-related applications through Feb. 24. The ordinance says the Land Development Code does not currently define data centers. It says the amendment establishes a common definition of “data center” and related terms only, as a first step before consideration of later text amendments and public hearings. Steve Childers, the city’s director of planning and development, said the city has not yet written a definition for data centers. He said the city needs that definition before it can establish rules for where data centers can go and how they can operate. “We’re just taking the time to get it right, taking the time to do the due diligence we need in order to be able to do the research, pull it all together and present council with a draft ordinance that they could consider,” Childers said. Any future regulations would still have to go through additional review and public hearings. How the ordinance defines data centers Under the proposed definition, a data center is a building, or a room or portion of a building, used to house information technology equipment for the storage, management, processing or transmission of digital data. The definition lists server farms, artificial intelligence training or processing, image processing, cloud computing, email services, and cryptocurrency or other digital-asset mining, among other uses. The definition also includes backup generators, energy storage systems, on-site electric generation, cooling equipment, electrical equipment, and any substations that primarily serve the data center. The ordinance would classify data centers into three types: - Accessory data center: Located within the principal building on the lot, with a data center floor area of no more than 20% of the building’s gross floor area. It serves only the owner or a tenant of the premises, does not sell, lease, or otherwise provide data storage, processing, or computing capacity to others, and has a maximum power demand of less than 1 megawatt. - Micro data center: Not an accessory data center, with a floor area of no more than 10,000 square feet and a maximum power demand of less than 5 megawatts. - Large-load data center: Not an accessory data center, with a maximum power demand of 5 megawatts or more or a floor area of more than 10,000 square feet. The ordinance says data centers other than accessory data centers that are on the same lot or premises, on adjacent lots, or under common ownership or control and share infrastructure or a point of interconnection with the electric utility would be treated as one data center. Their floor area and maximum power demand would be combined. The ordinance would take effect immediately upon passage. The Planning and Zoning Commission held a public hearing on the amendments Oct. 15 and recommended approval, with additional changes, by a vote of 7 to 0. Existing pause and public input City Council enacted Special Ordinance 28306 on June 29 to delay the acceptance and processing of applications relating to the evaluation, establishment, servicing or expansion of a data center facility until Nov. 17. The ordinance says the city held three public engagement sessions on data centers during the delay, and city staff is reviewing the feedback. The current moratorium has put at least one proposed project on hold. Trent Overhue, who was working to develop a data center at 2900 National Ave., asked a judge for permission to keep moving forward despite the moratorium. The Greene County Circuit Court denied the request for a preliminary injunction Nov. 9. When asked about a formal interview with KY3, Overhue declined. How data centers differ Matt Powell, executive director of the Missouri Cybersecurity Center of Excellence, said many people’s digital lives rely on data centers, from online banking to storing photos and shopping online. He said data centers support technology people use in everyday life, including banks giving customers access to their money, photos and family albums on phones, and GPS on phones. “You know that phrase, it’s on someone else’s computer. That’s essentially what it is,” Powell said. Powell said data centers have large amounts of storage capabilities and are used for accessing and storing people’s data. Powell said not all data centers are the same. Some primarily store information, while others use much more electricity to power the computing behind things like artificial intelligence. Powell said data centers are essentially hubs that allow data to flow throughout the world. “At one point it used to be thought of, well, the internet’s a bunch of invisible wires that connect everyone together,” Powell said. “Well, think of data centers as those hubs. You know, that data is going to ... it goes faster, it’s able to travel further and faster when we have hubs that support that data and push it along, kind of like a relay race, right? So it’s relaying information from one point to another.” The council meeting begins at 6:30 p.m. at the Regional Police-Fire Training Center on Bat

artigo.texto: BMW Group Malaysia and Universiti Malaya (UM) are taking their second-life EV battery initiative a step further. After rolling out a solar-powered mobile device charging station at UM Sentral in August, the collaboration has now deployed a larger Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) solution to power an Orang Asli village in Pahang. As part of the RE:GENERATE x Universiti Malaya initiative, the latest project uses retired BMW EV batteries and repurposed solar panels to provide 24-hour electricity to 20 households in the Semai Orang Asli community at Kampung Saweh, Pos Sinderut, Kuala Lipis. The new system not only reduces reliance on fuel-powered generators but also provides a practical example of how EV batteries can continue to serve a useful purpose beyond their automotive lifespan. From four hours of electricity to 24-hour power supply Prior to this, residents at Kampung Saweh relied on petrol and diesel generators, which typically operated for about four hours each night. Electricity usage was largely limited to basic needs such as lighting and fans, and each household were spending about RM10 per day on generator fuel. With the new solar-powered battery storage system, all 20 households now have access to electricity throughout the day and night, at a significantly lower operating cost. More importantly, the continuous power supply opens up possibilities for appliances such as refrigerators, which can make a practical difference to the community. According to BMW Group Malaysia, families who hunt or gather food previously had no reliable means of preserving perishable items such as meat. These items had to be consumed or shared with neighbours immediately to prevent spoilage. The system has been designed to support refrigerators as households acquire them. At the moment, televisions represent the highest individual electricity load in most homes. How does the second-life BMW EV battery system work? The energy storage system was developed by Associate Professor Dr. Tan Chia Kwang and his team of researchers and students at Universiti Malaya’s Power Energy Dedicated Advanced Centre (UMPEDAC). It consists of 30 repurposed BMW EV battery modules, supported by a combined 8kW of inverter power. The system supplies electricity to all 20 households from a single centralised point, with each household allocated 3kWh of energy per day. Instead of having separate battery storage systems for individual homes, the centralised setup allows available capacity to be shared between households based on their current demand. Besides reusing old EV batteries, the solution also utilises second-life solar panels that were retired early from commercial solar farms which still has considerable usable life. During the day, the solar panels charge the batteries, which store energy for use after sunset when household electricity demand is highest. The battery modules are housed in a structure built using wood and bamboo sourced from the surrounding environment. According to BMW Group Malaysia, the repurposed batteries are expected to serve the village for at least another five years under the current system design. This is comparable to or longer than the lifespan of new lead-acid batteries commonly used for rural electrification. The installation was carried out over five days from 23 to 27 October 2026, with the system going live during the team’s visit. Not all retired EV batteries are equal One of the challenges of repurposing EV batteries is that not every battery has the same remaining capacity or condition. According to Universiti Malaya, the research team has spent two years developing a methodology to evaluate and reconfigure used batteries for second-life applications. Each battery undergoes State of Health (SoH) testing at the cell level. Cells that have significantly degraded are removed, while those that meet the required performance thresholds are reassembled into new battery packs. The researchers found that newer-generation BMW batteries typically retain more usable energy, averaging 1.6kWh per pack, while older-generation batteries average around 0.5kWh. This allows the team to match battery packs to different applications based on their remaining capacity. Higher-capacity packs are used for more demanding applications such as rural electrification to power home appliances in off-grid villages. Meanwhile, lower-capacity packs can be used for simpler tasks such as charging smartphones. In August 2026, BMW Group Malaysia and Universiti Malaya deployed their first real-world installation under the partnership, a solar-powered smartphone charging station at the UM Sentral bus stop. The station uses three repurposed BMW battery modules with a combined capacity of 1.5kWh. These modules had retained just 30-40% of their original capacity, demonstrating that even heavily degraded EV batteries can still be useful for less demanding applications. BMW previously repurposed EV batteries for mobile EV charging This isn’t BMW Group Malaysia’s first attempt at giving retired EV batteries a second life. Back in May 2023, BMW Group Malaysia worked with EV Connection to introduce what it described as Malaysia’s first Mobile Charging Vehicle powered by repurposed BMW and MINI EV batteries. Unveiled at the Malaysia Autoshow 2023, the mobile charging solution uses 16 repurposed battery modules with approximately 70% State of Health. The latest rural electrification project builds on this concept by using retired EV batteries as a stationary energy storage solution for an off-grid community. According to Universiti Malaya, repurposing used EV batteries requires extensive testing, grading and modification due to differences in battery condition. The university also highlighted that the cost of supporting components remains substantial, despite receiving retired EV batteries from BMW and donated solar panels. artigo.texto: Irondale sets rules for data centers before any are proposed, but resident raises loophole concerns Irondale is putting rules in place for potential data centers before any companies come knocking. The City Council voted unanimously to approve an ordinance regulating data center development after a second reading and a chance for residents to comment. Mayor James Stewart Jr. said no data centers have been proposed in the city, and no companies have expressed interest in building one. The regulations follow a six- to seven-month study led by a city councilor. Stewart said the goal is to prepare for potential development while protecting residents. Under the ordinance, data center companies must pay for any necessary power grid upgrades, keep noise within a specified limit and use a closed-loop cooling system. The ordinance also establishes a community benefit agreement intended to support schools, infrastructure and nonprofit organizations and requires the data center company to complete a certification every year to hold it responsible. Stewart said he hopes the ordinance will help residents make informed decisions about data centers while providing safeguards for the community. “A lot of this has to do with education,” Stewart said. “We’re hoping that the ordinance provides that information. It gives you the opportunity to be able to educate our citizens more, but then it also, at the end of the day, protects our community.” The mayor said three residents spoke during the meeting, and one opposed bringing data centers to Irondale. That resident didn’t want to go on camera but expressed concerns about specific language data centers can use to find loopholes around the established regulations. She also feels like the six-to seven-month study is outdated and so much has changed with data centers since it was done. She said she felt like a moratorium on data centers would’ve been better, but Stewart said that would only allow for the city to do more research, which it's already done.

artigo.texto: Georgetown panel recommends denial of rezoning for northeast data center after outcry GEORGETOWN, Texas — Georgetown's Planning and Zoning Commission unanimously recommended denying a rezoning request Tuesday night for a proposed data center in northeast Georgetown, following opposition from residents concerned about the project's proximity to neighborhoods and future development. More than 100 people signed up to speak at Tuesday's meeting as commissioners considered a request to rezone approximately 28 acres near East University Avenue and Northeast Inner Loop. Commissioners ultimately voted unanimously to recommend denying the proposal, citing concerns about how close the data center would be to nearby neighborhoods and its potential impact on future development. Residents raised concerns about potential light and noise pollution, as well as how the project could affect the surrounding area. The proposal includes a data center, on-site generators and closed-loop cooling systems. A representative of the developer, Phillip Niels, said the project would use low-level lighting and was designed to limit noise compared to larger artificial intelligence data centers. ALSO| More camp safety law changes could be on their way in Texas Niels also said the project could generate millions of dollars in property tax revenue for the city. "If this project is built as planned, it will be the largest taxpayer in Georgetown," Niels said. "Should deliver 10 to 15 million dollars a year in property taxes." The rezoning request would increase the maximum allowed data center building footprint from 5,000 to 290,000 square feet. Among those opposing the location were Judy Fabry and Kerry Brun, who said they have lived about half a mile from the proposed site for more than 30 years. "It's too close to houses. It will ruin any other development in that area. And we need a grocery store out there," Fabry said. "There's a lot of downsides, I think. I don't even know what an upside of having a data center would be," Brun said. Despite the commission's unanimous recommendation to deny the rezoning request, the proposal is not yet officially rejected. Georgetown City Council is expected to consider the rezoning request and the commission's recommendation on Dec. 8. Because the Planning and Zoning Commission recommended denial, the City Council would need a 6-1 vote to overturn that recommendation and approve the rezoning request. This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

artigo.texto: For all the talk of this month’s election being about a referendum on President Donald Trump, voters had other considerations on their mind, too. Data centers and artificial intelligence had a “huge impact, huge impact,” state Rep.-elect Ryan Kominakis, D-Valparaiso, said. More than 500 state legislative seats were flipped nationwide, he said. “I’ve been in this for a while, and I’ve never seen anything like this ever,” state Rep. Chuck Moseley, D-Portage, said. “I find it hard to believe that that many people could be wrong,” his wife told him. Utilities and data centers were the main topic that came up when Kominakis was knocking on doors in his campaign to unseat incumbent Republican Ed Soliday. “A lot of people are frustrated with the data centers,” Kominakis said, with voters citing the one that had been proposed near Wheeler High School in Union Township and another whether Valparaiso had initially proposed a sports complex. “All these horror stories,” he said, and no regulations made voters wary. Adding to that is the $655 million and counting in tax revenue loss from state economic development giveaways to data center developers. “We’ve got to repeal that law or at bare minimum amend it,” Kominakis said. He has a Dec. 11 deadline to give the Legislative Services Agency, which drafts legislation, his proposal to repeal those tax breaks, require project labor agreements for union wages for data centers that receive scaled-back tax breaks, limit their locations so they can’t be near schools or neighborhoods, and require environmental protection. Kominakis, a Democrat, plans to seek his caucus leadership for advice on the direction his legislation takes. “I want to make sure we’re doing the right thing, making the correct strategic moves,” he said. He credits his Nov. 3 victory to Republicans staying home or switching sides as well as Democrats showing up. “Voters talked about it at the door. Not every door I knocked talked about data centers, but some did,” Moseley said. The Democratic incumbent won re-election. Voters’ concerns ranged from extending big money for tax credits and other incentives to questions about the noise data centers generate. “Everything, everything. He also said he’s against non-disclosure agreements. Houldieson previously told the Post-Tribune that he wants to focus on utility affordability at the statehouse. He’s unsure what legislation he’ll support or draft yet. “I’m thinking about all of that,” Houldieson said. “I’m still learning the ropes of the legislature, and I probably will be learning a lot for a while, so I can’t say what legislation I’m going to be putting forward.” State Rep.-elect Nick Neal, D-Crown Point, said it’s important to him that residents’ data center concerns are heard and that utility customers are protected as developments come in. artigo.texto: Data centers no Brasil terão que ter licença prévia dos EUA para comprar chips de IA da Nvidia Medida dos EUA também atinge Singapura, Malásia, Tailândia e Indonésia para impedir que empresas chinesas usem chips avançados da Nvidia Resumo - Departamento de Comércio passou a exigir licença prévia para a compra de chips avançados de IA da Nvidia. - Objetivo da medida é impedir que empresas chinesas e de Macau acessem tecnologia americana por meio de servidores no exterior. - A restrição atinge data centers no Brasil, Singapura, Malásia, Tailândia e Indonésia. - Exigência vale para centros que fornecem mais de 12 milhões de unidades de processamento a empresas de Macau ou do Grupo D:5 (como a China). - Norma foi adotada logo após um escândalo de espionagem forçar a renúncia de Jensen Huang do comando da Nvidia. O governo dos Estados Unidos emitiu nesta segunda-feira, dia 16, uma norma para impedir que empresas chinesas utilizem chips avançados de inteligência artificial (IA) dos EUA em centros de dados de outros países. Dentre os países afetados estão data centers no Brasil, Singapura, Malásia, Tailândia e Indonésia. Na prática, data centers que fornecem mais de 12 milhões de unidades de desempenho de processamento a empresas de Macau ou dos países do Grupo D:5, que inclui a China, precisam obter licença prévia do governo americano para comprarem chips avançados de IA da Nvidia. Conforme o Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), a norma evita que restrições a tecnologias sensíveis dos EUA sejam contornadas por data centers de países terceiros. As empresas norte-americanas que operam nesses países, incluindo o Brasil, mas bloqueiam o acesso a países restritos ficam isentas da exigência da licença. A medida, adotada pelo Departamento de Comércio americano, é tomada logo após um escândalo de espionagem ter forçado a renúncia de Jensen Huang como diretor-executivo da Nvidia, em meio a relatos de que ele ajudou a facilitar o acesso da China à tecnologia de sua empresa, em violação às normas americanas. Proibição à China Em virtude de medidas sucessivas dos governos de Joe Biden (2021-2025) e Donald Trump, está proibida a venda dos processadores de tecnologia americana mais avançados para empresas chinesas. Washington justifica essas restrições pelo receio de que a China desenvolva uma IA de ponta para fins militares e, mais recentemente, também para conter o avanço de Pequim para a superinteligência. A superinteligência marcaria o momento em que a IA superaria as capacidades humanas de raciocínio e compreensão, e muitos consideram que quem alcançar esse estágio primeiro obterá uma vantagem decisiva nos campos tecnológico e estratégico. O secretário de Comércio dos Estados Unidos, Howard Lutnick, foi acusado por vários observadores de ter trabalhado para flexibilizar as regras de exportação de chips americanos para a China. Na sexta-feira, 13, o secretário do Tesouro, Scott Bessent, criticou publicamente seu colega de governo por essa questão. O documento que apresenta as novas regras de exportação foi publicado pelo Departamento de Comércio, mas foi "redigido pelo Departamento do Tesouro e pelo Conselho de Segurança Nacional, a pedido de ambos", segundo um comunicado do governo americano. Impactos para o Brasil De acordo com o especialista em gestão e governança de riscos digitais, cibersegurança e proteção de dados digitais, Paulo Nascimento, na prática, os data centers brasileiros de grande porte precisam adquirir esses processadores de ponta. “Só que a partir de agora eles precisam de uma autorização dos EUA e essa exigência acaba sendo ativada quando esse poder computacional vai ultrapassando determinado limite, que é de 750 chips NVidia H-100”, exemplifica Nascimento. Ele aponta os principais riscos para os data centers instalados ou em processo de instalação no Ceará. “Primeiro é o atraso e o encarecimento dos projetos porque agora vai depender dessa licença americana, que pode ou não ser concedida. Segundo, a incerteza para novos investimentos. Os investidores vão pensar duas ou três vezes antes de colocar alguns bilhões em projetos que dependem de autorização de um outro país. E o terceiro risco, seria uma vantagem competitiva para as operadoras americanas, que estão isentas dessa exigência”, elenca. De acordo com o professor do Departamento de Telemática do Instituto Federal do Ceará (IFCE), campus Fortaleza, Wendell Rodrigues, a decisão pode, sim, afetar o País. “Isso não vai impactar quem já tenha esse acesso a esses chips, mas nas novas aquisições e novos projetos. Aqui mesmo no Instituto Federal a gente deve adquirir nos próximos meses toda uma plataforma baseada em chips avançados de inteligência artificial conhecida como GPUs”, cita. Para o idealizador do projeto Iracema Digital, Mauro Oliveira, “a regra inclui o Brasil por risco presumido de desvio, sem apresentar um caso concreto envolvendo o País. Somos suspeitos do que poderíamos fazer”. Ele lembra, contudo, que empresas sediadas nos EUA, ou controladas por matrizes americanas ficam dispensadas da licença. “A big tech americana instalada em solo brasileiro segue recebendo seus chips. A empresa brasileira entra na fila”, critica. Por sua vez, o diretor do Fórum Brasileiro de Internet das Coisas, Vivaldo José Breternitz, minimiza o impacto da decisão sobre o Brasil. “É mais oba-oba. Eu acho que o Trump tomou esse tipo de medida pensando nas eleições que aconteceram. Algum atraso pode ocorrer, algum aumento de custo pode ocorrer, mas nada que vá mudar radicalmente o cenário de investimentos nos data centers que estão sendo construídos aqui”, pondera. Já a Associação das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação e de Tecnologias Digitais do Brasil (Brasscom) disse, por meio de sua assessoria, que não comentaria sobre o assunto. O POVO também tentou contato com as principais empresas do setor de armazenamento de dados que atuam no Ceará, a Omnia e a Tecto Data Centers, e aguarda posicionamento para atualização posterior. (C

artigo.texto: The data center capital of the world is pressing pause on legislative approvals for the digital infrastructure facilities through as late as September of next year. The Loudoun County Board of Supervisors voted 7-1, with one abstaining, Tuesday evening to halt consideration of legislative applications for data centers and substations, with a retroactive effective date of Sept. 15. Thirty-three legislative applications are currently active, according to the resolution. Supervisor Kristen Umstattd, who represents the Leesburg District, voted against the motion, and Supervisor Caleb Kershner, who represents the Catoctin District, abstained. "Just the fact of the matter is that this development of data centers has moved a lot faster than the board has been able to respond," Supervisor Juli Briskman, who proposed the review that culminated in the resolution, said just before the vote. "And we did have a lot of missed opportunities to respond and get this under control, as our constituents have been begging us to do, and this is a golden opportunity to do that tonight," added Briskman, who represents the Algonkian District. Loudoun County is in the second phase of its impact study that would establish new guidance and standards for data centers and substations. The result of that study is expected to be released next spring. The county's pause comes as communities across the U.S. are fighting to slow down the rapidly spreading asset class. Next door to Loudoun, Prince William County in September drastically shrank its map for data centers that are allowed by right. Montgomery County instituted an 18-month data center freeze in July. New York instituted a yearlong moratorium for large-scale data centers, also in July, and at least seven more states are considering similar measures, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. Loudoun’s halting of legislative applications includes rezonings and special exceptions that need to be approved by the board. Administrative applications for things like site plans and subdivision plans would still be allowed to proceed. Data center moratoriums are not allowed in Virginia. But since the board has one year to review legislative applications under Loudoun's zoning ordinance, it's using that length of time to effect the pause. At Tuesday night's board meeting, Loudoun County Attorney Leo Rogers confirmed the legality of the pause that the county is undertaking, but said he does believe there is a "real threat of litigation" from data center applicants. The legislative effort dates back to July, when the supervisors asked county staff to look into whether instituting such a pause would be permissible. In September, after getting the green light from the county's attorney, the board voted to direct staff to draw up a resolution for the final vote. In March 2025, Loudoun took its first step in limiting data center development when it stripped by right zoning, requiring all data centers to go through a special exception process. Under that legislation, data centers in the works that had already been approved — 15 projects in the pipeline totaling 10.5M SF of development — can still proceed without going through that process. In 2025, Loudoun had about 53M SF of data centers, a 100% increase from five years earlier, according to county officials.

artigo.texto: Mercado global de bandejas para cabos (leitos para cabos): Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de bandejas para cabos até 2035, impulsionada pela demanda por gestão de cabos em data centers Resumo Segundo o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de bandejas para cabos, o mercado chega a 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compras mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de oferta mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de bandejas para cabos é um segmento fundamental da infraestrutura elétrica e do gerenciamento de cabos, oferecendo suporte estrutural rígido para o encaminhamento e a proteção de cabos de energia e de dados em edifícios, plantas industriais, data centers e sistemas de transporte. Em 2026, o mercado é moldado pela demanda constante de substituição em mercados de construção maduros e pela aceleração das instalações em projetos de infraestrutura digital e energia renovável. As bandejas para cabos — incluindo configurações tipo escada, calha, tela metálica, fundo sólido e ventiladas — são cada vez mais especificadas por sua capacidade de suporte de carga, propriedades de dissipação de calor e compatibilidade com práticas de construção modular. O horizonte de previsão até 2035 aponta para um crescimento moderado, porém resiliente, com os fundamentos da demanda migrando para lançamentos de cabos de maior densidade em data centers, códigos de segurança e combate a incêndio mais rigorosos em edifícios comerciais e a eletrificação de processos industriais. A escolha de materiais também está evoluindo, com as bandejas de alumínio e à base de polymer ganhando participação onde a resistência à corrosão e a redução de peso são relevantes. Este relatório oferece uma visão baseada em dados do tamanho do mercado, da segmentação, dos fluxos comerciais e da dinâmica competitiva, fornecendo a fabricantes, distribuidores e especificadores um arcabouço analítico transparente para a tomada de decisão até 2035. O cenário-base para o mercado mundial de bandejas para cabos prevê expansão constante de 2026 a 2035, com a demanda global crescendo a uma taxa composta de crescimento anual de aproximadamente 4,2%. O crescimento não é uniforme entre regiões ou tipos de produto; reflete, antes, uma rotação da construção comercial tradicional para aplicações em data centers, energia renovável e automação industrial. Nas economias avançadas, as atividades de substituição e modernização em edifícios e plantas existentes sustentam o volume de base, enquanto os mercados emergentes contribuem com demanda incremental por meio da construção de nova infraestrutura. A dinâmica do lado da oferta é moldada pela volatilidade dos preços do aço e do alumínio, pela utilização da capacidade de fabricação e pela transição contínua para acabamentos pré-galvanizados e com pintura a pó, que reduzem o tempo de instalação. Espera-se que a intensidade competitiva aumente à medida que fabricantes de metais e integradores de sistemas ampliem seus portfólios de gerenciamento de cabos por meio de aquisições e ofertas de serviços integrados. O índice de mercado, fixado em 100 em 2025, deve alcançar 151 até 2035, refletindo o crescimento acumulado de volume, e não a inflação de preços. Os riscos para as perspectivas incluem quedas no ciclo da construção, atrasos nos investimentos de capital em data centers e mudanças na política comercial que afetam os custos dos insumos metálicos. De modo geral, o mercado é mais bem caracterizado como maduro, mas em evolução, com potencial de alta atrelado às tendências de infraestrutura digital e eletrificação. Fatores de demanda e restrições Principais fatores de demanda - Rápida expansão de data centers de hiperescala e de colocation, que exigem gerenciamento de cabos de alta densidade e soluções de bandejas ventiladas para dissipação de calor - Eletrificação de processos industriais e modernização da automação, impulsionando a demanda por bandejas para cabos duráveis de aço e alumínio em ambientes de plantas - Instalações de energia renovável, incluindo parques solares e eólicos, onde os sistemas de suporte de cabos são essenciais para a coleta e a distribuição de energia - Códigos de construção e segurança contra incêndio mais rigorosos, que exigem suporte e separação adequados de cabos em construções comerciais e institucionais - Adensamento das redes de telecomunicações, incluindo small cells de 5G e expansão de fibra, que exige encaminhamento organizado de cabos em ambientes urbanos e suburbanos - Modernização da infraestrutura ferroviária e de transporte, incluindo sistemas de sinalização e energia que dependem de instalações robustas de bandejas para cabos Possíveis restrições ao crescimento - Volatilidade dos preços do aço e do alumínio, que comprime as margens dos fabricantes e atrasa as especificações de projetos - Ciclos longos de licenciamento e construção no setor imobiliário comercial, que podem adiar a demanda por instalação de bandejas para cabos - Disponibilidade de métodos substitutos de gerenciamento de cabos, como eletrodutos e canaletas, em certas aplicações de baixa densidade - Escassez de mão de obra qualificada em contratação elétrica, que pode retardar os prazos de instalação e afetar o cronograma dos projetos - Tarifas comerciais e requisitos de conteúdo regional que afetam os fluxos transfronteiriços de bandejas metálicas fabricadas Estrutura da demanda por setor de uso final Infraestrutura de data centers (participação estimada: 28%) Os data centers são o segmento de uso final de crescimento mais rápido para bandejas para cabos, impulsionado pela construção de instalações de hiperescala e de colocation para atender à computação

artigo.texto: Imagem ilustrativa Documento cita risco para o abastecimento de água e questiona o protocolo de R$ 10 bilhões assinado com a Atlas Renewable Energy Moradores, trabalhadores e entidades da sociedade civil de Uberaba lançaram uma petição pública que exige transparência e a realização de audiências públicas antes de qualquer licença, outorga ou benefício municipal para a instalação de megadata centers na Zona de Processamento de Exportação (ZPE) da cidade. O documento é uma reação ao anúncio da Prefeitura de que assinou um protocolo de intenções com a Atlas Renewable Energy para um megacomplexo de data centers, com investimento previsto de R$ 10 bilhões. Segundo os autores, poucas semanas antes do anúncio, o telejornal MGTV 2ª Edição noticiou o fechamento frequente de reservatórios e o pedido oficial para que a população economizasse água diante da crise hídrica. Choque de datas O principal argumento da petição é o descompasso entre dois cronogramas. Comunicados da Prefeitura, divulgados por veículos como o JM Online e o Regionalzão, projetam o início da operação do data center para 2028. Já a Resolução ARISB-MG nº 298, do Codau, prevê a conclusão das operações do Sistema de Abastecimento do Rio Grande apenas em 2030. Ao cruzar dados de consumo médio de água de Uberaba, do SINISA, com levantamentos técnicos divulgados pelo The Intercept Brasil, os autores calculam que o consumo diário de um megadata center equivale ao de 2.200 até mais de 36 mil residências. Para eles, operar a estrutura antes da conclusão da obra do Rio Grande colocaria em risco o abastecimento das moradias durante a estiagem. Protocolo não garante obra A petição também ressalta que o documento assinado é uma carta preliminar, sem obrigação de execução. Segundo os autores, citando o The Intercept Brasil e a BNamericas, a Atlas já divulgou anúncios bilionários semelhantes em Paracatu (R$ 35 bilhões), no Norte de Minas e no Rio de Janeiro, em disputa por clientes globais que ainda não fecharam contrato. Empregos e capital Com base em estudo da Fundação Getulio Vargas (FGV), o texto afirma que 85% das vagas geradas seriam temporárias, restritas à construção civil, e que menos de 4% seriam empregos permanentes em galpões altamente automatizados, beneficiados por isenções fiscais da ZPE e do regime federal Redata. A petição afirma ainda que cerca de 80% do capital investido não permanece na cidade, sendo destinado à compra de servidores e chips importados. Conta de luz e precedentes Os autores citam levantamentos da CBS News e da NPR segundo os quais o custo de obras de expansão da rede elétrica para atender centros de dados costuma ser repassado à tarifa dos consumidores residenciais. Afirmam também que, em cidades vizinhas como Paracatu e Uberlândia, projetos semelhantes avançaram sem audiências prévias e hoje são alvo de questionamentos na Assembleia Legislativa de Minas Gerais (ALMG) e de investigações do Ministério Público Federal (MPF). O que os signatários pedem - Transparência total: divulgação da íntegra dos protocolos de intenções e das estimativas de consumo de água e energia, sem cláusulas de sigilo comercial sobre recursos públicos e naturais. - Audiências públicas amplas: convocação pela Câmara Municipal e pelo Conselho Municipal de Meio Ambiente (Comam), com participação de moradores, sindicatos, universidades, produtores rurais e especialistas independentes. - Condicionante hídrica: proibição de licença ou operação de data centers de alto consumo antes da entrada em operação efetiva do Sistema Rio Grande, com exigência de refrigeração em circuito fechado, sem perda de água por evaporação. - Contrapartidas reais: definição clara de benefícios sociais, ambientais e de qualificação profissional para a população local. “Uberaba não pode decidir o futuro da sua água e da sua energia a toque de caixa”, conclui o texto, que convida a população a assinar e compartilhar. A Folha Uberaba solicitou um posicionamento da prefeitura e assim que for atendido, será inserido na matéria O link da petição: https://www.peticao.online/data_centers_na_zpe_de_uberaba_debate_publico_imediato?utm_source=whatsapp A prefeitura de Uberaba respondeu ao questionamento, veja a resposta na íntegras: A Prefeitura de Uberaba respeita o direito de manifestação do cidadão e está à disposição da comunidade para prestar esclarecimentos e dialogar. Nesse sentido, o Município informa que o projeto foi concebido desde a origem para promover o uso eficiente e responsável dos recursos hídricos, adotando soluções que reduzem a demanda por água e evitam a utilização da rede pública de abastecimento. O fornecimento de água ocorrerá por meio de fontes independentes, sem demanda direta sobre o sistema público de distribuição que atende à população e estando de acordo com todos os requisitos e formas de controle da legislação aplicável. Durante a operação, o sistema de resfriamento funcionará em circuito fechado, permitindo a recirculação contínua da água e reduzindo significativamente a necessidade de reposição. O projeto também prevê o reaproveitamento de água proveniente da Estação de Tratamento de Esgoto (ETE) para atividades de serviços gerais, como limpeza e manutenção, reduzindo ainda mais a necessidade de utilização de água potável. A combinação dessas soluções demonstra o compromisso do empreendimento com a eficiência, o reaproveitamento e o uso racional da água. Além disso, a instalação do empreendimento depende, entre outras etapas, do licenciamento ambiental, processo durante o qual o Conselho Municipal do Meio Ambiente (Comam) se manifestará por meio dos seus membros, que representam diferentes setores, incluindo a sociedade civil.

artigo.texto: Spartanburg County council takes up 6 data center development agreements Monday Residents speak for and against projects as council considers three final votes and three first votes SPARTANBURG COUNTY, S.C. (FOX Carolina) - Spartanburg County Council on Monday night took up six data center development agreements, with three up for final votes and three up for first votes, as residents spoke for and against the projects in council chambers. The agenda ran more than 700 pages and included 20 public hearings. Before the 5:15 p.m. public meeting, council met in executive session to discuss contractual terms of several development agreements. The three agreements up for final votes were scheduled for public hearings during the regular council meeting. Resident calls for council members to resign Spartanburg County resident Eric Allison, founder of the Facebook group No Data Centers in Spartanburg, has been leading opposition to data centers in the county. Allison called council members “cowards” and said every member should resign. “Our Spartanburg County Council, every member should be totally ashamed. They need to resign today. It’s a mess. In one meeting, 20 public hearings, 22 second and third votes to move projects forward. It’s absolutely insane,” Allison said. Allison said he believes council is sending residents a message: “We don’t listen to you. We don’t do what you want. We do what we want and our controllers want. Our ears are not for the people of Spartanburg County. Our ears are for other people.” Three of the 20 hearings involve data center development agreements. Valara agreement on South Pine Street The Valara data center at 4000 South Pine Street, which the agenda describes as a high-performance computing center, is under construction. Council took a final vote on a development agreement among the county, Numara LLC and Valara Holdings LLC. It was approved. The agreement will provide the company with long-term development certainty and establish limits on certain future county regulatory actions affecting the project. It will: - Lock in Valara’s development rights for 10 years, protecting the 457-megawatt project from certain future county regulations, moratoriums and zoning changes. - Require the county to determine within 10 days whether development applications are complete. Once an application is determined to be complete, the county would have 45 days to take final action. If the county fails to act within that period, the agreement says the application could be considered approved based on the submitted documentation. - Protect Valara’s ability to continue developing the property, including additional data center buildings, generators, substations and battery storage, subject to the agreement’s terms. In exchange, the company commits to noise mitigation, landscaping and at least one community meeting each year. The agreement calls for an investment of about $2.76 billion. The agreement identifies 27 full-time jobs as a target, not a guarantee. It also requires annual reporting to the county on investment, construction, utilities and employment. Fox Carolina contacted Valara by email to request an interview and a tour of the facility. Jones Road agreement A development agreement with 300 Jones Road Associates LLC for approximately 137 acres at or near 430 Jones Road also received final approval after a vote. The proposal calls for a data center with up to 65 megawatts of IT capacity, an anticipated investment of approximately $1.5 billion and 25 full-time jobs. The agreement also includes $9 million in community benefit payments over five years. The proposal has a history of county opposition. In June, Spartanburg County planning staff denied an earlier application for a data center at the Jones Road property, citing violations of the county’s Unified Land Management Ordinance. The county’s Board of Zoning Appeals upheld that denial on August 25. The developer is now pursuing the project under an exception to the county’s data center moratorium, adopted in September. The exception allows qualifying data centers of 65 megawatts or less on designated industrial park sites or former industrial properties to move forward if they meet additional requirements. The original denial was not overturned. Instead, the county subsequently adopted rules creating another path for certain smaller data center projects to seek approval through development agreements. Monday’s vote was the third and final reading. Tyger River Industrial Park proposals Project Spero was a proposed $3 billion data center development for the Tyger River Industrial Park. In February, Spartanburg County leaders announced they would not approve the tax incentives sought for the project, effectively derailing the proposal following significant public opposition. Jerry Tang, the executive associated with Project Spero, is now associated with four data center proposals in the same industrial park. One, AIB CLT1 at 389 Tyger River Industrial Drive, is an existing bitcoin mining operation proposing to convert its facility into a conventional data center. A final vote was held on Monday on a development agreement. It was approved. The proposed facility would have 50 megawatts of capacity and an estimated investment of $1.2 billion. The other three proposals, AIB CLT2, AIB CLT3 and AIB CLT4, were up for first readings. Each item on the agenda included a proposed special source credit agreement and development agreement. The agreements include tax incentives. Draft agreements indicate the incentives could run for 40 years. FOX Carolina contacted Tang by email to request an interview and a tour of the proposed development sites. artigo.texto: University of Dubuque students present semester-long data center research at community forum DUBUQUE, Iowa (KCRG) - As Dubuque County communities draft new zoning rules for data centers, University of Dubuque students shared semester-long research on the facilities with the public Tuesday night. The Data Center Community Forum at the Peter and Susan Smith Welcome Center featured projects from seven classes spanning aviation, environmental science, public policy, computing and theology. Junior Roland Preston, a flight operations and politics major from Des Moines, focused his research for his public policy and environmental ethics classes on the data center campus in Altoona, a facility he passes regularly on his drive home from college. “I chose the one in Altoona because I drive to and from Dubuque and back home in Des Moines, so I drive by that data center all the time,” Preston said. “So I wanted to actually take a look at that one specifically and kind of gather why was it built, what’s the impact on the local community, how’s the local community feel about it.” During his trips near the Altoona campus, Preston said he experienced firsthand one of the most common complaints raised by nearby residents. “If I get close to that campus in the Altoona area, you can hear it,” Preston said. “And I understand why people have concerns about it because it’s just this constant droning sound you hear. And I can imagine why it’s quite the inconvenience.” Dubuque County, the City of Dubuque and the City of Peosta all currently have temporary moratoriums halting data center construction while officials write ordinances governing water use, power demand and noise. Preston said those local pauses reflect how quickly the industry is moving compared to municipal policy. “This technology is outpacing our ability to regulate it,” Preston said. “And we need to stall it in its tracks right now, come up with a comprehensive way to regulate it, and then we can maybe allow it to keep happening.” “When Dubuque County, for example, talks about doing a moratorium on data centers, it is from that perspective that we have all these companies trying to come in ... and for them (the local governments) it feels like it’s the only way that they can put in meaningful regulation before companies start building,” he added. While Preston said he entered the semester with a favorable view of data centers, researching a specific facility gave him a more detailed understanding of community pushback. “When we talk about noise, talk about water issues, the impact on the community, I have a better understanding as to why people feel that way, especially now that I’ve taken a specific data center and looked at it very intentionally,” Preston said. Christine Darr, an associate professor of philosophy at the university, helped organize the forum after watching public meetings across the area grow increasingly heated. “We wanted to work together to help students understand a local issue, both locally and kind of nationwide,” Darr said. “We thought it would be a great opportunity to do some interdisciplinary work, so thinking about such a complex issue from a variety of perspectives, and then a great opportunity to kind of showcase our students and the great work that they do and offer something to the community.” Darr said combining fields like theology, aviation and environmental science was deliberate. “We thought it was an exciting opportunity to show how complex even something seemingly as simple as a data center might be,” Darr said. “And by bringing as many different disciplinary lenses, I think we did really kind of lift up all of the different ways that you can think about a particular issue, that nothing is one way or another way.” Following the student showcase, regional journalists Benjamin Fisher, Tom Kertscher of Wisconsin Watch and Grace Nieland of The Gazette held a panel discussion and Q&A on data center coverage and local policy. For Preston, presenting months of research to community members fulfilled a goal he set when he started college “It’s very nice researching something for months and then being able to talk to the public about it,” Preston said. Darr said she hopes attendees left the forum with a broader view of the debate. “I hope that people see that the issue is actually pretty complex, and also, I hope they walk away feeling as though they are part of a community that really cares about understanding issues, and trying to work together to understand things in a more nuanced way,” Darr said. artigo.texto: A multi-metallic oxide composite synthesized from nickel cobalt bimetallic oxide and magnesium-copper oxide has demonstrated high electrochemical activity for both water oxidation and asymmetric supercapacitor energy storage in alkaline environments. Synthesized as NiCo2O4/MgO-CuO, the material addresses limitations in the chemical fabrication of multi-metallic oxides for water electrolysis while leveraging the versatile redox properties recognized in transition metal oxides containing nickel and cobalt. The research team developed the composite using a chemical synthesis strategy combined with a modified hydrothermal process. This fabrication method utilized phytochemicals derived from lemon peel extract to facilitate the in situ growth of the NiCo2O4/MgO-CuO composite directly onto a nickel foam substrate, creating an integrated electrode structure intended for oxygen evolution reaction half-cell water splitting and asymmetric supercapacitor devices. The introduction of multi-metallic ions into the composite architecture induced electronic disorder and surface defects throughout the material. According to the study, the resulting presence of oxygen surface vacancies alongside trivalent cobalt (Co3+) and trivalent nickel (Ni3+) species contributed significantly to the material’s electrochemical performance and reaction kinetics in alkaline media. Structural validation of the NiCo2O4/MgO-CuO composite was carried out using multiple complementary characterization techniques. The researchers employed scanning electron microscopy, powder X-ray diffraction, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy, and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy, which together confirmed the multi-metal oxide composition and the tailor-made structural features of the synthesized electrode material. When evaluated for the oxygen evolution reaction in a 1 M potassium hydroxide electrolyte, the composite exhibited a low overpotential of 370 millivolts at a current density of 10 milliamperes per square centimeter. In addition to its catalytic efficiency during water oxidation testing, the electrode demonstrated operational durability by sustaining the same catalytic function over 40 continuous hours under alkaline conditions. In asymmetric supercapacitor testing conducted in 3 M potassium hydroxide, the NiCo2O4/MgO-CuO composite delivered a specific capacitance of 551.73 farads per gram. The assembled device attained an energy density of 193.97 watt-hours per kilogram at an applied current density of 1 ampere per gram, while exhibiting high cycling stability by retaining 96.9 percent of its original capacitance after 40,000 galvanic charge-discharge cycles. artigo.texto: Subgen AI’s subsidiary, Substrate AI, signs a grid connection agreement with i-DE (Iberdrola group) for its future AI data centre Source: MFN Subgen AI AB (“Subgen AI” or the “Company”) announces that its Spanish subsidiary, Substrate Artificial Inteligence S.A. (“Substrate AI”), has signed an project commission agreement (the “Grid Connection Agreement”) with i-DE Redes Eléctricas Inteligentes, S.A.U., the electricity distribution system operator belonging to the Iberdrola group (“Iberdrola”), for the execution of the facilities required to connect to the distribution grid, associated with 5 MW of granted access capacity for its future AI data centre in Talavera de la Reina, Spain. Under the Grid Connection Agreement, Substrate AI will pay Iberdrola EUR 174,000 plus VAT to reinforce and adapt the power grid. This Grid Connection Agreement is part of Substrate AI's strategy to build its own AI infrastructure in Spain and support a more sovereign and competitive European technology ecosystem. The Grid Connection Agreement is a key step towards securing 5 MW of electrical connection capacity for the future data centre. Once built, Substrate AI will have one of the essential elements for the development of its project: the availability of sufficient electrical power to deploy its artificial intelligence (AI) computing infrastructure. The Talavera data centre forms part of Substrate AI’s strategy to develop its own technological infrastructure in Spain, contributing to the growth of European computing capacity and to the deployment of more sovereign, secure and competitive artificial intelligence. The future availability of these 5 MW through the Grid Connection Agreement represents a decisive step forward in the preparation of the project and enables Substrate AI to continue progressing towards the next milestones required for its launch. With this initiative, Substrate AI reinforces its commitment to Spain as a strategic location for developing artificial intelligence infrastructure and helping to build a European technology ecosystem with greater capacity and autonomy. For further information, please see Substrate AI’s website: www.substrate.ai.

Dozens of countries - from big emerging economies to the world's poorest nations - are calling for the UN's new carbon market to reassess climate integrity rules, in a push that campaigners and researchers have blamed on industry lobbying. At COP31 talks on the Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism (PACM) this weekend, the Like-Minded Developing Countries – a group that includes Saudi Arabia, India and China – the Least Developed Countries (LDCs) and landlocked developing countries raised concerns about the requirements project developers must meet, according to sources familiar with the closed-door discussions. They warned about the cumulative weight of those requirements developed under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement as barriers to implementation. Several countries, including Singapore and some Latin American states, said rules must keep projects financially viable, while South Korea asked for proportionate requirements, the sources said. Their demands closely track arguments from carbon market industry groups, which claim PACM's conservative approach to counting emission reductions is so strict that few projects will ever come to fruition. Industry and NGOs lobby to weaken UN carbon credit rules in “coordinated” push In a letter published ahead of COP31, the lobby groups asked governments to "raise implementation concerns" and to request that the Supervisory Body - the UN body that oversees the market - assess the "combined impact" of its rules on the feasibility of projects. The letter was signed by the International Emissions Trading Association (IETA), a business group whose members include fossil fuel giants Shell, BP, Saudi Aramco and Chevron, along with the Project Developer Forum and the Wildlife Conservation Society, which develops forest conservation programmes. Draft text reflects industry demands Those demands are reflected in the first draft of the COP31 decision on the mechanism, published late on Saturday. To guard against over-crediting, PACM’s rules deliberately err on the side of issuing fewer credits when emissions cuts from projects are uncertain. The document asks the Supervisory Body to look at how these cautious assumptions add up across its rules and what that means for the number of credits, project costs and prices. The aim, it says, is to avoid "excessive compounding of conservative adjustments". Other parts of the draft tell the body not to make its rules too cautious or too rigid. That includes efforts to guard against the risk that carbon captured by a project is later released. Most of these passages add that environmental integrity must be maintained. Risk of another 'failure' "Weakening the rules is not climate ambition - it is a license to pollute,” said Erika Lennon, a senior attorney at the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL). “As we are on the brink of permanently breaching 1.5C, we cannot afford to turn the carbon market into another loophole for polluters,” she added. Axel Michaelowa, research director at Perspectives Climate Research, said that if attempts to weaken the rules succeed, it could lead to another failure of an international carbon market. Demand for credits rests on trust, he said, and the slightest doubt over integrity erodes buyers' willingness to pay. Calls to revise requirements "must be supported by scientific evidence, not unsupported claims of under-crediting - especially when these assumptions come from private actors whose revenues depend on the volume of transacted credits rather than real mitigation outcomes," Michaelowa said. The EU, Switzerland and Senegal are among a handful of countries pushing back against demands to re-assess the market rules, according to the sources, and are opposing requests to weigh up the profitability of projects or to lower standards. Cookstove credits in focus At the centre of the fight are new methodologies for projects that aim to cut emissions by distributing cleaner cookstoves - one of the carbon market’s most popular credit types and also one of its most criticised for overstating climate benefits. A 2024 study in Nature Sustainability found cookstove projects had been over-credited roughly tenfold. Under the rules adopted by the Supervisory Body in October, cookstove project developers are required to set aside part of their credits in a buffer pool, in case the forests they claim to save later burn or are cleared.
