One way to do that, Liang said, is to repurpose existing data centers. This approach âdisrupts the communities less,â he told Semaforâs Liz Rappaport. AI backlash has presented a formidable obstacle for the data center buildout. People voted to limit data center development in 40 out of 41 ballot measures across the US on Election Day, and some newly elected Democratic leaders have laid out plans to pass data-center moratoria. Existing data centers tend to be much smaller than the massive ones being built for AI, and repurposing old infrastructure will require the industry to be âmuch more energy-efficient in the chips that we build,â Liang said. Still, he said, itâs good for the industry to get more value out of what it has available now. âTo distribute the data center into existing environments where power already exists, the infrastructure already exists, the cooling already exists and fits within the ecosystem â itâs not a bad way to do it,â he said. Compute is a precious resource for companies right now. Voice AI company ElevenLabs CEO Mati Staniszewski told Rappaport that âcompute constraintâ in the near term is a real possibility.

artigo.texto: The International Business Aviation Council (IBAC) is urging its affiliated national associations to lobby their governments to demand political pressure to block changes to the European Union Emissions Trading Scheme (EU-ETS). The group, which represents business aviation at ICAO, has backed the EBAA’s opposition to proposals made by the European Commission’s Climate Action directorate-general on the grounds that changes would disproportionately affect the industry to the extent that some operators could find it impossible to comply with requirements. Under proposals issued in July, the introduction of a new de minimis emissions threshold of 1,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide per company annually would bring many additional smaller operators under the EU-ETS mandate. According to IBAC, some members of the European Parliament want to further lower the de minimis threshold for EU-ETS compliance to just 250 tonnes. The group said this would bring around 1,000 more operators under the requirements of the legislation. The EC also wants the scheme to apply to all flights from the European Economic Area to third-country destinations within a 5,000-kilometer (2,700-nm) radius of Frankfurt, Germany. IBAC says this will significantly increasing the number of flights from outside the European Union that would be subject to requirements. As part of its rebuttal of the proposed changes, EBAA has also protested that they will subject business aviation to broader carbon-pricing obligations than airlines by being denied access to sustainable aviation fuel allowances and to the use of book-and-claim options. The group has also complained that the new structure would take no account of other passenger and carbon taxes levied by individual European Union member states, such as France, Portugal, Italy and the Netherlands. IBAC director general Kurt Edwards has accused the EC of “sectoral bigotry” in consciously discriminating against business aircraft operators, which he said will be harmful to the viability of some companies. Edwards said excluding the industry from book-and-claim accounting for emissions is especially unreasonable since its companies commonly fly to airports where SAF is not available. “In their supporting text, the European Commission said that business aircraft operators have the means and the resources to buy SAF without providing evidence of that,” he told AIN. “Why strip away the benefit of taking advantage of [SAF] technology?” In what IBAC said would be a further divergence from the ICAO-backed CORSIA approach to achieving net-zero emissions for air transport by 2050, the EC intends to reduce the mtow threshold for EU-ETS from 5,700 kilograms (12,540 pounds) to 2,500 kilograms. Edwards said this will mean turboprop aircraft such as the Pilatus PC-12 and Daher TBM 980 would be covered by the scheme and its high cost of compliance and administration. At the EBAA Week event in Brussels this week, IBAC representatives will introduce a new vehicle-tonne-kilometer metric that they are proposing for business aviation. According to Bruce Parry, senior advisor for industry affairs with Bombardier Aerospace, this would be a fairer way to calculate the sector’s emissions than the passenger-kilometer metric devised with airlines in mind. Edwards said the EC’s allegedly discriminatory efforts to make EU-ETS compliance harder for business aviation companies are also unnecessary since the industry is strongly committed to decarbonization. “Part of the reasoning for excluding our operators from SAF allowances is that they believe we are more likely to electrify [aircraft] sooner, but this simply isn’t the incentive they think it is,” he concluded. Ultimately, if the EC presses ahead with the proposed changes, IBAC has indicated that the industry may be forced to take legal action to challenge the new rules on grounds of discrimination. In June, lawyers acting for Dassault Aviation, with EBAA support, successfully challenged the process by which the European Commission had excluded business aviation from its “taxonomy” definition of environmentally sustainable activity. The European Union General Court in Luxembourg ruled that the industry had been excluded in an unfair and discriminatory way.

artigo.texto: Jasper residents get a crash course on data centers, but some say the presentation leaned one-sided JASPER, Ind. (WFIE) - Dubois County residents got a closer look at data centers Tuesday night, but some who attended said the event wasn’t as neutral as advertised. Officials and developers gave a presentation Nov. 17 at Jasper’s Thyen-Clark Cultural Center. They explained what data centers are and how they work, and they weighed the pros and cons. Nancy Eckerle, executive director of the Jasper Chamber of Commerce, said she hoped people came with open minds. “I hope people are just educated and informed that they come here with an open mind that they are not biased in their opinion, but maybe they learned something. Maybe they learned something. They didn’t know if they were against data centers maybe they’ll learn something that will just open their eyes a little bit and if they’re definitely for them, they may learn something that says you know maybe we don’t need that here or whatever it might be.” Presentation focused on property values, water and power The night’s main speaker was Paul Wyman, owner of The Wyman Group, a full-service real estate firm in north central Indiana. He went into detail on how data centers affect property values, water and power. Officials said the event was meant to be a neutral learning experience. Many in the audience said it wasn’t. They said they felt a bias in favor of data centers. Jasper resident Maggie Stimming said she agrees data centers are coming, but she questioned some of what she heard. “I agree with him that we are going to have data centers. I don’t think there’s any doubt about that. We’re not gonna turn the clock back. The horse is out of the barn and we will have data centers, but how we do them is I think what he was trying to get across how we do them and that’s a good point to make however, some of his examples I felt were not really very good.” Environmental questions dominate Q&A After the presentation, many in the audience asked questions. Many of them focused on how data centers would affect the environment. Others asked why demand for data centers is so high in the area. Some residents left concerned. They said many environmental topics were not addressed. Jasper resident Rock Emmert said diesel pollution was his biggest concern. “He touched on a lot of reasons and methods how communities can demand the best possible like the best practices or the best available control technology but he didn’t address about the pollution aspect of diesel. That was my biggest concern about the whole presentation. Absolutely zero concern for public health and pollution.” Now again, this was just meant to be an educational experience, and no plans for a data center were discussed. But if one ever comes, we will keep you updated. Copyright 2026 WFIE. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Trending SNOQUALMIE, Wash. -- In the race to meet the nation's growing power demands, states and utilities are rapidly building new "battery farms" that can store energy for when customers need it most. But as the facilities grow, so too does community opposition. The systems store banks of batteries in buildings or shipping containers. While they can take many forms, developers are increasingly building large, multi-acre projects designed to meet the needs of local utilities. The electricity stored by such systems nationwide has grown tenfold since 2022, and it's projected to double again by the end of 2028. State lawmakers and renewable energy advocates say battery storage is urgently needed to stabilize the grid and support the transition to clean power. But in some communities, residents are wary of proposals to build industrial battery systems in their neighborhoods, noting that battery fires can produce toxic smoke and are difficult to extinguish. As the backlash has grown, nearly 200 communities have passed or proposed moratoriums to block battery farms from being built near them. Backers say modern systems are designed to be much safer than previous versions, with data showing that fire risk has dropped significantly. But some industry leaders fear the perception of danger -- along with a rising tide of community activism stirred by the buildout of data centers -- could threaten an industry that's becoming integral to the nation's energy future. 'Meteoric growth' Most energy storage on the U.S. grid takes the form of battery energy storage systems, commonly known as BESS. Such facilities host banks of batteries, typically lithium-ion -- a technology that has become more capable and cost-effective with the development of electric vehicles. At present, battery storage capacity nationwide exceeds 50 gigawatts, up from just 5 gigawatts at the beginning of 2022. Another 54 gigawatts is slated to come online in the next two and a half years. That projected total of more than 100 gigawatts would be enough to power roughly 75 million homes, although battery farms are designed to provide electricity for one to four hours, as opposed to the more continuous supply of conventional power plants. "The meteoric growth is continuing," said Noah Roberts, executive director of the U.S. Energy Storage Coalition, an industry group. "For state policymakers who are focused on the energy transition and decarbonizing the grid, (battery) storage is essential." Policymakers and energy planners have increasingly pushed for battery farms as more renewable energy sources have come online. Solar farms, for instance, can produce massive amounts of cheap electricity during the afternoon hours -- but peak demand is in the evening, when people get home from work and turn on household appliances. With batteries on the grid, that surplus solar energy can be stored and saved for when it's needed, instead of firing up more costly "peaker" gas plants to meet evening demand. Industry leaders say battery systems can also improve reliability and affordability, even in states without clean energy goals. They note that Texas and California are home to a majority of the battery projects on the grid so far. While typically on opposite ends of the political spectrum, both states produce large amounts of wind and solar energy, while facing heavy power demands that have at times required energy conservation measures and put the grid at risk of blackouts. Battery systems, backers say, have already stabilized their grids considerably. Adding to the appeal of battery farms is the fact that they can be put in place quickly, in a matter of months, compared with much longer timelines for other energy projects. "As we're dealing with a power supply crisis, energy storage is the obvious solution for adding capacity and getting more out of the grid that we've already paid for," Roberts said. State policies have been a driver of the industry's growth. Thirteen states have enacted targets requiring their utilities to deploy certain amounts of energy storage by specific dates. In Maryland, Democratic Del. Lorig Charkoudian authored a law in 2025 directing state regulators to issue bids for projects totaling 1,600 megawatts of energy storage. "It's basically a no-regret path," Charkoudian said in an interview earlier this year. "Over time once we bring more renewables on, they will be that much more valuable because there's battery storage." Charkoudian noted that the Trump administration has stalled permitting for offshore wind and other renewable projects, while phasing out clean energy tax credits. The federal push against those forms of energy has made battery farms a more attractive option, as they've met with less resistance and still qualify for a 30% tax credit. Community concerns For all of the potential that battery farms offer the grid, some communities are not eager to host them. Much of the opposition centers around the risk for out-of-control fires and toxic smoke. Most prominently, the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County, California, caught fire in early 2025, burned for several days and released 55,000 pounds of toxic metals into nearby wetlands. Lithium-ion batteries, when ignited, can trigger a reaction known as thermal runaway that is nearly impossible to extinguish. Across the country, community activists have been alarmed to see battery farms proposed near schools, playgrounds and senior care facilities. "They're making us collateral damage," said Phoenix Artemisia, an activist in Watsonville, California, who has helped lead efforts to oppose a proposed battery storage facility there. "We have 12 schools within two miles of us here, but these out-of-state developers are telling us what we're going to do in our backyard." The Watsonville project has stirred up significant community opposition, Artemisia said, prompting the developer to seek approval from state regulators in order to bypass local officials. Indust

artigo.texto: Swedish private markets fund manager EQT is acquiring US battery energy storage firm Flatiron Energy from Hull Street Energy (HSE). EQT said it has agreed to acquire Flatiron through its EQT Transition Infrastructure fund without disclosing financial terms. Flatiron, which was founded in 2021, develops and operates utility-scale energy storage projects across New England, New York and Mid-Atlantic power markets. Since HSE’s initial investment in 2022, Flatiron has expanded its portfolio nearly tenfold to 24GWh of capacity, been awarded 6GWh of long-term contracts and has 2GWh of batteries under construction. Flatiron joins an existing EQT battery storage platform that comprises Statera Energy in the UK and Ju:niz Energy in Germany. Benjamin Bygott-Webb, partner at EQT, said: “Battery storage has become essential to keeping the grid reliable and electricity affordable, as an ageing grid, a changing generation mix and rapidly growing power demand continue to put the system under strain. Flatiron has secured scarce, well-located sites and built a strong record in the communities where it operates. “Building on EQT’s deep experience investing in critical infrastructure, our expertise in scaling energy platforms and the opportunities for collaboration across the EQT infrastructure portfolio, we look forward to supporting the Flatiron team as they deliver their projects and bring more firm capacity to the region.” Sarah Wright, founder and managing partner at HSE, said: “This transaction underscores HSE’s approach to identifying attractive opportunities and creating long-term value in a rapidly growing and decarbonising power sector. “HSE is highly selective about the management teams we back, and Flatiron is an excellent illustration of why this matters. Because the Flatiron team has a strong track record in the sector and a rigorous, fundamentals-driven approach to setting strategy, they have been able to deliver material growth and value accretion.” Rob Brink, CEO of Flatiron Energy, said: “We started Flatiron with the mission to bring reliable energy where it’s needed most, in the communities that rely on it every day. “EQT is an exceptional firm with a strong track record of scaling platforms in the energy transition, and we couldn’t be more excited to partner with them on our next stage of growth.” Simpson Thacher & Bartlett and Santander served as legal and financial advisers to EQT, respectively, while Kirkland & Ellis and Guggenheim Securities advised Flatiron Energy. Faegre Drinker Biddle & Reath acted as legal counsel to HSE. To read the latest IPE Real Assets magazine click here.

artigo.texto: 1. The U.S. is tightening restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips by closing a loophole that lets Chinese firms obtain computing power through overseas data centers, shifting controls from the physical movement of chips to remote access to their computing capacity. [para. 1][para. 4] 2. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim rule on Monday requiring licenses for shipments of advanced AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world if they provide large amounts of computing power to companies headquartered in China or other restricted jurisdictions. The rule also imposes new licensing requirements specifically on exports to Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil, which the U.S. views as having a higher-than-normal risk of chip diversion. [para. 2][para. 3] 3. Under the new framework, exporters must seek U.S. approval if they know covered chips or servers are destined for a data center providing more than 12 million in aggregate total processing performance (TPP) to China-linked companies. This threshold applies to an individual facility or a group of linked data centers, regardless of the data center's location, and covers computing provided directly or indirectly to companies headquartered in China. [para. 5][para. 8] 4. Based on Nvidia product specifications and industry estimates, the 12 million TPP threshold is roughly equivalent to about 750 Nvidia H200 chips. While this is small compared with the tens of thousands of chips typically needed to train the most advanced AI models, it could still support substantial inference workloads that require less concentrated computing capacity. [para. 6][para. 7] 5. Data-center operators face new obligations after chips are delivered. If an overseas facility begins providing computing capacity above the threshold to covered Chinese entities, the owner, operator, or another involved party must obtain a license. Existing data centers already providing such services have 90 days from the rule's effective date to seek approval if they wish to continue, or they risk future U.S. export restrictions. Commercial recommendation systems, such as those used by online retailers, are exempt. [para. 9][para. 10][para. 11] 6. The separate licensing requirement for Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil could have a particularly large impact on Southeast Asia, which has become a major destination for AI data-center investment. Advanced chips shipped to these five countries will generally require U.S. approval, though companies headquartered in the U.S. or owned by U.S. parents can qualify for an exemption if they meet reporting requirements. Washington cited elevated risks of diversion to restricted users in these markets. [para. 12][para. 13][para. 14][para. 15] 7. Southeast Asia has grown rapidly as a computing hub as Chinese tech companies expand overseas and seek AI infrastructure. Singapore had more than 1.4 gigawatts (GW) of computing-infrastructure capacity in 2025, while Malaysia had about 1.06 GW, Indonesia 900 megawatts, and Thailand 620 megawatts. Regional capacity is expected to exceed 10 GW by 2030, up from more than 4.4 GW in 2025. [para. 16][para. 17] 8. Chinese technology companies including ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent have leased data-center capacity in Southeast Asia. Of roughly 1.5 GW of data-center projects approved in Thailand, as much as 60% to 70% are backed by Chinese investors or primarily serve major Chinese tech companies. In response, Malaysia plans legislation requiring data centers to disclose information such as operators, cloud customers, locations, electricity consumption, and GPU imports. Singapore said it is studying the new U.S. rules and engaging with affected companies and U.S. authorities. [para. 18][para. 19][para. 20][para. 21] 9. The rule also tightens requirements for semiconductor foundries and chip-packaging companies. Certain advanced chips designed by companies outside the U.S. and designated allied jurisdictions will be presumed to fall under U.S. export controls and to be intended for data-center use unless manufacturers or packaging companies can demonstrate otherwise. This builds on earlier restrictions aimed at preventing Chinese chip designers from using overseas foundries for advanced processors. [para. 22][para. 23][para. 24] 10. The Commerce Department formally rescinded the Biden administration's AI Diffusion Rule, a sweeping global framework unveiled in January 2025 that sought to divide countries into different tiers for access to advanced computing power. That rule never took effect; the Trump administration announced plans to abandon it in May 2025, arguing for a more targeted approach like the current interim rule. artigo.texto: BW ESS has partnered with French battery storage developer Wattmen to develop a battery energy storage system (BESS) portfolio of approximately 500 MW in France over the next three years. The partnership aims to expand BW ESS’ presence in the French energy storage market by developing large-scale, standalone battery storage projects connected to the transmission network. The collaboration will combine Wattmen’s local project origination and development expertise with BW ESS’ international experience in energy storage investment, project design and procurement. The companies will jointly work on advancing projects from the initial greenfield stage to ready-to-build status. This will include securing land rights, grid connections and the necessary regulatory authorisations required to move projects towards construction. The partnership will primarily focus on projects with connection capacities of at least 100 MW. The companies will priorities strategically located sites near grid connection points, with sufficient land availability to accommodate battery systems offering a minimum storage duration of four hours. This development strategy is intended to create a portfolio of large-scale energy storage assets capable of supporting the changing requirements of France’s electricity system. Under the partnership, Wattmen will lead local development activities, including identifying suitable project sites, negotiating land agreements, managing permitting processes and coordinating grid connections. The company will also work closely with landowners, local authorities and communities to facilitate project development. BW ESS will contribute its international energy storage experience, particularly in project design, investment and procurement strategy. The company operates across seven markets and brings experience in developing and managing battery storage projects at scale. Hazel Starmer-Jones, Development Director at BW ESS, said the partnership represents an important step in strengthening the company’s presence in France. She highlighted Wattmen’s technical capabilities and local market knowledge as important factors in selecting the development partner. Both companies aim to develop high-quality energy storage projects that can deliver long-term value while improving the flexibility and resilience of the French electricity system. Jean-Marc Guenée, CEO and Co-Founder of Wattmen, said the partnership combines complementary capabilities and a shared ambition to develop high-quality battery storage infrastructure. He noted that the collaboration would help advance strategically located projects and support the development of flexible energy infrastructure required for the energy transition. The agreement reflects BW ESS’ strategy of partnering with specialized local developers when entering and expanding in new markets. By combining local development capabilities with international investment and operational experience, the company aims to build a strong pipeline of energy storage projects. The latest partnership builds on BW ESS’ recent entry into France through the acquisition of two battery energy storage projects, each with a capacity of 100 MW and 400 MWh. These acquisitions, together with the new 500 MW development partnership, strengthen the company’s project pipeline and establish a foundation for further expansion in the French battery storage market. artigo.texto: Publicidade As novas restrições impostas pelos Estados Unidos à exportação de chips avançados para inteligência artificial adicionaram uma nova fonte de preocupação para os planos de expansão de data centers no Brasil e podem representar um obstáculo para a WEG (WEGE3), na avaliação do Bradesco BBI. A partir de 16 de novembro, fornecedores passarão a precisar de autorização do governo americano para exportar ao Brasil determinados processadores utilizados em data centers. A medida também alcança chips fabricados fora dos Estados Unidos quando desenvolvidos com tecnologia americana e faz parte dos esforços de Washington para evitar que empresas chinesas utilizem operações em terceiros países para contornar restrições tecnológicas impostas à China. Segundo a regulamentação do Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), Brasil, Singapura, Tailândia, Malásia e Indonésia foram classificados como países com risco acima do normal de desvio ilegal desses componentes para a China e Macau. Para o BBI, a notícia tem leitura negativa para a WEG, embora o banco não veja, por enquanto, necessidade de alterar suas estimativas, recomendação equivalente à compra ou o preço-alvo de R$ 62 para a ação. Na avaliação dos analistas, as restrições podem desacelerar a implementação de alguns projetos de data centers justamente em um momento em que o governo brasileiro tenta atrair investimentos para o setor por meio do programa ReData. Como a companhia fornece uma ampla gama de equipamentos para esse mercado, eventuais adiamentos poderiam postergar parte da demanda por seus produtos. O banco ressalta, contudo, que o impacto ainda é incerto e dependerá de fatores como a estrutura societária dos projetos, os usuários finais dos chips e as aplicações pretendidas. Além disso, a regulamentação prevê exceções para operações ligadas a empresas americanas e não representa uma proibição total das exportações para o Brasil. Continua depois da publicidade A preocupação surge em um momento de forte expansão do mercado local. Dados da Abinee citados pelo BBI mostram que as importações brasileiras de semicondutores somaram US$ 6,8 bilhões entre janeiro e setembro, alta de 51% na comparação anual. JPMorgan vê fundamentos intactos Apesar das preocupações de curto prazo envolvendo data centers, o JPMorgan segue otimista com a tese de investimento da WEG e reiterou recomendação overweight, equivalente à compra, elevando o preço-alvo para R$ 66 ao fim de 2027, ante R$ 56 anteriormente. O novo alvo implica potencial de valorização de cerca de 30% em relação aos níveis atuais. Para o banco americano, a empresa continua bem posicionada para acelerar o crescimento nos próximos anos, com expectativa de expansão da receita de 23% em 2027 e de 21% em 2028, depois de um crescimento estimado de apenas 3% em 2026. A tese é sustentada principalmente pelos negócios ligados a transformadores, sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias (BESS) e motores elétricos. Continua depois da publicidade Outro ponto destacado pelo JPMorgan é a proteção natural que a companhia possui contra a desvalorização do real. Mais de 60% das receitas da empresa são geradas fora do Brasil, sendo cerca de 30% provenientes da América do Norte. Segundo os cálculos do banco, cada depreciação de 5% do real acrescenta aproximadamente 4% ao EBITDA (lucro antes de juros, impostos, depreciações e amortizações) projetado da companhia. O JPMorgan também revisou para cima suas projeções financeiras após incorporar um cenário de câmbio mais depreciado. O banco elevou suas estimativas de EBITDA para 2027 em 6% e passou a trabalhar com crescimento de 27% nessa linha, além de prever lucro líquido e receitas acima do consenso de mercado para 2027 e 2028. Na visão dos analistas, a ação ainda negocia a múltiplos considerados atrativos, com desconto de cerca de 15% em relação à média histórica do período pós-pandemia. O banco argumenta ainda que a empresa tende a se beneficiar do atual ambiente doméstico por ser vista pelos investidores como uma companhia de alta qualidade, forte exposição ao dólar e menor dependência do ciclo econômico brasileiro. artigo.texto: Stars could disappear from the night sky because of space data centers – scientists warn of a threat Kyiv • UNN Tens of thousands of space data centers could change the appearance of the night sky and make astronomers’ work more difficult. Scientists also warn of collisions and orbital debris. The mass deployment of artificial intelligence data centers in Earth's orbit could radically change the appearance of the night sky. Scientists warn that satellites could become more visible than stars and create serious problems for astronomical observations. Axios reports this, citing a new scientific study, writes UNN. Details According to researchers' estimates, the deployment of tens of thousands of orbital data centers could result in artificial satellites becoming the brightest objects in the night sky across most regions of the world. In addition to light pollution, scientists warn of the risk of collisions between spacecraft traveling at about 27,000 km/h and an increase in the amount of orbital debris. Companies plan to launch tens of thousands of satellites According to Quilty Space, investment in space data centers increased from $197 million in 2025 to $1.11 billion in 2026. SpaceX has applied to create a network of 1 million satellites. Meanwhile, the Starcloud and Blue Origin projects envisage the potential deployment of 88,000 and 51,600 spacecraft, respectively. However, experts emphasize that the announced figures do not mean that all the satellites will actually be launched. The study's lead author, David Sandalow, urged companies to act cautiously, as the consequences of the mass deployment of data centers in space have yet to be sufficiently studied.

artigo.texto: Data centers são apenas um dos dez pilares para o Brasil disputar a liderança global em IA Monica Miglio Pedrosa Para se destacar globalmente na transformação pela inteligência artificial, o Brasil precisa desenvolver capacidade própria de produzir conhecimento e tecnologia. O Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter) pode atrair investimentos para ampliar a infraestrutura necessária a essa ambição. Mas os data centers por si só não garantem autonomia sobre os modelos de IA que vão transformar os negócios e participar de decisões estratégicas nas empresas. O alerta é de André Luís da Fonseca, coordenador do Centro de Estudos em Estratégia e Inovação (CEEI) do COPPEAD/UFRJ. Segundo o pesquisador, os data centers podem ampliar a capacidade de processamento no país, mas manter os dados e a estratégia em tecnologias contratadas por empresas privadas estrangeiras. Além disso, de acordo com o periódico Technological Forecasting & Social Change, a infraestrutura é apenas um dos dez elementos para construir um ecossistema completo. Os demais são cultura, demanda, financiamento, instituições formais, intermediários, conhecimento, liderança, redes e talento. “A pergunta que o país precisa fazer não é apenas onde os servidores vão ficar, mas quem vai ser dono do conhecimento que roda neles. Capacidade de processamento sem capacidade de orquestrar a IA é aluguel de infraestrutura, não soberania”, afirma. Confira, a seguir, a entrevista exclusiva para a [EXP]. [EXP] O que a instalação de data centers representa para a participação do Brasil na indústria de inteligência artificial? [André Luís da Fonseca] A indústria da IA funciona sobre uma pilha de elementos. No nível mais básico estão o espaço onde fica o data center, a licença da prefeitura, a água usada para refrigerar os servidores e a energia elétrica que eles consomem. É uma camada sem a qual o restante não existiria, mas de menor valor agregado. Quando isso é feito por uma organização de fora, é quase como se estivéssemos exportando sol, água, uso da terra e autorização ambiental. Não tem muita diferença, para todos os fins práticos, de exportar soja. É quase como se tivéssemos um monocultivo agrícola, só que computacional. Isso contribui para o PIB, traz riqueza que de outra forma não viria e, portanto, é recomendável. A questão é passar a sensação de que estamos tendo uma participação na cadeia produtiva maior do que essa atividade de fato representa. Estamos pegando um pedaço da receita da indústria por meio do fornecimento desses recursos. Isso, por si só, não está diminuindo a dependência. Como avalia as contrapartidas de pesquisa e desenvolvimento previstas no Redata? Existem efeitos negativos associados ao uso do solo, da água e dos demais recursos de determinado lugar, assim como alguém poderia argumentar que uma plantação de soja tem efeitos ambientais negativos. Então, você exige uma compensação adicional. O Redata faz isso direcionando 2% da aquisição de hardware para investimento em pesquisa e desenvolvimento no Brasil. Esse investimento contribui para o ecossistema de desenvolvimento local, o que é uma coisa boa. E a oferta de 10% da capacidade ser oferecida ao mercado interno? O que ela representa? É preciso entender que estamos falando de vender uma parte da capacidade, não de dar. É como convidar alguém para montar um negócio no seu prédio e dizer que ele terá a chance de vender também para os moradores. Não sei se podemos atribuir tanta importância a esses 10%. Para o governo brasileiro, que tem a questão de manter o processamento dos dados públicos aqui, isso garante a possibilidade de comprar esse espaço. Garante que haverá capacidade disponível para rodar no Brasil o processamento de IA associado aos serviços do governo. Mas essa oferta não é exclusiva para o governo, já que a iniciativa privada no país também pode comprar e usar. Há outros benefícios econômicos que merecem ser considerados? No caso específico do Nordeste, há a possibilidade de aproveitar energia elétrica renovável que está sendo desperdiçada. Você leva o data center para perto da turbina eólica ou da usina solar e deixa de depender de linhas de transmissão para consumir aquela energia. Ela passa a ser monetizada, vendida na forma de computação, o que também é positivo. Não estou dizendo que isso não deva ser feito. Estou dizendo que tem muito mais a ver com PIB e geração de receita do que com diminuição da dependência. O problema é achar que estamos atingindo um resultado maior do que de fato estamos. Por que manter os dados no Brasil não resolve a dependência tecnológica? Estamos vivendo um aumento muito grande da dependência. Nossas atividades individuais e profissionais estão sendo estruturadas sobre uma cognição computacional que não controlamos. A empresa não controla e o país não controla. A simples possibilidade de um modelo deixar de estar disponível já é um problema. A questão é que estamos estruturando nosso trabalho e nossa pesquisa acadêmica cada vez mais em parceria com sistemas computacionais que não controlamos. Não é o fato de os dados estarem aqui que vai nos proteger disso. A tomada de decisão dos brasileiros está sendo feita em parceria com esses sistemas, e isso é uma fonte adicional de dependência. O dado pode estar aqui e continuar não sendo seu, continuar sem o seu controle. Não estamos falando de uma refinaria de petróleo que você pode expropriar e dizer que agora é sua. É uma máquina administrada por pessoas que estão em outro lugar e que tomam decisões com base em agendas que, eventualmente, não são as nossas. Que mudanças nas condições de uso desses sistemas podem afetar quem depende deles? Pode mudar o preço, a regra, as categorias sociais representadas naquele software. Podem mudar as políticas de tratamento dos dados que fornecemos o tempo inteiro. E a regulação, por si só, não resolve isso. O que resolve é ter alternativa. A própria maneira de tomar a decisão está sendo dividida com sistemas que não

artigo.texto: Hyperscale data centers’ energy consumption, carbon emissions newly estimated by researchers New research reveals the electricity consumption and carbon emissions behind America’s hyperscale data centers rivals that of some U.S. states For immediate release: November 16, 2026 Boston, MA—Over the course of a year, hyperscale data centers (HDCs)—the largest and most powerful class of data centers, supporting services such as cloud computing, large language model training, and global deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) tools—are powered mostly by fossil fuels and use as much electricity as entire U.S. states, according to a new study led by Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Harvard Data Science Initiative. The study provides one of the first facility-level estimates of HDCs’ electricity use and carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions since the rise of AI. The study was published Nov. 16 in Nature Sustainability. “Data centers are growing incredibly fast, driven largely by AI, and decisions about where to build them and how to power them are being made right now. But there’s very little facility-level information about their environmental footprint,” said lead author Gianluca Guidi, postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics. “Our study helps fill that gap.” “Our goal is to give the public, policymakers, investors, and developers a much more concrete, up-to-date picture than was available before,” added corresponding author Francesca Dominici, Clarence James Gamble Professor of Biostatistics, Population, and Data Science and director of the Harvard Data Science Initiative. “Decisions about where data centers go and how they’re powered are critical environmental and public health decisions, and they should be made with good data.” While data centers are known to require significant electricity to run, few studies have examined this topic facility by facility, estimating not just how much electricity each HDC uses, but what fuels generated this electricity. For this study, the researchers used satellite imagery to build a list of 403 HDCs across the U.S. and estimated annual electricity consumption for each facility between May 2024 and April 2025 under a range of operating scenarios. They then used Environmental Protection Agency data to attribute carbon emissions to each HDC based on the mix of power plants in its regional grid. The study found that these HDCs, depending on how hard they were running, together used between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours of electricity—with the upper estimate approaching the amount some states, such as Indiana, Michigan, and Tennessee, use in a year. During the study period, HDC electricity demand corresponded to approximately 1.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption, and was associated with about 25.7 million metric tons of CO2—an amount two to three times higher than an earlier estimate for 2018. Today, electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely much higher than they were during the study period, the researchers say. “What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” Guidi said. “The data center boom hasn’t slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025. New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow. That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.” The study also found that roughly 54% of the electricity powering the HDCs was generated by fossil fuels—mainly natural gas (38%) and coal (15%)—and about a quarter of the electricity was in grid regions dirtier than average. The researchers noted substantial regional differences, with some HDCs relying much more heavily on carbon-intensive electricity than others. Many of the facilities were concentrated in geographic areas where electricity is generated heavily by coal-fired power plants. The researchers also noted that just four states—Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa—accounted for more than half of the electricity use studied. The study had limitations, including that there wasn’t enough available data to study all HDCs in the U.S., and that the data did not allow them to differentiate between power used for general-purpose versus AI-specialized operations at each HDC. The researchers also noted that the study didn’t directly measure the health effects associated with HDCs, but that is a subject they plan to pursue in future research. “Quantifying health impacts is an important next step,” said Dominici. “First, carbon dioxide drives climate change, which affects health through heat waves, wildfire smoke, flooding, and other pathways. Second, the fossil fuel power plants in the regional electricity systems associated with this demand also release other pollutants, such as fine particulate matter, nitrogen oxides, and sulfur dioxide, that are directly linked to heart and lung disease and premature death. So when data centers draw heavily on fossil fuel power, the people living near and downwind of those power plants may bear health costs, even if they’re far from the data center itself.” Article information “Assessing the Carbon Emissions and Energy Consumption of US Hyperscale Data Centers,” Gianluca Guidi, Francesca Dominici, Tiziano Squartini, Callaway Sprinkle, Jonathan Gilmour, Kevin Butler, Eric Bell, Scott Delaney, Falco J. Bargagli-Stoffi, Nature Sustainability, November 16, 2026, doi: 10.1038/s41893-026-01985-7 The study was supported by the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences–Harvard Center Pilot Project (P30ES000002), the National Institute on Aging (R01AG066793), and the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (R01ES034373). artigo.texto: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines is seeking a stronger foothold in Southeast Asia’s emerging carbon markets, with Aboitiz Foundation joining a regional framework as an Observer in a move that could open up opportunities for climate financing, carbon trading and investments in nature-based projects. Representing the CarbonPH Coalition and the Philippines Nature-based Solutions (NbS) Group, Aboitiz Foundation has joined the ASEAN Common Carbon Framework (ACCF) as an Observer, marking a step toward greater Philippine participation in regional carbon market development. The engagement coincided with the signing of the framework’s Memorandum of Collaboration (MoC) during the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, and the renewal of the agreement for another two years. The move provides Philippine stakeholders an avenue to contribute to discussions on carbon market standards, financing mechanisms and regional cooperation as Southeast Asian economies work toward more interconnected and credible carbon markets. “ASEAN has the natural capital and economic dynamism to become a significant player in global carbon markets. Through the CarbonPH Coalition and our work in nature-based solutions, we hope to contribute Philippine perspectives and practical experience to this regional effort,” said Ginggay Hontiveros-Malvar, Aboitiz chief reputation and sustainability officer and president of Aboitiz Foundation. “Our aim is to help build a carbon market where integrity attracts investment, climate action creates economic opportunity, and communities share in the value being created,” she added. The Philippines’ participation comes as the country works to strengthen its carbon market ecosystem through private-sector collaboration, knowledge-sharing and capacity-building initiatives. One such initiative is the CarbonPH Coalition, which brings together industry stakeholders to explore opportunities for credible carbon market development and nature-based climate solutions. Together with the NbS Group, the coalition is also advancing a long-term initiative focused on forest restoration, biodiversity conservation, watershed protection and community development, alongside the development of recommended governance frameworks. These efforts aim to position the Philippines to develop nature-based carbon projects that can attract climate financing while creating economic opportunities for communities involved in conservation and restoration. The country has significant potential given its extensive natural resources, but turning this natural capital into viable carbon assets will require credible project standards, transparent governance and mechanisms to ensure measurable environmental and social benefits. Established in 2024, the ACCF brings together carbon market organizations from Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia and Thailand, along with the ASEAN Alliance on Carbon Markets, to coordinate regional initiatives and promote high-integrity carbon market development. Under its 2026-2028 strategy, the framework is prioritizing broader ASEAN representation, alignment with international standards, stronger market infrastructure and technical cooperation to facilitate credible carbon financing and cross-border market development. The inclusion of Philippine private-sector stakeholders as Observers provides an opportunity to exchange expertise with established regional initiatives while bringing local experience in conservation, restoration and sustainable investment into the discussions. For the Philippines, the engagement could help bridge the gap between its natural capital and emerging financing opportunities in regional carbon markets. As ASEAN moves toward greater market connectivity, the challenge will be to ensure that carbon trading delivers more than emissions offsets by supporting investable climate solutions that protect ecosystems, strengthen local livelihoods and build long-term environmental resilience.

artigo.texto: The Lansing Town Board is set to decide whether to ban data centers on Wednesday, following a public hearing held on Tuesday. The vote comes after multiple lawsuits and months of review of the Lake Hawkeye data center slated to be built on the banks of Cayuga Lake at the former Cayuga power plant, located in Lansing. Lake Hawk Eye LLC, a subsidiary of data center developer TeraWulf, signed an 80-year lease for the property in August 2025. The ban was proposed at the end of a special meeting on Sep. 29, called by the Lansing Town Board to evaluate the impact of the data center moratorium signed by New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) in July. The moratorium prevents hyperscale data center proposals from receiving environmental permitting, a required step in the approval process, for one year. This was the first statewide data center moratorium signed in the United States. The proposed data center has been met with opposition by community members concerned about the potential noise, strain on the power grid produced by the project and the cost of litigation in the event that TeraWulf violated legal agreements with the town. Others have expressed agreement with the project, citing the potential for economic development as the data center would bring in jobs and millions of dollars in tax revenue. The question to build or ban the Lansing data center comes amid national debates on artificial intelligence and data center development regulation in the wake of the midterm elections. Voters across the country supported 41 ballot measures to restrict data center development on election night – only voters in North Dakota rejected adding industrial review to the data center approval process. Data centers manage, store and process information to support artificial intelligence and online platforms. TeraWulf plans to develop the physical campus with cooling and electrical systems and then will rent the site to a tenant such as an artificial intelligence company. In a Nov. 3 lawsuit, TeraWulf alleged the Lansing town supervisor failed to produce “legally sufficient” responses for two Freedom of Information Law requests. TeraWulf took legal action through its subsidiary, Lake Hawkeye LLC, filing an Article 78 petition with the Tompkins County Supreme Court. FOIL requests cost the town more than $200,000 from October 2025 through mid-June, a surge that can be largely attributed to transparency around the controversial Lake Hawkeye Data Center, according to town supervisor Ruth Groff. An earlier hearing held at the end of September heard over 30 comments, all of which opposed the project – except Pace Ralli, vice president of project development at TeraWulf. Following the comment period, the Town Board discussed worries that even with regulation, the town cannot afford to enforce their rules due to the cost of litigation. This is not the first legal action taken against the town board. In July, a member of the Lansing Zoning Advisory Committee, Laura Baker, alleged town board member Joe Wetmore misused his authority to block projects. Baker, represented by a legal firm that works with TeraWulf, filed the petition in June, accusing Wetmore of “manipulating” government processes to block projects he does not personally agree with, among other complaints. Wetmore is “not commenting on ongoing lawsuits,” he wrote in an email to The Sun. Two environmental advocacy groups, FLX Strong and Cayuga Lake Environmental Action Network, filed an Article 78 petition against the Lansing Town Zoning Board of Appeals and TeraWulf project developers in January. They allege the ZBA overstepped its authority by “allow[ing] the project to bypass rigorous environmental review,” according to the Ithaca Times. Almost 23,000 people have signed the No Data Center FLX petition that calls for the rejection of the data center development. The organization is set to hold a press conference before the public hearing at Lansing Middle School on Tuesday. The data center development involves construction through wetlands, potentially contaminating Cayuga Lake and increasing strain on the electrical grid, according to No Data Center FLX. “These people are not the enemy,” said Joe Scaglione III, an Ithaca resident, referencing TeraWulf. In an interview with The Sun, Scaglione said he met with five TeraWulf representatives, including Ralli, to tour the site and “ask them some hard questions.” He is concerned about property tax increases and said the data center will bring in $8.5 million in annual tax revenue and 150 permanent jobs that would replace the 150 positions terminated when the Cayuga Power Plant shut down in 2019. TeraWulf plans to prioritize hiring those who used to work at the plant, according to Scaglione. Beyond Tompkins One of the foremost issues during the midterm elections were “data centers and the price of gas and affordability and corruption,” according to Prof. Dan Lamb, public policy. He added that “allowing the Wild West with data centers is not serving the public well, and communities are getting exploited.” On the federal level, President Donald Trump signed an executive order in July to accelerate data center permits by expediting environment reviews to 10 days and providing financial support to development companies. The administration also proposed that the Environmental Protection Agency no longer require towns to solicit public feedback on applications for air pollution permits, including data centers, and allow the projections to begin development before procuring proper permits. New York State has home rule power, meaning municipalities have complete control over zoning law. This creates uneven data center and artificial intelligence regulation, according to Lamb. As a result, large development companies “weave around the difficult municipalities” and may even exploit communities — especially those with loose regulations, Lamb explained. artigo.texto: Publicidade O veículo de aquisição de data centers recém-listado da Blackstone adquiriu uma participação majoritária em duas joint ventures com a Amazon Web Services (AWS) em uma transação avaliada em cerca de US$ 5 bilhões. Em seu primeiro investimento, o Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust Inc. (BXDC) passará a deter 13 estruturas energizadas recém-construídas em dois campi de data centers da AWS localizados no norte de Indiana e no Mississippi, segundo Nick Pell, diretor-presidente do fundo. O BXDC ficará com uma participação de 75% nos ativos, enquanto a AWS manterá os 25% restantes. A divisão de computação em nuvem da Amazon arrendará todo o portfólio por um prazo inicial de 12 anos, com possibilidade de extensão para até 32 anos, de acordo com comunicado divulgado nesta segunda-feira. “Este acordo direto com a Amazon cria um roteiro para realizarmos mais operações desse tipo com hyperscalers ou desenvolvedores”, afirmou Pell em entrevista. Segundo ele, a joint venture assumirá dívida equivalente a 50% do valor da aquisição no fechamento da operação, prevista para ser concluída ainda este ano. As ações do BXDC avançavam quase 7% às 9h30 em Nova York. O fundo imobiliário reflete a ambição da Blackstone de se tornar uma das maiores financiadoras de infraestrutura para inteligência artificial do mundo, além de ampliar seu alcance entre investidores individuais. A gestora de ativos alternativos, que administra quase US$ 1,4 trilhão, construiu um portfólio de data centers avaliado em US$ 200 bilhões, que inclui a QTS Realty Trust, uma das principais empresas de construção e operação desse tipo de instalação. Continua depois da publicidade “Somente em 2027, estamos acompanhando mais de US$ 300 bilhões em novos data centers pertencentes a desenvolvedores e hyperscalers cuja entrega é esperada nos Estados Unidos”, disse Pell durante teleconferência com analistas. “Vemos ainda mais projetos surgindo em 2028 e nos anos seguintes.” Ele acrescentou que mais da metade dos novos data centers está planejada para polos emergentes, incluindo Richmond, na Virgínia, e San Antonio, no Texas, o que demonstra a expansão da demanda. Lançado em maio, o BXDC foi criado para adquirir data centers já estabilizados, avaliados entre US$ 250 milhões e US$ 1,5 bilhão, com contratos de locação de longo prazo assinados com hyperscalers. O fundo estima que esse mercado potencial alcance US$ 1 trilhão nos próximos cinco anos. Continua depois da publicidade “À medida que as restrições de oferta aumentam diante de uma demanda que continua muito forte, ativos já estabilizados, que já existem, já possuem energia disponível e já contam com um inquilino, tornam-se mais valiosos”, afirmou o diretor de investimentos do BXDC, Mike Forman. “Há muitos desenvolvedores e fundos fechados buscando vender ativos e reciclar capital. Estamos oferecendo uma alternativa para eles por meio do capital dos investidores públicos do BXDC”, acrescentou Pell. A vitória ampla do Partido Democrata nas eleições legislativas dos Estados Unidos tende a impulsionar iniciativas para estabelecer limites regulatórios ao crescimento dos data centers. A expansão dessas instalações tem enfrentado resistência organizada de comunidades locais, além da escassez de equipamentos, fatores que criam gargalos para novos projetos. Continua depois da publicidade Segundo relatório divulgado pelo JPMorgan Chase em maio, mais de 60% da capacidade de data centers prevista para ser concluída em 2027 ainda nem iniciou sua construção. Apesar disso, a demanda por infraestrutura de nuvem e inteligência artificial segue em expansão. A carteira de pedidos da AWS, indicador que mede contratos de computação em nuvem ainda não executados, alcança US$ 578 bilhões, afirmou o CEO da Amazon, Andy Jassy, após a divulgação dos resultados do terceiro trimestre em outubro. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P.

artigo.texto: AmpereHour Energy has announced its role as the Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) integration partner for IndiGrid’s recently commissioned 250 MW / 500 MWh standalone battery storage project in Rajasthan. Located in western Rajasthan, the project is connected to the 765 kV Bhadla-III pooling substation and represents another step towards expanding India’s utility-scale energy storage infrastructure. The project has a power capacity of 250 MW and an energy storage capacity of 500 MWh, enabling it to deliver electricity at its rated output for up to two hours. The facility is designed to store electricity when it is available and supply it during periods of higher demand. This capability is expected to support peak demand management, improve grid flexibility and facilitate the integration of renewable energy into the electricity network. AmpereHour Energy was responsible for engineering and integrating the project’s AC-coupled BESS. The system comprises modular 40 MWh / 20 MVA blocks and a centralized Power Plant Controller (PPC). The PPC coordinates plant operations and supports various grid applications, including peak shifting and frequency support. The entire facility is managed through AmpereHour Energy’s proprietary ELINA Energy Management System (EMS). The platform supports battery operations and coordinates system activities with state and regional load dispatch centres. This technology is designed to help manage energy storage operations while ensuring the facility responds to grid requirements. Commenting on the development, Rahul Shelke, Managing Director and Co-Founder of AmpereHour Energy, said that large-scale battery storage plays an important role in making electricity available when the grid requires it. He highlighted that projects of this scale are essential for developing a power system capable of accommodating higher renewable energy generation while responding to changing electricity demand. Shelke also expressed appreciation for the partnership with IndiGrid, noting that AmpereHour Energy contributed its BESS integration expertise and proprietary energy management technology to support the deployment. Harsh Shah, Managing Director of IndiGrid, stated that battery storage is becoming an important component of India’s long-term power planning as renewable energy accounts for a growing share of the country’s electricity mix. He noted that energy storage can support renewable energy integration while maintaining grid stability. Shah further described the commissioning of the 250 MW / 500 MWh facility as an important milestone for IndiGrid and its third BESS project. He also acknowledged AmpereHour Energy’s partnership and support in bringing the project into operation. The commissioning reflects India’s increasing focus on standalone battery energy storage infrastructure. As solar and wind power capacity expands, large-scale storage facilities are expected to play a greater role in balancing electricity supply and demand, managing peak loads and improving the reliability of renewable-powered electricity networks. artigo.texto: Spartanburg County Council approves three data center agreements, advances three more Spartanburg County Council has approved three proposed data center development agreements on third and final reading. The agreement for Valara Holdings LLC passed in a 3-2 vote, with Councilmen Monier Abusaft and Grant DeShields voting against it. The proposed 457-megawatt data center is planned for about 300 acres along South Pine Street. The project represents an anticipated investment of roughly $2.8 billion and is expected to create 27 full-time jobs. The agreements for AIB CLT1 LLC and 300 Jones Road Associates LLC both passed unanimously. AIB plans to replace its existing Bitcoin mining operation at Tyger River Industrial Park in Moore with a permanent data center building. The 50-megawatt project represents an anticipated $1.2 billion investment and is expected to create 28 jobs. The Jones Road project would redevelop about 137 acres of the former R.R. Donnelley property into a data center with up to 65 megawatts of capacity. The company anticipates investing $1.5 billion and creating 25 jobs. Council also gave initial approval to three additional data center development agreements proposed by AIB for the Tyger River Industrial Park in Moore. AIB CLT2, CLT3 and CLT4 all passed unanimously on first reading. Those proposals will need additional readings before receiving final approval. Monday's meeting drew a large crowd, with council chambers filled with residents speaking both for and against the proposed developments. Opponents raised concerns about potential noise and pollution, while supporters pointed to the economic benefits and additional revenue the projects could bring to the county.

artigo.texto: Data Center na Virgínia, EUA • 17 de março de 2025 REUTERS/Leah Millis Dois dias de treinamento culminam em uma cerimônia de entrega de diplomas. Empresas ansiosas para contratar os recém-formados já estão oferecendo vagas com salários superiores kmja US$ 100.000 por ano. Bem-vindo à economia dos centros de dados. Na corrida para construir a infraestrutura de IA dos Estados Unidos, as empresas de tecnologia estão com dificuldades para encontrar técnicos com as habilidades necessárias para instalar os sistemas de refrigeração, racks de servidores, equipamentos elétricos e cabos de fibra óptica essenciais para atender à demanda altíssima por essa tecnologia revolucionária. Mesmo com as mudanças no cenário político da IA — principalmente após as recentes eleições de meio de mandato — a falta de mão de obra disponível para dar continuidade aos projetos de data centers certamente superaria qualquer possível desaceleração na construção civil. Assim, o setor está se empenhando ao máximo para capacitar e contratar pessoas para preencher essas vagas cruciais. Diversas organizações sem fins lucrativos, empresas de ensino online e os quatro grandes gigantes da computação em nuvem com inteligência artificial — Amazon, Google, Meta e Microsoft — oferecem vários tipos de cursos de treinamento acelerado e gratuito para as habilidades técnicas necessárias para a construção de data centers. Algumas dessas posições podem pagar salários de seis dígitos. E muitos americanos nem sequer sabem que esses empregos existem. Formatura na sexta-feira. Orientação na segunda-feira. Javonntae Hill estudou design de videogames. Ele está na casa dos 30 anos e buscava uma carreira, mas não sabia bem por onde começar. A namorada dele viu um anúncio da America's Workforce Academy, um novo programa de treinamento que a Meta lançou em agosto para ajudar a suprir a falta de mão de obra qualificada. A empresa se dispôs a pagar a ele durante as quatro semanas de treinamento e garantiu a ele um emprego em um data center após a conclusão do curso. Hill resolveu tentar. Ao longo de um mês, em uma sala de aula com 30 pessoas, ele participou de uma combinação de aulas teóricas e treinamento prático, aprendendo como instalar e passar cabos de fibra óptica e de cobre, e o que cada cor de isolamento do cabo indicava. Ele estava nervoso: esperava conseguir reter todas aquelas informações para o novo emprego. “A formatura foi na sexta-feira”, disse Hill. “Comecei o período de integração na segunda-feira.” A Meta fez uma parceria com a Associated Builders and Contractors, uma associação comercial do setor da construção civil que treina trabalhadores há décadas. Ao contrário dos métodos de treinamento tradicionais, como escolas técnicas ou estágios, os cursos acelerados da ABC não são projetados para serem abrangentes; eles são projetados para colocar o maior número possível de pessoas para trabalhar em data centers. “É como no exército”, disse Joel Thames, chefe do grupo de segurança e força de trabalho da ABC. “O treinamento básico os prepara para qualquer cenário? Não. Mas oferece uma formação fundamental antes de começarem a trabalhar no local de trabalho.” Hill disse que seu nervosismo era infundado: ele chegou ao local de trabalho em Ohio superpreparado. E grato. "Eu poderia fazer isso pelo resto da minha vida", disse Hill. "Já vi anúncios de vagas disponíveis, mas tenho muita lealdade à Meta." O problema Apesar da crescente oposição pública e de uma onda de novos legisladores prometendo regulamentar sua expansão, a construção de centros de dados é praticamente imparável. De acordo com o economista Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, da Columbia Business School , espera-se que os gastos com infraestrutura de IA se aproximem de US$ 1 trilhão por ano , anualmente, num futuro próximo. Mas a construção enfrenta muitos obstáculos logísticos , incluindo licenças de construção, garantias de energia, materiais e financiamento. Mesmo as empresas de IA com os maiores recursos financeiros, capazes de superar esses obstáculos, encontram um problema constante: os Estados Unidos têm muito poucos profissionais qualificados para construir centros de dados — principalmente em algumas das localidades remotas ou rurais onde estão sendo construídos. Os Estados Unidos enfrentam uma escassez de 1 milhão de engenheiros necessários para atender às estimativas de construção de data centers, segundo estimativas da PwC. Muitos projetos, que já estavam prontos para serem iniciados, sofreram atrasos de meses enquanto as empresas reúnem equipes qualificadas para construí-los. De acordo com o Goldman Sachs, apenas cerca de metade da capacidade de computação de IA prevista para entrar em operação entre agora e 2028 deverá ser concluída dentro do prazo. Essa espera tem um custo elevado: para grandes centros de dados de IA, um mês de atraso pode custar desde algumas dezenas de milhões de dólares até bem mais de 100 milhões de dólares, dependendo da localização, da escala e dos termos do contrato, afirmou Mona Dajani, copresidente da área de infraestrutura, energia e imobiliário da Cooley. Assim, as empresas de IA estão enfrentando esse desafio abandonando a exigência de cursos técnicos de vários anos ou estágios remunerados, em favor de cursos acelerados e de alta intensidade, projetados especificamente para vagas na construção de data centers. Muitas oferecem os cursos gratuitamente. Um número crescente delas chega a pagar aos alunos para participarem dos cursos. As aulas podem durar de 15 semanas a apenas dois dias, dependendo da vaga. A demanda por mão de obra é tão grande que empresas de IA estão contratando alguns dos melhores graduados logo no dia seguinte à obtenção de suas certificações. artigo.texto: The Broken Arrow City Council voted Monday to extend its moratorium on new applications for data centers and to hire a consulting firm to help write permanent rules. The city wants rules in place before any data center company can apply to build in Broken Arrow. What the council approved Council members approved two things Monday: - A contract with Westwood Professional Services Inc. to study data centers and help write permanent zoning standards. - An extension of the moratorium through June 30, 2027, so the city can finish those rules before it accepts any applications. The study will focus on three things: where data centers could be allowed, protecting the city’s water and other infrastructure, and the long-term impact. Work since June In June, the City Council passed a six-month moratorium on data center applications that was set to expire Dec. 31. Since then, the city formed a data center study committee and met with Public Service Company of Oklahoma about how to power large data centers and plan for the infrastructure. The city also reviewed data center rules adopted by other cities, including Oklahoma City. City Attorney Trevor Dennis said the goal is to bring the council “a set of regulations and recommendations” for amending the zoning ordinance for data centers. Support for police chief during public comment One person also spoke during public comment in support of Police Chief Lance Arnold, who has been on paid administrative leave since Oct. 14 while the city conducts an internal investigation. Action on Arnold’s employment was not on the agenda Monday because the chief reports to the city manager, not the council. Data center moratorium timeline - April 30, 2026: The city publicly discloses a developer’s interest in building a data center in east Broken Arrow. - June 10, 2026: The prospective company walks away from its letter of intent to buy privately owned land in east Broken Arrow. - June 15, 2026: The council passes Ordinance No. 3929, a six-month moratorium on data center applications through Dec. 31. - Aug. 18, 2026: The city announces the formation of a Data Center Study Committee. - Oct. 20, 2026: City staff briefs the council on their regulatory study. - Nov. 16, 2026: The council approves a consulting contract with Westwood Professional Services and extends the moratorium up to six months through June 30, 2027.

artigo.texto: 17 de novembro de 2026, às 20:22 A CEO interina da Nvidia Colette Kress, que ocupava o cargo de diretora financeira, afirmou que é importante que os data centers atendam as comunidades nas regiões em que estiverem instalados, enquanto salientou que essas estruturas criam empregos. A ponderação foi feita em resposta a uma pergunta sobre o impacto da “onda azul”, termo que se refere ao Partido Democrata, que se saiu vitorioso nas eleições de meio de mandato nos Estados Unidos. A vitória democrata abre uma nova frente de incerteza para os investimentos em inteligência artificial (IA), com perspectiva de maior regulação sobre o setor e restrições à construção de data centers. A executiva comandou sua primeira webcast para comentar os resultados da gigante de chips de inteligência artificial nesta terça-feira, após assumir o posto principal da Nvidia interinamente diante da renúncia do ex-CEO Jensen Huang. A CEO interina ressaltou que a empresa continuará sendo “cautelosa” e “disciplinada” na forma como aloca capital daqui para frente. A Nvidia está “avaliando rigorosamente” futuros investimentos, compromissos e garantias, acrescentou. Kress, contudo, afirmou que a companhia seguirá dando apoio aos seus fornecedores, o que é uma prioridade, citando que alguns precisam de ajuda financeira para desenvolverem suas capacidades. A gigante de IA registrou um lucro líquido de US$ 65,29 bilhões no período, o dobro do valor registrado no mesmo período de 2026, conforme o balanço divulgado hoje. A receita do terceiro trimestre de 2027 também mais que dobrou em relação ao mesmo período do ano anterior, para US$ 115,8 bilhões, acima da previsão de US$ 108,9 bilhões da Factset. Veja também

artigo.texto: A eletrificação de automóveis, ônibus e caminhões pode movimentar mais de R$ 200 bilhões em investimentos no Brasil, segundo estimativa da BYD. A companhia aposta na redução dos custos operacionais dos veículos elétricos e na expansão da infraestrutura de recarga para impulsionar esse mercado, com planos de instalar mil carregadores ultrarrápidos no país até o fim de 2027. A projeção foi apresentada por Alexandre Baldy, vice-presidente da BYD, durante o 2º Fórum de Análise Setorial da Câmara de Comercialização de Energia Elétrica (CCEE). Na avaliação do executivo, o Brasil reúne condições para protagonizar uma das transições energéticas mais competitivas do mundo, devido à abundância de fontes renováveis e ao avanço das tecnologias de armazenamento. Baldy destacou que a decisão de compra dos consumidores é influenciada tanto por fatores relacionados à sustentabilidade quanto pela economia proporcionada pelos veículos elétricos. Segundo ele, rodar com um automóvel carregado na tomada de casa pode custar até nove vezes menos do que utilizar gasolina em um veículo a combustão. Mil carregadores ultrarrápidos até 2027 Como parte da aposta na expansão da mobilidade elétrica, a BYD pretende instalar mil carregadores ultrarrápidos no Brasil até o fim de 2027. A companhia lançou no país um equipamento com potência de 1,5 MW, associado a um banco de baterias que permite realizar recargas sem exigir uma infraestrutura de conexão à rede elétrica equivalente à potência máxima do carregador. O primeiro equipamento já está em operação em Brasília. Segundo Baldy, a tecnologia permite carregar a bateria de 50 kWh de um veículo de 20% a 80% em aproximadamente quatro minutos. A recarga de 10% a 97% pode ser realizada em cerca de oito minutos, proporcionando autonomia superior a 400 quilômetros, conforme o modelo. Na China, de acordo com o executivo, a BYD instalou 12 mil carregadores com essa tecnologia em um período de dez meses. A associação dos carregadores a sistemas de armazenamento é uma das alternativas para ampliar a infraestrutura de recarga, especialmente em locais onde a capacidade disponível na rede elétrica representa uma limitação. Ônibus elétricos têm custo de operação 65% menor Baldy também destacou o avanço da eletrificação do transporte coletivo em São Paulo, que já conta com mais de mil ônibus totalmente elétricos. Segundo o executivo, apesar dos desafios iniciais para adaptar as garagens e instalar os sistemas de recarga, os operadores que adotaram a tecnologia não demonstram interesse em retornar aos veículos movidos a diesel. Para a empresa, os ônibus elétricos apresentam custos de operação com eletricidade aproximadamente 65% inferiores aos gastos com diesel, além de despesas de manutenção cerca de 70% menores. A redução dos custos também começa a impulsionar a eletrificação dos segmentos de caminhões e veículos utilitários. O executivo mencionou ainda aplicações de baterias no transporte ferroviário. Os trens desenvolvidos pela BYD para o monotrilho da Linha 17-Ouro, em São Paulo, possuem sistemas próprios de armazenamento, que permitem continuar a operação até a estação seguinte em caso de interrupção do fornecimento externo de energia. Eletrificação pode reduzir emissões em São Paulo Além dos ganhos econômicos, Baldy destacou o potencial de redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa com a substituição de veículos a combustão por modelos elétricos. Como exemplo, citou a frota de São Paulo, que reúne mais de 12 mil ônibus e entre 3,8 milhões e 3,9 milhões de automóveis em circulação diariamente. Segundo estimativa apresentada pelo executivo, a substituição desses veículos por modelos elétricos poderia reduzir as emissões de carbono na cidade em aproximadamente 9 milhões de toneladas por ano. Baldy também mencionou o avanço da eletrificação nos serviços de transporte por aplicativo. De acordo com ele, uma empresa do segmento já possui quase 70% de sua frota eletrificada, sendo aproximadamente 62% composta por veículos da BYD. Para o vice-presidente da companhia, a combinação entre a expansão da infraestrutura de recarga, a redução dos custos de utilização e a disponibilidade de energia renovável deverá acelerar a eletrificação do transporte e ampliar as oportunidades de negócios no setor elétrico brasileiro.

artigo.texto: Elysia BESS Copilot for mines: dispatch, degradation and revenue notes for engineers Reviewed by Joe Ashwell First reported on International Mining – News 30 Second Briefing Elysia, Fortescue Zero’s battery intelligence division, has launched Elysia BESS Copilot to manage large, multi-site battery energy storage system portfolios at mines that are expanding faster than operations teams. The software ingests high-frequency BESS data to optimise dispatch, state-of-charge windows and degradation, targeting higher revenue capture from arbitrage and ancillary services while protecting cell life. For mine power engineers, it aims to cut manual portfolio tuning effort as installed MWh scale up, reducing chronic underperformance and operational complexity across hybrid diesel–renewables systems. Technical Brief - Elysia BESS Copilot is developed by Fortescue Zero’s dedicated battery intelligence division, Elysia. - Chronic underperformance is framed as compounding with every additional MWh of storage deployed. Our Take Fortescue Zero’s role in both this Elysia BESS Copilot piece and the recent Pilbara decarbonisation strategy shift (2025-12-03) suggests the software may be aimed at integrating with, or at least complementing, Fortescue’s evolving battery-electric haul fleet architecture rather than standalone grid projects. In our Software category, relatively few of the 43 stories intersect directly with mine haul electrification, so a Fortescue Zero–linked energy management product signals that mine-site BESS optimisation is moving from pilot tools into operational fleet-scale systems. The earlier installation of a Fortescue Zero battery-electric system into a Liebherr T 264 haul truck (2026-05-23) implies that any BESS Copilot deployment will need to handle highly transient, high-C-rate duty cycles, which is a more demanding optimisation problem than typical stationary industrial storage.
