artigo.texto: More than a dozen huge pieces of public land may soon be part of the United States’ arsenal in the global race for artificial intelligence supremacy. The Bureau of Land Management and the Department of Energy are considering leasing at least 17 public land parcels totaling 19,200 acres to developers that plan to build data centers and power infrastructure on the land, a Bisnow analysis of public records found. Just two companies are responsible for more than half of the filings. “This is a new strategy by the Trump administration,” said Chinonso Anozie, an assistant professor at the University of Houston Law Center. “What it would do is remove a lot of local opposition and local vetoes over some of these data centers, limiting what states and local communities can also do in challenging and stopping data centers.” Bisnow verified 17 proposed projects with the BLM and DOE that are either approved or pending authorization by cross-referencing federal agency records and press releases with data center trackers from two conservation and public lands advocacy groups: the Center for Western Priorities and More Than Just Parks. The majority of those projects, excluding separate land parcels for power stations, are in the western U.S., while a smattering of sites are in the Southeast. The filings show that developers are jumping on the opportunity to lease public lands, catalyzed by a July 2025 White House initiative to accelerate the country’s AI industry and by last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Using public lands also means the federal government can flex the supremacy clause, a constitutional provision that gives federal law priority over some state laws. This tool could help developers skirt a broad cultural pushback against data centers. Industry advocacy group Data Center Coalition praised the Trump administration and the DOE for the policy initiative. “The digital infrastructure that data centers provide is essential to advancing America’s global economic competitiveness, safeguarding national security, and maintaining the country’s edge in cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and many other 21st-century technologies,” Michele Nellenbach, the trade group’s vice president of federal affairs, said in a statement. But elected officials are already speaking out against leasing public lands for data center development in Idaho and Kentucky. A lack of local support could still hamper proposals far away from towns and cities, said John Boyd Jr., principal at site selection firm The Boyd Co. “Companies routinely look for some type of public-private partnership, whether that be sales tax abatements for the server equipment or property tax abatements,” Boyd said. “All of that requires county, city or state support.” Most of the companies that filed prelease applications with the BLM or have been selected for projects on DOE land didn't respond to Bisnow’s requests for comment. SB Energy In Ohio Part of a former uranium enrichment plant near the 2,200-person town of Piketon in southern Ohio is planned to become the world’s largest data center to date. SB Energy, a SoftBank Group company, broke ground on the 189-acre project in March and committed to building 10 gigawatts of new power generation connecting to the local grid. It expects to generate 10,000 construction jobs and 2,000 permanent jobs in the region. Known as the Portsmouth Site, it includes Department of Energy land. It is split between public land and some private land, according to a spokesperson for SB Energy. Valar Atomics In Utah Valar Atomics, a company focused on scaling nuclear energy for heavy industrial power, filed an application with BLM to build a 9,000-acre facility in Carbon County, Utah, NPR reported in September. BLM records confirm the filing but don't contain the project's acreage. The development, named Project Beehive, is planned to include data centers along with 456 small nuclear reactors and space to produce nuclear fuel and store nuclear waste on a Department of Energy site. A Brookfield Partnership In Kentucky A partnership between Brookfield, NextEra Energy Resources, Big Rivers Electric Corp., Jackson Purchase Energy Cooperative and Paducah Power System is planning an energy generation and AI campus on a 785-acre DOE site. Construction is expected to conclude on the former Superfund site in 2031, following remediation efforts that are needed because of the site’s decades of uranium enrichment operations, according to a release from the department. A spokesperson for the Paducah American Energy Hub told Bisnow in a statement that the team is “committed to working with all stakeholders.” “We have met with many local and state officials and look forward to engaging constructively with them and the community as a whole,” the spokesperson said. But Gov. Andy Beshear told Politico in August that the Trump administration excluded him from conversations about the $100B data center project and indicated a willingness to block or delay data centers from opening. While Beshear can’t stop the data center from happening, Anozie said, local governments can still make it difficult for projects to operate once they are built. “Where the states might have a way of regulating what is going on is using state environmental laws to challenge and to say, ‘Well, you didn't get the permit for this,’” he said. “But they cannot outrightly veto or zone out that area for a data center.” Amentum And DC Blox In South Carolina The Savannah River Site was one of 16 sites identified by the DOE in April 2025 to support the construction of data centers and the power infrastructure they require. The site was used to produce plutonium and tritium for nuclear weapons in the 1950s, Spectrum News reported. Efforts at the site have centered on environmental cleanup and managing nuclear materials, as well as research and development. A WEG apresentou o W30Slim Smart EC, motor com inversor integrado e 175 milímetros de comprimento axial destinado a aplicações como ventilação e refrigeração de data centers. Divulgada pela fabricante em 10 de novembro de 2026, a solução reúne acionamento eletrônico e ventilação própria para facilitar sua integração aos equipamentos que mantêm os servidores em condições adequadas de operação. A família oferece potências de 1,5 a 10 hp, equivalentes a aproximadamente 1,1 a 7,5 kW. Esses números representam potência mecânica de acionamento, não capacidade de refrigeração. O catálogo posiciona o modelo em aplicações com ventiladores radiais: ele movimenta o conjunto responsável pela circulação de ar, dentro de um sistema térmico mais amplo. O que os 17,5 centímetros representam A medida destacada corresponde ao comprimento ao longo do eixo. Portanto, não descreve o diâmetro nem todas as dimensões externas do equipamento. Para fabricantes de sistemas de ventilação, essa característica pode ampliar as possibilidades de montagem em espaços restritos, embora o resultado dependa da geometria do conjunto. A WEG classifica o produto como o mais compacto, leve e eficiente de sua categoria. Entretanto, os documentos consultados não apresentam uma comparação reproduzível com concorrentes, identificando modelos, condições de ensaio e diferenças percentuais. A afirmação permanece atribuída à fabricante, sem validação independente apresentada nesses materiais. Inversor integrado controla a velocidade O inversor incorporado permite ajustar a rotação conforme o comando recebido, reunindo motor e eletrônica de acionamento em uma solução integrada. Isso oferece ao fabricante do equipamento uma forma de controlar a movimentação de ar conforme as necessidades operacionais, em vez de trabalhar exclusivamente com uma velocidade fixa. Entre as interfaces especificadas estão sinais de 2–10 V, corrente de 4–20 mA e PWM, além de comunicação Modbus. Na prática, esses recursos permitem receber comandos e integrar o acionamento à automação da instalação. A documentação também relaciona proteções contra sobrecarga, sobretemperatura, sobretensão, subtensão e rotor bloqueado. O catálogo apresenta alternativas de rotação nominal que chegam a 3.600 rpm, com faixas ajustáveis conforme a versão. A seleção precisa considerar simultaneamente potência, velocidade e alimentação elétrica; o limite de 10 hp não deve ser entendido como disponível em qualquer configuração. Ventilação própria e proteção opcional Outro diferencial é a construção TEFC, com ventilação própria. Segundo a WEG, o motor não depende do fluxo de ar produzido pela aplicação para manter seu desempenho térmico. Essa independência é relevante quando o posicionamento do acionamento dificulta a passagem de ar sobre sua estrutura. O catálogo informa operação em ambientes de −25 °C a 50 °C e regime S1, destinado ao funcionamento contínuo. A proteção padrão é IP55; IP66 aparece como opção. Assim, a resistência ampliada a poeira e jatos fortes de água precisa ser confirmada na configuração adquirida. A documentação menciona níveis de eficiência IE5 e IE6, mas não fornece, na apresentação geral do W30Slim, uma tabela completa de rendimento por carga e rotação. Por isso, essas classificações não permitem calcular diretamente a redução da conta de eletricidade de uma instalação. Demanda energética cresce, mas economia exige medição O contexto comercial é global. No relatório Key Questions on Energy and AI, de 2026, a Agência Internacional de Energia estima que os data centers consumiram 485 TWh em 2025 e projeta aproximadamente 950 TWh em 2030. Os valores abrangem o setor inteiro, incluindo instalações que não são dedicadas à IA. Para avaliar o impacto dessa tecnologia na infraestrutura de inteligência artificial, ainda faltam resultados operacionais do modelo: economia medida sob condições comparáveis, efeito sobre a eficiência total da instalação, preço e retorno do investimento. Os materiais consultados descrevem especificações e aplicações previstas, mas não apresentam esses indicadores em um data center identificado nem detalham prazos de fornecimento para projetos no mercado brasileiro. artigo.texto: U.S. construction economists continue to marvel at the historic strength of the data-center market, with unprecedented growth in project value and industry domination never before experienced. Experts assembled for the Construction Economy Outlook Fall 2026, presented by ConstructConnect on Nov. 12, spoke in superlatives throughout the webinar. Even threats such as growing public resistance and the uncertainty of financing may only cool the pace of data-center growth, not arrest it, they suggested. “We continue to see just amazing, unprecedented growth in data centers,” said ConstructConnect chief economist Michael Guckes. “Even though we’ve seen some political pushback on data centers, I think it’s too late. I think the train has left the station. “Once you have a technology with this kind of power, and other countries are competing in this realm for it, there’s no going backwards with this.” Guckes reported in 2022, the first $1-billion data center broke ground; in 2024, the U.S. had the first project that surpassed $3 billion; the next year saw the first $10-billion project; and now, he said, “Amazingly enough, we saw more starts in just January than we did in all of 2024. This is also the first time where we’re seeing these campuses of $50 billion and greater breaking ground.” Guckes added, “So this industry is not only huge for construction, but it has completely transformed within its own ranks. “If you go back to pre-COVID, you were seeing about 10 to 12 per cent of all non-residential construction dollars heading into megaprojects and now it’s more than one out of every $4.” Guckes was joined by Ken Simonson, chief economist, Associated General Contractors of America; Richard Branch, chief economist, American Institute of Architects (AIA); and Kristy O’Brien, director of content acquisition, ConstructConnect. Paul Hart, vice-president of economic content with ConstructConnect, served as the moderator. 2027 looks brighter Overall, U.S. construction spending is expected to remain slow, Branch said. Non-residential building construction spending is forecast to decline 0.3 per cent in 2026 before increasing three per cent in 2027, he said. Commercial construction is expected to grow 4.8 per cent in 2026 and 5.8 per cent in 2027, while industrial construction is expected to decline 11.6 per cent in 2026 and 0.6 per cent in 2027. Institutional construction is forecast to rise 2.8 per cent and 2.7 per cent, respectively. The Fed is expected to raise rates in the next year. “We’re probably looking at another 50 basis points of rate hikes between now and at this point next year,” said Branch. “I do think, though, if we start to see oil prices come down, that we’ll start to see inflation peel back, and as inflation peels back, particularly if it gets closer to their two-per-cent target, I think we will start to see they’re loosening rates.” Strong commercial numbers are largely because of data centers, Branch said. Traditional office construction is expected to decline five per cent and four per cent this year and next, respectively, while warehouse spending is forecast to decline 1.7 per cent in 2026 before increasing 1.4 per cent in 2027. Guckes reported ConstructConnect’s October 2026 economic forecast projects U.S. GDP growth of 2.1 per cent in 2026, rising to 2.4 per cent in 2027 and 2.7 per cent each of the next three years. Guckes identified various headwinds facing the construction sector: Higher interest rates make it harder to build profitably, while slow labour growth restrains the economy’s expansion. Inflation hurts consumers and spending, casting a shadow over the construction economy. Costs, rates squeeze margins O’Brien reported higher costs and rates are squeezing margins even as demand holds. She said tariffs and trade disruption continues to buffet the U.S. construction sector. Steel and aluminum imports have faced 50 per cent tariffs since June 2025, while overall construction material prices are up 11.0 per cent year-over-year, the fastest spike since May 2022. Tax cuts and business-investment incentives in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act continue to support demand, O’Brien stated. Bid prices are up 5.4 per cent. According to Simonson, tariffs, immigration enforcement, federal deficits and interest rates are the four major risks to construction. The concern is tighter immigration enforcement will worsen labour shortages. The webinar wrapped up with further roundtable discussion of the topic of the day. Branch said, “I think where that moratorium issue comes more is in 2028 spending data. There again, I don’t see a decline. I don’t see a collapse. I see more of a flat market in 2028 rather than a slowdown.” O’Brien noted Texas is leading in data-center construction, followed by Virginia, North Carolina, Arkansas and the Midwest states. The sheer scale of the explosion, she said, brings constraints: power and water availability, public response and the cost of capital. Guckes said public pushback can be addressed in part through engineering. “Some of the solutions you talk about, noise, water, pollution of other types, a lot of those have engineering solutions…Those things generally just take money, and so far the data centers have access to a lot of it.”

artigo.texto: Tulsa, Broken Arrow leaders weigh data center regulations amid growing public concerns As debate intensifies across Green Country over hyperscale data centers, Tulsa and Broken Arrow, the region’s two largest cities, have voted to pause consideration of any new data center proposals while they work on regulations. Broken Arrow City Manager Michael Spurgeon said the city’s decision followed packed City Hall meetings and concerns that have surfaced in other communities. Broken Arrow leaders halted data center discussions through the end of the year while the city develops an official plan for how to handle developers. “I know the council shares the same concerns that I have that the public has about the detrimental effect that a data center could have on a community when it comes to for example, our utilities, the water usage, utility rates,” Spurgeon said. He said the city wants to take a deliberate approach before moving forward. “We need to go about this in a very methodical way to look at every aspect of of what the impact would be, whether it's financial, whether it's environmental, whether it's long term,” Spurgeon said. In Tulsa, city leaders raised similar concerns, including the prospect of data centers being built near neighborhoods with limited ability for elected officials to weigh in. During discussion, Tulsa City Councilor Laura Bellis said, “I totally agree with you 100 percent about putting a data center next to large subdivisions. It's just nonsense to me.” Councilors also pointed to zoning rules that could allow data centers in multiple areas near neighborhoods with little to no need for city leaders to provide input. Tulsa City Councilor Vanessa Hall-Harper said, “I'm just raising a question that we have some kind of say in it or not. Where it's already zoned, I don't think we do.” As more cities and towns face data center proposals, a push is growing at the state Capitol to establish statewide guardrails. Tulsa state Rep. Amanda Clinton said communities can feel pressured by promises of economic benefits while lacking the resources to negotiate with major tech companies. “They're between a rock and a hard place. You know, they have this carrot being dangled out of there that they're going to get better schools, better sidewalks, better roads. And that's very tempting. But they also know that they share a city attorney with, say, 4 or 5 other towns. So they're not really quite equipped to go up against, you know, a Google or an Amazon. And they just feel like they're outgunned,” Clinton said. At Clinton’s request, the Legislature held its first-ever interim study on data centers last fall. Then last spring, lawmakers passed the first bill placing a limit on data centers by requiring them to produce their own electricity rather than drawing from the grid and increasing demand. “If these large tech companies want more electricity, fine. You pay for it. We shouldn't have to pay for it,” Clinton said. Clinton said lawmakers still need to address issues including water use, potential impacts on property values, and residents’ ability to learn about proposals. She also said data companies have realized that using non-disclosure agreements to advance projects in Oklahoma has not helped. “I think that people just don't feel like they have any say so they don't have any buy in. Like these decisions are being made for them and around them,” Clinton said. Clinton said she plans to file new bills on data centers in the coming legislative session. She also said that in multiple states, exit polling of midterm voters showed data centers ranked just under the war in Iran and inflation as a top concern. “This is not a Republican or Democratic issue. This is an issue about what we want for our future and for our communities,” Clinton said. Tulsa and Broken Arrow leaders are expected to finalize data center regulations in the coming months. City leaders say it is not a matter of if a new proposal comes, but when. “Sometimes it can seem like you're a little bit behind, but eventually you start to see the cities will catch up and start having regulations and ordinances in place that will actually govern how you how those businesses can move forward,” Spurgeon said.

artigo.texto: Publicidade Washington — Semanas depois de os eleitores demonstrarem forte insatisfação com os data centers nas eleições de meio de mandato, o Congresso debate uma ampla reformulação das regras federais de licenciamento que poderia ajudar as empresas de tecnologia a construir essas instalações mais rapidamente. O projeto de lei aceleraria as análises ambientais federais de vários projetos de energia, incluindo linhas de transmissão e gasodutos, facilitando para os desenvolvedores a obtenção da energia necessária para operar os data centers. Mas essa ajuda vem com uma enorme contrapartida: os data centers também teriam de pagar muito mais pela eletricidade, segundo uma disposição do projeto que cobraria das instalações uma tarifa adicional pelo acesso à rede elétrica. A medida alteraria décadas de regras federais do setor elétrico e poderia gerar uma economia de bilhões de dólares na próxima década para as famílias e outros consumidores. Leia mais: Boom de data centers de IA enfrenta reação negativa nas urnas dos EUA Leia mais: A SpaceX planeja investir US$ 74 bi na construção de data centers no Texas e Arizona A iniciativa de impor custos mais altos aos data centers evidencia como a política em torno da inteligência artificial se tornou complexa em Washington. Data centers gigantescos e ávidos por energia estão se espalhando rapidamente pelo país, pressionando as redes elétricas e provocando indignação em muitas comunidades. Neste mês, os eleitores aprovaram pelo menos 40 iniciativas locais para restringir essas instalações. Continua depois da publicidade Prós e contras Alguns ambientalistas que se opõem ao projeto de licenciamento o classificaram como um benefício para as empresas de tecnologia, argumentando que a legislação poderia acelerar o desenvolvimento de data centers abastecidos por gás natural. O projeto reduziria o alcance de leis ambientais federais para acelerar a construção de diversos tipos de empreendimentos, incluindo gasodutos, projetos eólicos e solares, linhas de transmissão de alta tensão, estradas, transporte público e moradias. Em contraste, os defensores apresentaram o projeto como uma oportunidade de endurecer as regras para as empresas de IA. “O período em que os data centers não pagavam sua parte termina quando este projeto for aprovado”, disse o senador Sheldon Whitehouse, democrata de Rhode Island e um dos autores do projeto. “A partir de agora, os data centers terão de pagar pelos custos adicionais que impõem à rede quando entram em operação. Eles não poderão transferir todos esses custos adicionais para a base tarifária da concessionária e fazer com que sejam arcados pelos demais consumidores.” Continua depois da publicidade O setor de data centers, por sua vez, permaneceu relativamente calado. Embora diversos grupos empresariais, sindicatos e algumas empresas do Vale do Silício tenham apoiado o projeto, uma das principais entidades representativas do setor ainda não o fez. A Data Center Coalition, cujos membros incluem Amazon, Google, Meta e Microsoft, afirmou que ainda está analisando a legislação. “Continuamos avaliando suas implicações com nossos membros, que estão fazendo sua parte para promover a acessibilidade e o crescimento econômico ao investir centenas de bilhões de dólares nos Estados Unidos todos os anos”, disse Jon Hukill, porta-voz da coalizão. Muitos data centers desenvolvidos para treinar e operar modelos de IA de ponta podem consumir tanta eletricidade quanto pequenas cidades, o que provocou debates sobre quem deve pagar pelos bilhões de dólares necessários para construir as usinas e linhas de transmissão de que precisam. Continua depois da publicidade Historicamente, as concessionárias distribuíram o custo das melhorias na rede elétrica entre todos os seus clientes. Mas, à medida que a insatisfação com os data centers aumentou, o presidente Donald Trump e vários governadores pressionaram as gigantes da tecnologia a assumir a conta e não repassar esses custos às famílias. A maioria das empresas de IA prometeu fazer isso, embora esses compromissos de proteção aos consumidores possam ser difíceis de fiscalizar. Inseridas nas 494 páginas do projeto de lei de licenciamento estão várias disposições destinadas a dar mais força a essas promessas. Cobranças extras Uma das medidas determinaria que a Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, a agência federal americana responsável pela regulação do setor de energia, emitisse novas regras em até 90 dias. Essas regras cobrariam dos data centers tanto os custos de eventuais melhorias na rede necessárias para atendê-los quanto os custos de utilização da rede elétrica existente. Continua depois da publicidade Isso derrubaria princípios regulatórios antigos, em vigor desde 1994, que proíbem as concessionárias de cobrar duas vezes dos clientes pela mesma capacidade da rede. Na prática, o projeto afirma que os grandes data centers são diferentes e deveriam pagar potencialmente o dobro do que pagam atualmente. “É uma grande mudança em relação à forma como temos administrado a rede até agora, na qual os benefícios são amplamente compartilhados e socializamos os custos”, disse Robin Millican, diretor de programas de pesquisa e parcerias estratégicas do Center on Global Energy Policy, da Universidade Columbia. Outras disposições dariam aos reguladores estaduais mais liberdade para cobrar dos data centers valores adicionais pelas usinas de energia de que precisam e utilizar o dinheiro para conceder créditos nas contas das famílias. Pela primeira vez, o governo federal também seria obrigado a monitorar o consumo de energia dos data centers. Os políticos têm colocado os data centers no centro das discussões em parte porque a dimensão do boom da IA ameaça sobrecarregar as redes elétricas. As gigantes da tecnologia também priorizam a velocidade e frequentemente estão dispostas a pagar mais para obter energia mais rapidamente. artigo.texto: ABB Key player in electrification According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Battery Circuit Breakers market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global battery circuit breakers market is entering a phase of sustained expansion as electrification reshapes transportation, power generation, and industrial infrastructure. Valued for their ability to safely interrupt high direct current in battery-powered systems, these specialized protective devices are indispensable in electric vehicles, stationary energy storage, and renewable energy installations. Between 2026 and 2035, demand is forecast to rise at a robust pace, supported by policy-driven decarbonization targets, falling battery costs, and the proliferation of DC-coupled architectures. Asia-Pacific remains the largest and fastest-growing region, underpinned by China's dominance in EV and battery production, while North America and Europe accelerate investments in grid-scale storage and charging infrastructure. Technological shifts toward solid-state and hybrid breakers are expected to unlock higher voltage classes and faster response times, intensifying competition among established electrical majors and specialized innovators. Supply chains face pressure from copper price volatility and certification bottlenecks, but the overall outlook remains firmly positive. This report provides a data-driven assessment of market size, segmentation, competitive dynamics, and the strategic pathways to 2035. The baseline scenario for the battery circuit breakers market through 2035 assumes continued policy support for clean energy and electric mobility, alongside steady improvements in battery energy density and cost. Under this scenario, global demand grows at a compound annual rate in the high single digits, with the market index reaching approximately 210 by 2035 (2025=100). Electric vehicles are expected to remain the largest end-use sector, though stationary energy storage gains share as grid operators integrate more intermittent renewables. The product mix shifts gradually from thermal-magnetic toward solid-state and hybrid technologies, particularly in high-voltage EV and utility-scale storage applications. Regionally, Asia-Pacific retains its dominant position, but North America and Europe post faster growth rates as local manufacturing incentives and stricter safety standards take effect. Key risks to the baseline include slower-than-expected EV adoption in mature markets, prolonged raw material price volatility, and regulatory delays in certifying new breaker technologies. Nevertheless, the fundamental demand drivers—decarbonization, decentralization, and digitalization of power systems—remain intact, supporting a positive long-term trajectory. artigo.texto: Trending WHEELING - City officials in Wheeling have consistently heard from vocal opponents of data centers in recent months, but some of those same individuals stepped forward Tuesday night to express gratitude for comprehensive data center regulations introduced as new legislation before city council. Council heard the first reading of an ordinance to create Article 1365 of the city’s planning and zoning code, which outlines several pages of rules and regulations on data centers in Industrial districts. The legislation will establish a rigorous application process, requirements for development and performance standards, regulations for electrical power demands and water consumption, and guidelines on water reuse for closed-loop cooling systems. It additionally outlines rules for noise and air emissions, wastewater guidelines and regulations pertaining to other potential impacts associated with data center operations. For several months, local data center opponents have vocally stood against a planned development at the former Centre Foundry & Machine Company facility in the Wheeling neighborhood of Warwood along River Road. Silicon Foundation plans to redevelop the Centre Foundry site into a phased data center and energy technology campus. While opponents over the past several months have expressed criticism about the way the city has handled the situation surrounding the planned data center in Warwood, a handful of vocal community members came forward during Tuesday night’s meeting to acknowledge they view the new legislation as a step in the right direction. "This ordinance is a good effort to control if not prevent data centers in the city of Wheeling," said Warwood resident Polly Barks. "This effort to halt or mitigate Silicone Foundation’s disastrous effects on Warwood would not have happened without the sustained effort of our community, without coming together almost unanimously against data centers. I challenge any of you to find something that has been so uniquely unifying to the community, for better or for worse." Barks is among several Warwood residents who earlier this summer filed a civil lawsuit against Silicon Foundation in an effort to stop or at least pump the brakes on the development of the Centre Foundry site. She and others have been outspoken on the matter during public informational gatherings as well as during city council meetings. Barks and fellow colleagues have called for the city to pass a moratorium on data center development within the city - a move that Wheeling’s city solicitor maintains cannot be done legally. Officials have noted the Center Foundry site is properly zoned for data center use in an Industrial location. "Although it’s not a moratorium, I’m pleased that this provides a stop-gap that makes the city far less appealing to those coming in to exploit us for their own benefit to our detriment," Barks said. "Although I do disagree with the opening statement that, ‘the city recognizes that facilitating the development of data center service technology can be an economic development asset to the city and of significant benefit to the city and its residents. That’s subjective - we can agree to disagree on that." Barks applauded Ward 1 Councilman Tony Assaro, who represents the Warwood neighborhood, for listening to his constituents and representing their voice. "Tony has shown himself to be a faithful steward of the will of the people," Barks said. "For that we thank him and look forward to working with him further to make our community even better." Members of the Rules Committee of Council, the city administration, the city’s legal department and other council members all worked on the development of the data center regulations for several weeks. A draft of the document was made available on the city’s website, and city leaders welcomed suggestions from the public to make any adjustments to the regulations that may be deemed necessary or beneficial. The regulations were viewed as a result of community action, Barks noted, indicating the regulations attempting to address concerns expressed by vocal residents who do not want noise, higher utility bills, pollution or any other potential side effects data centers have reportedly brought to communities in other parts of the country. She credited people who wore anti-data center T-shirts, posted yard signs, signed petitions, attended events and let their voices be heard. "Residents have become activists," she said, noting this was the beginning of a fight against data centers throughout West Virginia, an effort unfolding "in a state that does not support the will of the people." Barks asked council to make a public statement about anticipated impact on the proposed data center at Centre Foundry. "Take credit for being the first city in West Virginia, to our knowledge, to adopt an ordinance against data centers, and lend your expertise elsewhere," she said. Amanda McWhorter of Triadelphia said she represents Ohio County on a statewide panel known as the West Virginia Data Center Accountability Project. "Thank you for listening to the community and working on this ordinance," McWhorter said. "I would love to be able to connect you to other communities, as well, with our group." McWhorter and Barks encouraged city leaders to work with other communities in the state and with Ohio County on similar efforts to regulate data centers on a local level. In West Virginia, House Bill 2014 - known as the Power Generation and Consumption Act of 2025, establishes state jurisdiction and outlines regulations on the state level for data centers planning to operate at 90 megawatts, which would be deemed as a "high impact data center." Wheeling’s new Article 1365 of the city planning and zoning code, could be used as a template for other communities faced with regulating the development of data centers below the "high-impact" threshold. artigo.texto: State launches India’s first SO2 Emissions Trading Scheme EMA is a collaboration between the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago (EPIC) and the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL) to scale emissions markets across the Global South MUMBAI: The Maharashtra government on Tuesday launched India’s first sulphur dioxide (SO2) Emissions Trading Scheme with the Emissions Market Accelerator (EMA) to reduce industrial pollution. The scheme comes on the heels of the successful implementation and evaluation of the world’s first particulate (PM2.5) pollution market in Surat in 2019. EMA is a collaboration between the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago (EPIC) and the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL) to scale emissions markets across the Global South. The Maharashtra Pollution Control Board (MPCB), which is implementing the scheme, has partnered with the University of Chicago Trust to incorporate artificial intelligence into environmental inspections. The announcement has come almost seven months after MPCB launched mock trading for the SO2 emissions trading market. According to its proponents, the new scheme will benefit approximately 130 million people by improving air quality in Maharashtra. Pankaja Munde, minister for environment and climate change, said at the launch, “We need to look at how technology, including AI, can help us monitor industrial pollution more intelligently.” Munde added that the state government’s role did not end with just regulating industries or controlling pollution. “We must also work alongside industry and encourage participation to create solutions that benefit both the environment and economic growth,” she said. Under the scheme, which covers 17 industrial sectors, MPCB will establish emission limits for participating industries and distribute emission permits, with each permit representing the right to emit a specified quantity of SO₂. Industries will have to monitor and report their emissions through Continuous Emissions Monitoring Systems, and at the end of each compliance period, surrender permits equivalent to their actual emissions. Industries that reduce emissions below their allocated permits can sell the surplus permits in the market. Conversely, industries that exceed their allocation can purchase additional permits from those with surplus. A statement from EPIC said that the selling of permits would create an economic incentive for “cleaner production and technological innovation”. For industries, the scheme provides a choice in how they meet environmental compliance requirements: either by investing in emission-control measures or purchasing permits. Siddhesh Ramdas Kadam, chairman of MPCB, said that the SO₂ emissions trading scheme was a “feather in the cap” for the state. “Our approach is not to control, but to grow together with industry,” he said. Professor Michael Greenstone, the Milton Friedman Distinguished Service Professor in Economics and director of EPIC and Co-Chair of EMA, said that a market like India could cut emissions while lowering costs for industry and helping the economy grow. Balaji Srinivasan, co-chair of EMA, who played a key role in coordinating the initiative, claimed that in the US, emissions trading had cut pollution by 96%. “So, other countries and Indian states are looking to the Maharashtra SO2 pollution market with enormous hope,” he said. Tithee Mukhoppadhyay, deputy executive director of J-PAL South Asia and advisor to EMA, said, “The Surat pilot proved that emissions trading cuts industrial pollution without hurting economic growth.” - ABOUT THE AUTHORSnehal Fernandes Snehal Fernandes is senior associate editor, who joined HT in 2006. She heads the Mumbai edition’s city reporting team that writes on civic and urban governance, transport and infrastructure, health, and education. She is also the National Science Editor. With a career spanning more than two decades, her expertise lies in writing on science and technology, space, environment, sustainable development, climate change, and nuclear energy. Her work consistently breaks down, and without oversimplyfying, science and research developments into an easy read for a broad audience. In 2009, she was among the very first journalist to report on the opposition to the Jaitapur nuclear power plant in Ratnagiri (Konkan) following the Indo- US civil nuclear agreement and consistently followed it with multiple stories from ground zero; wrote about the introduction and subsequent halt to the cultivation of genetically modified (BT) brinjal, and has interviewed Nobel laureates and award winning scientists. In 2012, she was awarded ‘The Press Club Award for Excellence in Journalism’ (Political category) for reports on the mining scam in Goa. Prior to HT, she wrote on education and transport at the Indian Express. She graduated in sociology from St Xavier's College, and firmly believes in the phrase by Karl Marx that ‘Religion is the opium of the people’. When she is not keeping a tab on the going-ons in Mumbai and the scientific world, you'll find her reading world news, or watching crime/espionage series or political dramas. She can repeatedly watch Kill Bill with the same interest as Planet of the Apes and Spiderman. artigo.texto: Com tecnologia da chinesa CATL, a expansão industrial em Belo Jardim permitirá fornecer sistemas de armazenamento com capacidade superior a 8 GWh, preparando a fabricante brasileira para atender aos grandes projetos do setor elétrico a partir de 2028. A Moura vai investir R$ 200 milhões em Pernambuco para ampliar sua fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, instalada em Belo Jardim, no Agreste do estado. O projeto inclui uma nova linha industrial, transferência de tecnologia da chinesa CATL e previsão de mais de 200 contratações, com início da produção ampliada esperado para 2027. Conhecida nacionalmente pelas baterias automotivas, a empresa agora pretende disputar espaço em um mercado que ganha importância com a expansão das usinas solares e eólicas: o armazenamento de eletricidade em equipamentos de grande porte. O investimento já está em execução. Segundo reportagem da Exame, publicada em 14 de novembro de 2026, a companhia prepara seu complexo industrial para atender aos projetos que disputarão o primeiro leilão brasileiro de armazenamento de energia em baterias. - Em apenas 81 minutos, leilões de energia movimentam R$ 14,25 bilhões, garantem eletricidade para os próximos anos e levantam uma pergunta incômoda sobre a conta de luz - Quem paga conta de luz no Nordeste pode ter alta de 9,58% em 2027, enquanto o Sul terá queda de 7,59%: a Thymos Energia projeta tarifa 2% menor na média do país - Montadores de subestação no Rio Grande do Norte esperam 2.299 vagas no Lote 7 da Axia, que tem 42 meses de obra e negocia até R$ 680 milhões com o BID para 3 compensadores síncronos em Açu e João Câmara - Operadores da Termocabo, em Pernambuco, vão trocar 250 toneladas diárias de óleo combustível por gás natural nos 3 motores da usina, convertidos pela Wärtsilä para um contrato de 10 anos A capacidade de fornecimento anunciada supera 8 gigawatts-hora (GWh), colocando a nova operação em uma escala industrial voltada ao atendimento de grandes empreendimentos do setor elétrico. Fábrica da Moura em Pernambuco receberá nova linha de produção e tecnologia chinesa A ampliação ocorre no complexo industrial de Belo Jardim, onde a Moura mantém uma de suas principais operações produtivas. O prédio destinado à expansão já está pronto, enquanto a nova linha industrial foi adquirida na China. A expectativa é iniciar a produção dos equipamentos no fim do primeiro semestre de 2027. A parceria com a CATL, uma das maiores fabricantes mundiais de baterias, divide responsabilidades entre as duas companhias. A chinesa fornece tecnologia de armazenamento e participa da comercialização dos sistemas. A Moura ficará responsável pela industrialização, montagem e integração dos equipamentos no Brasil. O processo envolve receber módulos de baterias e integrá-los em sistemas completos, instalados em contêineres industriais de aproximadamente 20 pés, equipados com refrigeração e proteção contra incêndios. De acordo com informações publicadas pelo Jornal do Commercio, a fabricação nacional também está relacionada às condições de financiamento do BNDES, que podem exigir índices de conteúdo local entre 50% e 60%. A produção em Pernambuco permitirá concentrar no Brasil atividades de engenharia, integração, testes e assistência técnica, fortalecendo a cadeia industrial brasileira de armazenamento de energia. Moura prepara mais de 200 contratações para ampliar produção de baterias em Pernambuco A ampliação da fábrica em Belo Jardim deve impulsionar a geração de empregos no Agreste pernambucano. A Moura prevê contratar e capacitar mais de 200 profissionais para atender à nova linha de produção de sistemas de armazenamento de energia, desenvolvida em parceria com a chinesa CATL. Atualmente, o grupo possui aproximadamente 7.400 funcionários, dos quais cerca de 3.500 trabalham no complexo fabril de Belo Jardim. As novas contratações acompanharão a expansão das atividades industriais, com demandas relacionadas à montagem, integração e operação de sistemas de baterias de grande porte. Com investimento de R$ 200 milhões e início da produção previsto para 2027, a expansão fortalecerá a estrutura industrial da Moura em Pernambuco, ampliará sua capacidade de fornecimento e criará novas oportunidades profissionais em um segmento estratégico para o setor elétrico brasileiro. Sistemas de armazenamento poderão alcançar mais de 8 GWh e atender grandes projetos elétricos O principal produto da expansão será o BESS (Battery Energy Storage System), sistema capaz de armazenar eletricidade e disponibilizá-la posteriormente, conforme a necessidade da rede. Esses equipamentos ganham relevância com o aumento da participação de fontes renováveis na matriz elétrica. Usinas solares concentram sua geração durante o dia, enquanto parques eólicos produzem de acordo com as condições de vento. O armazenamento permite aproveitar a energia gerada nesses períodos e disponibilizá-la em horários de maior demanda. As baterias contribuem para aumentar a flexibilidade operacional do sistema elétrico e favorecer a integração das fontes renováveis. A Moura desenvolve soluções de armazenamento desde meados da década passada e apresentou seu Moura BESS em 2019. Atualmente, a companhia acumula mais de 40 projetos instalados no Brasil, atendendo segmentos como indústria, agronegócio, saúde, saneamento e infraestrutura elétrica. A nova etapa representa uma mudança de escala. A empresa já trabalha com equipamentos de aproximadamente 30 MWh, enquanto a expansão foi planejada para atender projetos a partir de 120 MWh. Para dimensionar a diferença, um único sistema de 120 MWh pode reunir aproximadamente 20 contêineres de 20 pés com baterias, na configuração descrita pela companhia. artigo.texto: Ministry of Heavy Industries Receives 22 Bids for 10 GWh ACC Battery Manufacturing Capacity The tender covers 10 GWh of advanced chemistry cell manufacturing capacity for grid-scale stationary storage applications under India's ₹18,100 crore PLI scheme. The Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI) has received 22 bids for 10 GWh of advanced chemistry cell (ACC) manufacturing capacity under the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for ACC battery storage. The capacity has been earmarked for grid-scale stationary storage (GSSS) applications and forms part of India's broader target to establish 50 GWh of domestic ACC manufacturing capacity. The bids were submitted through a global tender floated on the Central Public Procurement (CPP) Portal to select companies for setting up giga-scale ACC manufacturing facilities in India. Technical bids were opened on November 11, 2026, at the Ministry of Heavy Industries in the presence of the participating bidders. The selection process is being conducted through a two-stage Quality and Cost Based Selection (QCBS) mechanism. The 22 bidders include ACME Solar Holdings, Amara Raja Advanced Cell Technologies, Avaada Electro, Exide Energy Solutions, Fujiyama Power Systems, GK Energy, Godawari New Energy, JPM Energy Solutions, JSW Neo Energy, Lineage Power, Mahendra Sponge and Power, and Megha Engineering and Infrastructures. Other companies that submitted bids include Nsure Reliable Power Solutions, Reliance Industries, Renew Photovoltaics, Sai Bioenergy, Shirdi Sai Electricals, Sun Drops Energia, Utex New Energy, Vikram Solar, Waaree Energy Storage Solutions and Zetsol Energy. PLI Scheme Targets 50 GWh of ACC Manufacturing Capacity The tender is part of the National Programme on Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) Battery Storage, approved by the Union Cabinet in May 2021 with a budgetary allocation of ₹18,100 crore. The programme aims to establish 50 GWh of domestic ACC manufacturing capacity and encourage domestic and international companies to set up manufacturing facilities in India. The 10 GWh allocation for grid-scale stationary storage is intended to address energy-storage requirements arising from the expansion of renewable energy capacity. The programme also seeks to strengthen domestic manufacturing capabilities and develop the local value chain for ACC technologies. The Request for Proposal (RFP) was issued on July 15, 2026, followed by a pre-bid conference on July 29. The deadline for submitting bids was November 10, with technical bids opened the following day. artigo.texto: Comissão de Meio Ambiente da FIERN debate segurança hídrica e condições para atrair data centers ao RN A segurança hídrica e os aspectos técnicos e regulatórios para a instalação de data centers no Rio Grande do Norte foram os principais temas discutidos na reunião da Comissão Temática de Meio Ambiente (COEMA) da FIERN, presidida pelo empresário Marcelo Rosado. A Secretaria de Estado do Meio Ambiente e dos Recursos Hídricos (Semarh) apresentou o trabalho de dimensionamento e manutenção dos reservatórios, além do planejamento para atender à expansão das atividades econômicas e ao abastecimento da população. “Eles mostraram o planejamento de como oferecer e ampliar a segurança, nesta área, para as novas indústrias, para as expansões residenciais, condomínios, loteamentos que poderão acontecer no estado do Rio Grande do Norte”, afirmou Rosado. O presidente da COEMA destacou que a sustentabilidade do sistema depende do uso adequado da água e dos recursos necessários para manter e ampliar a infraestrutura. Segundo ele, os investimentos precisam contemplar a redução do desperdício e o aumento da capacidade de armazenamento e abastecimento para atender à população e aos empreendimentos do estado. A apresentação sobre reservatórios, armazenamento, uso e distribuição da água foi conduzida pelo secretário de Estado do Meio Ambiente e dos Recursos Hídricos, Paulo Varella. Ele abordou iniciativas de recuperação de barragens, expansão de sistemas adutores, perfuração de poços e dessalinização. Entre as ações apresentadas está a previsão de recuperação de 28 barragens. Outro empreendimento apresentado foi o Projeto Seridó Norte, com 113 quilômetros de adutoras em execução. Os presidentes do Instituto de Desenvolvimento Sustentável e Meio Ambiente do Rio Grande do Norte (Idema), Werner Farkatt, e do Instituto de Gestão das Águas do Estado do Rio Grande do Norte (Igarn), José Procópio de Lucena, também participaram do encontro e destacaram a importância da sustentabilidade e do uso adequado dos sistemas hídricos. Data centers e atração de investimentos A discussão sobre data centers — instalações que abrigam equipamentos de processamento e armazenamento de dados — tratou das condições técnicas e ambientais para receber esses empreendimentos. Marcelo Rosado ressaltou que o Rio Grande do Norte tem diferenciais para disputar investimentos, mas precisa avançar nas políticas de atração e no debate sobre licenciamento. “Precisamos de mais discussão e, de alguma forma, criar políticas que consigam atrair mais investimento nessa área”, declarou Rosado, que também preside o Sindicato das Indústrias de Extração de Calcário, Fabricação de Cimento, Cal e de Argamassa do RN (SINECIM-RN) e é vice-presidente da FIERN. Na apresentação técnica, o especialista em gestão de data centers Júlio Lima abordou eficiência energética, fontes renováveis, resfriamento e uso responsável da água. Entre as alternativas apresentadas estavam o reaproveitamento de prédios e a adoção de sistemas de refrigeração que reduzam o consumo hídrico. Ele também destacou tecnologias voltadas à melhoria do desempenho ambiental das instalações e a importância de acompanhar indicadores que relacionam o consumo de energia, o uso de água e as emissões de carbono à energia utilizada pelos equipamentos de tecnologia da informação. Já o advogado e consultor jurídico Kepler Brito abordou a regulamentação do licenciamento ambiental de data centers aprovada pelo Conselho Estadual do Meio Ambiente (Conema). Ele explicou que o sistema de refrigeração é uma variável relevante na avaliação dos projetos, mas que a análise também deve considerar localização, consumo de água, efluentes, geradores, movimentação de terra e retirada de vegetação. “A resolução estabelece um enquadramento inicial, mas também preserva a análise técnica das características concretas do projeto. Estudos adicionais podem ser exigidos por decisão motivada e proporcional aos riscos, considerando o local, a tecnologia e outros elementos objetivos”, destacou Brito, em sua apresentação. Também participaram da reunião os presidentes do Sindicato da Indústria de Cervejas, Refrigerantes, Águas Minerais e Bebidas em Geral do Rio Grande do Norte (SICRAMIRN), Joafran Nobre; do Sindicato da Indústria de Panificação, Ivanaldo Maia; Francisco de Assis, representante do SINDIMÓVEIS na COEMA; e o assessor corporativo e gestor dos Conselhos e Comissões Temáticas, Ernani Bandeira.

artigo.texto: On November 16, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) released an interim final rule (IFR), “Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors” (RIN 0694-AK50). The IFR closes what the government sees as a gap in existing chip controls: companies in China and other countries of concern can rent US-designed computing power from data centers in third countries rather than import the chips themselves. BIS says the IFR aligns the treatment of remote access with existing controls on physical shipments. It also adds new license requirements for five countries viewed as diversion risks—Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil—tightens the rules for chip foundries and packagers, and formally rescinds the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. Consistent with Executive Order 14434, the rule uses “Super Intelligence” (SI) in place of “artificial intelligence.” The changes reach chipmakers, server makers, distributors, cloud and data center operators, and their customers, both in the US and abroad. BIS has indicated that the IFR is expected to be formally published and go into effect on November 19. Key changes - New data center end-use control (new §744.24). A license is now required to export, re-export, or transfer (in-country) advanced chips and servers (ECCNs 3A090 (other than 3A090.c), 4A090, and related .z items, software, and technology) if the exporter, re-exporter, or transferor has “knowledge” at the time of the shipment transaction that the item is destined to a data center anywhere in the world that provides or will provide access to more than 12 million “aggregate TPP” (total processing performance) to or for companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, China, another destination specified in Country Group D:5, or Macau. The threshold counts capacity at a single facility or across “linked data centers.” The new defined term “linked data center” includes digitally linked infrastructure, not just physically linked infrastructure. “For” such a company also captures instances where there is “knowledge” that a data center is providing remote access to a non-D:5 customer that in turn trains or provides SI models to a D:5 company. License applications will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis. - Heightened diligence expectations. BIS points out that “to satisfy the requirement that you do not have knowledge” for purposes of §744.24(a)(1), companies will be expected to obtain and be able to provide sufficient information from the foreign data center regarding that data center’s “know your customer” due diligence checks. Such diligence checks will include diligence on whether any data center customers are subject to direct or indirect ownership or control by persons located in, headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent is headquartered in, Macau or a destination specified in Country Group D:5. A data center’s refusal or inability to provide that information is a red flag that presumptively gives the exporter “knowledge” unless resolved. - No de minimis. Companies outside the US should note that the prohibitions under §744.24(a)(1) still apply when a US-origin item covered by paragraph (a) is incorporated into or commingled with a foreign-made item. Re-exporters and transferors cannot rely on the de minimis provisions if, at any point during the “development,” “production,” or “use” of the foreign-made item containing a US-origin item specified in paragraph (a), they have “knowledge” that the foreign-made item will be used for an end use prohibited under §744.24(a)(1). - Downstream notice and change-of-use authorization. Anyone who ships covered items without a license on or after the Federal Register publication date of this rule—expected on November 19—must notify the recipient in writing that a BIS authorization is required. Authorization is required if the item will be used to provide access to more than 12 million “aggregate TPP,” at a single data center or “through linked data centers” to or for companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, Macau or a destination specified in Country Group D:5. Changing an item’s end use from a permitted use to one prohibited under §744.24(a) is considered an in-country transfer and requires an Export Administration Regulations (EAR) authorization under §744.24. New recordkeeping obligations apply. - Narrow “commercial recommender system” carve-out. The new prohibition does not apply to a “commercial recommender system”—which BIS defines as an SI tool “exclusively designed and exclusively used to rank, filter, or suggest commercial products, services, or content to users based on user behavior, transaction history, or item attributes.” BIS explains that this term does not include any SI system designed or used to generate novel text, image, audio, video, software, or other content in response to user inputs, or any system that incorporates such model, regardless of whether the system also performs recommendation functions. Relying on the carve-out triggers a specific submission to BIS, which requires a description of the due diligence performed to ensure the computing power access is exclusively being provided for a commercial recommender system and additional data points. When this alert was published, the link that BIS included in the IFR for this submission was not yet functional. - 90-day deadline to obtain a license for existing arrangements. Data centers that already provide significant volume of compute power to companies headquartered, or with an ultimate parent headquartered, in Macau or Country Group D:5 and wish to continue providing these services must obtain a license within 90 days of the effective date of this rule or they may be subject to future export restrictions. - New license requirement for five diversion-risk countries. A license is now required for advanced SI items to or within Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil

artigo.texto: O co-CEO da Oracle, Mike Sicilia, reconheceu que a indústria de tecnologia cometeu um erro na forma de apresentar seus projetos de data centers às comunidades que recebem essas instalações. Durante o Fórum de Inovação da Fortune 500, realizado em Detroit, nos EUA, em 16 de novembro, o executivo afirmou que a estratégia de comunicação adotada pelas empresas não foi suficiente para conquistar o apoio da população. Segundo Sicilia, um dos problemas foi enviar representantes das sedes corporativas para explicar os projetos às cidades, sem estabelecer uma relação próxima com os moradores. “Não é assim que vamos conquistar corações e mentes”, disse. A declaração ocorre em meio à resistência crescente à construção de data centers, estruturas que concentram servidores e equipamentos responsáveis pelo processamento e armazenamento de grandes volumes de dados, incluindo as operações de inteligência artificial (IA). Resistência local pressiona expansão da infraestrutura de IA A oposição aos empreendimentos tem se refletido em decisões políticas locais. De acordo com o relato apresentado no evento, eleitores rejeitaram amplamente propostas de construção de data centers em eleições municipais nos EUA. A resistência representa um obstáculo para empresas de tecnologia que precisam ampliar sua capacidade computacional para atender à demanda por serviços de IA. Durante o fórum, executivos de diferentes setores também destacaram a importância de investimentos em infraestrutura física e operacional. O debate incluiu a necessidade de ampliar redes, fábricas, centros de dados e sistemas de distribuição, além de investir em educação, pesquisa, qualificação profissional e políticas públicas. Para o CEO da Honeywell, Vimal Kapur, décadas de automação em camadas criaram dificuldades para acompanhar a complexidade dos sistemas atuais. A discussão também chegou ao campo regulatório. O senador democrata John Hickenlooper, do Colorado, defendeu que os EUA mantenham a liderança mundial em IA, mas com mecanismos de segurança semelhantes aos utilizados na aviação. O encontro reuniu ainda representantes de empresas como Kraft Heinz, Delta e US Steel, que abordaram desafios relacionados a cadeias de suprimentos, falhas operacionais e políticas comerciais.

artigo.texto: The United States has crossed 200 GWh of cumulative installed energy storage capacity, with 14.3 GWh of new installations added in the third quarter (Q3) of 2026. The milestone highlights the growing deployment of battery energy storage systems (BESS) to support renewable energy integration and grid reliability. According to the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA), cumulative installations have reached 215.9 GWh. The country added 48.3 GWh during January-September 2026, registering 20% year-on-year growth. Utility-scale projects accounted for the largest share of Q3 additions at 12.2 GWh, followed by the commercial and industrial (C&I) segment at 1.3 GWh and residential installations at 746 MWh. US Energy Storage Deployment In Q3 2026 SEIA has raised its forecast for cumulative US energy storage deployment by 2030 to 708 GWh, an increase of 3.7% from its previous projection. Annual installations are expected to exceed 129 GWh by the end of the decade. The country is also expanding its domestic manufacturing capacity. US battery cell manufacturing capacity has reached 92.4 GWh, following a 50% increase, while battery module manufacturing capacity has crossed 109 GWh. India Targets 888 GWh Of Storage Capacity By 2035-36 The US milestone comes as India works towards significantly expanding its own energy storage capacity. According to the Central Electricity Authority (CEA), India is projected to require 888 GWh of energy storage by 2035-36, comprising 321 GWh of battery storage and 567 GWh of pumped storage projects (PSP). As of September 30, 2026, India had 14.54 GWh of operational BESS capacity. Another 78.96 GWh was under construction, 28.91 GWh had been awarded and 76.02 GWh was under tendering. India's BESS Project Status To support deployment, the Union Cabinet approved a Rs 14,500 crore viability gap funding (VGF) scheme on November 4, 2026, for 92 GWh of energy storage projects. This includes 30 GWh of BESS, 60 GWh of pumped storage and 2 GWh of emerging storage technologies. While the US has crossed the 200 GWh mark, India's immediate challenge remains converting its growing project pipeline into operational capacity. Timely execution, financing, domestic manufacturing and viable revenue models will be critical to achieving its long-term storage targets.

artigo.texto: Batteries are great for many applications, but they can’t do everything. For example, they aren’t ideal when you need fast and large bursts of electrical current (like regenerative braking in your car). They also don’t have very long life-spans (usually between 1,000 and 10,000 cycles) or work very well in cold temperatures. Fortunately, batteries can be paired with (and perhaps one day even be replaced by) an energy storage device that brings its own unique set of strengths. Enter the supercapacitor. What is a supercapacitor? “Supercapacitors are energy storage devices that work in a fundamentally different way than batteries. They store charge physically, not through chemical reactions,” explained Materials Science and Engineering Professor David Estrada. “Supercapacitors have a long life of a million cycles and they are very useful in high power applications, such as backup power that bridges short outages, wearable electronics and sensors, and in aerospace and defense applications for pulsed loads, actuators and emergency power systems.” And at Boise State, a team led by alum Fereshteh Rajabi Kouchi (PhD, materials science and engineering, 2025) under the supervision of Estrada, are expanding the future of supercapacitors through the invention of a new 2D metal alloy ink. Printing with nanomaterial inks for energy devices Supercapacitors for various flexible applications can be printed using 2D printing technologies and energy material inks. However, the material properties of the inks ultimately shape the end product’s abilities. “In the grand scheme of things, materials are the heart of any electronic system,” Estrada said, “whether it’s a micro-fabricated transistor or a printed energy storage device. Without understanding the materials properties, and how they are affected by a fabrication process, it’s near impossible to get repeatable and reliable results to translate research from the lab to the fab.” For Kouchi, the goal was to widen the range of possible inks for supercapacitors by using special alloys (a mixture of two or more metals). And to do that, she set about inventing a completely new type of alloy ink. “In our lab, I used an aerosol jet printer that transforms these inks into a fine mist and deposits them onto a surface in precise patterns,” Kouchi said. “The exciting part of my research is that by combining different elements at the atomic level, we can create new materials with improved properties and use them to develop better-performing energy storage devices.” Kouchi blended niobium, tantalum and sulfur in a novel 2-dimensional (2D) material ink, within the 2D transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) family of materials. 2D TMDs are materials that are three atoms thick where the metal layer is sandwiched between two layers of chalcogens atoms such as sulfur. What she and her team discovered was an alloy ink capable of being printed in patterns as small as 50 micrometers (about the diameter of a human hair), and that supercapacitors made from these inks could store far more charge than TMDs made from either metal alone. Importantly, the ink dried uniformly and met the material requirements to be printed on flexible substrates (like those used in wearable skin-based electronics). “Making a printable ink from a brand-new alloy meant solving several problems at once: keeping the nanosheets stable, preventing oxidation, and controlling how the droplets dry,” said Kouchi. “Seeing the alloy outperform both of its parent materials shows how the composition of 2-dimensional system can be used as a design tool for energy storage.” The research was supported by NASA EPSCoR, the National Science Foundation’s Center for Atomically Thin Multifunctional Coatings (ATOMIC), and the Penn State Two-Dimensional Crystal Consortium Materials Innovation Platform. Collaborators included The Pennsylvania State University, the University of Illinois Chicago, Tulane University, and Southern Methodist University. “This work shows that alloy engineering and additive manufacturing work well together,” said Estrada. “Fereshteh has created a general approach for taking newly discovered layered materials and turning them into printable inks, which brings flexible, miniaturized power sources for the Internet of Things closer to reality.” Kouchi’s discovery builds on Boise State’s decade-long history of stable, aerosol-jet-printable ink innovation. She previously reported a similar study on 2D transition metal carbides, known as MXenes, which showed excellent energy density – but lower power density than the alloy inks reported here. This research was conducted by Micron School of Materials Science and Engineering faculty and staff Fereshteh Rajabi Kouchi, Hailey Burgoyne, Tony Valayil Varghese, Ajay Pratap, Attila Rektor, Olivia Maryon, Mike Hurley and David Estrada with support from NASA EPSCoR, the National Science Foundation’s Center for Atomically Thin Multifunctional Coatings (ATOMIC), and the Penn State Two-Dimensional Crystal Consortium Materials Innovation Platform. Collaborators included The Pennsylvania State University, the University of Illinois Chicago, Tulane University and Southern Methodist University.

artigo.texto: Form Energy has appointed Lori Goler, former Chief People Officer at Meta, and Jon McNeill, a former senior executive at Tesla and Lyft, to its Board of Directors as the energy storage company prepares to expand manufacturing and commercial deployments of its iron-air battery technology. The appointments bring experience in organizational development, operations, sales, and scaling high-growth businesses. Goler currently serves as President of the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, while McNeill is Co-Founder and CEO of venture firm DVx Ventures. The appointments follow a significant period of financial and operational expansion for Form Energy, which is developing long-duration energy storage systems designed to improve electricity grid reliability and affordability. The company closed a $750 million Series G financing round in August 2026 and secured a $270 million credit facility in September to support manufacturing expansion and working capital requirements. The financing is supporting continued development of Form Factory 1, the company’s manufacturing facility in Weirton, West Virginia. Form Energy also expanded its executive leadership team with the appointments of Navneet Govil as Chief Financial Officer and Wes Sloan as Chief Operating Officer. Lori Goler Brings Experience Scaling Global Organizations Goler has served as President of the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative since 2025, overseeing its work across science and education. Previously, she spent 16 years at Meta, serving as Chief People Officer from 2008 through 2024. During that period, she led the company’s global workforce strategy and organizational operations through substantial growth and transformation. Earlier in her career, Goler served as General Manager of eBay Stores and led consumer marketing at eBay. She was also a founding executive at online retailer eStyle. She previously served on the board of Stanford Health Care from 2013 to 2022. Goler holds a bachelor’s degree from Yale University, an MBA from Harvard Business School, and a Master of Public Policy from Harvard Kennedy School. Form Energy expects her experience developing organizational structures and managing workforce expansion to support its growing manufacturing and commercial operations. Jon McNeill Brings Tesla And Lyft Operating Experience McNeill is Co-Founder and CEO of DVx Ventures, a venture firm focused on creating and scaling companies addressing large market opportunities. Previously, he served as Chief Operating Officer at Lyft between 2018 and 2019 and as President of Global Sales, Delivery and Service at Tesla from 2015 through 2018. Before joining Tesla, McNeill was CEO and chairman of the board at software company Enservio, where he served from 2006 to 2015. Throughout his career, he has founded and scaled six companies, many of which were subsequently acquired by publicly traded businesses. McNeill has served on the boards of Lululemon Athletica, CrossFit, and Asurion. He also previously served on the board of General Motors from 2022 through 2026. His additional board experience includes Cruise, Stash, Tekion, TIER Mobility, and TrueMotion. McNeill graduated from Northwestern University. Expanding Long-Duration Energy Storage Form Energy is developing iron-air battery systems designed to provide approximately 100 hours of energy storage. The technology uses iron, water, and air, materials the company describes as among the most abundant and affordable resources available. The batteries are designed to store electricity and discharge it over extended periods, providing a potential solution for balancing renewable energy generation and electricity demand. Long-duration storage could help utilities manage periods when wind and solar generation are limited, while improving the resilience of electricity networks. Form Energy is manufacturing its systems at Form Factory 1 in West Virginia as it prepares to serve customers across the United States and internationally. The addition of Goler and McNeill comes as the company moves from technology development toward broader commercial production and deployment. KEY QUOTE: “Lori and Jon have each led organizations through critical periods of rapid growth and I am pleased to welcome them to the Board. Lori spent 16 years at Meta building a global workforce and culture, and as our team grows, that experience will be invaluable. Jon has scaled operations, sales, and delivery at Tesla and Lyft, which is just what we need as we continue to ramp production and deploy iron-air batteries to customers across the United States and internationally. Their perspectives will guide how we grow, and I’m looking forward to working closely with both.” Mateo Jaramillo, Co-Founder And CEO Of Form Energy

artigo.texto: Siga A Crítica de Campo Grande no Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. Siga A Crítica de Campo Grande no Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. Veja o resumo da notícia - Data centers dos EUA emitiram 25,7 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ entre maio de 2024 e abril de 2025, volume similar ao de Dinamarca e Bolívia. - Estudo liderado por Harvard analisou 403 grandes instalações, que consumiram quase 2% da eletricidade usada no país no período. - Combustíveis fósseis, sobretudo gás natural e carvão, originaram 54% da energia associada ao funcionamento dessas estruturas. - Virgínia, Iowa e Ohio concentraram cerca de metade das emissões, enquanto o Oregon teve menor intensidade de carbono. - Pesquisadores usaram imagens de satélite e plantas de edifícios, o que expôs a falta de transparência das empresas do setor. - Oposição de comunidades bloqueou ou atrasou 70 projetos em 25 estados, que somam investimentos estimados em US$ 271 bilhões. - Especialistas defendem que grandes operadores divulguem consumo de eletricidade e emissões para permitir maior fiscalização. Os maiores data centers dos Estados Unidos responderam por emissões estimadas em 25,7 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono (CO₂) entre maio de 2024 e abril de 2025. O volume é comparável às emissões anuais de países como Dinamarca e Bolívia, segundo estudo publicado nesta segunda-feira (16) na revista científica Nature Sustainability. A pesquisa, conduzida por uma equipe liderada pela Universidade Harvard, analisou 403 grandes centros de processamento de dados. Juntas, essas instalações consumiram quase 2% de toda a eletricidade utilizada nos Estados Unidos durante o período. Além disso, os pesquisadores identificaram que 54% da energia associada ao funcionamento dessas estruturas teve origem em combustíveis fósseis, principalmente gás natural e carvão. Dessa forma, a expansão da inteligência artificial amplia o debate sobre o consumo energético e os impactos ambientais da infraestrutura digital. Consumo de energia varia conforme a localização O levantamento mostrou que a localização dos data centers influencia diretamente suas emissões de carbono. Isso ocorre porque cada região americana utiliza diferentes fontes para produzir eletricidade. Na Virgínia, em Iowa e em Ohio, por exemplo, as instalações concentraram aproximadamente metade das emissões estimadas no estudo. Por outro lado, centros de dados localizados no Oregon apresentaram menor intensidade de carbono, devido à maior participação de fontes de energia sem combustíveis fósseis. Para chegar aos resultados, os pesquisadores analisaram imagens de satélite, plantas de edifícios e informações sobre a capacidade elétrica das instalações. Em seguida, calcularam o consumo estimado e relacionaram os dados à composição da matriz energética regional. Entretanto, o trabalho também revelou dificuldades para acessar informações sobre o setor. Segundo Gianluca Guidi, pesquisador de Harvard que liderou o estudo, a necessidade de reconstruir dados sobre as instalações demonstra a falta de transparência das empresas. Além disso, os números podem estar abaixo do impacto real da atividade. Isso porque o levantamento não inclui todos os centros de dados existentes nos Estados Unidos nem instalações que utilizam exclusivamente sistemas próprios de geração de energia. Expansão da IA aumenta pressão por transparência O crescimento acelerado da inteligência artificial impulsiona a construção de novos data centers, estruturas responsáveis pelo armazenamento e processamento de grandes volumes de informações. Entretanto, a expansão também enfrenta resistência de comunidades preocupadas com o consumo de energia e os impactos ambientais. Entre março de 2024 e o início de novembro de 2026, movimentos de oposição conseguiram bloquear ou atrasar pelo menos 70 projetos em 25 estados americanos, segundo levantamento da consultoria Relae. Esses empreendimentos representam investimentos estimados em US$ 271 bilhões. Além disso, parte das críticas envolve a falta de informações públicas sobre o funcionamento das instalações e seus efeitos nas regiões onde pretendem operar. Diante desse cenário, pesquisadores defendem regras mais rigorosas de transparência. A proposta é exigir que grandes operadores divulguem informações sobre consumo de eletricidade e emissões de carbono, permitindo maior fiscalização. O estudo também retrata um setor em rápida transformação. Desde o encerramento do período analisado, pelo menos 250 novos data centers entraram em operação nos Estados Unidos, conforme dados da empresa Cleanview. Assim, os resultados reforçam a necessidade de acompanhar os efeitos ambientais da expansão tecnológica. Embora a inteligência artificial ofereça novas possibilidades econômicas e produtivas, seu crescimento também exige investimentos em fontes de energia menos poluentes e maior transparência sobre o consumo de recursos.
